en: The First Daily Lesson of the First Chapter in the *Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā* composed by Vācaspatimiśra.
*Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā*.

Pervading all, possessing all powers, wielder of the Pināka bow, Lord of the universe, creator of the universe, whose form is the universe, knower of all, the agent of the dissolution of the universe, and the one worshipped by all— may He grant our desired object.
I bow to the Protector Akṣapāda, who possesses mastery over dharma, consciousness, dispassion, and sovereign power; he is a treasury of the purities of speech.
Under the very guise of a commentary on the text, we shall compose the *Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā*, in which all defects have been eliminated.
I desire some merit from the rescue of the exceedingly aged cows of Uddyotakara, which have sunk into the mire of difficult and poorly composed treatises.

NyS 1.1.1: From the knowledge of the true nature of the means of valid cognition, the objects of valid cognition, doubt, purpose, example, tenet, member [of a syllogism], reasoning, ascertainment, discussion, sophistry, cavil, fallacies of the reason, quibbles, futile rejoinders, and points of defeat, there is the attainment of the supreme good.

Now, wishing to dispel the doubt—"Since the treatise concerning the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) has been composed by the Blessed Akṣapāda and explained by the Blessed Pakṣilasvāmin, what else remains for which the *Vārttika* should be undertaken?"—he demonstrates the purpose of commencing the *Vārttika* by first restating the purpose of the treatise as stated by the author of the *Sūtras*: "That which Akṣapāda... [and so forth].
Thus it is said.
Although this has already been elucidated by the author of the *Bhāṣya*,

nevertheless, the treatise has been obscured by later scholars such as Dignāga and others through the raising of a dense darkness of fallacious arguments; therefore, Uddyotakara removes that [obscuration] by means of the illumination of his own work.

"An undertaking is purposeful" means that the restatement of the purpose mentioned in the Sūtra is intended to demonstrate that one's own composition possesses a purpose by way of elucidating the treatise with a purpose— a prerequisite for the engagement of discerning persons— since mere elucidation, being common to works such as the *Kākadantaparīkṣā* (The Examination of a Crow’s Teeth), does not serve as a basis for the engagement of discerning persons.
And here, "peace" (*śama*) is the absolute cessation of suffering, which is divided into twenty-one types; [the treatise is] for that purpose.
For whom? For the world (*jagat*).
For the Blessed One, the Sage, being supremely compassionate, composed this treatise out of a desire to uplift the very world submerged in the mire of suffering.
In that case, if no one were to engage [with it], what would happen to the treatise?
Nor is there any fault on the part of this treasury of asceticism for instructing persons who are not qualified.
Likewise, Viśvāmitra performed a sacrifice for Triśaṅku, and Viśvāmitra married Akṣamālā, who was born from an outcaste womb;
for such indeed was the power of their asceticism that even such sins as these were dissolved away.
And this consequence does not apply to those of us whose asceticism is weak.

For just because the digestive heat of elephants digests food such as banyan wood, it does not follow that our own digestive heat must function in the same way. "Ignorance of bad logicians" refers to the ignorance instilled by bad logicians such as Dignāga and others.

Although the salutation to the chosen deity was performed by the most refined author of the Vārttika—a practice obtained through an unbroken succession of the conduct of the learned—it has not been included in this treatise.
Indeed, no other auspicious rite has been inserted into the treatise either;
however, because it is so well known, the students will understand it as being like any other auspicious act. Thus, everything is clear.

In this regard, having briefly restated the first aphorism, he states its purport: "The attainment of the supreme good results from the knowledge of the true nature of the categories, such as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)," etc.; this is the opening aphorism of the treatise.
This constitutes the statement regarding the connection (*abhisaṃbandha*) of that treatise.
By the inclusion of the word "first" (*ādi*), it is shown that it is proper to provide an explanation of the very first [aphorism] as it occurs in sequence, and not of the second and so forth.

The intended connection is "abhisaṃbandha," which is the relationship of cause and effect between the treatise and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). This aphoristic statement is the "statement of connection" (*ābhisaṃbandhavākya*) for that [relationship].

Regarding the phrase "from the knowledge of the reality of categories such as the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇādipadārthatattvajñānāt*), "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is defined by the etymology "that by which something is known. Thus, "knowledge of reality" refers to the treatise (*śāstra*).
The ablative case indicates its status as a cause.

For it is not by its mere nature—like a poison-neutralizing mantra—that this [treatise], when its meaning is not intended to be understood, becomes a cause for the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*); rather, the treatise is designated as such because it is the instrument for the comprehension of the reality of the categories.
But not by its own nature.

Therefore, it is established that when the treatise is to bring about the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), the comprehension of the reality of the categories beginning with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) constitutes its intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*).
And thus, the reality of the categories such as the means of valid cognition is to be understood.

And since the treatise (*śāstra*) is that which teaches, the relationship between the reality of categories such as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth—which are the objects to be known—and the treatise itself—which is the knower—is indicated; likewise, the relationship characterized by the cause-and-effect connection between the knowledge of the reality of categories such as the means of valid cognition and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) is indicated. Thus, this constitutes the purpose of the first aphorism (*sūtra*), which is to set forth the subject matter (*abhidheya*), the relationship (*saṃbandha*), and the purpose (*prayojana*).
Furthermore, how the knowledge of the reality of the six categories serves as a means for attaining the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) will be explained later.
Once the status of the Sage as a reliable authority (*āpta*) has been ascertained, people will ascertain the purpose and other factors from his words and proceed to act.
However, if his status as a reliable authority is not ascertained, action would result from doubt regarding the matter.

It is not correct to argue that activity toward agriculture and the like would not occur even for those who have already obtained grain and other crops, on the grounds that such a statement is useless because the non-production of fruit is logically established due to intervening obstacles such as drought;
for doubt does not arise without depending upon the recollection of specific details.
But since the recollection of specific details arises from the sentence, it is not purposeless.

Having thus stated the purport of the first aphorism, he states the purport of the opening sentence of the commentary: "When there is comprehension of an object through a means of valid cognition," and so forth; this is the sentence of *anusandhāna* (reconnection). It refers to the reconnection—that is, the joining together—following (*anu*) the disjunction (*sandhāna*) of that treatise, which was originally joined with the aphorism for the attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), due to a suspicion of its disjunction from some cause or other.
His statement is a statement of investigation.

In this regard, it is indeed suspected as follows: that which teaches a means impossible to carry out is useless, just like a statement teaching the ornamentation of the crest of the serpent Takṣaka with a blue lotus;
and such is this scripture.

For indeed, the knowledge of the reality (*tattvajñāna*) of the categories beginning with the objects of cognition (*prameya*) depends upon the knowledge of the reality of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

For a means of valid cognition, if its reality is not ascertained, is not capable of determining its own object merely by virtue of being a cognizer; for that much alone is common to fallacious means of cognition (*tadābhāsa*).
Rather, it is by way of non-deviation (*avyabhicāritva*), which inheres in the same substrate as the quality of being a cognizer.
For that alone is validity;
and that is impossible to ascertain. And because that is not ascertained, the objects of cognition and so forth are difficult to ascertain.
For instance, is the validity of cognition determined intrinsically (*svataḥ*) or extrinsically (*parataḥ*)?
The first alternative is not tenable;
for a cognition that is self-cognizing (*svasaṃvedana*) could not possibly apprehend itself.
Nor is its validity [established] prior to that;
nor can another cognition apprehend it as "that cognition."
Nor, however, does it [establish validity] by virtue of its non-deviation;
for the mere quality of being a cognition is common to that which appears as such [but is invalid], and thus there is no determination of validity from itself (*svataḥ*).
By this, the apprehension of non-deviation is also refuted even in the system of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*).
Nor [is it established] from another;
for one would have to admit either that another cognition has that [object] as its domain,
or a cognition manifesting causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
Or, it might be the perception of another object that is invariably concomitant with that [first] object.
Yet, since all such [subsequent cognitions] would be confused and their validity not ascertained by themselves, how could they clarify the initial impelling cognition?
Or, if its validity were self-evident, what wrong has the impelling cognition done that the same [self-evident validity] should not apply to it as well?
And it has already been explained that validity is not known intrinsically (*svataḥ*).

Since the validity of cognition is difficult to ascertain through the aforementioned sequence, what then can be said of the sense organs and so forth, whose status as valid means of knowledge is manifested by their effect—namely, non-erroneous cognition? Therefore, let practical activities based on those things whose objects are perceived proceed as they may, even from a state of doubt.
However, Vedic practices whose purposes are unseen (adṛṣṭārtha) are accomplished through great expenditure of wealth and effort; thus, they have become like water poured out upon sand.

Therefore, it might be argued that the scripture is not connected with the supreme good (niḥśreyasa) by means of making known the true nature of categories such as the instruments of knowledge (pramāṇa).
This very doubt has been dispelled by the author of the Bhāṣya through the opening sentence, which explains the means for knowing validity.
For it is said that "the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) possesses its object" (*arthavat*); here, the suffix *matup* denotes a permanent connection (*nityayoga*).
And this permanence is non-deviation (*avyabhicāritā*).
Therefore, the meaning is that it is non-deviant with respect to the object.

And this very non-deviation from the object is the defining characteristic of a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), namely: the non-contradiction regarding the nature and the mode of the object as presented by it, across different places, times, persons, and circumstances.
The reason for this is "due to the efficacy of purposeful action" (*pravṛttisāmarthyāt*), which means because it generates an efficacious activity.
If, on the other hand, this [scripture] were not possessed of such meaning, it would not have prompted effective activity,
just like a fallacious means of valid cognition (pramāṇābhāsa); thus, this is a negative reason (vyatirekī hetuḥ).
Or it is both positive and negative (anvayavyatirekī),
since, given that inference is intrinsically valid, the positive concomitance (anvaya) is also possible.
However, the capacity of a means of knowledge to produce activity is not direct.

But rather, [the author] says "by way of generating the comprehension of the object" (*arthapratipattijananadvāreṇa*), stating: "when there is comprehension of the object through a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇato 'rthapratipattau*). We shall demonstrate the justification for all of this on the occasion of explaining the *Vārttika*.
It might be argued:

"Granted that categories such as the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and so forth are capable of being known, they are not taught by this treatise; therefore, there is no connection between the treatise and the supreme good (niḥśreyasa). To this, he says: "Because the treatise declares the welfare of man."
Although he will later describe the highest good as the absolute cessation of suffering,

nevertheless, in this context, it is that [cessation] together with its means that is intended by the word "highest good" (śreyaḥ), because the mere [cessation] alone is not the subject matter of the treatise.
This is the meaning:

It is established by experience that this treatise (*śāstra*) sets forth the supreme human goal (*puruṣa-śreyaḥ*) together with its means; however, it might be subject to denial on the grounds that it is impossible to put into practice.

By the words "if that impossibility of practice is removed by means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇataḥ*), etc., it is shown that the treatise is indeed connected with the attainment of the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*).

He explains the introductory statement beginning with "of the treatise" (*śāstrasya*) and so forth, using the passage from "the treatise, moreover" (*śāstraṃ punar*) up to "by enjoyment through exhaustion" (*upabhogāt prakṣayeṇa*).
By mentioning words that denote the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so on, he also indicates their definitions and their critical examinations (*parīkṣā*).
Thus, there is no contradiction in stating that the treatise consists of five chapters (*pañcādhyāyī*).

By the phrase "five [or more] letters" (*pañcādhyakṣī*), the arrangement (*vyūha*)—that is, the appropriate sequence of a collection—is indicated. He states the nature of the word (*pada*) which serves as the indicator: "Furthermore, a word here is a collection of phonemes (*varṇa*) mounted upon memory, delimited by the communication of a single meaning."

In this way, the collection of the words of a *sūtra*—which have as their intermediate operation the recollection of their own respective meanings and which are delimited by the function of conveying a sentence-meaning consisting of a single referent qualified by various word-referents—is to be understood.
And thus, in some cases, the unity of several *sūtra*-sentences through a single meaning constitutes a "collection," which is a *prakaraṇa* (section).
Furthermore, the collection of *prakaraṇas* through a certain internal coherence of their own meanings constitutes an *āhnika* (daily lesson).
In this manner, it should be understood in each respective case.
Furthermore, we shall briefly demonstrate these connections—namely, those between the topics (*prakaraṇa*), the daily lessons (*āhnika*), and the chapters (*adhyāya*)—in their appropriate places.

Having thus shown the nature of the treatise (*śāstra*), [the author] explains its purpose, for the status of the treatise as an indicator of human excellence cannot be established without explaining its meaning: "But surely, since the categories such as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are infinite for each individual, they would be difficult to know; therefore, the uselessness of the treatise remains as it was. To this he says: "Consisting of sixteen.

"Self" (*ātman*) means essential nature (*svabhāva*); that is to say, it is the specific universal (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*) such as "being a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇatva*) and so forth, belonging to the means of valid cognition and the rest.
This is what is meant:

although there is an infinity [of categories] due to internal subdivisions, they are not difficult to understand because they are subsumed under their own specific and general characteristics. Since its subject matters—such as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth—are thus accessible, this treatise (*śāstra*) expounds the highest good for man (*puruṣaśreyaḥ*).
This might be the case:
are categories such as the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and so forth established by valid authority (prāmāṇika) or not established by valid authority (aprāmāṇika)?
If they were not established by valid authority, being constructed merely by imagination, how could they lead to the supreme good (niḥśreyasa)?

Nor are there sixteen-fold conceptualizations, because the *Kośa* has infinite scope; or, if they were authoritative, they would be established by the very means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), rendering the treatise useless. Therefore, he says: "perception" (*pratyakṣa*).
By the inclusion of what is apprehended through perception and inference, non-authoritativeness is refuted.
Therefore, it is said: "the reality of things.
Categories such as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth are not objects of comparison (*upamāna*); thus, comparison has not been introduced [as a separate means].

Although the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), characterized by the self (*ātman*) up to liberation (*apavarga*), are derived from scripture (*āgama*), nevertheless, since scripture is composed by a trustworthy person (*āpta*), there exists within it either inference (*anumāna*) or perception (*pratyakṣa*) as its underlying basis; thus, [only] perception and inference [are established].
[This] has been shown. Now, it was argued that if [the categories] are established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then the treatise (*śāstra*) is redundant; to this he says: "Its object.
Even though worldly people employ means of valid cognition in their practical dealings, being devoid of the analytical intellect (*vainayika-buddhi*), they do not discern these categories.
Because these [faculties] are not isolated, they do not conduce to the supreme good; thus it is said "not attained.
Internal capacity consists of such qualities as the desire to hear [the truth] and so forth.
It is said to belong to the person (*puruṣa*).

In that context, in order to identify the specific person intended, [the author] shows the possible types of persons with the words "The person, moreover... He shows those to be abandoned with the word "therein...
and states those to be accepted with the word "the other..."
Expectation is the desire to know (*jijñāsā*).
That exists first for an object that is doubted;
but for one who is conflicted, it arises when the object is being examined before witnesses through debate (*jalpa*) and destructive criticism (*vitaṇḍā*), once the sense of ego has dissolved.

For one who has developed a desire to know and is thus expectant—even if not yet fully understood—once doubt has been induced by some means and they have been made expectant, they become the object to be communicated.
This is what was stated: "The others, being expectant, are the objects to be communicated."
Even though [the truth] is not doubted, it is presented by the compassionate one after having made it appear doubtful for the sake of establishing that reality.
Therefore, with reference to what dependent [person] has the treatise proceeded?
And thus, there would be no engagement with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) on the part of the cognizers; to this he says: "When those... [te yadā].
When those desiring to know a certain object depend upon the sense faculties and so forth, they are to be established by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The same should be applied to the subsequent [means of knowledge] as well.

This is the intended meaning: here, "desire to know" (jijñāsā) is not intended to mean the inquiry into objects useful for a visible purpose, but rather the inquiry into categories of existence that are useful for the supreme good (niḥśreyasa).
And that [desire] is the cause for engaging with this very treatise, and not with any other.
This is what was stated by the words "But when...
The ellipsis to be supplied is: "those who desire to know the means for attaining the supreme human goal."

In this context, in order to determine the desired ultimate good (*śreyas*), he states the means of valid cognition for that which is merely the good: "The good, moreover, is happiness and the cessation of what is harmful.
He further explains its internal subdivisions: "That good, being divided, is established as twofold—happiness and the cessation of suffering.
He states this by way of the distinction between the seen (*dṛṣṭa*) and the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*).
It is not collectively, but rather individually, that [the objects] are stated; thus he says: "Visible happiness" is that which arises from the enjoyment of garlands, sandalwood, women, and so forth;
"invisible happiness" is heaven and the like.
In this same way, the cessation of suffering is also to be construed as both visible and invisible excellence (*śreya*), due to the elision of the word "and" (*ca*).

He states the distinction between the seen and the unseen regarding the cessation of the harmful and the attainment of the beneficial—whether that cessation is ultimate or non-ultimate—as follows: "The cessation of the harmful also...
He specifies the desired benefit as "ultimate.
The word "again" (punar) illuminates this specification.
The absoluteness of cessation is the non-arising again of that which has ceased; and it is characterized by the cessation of the effect, the cause, and their concomitants,
for an effect is never produced without a cause.
This has been stated as: "by the destruction of the twenty-one-fold suffering.
And he describes the modes by which the twenty-one things, beginning with the body, constitute suffering through their division into secondary and primary types: "twenty-one-fold," etc.
The sixth sense-faculty is the mind (*manas*).

Its objects are desire, aversion, and effort. Although the body is also an object, its nature as a cause of suffering is of a different kind; thus he says "the body. The portion of the self delimited by the body is the locus of suffering; therefore, the body is called the locus of suffering. He states the reason for the metaphorical designation of the senses, objects, cognitions, and so forth, as being suffering itself: "the senses," etc.
In this context, first of all, the sense faculties (indriya) are so called because they perceive objects such as odors; the objects (viṣaya) are so called because they are what is perceived.
However, the cognitions (buddhi) are metaphorically designated as suffering because they are the direct instruments for producing suffering.
He states the seed for the metaphorical designation of pleasure as suffering: "Pleasure," he says.
Dependence on external means, perishability, and desire are the causes of suffering that accompany all pleasures;
therefore, even pleasure is accompanied by suffering.
He states the means for the removal of suffering in the manner described: "The removal of that [suffering]...

Indeed, one whose path of supreme logic has been purified by the knowledge of reality regarding doubt and so forth, and who—through the cultivation of the twelvefold objects of knowledge consisting of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted—has, by means of discriminative discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*), wiped away the attachment to all defects that cause worldly activity, does not, being inactive, produce a new accumulation of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*) which is the cause of the body, senses, and so forth.

And by the power of the ripening of discriminative discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*), one exhausts even that infinite accumulation of merit and demerit acquired through the beginningless succession of existences— which, though its time of fruition is indefinite— by manifesting bodies that partake in various respective experiences and thereby undergoing those specific fruits;
for meditative absorption (*samādhi*) possesses an inconceivable excellence of power.
As the venerable ones have said:
"For who, apart from the power of yoga, can drink up the ocean like Agastya,
and create the Daṇḍaka forest like him?"
As stated in the *Yogabhāṣya* on sūtra 8.10:
"This absolute cessation of suffering is the highest good (*śreyas*)."
This has been stated: "Because the scripture is that which declares the highest good of man."
It might be argued:
the absolute cessation of suffering alone is the supreme good (*śreyas*), as it serves as a factor for engaging in meritorious deeds;
however, since this [state] involves the absolute cessation of pleasure just as it does of suffering, how can it be considered the supreme good?
And how is this a factor for the engagement of a discerning person? To this he says: "Persons possess passion and so forth.

Although this is not a factor for the engagement of ordinary worldlings who possess passion and so forth—for they, out of sweetness, might consume even food mixed with honey and poison, thinking, "May it be delightful at first; may the poison not kill me, or may it not kill me"—[nevertheless, for the discerning, it is a factor].
Let us first consider immediate pleasure;
for who, indeed, would cast what is in his hand to his feet? Thinking thus, one enjoys it.
But the discerning, reflecting upon the future, abandon even heaven, regarding it as comparable to the shadow cast by the expanded hood of an angry serpent.
Therefore, let it not be that this [knowledge] is a factor for the activity of those possessed of passion and so forth;
rather, it will be so for those who possess discernment.
Furthermore, the means for instilling discernment even in those who lack it—namely, those who have not yet understood or who have misunderstood—has been explained previously.
In this context, discrimination (*viveka*) and dispassion (*vairāgya*) are intended merely as preliminary factors for the engagement with the treatise.
Engagement is of two kinds: uniformity and duality.
The distinction between persons arises from passion and dispassion.

Since all happiness that is to be attained is inevitably mixed with suffering, it is cast into the category of the undesirable; therefore, for those possessed of discernment, their activity is of a single form, consisting solely in the prevention of the undesirable.
However, it has been stated that the activity of those lacking discernment is of two forms.

Having thus explained the purport of the statement beginning with "the comprehension of an object through a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇato ’rthapratipatti*) by means of this elaboration, he prepares the ground to explain its constituent part, "by the capacity for purposeful action" (*pravṛttisāmarthyāt*). He does so by stating, "even of purposeful action," thereby presenting the capacity for action characterized by passion and so forth as the observed cause;
however, this is not [the case] for those free from passion (*vītarāga*).

For the connection between the activity of that [means] and the fruit characterized as the stainlessness of the supreme good (niḥśreyasa) is not observed, because the supreme good is non-worldly (alaukika).
It is incorrect to say that a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is useless because it lacks an object;
for to say "the means of valid cognition is useless" is a contradiction. Therefore, he says: "First of all, the means of valid cognition..."
For an invalid means of knowledge (apramāṇa) does not lead to purposeful action when it is apprehended as "invalid. What then [is required]? It must be apprehended as "valid" (pramāṇa).

And there can be no misconception of an invalid means of knowledge as being valid without some similarity to a valid means of knowledge and so forth; therefore, he asks about that similarity: "What then?"
The answer is: its nature as a delimiting factor of the universal.
To explain that, he says: "even by means of a valid cognition.
Even the cognition of silver delimits the white, shining, existent substance present before one.
The cognition of mother-of-pearl is also [an instance of this].
The point is that the relationship of sublation between two cognitions occurs solely through the superimposition and subsequent negation of silver upon one and the same object.
Thus, in both cases, the activity [of the cognition] proceeds from a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) alone.
He says that [the means of knowledge] is not one that deviates from its object without being a valid cognition—namely, "this is the cognizer.
Therefore, the intention is that the successful activity (*samartha-pravṛtti*) is established as the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of unsuccessful activity.

And thus, he states that successful activity, which is endowed with the exclusion of unsuccessful activity, is the reason for the validity—that is, the non-deviation from the object—of the means of knowledge: "Furthermore, because of that successful activity as its cause, the means of knowledge possesses validity, which is the non-deviation from the object."
But even that which is immediately adjacent is not connected if it lacks the capacity for conjunction.
He restates the initial statement in order to raise an objection: "by means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇataḥ*).
He raises the objection: "mutually" (*paraspara-*) [dependent]. He resolves it: "no" (*na*).
He analyzes the objection: "If [it were] by means of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
First of all, the mere apprehension of an object is not the cause of purposeful activity; rather, it is the ascertainment (*viniścaya*) of that object. And yet, that alone is not sufficient.

Rather, it is the determination—accompanied by an inference that this present object, being of the same class as those previously observed to be causes of the highest good (*śreyas*), must itself be a cause of the highest good—that serves as the motive for action.

This determination, which arises from the apprehension of an object through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and is conjoined with the inference of its being a means to the highest good, has been described as the cause of effective activity.
Furthermore, the determination of an object does not occur without the ascertainment of the validity (*prāmāṇya*) [of the cognition].

Furthermore, the ascertainment of validity and the apprehension of the pervasion (vyāpti) which is the basis for the inference that [the Veda] is a cause of the highest good (śreyaḥ) cannot exist without effective activity;
nor can effective activity exist without those two. Thus, there is a mutual dependence (parasparāśrayatā).
This is what was stated:

First, one might ask: since the comprehension of an object through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is preceded by a definitive ascertainment that depends upon a suitable means, why does it comprehend and ascertain [the object] without the capacity for purposeful action (*pravṛttisāmarthya*), [thinking] "this is indeed the desired means" and "this is indeed water"? He provides the resolution by analyzing [the objection]: "And that is not so."
As for what was stated—

that because the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is difficult to ascertain and there is consequently no certainty regarding the object, there can be no efficacy of purposeful action— to that we reply: True.
Intrinsic validity cannot be determined;
rather, extrinsic validity is understood—much like the efficacy of action—in those cases where the object is perceived and one is not in a state of non-habituation.
However, action depends upon the cognition of the object, not upon the ascertainment of the object.
For even those who possess discernment act out of doubt regarding the result;
indeed, those who act even while certain that there is a means do not fail to doubt the future fruit.
Thus, although they act while still doubting, they determine the validity of the means through the efficacy of their action.

Because of the capacity for successful activity (*pravṛtti-sāmarthya*) of another instance of that same class which has undergone repeated practice, one ascertains its validity even before [the activity occurs] by means of the mark (*liṅga*) of belonging to that same class; thus, through the determination of the object, people proceed to act.

In this way, having ascertained the validity of mantras and Ayurveda—which have perceptible objects—by means of the capacity for successful activity, one likewise [ascertains the validity] of another instance of that same class spoken by a reliable person (*āpta*), even if its object is imperceptible (*adṛṣṭārtha*).

It will be explained that the determination of the Veda’s authority is established by its being the word of a reliable person (*āpta*), even without the capacity for [immediate] activity. Furthermore,

those who possess discernment do not examine the knowledge of the result itself, because any kind of result whatsoever is desired, and since the definition of a result is simply that which is desired, they examine its status as a means to that [result].
For instance: there is the cognition of water;
for one who is thirsty, there is activity toward it; and for one who has engaged in that activity, there is the attainment of it.
The knower is satisfied merely by drinking what is trustworthy and by the resulting allaying of his thirst;
he does not further investigate even that cessation of thirst.
Some say that this is because even such [knowledge] as that is desired;
however, we say that even the knowledge of the result, by virtue of having reached the stage of practice, has its non-deviation determined through the mark (*liṅga*) of belonging to that same class.
Thus, it proceeds from that which preceded it, to that which preceded that, and to that which preceded even further.

Nor should it be argued that there is an infinite regress because, in order to determine the validity of the present cognition of a result, one must at this very moment determine the validity of a previous cognition of a result by virtue of its belonging to the same class. This need not be said.
Because, by virtue of its similarity to what preceded it, the validity of the earlier [scripture] was already determined;

likewise, by virtue of its similarity to what preceded that, the validity of the earlier-than-that was determined; and likewise, by virtue of its similarity to what preceded that, the validity of the earliest was determined. Thus, the resolution here lies precisely in the beginninglessness [of the tradition].

Among these, that knowledge of the result which is suspected of being fallible because it is equivalent to the experience of dreams and the like is in a state of non-habituation (*anabhyāsadaśāpanna*).

Therefore, in that case, the capacity for successful action (*pravṛttisāmarthya*) must be relied upon to determine its validity; thus, the beginninglessness of both the comprehension of the object and the capacity for action has been stated.

As for inference, however—whether it arises from the mark of the capacity for successful action or from another [mark]—its validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ*), since all suspicion of fallibility has been removed due to its originating from a mark that is inherently non-deviant with respect to the object to be inferred.

For a cognition having the form of a mark does not arise without the mark, nor does a mark exist without the possessor of the mark; thus, a steady cognition is possible only when it arises from a mark whose non-deviation has been grasped by itself.
Sensory perception, however, even though it arises from an object, does not [arise] from one whose non-deviation has been grasped.
Rather, it arises from that which exists merely by its presence.
Furthermore, other causes such as the sense faculties and so forth are not invariably concomitant with the object as it is apprehended; nor are they invariably concomitant with the object.
Verbal cognition, however, does not arise from the object.
For even in the absence of that [invariable relation], the word exists;

furthermore, unlike a logical mark (*liṅga*), a word does not possess an invariable concomitance with its object, but rather conveys the meaning of a sentence by communicating the meaning of the word-constituents through the mere grasping of convention (*saṅketa*).
Therefore, there is no apprehension of non-deviation *per se* for either perceptual or verbal cognition.

For the sake of ensuring non-deviation from the object, one must rely on a logical mark (*liṅga*), such as the efficacy of purposeful action (*pravṛttisāmarthya*) or the fact of belonging to that same class (*tajjātīyatva*).

And since the mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*) which grasps the logical mark of belonging to that same class within the cognition—being of such a nature that its deviation has never been observed and thus having all suspicion of error completely eliminated—is itself [non-deviating], it is *svataḥ* [intrinsically valid].
Validity is thus established, and there is no infinite regress. By this, analogy (upamāna) is also explained.

Furthermore, by stating that cognition is non-deviant with respect to its object, it should be understood that the sense faculties and other causes of that cognition are also declared to possess the status of valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
For their validity consists in nothing other than being the producers of non-erroneous cognition.

Nor is it correct to ask how the sense faculties and so forth—which are themselves subject to error regarding their objects—can produce cognitions that are non-erroneous with respect to their objects;
for it is impossible to either determine the essential nature of a cause or to subject it to such an inquiry.

Therefore, because there is doubt regarding the object when one has not reached a state of familiarity, validity with respect to the apprehension of the object arises from the possibility of successful activity; and since for that which has reached a state of familiarity, validity is inferred through its belonging to the same class as [previously known] knowledge of successful activity, while for that which has not reached a state of familiarity,

validity is inferred by means of another cognition of the capacity for successful activity— and because this process is beginningless— there is no regressus ad infinitum regarding the apprehension of the object and the capacity for successful activity.
It is argued that there is mutual dependence;
for the object's status as a sought-after means and the capacity for the operation of inference are mutually dependent.
In that case as well, the fault of infinite regress remains unavoidable.
For as soon as a newborn infant sees a breast, the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by experiences of that same kind from a previous birth manifests;
from that, memory arises;
and from that, the inference that it is a means to what is desired.
From that comes activity;
from that comes its capacity.
Thus, in each preceding birth, because there is no beginning, they do not depend upon one another like a seed and a sprout.
Regarding the phrase "the comprehension of the meaning":
the comprehension of the meaning refers to the comprehension that the object is a sought-after means [to an end].
Therefore, everything is clear.

Thus, by means of this stated sequence, the interpretation of the phrase "when an object is apprehended through a means of valid cognition" as referring to the inquiry into the treatise (*śāstra*) has been established. Now, he states another intended meaning of this very same [phrase]: "Or, [it refers to] the operation of the means of valid cognition. Here, the following doubt might be raised: for the Sage [Gautama], through this treatise, directly and by way of explaining perception, doubt, and so forth, [established] the science of inquiry (*anvīkṣikī*).

He expounded Nyāya— also known by the name Anumāna— which elucidates the twelvefold objects of knowledge existing as things to be abandoned or accepted— for the sake of attaining the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).

Yet, the attainment of the supreme good does not result merely from the ascertainment of the true nature of the objects of knowledge through the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) according to Nyāya.

However, through such practices as cultivating the perception of suffering regarding the ten objects of cognition— excluding the beginning and the end— and cultivating the true nature of the self, there occurs, by way of the gradual ripening of dispassion and the direct realization of the reality of the self, the non-arising of previously unproduced dharma and adharma, and the exhaustion of those already produced through their experience.

And thus, because it is an internal factor (*antaraṅga*) with respect to the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), activity (*pravṛtti*) itself is more powerful than the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or the system of reasoning (*nyāya*); not reasoning. Therefore, it is activity alone that must be explained, and not the means of valid cognition, even though the latter is a cause of the supreme good, because it is an external factor to activity. In this regard, the following applies: when there is comprehension of an object through the means of valid cognition, the efficacy of activity consists in its connection with the result.
But it is not the case that there is cognition of an unreal object by means of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, a valid means of knowledge is purposeful and effective, just like the activity [it prompts].
This is what is meant:
Just as activity is more powerful due to its being internal, so too is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) [more powerful] due to its being the root cause;
for activity arising from what is not a means of valid cognition is not connected with a result.
Therefore, both are equal.

Nevertheless, since activity (*pravṛtti*) is also elucidated by means of the elucidation of the instruments of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it was the elucidation of the *pramāṇas* that was undertaken by this treatise,
and not that of activity. Furthermore, the general statement [regarding the purpose] is ultimately intended for the sake of the system of logic (*nyāya*).
"Because that alone is the subject under discussion.
Previously, it was stated that this is a continuous discourse (*anusandhānavākya*) because its purpose is to establish the means for knowing validity.
Now, he demonstrates its nature as a continuous discourse by way of responding to an objection from another—beginning with the words "The worldly practice... (*lokavṛtta*).
For indeed, one who rejects the means for the apprehension of valid cognition must be questioned as follows:
"Do you reject the means for the knowledge of valid cognition by means of a valid cognition, or by means of what is not a valid cognition?"
If he should say "by means of a valid cognition," he should be answered: "Since you do not know the means for the knowledge of a valid cognition, how can you speak thus?"
If it is argued that [the cognition] is "without a means of valid cognition" (*apramāṇena*), then one must proceed by way of permission (*anujñayā*).
Or, if it is argued that it is "with a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇena*) but one whose validity has not been apprehended,
there is a contradiction between the two mental states (*manasayoḥ visaṃvādaḥ*).
Therefore, even if you do not desire it, you must follow worldly convention;

otherwise, being neither a worldly person nor an investigator, you would be disregarded like a madman. Thus, this worldly convention is restated in this commentary (*bhāṣya*) in order to inform the objector that the comprehension of an object occurs through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Since a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) possesses the capacity for purposeful activity (pravṛtti-sāmarthya), it is the worldly convention that every cognizer, having ascertained an object through the fact that its meaning is understood by means of a pramāṇa, engages with it and thereby obtains a result. This [convention] is restated by the sentence beginning with "tat pramāṇataḥ" by way of demonstrating its cause.
He prepares the ground to state another intended meaning of this very commentary with the words "heyahāna" (the abandonment of what is to be abandoned).

The word *artha*—meaning the term *artha*—is established in the rule *pramāṇato 'rthapratipattau*. Those [words] for which it serves as the basis (*pada*) are "tathā. Such is the explanation of this portion of the Vārttika text.
However, in the case of what is found in the Bhāṣya, it will be otherwise:
"the means is the treatise" (*śāstra*). Here, the word *śāstra* refers to its meaning [i.e., the means].
Since the *artha* (subject matter) also constitutes the body of the treatise (*śāstra*) just like the words themselves,

and since the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of cognition (*prameya*) are included here by the terms "that which is to be abandoned" (*heya*), "the abandonment" (*hāna*), and "that which is to be attained" (*adhigantavya*), the term *śāstra* applies— according to the maxim of "the cow and the bull"— to everything from doubt (*saṃśaya*) up to the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
Therefore, by the term "means" (*upāya*), everything from doubt up to the points of defeat is indeed expressed.
He explains the summary statement (grahaṇakavākya) with the words "that which is to be abandoned" (heyam).
He states the intended meaning (tātparya) with the words "and in this" (etasmiṃśca).
By the word "and" (ca), he indicates another fourfold group consisting of the means of knowledge (pramāṇa), valid cognition (pramā), the knower (pramātṛ), and the object of knowledge (prameya).

In this regard, this commentary is intended to demonstrate the primacy of *pramāṇa* (the means of valid cognition) among the fourfold group beginning with *pramāṇa*, which is indicated by the term "object" (*artha*) within the fourfold group beginning with "that which is to be abandoned" (*heya*).
Although the comprehension of the reality of both sets of fourfold groups is the cause for attaining the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), nevertheless, *pramāṇa* alone is primary.
Because the establishment of the others is rooted in that;
this is what was meant by the statement "it is meaningful."

The suffix *matup* is used in the sense of excellence (*atiśāyana*). A means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is "possessing a purpose" by virtue of its excellence relative to the knower (*pramātṛ*) and so forth, and relative to what is to be avoided (*heya*) and so forth. Why? Because when an object is apprehended through a means of valid cognition, the knower who has acted upon it obtains something other than that [previously known].
And because valid cognition (*pramā*) is its effect;
this is what was stated: "due to the efficacy of purposeful action" (*pravṛttisāmarthyāt*).
Therefore, because of its primacy, valid cognition is mentioned first, prior to the two groups of three [categories], according to the distinction of what is intended to be expressed.

By this, [the author] refutes what some say: "If priority is due to predominance, then it belongs to the object of cognition (*prameya*) alone; if, however, it is due to being a means, then it belongs to doubt and the rest, because they are the means for the instruments of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)."
And why is the instrument of knowledge (pramāṇa) primary over the knower (pramātṛ) and the other factors?
That [objection] is refuted,
because even the means of knowledge, such as doubt and so forth, are dependent upon the instrument of knowledge itself.
Surely it has been understood that the fourfold group beginning with "that which is to be abandoned" (heya) has been shown by way of the "objects" (artha); however,
he asks— "How, then?"— in order to inquire how the fourfold group beginning with "the means of valid cognition" (pramāṇa) has been demonstrated.
The subsequent [cognition] consists in the comprehension of the means of valid cognition and the objects to be cognized.

Having thus explained the overall purport (*tātparya*), he begins to explain the meaning of the individual parts: "This very statement is presented part by part and described—that is, explained—part by part.

Since its constituent parts are to be explained, he first elucidates the phrase "from the perspective of the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇataḥ*) because of its priority, saying: "In that regard...
He analyzes [the term]: this [suffix] *-taḥ* in *pramāṇataḥ* is the ablative case expressing cause (*nimitta-pañcamī*).
If it is asked why "by what means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇāt*) was not stated when the fifth case is used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta*), he says: "of this" (*asya*).
The expression "by means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇataḥ*) is for the purpose of pervading the number (*vacana*) and for the purpose of pervading the case-ending (*vibhakti*).
We consider that it is for the purpose of pervading the number.
But it is not for the sake of pervading all case endings (*vibhakti*), because *tasi* does not exist apart from the fifth case (*pañcamī*). To this he asks: "How then?
He answers: "It is obtained."

He asks about the purpose of pervasion (vyāpti): "What is established? The answer is: "Through the pervasion of the statement, there is both convergence (saṃplava) and systematic distinction (vyavasthā).
He analyzes these two by means of the phrase "by the instrument of knowledge" (pramāṇena).

Where there is a convergence (*saṃplava*) of two or more means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), each one of them possesses the capacity to establish comprehension; thus, even at the occasion of discussing convergence, the word "by means of a pramāṇa" (*pramāṇena*) was employed to express this.

For this very reason, in the context of the restriction (*vyavasthā*), the restrictive particle *eva* is used as in "by means of a pramāṇa alone" (*pramāṇenaiva*). He states the purpose of the pervasion of case-endings (*vibhakti-vyāpti*): "Through the pervasion of case-endings, the state of being a cause (*hetutva*) and the state of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) [are distinguished]."
The word "is understood" (*gamyate*) is supplied [from the previous context].
He analyzes that: "The attainment of an object arises from a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇāt*); thus, its status as a cause (*hetutva*) is understood.
"By means of a means of valid cognition, the attainment of an object arises" (*pramāṇena*); thus, its nature as an instrument (*karaṇa*) is understood—this is the connection.
Why, then, is the sense of "instrument" understood? To this he says: "by means of a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇena*).
This is because it is the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*) in accomplishing the apprehension of an object.

Furthermore, the expression of the causal state—which is inseparable from the state of being an instrument—by means of the ablative case is intended to negate the identity (*tādātmya*) between the means of valid cognition and its result.
Since the relationship of cause and effect has as its locus a distinction [between entities],
it is certainly not the case that the axe itself is the act of cutting.

Furthermore, in order to show that it is appropriate for this [instrument]— which is restated as having the status of an instrument (karaṇa) based on the nominal stem of the word *pramāṇa*— to be explained as being more eminent than other causal factors of valid cognition (*pramākāraka*), and to be primary, he raises the objection regarding the convergence [of means of knowledge] with the words "convergence" (*saṃplava*).
He refutes [the objection] with "No.
He analyzes the objection with "It might be thought.
Those whose objects are distinguished—that is, distinct—are "tathā" (so).
The plural number is intended to refer to the internal distinctions within the category [of perception].
For perception, which arises from the capacity of the object, has the object as its domain.
That alone is the object within the domain of perception which, through its presence and absence, causes the manifestation in cognition to conform to itself.
Furthermore, a universal cannot be such as to have its capacity for all causal efficiency entirely negated;
rather, it must be a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
For that alone is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*).

Since a real entity is characterized by causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*), its very own unique characteristic (*asādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*) is as follows: because it does not persist across space, that which is non-spatial is atomhood (*paramāṇutva*);
and because it does not persist across time, it is momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*).
Therefore, perception has the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object;
and the particular characteristic is not the domain of inference either,
for that [inference] is caused by a logical mark (*liṅga*) whose invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*) has already been apprehended.

Furthermore, since the relationship of contrariety—characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*)—has as its object the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) and is impossible to grasp, one must rely upon general properties (*sāmānyadharma*).
Yet, a single universal cannot possibly exist as something associated with multiple locations, times, and states.

Therefore, it must be accepted that the object of inference is either the basis for conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising from beginningless latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), or the externality of the conceptual form itself, which is unreal.

And that [conceptual image] is based on the exclusion of others (anyavyāvṛtti) because it is common to both existence and non-existence, because it resembles external objects, and because its manifestation is restricted.
Indeed, whatever is common to both existence and non-existence is necessarily based on the exclusion of others, just as, for example, incorporeality is.
That [conceptual object] is common to both existence, such as consciousness and so forth, and non-existence, such as a rabbit's horn and so forth.
And there exists a domain of conceptualization that is common to both existence and non-existence, namely: "the pot exists" and "the pot does not exist.
If, however, existence were exclusively unique (asādhāraṇa), the word "exists" would not be employed.
Because it would be a tautology;
nor should one say "it does not exist," because that would be contradictory.
The same should be stated regarding the non-exclusivity of non-existence as well.

Nor is it maintained that there is a similarity with a particular (svalakṣaṇa) for that which is false and devoid of all causal efficiency, because [such similarity] consists in the exclusion of others (anyavyāvṛtti).
Furthermore, the determinate cognition and designation "cow" do not occur without the exclusion of non-cows and the like.

Therefore, inference—which takes as its object a universal consisting of the form of the exclusion of others, which is internal yet immersed in externality due to the non-apprehension of its difference from the external—induces activity toward the external world.

And because it leads to the external object through a causal chain despite external obstructions, being concordant with reality, it is a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) even though it is erroneous, by virtue of the cognizer’s intention.
Therefore, its object is not the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*);
furthermore, it has already been explained that perception (*pratyakṣa*) does not have the universal characteristic (*sāmānya*) as its object.
And there is no means of valid cognition other than these two, because any existing means of valid cognition is included within these very two;
for if it were not so included, its status as a means of valid cognition would be untenable.
And there is no other object of cognition (prameya) apart from the universal and the particular wherein these two could be merged; this is the meaning.
He explains the statement of summary: "And this is not so.
How this is so will be explained here and there.
A "distinction" (viśeṣa) is that which excludes [other possibilities].
And that [object], such as a curved hollow and so forth, is the final one.

He states examples of the confusion of definitions—beginning with "like the sense organs"—and, not tolerating the convergence [of means of knowledge], he says: "because it has already been apprehended."
"By one who is concentrated, not otherwise. He explains the objection with the words "If... etc.

It might be argued that there is no pointlessness [in further cognitions] because, since cognitions perish very rapidly, another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is purposeful with respect to the production of a subsequent cognition whose object is that same thing; to this he says: "by a means of knowledge which makes known an object already known."
Even though cognitions are extremely swift to perish,

nevertheless, because a continuous stream of recollection regarding that object arises from the very stable mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the apprehension of the object through the generation of a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the object already apprehended would be apprehended once again by the means of valid cognition; thus,
it would be like grinding what has already been ground.
He restates the statement regarding meditative concentration (*samādhi*) in order to explain it—namely, "not otherwise.
He explains: "We do not say [it is] so.
This is the intended meaning (*abhisandhi*).
For the causes of valid cognition are not discerning agents, such that they would reflect in this way: "Let us produce a valid cognition for someone else; we shall remain indifferent here."

Nor can the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), which have acquired their birth through the power of their own causes, cease on the grounds that "this object has been shown by one of our means of valid cognition, so enough with us"; for since the cognizer is conscious, [the objection] that this is improper is not tenable. If it is argued: "No," [we reply: no.
Because this [means of knowledge] seeks to cognize a most beloved object again and again,
and because it also cognizes objects of cognition that are not sought to be known, such as the words of wicked people;
therefore, the engagement or non-engagement of a means of knowledge with an object does not depend on the intention of the cognizer.
Rather, it is due to its capacity;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that sufferings such as being burned by fire would not be perceptible.
The four means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) function depending upon the desire to know (pramitsā); if the cognizer (pramātṛ) does not employ them, what has happened to the means of valid cognition?
For it is not the case that because water is not drunk by one who is thirsty, its power to quench thirst is thereby lost.
Therefore, valid cognition (pramā) is the cognition produced by the assemblage of present causes.

And the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that produce those [cognitions] have the same object; moreover, by this [statement], he has demonstrated a difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), otherwise [as shown] by the passage beginning with "by perception" (*pratyakṣeṇa*).
Although there is also a difference in mode, such as direct manifestation (*sākṣātkāra*) versus non-manifestation (*asākṣātkāra*), and so forth.
Nevertheless, it has not been mentioned here because it is irrelevant to the present context.

For if it were said that "the substance is grasped by the skin" and thus the eye is rendered superfluous, or if it were said that "it is grasped by the eye" and thus the skin is rendered superfluous, [then the point would be lost].
Otherwise, neither the cognition of form nor the cognition of touch would arise;

for that purpose, either the eye or the skin must be admitted. Thus, although there is redundancy in the case of overlapping [functions], there is no redundancy in the case of their specific determination; this is what he means by saying "in respect of other objects."
He concludes the subject under discussion with the words "Therefore."

Having defined the meaning of the case-endings, he introduces the definition of the meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadika) with the words "pramāṇa... etc. Here, "avadhāraṇa" means that by which something is determined; it is "vicāra" (investigation).
For the sake of investigation, he asks about both the state of being (bhāva) and the agent of being (bhavitṛ) with the words "kiṃ punar... etc.
Some say that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which makes known an object not yet apprehended;
others maintain that it is the conformity of the object to a cognition possessing an aspect (*sākāra-vijñāna*);
while still others hold that it is the capacity of a cognition devoid of aspects (*anākāra-vijñāna*) itself to manifest its own nature.
The elders say that it is the means of apprehension (*upalabdhisādhana*). Therefore, because there is doubt due to conflicting views, a question is asked.
By the explanation of the question regarding the "being" (*bhāva*), the question regarding the "possessor of being" (*bhavitṛ*) is explained.
The answer is: A means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the cause of apprehension (*upalabdhi*).

Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of including doubt and error as causes of apprehension, because of the governing rule [of the definition] that it must be "like the object" (*arthavat*).
Because those two [conceptions] lack purposefulness due to their deviation from the object indicated by words;
for indeed, an entity that is being conceptualized neither exists nor is it employed in causal operations.
This might be so:
it would follow that even the cause of memory possesses validity,
for it is not the case that this [cause] is not a cause of apprehension.

Nor is it correct to claim that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) lacks validity because it lacks the cooperation of an object (*arthasahakāritā*), since this would entail the undesirable consequence that a river flood and the movement of ants with their eggs— which serve as signs (*liṅga*) for past and future rain— would not be valid cognitions, nor would a word whose object is past or future be a valid cognition, despite its lack of cooperation with an [actual] object.

If it is argued that, through some connection with an object—whether by way of being an indicator (*jñāpaka*) or an effect (*kārya*)—the same [status] applies to the mental impression (*saṃskāra*), then its validity as a cause for the apprehension in the form of memory would also follow.

This is not so, because it has been excluded by the term "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*). For a means of valid cognition is the instrument for producing valid knowledge (*pramā*), and memory is not valid knowledge.
For the relationship between a word and its meaning is determined by worldly convention.
And the world designates as "valid cognition" (pramā) only that apprehension which is distinct from memory—arising solely from mental impressions—and which does not deviate from the object.
Therefore, since a means of valid cognition is the cause of such [non-deviating] apprehension, there is no over-extension to the cause of memory.

We do not respect the claim that the validity of successive cognitions (*dhārāvāhika-vijñāna*)— which have as their object an already apprehended thing and whose status as valid means of knowledge is well-established in the world— is undermined by the requirement that a valid cognition must apprehend an object not yet apprehended.
Nor is it logical to argue that successive cognitions apprehend an unapprehended object due to a difference in time,
for we, with our physical eyes, cannot perceive such extremely subtle divisions of time.

Nor should it be said that the subsequent cognitions lack authority because the object has already been indicated by the first cognition, because the person has already been prompted to act, and because the object has already been attained;
for the attainment of an object by a cognition is nothing other than its prompting [the person toward it].
Furthermore, instigation (*pravartana*) is nothing other than the manifestation of the object (*arthapradarśana*).
Therefore, cognition, whose function consists solely in the manifestation of the object, is both that which instigates and that which leads to attainment.

And since this manifestation is no different for subsequent cognitions than it was for the preceding one, why is it that only the first cognition is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and not the subsequent ones as well?
If, however, validity were dependent upon a person, it would follow that cognitions such as those of the moon and stars— which do not depend on a person— would lack validity.
Nor is that [cognition] required by a person because its object is too distant and thus to be discarded,
since its object belongs to the category of things that are to be disregarded.

It will be explained that even that which is to be disregarded (*upekṣaṇīya*) is not to be abandoned merely because it is not to be adopted; rather, it is to be regarded as something to be abandoned [in the sense of being recognized].

Furthermore, by asserting that the cause of apprehension (*upalabdhi-hetu*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the views that a means of valid cognition consists in "the reaching of an object not yet cognized," "conformity with the object," or "the power to illuminate both self and non-self" are refuted.
It will be explained that since there is only apprehension, [the aforementioned definitions] are to be abandoned.

By stating that the cause of apprehension (*upalabdhi*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the following [definitions] are refuted: that the means of valid cognition consists in "cognizing an object not yet cognized," or "conformity with the object" (*arthasārūpya*), or "the power to illuminate both itself and the non-self. This is because the term "means of valid cognition" is applied to anything other than mere apprehension—that is, to that which does not deviate from the object—and because by using the term "cause" (*hetu*), conformity and power (which are non-different from the result) are excluded; for a relationship of cause and effect is untenable if there is identity (*tādātmya*).
And being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consists in being the cause of apprehension (*upalabdhi*). By the explanation of the "agent" (*bhavitṛ*), the "action" (*bhāva*) has been explained.
Thus, in this way, whether it be knowledge (*jñāna*) or non-knowledge (*ajñāna*), that which is the cause of apprehension is the means of valid cognition.
It is established that its state is its reality (tattva).
He raises an objection on the grounds of over-extension with the words "because of their being equal. He provides the solution with the words "this is the distinction.
This is the meaning:
Every agent performs an operation within the sphere of an instrument, but does not operate directly upon the result.
Furthermore, the instrument is established as being of two kinds: accomplished and unaccomplished.
Among these, an accomplished instrument, such as an axe, is said to "cut wood" when, having repeatedly raised it for the purpose of splitting the wood, one brings it down upon the wood.
However, the splitting of the wood is not the direct object of the agent's operation;

rather, the agent's operation—characterized by raising and lowering—is the conjunction of the axe, which serves as the instrument and possesses touch and momentum, and this operation has the axe itself as its object.
In the same way, the agent who desires heaven does not operate directly upon heaven.
However, that instrument establishes the sacrifice which is not yet established.

Heaven, moreover, arises directly from the very operation of the sacrifice—termed the *apūrva* (unprecedented result)—which is the locus of consciousness and which attains a specific transformation through differences of place, time, and state.
Similarly here as well, the cognizer [establishes] the sense organs and so forth, which are already established.

Furthermore, the sense-organ and so forth, by operating upon or producing that [cognition] which is yet unestablished, fulfill their purpose only as instruments (*karaṇa*). Since the instrument—whether it be the sense-organ or its contact with the object—does not fulfill its purpose elsewhere, it exerts its activity directly toward the fruit, which is perception itself.
As for the object of cognition (*prameya*), it does not even possess the status of being a cause for perception in any instance other than through direct perception.
Even in that case, the object of cognition (prameya) is useful only for establishing the connection with the sense faculty;
however, it is the sense faculty itself, or the respective contact (*sannikarṣa*) and so forth, that is the direct cause of valid cognition (*pramā*).
Therefore, this is established: the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) is not the direct cause of valid cognition, because he is the agent (*kartṛ*).
Whosoever is an agent, none of them is a direct cause of the result, just as the axe, the sacrificer, and so forth;
and this [agent] is likewise.
Therefore, it is so:
likewise, the object of cognition (prameya) is not the direct cause of the means of valid cognition (pramā), because it is an object of cognition.
Whatever is an object of cognition, all that is not the cause of its own cognition, just like the object of inference and so forth;
and this [subject] is such;
therefore, it is so.
Thus, this is the fulfillment and non-fulfillment of the purpose of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) and the object of cognition (*prameya*);
therefore, that [means of valid cognition] alone is the cause of the result (*phala*).
However, since the cognizer and the object of cognition proceed for the sake of the result, they are in some sense its causes.
He objects: "By non-action.
The meaning is that a non-acting agent cannot even encompass a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
He replies: "No."

Regarding the phrase "indriyārtha": when cognition is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the meaning is "at the time of the arising of that cognition which is the means of valid knowledge. He raises an objection again: "If, then... and so forth.
He refutes this with the words "even in that case.
He objects: "If the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) exists because the cognizer (pramātṛ) and the object of cognition (prameya) exist.
The meaning is that, since there can be no valid cognition (pramā) without a means of valid cognition, the cognizer and the object of cognition themselves would remain unestablished.
He asks: "How so? The answer is: "Because it is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
Why does the object itself not become the causal factor (kāraka) merely by its own nature?
And since that [capacity] exists even prior to its connection with an action, he says: "nor is it merely a substance.
Let it be, then, that its intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*) is the *kāraka* with respect to the primary action to be accomplished.
Since that [instrument] also serves as a cause for the primary action, he says: "And it is not merely an action.
For Devadatta is not an axe by his own nature, nor is his activity—such as raising and lowering—of the same nature as a clod of earth or similar objects.
To the question, "Where, then, does the term 'kāraka' (agent/causal factor) apply?", he says: "For the term 'kāraka'...
The term *kāraka* applies to a cause (*hetu*) that accomplishes the primary action and is connected with specific intermediate actions.

For instance, when the result is the act of splitting into two (*dvaidhībhāva*), which is the primary operation, the intermediate operations within the scope of the agent's instrument—such as raising and striking—are what constitute the *kāraka*.
And in the case of the action of cutting wood, the intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*) is precisely the contact with an axe that is harsh to the touch, swift, and exceedingly sharp.
For by means of that [contact], the wood undergoes bifurcation through the disjunction of its parts, which arises from the motion of its own constituent members.

Having thus established in general that "an instrument (*kāraka*) is that which is endowed with both an intermediate and a primary operation," he applies this to the present context: "and the words 'knower' (*pramātṛ*) and 'object of knowledge' (*prameya*."
To this much, [the opponent] objects that the action is the primary action;
[the author] refutes this, saying: "No, as in the case of words such as 'cook' (pācaka)."
Indeed, this relationship between word and meaning is determined by worldly convention.
And the world employs words denoting grammatical factors (*kāraka*) with the intention of expressing merely the connection to past, future, or present actions—
as in "bring the cook" and "he will cook."
The observation that the usage of the term "cook" (pācaka) is seen equally as referring to the three times— both in the expressions "this cook cooked" and "this cook cooks"—
is for what reason? It is because Devadatta and others possess an inherent capacity (svarūpa-śakti) toward the connection with cooking, even when they are not currently cooking.

For the causal capacity of factors (*kāraka*) with respect to the production of an effect is twofold: their own essential nature (*svarūpa*) and the conjunction of the collection of auxiliary conditions (*sahakāri-grāma*).

Among these, since the words "causal factor" (*kāraka*) apply even when the conjunction of the collection of auxiliaries is absent, and since they do not apply when—despite the presence of an essential nature that persists through the three times—an effect connected to the three times is impossible, it follows that the essential nature itself, as delimited by an effect connected to the three times, is the basis for the application of the words "causal factor."
Regarding the term "nimitta" (cause):

even in the absence of a connection between the present cause of valid cognition (*pramā*) and the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the application of the terms "knower" (*pramātṛ*) and "object of knowledge" (*prameya*) is possible; thus, it is established that the means of valid cognition is produced by the knower and the object of knowledge.
That means of valid cognition is the direct instrument for apprehension (*upalabdhi*).
Thus it is established that [the self] is neither the knower nor the object of knowledge.

And even though the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) and the object of cognition (*prameya*) are means for apprehension (*upalabdhi-sādhana*), there is no over-extension [of the definition] to them in the phrase "the cause of apprehension," because the effect is understood to reside in that which is the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*) among the various instruments, since it is that which is manifested through its excellence; thus he says: "Or, because of being the most effective instrument" (*sādhakatamatvād vā*). He asks about the meaning of "most effective instrument": "But what [is it]? (*kaḥ punar iti*).

The answer: The meaning of "the most effective instrument" (*sādhakatama*) is that the presence or absence of the effect, namely valid cognition (*pramā*), corresponds to the presence or absence of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
There is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) because of the intended non-difference between the definiendum (*lakṣya*) and the definition (*lakṣaṇa*);

however, it is not the case that the positive and negative concomitance of the knower (*pramātṛ*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*) also constitutes the positive and negative concomitance of the valid cognition. Therefore, he says: "not in the knower."

The relationship of the production of valid cognition (*pramā*) with the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) and the object of cognition (*prameya*) is one of exclusion of other connections (*anyayogavyavaccheda*). However, the relationship of the production of valid cognition with the instrument of cognition (*pramāṇa*) is by way of both the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) and the exclusion of connection with others (*anyayogavyavaccheda*); such is the excellence of the instrument of cognition.
For the functions of the cognizer and the object of cognition are exhausted in the instrument of cognition and do not operate upon the valid cognition itself.

Therefore, because obstacles may arise, valid cognition (*pramā*) does not necessarily occur even when there is the operation of the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) and the object of cognition (*prameya*). However, when there is the operation of the instrument of cognition (*pramāṇa*), valid cognition certainly occurs. He states another alternative: "Or rather, that which possesses [the capacity] by means of which one cognizes is the excellence (*atiśaya*).
By saying "one cognizes" (*pramimīte*), he indicates an independent agent (*kartṛ*) in order to distinguish it from the instrument (*karaṇa*) which is to be explained.
And the phrase "yadvān eva" (only that which possesses *yad*) is restrictive;
therein, "yadvān" excludes any other agent,
for an agent is not "possessor-of-an-agent."
Rather, it must possess a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇavat*).
For a basis that is independent is supported by that which is dependent;
indeed, it has been explained that an instrument is dependent upon an agent.
The knower may in some cases possess the object of knowledge because the object of knowledge is dependent upon him; however,
he does not *always* possess the object of knowledge,
since in the case of inference and other means of cognition, the object of knowledge has already passed away and thus the state of possessing it is lost.
But the result of the restriction is that one who possesses the knowledge of the inferential mark (*liṅga*) and so forth is never [without it].
This is the distinction of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) from the knower (*pramātṛ*) and the object of cognition (*prameya*).
And he demonstrates the superiority of this very distinction through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) by saying: "When the means of valid cognition exists... and so on.
[Kalpataru says: "Satārveti.

The distinction here is that whereas in the previous [verse] an excellence characterized primarily by positive affirmation (*bhāva*) was shown for such a person, here an excellence characterized primarily by negation (*vyatireka*) is shown for that very same person.
The meaning is that it is without an agent and without a cause.
