He states that the specific definitions of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), such as perception and the rest, are mentioned immediately after [the general definition] because they serve as the cause for the classification and enumeration of their implied general characteristics—thus he says, "Now, of those which have been distinguished.
Among those, because of its priority, the definition of perception is the sūtra beginning with "produced by the contact of the sense-organ and the object," and so forth.
He states its intended meaning: "the meaning of the sūtra" refers to the purpose of the sūtra.
It is the quality of distinguishing between what is of the same class and what is of a different class.
That which is of the same class includes inference and so forth; that which is of a different class includes fallacious perception, objects of knowledge, and so forth.
The "particularity" (*viśeṣa*) is that which distinguishes [an object] from those [others];
this is the purpose of this Sūtra.
Indeed, for one who—due to some delusion—is unable to grasp that form as distinguished from things of both similar and dissimilar classes, [this Sūtra is intended].
Thus, it is made known by this definition that perception is characterized in such a manner. Therefore,
this sūtra is intended to prescribe a definition by way of restating mere perception— already established in its general form— as something distinct [from other means of knowledge].

However, since its definition has been understood from this [previous] source, one grasps the true nature of perception by distinguishing it through that very [definition]; thus, the meaning of the Sūtra is stated as the exclusion of similar and dissimilar classes.

And here, having supplied the word "which" (*yat*), because of the constant connection between "that which" and "that" (*tad*), the term "perception"—which denotes the instrument of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—should be applied as "that is perception.

In this way, even on the view that cognition is the instrument of knowledge (*jñānapramāṇya-pakṣa*), that object-cognition which is the result of perception (*pratyakṣaphala*) is the consideration of the mark (*liṅgaparāmarśa*).

Or rather, since that [result] also possesses the quality of being produced by the contact between the sense organ and its object, it serves as a qualification of the means of valid cognition; thus, the definition is not under-extended.
He asks about the meaning of the words of the Sūtra with "Now" (*atha*). The answer is "The sense-faculties" (*indriya*).
He enumerates the specific varieties obtainable through the mention of "contact" (*sannikarṣa*) with the words "Contact, moreover... (*sannikarṣaḥ punar iti*).
By the inclusion of the word "again" (punaḥ) along with the terms "conjunction" (saṃyoga) and "inherence" (samavāya), he excludes [other relations].
For if only the term "conjunction" were included, inherence would not be obtained; nor, if only the term "inherence" were included, would conjunction be obtained.
By including the term *sannikarṣa* (contact), however, the desired [definition] is obtained.
By the inclusion of the word *artha* (object), the suitability of the nature of the knowable (*jñeya*) as that which is sought after is shown.

Since this [suitability] does not exist for atoms, space, and so forth, even though conjunction and other [contacts] may exist, these are not "contact with an object" (*arthasannikarṣa*); thus, they are excluded.
By the inclusion of the term "arisen" (*utpanna*), it is indicated that the sense-object contact (*sannikarṣa*) must be productive [of cognition].
Consequently, even though the object possesses its own intrinsic fitness, this excludes those contacts—such as "contact with what is conjoined" (*saṃyukta-saṃyoga*)—that are not productive.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that a sense organ conjoined with a wall would perceive a jar or similar object conjoined with that wall but separated by it, as well as the color and other qualities inherent (*samaveta*) in that jar.
Nor is it correct to maintain that there are only three types of contact— namely, conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence in the conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), and inherence (*samavāya*)—
because this contradicts both independent reasoning and experience.
For those who accept similarity as a distinct category, separate from generality (*sāmānya*) and residing in substances, qualities, and actions, [would find such a restriction untenable].
How could the mutual similarity between those various distinctions of form and so forth be perceived?
For it is not in contact with the sense faculty,
nor is it inherent in that which is in contact with the sense faculty.
Therefore, the fourth [type of inherence], namely inherence in that which is conjoined with that in which something inheres (*saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya*), must be accepted;
otherwise, there would be a contradiction of independence and a contradiction of experience.
For universals and particulars, such as "color-ness" and "odor-ness," are indeed experienced as recurring [in various instances];
these would not be experienced in their respective individual manifestations—which are mutually distinct—if there were no other [kind of] contact.
If, however, out of audacity they say that they are not experienced at all, [then...]
Then it must be answered: from what source does this difference in designation—such as "color" or "smell"—arise with respect to these infinite individual manifestations of color, smell, and so forth?

If it is argued that this is based on limiting conditions (*upādhi*) such as visibility (*cākṣuṣatva*), we say no; for there can be no cognition of a qualified object (*upahita-pratyaya*) when the qualifying condition has not been apprehended (*ananusaṃhita-upādhi*).

Indeed, one does not designate someone as "the staff-bearer" (daṇḍin) based on a cognition of the staff alone when it is not being attended to. Nor do the sense organs, which are themselves supersensible, ever become objects of sensory perception.

Therefore, there must exist a perception of universals such as "color-ness" (rūpatva) by means of the sense organ, upon which basis certain specific designations apply to certain specific individuals; thus, another type of contact (sannikarṣa) is established.
And by way of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇabhāva*), both the qualifier of that which is conjoined (*saṃyuktaviśeṣaṇa*) and the qualifier of that which is inherent (*samavetaviśeṣaṇa*) are included.
He demonstrates the specific kind of contact that occurs with each respective sense organ—therein, "the eye" [is mentioned].
Sound has space as its quality;
the portion of space delimited by the ear-cavity is the sense of hearing (śrotra).

It will be demonstrated more thoroughly in the second [chapter] that it is only the first sound that is born from conjunction and disjunction, its production in the auditory organ through a continuous series is inherence, and so forth; furthermore, parts and wholes,
qualities and their possessors, actions and their agents, and universals and their instances are experienced as being mutually connected.
Otherwise, there would not be such [conceptions] as "the cloth in the threads," "the white cloth," or "the cloth moves."

If you argue that there would be the cognition and designation "the cloth is a substance," and that the knowledge of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in such cases as "the white cloth" is not a knowledge of a relation (*saṃbandha*),
then what indeed is this coreferentiality?
If it is argued that they are identical— that is not so,
because the second cognition and designation would be redundant. And yet, cognizers consider them to be non-redundant.
When one perceives one thing, they desire to perceive another;
yet it is not logical for a single entity to possess a dual nature,
because duality— which is necessarily dependent upon difference— is impossible within a single self due to contradiction.
Therefore, two distinct entities appear in a relation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) precisely because they are related;
for if they were unrelated, such a relation would be impossible, as in the case of "cow" and "horse.
If it is argued that even if they are related, there would be the consequence of non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), as in the case of "curd in a bowl"—we say no.

Because, despite the non-difference of the relation, the distinction between grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) is established through the difference in the mode of operation of words;
for the word "curd" never occurs with reference to a bowl, nor does the word "bowl" occur with reference to curd.
However, words such as "fragrant," "sweet," and "white" do occur with reference to cloth and other objects by taking their own denotata as the causal basis (*nimitta*).
In this way, words such as "cloth" also apply to a substance by taking its genus and so forth as their basis; thus, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

Consequently, even though they share a common substratum, the bases for their application (*pravṛttinimitta*) do not possess identity with one another, nor do they possess identity with the substance.
However, a single substance is cognized as being denoted by those various [words].
Because words function with respect to that one substance, there arises the illusion of identity among their referents.
Due to their inseparable connection (*ayutasiddhi*), however, the clear manifestation of their distinction is not as evident as it is in the case of "curd in a bowl."

Thus, there exists an experience of connection, and since that experience of connection does not occur without a connected object, the connection itself is experienced; and that [connection] is inherence (samavāya), brought about by the fulfillment of conditions such as inseparable existence (ayutasiddhi).
Nor does it have another inherence, because it is not a state [of a substance];
nor is there conjunction of it with a sense organ, because it is not a substance.
Nor can there be a cognition of that which is unrelated,
because it has been established that the sense organs function by reaching their objects;
therefore, the relation of qualifier and qualified remains as the only possibility.
Now, this relationship of qualifier and qualified is observed elsewhere to be preceded by another relation;
so why should another relation not be postulated here as well? And thus, it has been stated, there would be an infinite regress.
And there is no apprehension of that which is not connected to a sense faculty;
therefore, it is established that the relation of qualifier and qualified must be accepted as existing even without any other [physical] connection.

Thus, even in the case of non-existence (*abhāva*), that which is either conjoined with a sense faculty (*indriya-saṃyukta*) or inherent in it (*indriya-samaveta*)— such as "there is no jar on the ground" or "there is no grave accent (*anudātta-svara*) in the syllable *na*"— is apprehended through sensory proximity (*indriya-pratyāsatti*) by virtue of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇabhāva*) of that which is conjoined or inherent.
Nor is it correct to claim that the non-existence of a jar is merely the form of the ground itself and not a distinct entity (*arthāntara*).
Even when a jar or other object is present, the ground still exists;
moreover, its "isolation" (*kaivalya*) is not a property of that ground which is opposed to the presence of a jar and distinct from the absence of a jar.
Furthermore, it is not tenable to claim that the perception of the ground while a visible jar is present constitutes "isolation" as the cause for the conventional usage of "absence."
For in this way, even the apprehension of a floor-surface conjoined with a jar would have to initiate the conventional usage of the "absence of a jar" by means of [calling it] "isolation.
Indeed, at that time, the invisible jar is not being perceived.

But if the qualification "not being perceived while perceptible" is used, what has the absence of perception (upalabhyābhāva) done wrong that one must resort to the absence of apprehension (upalambhābhāva) to set it aside?
Therefore, non-existence must also be accepted as a reality, just like existence;
and that [non-existence] is perceived because its cognition occurs when the sense organs are operative.

Nor is it correct to argue that sensory contact with an object is incapable of producing the cognition of absence when it is interrupted by the recollection of a counter-positive, as we shall demonstrate later.

Regarding the establishment of conceptual perception (*savikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) as valid, just as the recollection of words, the prior apprehension of the object, and the synthesis (*anusandhāna*) do not obstruct the operation of the sense faculty,
nor is there any deficiency in the recollection of words and so forth,
because they serve as auxiliary factors for the conceptualization of the ground.
According to the maxim that "one's own limb is not an obstacle," it is correct to say that the jar is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*);
but of what, then, is the jar the counter-correlate?
If it is argued that this refers to the absence of that [cognition], let it be so; however,
for the experience of the absence of a jar, the cause is the recollection of the jar, which is not the counter-correlate (pratiyogin), but rather the sub-correlate (anuyogin) itself.

Now, consider the case where Caitra, having merely perceived his own form and having gone outside while recollecting the house and other objects, is asked by someone: "Friend, who was there in your house at that time, Maitra?

Although Caitra had not previously apprehended the absence of Maitra due to the lack of recollection of the counter-positive (Maitra), he reflects for a moment upon the memory of Maitra produced by that question, realizes that absence, and says: [Maitra was not there].
O Mitra,
in that case, there was no Maitra.

Thus, the cognition of non-existence arising when there is no contact between the sense faculty and its object establishes a means of valid cognition called "non-existence" (abhāva), which is distinct from perception and the other [means of knowledge].

This is not so; for, having apprehended Maitra’s absence of recollection regarding that which ought to be remembered through the mental contact characterized as a qualification of a conjoined object, one then infers his absence by means of that mark (liṅga), because at that time Maitra’s house was perceived while Maitra—who is capable of being known—was not known.
Thus, that house at that time was devoid of Maitra, since the house was being cognized while Maitra, who is fit to be known, was not.
Whatever is known in the absence of something that ought to be known is devoid of that thing;
for example, a floor is devoid of a jar,
and so too is this house.
Therefore, it is so.
Furthermore, it is not the case that whatever is sometimes inferential must necessarily be inaccessible to the senses,
because of the established principle of the convergence of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-saṃplava*).
Thus, because it stands in a relationship of qualification with that [non-existence], non-existence is an object of sensory cognition.
He states the purpose of employing the term *sannikarṣa* (contact) instead of the terms *saṃyoga* (conjunction) and *samavāya* (inherence): "This is the word *sannikarṣa*."

By this preceding discussion, the Bhāṣya passage—"the cognition which arises from the contact of a sense-organ with its object is perception"—has been explained. Now, he explains the objection in the Bhāṣya beginning with "In that case, then... (na tarhi): "If [it is defined as] 'from the sense-object...
The meaning is that, since the author of the Sūtra was engaged in stating the causes of perceptual cognition, if he were to state only a single part of it, he would be unskilled.
He shows other causes with the words "tadyathā" (for example):
the conjunction of the object, the eye, and light;
and the form residing therein.
For it is an established principle that the eyes perceive a substance by means of their own form;
whether it be its magnitude (*mahattva*) or its possession of multiple substances (*anekadravyavattva*),
since its parts consist of multiple substances.
The possession of that [magnitude] belongs only to a large composite whole (*avayavin*), not to a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*);
therefore, it is logical that there is indeed an alternative [explanation] for the coexistence of magnitude and the state of having multiple constituent substances as being mutually independent.

Even though the visual organ, which is a composite whole composed of light, possesses such characteristics, it does not possess visibility; therefore, it is stated: "the refinement (*saṃskāra*) is of the nature of perception."
The formative force (saṃskāra) is said to arise from the causes of merit and demerit (dharmādharmanimitta) and has perception as its result;
yet it does not exist in the eye,
because by the power of the unseen (adṛṣṭa), its color and tangibility are unmanifest— this is the meaning.
He refutes this, saying that [these things] should not be mentioned.
For the author of the Sūtras, being engaged in formulating the definition of perception, would mention only that which is its specific cause;
he would not mention even that which is a common cause of it.
For that is not its defining characteristic because it is over-extensive; this is the meaning.
By this, the commentary beginning with "not this" and so forth has been explained.
If an uncommon cause were to be adopted as the definition of perception, alas! [it would lead to absurdities].
He raises an objection, suggesting that there is yet another unique cause for this [cognition] which should also be accepted—namely, "then it is the contact between the sense organ and the mind.
By this, it should be understood that the meaning of the commentary's statement, "then it is of the mind," has been explained. He refutes this: "No."
"By this very [means]" means by the contact between the sense-organ and the object alone;
for that contact between the sense-organ and the mind has already been stated.
Whatever is to be accomplished by that statement has already been performed by it.
However, the contact between the sense organ and the mind is unable to accomplish that which is to be accomplished [by the sense-object contact];
furthermore, in the case of mental cognition of pleasure and so forth, there is no contact between the sense organ and the mind.
On the other hand, the contact between the sense organ and its object is all-pervasive.
For he will indeed state that the mind possesses the status of a sense-organ (*indriya*), and that pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth possess the status of objects (*artha*) is already established.
Now, having provisionally accepted [the opponent's claim of] pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*), he states another rebuttal: "indriyārtha... and so on.

Although the sense organ is present even in the contact between the sense organ and the mind, it is the specific determinant (*viśeṣaka*) of perceptual knowledge because perceptual knowledge is designated by means of the sense organ as "sense-knowledge" (*indriyajñāna*);

nevertheless, because there is no designation by means of the mind, the mind is not a specific determinant therein. However, in the case of the contact between the sense organ and its object, both are specific determinants, since perceptual knowledge is designated by means of both.
This is the distinction of this [type of contact] from the contact between the sense organ and the mind.
He raises an objection with the words "But when... (*yadā tu*). The word "but" (*tu*) sets aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
For when cognitions arise in the self of a yogin through the conjunction of the self and the mind, those [cognitions] are indeed designated by the self as "cognitions of the self" (*ātmabuddhayaḥ*).
Furthermore, they are designated by means of the mind as "mental cognitions" (*manobuddhi*).

Therefore, because they are designated by both [the sense organ and the mind], both serve as qualifiers; the meaning is that, like the contact between the sense organ and its object, the contact between the self and the mind must also be stated.
He offers a rebuttal with the words "And as for that which... (*yacca*).
The particle *ca* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*).
The meaning is that whatever is unique (*asādhāraṇa*) receives its designation; thus, cognition is designated by way of being the cause.

This is what is meant: just as cognition is designated by means of the eye as "visual" (*cākṣuṣa*) because the eye is a sense-faculty (*indriya*), so too cognition is designated by means of the mind as "mental" (*mānasa*) because the mind is a sense-faculty.
Likewise, just as cognition is designated by means of its object, form (*rūpa*), as "cognition of form" (*rūpajñāna*).
Likewise, it is designated by its object as "knowledge of the self" (*ātmajñāna*);
in that case, those two [the self and the knowledge] possess exclusivity (*asādhāraṇatva*) alone.
However, where another sense organ itself is exclusive, [the designation is made by that].
Or rather, in that case, it is not the object—such as a mark (*liṅga*) and so forth—but the self (*ātman*) who is the knower;
for instance, in the cognition of color and so on, or in inferential cognition and the like, there is no designation of it as "mental cognition" or "self-cognition.
For what reason? Because those two [the object and the self] are common to both [types of cognition].

The contact between the self and the mind, however, is already included within the contact between the sense organ and its object; it is not the subsumer of the contact between the sense organ and its object, because it does not pervade it.
The author presents the rebuttal of the partialist (ekadeśin): "Or rather, there is no non-perception of the contact between the sense organ and the mind because of non-difference despite difference.

For instance, when the women of the city, out of curiosity, with their minds intent and their lotus-eyes wide open and motionless, gaze through the windows of the palace rows at the king entering through the main gate with his army and vehicles after a very long absence."

At that time, indeed, through a single conjunction of the sense organ and the mind, assisted by successive contacts with multiple objects of the senses, distinct and successive perceptions of elephants, horses, and so forth arise;
this is what he says with the words "because. He raises an objection with the words "if."

For when a cow moves slowly from a distance, one perceives "the white cow" through the sense-object contact of inherence-in-the-conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*); then, as one draws closer, one also cognizes "it is moving" through that very same contact of inherence-in-the-conjoined.
Therefore, although there is a difference between the perceptual cognitions of "white" and "moving," the sense-object contact does not differ.

Therefore, since the contact between the sense organ and the object is common [to both perception and inference], the conjunction of the sense organ and the mind must also be mentioned there; this is the meaning.
He refutes this: "It need not be mentioned.
Why? Because the answer has already been stated."
He analyzes that [point] with the words "stated," etc.

Now, one might object: "Granted that the stated reply has been given, the objection to the statement ‘because there is non-difference in difference’ must still be resolved. To this he says: "And because it is not accepted. This is the view of a certain school (ekadeśin), which we do not accept.
Therefore, the meaning is that it need not be addressed.

[Objection: In that case, is the commentary—which states that this [reason] is not mentioned because it is common to both, since the perceptual cognition being divided does not itself divide—not indeed untenable?
[Reply: No; he says: "And there is no mention of the contact between the sense organ and the mind because it is common [to both cases]."
He asks: "By what? The answer is: "By the self and the mind.
He asks again: "What, moreover, is this similarity?"
The answer is: it has been stated that there is an absence of designation. Therefore, this is the meaning of the Bhāṣya:

for perceptual cognition—whether it be the cognition of color or designated as "cognition of color" or "visual consciousness"—this conjunction of the sense-organ and the mind is [the cause], just like the conjunction of the self and the mind.
It is not divided;
for it is divided in this way only if its own [referent] is distinguished from others by means of a designation that expresses its own related entity.
Nor would knowledge, even when qualified by a qualifier, be distinguished from other [types of knowledge].

However, there is no designation for this [knowledge] based on the sense organ and the mind individually— as its bases for contact— such as the designation "knowledge of form" or "visual knowledge" based on the sense organ and the object as their respective bases for contact.

Therefore, the absence of a specific designation [for the contact between the mind and the self] implies that the contact between the sense organ and the mind is equal to the contact between the self and the mind;
because of this equality, it was not mentioned.

He shows another alternative in the case of equality [of the two objects]: "or it is the state of having a supersensuous substratum. For a definition is well-known, as smoke is of fire; however, contact with a substratum of two supersensuous things is not well-known in that way, because contact between a sense organ and an object is well-known only in relation to one [object] which is connected to the sense organ.
However, because both the sense faculty and the mind are beyond the reach of the senses,
the self,
although distinct from the body and other such things, is indeed perceptible to the yogin.
Nevertheless, since it is not so for people like us, it is said to be "beyond the senses" (*atīndriya*).

Thus, having stated by its very nature that [the self] has as its substrate something beyond the senses, he expresses this same quality of having a substrate beyond the senses through the two [characteristics] of not residing in objects and residing in the mind—namely, "or, not residing in objects.
He concludes with "therefore," which is the reason stated in the Bhāṣya: "because of being common."
"Because its purpose has been fulfilled"—this is what was stated by [the author] himself.
He objects: "The claim that [perception] arises from the contact of the sense organ with its object is incorrect.
He analyzes the reason, "because of the apprehension of distance," by stating: "in the case of what is remote.
Now, it might be argued that the object is not actually remote.
Because the eye reaches that [object], he says: "But not by the eye.
Why? To this he says: "Of a particular element.
The external particular element is light.
Its clarity consists in the non-obstruction of the sense-faculties; this is its distinction from walls and the like, for it is indeed present in such transparent things as glass and mica.
It might be argued:
"There exists a specific kind of earth characterized by the black antelope (*kṛṣṇasāra*), which [is also found] even in the case of one whose vision is clear."
Therefore, it might follow that there would also be perception of form [by other senses]; to this he says: "preceded by thirst for that.
For thirst for the enjoyment of form extends its scope even to the black pupil (*kṛṣṇasāra*), which is the instrument for that [perception].
This is what is meant: a particular element (*bhūtaviśeṣa*), depending upon karma, perceives form; thus it is called the "eye" (*cakṣus*).
But because of the destruction of karma, for one whose vision is clear, form is not seen; thus, it is not the eye [itself].
[The opponent asks: "Let the eyeball itself be the eye; what follows from this? To this he says: "And not...
The meaning is that the eyeball is indeed experienced as being spatially distinct [from the visual consciousness].
Thus, in this way, the perception of an object as having an interval [between it and the sense organ] has been stated as the reason for its acting without reaching [the object].
Some, however, state that "with an interval" (*sāntaram*) is a qualification of the perception; he introduces their view with the words "others, however.

He demonstrates the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of this [reason] with the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyaya*) by saying "for [it is not seen] in those [senses] which act by reaching [their object]," and he states its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) by saying "but it is observed..."

As for the argument stated—that [the sense organ] acts without reaching [its object] because it perceives something larger [than itself]—that is analyzed as follows: "pṛthutara... (larger...). For a conjunction based on two substrata conforms only to the smaller of the two conjoined entities.
It is not large;
for the conjunctions of chariots and such things never pervade space, lest there be the perception of chariots and the like, as well as their conjunctions, everywhere.
Consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving only that much which is pervaded by the globular mass of the kingdom, forest, and so forth.

He states another reason: "Direction" (diś). He demonstrates that this too functions as a means of cognition through the method of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*): "if [the sense organ] were to function by reaching [its object]" (*yadi prāpyakārī*).
He states another reason as well: "sannikṛṣṭa" (proximate), etc.

Although there is no distinction among the individual moments of motion (*gati-kṣaṇa*) in terms of their swiftness regarding the production of disjunction from and conjunction with another location for their own substratum, nor is there any distinction in their proximity to that substratum, nevertheless, the collection of sequential moments of motion—beginning from the disjunction from the point of departure (*apādāna*) up until the attainment of the destination to be reached—is what constitutes "motion" (*gati*) here.
This is what is intended.

Its "having intervals" means slowness or delay; whereas "continuity" means dexterity or swiftness. Even while performing this very movement without interruption, one who does not break it reaches the proximate point quickly.
It is not simultaneous with what is distant,
but rather, that which is distant [is perceived] after a long time.
As it was said by Digrāga:
If there were contact [between the object and the sense organ], there would be no perception of distance, nor of something additional [such as the intervening space].
If it is argued that "the perception of distance is logical because the sense organ exists externally," to this it is said:
The sense organ does not exist outside its physical basis; rather, the sense organ is located precisely where the basis is.
Why?
Because of the application of medical treatment and so forth to that very location.
Moreover, even if it existed externally, it would have no power to perceive the object;
for if it did possess such power, one would continue to see it even after closing one's eyes upon having opened them.
And if it were so, one would see form even with eyes closed; therefore, because there is seeing upon opening [the eyes], the external sense faculty exists.
In this regard, the author of the *Vārttika*, having analyzed the reason "because of the perception of intervals," refutes it with the words "As for what was first...

Indeed, "having an interval" (sāntaratā) is associated with non-contact (*aprāpti*). He characterizes non-contact because the meaning of the reason is implied by the meaning of the thesis through non-difference.
As it has been said: "It does not differ from the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*).

Although there is a distinction based on being expressed by the words of the reason (*hetu*) and the proposition, this relationship of the implied and the impeller (*ākṣepyākṣepakabhāva*) should be understood as a figurative designation (*upacāra*).
This is because of its obstructive nature; that is to say, of things such as walls, which possess form and have the nature of non-transparency.
However, that light whose nature is clarity is not perceived; rather, only its color-form (*rūpamātra*) is seen by one with wide-open eyes.
And the substance (*dravya*) which is the substratum of that [color-form] will be established later.
Furthermore, a quality is not distinct from the substance;
let there be no distinction of the substance from its odor and so forth,
yet let it not be the case that they do not exist in a substance that is without interval.
Because it is separated by its own qualities (*guṇa*).

Furthermore, neither the initial perception (*ālocana*) nor the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which arise immediately [after the senses], await the inference of a substance such that the substance inferred from the cognition of color would constitute an interval between the sense organ and the object, both of which are substances.
Moreover, if the substance were not being perceived, how could color alone—being perceived independently like smell and so forth—cause one to infer its own substratum in the interval?
Is it because the substrata, such as space and so forth, are not perceived?

Therefore, the refutation that will be stated—based merely on the superimposition of the non-perceptibility of the substance of fire whose parts are detached—should be understood as a refutation regarding ultimate reality (*pāramārthika*), whereas the [other] refutation is one of being established otherwise (*anyathāsiddhatva*).
Now, if it is argued that "non-existence" is what is expressed by the word *antara*, [the response follows].
The point is that for us, space does not exist as something other than the absence of corporeal substance (*mūrtadravyābhāva*).

He refutes this: that [absence] is not an independent object of visual perception; rather, non-existence (*abhāva*) must be apprehended between the sense organ and its object, and the apprehension of the object together with that [non-existence] constitutes "apprehension with an interval" (*sāntaragrahaṇa*).

Furthermore, there is no apprehension of anything—whether conjoined or inherent—between the sense organ and its object, such that non-existence could be apprehended in dependence upon it; this is the point.
It might be argued as follows:
let there be no intervening object that is either conjoined (*saṃyukta*) or inherent (*samaveta*); rather, it is the qualified object itself, such as color and so forth, that is being perceived.
This absence depends upon that [qualified object] and will be defined as its qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).
And since, for that reason, the apprehension of an interval would be possible, he says: "In the case of simultaneous perception with that.
For even by means of sense organs such as the skin which function through contact (*prāpyakārin*), water that is extremely cold is perceived as qualified by the absence of heat;
nor is there a lack of functioning through contact in the case of these sense organs here.
Therefore, it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
This was stated with the admission of positive concomitance (*anvaya*); however, the intention is that in the absence of positive concomitance, it is contradictory (*viruddha*).
Nor is there an intervening luminous form by which there might be a perception of something at a distance; thus he says: "And there is no other way.
How this is so has been demonstrated below.
Regarding those who offer the reason that "the perception [of objects] occurs with intervals," he states the refutation against them with the words "by whomsoever...
He states the reason for [the argument's] being established otherwise with the words "the body..."
Indeed, selves delimited by the body have the body as their abode; conceiving the body itself to be the self, they experience objects.
In that regard, whatever is experienced as unconnected with the body is conceived as being "at a distance.
Let there be a connection with the sense organs, [but the object remains distant].
Or rather, let it not be so;
the meaning is that due to its connection with the body, there is no misconception of its having internal spaces in relation to touch and other sensations.
He refutes another reason with the words "as for what [was said] also."
Regarding the phrase "by mere relation":
the inclusion of the word "mere" (mātra) is for the purpose of pervading all four types of relations.
For example, the relation between a sense faculty and its object;
Of the object by means of the parts of the sense-organ; of the sense-organ by means of the parts of the object;
and of the parts of the object by means of the parts of the sense-organ.
And since this [process] does not occur without a state of being broad-tipped, a broad-tippedness is indicated;
just as light, though concentrated in the region of a wick, spreads and pervades the interior of a palace.
For what reason is that?
Regarding the phrase "because of its narrow tip":
although it spreads out by its very nature, it does not produce a cognition that conforms to its own dimensions, but rather one that conforms to the distinctions of the object.
For cognitions are defined in dependence upon the definition of their objects, not in dependence upon the definition of the sense organs.
Thus it has been said: "A cognition conforms to the distinction of its object."
He refutes another reason as well with the words "yat punar" (as for what [has been said] again).

This refers to one who, while situated within the body and its objects, takes into account the lesser or greater number of *saṃyuktasaṃyogas* (conjunctions with that which is conjoined) involving the earth and other elements.

Furthermore, the state of being distant or near for birds moving one above the other is to be understood through the lesser or greater number of *saṃyuktasaṃyogas* among the most abundant parts of the constituent portions of light.
Moreover, that composite whole consisting of such light-particles must be perceptible; otherwise, as has been stated, it would be impossible to infer it through its color alone.
Furthermore, for birds flying one above another, there would be no cognition of distance or proximity, nor would there be the perception, "The bird here has arrived," or "It has not."

Therefore, it should be understood that here too the refutation is simply "established otherwise" (*anyathāsiddhi*), just as in the case of [the argument] regarding the perception of [an object] together with or without [something else].
He refutes another reason as well with the words "yat punar" (as for what [you said] again):
the simultaneous apprehension is unestablished,
while the mere conceit thereof is established otherwise.

For the excellence of speed belonging to light is indeed inconceivable due to its extreme swiftness; thus, when the orb of the sun merely ascends the peak of the mountain of sunrise, ordinary people have the conviction that light has already entered the interiors of their houses.
And since visual light is of such a nature, even though it travels sequentially, it is perceived as being simultaneous in various places.
Nor is it logical that multiple conjunctions with distant and near objects could occur simultaneously from a single action alone.
For that [action], in order to produce its own effect, depends upon proximity to its own substratum;
otherwise, the action of Devadatta situated in Madhurā would connect Devadatta with Pāṭaliputra.
Even the action born from the latent impression called velocity (*vega*) does not suddenly join the arrow with the intermediate space and the target.
Therefore, the conceit of simultaneity is indeed false. [The opponent] objects: "But how so?
For there is indeed a conceit of simultaneity in the perception of the branch and the moon.
And this [cognition] cannot be said to be false when there is no sublation;
thus, this uncontradicted cognition makes known the fact that the eye functions without reaching its object—this is the meaning.
He refutes [this objection] with the words "this... [idam iti].

If the sense faculty were to apprehend an object without reaching it, what obstacle such as a wall or a mat could it remove, such that it would fail to apprehend an object because it is obstructed by it?
But if there is reaching, then— as in the case of tangible objects— this very [obstacle], being devoid of translucency, acts as its impediment, and thus it does not reach the object.
And it does not grasp what has not been reached.
As for the application [of this principle]: the eye and the ear perform their respective functions upon reaching their own objects.
Because if it were a producer, it would not produce when that [object] is not reached; for whatever is a producer,
if it does not produce something when that thing is not reached,
it produces it only upon reaching it— just as a potter, who is the producer of a pot, does not make the pot when he has not reached the clay, but makes it only upon reaching it.
And so it is; therefore, it is thus.
He states another argument: "Conformity with distance and proximity.
That is, it is not perceived at a distance, yet it is perceived when near.
If there were no distinction regarding non-attainment (*aprāpti*), perception would occur even at a distance; or, conversely, if there were no perception, it would not occur even nearby.
But if there is attainment (*prāpti*), then as it travels to a distance, it becomes diminished and thus does not grasp the object that has been reached, because it is non-luminous (*ataijasam*).
Even a luminous object, when overwhelmed, is not perceived— just as the light of a torch is not seen at midday;
however, the orb of the sun, being unoverwhelmed, is indeed perceived.
He objects: "Because of becoming an object.

For such a moment of the sense-organ and the moment of the object, produced or transformed from their own causes, are capable [of the relationship] such that the state of grasper and grasped exists between them even without contact.
Moreover, those two [the sense organs] are not such when they are obstructed or distant;
therefore, what is the point of postulating an attainment that is not actually perceived? He answers this: "And that is not so."
For the momentary destruction and transformation of entities are indeed established.

Therefore, for entities possessing stability, what remains as the basis for the production of cognition is either their own essential capacity (*svarūpayogyatā*), such as magnitude and so forth, or the completeness of auxiliary conditions (*sahakārisākalya*).
In that regard, if one were to maintain that it is merely their essential capacity, [then...]
In that case, whatever [cause] produced the cognition when it was immediate and proximate must produce the cognition in exactly the same way even when it is remote and obstructed;
for its intrinsic capacity (svarūpayogyatā) remains at that time as well.
The completeness of auxiliary conditions (sahakārisākalya), however, is simply "attainment" (prāpti).
Therefore, it is well said that there can be no status as an object without a connection.
The one who is doubtful asks: "Now, regarding the state of acting by reaching [the object]? This is the underlying intention:
It is observed that in the case of a potter and the like, who act by reaching their object, one who is distant or obstructed does not act;
therefore, it is also observed that in the case of those that act without reaching their object, such as the eye and the magnet, a distant or obstructed iron is attracted by the magnet.
Consequently, the proof for this must be stated. The answer is: the very fact of being a sense organ (*indriyatva*) is the proof.
He states that very [argument] as being endowed with five members: "acting by reaching" (*prāpyakārī*).

If, however, someone were to raise the objection that the example is deficient in the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatva*) because the skin and other [senses] act without reaching their objects (*aprāpyakāritva*), he replies: "But then, nothing at all... and so forth.
He asks: "Now" (atha).
For causes perform their own effects solely through their inherent capacity (yogyatā);
whereas actual contact (prāpti), however, depends upon a pervasion (vyāpti) that is itself necessitated by the capacity of their essential natures (svarūpa-yogyatā).
The point is that its pervasiveness is not inherent. The reply is: "That too," etc.
It has already been stated that the completeness of auxiliary factors (*sahakāri-sākalya*) does not exceed [the nature of] attainment (*prāpti*).
Only the intrinsic capacity (*svarūpayogyatā*) needs to be stated;
and since that exists even for [causes] when they are separate, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the production of an effect from those causes situated here and there.
Furthermore, one must admit a distinction in the operation (*vṛttibheda*) of the magnet, just as there is for the eye.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even iron situated at a distance or separated by an obstacle would be attracted.
Nor does it attract iron when accompanied by the absence of separation and distance;
for it is not the case that it now fails to attract because of the absence of that absence of separation and distance.
For it is precisely attainment (*prāpti*) that is understood to be functional toward the production of an effect in various instances;
moreover, the view that mere capacity (*yogyatāmātra*) serves as the limiting condition (*upādhi*) has already been refuted.
Furthermore, how attainment is a property distinct from the substance itself will be explained later.
Therefore, everything is clear.
He concludes with the words "therefore" (tasmāt).
As for the argument that visibility and invisibility [of the self] result from the benefit or injury to the black antelope skin (the eye), it is said in response to that:

The sense-faculty is the substratum of that [consciousness]; thus, by the benefit or injury to its substratum, there is benefit or injury to it, just as the benefit or injury to the fruit of a *kūṣmāṇḍa* creeper occurs through the watering or cutting of the creeper itself.
For this very reason, it is established that even a view (*dṛṣṭi*) which has issued outward is capable of producing an effect only if its root is not severed, but not if its root is severed.

He asks: "Now, regarding 'knowledge' (jñāna)"—the point is that when the definition is being prescribed by restating the definition already designated as "perception" (pratyakṣa), it is already understood in common worldly usage that this [definition] refers specifically to knowledge, because that which causes direct intuition (sākṣātkārin) is called perception. The answer is: "In order to exclude pleasure and so forth."

For that alone is called a valid definition (*lakṣaṇa*) from which the exclusion of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) and under-extension (*avyāpti*) is understood from the words of the definition itself, without depending on the definiendum (*lakṣya*).
The point is that if the establishment of a definition depends upon the definiendum, there would either be mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*) or an infinite regress (*agati*).
If it is argued that pleasure and the like cannot be excluded from the category of consciousness because they arise from causes non-different from those of consciousness— no,
for their arising from non-different causes is unproven.
Indeed, the causal complex (sāmagrī) that produces the cognition of the touch of sandalwood is not the same as that which produces the pleasure [thereof].
For even one afflicted by cold experiences the cognition of a cold touch through contact with sandalwood; likewise, pleasure would also arise for this person [the yogin].

If it is argued that despite a difference in the intermediate causal complex (*sāmagrī*), these cognitions belong to the same class because they are produced from sense-faculty, object, and attention (*manaskāra*)—we say no, because it is logically established that a difference in the effect can occur even when some of its causes remain identical, and thus such a difference is not accidental.
Furthermore, the effort expended in pursuing a distinction between causes is for the sake of that [very point].
Nor is it logical to claim non-difference based on the non-difference of the material cause (*upādāna*),
because you yourself accept that even distinct cognitions can have a single immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) as their material cause.
Moreover, since there is no difference in the material cause (*upādāna*), yet a difference in the effect arises from some difference in the causal factors (*kāraṇa*), what contradiction is there?

For this very reason, our established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that even though the material cause—the pot—is non-different, the smell, color, taste, and touch produced are of distinct classes due to the difference among the causes: namely, the heat (otherwise known as *auṣṇya*) of fire, its conjunction with the pot, and the destructions of the previous color and other qualities.

Therefore, it is most fitting that pleasure and the like—which, by not being directed toward objects, belong to a different genus from cognitions directed toward objects, and which are mutually distinct through their respective characteristics such as being experienced as agreeable—are perceived by mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) independent of a desire to know, due to the intensity of the mental impulse. This is indeed delightful.
It might be argued as follows:
even in the absence of contact between the sense organ and its object, pleasure and pain are observed in dreams solely from cognition itself;

and even where there is contact between the sense organ and its object, cognition is also present there. Therefore, cognition alone is the cause of pleasure and pain, because its causal capacity has already been established.

However, [the opponent claims] that because the contact between the sense-faculty and its object is established otherwise as being useful only for the mere production of cognition, its presence or absence [does not determine the truth of the cognition].

This is incorrect, because the production of pleasure and pain in a dream-like state (svapnāntika) is not established; for that cognition, like the cognition of an object [in a waking state], is false.

For just as in that case, the distortion consists precisely in the recollection of a beloved woman, so too here, the distortion consists in the recollection of the pleasure experienced in a previous birth.

Furthermore, it is the very arising of the cognition of pleasure or pain that constitutes the application of merit (*dharma*) or demerit (*adharma*), and not the actual production of pleasure or pain itself.

Nor does any other form of knowledge—such as mere mental longing—produce a particular kind of pleasure like that which arises from the enjoyment of an object when there is no contact between the sense organ and its object.
When there is contact between the sense faculty and its object, mere cognition alone is its cause;
it has already been stated that this is because no distinction of pleasure arises from the cause of cognition.
If it is argued that the direct perception of the object is the cause for its production, and not merely the cognition of the object?

O Destroyer, even for the Lord, for that venerable one, and for those of great intelligence endowed with the supernatural power of yoga, there exists direct perception of all things; thus, it would follow that even for them, an accumulation of the arising of pleasure and pain would occur, provided there is no application of a counteractive concentration (*pratipakṣadhāraṇā*).
Therefore, the contact between the sense-faculties and their objects must also be accepted as a cause for the arising of pleasure and pain.
And since that [capacity] does not exist for the perfected ones (*siddhas*) even though they possess direct perception of objects, there is no arising of pleasure or pain for them.

Furthermore, if one were to establish the non-causality of preceding factors by taking the final factor as the criterion, it would follow that even threads and the like are not causes with respect to cloth and so forth;
for such cloth arises solely from a particular conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and the threads and other materials are useful only in producing that particular conjunction.
However, it is the same in that the causality of that [pleasure] belongs to the contact (*sannikarṣa*) when it is accompanied by initial perception (*ālocana*), just as it does for the latter.

As the experts in categories (*padārthavid*) have said: "When there is proximity to an object such as a garland that is intended, pleasure arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending upon the perception of a desired object, the contact between sense-faculty and object, and factors such as merit (*dharma*); that which produces favor, attachment, and clarity of the eyes and so forth is pleasure."
Therefore, it has been well said that the term "knowledge" is included for the purpose of excluding pleasure and the like.
In this context, there are two types of perception: the non-conceptual and the conceptual.

Although both are included under the definition "knowledge arising from the contact of a sense-organ with its object that is non-erroneous," they are also mentioned by their own specific names because there are differing views regarding them.

In that context, the non-conceptual [perception] has as its object that which is inexpressible, while the conceptual [perception] has as its object that which consists of a determinate judgment (*vyavasāyātmaka*).
Here, "designation" (*vyapadeśa*) refers to a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) or a secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*), such as name, genus, and so forth.
That [object] is to be designated (*vyapadeśya*), meaning it is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*).

For example: "This is Ḍittha," "This is a cow," "This is white," "This one has a water-pot," "This one is going"—all conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) functions with respect to objects by way of the relationship between qualifier and qualificand.
That which does not have a non-existent designatum is "non-designatable" (*avyapadeśya*); it is that which penetrates the intrinsic nature of the universal (*jāti*) and so forth.
However, it does not, that is to say, apprehend a mutual relationship of qualifier and qualified between genus and the other categories.

In this regard, the author of the Bhāṣya sets forth [the following] in order to refute the view of those who maintain that there is nothing devoid of a name and free from conceptual construction: "Names and words indeed correspond to their referents;
all objects, in every way, at all times, and in all places, are accompanied by names.
There is no object whatsoever that is ever, anywhere, or in any manner, dissociated from a name."
By this, he asserts the identity of objects with their names.
He states the reason for this: "because the cognition of the object occurs through them.

For when objects are being cognized, they are understood as being endowed with their names through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), such that one says, "the object is 'cow'," or "the object is 'horse'."
Furthermore, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is not tenable on the basis of being a means (*upāya*).
For the eye and other [faculties], while coreferential [with their objects], do not experience form and so forth;
nor does a means, when it is itself being known, experience coreferentiality with that which is to be attained (*upeya*).

For it is not the case that one thinks, "This is smoke; therefore, there is fire"; rather, one thinks, "This is smoke; because it is smoke, fire is inferred. Furthermore, in the case of an object of inference and the like which is not based on a word, there would be no cognition through the association with a word, yet such cognition does exist. Therefore, [the word] is that from which there arises the cognition of an object as being in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with those names.

Therefore, objects have names as their very essence. Furthermore, in the case of [objects such as] cows and [musical notes such as] *ṣaḍja*, because the cognition of the object is withdrawn when the word is withdrawn, and because the cognition of the object is enhanced when the word is enhanced—and since the enhancement of a cognition is dependent upon the enhancement of that which is to be cognized—the enhancement of the object follows from the enhancement of its name. Thus, the object [is enhanced].
It brings about identity with that.
This very thing is "equal cognition" (*samaḥ pratyayaḥ*), which means "cognition that is equal to or exceeding [the object]" (*samadhikaḥ pratyayaḥ*).
There is a cognition of the referent by virtue of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the name.
However, identity with the name is not established by this much alone.

For there exists a cognition of "silver" through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a substance present before one, yet by this much alone, the mother-of-pearl does not become identical in nature to silver; therefore, he says: "And from the cognition of the object, there is practical activity. The meaning is that, being a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) due to its non-discrepancy (*avisamvāda*), it establishes the identity of objects with their names.

Having thus established in general the identity of objects with their names, he applies this to the present case: "In that regard, this cognition of an object arising from the contact of the sense organ with its object occurs in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with objects such as 'form' or 'taste. Let it be so; but what follows from this? To this he replies: "And the words 'form,' 'taste,' and so on, are the names of the objects."
To the question, "What follows from this?", he says: "By that [name], the cognition is designated.
He states the aforementioned designation along with its explanation: "one knows it as 'form' (rūpa), one knows it as 'taste' (rasa).

Thus, since objects consist of their designations, even the bare perception (*ālocana*) directed toward them has the designation as its object; consequently, being designated by a name, it would follow that such a cognition is verbal (*śābda*), which is undesirable.
Verbal cognition is not so called because it has sound as its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), but rather because it is produced from sound;
and in this context, sound is the producer by virtue of being the object, due to its identity with the referent.
And thus, the intended meaning is that there exists no non-conceptual [cognition] devoid of words.
Accordingly, they have said:
"There is no cognition in the world that is without the accompaniment of words."
All knowledge is understood as if it were permeated by sound.
Even the knowledge of infants, the mute, and others arises precisely through the infusion of words, by virtue of the beginningless mental impression (*bhāvanā*) of words; as it has been said:
"The initial arrangement of the organs and the upward movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*)."
And there is no striking of locations without the cultivation of sound.
Thus, its refutation has been indicated by the term "avyapadeśya" (non-verbalizable), which— situated within the definition— has the sense of excluding reflective cognition (*ālocana-jñāna*).
Therefore, the Commentator, though it was appropriate to state this during the section on examination (*parīkṣā-parvan*), did not wait for that occasion out of a fondness for elegant expression.
He states this precisely at the occasion for defining the characteristics [of perception].
Therefore, he says: "It is that which is non-verbalizable" (*avyapadeśyam*).

Even though the meaning has already been indicated by that [definition], he employs the term "non-verbalizable" (*avyapadeśya*) to address the following: namely, that when the relationship between word and object is not applied, there is a cognition of the object.
That is not designated by means of a word expressing a name.
This is the underlying intention:

when the nature of form and so forth is expressed through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), is it being said that they consist of the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*), or rather that they consist of the distinct words such as "cow" and so on which are currently being uttered?
It cannot be the first [alternative].

This is the argument: For ordinary people, there is no perception of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between color-form (*rūpa*) and the like and the *Śabdabrahman*, which transcends the entire range of vision accessible to persons such as ourselves.

Furthermore, if identity were established through coreferentiality with a word that is actually being heard, then in the cognitions of color-form and so forth belonging to infants, the mute, and others—who have no connection with the word—there would not be even a trace of the scent of a word being heard.
But let alone their grammatical coreferentiality [with the object];
nor is it tenable to claim that even for those [sensory cognitions], there is coreferentiality with the object through the persistence of verbal impressions (*śabdabhāvanā*) from a previous life.
For indeed, it is impossible for a word, whose nature consists of form and so forth, to possess either clarity or lack of clarity regarding form and so forth.

For it would follow that there is a distinction [between the two cognitions] due to their simultaneous association with contradictory properties in the form of clarity (*vaiśadya*) and lack of clarity (*avaiśadya*). If, however, there were clarity, then even one who is unlearned (*avyutpanna*) would engage in linguistic usage through words just like one who is learned (*vyutpanna*),
and would not depend upon the apprehension of the relationship [between word and meaning].
Furthermore, there is no denotative capacity of words other than identity (tādātmya) such that it would require the apprehension of a relation;
nor, even in the case of identity, can there be a signifier-signified relationship between things whose differences are merely conceptualized.
If that were so, grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) would not be possible.
For it is impossible for there to be both the conceptualization of difference and the manifestation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) simultaneously.
Therefore, for those who are untrained, there exists a non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) of forms and so forth that is devoid of words.
This is not only the case for the untrained;...
He states that [the relation] exists even for those who are proficient: "And even when the relationship between word and object has been grasped.

Having already stated half of this very point in order to refute coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), he describes the nature of the grasping of the relationship: "This phoneme *ga*, etc., is the name of this object whose form consists of possessing a dewlap and so forth.
The particle *iti* primarily serves to refer back to the cognition.

And thus, the meaning is that "this" refers to the individual entity (piṇḍabheda) named Ḍittha, which is connected with various places, times, and states, and is present in a proximate place and time; it is not, however, the cognition that "this individual entity is the word Ḍittha.
For while words generally have their primary reference directed toward objects, that [general rule] is set aside in certain cases by words such as "again" (punaḥ) and so forth.

Even in cases where a relationship is presented through non-difference, as in "This is Ḍittha," there too the word refers to the state of being denotable and not to its own form; it is like [the statement] "The Vāhīka is a cow," which refers to the connection with a quality that is being indicated.
And by that alone, the Vāhīka does not actually become a cow.

Therefore, because the relationship is grasped only between two distinct things—the word and the object—and because linguistic usage is rooted in that [relationship], even a cognition preceded by a word does not possess the word as its own co-referentiality. As for the fact that a word occurs prior to a cognition even when the word is not the means [of that cognition]: for one who has grasped the convention, when the mere object is first perceived through sensory contact with the object by means of a non-conceptualizing (ālocana) perception devoid of association with a word, that particularity of the object becomes an object of the word due to its connection with the particularity of the word.
The latent predisposition (*saṃskāra*) is awakened;
once awakened, it produces the recollection of words.
Consequently, for one who is proficient [in language], subsequent cognitions—even those that do not rely on words—arise preceded by words, following upon non-conceptual [perception].
As they have said:
"That perception and recollection which occurs there is not itself caused by something else;
for it is only when the aggregate (piṇḍa) itself has been seen that it is capable of causing the recollection of the name."

Therefore, even for one who is proficient [in language], the cognition of the object must first occur independently of the name, so that the name may subsequently be remembered. This has been stated: "Even when the relationship between word and object is grasped—namely, that 'this word is the name of this object'—when that object is perceived prior to the recollection of its name, it is apprehended without conceptual construction (avikalpena); at that time, it does not differ from the knowledge of the object obtained previously during the stage of non-proficiency."
Since it is not distinguished [from the object], the cognition of that object is of exactly that same nature.

Now, when cognition—which must be designated by its own intrinsic form (*svarūpa*) for the sake of conventional usage characterized by the communication of others and so forth—is instead designated by the designation of the object, we understand from this that it possesses the form of the object's designation;
how, then, does it come to possess the form of the object?
If there were no difference between the object and its designation, then identity would again follow; therefore, he says: "But of that...
The meaning is that cognition, which indeed possesses the very form of the object, is designated by the designation of the object, because otherwise it would be impossible [to designate it].
It is being perceived by another.
He concludes: "Therefore... [etc.]

Thus, at the time of cognizing the object, that conventional term does not function by way of being perceived; however, at the time of linguistic usage—that is, at the time of communicating to another—it functions as a cause.
Therefore, the application of names to various individuals by cowherds, shepherds, and others is the cause for the excellence of linguistic practice regarding them.
It is also indicated that [the word "avyapadeśya"] is not a cause for the excellence of the object.

Therefore, with the intention that the term "avyapadeśya" (inexpressible) serves to exclude non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣa*), he concludes—stating that this very non-conceptual [perception] is devoid of the accompaniment of words—with the words "Therefore...
The author of the *Vārttika* explains this *bhāṣya* according to its intended meaning (*tātparya*) as follows: "And that [is] from the sense-organ and the object..."
Cognition conforms to the distinctions of its objects; thus, it does not attain the nature of sound.
For visual cognition of form is restricted to form alone and does not operate upon sound;
likewise, auditory cognition is restricted to sound alone and does not operate upon form and the like.
If, moreover, this [object] such as form were of the nature of sound, then the auditory cognition, which grasps sound, would also operate with respect to form and so forth;
or, failing to operate, it would subvert the nature of sound in form and the other [objects].
Moreover, if form and the other [sensory objects] were of the nature of sound as they are heard,
then they too would be graspable by hearing; consequently, even a blind person would perceive form,
for he possesses both the sense of hearing and the cognition of sound.
In that case, even a deaf person would perceive sound;
for he possesses both the eye and the cognition of form.
Furthermore, there is the fallacy of arriving at the opposite of what was intended, because the object "absence of sound" would itself be a sound.
Alternatively, if it were non-verbal, that very object would follow as being distinct from the word;
likewise, the word "non-existence" would have "non-existence" as its object,
and thus it would not be a non-existence.
Because sound exists,
consciousness that conforms to the object would not occur;
yet it does exist.
Therefore, objects do not have the nature of words;
by the phrase "at the time of their arising," he first excludes the [view] that they are permeated by words.
He states the explanation of the "partialist" (ekadeśin): "But others [say]...

For, by means of the mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the contact between sense faculty and object, that cognition of the sense faculty which arises would also be subject to the definition of perception; thus, it would follow as a consequence that such cognition is perception. To exclude this, the term "non-verbalized" (*avyapadeśya*) is used.
"Verbalization" (*apadeśa*) refers to the statement of a reason (*hetu*).

That very [object] is distinguished from its appearances; this is the designation (*vyapadeśa*). Its effect is the cognition of the inferable (*anumeya*) by way of making the reason known; this is what is to be designated.
By stating "not to be designated" (*avyapadeśya*), that which does not arise from a logical mark (*aliṅga*)—namely, inference—is excluded; such is the meaning.
He refutes the view of that partial proponent (ekadeśin) with the words, "And that is not so. Now, one might object:

even the cognition of the movement of the sense organ is produced from a mark (liṅga) through the contact of the sense organ with its object; to this he replies: "For [the cognition] of the inferable [object]... This does not arise from the contact of the sense organ with its object, but rather from the cognition of that [movement].
For this very reason, even when the mark (liṅga), such as smoke, is past, the cognition of the object to be inferred arises from the mere recollection of it.
The point is that when the primary sense of the term "contact" (sannikarṣa) is possible, it is not appropriate to resort to a figurative definition (jñānalakṣaṇā).
He concludes with the word "ataḥ" (therefore).

And failing to understand this Vārttika text, they supply the words "with regard to the objects of the senses" (*indriyaviṣayeṣu*) into the Sūtra for the purpose of excluding the cognition of the movement of the sense organs.

Stating the intended meaning of the term *avyabhicārin* (non-erroneous), which follows in sequence, he also states the intended meaning of the Bhāṣya: "In summer, [the perception of] mirages," and so forth.

Although cognitions that are erroneous have already been excluded by the general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), and the specific definition (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*) depends upon that, otherwise the term *avyabhicārin* would have to be included even in the words for inference (*anumāna*) and the like.
Nevertheless, since [the point] is already established, this undertaking is for the purpose of restriction.
For there are two ways in which means of valid cognition function:
some establish valid knowledge by their mere existence, such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
For it is not the grasping of the eyes and so forth that is required, but rather their very existence;
whereas inference and the other means of knowledge are instruments of valid cognition through their own cognitions.

Indeed, neither a logical mark (*liṅga*), nor a word (*śabda*), nor similarity accompanied by authoritative testimony (*āgama*) produces valid cognition (*pramā*) with respect to its respective object unless it has been apprehended;
for in the case of inference, the production of valid cognition depends on the prior apprehension of the non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) of the object, and not otherwise.
From that, valid cognition is established.
Although, in the case of words and the like, there is no dependence on grasping the non-deviation from the object for the production of valid cognition,
nevertheless, it is possible [to have such dependence] even for that which has its meaning not concealed and whose meaning is immediately perceived when situated within a mantra,
as in: *sṛṇyeva jarbharī turpharītū*.
In this way, because such mantras were composed by authoritative persons, one may grasp their general non-deviation from reality;
for the default tendency of words is to be directed toward meaning.
For this very reason, people determine the meaning from them with the aid of etymology, philology, and grammar.

In this way, just as with the phrase "the mudgaparṇī is like the mudga-stalk," from the mere hearing of the authoritative statement (āptavākya), it is possible to ascertain that the cognition of similarity to the mudga-stalk— which, though its fruit has not yet been produced— is non-deviant from its object; however,
for the means of knowledge that is perception (pratyakṣa), the apprehension of an entirely transcendent nature is itself difficult to obtain prior to the arising of the valid cognition.
But prior to that, its non-deviation from the object [must be established];

and although, even on the view that cognition itself is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), that cognition of it is easily accessible by the mind (*manas*), nevertheless, that alone is not the means of valid knowledge.

Rather, because it is assisted by the unique contact between the sense faculty and its object, that [cognition] which has such assistance is indeed indirect (*parokṣa*). Therefore, the non-erroneousness of perception as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is known only through its non-deviation from its result, not by way of its own intrinsic nature (*svarūpataḥ*). Thus, the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" (*avyabhicāri*) is intended to demonstrate the unique characteristic of perception, which distinguishes it from other means of valid cognition.
Alternatively, the non-deviation of perception itself is the cause for the non-deviation of inference and other means of knowledge.

For it is impossible that an inference—whose property-of-the-subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) has been grasped by a non-deviating perception and whose invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) has been grasped by perception aided by reasoning (*tarka*)—should deviate.
As for an inference whose object is sublated or which is countered by an opposing argument (*satpratipakṣita*), [it is not non-deviating].
Even if that [inference] was not initially undermined by a defect in the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*),
it is nevertheless perceived as such after its refutation;
and thus, the perception that grasps the pervasion is itself subject to deviation (*vyabhicārin*) in that case as well.
Thus, scripture (*āgama*) as well—whether directly or through a traditional lineage—is preceded by perception; therefore, it errs precisely because that [perception] errs.
By the very fact of the error of scripture, the error of analogy (*upamāna*) is also explained.

Consequently, since the non-erroneousness of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) exists only when perception is non-erroneous, he employed the qualifier "non-erroneous" (*avyabhicārin*) specifically for perception.
Not so for the other means of valid cognition;
for it is impossible that their basis— direct perception— is non-erroneous while they themselves are erroneous.
This, then, is the distinction of perception from other means of valid cognition.
As the author of the Mīmāṃsā-vārttika said:
"By its non-deviation [from reality] and by the power of its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)."
Inference is not examined here because its non-deviation is already well-established.
Thus it is said.
Therefore, the commentary stating "in summer, [it is] mirages" is well-said;
and to refute that, this is stated: "non-deviant."
He asks: "What is this? The answer is: "That which [occurs] in this.
And this has been established in the second sūtra.
He refutes it again, saying: "And that is not so.
He asks: "Why? The answer is: "Because of the object (artha)."
He clarifies that very point with the words "that which is that" (yattat).
And here, it is not the non-conceptual [cognition] that is erroneous, but rather the conceptual; thus he says: "those rays," and so forth.

Having perceived the shimmering rays with the sense faculty and having grasped them through non-conceptual [perception] as they move up and down, one subsequently errs therein due to the defect of impairment; thus, his conceptual cognition arises as an illusion.
Therefore, it is the cognition that is deceptive, not the object.
As the authors of the Nirukta have said: "It is not the fault of the post that a blind man does not see it;
rather, that is the fault of the person."
By the very term "non-deviant" (avyabhicārin), even doubtful cognition is excluded.
Indeed, a doubtful cognition, which has as its object a thing that is being conceptualized in various ways, does not cause one to attain that thing in its actual form.
And how can that which does not cause attainment be said to have "correspondence" (saṃvāda) with what was indicated?
And how can that which is non-concordant (*asaṃvādaka*) be non-deviant (*avyabhicārin*)?

Therefore, since doubt-cognition (*saṃśayajñāna*) has already been excluded by the term "non-deviant" alone, the inclusion of the term "determinate in nature" (*vyavasāyātmaka*)—employed for the purpose of indicating determinate perception (*savikalpakapratyakṣa*)—serves as a secondary exclusion (*anvācīna*) of the perceptual status of doubt-cognition.
It is just as when one says: "Go to the forest to fetch firewood."
The phrase "you will bring vegetables" implies the bringing of vegetables as a secondary consequence; yet that alone is not what the sender intends to enjoin. It is the same here as well:
the word *vyavasāyātmaka* (of the nature of determination) is the direct denoter of conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*).
For indeed, "ascertainment" (*vyavasāya*), "certainty" (*viniścaya*), and "conceptualization" (*vikalpa*) are synonymous.
That which has this very [conceptualization] as its nature is determinate perception (*savikalpaka-pratyakṣa*).
