Since this is extremely clear and is thus understood by the students themselves, it has not been explained by either the author of the *Bhāṣya* or the author of the *Vārttika*, yet we shall explain it.
This has been explained in such a manner, according to the rule and according to the facts, by those who are intent on following the path led by the teacher Trilocana.
It might be argued as follows:
perception cannot be of the nature of a determinate judgment (*vyavasāya*),
for it has a manifestation that is capable of being associated with verbal expression.
Furthermore, it is not possible to associate with verbal expression a cognition that has arisen from the sense faculty and its object and which manifests the appearance of that object;
for words do not exist within the object, nor do they constitute the very nature of the object.
Thus it has been stated that even for one who is unskilled [in language], linguistic usage would occur as if they were skilled;
nor is verbal expression a property of consciousness that does not touch upon the object,
because it is applied to objects.
Therefore, the cognition arising from that object must manifest the object itself and not the verbal expression.
For a perception arising from a visible form does not manifest it as accompanied by taste.

Consequently, conceptual cognition—which manifests an object associated with verbal expression while being independent of such association—is produced by the latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) of conceptualization and grasps an indeterminate object.

Discarding their own mental activity characterized by conceptual construction (utprekṣā), perceivers proceed while prioritizing the operation of direct experience— since [the cognition] originates from experience— and they regard it as being that very experience.
Thus, this is established:
That which arises through the power of an object does not follow the conceptualization of words,
just as non-conceptual [perception].

The conceptual constructions under dispute have their birth obtained through the power of the object (*arthasāmarthya*); this is a *prasaṅgasādhana* consisting in the perception of what is pervaded by the contradictory [of the probandum].
For that which is to be negated—namely, being followed by verbal conceptualization—is contradicted by not being followed by it;
therefore, being born from the power of the object is pervaded by that [non-association with verbal conceptualization].
The perception of that [object], by giving rise to its non-concomitance [with conceptualization], excludes its concomitance with it.
Now, if the concomitance of these cognitions with verbal expression is directly perceived, it cannot be denied;
alas, sir!
"Therefore, it is not produced by the capacity of the object"—this is the contrapositive of the reductio (*prasaṅga-viparyaya*).
For instance, whatever is accompanied by the conceptualization of verbal expression is not produced by the capacity of the object, such as the conceptual cognition of Īśvara, Pradhāna, and so forth.
And these conceptualizations under dispute are likewise [accompanied by verbal expression]; thus, there is the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpaka-viruddhopalabdhi*).

The state of being produced by the capacity of the object (*arthasāmarthya*), which is to be negated, is pervaded by the non-concomitance with the conceptualization of its verbal expression; and its opposite is the state of being concomitant with that [verbal expression].
Nor is there any doubt regarding the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*):
for that which is produced by the capacity of the object would necessarily conform to the form of the object, not to the form of the word.
For it has already been stated that words do not exist within the object, nor are they identical with its nature.
If consciousness were to imitate forms that are unrelated [to the object], then by imitating all forms, there would follow the absurdity of everyone being omniscient.

If it is argued that, through the power of convention (*saṅketa*), words are connected to objects; and when an object is perceived, because of the recollection of those [words], there is a cognition associated with them?
In that case, one should remind them of that very thing with which they have made their convention;
and it is precisely that pervasive universal with which they have made their convention,
yet that has not been perceived.
However, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the domain of perception;
for that alone is the cause of consciousness as ultimate reality (*paramārthasat*),
and not the universal (*sāmānya*).
For that [universal] is devoid of all causal capacity because it is unreal.
Therefore, there is no connection of words with that which is perceived,
and that with which there is a connection is not perceived.
Moreover, if that which is perceived were expressible by words, then it would be cognized even from a sentence such as "fire is hot," just as it is from the act of seeing.
And thus, if it were cognized through words as well, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the removal of cold.
Furthermore, the inferential mark (*liṅga*) and words have the universal (*sāmānya*) as their object, whereas the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) is like a real universal.

If it is argued that such is the cause of that perception—namely, because the indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) produced by the first impact of the sense organ perceives the object as possessing a genus (*jāti*), there arises a recollection of a word whose relationship [to the object] has been previously apprehended;

and thus, a conceptual cognition (*vikalpa-pratyaya*) produced by the contact of the sense organ with its object arises, taking the form "this is a cow," which apprehends a substance qualified by the genus denoted by that word? As they say:
"By means of indeterminate cognition, even though the object is of a dual nature..."
The apprehension [of the object]— as stated in the *Ślokavārttika*, Pratyakṣa 118—
and likewise, the cognition by which the object is subsequently determined through its properties such as genus and so forth, that too is accepted as perception (*pratyakṣa*).
[As stated] in the *Ślokavārttika*, *Pratyakṣa* 120:
"That is not so, because the universal (*jāti*) and so forth are not apprehended by indeterminate perception (*avikalpaka*) through a distinction from the individual (*piṇḍa*).

For neither the universal and the possessor of the universal, nor action and the agent of action, nor quality and the possessor of the quality, nor their inherence (*samavāya*), appear as distinct [from one another]."
Furthermore, it is impossible for two things that do not appear in isolation to be joined together by one who does not perceive them as distinct, like milk and water.

Therefore, we consider it logical that a single, undivided particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) is conceptualized in such a way through the distinctions of genus (*jāti*) and so forth, which are superimposed by the beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Moreover, even if two ultimately real entities were perceived, how could there be a relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) between them?
For two fingers, being objects of a single cognition, do not enter into a relationship of qualifier and qualified with one another.
Indeed, the qualifier is that which assists, and the qualified is that which is assisted;
otherwise, their relationship as such would not exist.
Furthermore, the relationship of signifier and signified, or the relationship of cause and effect, is not possible between two things mounted upon a single cognition,
because both of them exist simultaneously and thus lack the necessary restriction of temporal sequence.

Moreover, if universals and other limiting adjuncts were inherent in a real entity, then for a single entity there would have to be its existence, its substantiality, and its earthiness [all at once].

Since "treeness," "śiṃśapā-ness," and so forth are all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), it follows that if one perceives an object as qualified by a single adjunct from a distance, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of perceiving it as qualified by all adjuncts.
For the relationship between the locus and the located (*ādhārādheyabhāva*) is essentially rooted in assistance (*upakāra*).
Indeed, a bowl is the locus of a jujube fruit—which possesses the property of falling—by placing that fruit, which is naturally prone to fall, in its proximity so that it no longer falls.
Similarly here as well, the substance must benefit its adjuncts, such as the universal and so forth;
yet it does not benefit them by means of other powers.
For if one were to postulate further powers even when there is a benefit from those [other] powers, it would result in an infinite regress.

Therefore, it must be stated that the very nature (svabhāva) of a substance is that which, having its birth dependent upon its own causes, is such that it assists many limiting adjuncts (upādhi). And thus, when that substance—which is capable of assisting existence—is apprehended, its very same nature is also capable of assisting substantiality (dravyatva) and so forth; consequently, [the cognition] delimited by that nature, being a conceptual construction of existence, penetrates the ultimately real substance.

Since all [properties] such as substantiality (*dravyatva*), earth-ness (*pārthivatva*), tree-ness (*vṛkṣatva*), and śiṃśapā-ness (*śiṃśapātva*) have been made objects [of the cognition], other conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) are rendered purposeless.
As it has been said:
"Even for one who holds that an object, though distinct, is grasped by a cognition through various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)."
When there is the apprehension of an entity whose nature is differentiated by the assistance provided by various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*),
what aspect of that assisted object— which exists in its entirety— could remain undetermined?
When one thing that provides assistance is to be grasped, no other assistances [are required] beyond that;
since those [other things] are unseen when that [one] is seen, if that one is grasped, there is the grasping of the whole.
Thus [it is said].
For us, however, conceptual constructions—which have the latencies of beginningless conceptualization as their material cause—grasp both that which they apprehend and that which they determine;
yet since both of these consist in the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) and are therefore non-entities, even when they grasp something, they do not grasp an entity that is ultimately real.

However, because they operate upon that [object] through a traditional succession based on a connection with the actual entity (*vastu*), and because they cause one to attain it, they do not deceive the world.

Therefore, since conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) do not adhere to the existence of the entity itself, there is no redundancy. Furthermore, when an object has been perceived by the sense faculty, the sense faculty and the object—whose operation is immediately preceded by the recollection of words—are not capable of producing even a conceptual cognition.
As it has been said:
"Even when an object is being engaged, if the sensory cognition were to depend upon the application of a word through memory, that object would become obscured."
Nor does the very same sense organ that produced the initial perception produce the conceptual cognition by acting as a cooperative cause for memory;
nor is memory an intervening factor, according to the principle that "one's own limb is not an intervention."
Since that which was previously not a producer of cognition remains [non-producer] even later due to the lack of any difference in its functional capacity,
it is certainly not the case that the past becomes an object of the sense faculty.
Nor can this [present object] be brought within range by even a thousand means;
nor is it possible for memory, whose domain is the past, to take as its object a present thing never experienced before.
And if that were its domain, it would follow that even the blind would have direct perception of forms, as it has been said:
Therefore, even when the sense organ has perished, there would be visual cognition.
Thus, in this way, the conceptual constructions of name, genus, quality, and action have been refuted by means of direct perception.
The conceptual construction of substance, such as "the man with a staff" (daṇḍī), is also [refuted].
Having grasped the qualifier, the qualified, their relation, and the conventional state of affairs,
and having synthesized these, one cognizes it in that way and not otherwise.
Furthermore, sensory cognition cannot sustain such a complex array of operations, for it arises by the power of a proximate object and is thus non-discursive (*avicāraka*).

Moreover, this [discursive synthesis] is simply impossible for those possessing universals, qualities, and actions, because—since neither the distinction between forms nor their relation appears—it is illogical to effect a synthesis; as it has been said, "this is like milk and water for one who does not perceive them as distinct."
Therefore, perception is not that conceptual construction.
To this it is replied:

as for what was stated— that there is a contradiction between being produced by the capacity of an object and having a manifestation capable of association with verbal expression— we say in response to that:
There would be a contradiction if the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) alone were the object;
however, this is not the case.
For [the author] will establish that the object possesses a universal (*jāti*) and so forth, is ultimately real, stable, and capable of being associated with verbal expression.

Therefore, there is no contradiction in [the fact that] the cognition produced by that [perception] is both born from the capacity of the object and possesses an appearance capable of being associated with verbal expression.
Thus, the *reductio ad absurdum* (prasaṅgasādhana) has a doubtful negative concomitance (*sandigdhavyatirekitā*).
Furthermore, it is not correct to claim that conceptual constructions—which imagine universals and the like as distinct from substances and so forth—are not born from the capacity of the object.
For their difference from the substance will also be established by you;
and how there is coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) among those words denoting them despite their difference has already been demonstrated above.

Nor is it logical to claim that conceptual constructions (*vikalpāḥ*) are not born of reality because one imagines non-difference—such as "this is Ḍittha"—through a word that is [in fact] different [from the object].

This has already been stated during the explanation of the term *avyapadeśya* (non-verbal): it is not that two objects are connected within a single sensory cognition by way of the non-difference of their words; rather, an object first perceived through indeterminate observation (*ālocana*), possessing both general and particular characteristics, causes one to remember one's own state at the time when the linguistic convention was grasped, and thereby necessarily causes one to remember the word existing at that time as well.
However, the recollection of words has no utility whatsoever regarding the production of sense-born conceptualization (*vikalpa*);
otherwise, infants, the mute, and others would not possess sense-born conceptualization due to the absence of the recollection of words.
Rather, it is the recollection of the state [of the object] existing at the time of the convention that is useful.
Because a single object, which possesses distinct states at different times—both past and present—is apprehended by a conceptualization born of the senses;
whereas a word, arriving merely by chance, does not insert itself into that sensory conceptualization.
As it has been said:
That very same physical body which was previously remembered by means of the word "Devadatta" and so forth residing in the heart, is now seen with the eye as well.
For by this [statement], he demonstrates that the oneness existing between the prior and posterior states of the lump is within the range of sensory perception and conceptual construction,
but not even the application of a word.
Likewise,
For even when a name is being remembered, it does not subvert the perceptuality of the named object. Why is that?
That state on the bank is not capable of concealing its true form.

The meaning is that [the conceptual cognition] does not obstruct the operation of the object and the sense faculty. Nor is it correct to say that the contact between the sense faculty and the object is not the cause of conceptual construction because it depends upon the recollection of a prior state; for:
"Nothing arises from a single cause; everything arises from a causal complex" (Pra.vā.
3.53)—thus you yourselves have said.
Otherwise, even a non-conceptual [cognition] would not be produced by the sense faculty and the object when they depend upon the attention of the world.
As for the fact that it did not produce [the effect] at first, that is due to the absence of the auxiliary conditions for recollection;

for it is not the case that because a seed remaining in a granary does not produce a sprout, it therefore ceases to be a producer when its collection of auxiliary conditions, such as soil and so forth, is present.
Furthermore, we shall demonstrate in the *Kṣaṇabhaṅgabhaṅga* that the conjunction of contradictory properties characterized by being a producer and a non-producer is not a cause of difference.
This might be so:
the past state is not within the range of the sense faculties, because they are restricted to present objects;

nor is a present object the range of memory, because memory—arising from the awakening of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by a prior experience—is restricted to the object of that previous experience.
Therefore, because their objects are distinct, memory does not function as a cooperative cause for the sense faculty.
For even a thousand factors such as the eye or a lamp, which have color-form (*rūpa*) as their object, cannot become cooperative causes for the ear, which has sound (*śabda*) as its object.

In that case, according to you, when a visual cognition of color-form arises immediately after a cognition of odor, would that cognition of odor not be the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*)?
For even in that case, the eye, which has visible form as its object, cannot be a cooperative cause for a cognition whose object is odor,
precisely because their objects are distinct.
If it were argued that the causal relationship, being based on positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), does not require the objects to be identical;
That is the same for us as well.
[Objection: But since its state of being qualified by a past condition is not in contact with the sense organ, how can it be perceptual?
[Response: Is it then the case that whatever is connected to a sense organ is perceptual?
If that were so, then space, atoms, and so forth would also be conjoined with it, and they too would consequently result in being perceived.
Therefore, only that which is the object of sensory cognition is perceptible;
it is not merely that which is conjoined with the sense organ.
But how can a sense faculty that is not in contact [with its object] produce cognition therein?
And how is that cognition direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)?
If it is indeed direct perception, [then...]
How does the definition "produced by the contact of a sense faculty with its object" encompass perception, given that this very perception is not covered by the definition?
Let it be that the object's existence at a prior time is not the range of the sense faculty.

Nevertheless, that which is produced by sense-object contact assisted by memory and assisted by latent impressions (saṃskāra) does not qualify as "produced by sense-object contact" [in the strict sense].
Thus, this definition is not under-extended.
But how can a cognition that apprehends both prior and posterior states be one,
given the difference in its objects and the association with contradictory properties characterized by mediacy (*pārokṣya*) and immediacy (*apārokṣya*)? For instance, "that" (*tad*) denotes mediacy.
And there is the direct realization that "this is it. Furthermore, there can be no unity even when associated with contradictory properties,
for that would entail the absurd consequence that the three worlds are one.
Furthermore, there is a distinction of objects because of the contradiction between the connection of a single thing with a prior place and time and its connection with a subsequent place and time.
For instance, when a single ruby is being perceived, its absence is excluded;
if it were not excluded, then its presence could not be determined.
Because that [non-existence] consists in the exclusion of its own nature (*svābhāvavyavaccheda*),
and because emeralds and other such things are invariably concomitant with the absence of that [nature], they too are all excluded.
If, however, they were not excluded, [the definition would fail].

That very [entity] would consist of topaz and so forth; thus, it would result in the impossible situation where the absence of ruby—which is invariably concomitant with that [topaz, etc.]—would itself be a ruby.
Likewise, when its connection with a previous place and time is apprehended, through the process of excluding its absence therein, its connection with another place and time is excluded;
[this exclusion] is non-deviant from the absence of connection with the previous place and time.
And thus, it does not have as its intrinsic nature a connection with that place or time;
nevertheless, if it were to have an intrinsic nature other than that connection with that place and time, then in that case, it would simply be something else.
Otherwise, it would result in an untenable contradiction.
Therefore, since the connection with a subsequent place and time is distinct from the connection with a prior place and time, the difference in objects is established.
To this it is replied:
if, due to the distinction between the properties of being mediated and unmediated, the cognition that reflects upon prior and subsequent states were to differ, then— alas!— it would follow that...
Even that [notion] "that" would be differentiated;
for it too is both remote and non-remote, conceptual and non-conceptual.
With respect to the object, it is remote and conceptual; but with respect to itself, it is non-conceptual and non-remote.

If it is argued that there is a contradiction because the objects [of cognition] are different—[we reply: no; for even here, that single cognition [perceives] that very same single entity as being either remote or immediate in relation to its prior space and time, and [as being the same] in relation to another space and time.
What contradiction is there?
As for the claim that a difference in objects is stated due to the difference in the relations of space and time, [that too is untenable].
That too is incorrect; for it is logical that when the nature of a ruby is apprehended, its absence is excluded,
because things consist in the exclusion of their own non-existence, and if that were not excluded, it would follow that their very nature is not apprehended.
But why are emeralds and the like excluded?
If you say it is because of their invariable concomitance with the absence of rubies,
then from where does this knowledge of that invariable concomitance with absence arise?
If it is argued that this is because the two are never perceived as identical—then in that case, where identity is indeed perceived, there can be no invariable concomitance with its absence;
and thus, a ruby (*padmarāga*) experienced as identical by a sensory conceptualization (*vikalpa*) associated with prior and subsequent places and times cannot be something different.

Therefore, while the prior and subsequent places and times, or their connection, may well differ from one another due to their invariable concomitance with mutual absence, [the object itself remains the same].
Because those two never appear as identical with it;
nor does the ruby possess a nature inherent in them,
since it is distinct from both of them.
Furthermore, the differentiation of one thing does not induce differentiation in another, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Nor is it correct to argue that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—which consists in the reflective awareness of preceding and succeeding states—is not born of the senses even in the absence of sense-object contact; [for it is clearly so].

Likewise, even a non-conceptual [cognition] is observed in one afflicted by desire who contemplates a beloved woman, occurring even without sensory contact with that object; therefore, [if your definition were correct], cognitions whose nature is the experience of blue and so forth would also result in being non-conceptual and not born of the senses.
However, if you were to state some distinction between the experience of blue and so forth and the experience of the beloved woman, [the argument would hold].

In that case, there is indeed a distinction for us between the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) arising from non-sensory sources—the operations of imagination—and the visual operations arising from the senses.

Furthermore, it is not logical to maintain that the visual operation present within a conceptual construction, when experienced, must necessarily be a qualification (*upādhi*) of a non-conceptual [perception], provided such a possibility exists.

For all cognitions born of the senses—whether conceptual or non-conceptual, whether occurring in a continuous stream (*dhārāvāhinī*) or otherwise—arise and perish while apprehending a single object, either simultaneously or without mutual dependence.
We do not observe that these [cognitions] stand in a relationship of mutual following as the pursued and the pursuer.
Therefore, we consider it logical that conceptual constructions (vikalpas) arising from the contact of the sense organs with their objects are nothing other than the operation of perception itself.

Furthermore, even though both verbal cognition and perception have real entities as their domain, there is no lack of distinction between the two cognitions, because the difference between mediacy (pārokṣya) and immediacy (apārokṣya) is established by the difference in their causes.
Furthermore, the removal of cold produced by contact with fire cannot arise from the cognition of fire;
nor does it follow that when that [fire] is apprehended as qualified by one adjunct, such as existence (*sattva*), there must be an apprehension of it as qualified by another adjunct.

For the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a substance is qualified by adventitious attributes (*upādhi*), but the attributes themselves, nor the state of being qualified by them, constitute its intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, that which is related to the intrinsic nature is not itself the intrinsic nature.
In that case, there would be a contradiction with reality;
for a thing cannot be related to itself.
Furthermore, the cognition of form has the property of grasping an object, and while it has multiple atoms as its object, it does not have the nature of those atoms.

Or, if those [atoms] possessed that [consciousness] as their intrinsic nature, then because there would be no distinction with respect to all [beings], all those atoms would necessarily be known by everyone.
Nor should it be said that the form-atoms are the objects of one's own cognition while remaining entirely unconnected to it;
for if that which is unconnected were an object, it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

If it is argued that the relationship between the object and the cognition is simply their very nature (svabhāva)—such that the object is the "objectified" and the cognition is the "subjectifier"—then, alas, let the relationship between the attribute and the substratum also be merely their very nature. Even so, as in the case of the cognition and the object, there is no identity of essence (svarūpābheda).
However, in our refutation of momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga) and transformation (pariṇāma), we shall establish a relationship distinct from mere nature.
Therefore, when there is the apprehension of [an object] as endowed with one limiting adjunct (upādhi), it does not follow that there must be a cognition of it as endowed with all limiting adjuncts.

Regarding the claim that there can be no relationship of qualifier and qualified between two things that are objects of a single cognition, we reply: even if they are objects of distinct cognitions, such a relationship is not impossible.
For indeed, a cognition of a qualifier that does not have the qualified object as its content cannot delimit that qualified object;
likewise, how could a cognition of the qualified object that does not have the qualifier as its content delimit its own object,
since the two are ignorant of each other's nature?

From those two arises a latent impression (*vāsanā*), and from that, a mental cognition (*mānasapratyaya*) is produced which takes the form of the relationship between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*).
If it is argued that the relationship between qualifier and qualified does not exist as a reality?
Let the consideration of whether this is real or unreal be set aside for now; indeed, this will be addressed further below. As for the effort you have made regarding its being mental in nature:
Let it rather be produced by the sense-faculty itself; for if that were the case, its status as having the function of seeing would be directly established.
Otherwise, one would have to postulate an intermediary consisting of non-conceptual [perception].
Now, one might object: how can sensory cognition, which is non-discursive (*avicāraka*), synthesize the entire range of qualifiers, qualificands, and so forth?
Ah, my friend! Is even mental cognition capable of synthesizing them?
If you say it does, because the mind—which is its cause—has all things as its object;
If the preceding consciousness is the mind (*manas*),
how can it have all things as its object?
For us, however, although the mind has all things as its object, it is not a deliberative faculty because it is insentient.
Therefore, the self alone is the substratum of all cognitions and the impressions produced by them; it is the rememberer and the synthesizer.
As it has been said:
"Cognition resides in the self alone, for it is that which is understood here to be the knower."
And its capacity for recollection, as well as for the reconnection [of broken mantras] and so forth, exists.

Ślokavārttika, Pratyakṣa, verse 122: Having perceived through the contact of the sense organ with its object an object that possesses a genus but is initially indistinct, he— aided by the recollection of a previous individual entity arising from the awakening of latent impressions—
first conceptualizes it with the eye as "this is a cow."
As it has been said:
"The sense-faculty is the instrument of cognition, and the conscious self is the agent;
and because it possesses the capacity for memory, it will conceive of all objects."
Thus, although there is no relationship of benefactor and beneficiary in the form of a signified-signifier relationship when both are cognizable by a single cognition,
nevertheless,
the very fact that the perception of the object and the subsequent recollection produce a cognition that apprehends the qualifier-qualified relationship constitutes their status as benefactors.
For even though the two objects exist in the relation of the form and that which possesses the form, they are not grasped in that manner by a cognition arising from mere first impression;
rather, they are grasped only in their own essential nature (*svarūpa*). Indeed, it is not the case that everything that exists must be grasped.
Therefore, even when only a portion of that [object] is grasped, there is no lack of validity.

However, conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*), which arises from the aforementioned causal complex, constructs the substance by way of its form as a genus (*jāti*) and so forth, and by way of its form as a substance; although it arises subsequently, it is indeed perception because it originates from the contact between the sense organ and the object.
Furthermore, we shall demonstrate that even for that which is non-sequential, the production of effects sequentially is possible by virtue of the convergence of various sequential auxiliary causes.

Thus, this is established: the conceptual constructions under dispute are direct perceptions with respect to their own objects, because they arise from the contact of the sense organs with their objects while being non-erroneous;
whatever is such is directly perceived, like the initial sensory apprehension (*ālocana*), and this [subject] is likewise so.
Therefore, it is so.

Therefore, it is established that the term "of the nature of ascertainment" (*vyavasāyātmaka*) is intended to include determinate perception (*savikalpaka-pratyakṣa*). Since this inclusion of determinate perception is a secondary implication (*anvācīyamāna*), its exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) is also implied.

To explain that which is to be excluded, [the author], having restated the commentary (*bhāṣya*), states the meaning of the term "of the nature of ascertainment" as a secondary implication itself: "From afar by the eye... and so forth.

Not wishing to explain the commentary with the thought that "this should not be so considered," he raises an objection: "not of doubt. [The opponent asks: But when there is contact between the sense organ and its object, how can the cognition arising regarding a substance present before one—whether as "smoke" or as "dust"—be said not to be produced by the sense organ? To this he replies: "For it is not... Why is it mental? To this he replies: "Because it is a state of uncertainty (saṃśītiḥ)."

For the root *śī* preceded by the prefix *sam*, when ending in an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), functions in the sense of a deliberation that depends upon specific distinctions; and this [root], superimposing two mutually contradictory properties remembered as residing in a single substratum, does not determine either one of them.
Thus, the operation of the sense faculty consists merely in presenting the substratum.
However, it is only through the mind, acting in conjunction with memory, that a person experiences doubt.

For this very reason, when someone with wide-open eyes, having momentarily perceived some substrate possessing a common property due to a flash of lightning, becomes doubtful in the darkness, this doubt is purely mental and not born of the senses; such is the meaning.
Refuting this, he explains the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "And this is not so" as follows: "And that is not thus."
Why [is it said] "of doubt"?—[the text says] "but both. The word "but" (tu) excludes the notion that [doubt] has the mind alone as its cause.
By this, the commentary beginning with "for by this eye... has been explained.
The meaning is that, although perceiving the subject as possessing common properties, one does not ascertain it;
this refers to the case where there is doubt regarding its specific qualities.

"Perceived by the sense organ" means perceived as something proximate, since perception is preceded by sensory contact; "perceives with the mind" means one knows it by means of the eye as an auxiliary.

Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states: "That non-determination by the mind which is preceded by the non-determination of the sense organ, and which consists merely of a deliberation requiring further specification—that is doubt, not the former [non-apprehension].
This term "non-determination" (anavadhāraṇa) denotes the cognition of doubt; it is applied metaphorically to the contact between the sense organ and the object, which is its own cause.
For doubt is observed even when the operation of the sense organs has ceased;
thus the objector maintains that doubt does not arise from the sense organs even when their operation is present.

Therefore, between these two types of doubtful cognition, that which is preceded by the determination of the sense organ and the contact of the sense organ with its object, yet remains an indetermination by the mind—that is what is meant by "doubtful cognition."
"Not previously" means that the doubtful cognition which remains in the mind as an example for one whose sensory activity has ceased is what is suspected;
he explains this very commentary with the words: "In that case, [the cognition] which [arises] from the sense-organ and the object..."
The term *indriyārthasannikarṣa* (contact between sense-organ and object) and *anavadhāraṇam* (non-determination) form a *karmadhāraya* compound.
The meaning is that doubt-cognition is a non-determination by the mind preceded by that [contact].
[Objection: But surely the sense organ is not its cause, since its operation is mediated by memory; to this he says: "For of that...
This has been established below, namely, that memory does not intervene in the operation of the sense organ.
[The phrase] "But previously... refers to the following.
Its priority is established by way of illustration.
It might be argued as follows: one must accept that the mind alone functions with respect to external objects independently of the [physical] sense-faculties;
otherwise, the cognition "I know the jar" would be without a cause.
It is not, first of all, born of the sense faculties,
because the eyes and other senses do not operate with respect to internal cognition;
nor does it fall within the category of inference and the like.
Because of the absence of [inferential] marks and so forth,
this must therefore be a mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*).
And if the mind were not to operate toward external objects such as a jar, [it would not perceive them].
How could there be the thought "What is this pot"?
There would only be the thought "I know.
And there can be no determination of the nature of cognition without the determination of the object.
Therefore, suspecting that the mind has both external and internal objects— and thus that every doubt is mental— the author of the Bhāṣya says:
"And in all cases where there is an object of perception..."

Although such a reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) is mental, it nevertheless depends upon the eyes and other sense organs for the prior arising of the primary cognition (*vyavasāya*), because [otherwise] there would be no blind or deaf persons;
otherwise, it would follow that blind, deaf, and so forth, do not exist.
Thus, the point is that even in the production of a doubtful cognition, the contact between the sense organ and its object must be depended upon.
This very point has been explained by the Vārttika beginning with "tasya hi" and so forth.
The Bhāṣya, beginning with "in the case of the self and so forth," aims to refute the definition by showing its lack of pervasiveness;
he explains that [Bhāṣya] with the words "indriyārtha... [and so on]. He raises an objection: "But how [is this so]?"
He refutes this with the words "the sense-faculties" (*indriya*).
Let there be no [objection] regarding the reading in the *Indriya-sūtra*;
for that indeed is the definition of the external sense-faculties.
And because the internal organ is the mind, he says "and separately.
Furthermore, there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding pleasure and so forth;
therefore, by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), they are indeed perceptible. Thus he says: "and [they] are perceived."

[Objection: But surely these are not objects of cognition (*prameya*), because they are established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). Therefore, what is the use of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) here for the sake of an object of cognition? To this he says: "And not of those... [Objection: But was it not already stated that, by virtue of being self-awareness, these do not possess the status of being the objects of a cognitive act (*pramākarmabhāva*)? To this he says: "And there is no other way," for their state of being self-awareness consists precisely in their being awareness (*saṃvedanatvena*).
And it has been stated below that these are not consciousness; such is the intended meaning.
He concludes the objection with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*).
In the Bhāṣya, the two groups—beginning with "the self and so forth" and "pleasure and so forth"—are intended to represent the eternal and the non-eternal respectively.
The self, pleasure, pain, and so forth are eternal, while pleasure, pain, and so forth are impermanent. This has been stated by Dignāga:
"Pleasure and the like are not objects of cognition (*prameya*), nor is the mind another sense faculty."
And that is not possible, because it is prohibited by the *Ghrāṇādi-sūtra*, which is intended to effect a distinction; this is the sense.
[As stated in] the *Samādhi-bhāṣya*: "Indeed, for one who possesses a faculty..."
Desiring to explain that [point], he asks with a hidden intention: "And who is it that says this?
The objector replies: "The sense-objects, etc.
The respondent says: "This is not a fault."
Having exposed the seed of the latent disposition (anuśaya) of the objector, he refutes him with the words: "As for [the statement] 'in the Sūtra'...
This Sūtra concerning the nose and so forth is not intended to provide a classification; rather, it is intended to provide a definition (lakṣaṇa).
And in that case, the sense-faculty of the mind (*manas*) is also not characterized [as such], because it is of a different nature; this is the meaning.
He states the difference in nature: "the difference in nature" (*vaidharmyam*).
Therein he provides the proof: "But [the cognition] has all things as its object.
He refutes another point of dissimilarity with the words: "material" (*bhautika*).
For the two specific qualities of an effect are its being material and its being non-material.
That which is an effect of the primary elements is derivative matter (*bhautika*).
That which is not an effect of the primary elements is non-derivative matter (*abhautika*).
Furthermore, the negation of being an effect of the primary elements implies that it is an effect of something other than them.
This is because the negation of a specific attribute necessarily implies the admission of another specific attribute;
otherwise, it would be stated that it is simply "not an effect," rather than "not composed of the elements."
Therefore, the meaning is that for the mind, which is not an effect, being non-material (abhautikatva) is a property contradictory to being an effect.
Furthermore, because of its dissimilarity [to the ear], one should not say that the ear is like the mind; thus he says: "And in the case of the ear.
He raises an objection: "In its own object."

The meaning is that the difference [in nature] lies in the fact that the elements beginning with the sense of smell and ending with the ear are indeed elemental (bhūta), whereas the mind (manas) is not an element.
He refutes this, saying: "And that is not so."

For the author of the Vārttika will demonstrate that there is no suffix whatsoever that is purely *svārthika* (denoting its own meaning); this is the sense. He restates the reason for the objection with the words "yat puras" ("that which was previously [stated]"); he refutes it with the words "na nāsti" ("it is not non-existent").
Thus, the commentary beginning with "provided there is contact between the sense organ and its object" has been explained.

Furthermore, regarding that other point of dissimilarity stated by the author of the Bhāṣya concerning the mind (*manas*) as compared to the olfactory organ and the rest—that too he refutes by looking back like a lion (retrospectively)—with the words "of those possessing qualities.
Just as the olfactory organs and the others perceive external odors and so forth by means of their own respective qualities such as smell, [the mind does not do so].
The ear does not perceive an external sound by means of its own quality, which is sound;
therefore, like the mind, the ear should not be included in the Sūtra concerning the sense organs such as the nose. This is the meaning.
He concludes the intended point of dissimilarity among those mentioned in the Bhāṣya with the words "therefore."

The intended meaning of the restriction is that the dissimilarity characterized by being elemental (*bhūtatva*) and non-elemental (*abhūtatva*) cannot be stated by means of apprehending materiality (*bhautikatva*) and non-materiality (*abhautikatva*).

[Objection: Since cognitions do not arise simultaneously, it is understood that there exists a mind (*manas*) which is the cause of cognition; however, its status as a sense-organ (*indriyatva*) is not [established].

And since, if that [existence] were not understood, it would be impossible to say that the cognition of pleasure and so forth arises from the contact of the sense-organ with its object, he says: "In another system" (*tantrāntare*).
A *tantra* is a treatise (*śāstra*), because by means of it reality (*tattva*) is woven (*tantryate*) or explained.
By this, the commentary beginning with "and of the mind" (*manasaśca*) has been explained.
This has been refuted by Dignāga: "If [the word] 'not prohibited' is included [in the definition], then the mention of 'other sense organs' is redundant."
He introduces [the objection] in order to refute it: "Not by means of the remainder" (*na śeṣa*).
He refutes that: "Not by means of the technical principles of the system" (*na tantrayukti*).
Since everything is established in other systems and in the world, there is no such thing as "one's own doctrine" (*svamata*) when nothing remains to be stated.

For it is held that the mark [of inference] is speech; and one cannot state a mere negation regarding what is not consented to, because the determination of non-existence (abhāva) is dependent upon the determination of existence (bhāva). This is the underlying sense. He concludes the established point with the words "therefore" (tasmāt).
He concludes the subject under discussion with the word "tat" (that).
Having thus explained the words defining the characteristics, he reflects on them with the words "all together.
He states his intended meaning: "the Commentator says 'all together'. He provides the reason: "because..."

For the definition of perception—"knowledge arising from the contact of a sense-organ with its object, which is non-erroneous"—can indeed be defined as distinctively excluded from both similar and dissimilar classes without exception.
Indeed, it is not possible for the cognition "this is that horse" to be produced by a sense-organ [if it were] produced by a word;
for that [cognition] is said to have either a substance or [a universal] as its object.
[The cognition] has either "expressibility" as its object,
or it has a substance qualified by expressibility as its object.
In that case, since a substance is exclusively perceptual and not verbal, it is impossible to exclude [the possibility of] such a cognition.
And this is undesirable.
Furthermore, knowledge whose object is the state of being denotable is nothing other than verbal cognition;
otherwise, even a forest-dweller who has never heard the word "horse" would grasp that the horse is denotable by the word "horse" merely through the sensory contact with the animal itself.
Even the cognition of a substance qualified by expressibility is purely verbal,
just as the cognition of smoke qualified by fire is inferential; otherwise, if that were sensory, no further effort would need to be undertaken to refute it.
Now, "denotability" (vācyatva) is not some supersensible property as it is for the Mīmāṃsakas;
rather, it is merely a convention that "this [word] is to be understood from that [object].
Even so, it resides in the word itself.
Now, if this too were merely sensory,
then the verse taught by the Guru should be recited therein:
"If it is verbal because it is born from sound, then it is perception because it is born from the sense organs."
For since it has the nature of a clear apprehension, it is rightly considered sensory.
Thus, the term *avyapadeśya* (non-verbalizable) is not intended to exclude knowledge born of both [senses and words]. However,

since determinate (*savikalpaka*) cognition is already excluded by the term *vyavasāyātmaka* (of the nature of ascertainment), it is possible that indeterminate (*nirvikalpaka*) cognition might be rendered non-perceptual.

Thinking that [the definition] might exclude even indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*) by means of the term "inexpressible" (*avyapadeśya*), the word "verbal" (*śābda*) was stated so as to include the exclusion of the commingling of words even in the case of indeterminate perception.

Likewise, thinking that if indeterminate perception were excluded by the term "inexpressible," then determinate perception (*savikalpaka*) produced by the senses might be excluded from the category of perception, the term "doubtful" (*saṃśaya*) was stated so as to include the exclusion of the perceptual nature of doubtful cognition by means of the term "of the nature of ascertainment" (*vyavasāyātmaka*).
Having shown the positive concomitance (*anvaya*), he states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with the words "If...
He concludes with "Therefore... Therein, he enumerates the thirty crores of things to be abandoned (*heya*).

By taking "produced by the contact of the sense-organ with its object" (*indriyārthasannikarṣotpanna*) as the fixed term (*dhruva*) within the group of two words, there are four permutations (*koṭi*) through connection with each of the single words beginning with "knowledge" (*jñāna*).
Taking "knowledge" as the fixed term, there are three permutations through connection with each of the single words beginning with "inexpressible" (*avyapadeśya*).
Likewise, taking "inexpressible" as the fixed term, there are two permutations through connection with each of the single words beginning with "non-erroneous" (*avyabhicārin*).
In the case of a relationship consisting of non-erroneous ascertainment (*avyabhicārivyavasāyātmaka*), there are ten [possibilities].
Even by taking three terms together, there are exactly ten.

Having fixed the phrase "knowledge produced from the contact of sense-faculty and object" (*indriyārthasannikarṣotpannaṃ jñānam*), there are three groups of possibilities when each term beginning with "non-verbalizable" (*avyapadeśya*) is combined one by one.

Taking "knowledge that is non-verbalizable" as fixed, there are two categories through the connection with the words "non-erroneous" and so forth; however, when the words "non-erroneous" and "non-verbalizable" are connected with the word "determinate," there is one category. When the words "produced by sense-object contact" and "non-verbalizable" are fixed, there are two categories through the connection of each of the words "non-erroneous" and so forth. Furthermore, when the two fixed words "non-erroneous" and "determinate" are each connected with the words "produced by sense-object contact" and "knowledge," there are two categories.
Thus, by taking three terms, there are ten *koṭis*;
by taking four terms, there are five.

Having fixed [the definition] as "knowledge produced from the contact of sense-organ and object which is non-verbal," there are two *koṭis* for each connection with "non-erroneous" (*avyabhicārin*) and so forth.
Excluding the term *avyapadeśya*, there is one extreme; excluding the term *jñāna*, there is another;
and excluding the term *indriyārthasannikarṣotpanna*, however, there is the fifth.

He asks: "Why, by the inclusion of five terms and the inclusion of the thirty-first alternative (*koṭi*), are the other alternatives excluded? The meaning is: for there is no word here that expresses such an exclusion. The answer is: "By way of distinction" (*viśeṣa*).
In the context of providing a specific counter-argument, the presentation of the negation of the remainder is for the sake of obtaining an illustrative example.
"Acceptance of one part" means that among the thirty-one alternatives (*koṭi*), the thirty-first alternative is the "one part.
Alternatively, it refers to the prescription of the remainder.
The word "vā" has the sense of "iva" (like).
Having thus established the definition of perception, he now introduces the definition of perception according to Vasubandhu in order to refute it, saying: "Others, however...
He explains the definition [with the words] "from that object" (*tato 'rthāt*).
Because of the constant connection between the relative pronoun *yat* and the demonstrative *tat*, whatever cognition is designated by reference to whichever object, [that cognition is perception].

If that [cognition] arises from that very object itself and not from another object unrelated to the designation, then it is perception. For this very reason, the cognition of mother-of-pearl— which is designated as "silver" by means of an object other than itself, namely the form of the mother-of-pearl, which is unrelated to that designation— is not perception,
because the designation does not arise from its own source.

Because the silver that serves as the designator is impossible there, the exclusion of this pseudo-perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*) is well-established; therefore, setting that aside, he states the exclusion of inference (*anumāna*) with the words "by this" (*etena*).
Why? Because that cognition does not become an inference from that very fire which is the designator.
However, [the inference occurs] where fire exists;

and thus, where smoke has ceased immediately upon being seen because of the cessation of fire, there the cognition arises from another—namely, from smoke that is being remembered—even though the fire, which is the designator, is absent.
Therefore, in the phrase "from that object" (*tato 'rthāt*), the word "from that" (*tataḥ*) is a qualifier of the object (*artha*).
And the particle *eva*, when conjoined with that [word], functions to exclude non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*), as in the example: "Caitra is indeed a possessor of wealth.
Therefore, the meaning is that wherever there is a lack of connection with that [perceptibility], it is not perceived.
He refutes this definition: "In this [definition], the inclusion of the word 'object' (artha) is purposeless;
for the designation 'cognition' cannot occur either by means of the self or by means of the sense organ.
He raises an objection: "It is for the sake of restriction (avadhāraṇa)."
This restriction is by means of the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*),
and [it applies] to the qualifier;
for the particle *eva* when connected with a qualifier excludes non-connection.

The point is that if the substantive (*arthapada*) were absent, to what would this qualification belong? Thus, the particle *eva* (only), when connected with a qualifier, could not exclude non-connection. He refutes this, saying "that is not so," because a pronoun such as "therefore" (*tataḥ*) depends upon a proximate substantive.

Otherwise, because the denotation would not be complete, that which is designated by it—the substantive (viśeṣya) connected with the designation—is necessarily obtained; thus, its status as a qualifier (viśeṣaṇatva) is indeed established.
However, thinking that there is no fault even in merely restricting [the meaning] while granting [the opponent's position], the example "one who eats water" (abbhakṣa) was cited.
For even in the case of excluding others, only that which is contradictory is excluded.
It is not merely something else;
as they have said:
"A restriction is postulated because of its contradiction with that [other], not because of what is non-contradictory."
Thus it is said.
It might be argued as follows: if one were to say "from that" (*tataḥ*), it would mean "from whatever [cause]";

and since inference and other means of knowledge also arise from that—namely, from the cognition of the inferential mark (*liṅga*) and so forth—it would follow that they too are perception. To exclude this consequence, one must say "from the object" (*arthāt*).
For that [cognition] does not arise from the object, but rather is indeed direct perception;
therefore, he says: "by this."

Having anticipated the objection, "To whom does that [cognition] belong?", the exclusion of inference and other means of knowledge through the force of the word *tataḥ* (from that) has also been answered.
Furthermore, he refutes that other alternative exclusion of the word *tataḥ* which was mentioned, with the words: "As for that which... (*yatpunaretat*).
If that cognition which is designated as belonging to something is [considered] perception, then the cognition "this is a jar" would also follow as being perception,
for that too is designated as belonging to the jar.

But it does not arise from that jar; because the jar cannot withstand analysis and thus lacks ultimate existence, it lacks the status of being a cause for consciousness as a conventionally existent thing.
Therefore, in order to exclude that [cause], the word "from that" (tataḥ) was stated.
We do not understand how this [position] has been rejected.
He raises an objection with the words "If..."—
namely, that atoms of form and so forth, which arise in immediate succession, are ultimately real and distinct, and are the producers of their own non-conceptual cognition.

However, the conceptual cognition "jar," which arises subsequent to non-conceptual perception, conceals their diversity by means of its own form; it is called a "conventional reality" (*saṃvṛti*) because it presents those very [elements] such as color-form and so forth—which perform a single function such as carrying water—as if they were distinct entities.
He refutes this, saying: "Indeed, not from color-form and the rest..."
He exposes the seed of the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) with the words "even so" (*athāpi*).
He refutes [the opponent's view] with the words "like a sweetmeat for the mind" (*manomodaka*); [the opponent asks], "Let them be distinct; what does it matter if they are?
To this he replies, "And all..."—whatever you consider to be conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and whatever is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), all that arises from its own object.

Therefore, the inclusion of the word "from that" (tataḥ) for the purpose of excluding conventional reality (saṃv�rti) is redundant. One might object: "Let it not be for the purpose of excluding conventional reality;
rather, it will serve to exclude false cognition (mithyājñāna). To this he replies: "But surely false cognition arises even from what is not [the object]?"
Just as the object present before one is designated as "this" and not as "silver," yet not as "mother-of-pearl," so too,
although that cognition is designated in its general form, [it is not designated as such in its specific form].

And thus it follows: even though [a thing] arises from that, nevertheless, insofar as it is designated by a qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*) from which it does not arise, it is said to be "from that which is other than that.
Therefore, that alone from which something arises is perception (*pratyakṣa*).
And false cognition is not like this;
for the meaning is that it arises from various [different] sources.
He refutes [this objection]: "For that is not a false cognition because it arises from that which is not that—namely, from a superimposed form which does not exist there."
However, that from which it arises— namely, from that very universal form (sāmānyarūpa) to which "this" is designated—
is its [the cognition's] object insofar as it appears in a perceptible form, though it is superimposed upon that [object].
This has been stated as: "that which is not that appears as that.

And thus, because only the word denoting the *lakṣya* (the object to be defined) remains, there is an absence of a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*); so he says: "therefore, the inclusion [of the definition]. Likewise, he states that there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*): "and thus."
Having accepted [the opponent's position], he states another refutation: "Even though this may be so," and so forth.
For that from which cognition arises is the apprehended object (*grāhya*) as the cause, and the apprehending consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the effect.
Because those two do not exist simultaneously, a cognition appearing as present would be false with respect to a past object and thus could not be perception;
furthermore, because there can be no relationship of cause and effect between things existing at the same time,
the sense is that [the cognition] does not arise from that object.
He raises an objection: "destruction and production.
Because all things are momentary, the destruction of the cause and the production of the effect occur at the same time;
nevertheless, the causality of the object of cognition remains even when it belongs to a different time.
Its state of being an object (*grāhyatva*) consists solely in its producing a cognition similar to itself, and nothing else; as it has been said:
"If it is asked how that which exists at a different time can be an object, they understand 'being an object' [in this sense]."
Those who know the reasoning [of causality] maintain that it is precisely the state of being a cause that is capable of imparting its form to the cognition.
As stated in *Pra.vā.* 2.2.47:
"Nor does it follow from this much that [the cognition] is false,
because the blue form produced by the object is actually present"— this is the intended meaning.
He refutes this, saying: "And that is not so.
The definition of momentariness as being devoid of any temporal parts (kalā) in prior or subsequent time does not apply anywhere;
for even things like lightning or a flash of light, though quickly perishing, persist for two or three moments, and so forth—this is the meaning.
He states that the previously mentioned objection remains exactly as it was: "And [if] destroyed...
Blue and so forth, which are not the locus of egoity, are experienced as being of the nature of non-pleasure and so on, distinct from consciousness, and not as having consciousness as their essence.
And likewise, if the apprehension of a separation were false,
then how could this cognition be a perception with respect to that [separation], given that it is false,
since such a state belongs only to the distinction of correct cognition?
Nor is the experience of an object's beneficial form the experience of the object itself,

for that would entail the consequence of it being merely figurative. Furthermore, the modes of speech characterized as primary or secondary cannot be applied to cognitions, because they belong to different domains.
Therefore, it must be stated that cognition, being formless, takes as its object something distinct from itself.

If that [object] were the cause, then there would be the perception of what has already perished; and thus, by taking as its object what is not present while appearing as if present, it would follow that it is false and lacks the status of direct perception (pratyakṣatva). This is the intended meaning. Furthermore, even in the case of simultaneity, there is no illustrative example.
He raises an objection: "If it is argued that [this is] equal, because everything is included within the position of momentariness," he refutes it with: "And that..."
Now he presents Dignāga’s definition—“the other”—and asks about the nature of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) in order to refute it: “Now, what is this?
The proponent of the definition replies: “It is that which is associated with a name (*nāman*).”

For in the case of arbitrary words (*yadṛcchāśabda*), an object qualified by a name is expressed, such as "Ḍittha"; in the case of genus-words (*jātiśabda*), [an object] is expressed by way of its genus, such as "this is a cow";
and in the case of quality-words (*guṇaśabda*), [an object] is expressed by way of its quality, such as "white."
In the case of action-words, [the object is qualified] by the action, as in "cook";
in the case of substance-words, it is by the substance, as in "staff-bearer" or "horned.
That cognition in which this conceptual construction (kalpanā)—whether by way of its object or its own form—is absent is perception (pratyakṣa) as excluded from such construction.
This is what he says: that which indeed is not designated by name, nor defined by its meaning or its essential nature, nor described by genus and so forth;
and to ensure non-deviation, he states its status as the cause of the object—namely, "conforming to the nature of the object";
and he states its status as a means of valid cognition—namely, "that which delimits and establishes."
He demonstrates its nature as knowledge: it is to be personally experienced, and by that very self-awareness, its freedom from conceptual construction is also established.
As it has been said:
"Perception, which is free from conceptual construction, is established by perception itself."
Thus:
"That is perception.
He refutes this by examining the subject and the definition, the individual words and their collective function—namely, "those [who say] 'this is... etc.
Now, [it is] not so;
for words have conceptual construction as their source and they adhere to that which is their objective domain— namely,
that which conceptual constructions grasp.
Furthermore, both that which is determined [by conceptual thought] and that which is excluded from others are non-entities (avastu) in the form of exclusions;
therefore, conceptual constructions and words do not take as their object that non-conceptual cognition or its object which is ultimately real—this is the intended meaning.
Moreover, if this [ultimate reality] were inexpressible, there would be a contradiction with the scripture whose authority you yourself accept; thus he says: "impermanence, etc. (anityādi).
He raises an objection with "atha" (now/if);
that is to say, he means that its own specific form is excluded. He then refutes this with "sarve 'rthāḥ" (all objects).

For it is not the case that Dignāga established the definition of perception and so forth with reference to correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*) in the same way that Kīrti did, such that [the term] "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*) would be restricted to cognition based on that specific context; this is the intended meaning.

Now, one might object: "If the thing-in-itself (*svarūpa*) were not expressed, then it would follow that the object is inexpressible, and consequently, verbal discourse (*śābdo vyavahāra*) would become unreal. To this he says: "And of everything... (*sarvasya ca*).

There are three categories of entities based on the distinction between the universal (*sāmānya*), the particular (*viśeṣa*), and that which possesses them (*tadvat*). With reference to the entity that possesses these, it is said: "there are two aspects.
This means that it is designated by the aspect of the universal alone as being "endowed with the universal."
"Brahmin" means one who possesses the genus (jāti) of humanity; it was stated that [the self] cannot be designated by way of its own nature, with reference to a specific form.
The intended meaning is that it is not so in every respect.
He applies this to the present context with the word "thus" (*evam*).
Anticipating the previously mentioned over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), he resolves it with the words "if, however" (*yadi ca*).

Now, one might object—as with the word "aśvakarṇa" and others—that the term *kalpanāpoḍha* (free from conceptual construction) is an unanalyzed (avyutpanna) expression denoting the very nature of perception; thus he raises the doubt with "Now" (*atha*).
He refutes this with "Even so" (*evam api*).
Let it be that the word *kalpanāpoḍha* is either unanalyzed or not.
However, perception must be sought as something inexpressible;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that conceptual construction (vikalpa) is also perception.
And thus, there is a contradiction (vyāghāta); this is the meaning.
He refutes Jaimini’s definition of perception with the words "satsaṃprayoga" (contact with the existent).
As it stands, this definition is over-extensive (*ativyāpti*), because even by the word "sat," the correctness of the contact is implied;
and that correctness is equally present even in a false cognition.
Even when there is a reversal, because the object of cognition is presented by the intellect,
the word "that" refers to the object of cognition;
and even in the case of false cognition, there exists a connection between the sense faculties and the object of cognition.
For that which is to be cognized (*bodhya*) is the substance present before one.
Now, there exists no such connection between the sense organs as there is for that which is to be cognized, because the qualifier "silver-ness" (*rajatatva*) is not present.
Indeed, non-pervasion is a defect of the definition,
because in the case of recognition, the aspect of "that-ness" (tattā) is not in contact with the sense faculty.
Moreover, in the Prābhākara view, inferential and other such cognitions would not be perceptual with respect to the self,
for they are certainly not produced by the contact of a real object [with the senses].
Therefore, this point too should be reflected upon by the wise.
He states that the definition of Vārṣagaṇya is also incorrect: "The function of the ear and so forth.
For indeed, the function of the five sense organs is held to be mere observation when they have been transformed into the form of their objects;
and since that [mere observation] pervades doubt and other such states, it is not a valid definition.
Thus it is established that "produced from the contact of the sense-faculty and the object" is precisely this definition; the definition of perception is hereby completed. //4//
Now, inference preceded by that [perception] is of three kinds: namely, the *pūrvavat*, the *śeṣavat*, and the *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*.

Immediately after the definition of perception (*pratyakṣa*), he recites the aphorism concerning the definition of inference (*anumāna*): "Now, inference, preceded by that [perception], is of three kinds. Here, the term "inference" is a restatement of the object of definition (*lakṣya*)—which is a specific type of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—as something already established. This very fact decisively rejects the claim that inference lacks validity on the grounds that it is not a means of valid cognition.

For it is only through the similarity of certain individual instances to other instances whose validity or invalidity has been ascertained that one may establish the validity or invalidity of those particular instances.
Furthermore, since inference is precisely that which possesses perceived similarity (*dṛṣṭasādharmya*), how can it be invalid by its own means?
Moreover, the employment of the statement "inference is not a valid means of knowledge" is meaningful only with respect to a person who is ignorant, mistaken, or doubtful;
yet, the states of doubt, ignorance, and error residing in another person—unlike their physical attributes such as fairness of complexion—are not perceived through direct perception.
Nor are they understood from that statement,
because it is accepted that even a statement, being other than perception, lacks authority;
for a statement uttered without reference to a specific person is meaningless.
Otherwise, one would be like a madman whose words are not to be heeded, as if saying, "This person is neither a worldly man nor an investigator.
As for the remainder, it will be explained in the section on investigation (*parīkṣā*).
Therefore, even against one's will, inference must be accepted as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Having restated the definition of inference—which consists in its division according to the types of valid cognition—as "that which is preceded by that" (tatpūrvakam), he prescribes the defining characteristic.

The word "atha" (now) indicates immediate succession; thus, the meaning is that perception, which was previously mentioned, is the cause of inference, and now inference, which possesses that cause, is being explained.
He states the purport of the *Lakṣaṇasūtra*: "By means of inference," etc.
He clarifies that very point: "By this," etc.
Those of the same class are perception and the other [means of valid cognition] by virtue of being means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And there are those of a different class, such as fallacious inferences (*anumānābhāsa*) and the like—
for example, [the reasons] such as "existence" (*sattva*) when "momentariness" and so forth are the properties to be proven (*sādhya*).
It might be argued that this definition of "being preceded by that" (*tatpūrvakatva*) is over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*).
For the word "that" (tat) refers to perception because of its immediate proximity.
And thus, since inference—as well as scripture, memory, doubt, and error—likewise possesses the quality of being preceded by perception, they too would result in being classified as inference.
Furthermore, an inference preceded by another inference and so forth would not be preceded by perception, and thus it would not be inference.
Because it is not pervaded by the definition of inference, this [definition] is therefore neither too narrow nor too broad; thus, he says: "that which is preceded by that" (*tatpūrvakam*).
By repeating the phrase "preceded by that," three grammatical analyses (*vigraha*) are demonstrated.

In that case, regarding the first analysis (*vigraha*), one should connect "those" (*tāni*)—skipping the immediately following sūtra—with the *pratyakṣa* (perception) and other categories found in the *vibhāga-sūtra*, because they are appropriate [to be so connected].
As they have said:
"Whichever thing has a semantic connection with another, that connection exists for it even if it is situated at a distance."
Thus, by this, the lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the definition has been avoided.
He says this very thing with the words "when those... [referring to the sūtra].
Now, one might object that this contradicts the Bhāṣya statement, "this is preceded by perception" (*pratyakṣapūrvakam*); therefore, he says: "by way of a traditional succession" (*pāramparyeṇa*).
For the author of the Bhāṣya has stated that [the means of knowledge] are preceded by perception through a traditional succession;
therefore, there is no contradiction.
To exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*), he explains the second analysis [of the compound], beginning with "even when."
In the analysis of the compound *te*, only the word *pratyakṣa* from the immediately preceding sūtra is connected [to it].

And just as there are two types of perception (*pratyakṣa*) which are prior to that perception— the inferential cognition of the consideration of the mark (*liṅgaparāmarśajñāna*) which is the fruit of perception— this very [inferential cognition] is "that which has perception as its antecedent" (*tatpūrvaka*).
For that [cognition], although it is perception with respect to its own object, constitutes an inferential cognition regarding the object to be inferred;
thus, it is called "that" (tad).
The mention of "perception" (pratyakṣa) is for the purpose of illustration.
The phrase "in inference," and so forth, should also be understood here.
It might be argued as follows:
at the time of grasping the relationship [between word and meaning], perception first has the word and its referent as its object.
Now, when there is a second perception regarding that object, the memory that arises concerning that term is also preceded by two perceptions.

Likewise, the memory of the relationship between the mark (*liṅga*) and the marked (*liṅgin*) is also preceded by two perceptions; thus, the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) remains exactly as it was. With this intention, he asks: "Which two? The answer is: "The mark," and so forth.
In all cases of doubt, this principle applies:
"The specific determination arises from the explanation, for there is no non-characteristic due to doubt.
The meaning is that at the time of recollecting the pervasion (*vyāpti*), the perception of the second mark (*liṅga*) does not exist even in a state of perishing.

Because the impression of pervasion (*vyāpti-saṃskāra*), having been awakened by the conventional agreement (*samaya*), is destroyed at the time of the recollection of pervasion by its own produced impression;

and even if there were simultaneity between the second perception of the mark (*liṅga*)—which is in a state of perishing—and the recollection of pervasion, their mutual connection is impossible because they are unaware of each other's condition.
Nor is it tenable to say that the Self (*ātman*) connects them.
Indeed, this [cognition] would be produced by way of its function (*vṛtti*),

not by way of its own nature (*svarūpa*). Therefore, one must accept a third kind of perception, namely the reflective cognition (*parāmarśajñāna*) produced from both [the sense organ and the object], which arises from the contact between the sense faculty and the object.

"From the second [perception] for one who has the desire to know (*bubhutsu*). The phrase "for one who has the desire to know" is stated in order to show that the desire to know is also a cause for the arising of inferential knowledge (*anumāna-jñāna*).

In the statement, "The first perception is the observation of the relationship between the mark (*liṅga*) and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*)," the word "relationship" refers to the relationship that is a constituent part of inference.

Intending to refute the various alternative views regarding the relationship [between reason and probandum] propounded by others— which are not constituent parts of inference— he states that perception is its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For some say that inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), based on identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*), is the constituent part of inference.
For an object is of two kinds:
perceptible and imperceptible.
Among these, that which directly imparts its own form to the intellect is perceptible.
For that [object] is the producer of the cognition whose object it is; thus, it is logical that cognition—failing to find its own self without that [object]—establishes its existence.
But an imperceptible [object], lacking the capacity to directly present its own form to the cognition, is simply not logically apprehended.
Furthermore, it is not logical to postulate one thing upon the perception of another.
Because it would lead to an over-extension [of the principle].
However, by virtue of being inseparable (*nāntarīyakatayā*), one thing may cause another to be known;
for that which has an established nature connected [to the other] indicates the presence of such a nature.
Furthermore, that necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is not to be determined by mere observation and non-observation;
for if it were so, there would also be the following inference: "He is dark-skinned because he is the son of Maitra, like the observed group of Maitra’s sons.
For in this case as well, observation and non-observation do indeed exist.
