Therefore, the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is based solely on identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*). As it has been said: "The restriction of inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) arises from either the relation of cause and effect or from an essential nature (*svabhāva*) as the regulator; it is established by observation, not by non-observation."
And thus, without a conceptualization of the mark (liṅga), there is no conceptualization of the bearer of the mark (liṅgin);
without the experience of the mark, there is no conceptualization of the mark;
and without the mark itself, there is no experience of the mark.

And since there is no inferential mark (*liṅga*) that is not invariably concomitant with the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*), even though the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the *liṅgin* does not appear [directly], the conceptual cognition of inference is non-erroneous with respect to it because of its indirect connection thereto. This is the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).
The form "when this exists, it occurs; even when others exist, if this is absent, it does not occur" is not distinct from positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
And those two are determined by a conceptual construction (vikalpa) that arises subsequent to direct perception (pratyakṣa).
For instance, when fire exists, the very act of direct perception—whose function is followed by conceptualization—ascertains that "there is smoke";
and likewise, when fire is absent, it is also direct perception itself [that determines] that "there is no smoke."

For the non-perception of fire and smoke are not distinct from one another; therefore, because there is the perception of a thing devoid of them, there is no other exclusion (*vyatireka*) for these two than that very thing devoid of them.
Likewise, identity (*tādātmya*) must also be ascertained through the application of a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) in the case of the contrary.
Just as the identity of existence with momentariness is determined through the non-perception of its pervaders—succession and simultaneity—in the case of the contrary [non-momentary] entity;
therefore, the necessary connection (pratibandha) exists only through identity and causality, and not otherwise.
To this it is replied:

It is true that whatever is seen anywhere, if there is an invariable connection (pratibandha) between it and something else, we grant that for one who knows that connection, it is an indicator of that [connected thing] in that context.
However, that very restriction cannot be established by way of "arising from that" (*tadutpatti*).
What, then, is this "arising from that" of the smoke? Is it its existence immediately after fire?
Since such a thing exists even for a donkey, smoke might be dependent upon that [donkey] as well. If it is argued that [the smoke] exists immediately after that [fire],
and that although it occurs after a donkey, it does not exist immediately after the donkey;
Because even when that [fire] exists, smoke is absent if fire is absent;
and because even when that [fire] is absent, smoke is present when there is fire accompanied by wet fuel (*ādrendhana*).
Now, although the conformity of smoke to the presence and absence of fire has been observed there, how can its existence in other places and so forth be established?
For instance, smoke is observed repeatedly when a donkey is seen, and it is not observed in its absence; yet that smoke is not the effect of that donkey.
For smoke of that very same kind exists when fire is present even without a donkey; yet,

even this being so, one who perceives no restrictive rule must necessarily entertain the doubt that smoke of that same kind might arise from a *piśāca* alone in some place or other, even in the absence of fire, just as it does from a donkey.
Moreover, mere existence is not the determining factor, because that is no different even in the case of donkeys and the like;
furthermore, a restriction such as "immediately after that" is impossible without first removing doubt.
But if the doubt were removed by means of a restrictive determination (avadhāraṇa), there would be the consequence of mutual dependence (parasparāśraya).
It might be argued as follows:
whatever smoke is observed, all of it arises immediately after fire accompanied by moist fuel, and not immediately after a *piśāca*.

And since that smoke, being occasional, requires a cause, it takes as its cause precisely that which is understood to follow immediately after it, provided that no deviation from this rule has been perceived.
But it is not like a donkey or similar animals, which deviate from their perceived connection;
nor is it like a piśāca or similar beings, which have never been perceived before in any way.
If smoke were not caused by that [fire], why is it that smoke is not observed anywhere even in the absence of fire?
Now, if that [fire] is in every way accompanied by fire,
then, being like the fuel, why is fire also not a cause?
If it is a cause, how can there be any suspicion of the existence of smoke in its absence?
For an effect that lacks a cause would have to be either eternally existent or eternally non-existent, because it would be independent [of anything else]; it could not be occasional.
Nor is it produced by multiple causes, for that would entail the consequence of it being causeless.
Indeed, smoke's status as an effect of fire consists precisely in its existence immediately following fire.
If the meaning of the particle *eva* were not to apply even immediately after "non-fire," then it would not be the effect of fire;
likewise, it would not be the effect of anything else either.
For it does not arise immediately after something other [than fire].
Because it would also exist immediately after fire,
smoke would consequently be causeless;
and thus, its occasional occurrence would be contradicted.
True; this would indeed be the case if its being an effect were established. However, that very fact—that [the effect] exists immediately after that [cause]—does not exist.
For although smoke is never perceived without fire, and although [a jar] is never perceived immediately after a *piśāca* (since they are unperceivable), [the causal relation is not thereby proven].
Nevertheless, smoke would here be merely a "demon-like effect" (*piśācakārya*), where fire has somehow descended from its own cause like a donkey, but it is not the producer of smoke.
Therefore, even in the absence of that [fire], smoke of that same kind—born from a different cause—might occasionally arise; thus, the doubt is simply not removed.
You cannot reasonably say, "When what is seen is possible, it is not right to postulate what is unseen."
Because that which has reached the condition of being unperceivable (anupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta) cannot be refuted,
and other types of non-perception likewise lack the power to negate it;
therefore, since there is no restriction such as "only immediately after," a determination of the causal relation (kāryakāraṇabhāva) of this nature is not tenable.

Furthermore, it is not the case that whatever is perceived immediately after being accompanied by something else must, when arising from that same thing in the absence of that other, belong to a different class.
For it has been stated that the smoke produced from fire accompanied by a donkey is exactly the same as that produced from fire devoid of it.
Therefore, this demoness of doubt, attacking the certainty of causal origination which serves as its own repeller, cannot be warded off.

Furthermore, even if there were certainty regarding its arising, why would the effect not occur without a cause? And if it is argued that, such being the case, the occasional nature [of the effect] would be undermined due to its independence— just as it has been said:
A thing must be either eternally existent or non-existent, because it does not depend on anything else;
for it is only through dependence that the occasional occurrence of entities is possible.
Thus [it is said].
Let it be, then, that the relationship, being intrinsic and independent of anything else, is the non-deviating factor that serves as a limb of the means of cognition (*gamaka*).
And let that [relationship] be whatever it may be.
Enough with the effort expended in determining the relationship between cause and effect;
we shall demonstrate exactly how this is so right here.
Moreover, when a cause is inferred from its effect, it must be inferred as existing prior to that [effect],
and not as being simultaneous with it; for the existence of the cause at the time of the effect is not a factor in the production of the effect.
Rather, it belongs to a time prior to that;
for the difference in the river's flood does not indicate rain occurring at the very moment of its own existence, but rather rain from a time prior to it;
at that [present] time, however, it is not the cause of that [rain].

For this very reason, those who are doubtful regarding the year existing at that time— due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that either establishes or subverts it— do not engage in activity seeking that [year]. Likewise, fire inferred from smoke would be inferred as existing only at a time prior to that [perception], and not as existing in the present time.
And this being the case, those seeking that [color] would not engage in it without hesitation.
Furthermore, inferents infer a form distinct from taste as being simultaneous with the taste;
yet there is neither a causal relationship nor identity between these two.
If it were argued that the momentary flavor arises from the preceding moments of form, flavor, odor, and touch,
then that [flavor], while inferring its own cause— the preceding moment of form— infers only that which is of the same nature as that by which it was produced.
And that [moment of taste], being the very cause of its own cause—which is the moment of color simultaneous with the moment of the inferring [taste]—makes known precisely such [a moment of color].
Thus, the inference of the color simultaneous with the effect is established.
By this, the inference from smoke is explained.
As it has been said:
"The cognition of form and so forth, which depend on a single causal complex and are themselves non-existent [as external objects],
occurs through the inference of the properties of the cause, just like [the inference of] the transformation of fuel by means of smoke."
Thus it is said.

To this it is replied: Is this moment of form, which is simultaneous with the causal essence of the inference, the very nature (*svabhāva*) of that preceding moment of form which produced it, or is it a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of that nature which is not itself its nature?
It cannot be intrinsic nature (svabhāva),
because the relationship of producer and produced is impossible in the case of a single, non-different entity, since that relationship depends upon difference.
How can that which does not possess the same nature as it [the cause] be included within its inference?

If you argue that this is because it delimits it, then surely even by this much, this form—which exists at the same time [as the effect]—cannot have the status of a cause; so how could the effect be understood from the reason?
If it is argued that this absence (asvabhāva), though itself devoid of intrinsic nature, is implied by the specific nature of the cause through its status as a qualifier—
well, "implied" (ākṣipyate) and "made known" (jñāpyate) are not different in meaning.
Does this occur prior to the inference from the cause, or at the time of the inference, or afterwards?

First of all, it does not [indicate the cause] prior [to its own cognition], for a cause does not indicate [its effect] by its mere existence, as that would lead to over-extension; rather, it indicates it through its own cognition. And the effect is not the indicator of this [cause].
It has been stated that [the reason] is not a cause;
for this very reason, it is also non-informative at the time of inference,
because it becomes informative only through its own cognition.

Furthermore, since two cognitions that exist simultaneously lack the relationship of cause and effect—just like the left and right horns of an ox—it follows that from the taste, which is the effect, its cause, the visible form, must be inferred. Thus, inference of an effect from a cause is something other than [the relations of] identity (*tādātmya*) and origination (*tadutpatti*); therefore, the establishment of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) does not occur through these two alone.
Furthermore, this inference of form from taste belongs to worldly people;
yet these individuals, whose eyes perceive only gross matter, do not discern the mutual distinctions between moments.
And failing to discern them, they are unable to infer the form—which is the cause of the taste—on the basis of its capacity to produce a manifested form.
Furthermore, it is not proper for investigators to alter the nature of the object of definition (lakṣya) merely to conform to the definition (lakṣaṇa);
for such [alterations] do not constitute reality for those who have transcended worldly conventions.
As they have said:
It is appropriate for investigators merely to follow established consensus;
they should not negate that which is established for all the world by means of a definition.
Thus it is said.
Moreover, today’s rising of the sun [is inferred] by yesterday’s rising of the sun, and the rising of the moon [is inferred] by the simultaneous swelling of the ocean.
In the case of the eighth lunar mansion at sunset or sunrise being seen by the observation of a central asterism,
there is neither a causal relationship nor identity; nevertheless, a relationship of indicator and indicated is observed.
Moreover, even if there were identity (*tādātmya*), how could there be the relationship of the signifier and the signified?
For it is not logical that the very same thing should be both the object (*karman*) and the agent (*kartṛ*),
since that [relationship] depends upon difference.

If it is argued that although *vṛkṣatva* (treeness) and *śiṃśapātva* (śiṃśapā-ness) are not distinct in the ultimate sense, there nevertheless exists the relationship of the signified and the signifier (*gamyagamakabhāva*) between these two conceptually differentiated states—due respectively to the exclusion and non-exclusion of other differences—that is not so;
for we shall demonstrate that the distinction between *vṛkṣatva* and *śiṃśapātva* is indeed real.
Furthermore, even a conceptual form, when subjected to analysis, is not distinct in the same way that it is not non-distinct.
Otherwise, it would follow that even a real entity is insubstantial;
for that which is merely conceptual lacks reality and thus cannot constitute a true essence.
Therefore, there is no identity between a real entity and those things established by conceptual construction.
Nor [do they arise] from one another;
for if that were the case, it would follow that conceptual constructions such as "existent," "substance," "earthen," "tree," and "śiṃśapā" would be synonyms.
It might be argued as follows:

although these [cognitions] delineate difference among things that are devoid of any distinction in conceptual construction, they nevertheless apprehend their mutual non-difference because they possess the form of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*);
for such coreferentiality would be impossible if non-difference were not delineated.
And thus, identity is established;
this is incorrect, for it has been stated that grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) does not prove the non-difference of entities.
For words such as "genus" (jāti) and so forth function with respect to a substance by taking genus and the like as their causal basis;
and since that substratum (adhikaraṇa) is one, they attain grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya),
yet they do not mutually mix the genus and the other factors either.
This same principle applies even to conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) whose objects are identical to those of words.

Therefore, it is established that where there is the relationship of the signified and the signifier (*gamyagamakabhāva*), there is no identity (*tādātmya*); and where there is identity, there is no relationship of the signified and the signifier.

However, for the sake of a fool who— having learned the linguistic usage of "śiṃśapā" but not yet having learned the linguistic usage of "tree"— has observed the word "tree" applied to a tall śiṃśapā and thus believes that height alone is the ground for the application of the word "tree," it is established merely by way of being a śiṃśapā that it should be treated as a tree;
for even in the case of a short śiṃśapā, it must be designated as a "tree."
Because "treeness" is invariably concomitant with "simśapā-ness" alone;
even there, if the conventional usage is what is to be proven, that [usage] is distinct from the simśapā, and thus there is no identity.
If it is argued that [the capacity for conventional usage] exists,
since that [capacity] is non-different from the *śiṃśapā* tree itself, there can be no relationship of indicator and indicated (*gamya-gamakabhāva*).
Furthermore, this has already been stated regarding the difference in exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*).
Therefore, the claim that the necessary connection [of logical reasons] consists in identity (*tādātmya*) and origination from that (*tadutpatti*) is merely a wishful thought.

Furthermore, the fourfold relation described by the Vaiśeṣikas—"this is the effect of that," "this is the cause of that," "this is related to that," and "this is inherent in the same object as that"—is inferential (Vai. Sū. 9.2.1).
Thus, since all [categories] are already subsumed here by the term "related" (*saṃbandhin*) alone, the mention of "subsidiary" (*śeṣa*) is redundant.
Nor is there an over-extension (*atiprasakti*) of what is denoted by the term "related" that needs to be excluded by the terms for "subsidiaries.
If that were the case, let there be only the terms for "subsidiaries"; what is the use of the term "related"?
For it is precisely from those [four types] that the various distinctions of relations are understood;
yet, if this were the case, the relation that serves as a factor for inference would not be fourfold,
whereas that is indeed accepted.
Furthermore, if the term "related thing" (*saṃbandhipada*) were taken to include every related thing whatsoever, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*).
Moreover, how could past rain be contradictory to the conjunction of wind and clouds which has not yet occurred?
For that [conjunction] is actually conducive to it. Likewise, future rain is not opposed to the conjunction of wind and clouds that has already occurred.
Thus, the victory of the mongoose over the snake is not contradictory to the fact that the snake was not [truly] defeated;
nor is this [victory] non-existent in relation to what is non-existent. However, for those things that are truly contradictory—
Among those, it does not possess even the characteristic mark of any one of them; rather, it is simply a rejection [of them].
By these very [reasons]— namely,
by those consisting of measure, cause, conjunction, opposition, and coexistence,
as well as by those such as owner and owned, or victim and executioner— the Sāṃkhyas' inference is sevenfold.
It should be understood that this [objection] has also been refuted.

Therefore, regardless of what that specific relation may be, it is logical that only that whose relation is intrinsic and necessary is the signifier (*gamaka*), while the other related term is the signified (*gamya*).
For instance, the relation of smoke and the like with fire and the like is intrinsic.
But this is not the case for fire and the like with respect to smoke and the like; for those [fires] are perceived even without smoke and the like,
whereas when they experience a connection with fuel and so forth, [they are perceived as such].
At that time, they are connected with smoke and so forth.
Therefore, the connection of fire and the like with wet fuel and so on is produced by adventitious conditions (*upādhi*) and is not inherent; consequently, it is not necessary.
However, the connection of smoke and the like with fire and the like is inherent.
Because that limiting condition (*upādhi*) is not perceived,

and because no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is observed anywhere, it is reasonable [to hold] that even pride (*māna*), being suspected as a limiting condition due to the absence of both proving and subverting means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)— since it is unfit for perception— obstructs the inherent nature (*svābhāvikatva*) of the connection.
"Since those who perceive no restrictive factor must necessarily entertain doubt," this needle of doubt—

having been granted such an opportunity by the transgression of the boundaries of worldly means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)— has found its opening; thus, there would be no place where one could act with the thought "this does not exist," because everywhere something is a ground for doubt regarding some kind of harm.
Furthermore, for prudent people, the apprehension of harm is a necessary factor for desisting from action;
for even when consuming wholesome food and drink, death and other calamities are observed to occur.
Therefore, one who maintains the worldly course according to authoritative tradition must entertain doubts in accordance with what is observed.
Nor does it arise from what has not been seen before; for doubt depends upon the recollection of specific characteristics, and it does not occur in the absence of such recollection.
Furthermore, memory cannot occur with respect to that which has never been experienced before.

Therefore, having searched diligently for a limiting condition (upādhi) and failing to perceive one, we conclude that it does not exist and thus determine that the relationship is intrinsic (svābhāvika).
It might be argued:
if an intrinsic connection were to exist between one thing and another through the assistance of something else, then everything would be intrinsically connected with everything else.
And thus, everything would be understood from everything.
Furthermore, if one thing has another as its effect, why does everything not become the effect of everything?
Because there is no distinction from otherness;
and consequently, that same over-extension (atiprasaṅga) would follow.
If it should be argued:
The intrinsic natures of entities are not to be questioned;
therefore, even though there is no distinction in their being "other," only certain things are causes and only certain things are effects.

But surely this questioning of intrinsic natures is exactly the same even for distinct things that do not stand in a cause-and-effect relationship, provided they are connected by an essential nature (*svabhāvapratibandha*).
Therefore, this is trivial.
Furthermore, what kind of intrinsic relationship is grasped by means of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
In the case of things related through perception, it is grasped by perception.
As it has been said: "The first [cognition] is the perception of the relationship between the mark (liṅga) and the bearer of the mark (liṅgin).

When one first perceives the connection between fire and smoke—both of which are accompanied by fuel—one then considers whether the relationship of both is innate (svābhāvika) or adventitious (aupādhika);
or whether the relationship of smoke is adventitious while that of fire is innate.
It is impossible to determine that fire has a conditional relationship with smoke while smoke has an intrinsic one;

for in that regard, since fire without wet fuel is seen in cases such as a red-hot iron ball even without smoke, it is concluded that its connection with smoke is conditioned by wet fuel and not intrinsic.

However, because a specific kind of smoke is not perceived without fire, and because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for postulating an unperceived limiting condition (*upādhi*), and because if doubt— which depends on the recollection of a specific instance— were to arise regarding something never before perceived, it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) and the cessation of the activity of prudent people, an intrinsic relation (*svābhāvika-sambandha*) is determined. This determination is not mental (*mānasa*).
If the mind were to operate toward external objects independently, it would follow that there would be no such thing as the blind or the deaf; furthermore,
if its operation depended upon repeated observation, it would result in the admission of another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa),
for the mind does not constitute mental perception merely by being the instrumental cause.
If that were the case, nothing would be mental,
because the mere act of cognition has the mind as its cause. However,

when a specific designation of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is applied in dependence upon its respective uncommon cause (*asādhāraṇakāraṇa*), then here too, since repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*) is the uncommon cause, it becomes a distinct means of knowledge.

Therefore, we consider it logical that the sense organ itself—aided by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by repeated observation—is the grasper of the natural relationship between smoke and fire, just as one perceives the true nature of the distinction between genuine gems.

In the same way, regarding those things whose relationships are known through other means of knowledge, those very means of knowledge themselves, aided by repeated observation according to their respective domains, should be inferred as the valid cognizers (*pramāṇa*) for grasping the natural relationship.
Furthermore, if reasons (*hetu*) that are intrinsically connected to their own probanda were to exist without those probanda, [they would lose their status as valid reasons].

Wherever those [reasons] are observed that, aided by logical reasoning (*tarka*), have their doubt regarding the presence of the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyavyatireka*) eliminated—such that they would otherwise fall away from their very nature—they necessarily present their own probandum.
Furthermore, it is not possible for sons of Maitra and the like to have an essential connection (*svābhāvikapratibandha*) with dark complexion and so forth;

because the specific transformation of food and drink exists as a limiting condition (*upādhi*) between the dark complexion and the relationship with being a son of Maitra, "being a son of Maitra" is not a valid indicator (*agamaka*).

By this, other relations based on limiting conditions (*upādhi*)—such as "the ripe fruits at the top of this tree [are connected to the tree] because they originate from that tree, like fallen fruits"—are also explained.
Therefore, everything is clear.
Now, one might ask: how is the final perception assisted by two past perceptions? To this, he says: "and by memory.
The word "and" (ca) has the sense of a reason (*hetu*).
Although the observation of the mark (*liṅga*) has passed away in its own form, [it is grasped through memory].
Nevertheless, the memory produced by those two assists [the cognition], because it is for this reason that one is assisted by them.
And assistance is indeed an instrument (*karaṇa*).

That cognition of the mark (*liṅga*) which is produced by the sense organ—assisted by the recollection of the connection (*sambandha-smṛti*)—and which is inseparably connected (*avinābhūta*) with its own probandum, is *parāmarśa*.
Thus it is called.
Furthermore, the fourth member of the syllogism, which has as its object precisely that kind of mark (liṅga), is called the application (upanaya).
Here he asks: "But what [is it]?"
The meaning of the term *anumāna* is not, first of all, inference (*anumiti*).
Indeed, the consideration of the mark (*liṅgaparāmarśa*) is not inference,
because it is the result of perception.
Therefore, it must be stated that [the suffix -ana] has the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*), in the sense of "that by which one infers.

And since that [instrument] has the mark (*liṅga*) as its object, while the action (*kriyā*) has the thing to be inferred (*liṅgin*) as its object, there is no relationship of action and instrument due to this discrepancy in their objects—this is the point.
The answer is: "it is inferred" (*anumīyate*).
With that very intention, he asks: "But what [is it]? The answer is: "Fire.
The questioner reveals his own intention: "But how can it have another object?"

The response of the proponent of the "partial" view (ekadeśin) is: "No, because there is no such restriction. An axe is wielded by an agent with reference to the tree as a whole, not with reference to its parts;
therefore, the axe has the tree as its object, not its parts as its object.
The sense is that bifurcation occurs in the parts, not in the tree, because the latter would thereby perish;
however, in some cases, it refers to that which is the object [of the action].
The conjunction with fire, which depends on heat, is the instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the rice grains;
the cooking (*pāka*), which consists in the transformation of color and other qualities, occurs in those very same grains.
By means of the rice grain, one indicates the pot.

Not only is there no rule that [the instrument] must have the same object as [the agent], but there is also no rule that the agent and the instrument must be distinct; thus, in the context of explaining this lack of restriction, he says: "In some cases, however... "Abiding" (sthiti) means either inherence (samavāya) in the parts or conjunction (saṃyoga) in a specific location.

Having stated such a lack of restriction by way of an example, he applies it to the case at hand: "In the same way, for that which has another object"—that is, the cognition (pramiti), which is the activity having fire as its object, [arises] from a means of knowledge (pramāṇa) having smoke as its object.
When knowledge whose object is fire alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he says there: "But in some cases...
He raises an objection: "But what [is the case]?
Here he states the reason: "Because it has already been cognized."
The answer is: "It is cognized. He analyzes this by saying, "as something to be abandoned.
The proponent of restriction (niyamavādī) refutes the view of the partial proponent of non-restriction (aniyamavādin) by saying, "That is not so."
He states the reason: "of the means of valid cognition and its fruit.

If the instrument had one object and the action had another object, then there would be the over-extension (atiprasaṅga) that even when an axe is applied to a *khadira* tree for the purpose of cutting, the act of cutting might occur in a *panasa* tree or elsewhere.
Even though the agent employs the axe with the tree as the intended object, nevertheless, this [axe] reaches not only the tree but also its parts; thus, it has those [parts] as its object as well.

Therefore, by means of the splitting of its own parts, it also produces the action of splitting directed toward the tree; thus, there is no lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) between the instrument and the result.

Likewise, although the cognition of the mark (*liṅga*) has the mark as its object, it has perception as its result, because that [mark], being connected to it, falls within the scope of mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*).
Because that [the possessor of the mark] cannot be defined without defining the mark (*liṅga*),
it is not the case that the cognition of the mark cannot be defined without the possessor of the mark.
Therefore, by virtue of being an integral part of the process of comprehension, the possessor of the mark is not the object of the cognition of the mark.
However, it is indeed the mark (liṅga) itself;
nevertheless, because it generates the cognition of the object that possesses the mark (liṅgin), the knowledge of the mark has the possessor of the mark as its object.
And there is no over-extension [of this definition].
Because it possesses an essential connection with the probandum, the indicator (liṅga) [is related] to that which is to be indicated (liṅgin).
Therefore, the status of being an object is twofold: by way of being a concomitant of cognition and by way of being that which is to be communicated.
In this regard, the distinction is that the former [refers] to the result, while the latter refers to the validity [of the means of knowledge].
Therefore, it has been well said: "Because no difference in object between the means of knowledge and its result is admitted."
However, the distinction between the agent and the instrument will be shown later.

Thus, having established the two analyses—*tāni te* (those [means] for him)—as being mutually dependent, he establishes the other two analyses—*tāni tad* (those [means] for that)—as being mutually dependent with the words: "But when...
The analysis is: the perception of the relationship between the mark (*liṅga*) and the marked (*liṅgin*), the perception of the immediate mark, and the recollection of that [relationship].
In this regard as well, when all doubts arise, this principle applies:
"The specific meaning is understood through the commentary, for there is no definition [of a rule] based on doubt"—this is the intended sense.

Now, if the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*) have the same object, then only that object which has already been made the object of the reflective cognition (*parāmarśajñāna*) should be made the object [of the resulting inference], and nothing else.

Since that [object] is precisely the object of the means of valid cognition, namely perception (*pratyakṣa*), what is the use of inference? With this intention, he asks: "But what [is it]?"—meaning, by that reflective cognition of the mark (*liṅga*) as qualified by those [other factors].
The answer: "The remaining object" (śeṣo 'rthaḥ).

That which is other than the mark (liṅga) known through perception is the bearer of the mark (liṅgin); and it has been stated that the consideration of the mark (liṅgaparāmarśa) has that as its object.
He asks: in the term "inference" (anumāna), what is the grammatical factor (kāraka)?
The sense is that it is only the instrumental factor (*karaṇa-kāraka*) that is appropriate as "that by which [something] is inferred" (*anumīyate 'nena*),
because that alone is preceded by the perception of the mark (*liṅga-darśana*) and the recollection of the [invariable] concomitance;

whereas inference (*anumiti*) is not "inference" (*anumāna*) [as the instrument], since it is the operation of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa-vyāpāra*), and thus is not the cause of that [cognition], being distinct from the instrumental factor and not preceded by it.
The answer is: it is either an entity (bhāva) or an instrument (karaṇa).
[Objection: But was it not stated that an entity is not a causal factor (kāraka)? To this he says: "When... It is not only substances and the like that possess the status of being causal factors.
Moreover, it applies to the operation as well;
otherwise, in the case of names of rituals such as *udbhid* and others, the instrumental case expressing the cause would not be heard,
as in "one should sacrifice with the *udbhid*" (*udbhidā yajeta*) or "one should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*darśapūrṇamāsābhyāṃ yajeta*), and so forth.
For even that which is already established can serve as the cause for the cultivation of its result;
likewise, it is possible for a cognition of fire that has already been established to function as the cause for cognitions of avoidance and so forth.

And according to this interpretation, regarding the phrase "preceded by that," at the time of determining the connection with avoidance and so forth, there is first the perception of the mark (liṅga), namely the nature of fire.
Now, one should consider as a single unit these three: inference as the second [member], the recollection of the relation, and the resulting consideration (*parāmarśa*).
For the consideration of the mark (*liṅgaparāmarśa*) consists in the thought, "And so, this fire being inferred is preceded by that [mark]."
Therefore, the cognition that "fire is to be accepted because it performs functions such as burning and cooking" is the fruit of inference;
and thus, its being preceded by that [perception] is also established—this is the intended meaning.
He states the fruit according to the view that the instrument (*karaṇa*) is the causal factor (*kāraka*): "when it is the instrument."
Here he reflects on the word "liṅga" (the mark):
doubt arises from observing a common property, namely that [the mark] is the cause of inference preceded by that [perception].
In this regard, he states the opinion of one who is like a teacher: "First, some [say]... and so forth.

Even when the other [factors] are present, because memory is absent, inference does not arise; therefore, memory itself is inference, while the others are merely its auxiliaries—this is the meaning. He states another opinion with the words "another [says]."

The meaning is that even when the other [factors] are present, inference does not arise without the consideration of the logical mark (liṅgaparāmarśa); therefore, the consideration of the logical mark itself is inference, as assisted by the others.
He states his own view: "We, however," and so forth.

The meaning is that the relationship of subordinate and principal cannot be distinguished through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), because those two are equal in all cases. To the question, "In that case, does the relationship of subordinate and principal not exist at all? he replies: "Principal... [and so forth].
The meaning is that neither positive concomitance (*anvaya*) nor negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) are effective here, nor is any other logical principle;
thus he asks: "But what is it here?
and provides the answer: "Immediate succession" (*ānantarya*).
Nothing here is hidden.
He raises the objection of over-extension with the words "yadi" (if).
[The opponent objects: "Let it be that the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) preceded by two perceptions constitutes inference;
by that too, the remaining object will be inferred. To this he replies: the meaning is that it is the cause of memory, not the cause of inference.
He refutes this, saying: "This is not a fault.
Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is qualified cognition; and the qualification is its difference from memory, for a cognition produced by the contact of the sense organ with its object is not memory.
Because that [cognition] arises solely from its own formative impressions (*saṃskāra*) and does not arise from anything else,
its own cause is thereby distinguished by that cognition;
for in the *Pratyakṣasūtra*, the word "from which" (*yataḥ*) is to be supplied.

Therefore, even here, what is intended is a cognition other than memory that is qualified by its own specific cause. And since a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), even though preceded by perception, is not the cause of such a cognition, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) does not apply to it; this is the meaning. He excludes the undesirable consequence regarding a definitive judgment (*nirṇaya*) when its fruit has not yet been produced, stating: "in a definitive judgment."

The definition of the specific means of valid cognition (*viśeṣapramāṇa*), preceded by the general definition of the means of valid cognition as implied in the *Vibhāga-sūtra*, proceeds in dependence upon that [general definition]. It cannot operate toward a mere ascertainment (*nirṇaya*) that is not yet a means of valid cognition because its fruit has not been produced;
rather, the point is that an ascertainment whose fruit has been produced is indeed a means of valid cognition itself.
Because it delimits its own object, the fruit is the very act of delimitation, which is itself the delimiting agent.
It is a suffix used in the sense of the base word itself (a svārthika suffix).
Out of respect for the weight of the meaning, the author of the Vārttika, having set forth the phrase "of three kinds" from the Sūtra, explains it as follows: "It is of three kinds.
He defines the *anvayavyatirekin* (the reason that possesses both positive and negative concomitance) with the word "therein":
the intended establishment [of the probandum] is the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).
Arising from that same class is positive concomitance (*anvaya*);
non-occurrence in the dissimilar class is negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

Since it must be shown as being excluded from both mere positive concomitance and mere negative concomitance, it is the "positive-negative" (*anvayavyatirekin*) [reason]. Thus, although the two forms of the reason—namely, having an unsublated object (*abādhitaviṣayatva*) and not being countered by an opposing argument (*asatpratipakṣatva*)—are common to all three types of reasons, [the anvayavyatirekin is distinguished by its dual concomitance].
They have not been shown;

for without the intended cognition, it is impossible to perceive positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), namely, the occurrence in those of the same class and the exclusion from those of a different class. Therefore, the intended [subject] is employed.
And by way of that discussion, its being a property of that [subject] (*taddharmatā*), though common to all three types of reasons, has also been demonstrated.
He states an example of this with the word "as follows" (*yathā*).
Since the reason "because of being perceptible" (*pratyakṣatvāt*) exists in the case of the eternal self (*ātman*), he says "by means of external instruments" (*bāhyakaraṇa*).
Even so, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to universals and particulars such as "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*); therefore, he says "possessing universals and particulars" (*sāmānyaviśeṣavattve*).
Nevertheless, since there is a deviation [of the definition] in the case of atoms—which are external objects of perception for yogins—it is said: "for those such as ourselves.

Thus, this [reason] is concomitant with both positive and negative instances (*anvaya-vyatirekin*), as it is present in eternal things like space and absent in non-eternal things like jars. He defines the purely positive (*anvayin*) reason: "the positive," etc.
Regarding the phrase "devoid of the opposing side" (*vipakṣahīna*):
by means of the absence of the opposing side, he demonstrates the absence of any exclusion from it.
It has been stated that non-existence is determined by two positive entities, not by a single one.
For that reason, since the very counter-instance from which there would be a cessation does not exist, how could there be a cessation?
For everything other than the subject (pakṣa) is indeed a similar instance (sapakṣa). If it is argued that there is no cessation?
If it is argued that the reason (hetu) must nevertheless function there, because its functioning consists in the negation of non-functioning—

this is a fine saying: "How can one even suspect that something which lacks any designation (nirupākhyam) and for which even the status of being the locus of absence is impossible, could be the locus of existence?"
Indeed, no sensible person suspects that one who is about to die and is incapable even of swallowing water would be capable of eating a fried cake.
Therefore, do existence and non-existence not consist in the mutual absence of one another, such that the affirmation of one would occur through the negation of the other?
True; wherever one of these two is negated or affirmed, there the affirmation or negation of the other necessarily follows.
However, in this context, there is no negation of anything from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
Nor is a reason’s negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) that is devoid of any designation (*nirupākhya*) being negated here.
But is it not the case that the statement "that which is devoid of designation is the locus of negation" contradicts its own practice?
And we do not, in reality, negate the absence of the reason or the reason itself in that which is indefinable (*nirūpākhya*), nor do we establish a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with it.
Indeed, this [indefinable thing], being incapable of being an object of any cognition whatsoever, is of no use anywhere;
for if it were to have utility, it would not be indefinable.
What, then, is the meaning of this statement: "How is there no negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of the reason in that which is indefinable (*nirūpākhya*)?
Or rather, what is the meaning of this "negative concomitance of the reason in the indefinable" that you have uttered?
Indeed, for those whose speech lacks heart, the rebuttals likewise lack heart.

For there is a worldly proverb that "the offering must correspond to the recipient," and it has been established during the day of critical examination in the section on *anyathākhyāti* that things never before perceived cannot fall within the scope of conceptual construction.
Furthermore, since the distinction [between the subject and the property] has a conceptualized object and is itself conceptual, it is not a constituent part of inference.

For a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) endowed with an intrinsic nature is capable of producing the fruit that is the knowledge of reality, but not by virtue of an accomplishment of a conceptualized form,
because such [conceptual accomplishment] is easily found everywhere.
Furthermore, it will be demonstrated that inference has reality as its object.

Therefore, whether there is an absence of the reason from an indefinable counter-example (*vipakṣa*), or an absence [of the probandum] from it, or the occurrence of the reason within it, those with refined sensibilities ought to remain silent;
yet this does not imply that the reason lacks the capacity to prove [the conclusion].
For it is not the mere fact that there is a negative concomitance (vyatireka) that makes something a prover;
otherwise, even the "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa) reason would be a prover.
Rather, it is by virtue of possessing an intrinsic connection (svābhāvikasaṃbandha) with its own probandum.

And since that [pervasion] can be known through positive concomitance alone—provided it is free from any limiting condition (upādhi)—just as it can be known through both positive and negative concomitance, there is no need for negative concomitance here.

However, if there is the possibility of a counter-example (vipakṣa), then one must employ the apprehension of negative concomitance even there, in order to dispel the suspicion of the reason's presence in such cases; thus all is clear.
He states an example: "as follows" (*yathā*).
In our own system, however, [the following] should be understood: "The particular is denotable because it is an object of knowledge (*prameya*), like the universal";
"atoms, space, and so forth are perceptible to someone because they are objects of knowledge, like a jar," and so on.

Because everything that is divided by the distinction between existence and non-existence is included, each according to its own nature, within either the similar class (*sapakṣa*) or the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), there is no absence of a dissimilar instance (*vipakṣābhāva*).
He defines the purely negative reason (*vyatirekin*) with the words "the purely negative" (*vyatirekī*).

The author of the *Vārttika* will explain this purely negative reason on the occasion of explaining the definition of the members of the syllogism (*hetvavayava*); therefore, it is not explained here.

Having thus defined and explained that [the inference] is of three kinds, he now explains it as a single coherent statement beginning with "pūrvavat" (based on what precedes), or alternatively, as "trividham" (of three kinds).
Because the statement of the probandum (*sādhya*) was previously established in all three modes, that which has the probandum as its prior [basis] by way of being its locus is "pūrvavat.
However, even the reason "atoms are impermanent because they possess odor, like a jar" would [otherwise] be such a case.

For there is indeed something to be proven even for that [reason], since the impermanence of the atoms of earth is also intended to be established; therefore, he says: "by way of pervasion" (*vyāptyā*).
There is a probandum for the possession of odor, but not by way of pervasion.

Because it exists as a function of the earth-element alone, that [property] is absent in four atoms; since the probandum has already been accounted for, "the remainder" refers to something other than that which is of the same class as it,
meaning it is similar by way of the generality of the probandum.
This is what he says: "the probandum and that which belongs to its class."
Having analyzed the words, he states the meaning: "the name is as before.
He explains by including [the category] "not perceived through general observation" (*sāmānyato'dṛṣṭam*): "and through general observation" (*sāmānyataśca*).
And thus, an inference whose object is sublated as well as one that is "equal in force" (*prakaraṇasama*) would [otherwise] be [valid]; therefore, he says: "by the word 'and'.
In the *Vārttika*, the word "and" has already indicated the state of having no counter-inference (*asatpratipakṣatva*).

By that word "and" occurring in the *Sūtra*, it is stated that two characteristics—the state of having an unsublated object (*abādhitaviṣayatva*) and the state of having no counter-inference (*asatpratipakṣatva*)—are conjoined.
Now, one might object that if this is so, then even the threefold reason would possess five characteristics; to this he says: "In this way.

What is meant is this: having established as constant [the requirements] that the object is not sublated (*abādhitaviṣaya*), that there is no counter-argument (*asatpratipakṣa*), and that it is "like the former" (*pūrvavat*), "the remainder" (*śeṣavat*) constitutes one variety, and "perceived through general correlation" (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*) constitutes the second.
And the third is *śeṣavat-sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*;
thus, inference is of three kinds.
Among these, two possess four characteristics.
"One has five characteristics.
Having thus explained the Sūtra according to his own view, he explains it according to the view of the author of the Bhāṣya with the words "Or rather" (atha vā).
He explains its essential nature in order to raise an objection with the word "therein" (tatra).
The cause is prior to the effect. That which exists as the object (*viṣaya*) for the inferential cognition that reflects upon it is "pūrvavat" (the "prior-like"); this is the meaning.

He challenges [this definition] by means of an alternative analysis: "If, first of all..."—the sense being that [if this were so], there would be the unwanted consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [everything] being an inference.
Fearing an over-extension of the argument, he proposes an alternative hypothesis with the words "But then...
He refutes it with "This too...
and adds another refutation with "And because a cause is observed."
The meaning is that a reason whose locus is unestablished is not a means of cognition.
He refutes this with "no";
the sense is that neither of these two [conditions] is accepted.
What, then, is accepted? To this he says: "But the effect... He extends this same principle to other cases as well with the word "thus" (evam).
He asks: "How?"
The answer is: "Of the two.
By the word "prior," which denotes the cause, the effect is also implied by virtue of being its correlative.
Therefore, since both have been implied, the explanation is that [the relationship] exists by way of inference through the application of the cause.
He states the example with the words "the example" (*udāharaṇam*).
Although a mere cause may deviate from the production of an effect,
nevertheless, one must be discerning regarding that kind of cause which does not so deviate.
Otherwise, even mere smoke would deviate from the existence of fire, and thus a specific kind of smoke would not be a means of cognition.
Furthermore, regarding the inference of color from taste, we have already established for the Vaināśikas that this is an inference of an effect from its cause.
Moreover, since a cloth is produced immediately after the final conjunction of the threads, it is possible there as well to infer the effect from the cause.

Indeed, when this person— having already awakened the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) from another source and possessing the recollection of pervasion (*vyāpti*)— perceives, through sensory contact, that "it is thus" with respect to the final thread at the very moment an action has arisen in the other contiguous threads,
at that same time there is the disjunction (*vibhāga*) from the action; this constitutes one point in time.

Now, when the destruction of the prior conjunction occurs due to disjunction, then, through the act of reflection (*parāmarśa*), there arises the production of an inference that "this action is necessarily characterized by the cloth [to be produced]"; this constitutes one moment.
Then, there is the conjunction of the final thread with the [other] threads.
Now, regarding the production of the cloth:
therein occurs the production of color and so forth;
then there is the direct perception. Thus, direct perception occurs in the fourth moment, subsequent to the production of the inference.
If, however, it is maintained that the observation occurs immediately after the production of the action, even so, perception arises in the third moment; thus, inference is not out of place.
Moreover, a deaf person, having struck the surface of a drum with his own hand, infers without hesitation its effect—the sound—from the very cause of the impact, which is the sound itself.
In this manner, other inferences from cause to effect should also be inferred accordingly.
He states the example of *śeṣavat* (inference by remainder) with the words "of the river," etc. He raises an objection: "But how [is this so]? He replies: "No."

Inference (*anumāna*) is that by which something is inferred, such as the swelling of a river; however, it is not the case that past rain is being inferred from a specific flood, for at the time of the inference, it is impossible to ascertain that the rain has already ceased.

Nor can it be present, because its passing away is possible even at that time. Likewise, future [non-existence] is also merely doubtful due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) to establish or refute it.
Therefore, since the three times cannot be ascertained, inference is untenable; to this he says: "It will be."
For the priority of the cause over its effect can indeed be ascertained by means of the effect as a logical mark (*liṅga*).
Therefore, doubt regarding whether [the cause] is past and so forth brings about a deficiency [in the argument].
The phrase "anyone whatsoever" intends those who are capable [of such cognition].
And that [reason] is pervaded by the certainty of the effect beforehand; this is the meaning.
The example of *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* given by the author of the Bhāṣya is difficult to understand and is actually included within the category of *śeṣavat*.
This is because here too, one infers the motion— the cause— of the sun from its arrival at another location, which is its effect.
The threefold nature of inference does not follow merely from this [classification], because it would result in an infinite number of types due to the infinity of possible examples.

Therefore, the author of the Vārttika, disapproving of the commentator's (Bhāṣyakāra) explanation, provides another explanation and offers a different example, beginning with: "That which is called 'perceived through generality' (sāmānyatodṛṣṭa)..."
A property (*dharma*) qualified by a probans (*sādhanadharma*) which is invariably concomitant with the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is understood as the means of cognition (*gamaka*).
For it is a property qualified by a reason (*hetu*) that is the cognizer, and it is a property qualified by the property one wishes to know that is the object of cognition (*gamya*).
As they have said:
"That very same thing, being of a dual nature, is held to be both the object to be known and the means of knowing;
by its unestablished part it is the object to be known, and by its established part it is the indicator."

Thus, the state of being inseparable (*avinābhāvitva*)— that is, the state of being intrinsically connected (*svabhāvapratibaddhatva*)— is common to all reasons (*hetu*). In this context, with the intention of expressing the non-difference between the property (*dharma*) and the locus (*dharmin*), the reason itself is stated as the general characteristic.

Inference (*anumāna*) is the perceived form of the subject (*dharmin*) as delimited by a cause that is generally and invariably concomitant; this is "inference from what is generally observed" (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭam anumānam*).

The suffix *-tas* here is used in the sense of the third case (*tṛtīyā*). This [type of inference] also brings about the understanding of the *pūrvavat* and *śeṣavat* types; however, due to the proximity of those specific terms, it sets aside those two according to the maxim of the "cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*) and applies itself elsewhere.
This has been stated as "by that which does not stand in the relation of cause and effect.
He provides an illustration: "as by the crane."
Having set forth the example provided by the author of the Bhāṣya, he objects with the words "others, however.
He refers to that [example] as "one who possesses motion.
He points out the reason: "because it has reached the conditions for perception."

For the "attainment of the conditions for perception" (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpti*)—which consists in the inherence in a single substratum with a specific magnitude and form of an action—is the fitness for direct perception (*pratyakṣopalabdhiyogyatā*). He answers: "This is not so. The sun possesses motion toward another location because, while being a substance, it is not an object of the notions of decrease or increase, and it is perceived by one facing east.

And because of its connection with the location facing it, even for one who has not yet taken a step toward it, [the object] becomes the object of that cognition after turning around, like a gem or similar thing;
for if it is argued that "because it is the object of that cognition," there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) by way of a post standing in front,
since that too becomes the object of recognition while remaining in that very place.
To exclude that [possibility], the word "parivṛtya" (having turned around) was stated.
Nevertheless, there is still deviation due to qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth;
to exclude that, the qualification "provided it is a substance" (*dravyatve sati*) is added.
Nevertheless, there is a deviation [from the rule] in the case of lamps and the like, which perish very quickly;
to exclude those, the qualification "provided they are not objects of cognitions of decrease or increase" is added.
Even so, there is a deviation in the case of a pillar standing behind [an object].
To exclude that [possibility], the qualification "being perceivable while facing east" is added;
and "perceivability" here means being the object of perception,
which is intended to be past in this context.
Otherwise, there would be a deviation [in the rule] due to the Snowy Mountain (Himālaya), which reaches the tides of both the eastern and western oceans;
for although this mountain also, upon revolving, transcends the state of being perceived by one who possesses that cognition, it is nevertheless perceived at that time by another person.
There is an asymmetry in that the orb of the sun, while hanging upon the crest of the western mountain (*astācala*), is not within the range of perception for anyone in the east;
nevertheless, if the observer himself, having approached from the front of a palace situated before him and facing west, stands behind it,
then there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) from the stated definition of the reason (*hetu*).

To exclude that [possibility], the qualification "one whose foot-movement has not yet arisen" is added. The ablative case in the phrase "because of connection with the space facing it" is used in the sense of an elided *lyap* suffix (i.e., *abhimukhadeśāt* = *abhimukhadeśam upagamya*). Thus, it refers to one for whom a foot-movement directed toward the space facing oneself has not yet arisen.
The sense is that, with reference to him, this person, moving on foot, is behind the palace. He states another means for reaching another place— namely, "to another place"—
and it should also be understood as "the non-destruction of existence."
However, as for those who cannot tolerate this succession of inferences and instead maintain that the directions are perceptible,
and who seek to inform one who is in disagreement by means of inference, he sets forth their view with the words "But some... and so on.
He refutes this, saying "And that is not so.
By one who suspects that even formless things such as the self's own pleasure are perceptible, it is stated [in the text] "by the external instrument.
He asks: "How then?"
The answer is: "Direction and place," etc.

The meaning is that because the pointing with a finger is established through other means (anyathāsiddha), there is no natural necessary connection (svābhāvika-pratibandha) between the pointing and the perception of direction.
This might be so;

[one might ask] why it is said that [the cognition occurs] "in relation to those connected with direction and place" when direction itself is not perceived? To this he says: "by means of the sun. To analyze that, he says: "this is the east."

Furthermore, this perception [of the sun]— from its rising until its setting, regarding the movement of the solar orb from one location to another— is produced as something distinct from the operation of the sense faculties, despite the fact that it arises through a series of inferential arguments (daṇḍakānumāna) such as "if it were not a perceptible substance," and so forth;

therefore, let it be granted that space, direction, and the like are not objects of direct perception, nevertheless, those very same [senses] [perceive] the solar orb situated in the midst of its intensely clear mass of rays radiating all around.

It is logical that the conjunctions and disjunctions of those perceptible [rays] with the perceptible solar disc will themselves be perceptible, since the divisions of the portions of the rays occupy perceptible locations.
However, it should be understood that this was not stated because it is too obvious; rather, another unexplored path has been shown for the sake of instructing the student.

Thus, inference from touch based on color, or the inference of "treeness" based on hearing the term "śiṃśapā," and so forth, should be understood as being subsumed under *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* (inference based on general observation).
He states another explanation according to his own view: "Alternatively, it is threefold. He divides that [threefold nature] as follows: "The well-known" (*prasiddha*).
Even though it exists in one part of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśa*), it is established (*siddha*).
The meaning is that [the reason] is established as pervading the entire subject (*pakṣavyāpaka*) by excellence.

Although the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is completed within five or four characteristics of the logical mark (*liṅga*), and thus all forms of the mark are subsumed under invariable concomitance alone, nevertheless, here, by means of the two terms "well-known" (*prasiddha*) and "existent" (*sat*), two [characteristics] are subsumed; then, according to the maxim of the "cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*), setting those aside, he subsumes [the remaining three]: absence from the counter-subject (*vipakṣavyatireka*), the absence of a counter-balancing argument (*asatpratipakṣatva*), and the state of having an unsublated object (*abādhitaviṣayatva*).
Here too, there is a connection between four or five types of evidence (*liṅga*) as far as possible.

By this sequence, the disagreements of the proponents of inference regarding its essential nature (*svarūpa*), number, and result have been refuted. Among those, the phrase "preceded by that" (*tatpūrvakam*) addresses the disagreement concerning its essential nature.

By the power of the etymological definition of the designation "inference" (anumāna), disagreement regarding its result is [resolved]. By the statement "it is threefold," disagreement regarding its number—specifically by excluding numbers fewer or greater than three—is refuted.

If someone were to argue that because internal subdivisions are infinite, inference is impossible to define due to that infinity, then in order to refute that, the threefold nature of inference is stated; thus he states another intended meaning of the word "threefold" with the words "or rather" (*atha vā*).
The meaning is: since it is restricted by its threefold nature, it is therefore possible to define.
"Sound is impermanent because it is produced"—this [reason] exists only in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).
"Sound is impermanent because it is not preceded by our perception"—this [reason] both exists and does not exist in the similar instances.
Thus, this is the two-fold *anvaya-vyatirekin* (positive-negative) reason.
Likewise, the positive (anvayin) [reason] is also of two kinds. Among these, that which exists only in the similar instances (sapakṣa) is as follows:
for example, "atoms and so forth are perceptible to someone, because they are objects of cognition, like a jar."
Likewise, it exists or does not exist in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), just as [the reason] exists in that very same probandum (*sādhya*) like a jar and so forth.
The difference in time (*kālabheda*) refers to the three times (*traikālya*).
The difference in persons (*puruṣabheda*) consists of those who have understood, those who have not understood, those who are doubtful, and those who are mistaken.

Having previously restated "pūrvavat" as "like the established" (*siddhavat*) and provided its illustration, [the author] now states its true meaning by refuting the appearance of its meaning through a series of questions— beginning with "It has been said 'pūrvavat'.
The meaning is that there would otherwise be a contradiction with the Bhāṣya.
He applies the explanation of "pūrvavat" (as before) here as well to "śeṣavat" (the remainder).
He extends [the principle of] "sāmānyatodṛṣṭa" (knowledge based on general observation) by stating, "in this same way, in the cases of śeṣavat and the others.
Alternatively, "pūrvavat" refers to the Bhāṣya.
Its meaning is as follows: it exists in the same manner as the preceding [case], thus it is "pūrvavat" (like the previous).
And since the suffix -vat is used in the sense of equality of action, the equality of action is thereby demonstrated.
Regarding the phrase "wherein":
previously, the perception of one thing was observed along with the perception of another in the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*);
the expression "as previously, of the two that have become perceptible" is an illustration of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in general.

Thus, by the observation of one property (the probans) among two properties in the subject of the thesis (the minor term), there occurs an inference—namely, the cognition—of the other property, which is the property to be proven; this constitutes the equality of the action.
Having thus restated this Bhāṣya, he explains it with the words "Or rather" (*atha vā*).

In this regard, Dignāga, having refuted both the inference of a distinct property in the form of fire from smoke and the inference of a relationship between fire and its location, established the inference of a location qualified by fire. Thus he said:
"Some hold that a distinct property is the object of cognition because of the non-deviation of the mark."
Some maintain that there is a relationship [between the two], because the property and the property-bearer are already established.
If the logical mark (liṅga) is well-known in relation to the property (dharma), what else is measured by it?
Or, if it is known in relation to the subject (dharmī), why is that very subject not itself the object of inference?
Even if there were a relation, the two [factors] would not exist; the genitive case-ending would be heard [only] in that which possesses it.
Since it is not denotable because it is already assisted [by the word], it cannot be connected with gender.
For a logical mark (liṅga) is not perceived as a property of a relation;
rather, the meaning is that it is conjoined with a location.
In that regard, the non-deviation of the logical mark is observed through its property elsewhere.

"In that case, that which is well-known will lead one to understand the subject (dharmin) as being endowed with it. Having introduced the interpretations refuted by Dignāga, as well as other alternative interpretations, and having presented the interpretation established by Dignāga, [the author] refutes them: "But others [say]... because the relationship between property (dharma) and subject (dharmin) is untenable; for it is by means of the property that the subject is to be understood.
The meaning is that otherwise there would be an over-extension (*atiprasakti*).
And the sense is "by way of the location's own nature.
He raises an objection: "But even this... [etc.]
He refutes this, saying: "And that is not so.
Is it some unspecified location possessing fire that is to be proven, or is it a specific location possessing smoke?
Regarding that, he states the refutation of the previous position: "Because it does not have that property" (*ataddharmāt*).
The meaning is that whatever place is established as possessing fire does not necessarily have smoke as its property.
And he says: "Nor [is this] from fire," because this [fire] is already established (*siddhatvāt*).
He entertains a second alternative— namely, "this"—
and refutes it with: "No, because of that."
He analyzes the doubt with the words "deśa" (place), etc.
He analyzes the refutation with the words "na hyayam" (for this one does not), etc. For this proponent Dignāga does not perceive a specific place as the locus of the smoke.
For in his view, there is no such thing as a composite whole called "mountain" upon which smoke could be perceived;
rather, the mountain consists of atoms that are extremely subtle and beyond the reach of the senses.
Smoke, likewise, is of the same nature.
As he will state: "Because the whole is not established, there is no apprehension of all [its parts]" (2.1.34).

Even for those who hold that the whole possesses spatial extension and is perceptible, the point is that once one perceives a streak of smoke reaching the clouds as it moves through the sky, it is impossible to infer those parts whose locations have not been perceived.
He raises an objection with the words "by way of invariable concomitance" (avinābhāvena).
He analyzes that very point with the words "nevertheless" (athāpi).
He refutes it with the words "that is not so" (tan na).
He conceptualizes: "between fire and smoke.
He takes recourse in the relation of cause and effect: "let it be so. He refutes it: "that is not so."
For fire is inferred from smoke;
however, the existence of an effect is not pervaded by the existence of its efficient cause.
Indeed, it is not the case that whenever or wherever there is a cloth, [there must be a weaver].
Or, in that case, there would be a weaver;
nor [is it established] by the existence of the non-inherent cause,
for it is not the case that whenever there is conjunction, there is action.

Therefore, it must be stated that the effect is inseparably connected (*avinābhāva*) with its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*). To this, the following objection is raised: "Because it does not reside therein" (*atadvṛttitvāt*).
He refutes the inseparable connection based on inherence in a single object (*ekārthasamavāya*) by stating: "Not in one" (*naika*).
For "inherence in a single object" is twofold:
either the inherence of a single object, or inherence in a single object.
Therein, he refutes the first alternative with the words "by those two.
For if some single object were produced by these two—fire and fuel—then it would inhere in them;
however, this is not the case. This is the meaning.
He refutes the second alternative with the words "na ca tāv" (nor are those two). [Objection:
Then are fire and smoke simply unrelated?
In that case, there would be a contradiction with empirical experience.
To this he says: "merely a relation" (saṃbandhamātram).
This means conjunction (saṃyoga). If that is so, then that very thing [is the case].
Let this be understood; therefore he says: "That too. He asks: "How?
The answer: "If, first of all..."
He formulates the argument:
"There is a connection between fire and smoke, because of smoke. He refutes it: "That is not so, because it is unestablished."
By this, he demonstrates the inconclusiveness [of the reason].
He anticipates another possible connection—namely, "like color and touch"—[arguing that they coexist in a substance].
For in the Buddhist tenet, there is no such thing as a "substance" (dravya) in which color and touch are inherent (samaveta).
The meaning is that fire and smoke are likewise necessarily concomitant because they depend upon a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
He refutes this, saying: "Not for both."

By refuting the co-occurrence of both [fire and smoke], the statement "where there is smoke, there is fire" is also rejected, because that too is a specific instance of co-occurrence; thus he says: "where there is smoke.
Since there is no other alternative, he concludes: "and not..."
He raises an objection with the words "In the world," and he refutes it with "It does not exist.
For instance, where a streak of smoke situated on a mountain slope is seen rising continuously, [it is perceived as such].
In that case, it is a matter of common worldly experience that the very place itself, as qualified by that [smoke], is what is inferred; so what more need be said here?

However, where, due to the great distance of that smoke, its abundance is such that the place is not seen, but the smoke alone is observed licking the sky and, as it were, smearing the circle of the clouds—

In that case, because one is weary of the effort required for inference based on location, it is the very particular smoke being perceived that is established as possessing fire by means of those properties—such as continuity, upward movement, and so forth—which are inherent in the same substrate as the universal "smokeness. Thus he says: "by a particular smoke" (*dhūmaviśeṣeṇa*).
A "particular" (*viśeṣa*) is that by which something is distinguished; here, it refers to continuity, upward movement, and the like.
The meaning is that by means of that [qualification], smoke—which might otherwise deviate from fire merely because it is smoke—is distinguished as being invariably concomitant with fire.
The remainder of the text has its meaning self-evident.
"Residual" (*śeṣavat*) means "by elimination" (*pariśeṣa*).
Since "substantiality" (*dravyatva*) and "action-ness" (*karmatva*) have already been ruled out in the case of sound, "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*)—which is distinct from those two—is the remainder.
That [inference] which has this as its object to be established is [the inference] "by elimination."
That [argument] is like the "residue" (śeṣavat).
In that regard, sound is not a substance, because it inheres in a single substance.
For substance is indeed of two kinds.
It is both without substance and with multiple substances.
That which is without substance is the atom and so forth;
that which has multiple substances is the pot and so forth.
Sound, however, has a single substance as its substratum;
therefore, it is not a substance like color and so forth,
nor is it motion, because it is the cause of another sound.
This commentary raises an objection with the words "action" (karma), and answers it with "no.
It then demonstrates another meaning of this [objection] with the words "because it originates from that which is of the same class" (samānajātīyārambhakatvāt).
That which initiates an effect of its own kind is not *karman*,
just as color and other qualities are not;
furthermore, because it is an effect, sound possesses an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*).
And since earth and the other elements are negated therein, space (*nabhas*) is its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*).
Nor does this [sound] pervade space, because it would follow that it would be perceived everywhere;
therefore, it is non-pervasive.
The auditory faculty (*śrotra*) is the ether (*nabhas*) situated near the ear-cavity (*karṇaśaṣkulī*).
Sound is inherent (*samaveta*) in that region of ether through the mediation of contact with the palate and other [articulatory organs].
Furthermore, the auditory faculty functions by reaching its object (*prāpyakārin*).
Furthermore, that [sound] does not reach a portion of space obstructed by the speaker's mouth;
nor can sound, being a non-substance (*adravya*), travel and come into contact with the ear.

Therefore, it is established that—by way of the sequence of waves and ripples, through a succession of initiations of other sounds in spaces immediately adjacent to its own location—it perceives the sound produced at the location of the ear, because it initiates [sounds] of its own kind.
However, this example of *pariśeṣa* (presumption by elimination) is not to be respected;
for *pariśeṣa* is merely another name for the *vyatirekin* (negative-only) inference.

This [inference], on the other hand, is both positive and negative (*anvayavyatirekī*), because—given its exclusion from being a substance or an action—the non-difference from "existent" and so forth exists in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), such as color and the like.
Because [desire and so forth] are absent in the counter-example, such as the universal (sāmānya) and so on;
therefore, the example by elimination (pariśeṣa) for proving that desire and the rest are dependent upon a self (ātmatantratā) is to be understood.
And this he will state immediately hereafter.
Having restated the commentary beginning with "that which is called *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*," he raises an objection:
"How then does inference operate here?
The meaning is that it is because no connection of any inferential mark (*liṅga*) is observed with something that is eternally beyond the senses.
And as for the term "contradicted":
would that [subject] indeed be established by its own nature, which is absolutely unperceived, or rather as a qualification of a perceived locus?
In the former case, there is a contradiction, because it has not been previously unperceived; in the latter case, it is doubtful,
for doubt depends upon the recollection of specific characteristics and cannot possibly exist regarding something that was never previously perceived as possessing such properties.
The point is that no one indeed has any doubt regarding a substance on account of its being like the seventh flavor. He provides the resolution: "Not [of that which is] functioning as a qualifier.
To begin with, it is not inferred in its own essential form (svarūpa), whereby the statement "it is not unperceived" would be contradicted.
