However, it serves as a qualifier for the subject (*dharmin*) that has been perceived.
Nor does this result in a lack of distinction between all forms of inference,
because this [inference] is never perceived by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) by people such as ourselves with respect to the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*).

The meaning is that, however, because it is possible to grasp the essential connection (*svābhāvikapratibandha*) of the probans through something of the same class observed in the subject of the example—either by direct perception or by another means of knowledge—he states an illustration: "as [the self is known] by means of desire and so forth. He analyzes this as follows: "Desire and the rest are indeed the subjects (*dharmin*), and they are perceived by mental direct perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*)."
The self (*ātman*) is their qualifier. Why? Because it is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) as a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatayā*);
therefore, it follows that desire and the rest are to be proven as qualified by the self (*ātmaviśiṣṭāḥ*).
He demonstrates the property to be proven (sādhanadharma) residing in that [subject] by stating, "the quality-ness (guṇatva) of desire and so forth.
Now, one might raise the objection: "It has been stated that there can be no subject of doubt regarding a property to be proven that has never before been perceived;

and since the self (ātman) has never been perceived, how can desires and so forth, as qualified by it, be the subject of a formal argument (nyāya)? Anticipating this doubt, he indicates the formal application (prayoga) by stating, "they are dependent on another" (paratantrāḥ).
The meaning is that one should not assume there to be dependence on a self (*ātmapāratantrya*) in that case; rather, only dependence in general (*pāratantryamātra*) is established.
Therefore, the scope of the inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*) is merely dependence.

For those who maintain that the self is to be inferred from desire and so forth, the dependence of these [mental states] upon [the self] is never within the range of our direct perception, because their substratum— the other [i.e., the self]— is eternally beyond the senses.

Having thus illustrated the inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*), he presents the illustration of the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*) as the ultimate reality by means of a question, beginning with the words "pāratantrye" (in dependence).

For when the status of being a quality belonging to the eight substances has been removed by subverting arguments, the very nature of being a quality (*guṇatva*) serves as the negative-only reason (*vyatirekī hetu*) for proving dependence upon a self (*ātmapāratantrya*).
And although this self is not established by its own nature, [it is nonetheless proven].

Nevertheless, although it is referred to by terms such as "distinct from the eight substances" (*dravyāṣṭakavyatireka*) and so forth—which are not very remote [from its actual nature]—it is capable of qualifying [the subject], and it can induce doubt, which is a necessary factor for the operation of logic; thus, the Bhāṣya here is faultless.
The meaning of the statement "it is threefold precisely because of the mention of division" is as follows:

Since the threefold nature [of inference] is already established by the very statement of its classification, for what purpose is the mention of "pūrvavat" and so forth included in the sūtra? To this, the response is as follows: the "statement of the threefold" refers to the utterance of the three types beginning with *pūrvavat*.
By means of a concise sūtra, there is a brief expression of this vast threefold [inference], which has a great scope and encompasses the objects of the past, future, and present.

By the mere expression "preceded by that" (*tatpūrvakam*), the author of the Sūtras—considering himself to have achieved the ultimate brevity of expression (*vākyalāghava*)—shows no regard for another kind of brevity; this serves as an illustration for one who wishes to instruct his disciples. And so it is with this:

the construction is that [the author] proceeded with such a variety of syntactical variations (*vākyavikalpa*) as a matter of stylistic diversity (*vaicitrya*), and this is his established practice (*samācāra*).
Thus far, inference based on the difference in characteristics has been shown to be distinct from perception.

However, the author of the Bhāṣya states that it is also distinct by virtue of the difference in their objects: "Perception has an existent object, whereas inference has both existent and non-existent objects.
The word "and" (ca) conjoins this difference in objects.
"Existent" refers to the present;
"non-existent" refers to the past and the future.
For worldly perception has only the present as its object.
Inference, however, has the three periods of time as its object.

Although perception also has non-existent things as its objects when it functions toward the negation of the past and future— which are currently being negated— it is nevertheless said to have existent things as its objects insofar as it does not function toward those two [past and future] things that are being negated.
However, inference operates even with respect to those two; it is on this basis alone that it is said to have a non-existent object.
He raises an objection to this by stating, "and [it has] an existent object.

For it is not the case that a property whose general form is unperceived is eligible for the operation of logic; rather, a property must be perceived in its general aspect while remaining undetermined in its specific details.

The meaning is not that the universal (*sāmānya*) has not been perceived; rather, there can be no perception of a non-existent, independent [universal] by means of a universal. He anticipates the second alternative with the word "atha" (now/if).
In order to refute this, he states the threefold nature of phenomena (*dharma*) with the words "phenomena" (*dharmāḥ*).
He analyzes them with the word "therein" (*tatra*).
He asks: "But how [is it]? (*kathaṃ punar*)?
For if inherence were independent, it would not be a qualifier of anything;
and thus, the point is that it would not be perceived as a qualifier.
The answer is: because there is no other inherence (samavāya).
We do not deny that it possesses the status of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*) in its own right; rather, the meaning is that it does not possess [inherence as] its mode of existence (*vṛtti*).
But why is another inherence (*samavāya*) not admitted for this [inherence]? To this he says: "Now" (*atha*).
He asks: "What is this?
For the so-called "consequence of infinite regress" (*anavasthā-prasaṅga*) is indeed a form of reasoning (*tarka*).
The meaning is that this [reasoning] alone is not sufficient for a definitive conclusion without the aid of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
The reply is: there is no doubt;
rather, such reasoning certainly exists.
He says this: "five.
This word *pañcapadārthavṛtti* refers to the atom (*paramāṇu*) by way of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, but it refers to inherence (*samavāya*) by way of a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) compound.

Nor is the mere non-difference of the word [denoting the relation] in any way a constituent of inference; for, lest the horns of cows and other animals also follow from the similarity of the word "cow" (go), he states another argument out of dissatisfaction [with the previous one]: "Inherence is non-dependent.
Here, being the cause means being the basis for the cognition "here" (iha).
Lest there be an inconclusive [reason] due to conjunction (*saṃyoga*), it is stated: "provided that it is pervasive" (*vyāpakatve sati*).
Pervasiveness is the state of being perceived everywhere when other causes for perception are present;
and this is indistinguishable in the case of the cognition, the self, and inherence (*samavāya*) here.
He asks about the reasoning (*tarka*) that constitutes the methodological procedure (*itikartavyatā*): "But if... The answer is: "The effect.
In order to introduce the consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā-prasaṅga*), the consequence of having no substratum (*anādhāratva-prasaṅga*) was previously stated.
It might be argued:

"Let it be that the effect, prior to its existence, is unattached and later becomes attached [to its cause], just as a cloth, having arisen from threads joined with a shuttle, later becomes attached to the shuttle. To this, he says: "And inherence... (samavāyaśca).
The meaning is that the consequence of infinite regress (anavasthā-prasaṅga) has been stated previously.
He raises an objection: "Because it is an attainment" (prāptitvāt).

The meaning is that since it possesses a means of valid cognition (pramāṇavat), the occurrence of inherence (samavāya-vṛtti) has been attained; therefore, it cannot be abandoned for fear of infinite regress.
He dispels doubt by means of an inquiry: "What is this?

The meaning is that, although "attainment" (*prāpti*) has been excluded from the case of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), the relation is inherent because the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of "being an effect," which necessitates it, still exists.
Now, as to why it is not also a property of attainment (*prāptidharma*), he says: "If, however, this... and so forth.
Now, one might ask: why is this infinite regress not accepted here as well, just as it is in the case of the seed and the sprout? To this he says: "And this infinite regress...

An infinite regress can be established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in cases that are "not first-time" (*anidamprathama*), because they are beginningless; however, it cannot be established in cases that are "first-time" (*idamprathama*), because, being characterized by a beginning, its certainty is impossible.
This has been stated as "due to the absence of a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇābhāvāt*).
Furthermore, there is a contradiction with the treatise (*śāstra*) if one were to accept another inherence (*samavāya*); thus he says, "And inherence...
The treatise states that the reality (*tattva*)—that is, the oneness (*ekatva*)—of inherence is explained by its existence (*bhāva*), which is to say, by its beingness (*sattva*).
The meaning is that it would be contradicted by one who attempts to establish its multiplicity.
He raises an objection: "Upon the cessation of the relata," and thus it perishes.
The meaning is that when that [entity] has perished, what is seen is something else produced from it; thus, the manifoldness of inherence (*samavāya*) is established.
He refutes this, saying: "It is not non-existent.
Here, "manifestation" (*khyāti*) means apprehension (*upalabdhi*).
Why? Because of its being uncreated (*akṛtakatva*).
From where does this very state of being uncreated arise? To this he says: "it is uncreated. [The reason is:
because it possesses a substratum, like the relation of the uncreated with its own material cause (*upādāna*); this is a negative-only (*vyatirekin*) logical reason (*hetu*).
He states the non-deviation from negative concomitance (vyatireka-avyabhicāra) with the words "If this...
Indeed, this inherence (samavāya) arises together with its auxiliary cause,
not with the effect.
For form and touch, though they arise simultaneously, are not mutually connected;
rather, there is a co-inherence of the two in a single object.
Yet even that co-inherence does not exist within the act of inherence itself.
Even though it exists, it does not produce the effect as its substratum;
therefore, if they were to arise simultaneously, the effect would be without a substratum. He raises this objection with the words "Now, if... (atheti).

The meaning is that inherence, having arisen prior to the effect, will subsequently bring about the effect—which is being produced—as something residing in its material cause, by the power of the causes of the effect.
He refutes this with the words "even so" (*tathāpi*).
For an effect in the form of an existent entity arises from three causes.
Furthermore, since the effect and the cause must be stated to be the inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of inherence (*samavāya*),
it is not tenable that the effect is the cause of an inherence that has already arisen prior to the effect;
nor is it correct to say that its birth arises from a mere efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*).

Because the arising of any entity is everywhere necessarily preceded by three types of causes, it has been well said that since inherence lacks both inherent and non-inherent causes, it cannot arise prior to its effect; nevertheless, it must be stated "of what [is it the cause]? He raises an objection with "Now, if... (atha).
He refutes this with the words "kārya" (effect), etc.
Nor is it logical to claim that the inherence of the effect in its cause occurs subsequently, like the conjunction of a cloth and a shuttle;
for while a conjunction produced by conjunction can arise from three causes, this [inherence] cannot have three causes without another inherence.
The sense is that otherwise there would be the consequence of an infinite regress.
He concludes with "therefore" (tasmāt).
And thus, the objection arises: it is not understood with what intention it was stated that [the cognition] has a non-existent object.
He explains [the point] with the words "there, that which is being negated.
When the past and the future are currently being negated, it is said that the inference regarding them has a non-existent object (*asad-viṣaya*).
Let the negation of that [past and future], however, be within the range of perception (*pratyakṣa-gocara*).
Nevertheless, the meaning is that the distinction of objects is established.
Furthermore, in this context, this sequence of the threefold nature of phenomena is twofold: namely, that which is being enjoined and that which is being prohibited.
Even when being prescribed, it is twofold: dependent (*paratantra*) and independent (*svatantra*).
Furthermore, the status of the independent [term] as a property (*dharma*) should be understood as intended merely for the sake of specification (*viśeṣaṇatva*).
But is it not the case that even when something is being produced, it may be non-existent yet perceptible at some point?
For example, while a potter is at work, a jar is being born;
indeed, one with wide-open eyes perceives at that time, "the jar is coming into existence."

And that [entity] is not existent at that time, because the coming-into-being of an existent thing cannot have a non-agent as its cause, just like the act of going; thus he raises the objection: "it comes into being."
He refutes this, saying: "No, because it is that which is being born.
This is because one does not admit the existence or non-existence of an object that is currently being born and is the subject of an injunction.
However, its non-existence is indeed accepted by virtue of its being the object of negation.
To the question, "What then is the meaning of the word *bhavati*? he says: "it exists" (*bhavati*).

As for the common worldly usage, "the jar is born" (*ghaṭo jāyate*), it must be explained by applying the word "jar" metaphorically to the parts of the jar and to the jar itself, since those [parts] are already established and thus function as the agent [of the action].
He summarizes: "Thus, for now..."
Having established his own definition [of inference], he sets forth the following to refute the definition of others: "But others...
He states its meaning: "The meaning of this is...
He refutes it: "In this regard..."
Having analyzed the compound as appropriate, he refutes it with the words "if [it is argued that] it is an invariably concomitant object.
Existence (*sattva*) is the state of being accessible to a cognition whose object is a positive affirmation (*vidhi*),
and not a universal (*sāmānya*).

The meaning is that there could be an inference of impermanence from properties such as existence (*sattva*)— which are invariably concomitant with impermanence— by means of the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), which is itself invariably concomitant with them;
however, this is not possible, because those [properties] deviate (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of eternal things such as space (*ākāśa*).
Nevertheless, the compound is incapable [of expressing the intended meaning].
Previously, the objection was stated merely on the grounds of the excess of meaning;
now, however, the impossibility of the qualifying compound is established by the reason of that excess of meaning—thus there is no redundancy.
A qualifier is frequently compounded with the qualified.

In this context, since either the mention of the qualifier alone or the mention of the qualified alone would result in the meaning of the other being understood by implication, the purpose of mentioning both terms is so that a compound may occur in cases where there is deviation (vyabhicāra) for each individually, but non-deviation when they are taken together.
The meaning is that since that [mutual relation] does not exist here, the formation of the compound is untenable.
"Sāmarthya" (semantic competency) is the connection with a purpose. He raises an objection: "In the case of a single word... and so forth.
He refutes this with the words "here too":
the individual (vyakti) is the primary element because it is the qualificand (viśeṣya), while the genus (jāti) is subordinate because it is the qualifier (viśeṣaṇa).
When the word "earth" is uttered, doubt arises.

Is it intended that "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*) is the universal (*sāmānya*) of this [substance], as in the injunction "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*), or rather is it the substance qualified by that [universal], as in "he cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*)?
In this regard, the following occurs: "substance" (dravya).
For that [term] distinguishes earth from the general-particular (sāmānyaviśeṣa) of "earth-ness" (pṛthivītva).
Likewise, when "substance" is also stated, upon the inquiry whether it refers to the generality of "substanceness" (dravyatva) or to an individual instance, the term "earth" presents itself.
Substantiality (*dravyatva*) is not a universal, but rather earth (*pṛthivī*).
Furthermore, there is no co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between substantiality and earthness;
for it does not occur that "earthness is substantiality."

Therefore, because grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is possible, there is the attainment of a single individual instance of the primary meaning. In this case, however, the object does not deviate from its inseparable concomitance (nāntarīyakatva), but inseparable concomitance itself does not deviate from the object.
For it is impossible that there could be something which is both an inseparable concomitant (*nāntarīyaka*) and not an object (*artha*),
because it is impossible for that which is denoted by the term "inseparable concomitant" to be non-denotable.
Even if the word *artha* refers to a real entity (*vastu*), since a thing to be indicated (*lakṣya*) is impossible [in that case], the definition would have no subject matter.
For in the system of Dignāga, there is no real entity whatsoever that constitutes a valid reason (*saddhetu*) without being invariably concomitant (*nāntarīyaka*).
As he said:

"This entire relationship between the means of inference and the object of inference exists through a subject-attribute (*dharmin-dharma*) relation established within the intellect; it does not depend upon external existence or non-existence."
And it is non-pervasive;
for the meaning is that it is not the case that only a real entity is inseparable [from its effect], since even a non-existent thing can be inseparable [from its cause].
He states another refutation: "And [the phrase] 'of one who knows that'...

When it is said, "the perception of that which is inseparable," it is understood through the very power of the words themselves as "the perception of an object qualified by inseparability," because as long as it is possible, there is no abandoning of the literal meaning of the words.

The meaning is this: since the perception of the three-fold mark (trirūpaliṅga) is already established, what else remains that must be included for the sake of those who know [the system]? He explains this very point by way of negation with the words "for not" (na hi). He extends this refutation of the definition to other definitions as well with the word "by this" (etena).
He asks: "Who?"—for in this definition there is no mention of "those who know that," and thus [the objection] remains unrefuted; such is the sense.
The answer begins with "Just as" (*yathā*).
He refutes their example with the words "the example" (*udāharaṇam*).
Thus, having refuted Dignāga’s definition by this means, the definitions of others have also been refuted.

Now, in order to elaborate upon his own definition, Dignāga sets forth the statement beginning with "in the object of inference (anumeya) and what is similar to it," and then refutes it—saying "others, however" (apare tu).
He is called "another" (apara) in relation to the author of the immediately preceding definition. [Dignāga] raises an objection, saying "the object of inference" (anumeya).
The meaning is that it is not possible to say of something that exists in the object of inference (anumeya) both as existent and non-existent that it is "existent.
He provides the resolution: "there is no such undesirable consequence" (nāprasaṅga).

If this were the case, then that which exists in two ways in the counter-example (vipakṣa) would be a reason (hetu) that does not occur in the counter-example, and thus it would not be "erroneous" (savyabhicāra); such is the meaning. He objects again: "It should not be stated. Why? Because of the exclusion resulting from the restriction (avadhāraṇa).

The sense is that, because the presence [of the reason] in the inferable object (*anumeya*) is restricted by the restriction "only in the inferable object," how could there be the possibility of it occurring in only a part of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśavṛtti*)?
To refute this, he analyzes the possibilities as they occur, beginning with "in the inferable object.
Therein, he analyzes the intention of the first alternative, asking: "But what, then, is meant by this?"
The impossibility— that is, the absolute impossibility— is refuted; just as it is understood that a blue lotus exists and does not absolutely not exist,
but it is not understood that the lotus is exclusively blue and not non-blue.
Nor is it the case that only the lotus is blue and nothing else.
Now, regarding the term "possibility" (sambhava):
the meaning is that it refers to positive concomitance (anvaya) and not to negative concomitance (vyatireka).
He refutes these two alternatives with the words "and in both ways.
He states another refutation: "nor does it subsist in one part.
For by the exclusion of absolute non-connection, non-connection itself is not excluded.
Nor does the mere prescription of possibility exclude impossibility;
therefore, because the non-exclusion of [impossible] connection remains, the meaning is that the fallacy of inference consisting in partial occurrence is not excluded.
It might be argued:
this restrictive particle (*evakāra*), being connected with the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), can only apply to that which is inferable (*anumeya*),
just as in the expression "Pārtha alone is the archer."
Furthermore, this exclusion of connection with anything else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*) cannot be obtained without the particle *eva*.

Therefore, the restriction is not redundant; to this he says: "And there is the sublation of the subsequent term. For it is impossible that [the reason] exists only in the inferable (*anumeya*) and in what is similar to it (*tattulya*).
Therefore, there is a sublation of the [proposition] "it is similar to that. The word "and" (ca) conjoins the refutation that [the reason] does not reside in a single part [of the subject].

Having refuted, as far as possible, the first position—that existence [of the reason] must be in the inferable object (*anumeya*) itself—he introduces the second position to refute it with the words "Now, the reply" (*athottaram*). He demonstrates its purpose with the words "its pervasion" (*tasya vyāpti*); the meaning is that it shows the pervasion (*vyāpti*). Indeed, the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) connected with the qualifier "existence alone" (*sadbhāva eva*), by excluding non-connection (*ayoga*) and non-pervasion (*avyāpti*), demonstrates pervasion.

And thus, the meaning is that pervasion (vyāpti) is its sense. He refutes this: even so, that which is to be inferred (anumeya) is determined; [but] existence (sadbhāva), as a property (dharma) of possibility, is not [determined] by means of pervasion.
He states the reason: "Since the restrictive particle *eva* is employed, the restriction applies to something other than that."
"Do not fixate on the actual existence [of the reason]; rather, let the inferable object be fixed.
To the question, "What follows from this?", he says: "And by way of the pervasion of possibility (*saṃbhavavyāpti*).
For the inferable object, once it has been fixed, does not exist elsewhere apart from the presence of a valid reason.

Consequently, the object of inference becomes determined through the presence of the reason and its pervasion; however, the presence of the reason remains undetermined, being spread across everything— both in similar instances and in dissimilar instances— and it may, in some cases, pervade both the similar and the dissimilar instances.
Some [reasons] function as partial [pervaders].

Therefore, for the purpose of negating this possible reason—which might otherwise apply even to the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa)—it is appropriate to say "it does not exist when [the property] is absent.
However, since its application to what is similar to that (tattulya) is not negated, it is simply accepted; thus, the statement "its presence in what is similar" is redundant. This is the meaning.
It might be argued:

"Even if the existence of the reason in what is similar to that [subject] is established by its presence in the subject, the statement 'existence in what is similar to that' is for the purpose of ensuring that the reason exists there through pervasion (vyāpti).
To this, he says: "And in what is similar to that... [and so forth].

If, however, pervasion (vyāpti) were intended [by the definition], then "being produced immediately after an effort" would not be a valid reason when "being produced" is the property to be proven; for the latter does not pervade the similar instances (sapakṣa). This is the point. He raises an objection: "Now, [regarding] 'that which is similar to it'..."
He refutes [the opponent's position] by means of an alternative analysis: "But what here?"—
is there a sublation of the former due to contradiction,
or of the latter due to tautology?
He provides an illustration of the contradiction with the preceding phrase: "For it does not exist [in the dissimilar instance].

By the statement "existence in the inferable object" (*anumeye sadbhāva*), once the presence of the reason in the inferable object has been established, the restrictive conjunction "existence only in what is similar to that" (*tattulya eva sadbhāva*) excludes its occurrence from the mere dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), but not from the inferable object itself.
If it is argued that "just as [the scripture] says, 'In the beginning, she gave birth to two sons of her own accord, Nara and Nārāyaṇa,'" then the author replies: "so too here.

For when a restrictive particle (*evakāra*) is used with a cumulative restriction (*samuccīyamāna-avadhāraṇa*), it is connected with what is similar to it through the exclusion of other possibilities (*anyayoga-vyavaccheda*); likewise, it would also be connected with that which is to be inferred (*anumeya*).
In that case, even a reason that subsists in only one part of the object to be inferred (anumeya) would be valid.

For indeed, the particle *eva* in the expression "Nara and Nārāyaṇa alone" does not connect with Nārāyaṇa through the exclusion of connection with others (*anyayogavyavaccheda*), nor does it connect with Nara through the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*); such is the intended meaning.

Now, one who desires a connection for the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) without variety might suspect that just as there is an exclusion of what is otherwise possible (*yathāyogavyavaccheda*) regarding the object of inference (*anumeya*), so too should the connection be stated regarding its similar instance (*tattulya*) by means of an exclusion of what is impossible (*ayogavyavaccheda*). To this, he replies: "Regarding its similar instance.
He refutes it: "Regarding its similar instance."
He elaborates on that very point with the words "he" (saḥ):
the meaning is "in your [Buddhist] system.
Furthermore, it is not possible to state, by way of restating that "it exists only where the probandum exists," that "it must exist only in what is similar to that."
For it is not possible to qualify inference;
for if that were the case, and another effort were undertaken to qualify it, there would be the undesirable consequence of a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*).
As, for example:

Regarding the passage, "If both sacrificial oblations (*havir*) of one who has performed the *darśapūrṇamāsa* should suffer damage (*ārti*), he should offer five *śarāva*-measurements of rice (*odana*) to Indra," although the qualification of the oblation by means of its "damage" must be sought because damage cannot be apprehended in its own form,

nevertheless, it is not possible to qualify the oblation as being "both" without another effort. Thus, for fear of a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*), the state of being "both," even though it appears [in the text], is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*).
Thus, it is not intended that the mother also be inferred.

Alternatively, having accepted a split in the sentences precisely because of that intention, one subsequently maintains the establishment of the desired meaning through the syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) of the sentences.
And there is no absence of syntactic unity between the two sentences due to contradiction.

Since the exclusion of connection with anything else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*) is established even by having as its object merely the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), a contradiction is not proven [by the mere fact that the reason exists in the similar instance].
Therefore, because words have the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) as their meaning, a contradiction must be stated.
For instance, in the case of "existence in the inferable" (*anumeye sadbhāvaḥ*), it means existence in the inferable alone, and not in the non-inferable.
The meaning of the term is that existence itself is not non-existence;
thus, the absence of the reason in both the similar instance (*tattulya*) and the counter-instance (*vipakṣa*) has been shown.
Likewise, in the case of "existence in the similar instance" (*tattulye sadbhāva*), it means existence only in the similar instance and not in what is not the similar instance.
The meaning of the term is that there is existence itself, not non-existence;
thus, it is stated that [the probans] does not exist in the object of inference (*anumeya*).
Furthermore, there can be no conjunction between the object of inference and an object similar to it, as these two are mutually exclusive.
If it is argued that because both [terms] are intended merely to exclude their respective opposites, there exists a mutual conjunction [of the two exclusions], we say no;

for then the consequence would follow that even the pair "tree" and "cow"—which have the same referent insofar as they are both merely intended to exclude elephants and so forth—would exhibit grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
Therefore, because of this contradiction, an emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*) that conjoins the two is not tenable.
Furthermore, Dignāga did not accept a restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*) used in conjunction with a cumulative sense (*samuccīyamāna*),
as he stated when refuting the definition of the Vaiśeṣikas:
"If only form (*rūpa*) were visible, then substance (*dravya*) would not be visible."

Furthermore, this would contradict the statement regarding the visual perception of a substance in Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 4.1.6: "And likewise, there is perception [of a substance] due to its inherence in many large substances and due to color. Thus, the definition of the visual perceptibility of a substance would be undermined.

For in this case, it is possible to state a restrictive conjunction (samuccīyamānāvadhāraṇa) such that "only visible form, accompanied by a substance possessing form, is perceptible to the eye, and not smell, taste, and so forth.
Therefore, Kīrti’s independent statement of a restrictive conjunction is incorrect; enough with this elaboration.
He refutes the claim that "what is non-existent is non-existent" with the word "non-existent.
Why? Because that which is non-existent is void and does not exist of its own accord;
therefore, it cannot be designated as "existent" or even as "non-existent."

"Let it be so; nevertheless, why does exclusion from that [non-existent] reason not occur? To this he says: "For it is not non-existent," and so forth. How this is so has been stated by us on the occasion of establishing the positive concomitant (anvayin) reason. Having refuted this in its own form, and intending to refute the restriction contained therein, he restates it and subjects it to an alternative analysis: "What is being restricted?"
He refutes the first alternative with the words "If, for a start..."—
the meaning is that by this [statement], it is understood that existence is exactly equal to that [non-existence].
He refutes the second alternative with the words "If, for a start..."
The meaning is that by the phrase "existence is exactly equal to that," this is understood. He refutes the second alternative with the words "but if, however" (*atha punar*).
This reason—"this is a cow because it has horns"—does not exist at all in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*).
Because it pervades both the subject and the similar instances;
yet it is not entirely non-existent, since it occurs in some parts of the dissimilar instances, such as buffaloes and the like.
Therefore, this too would be a reason [for the non-existence of the probandum], namely that "the counter-position itself does not exist.
Having thus refuted the meaning of the individual members, he introduces the refutation of the collective meaning with the words: "Furthermore, by the exclusion of one or two terms...
In that regard, by the exclusion of one term, there are three positions.
By excluding two [of the three characteristics], there are three; thus, the group of six is formed. By excluding those [six], the group of seven is grasped.

For example, if it were stated only that "the reason must exist in the inferable object" (anumeya), then even something like "sound is eternal because it is produced"—which lacks presence in what is similar to it (tattulya) and possesses occurrence in the dissimilar (vipakṣa)—would also be a valid reason.

If it were said that [the reason] exists in what is similar to the subject (*tattulye asti*), then even that which occurs in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣavṛtti*) and that which is not a property of the subject (*apakṣadharma*) would become a valid reason, as in the case: "Sound is eternal because it is visible, like a universal. If it were said that [the reason] does not exist in what is not the subject (*nāstitāsatī*), then that which is not a property of the subject and does not exist in what is similar to the subject would also become a valid reason, as in the case: "Sound is eternal because it is non-existent."

If it were stated merely as "in the subject (anumeya) and in what is similar to it (tattulya)," then the reason "sound is impermanent because it is knowable" (prameyatvāt) would become a reason that occurs in the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa).

If it were stated merely as "it exists in the subject and does not exist where it is absent," then the reason "sound is eternal because, while possessing a genus (jātimattva), it is audible" (śrāvaṇatvāt) would also become a valid reason, even though it lacks occurrence in what is similar to the subject.

If it were merely stated that "it exists when [the property] is present in what is similar to that, and does not exist when it is absent," then the reason "atoms are impermanent because they are produced" would be a reason that lacks the property of the subject (*apakṣadharma*). To prevent all such [faults], the purpose of employing the term "composite" (*samudāya*) is [to include the subject]. He refutes this [position] with the words "this too... (*etadapi*).
The positive concomitant (anvayin) that possesses two forms—by virtue of either pervading or not pervading the similar instances (sapakṣa)—is of two kinds.
Now he refutes the Sāṃkhya definition of inference with the words "by this":
the relation (*saṃbandha*) is the inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) of the probans with the probandum;
[this is] from that perception which has been ascertained by a more reliable means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Nevertheless, since it would follow that even two contradictory non-erroneous reasons (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*), which are invariably concomitant (*avinābhūta*) with respect to a single locus (*dharmin*), would possess the status of valid reasons (*hetu*), it was stated: "from one.
This refers to the establishment of the remainder, namely the object of inference (*anumeya*).
By this [statement], it is said that [the reason] was not employed merely because of a commonality of being unestablished (*anupapannatva*).
He asks about the lack of establishment: "How?
He states the lack of establishment as it occurs: "For not... and so forth.
If the word "perception" (pratyakṣa) denotes cognition, and that cognition is qualified by oneness,
then this objection applies.
However, if "from one" (ekasmāt) is a qualification of the relation, [then the objection does not apply].
Furthermore, the word "perception" (pratyakṣa) refers to the object of knowledge and not to the act of knowing;
having set forth this point, he refutes it with the words "But even so, because of the connection" (athāpi saṃbandhāt).
He then raises an objection with the word "Now" (atha).
The meaning is that the perceptibility of the relationship was stated previously, but not at the time of inference.
He refutes this: "Even so, it would follow that there could be inference for one who previously perceived the relationship but does not perceive the probans (liṅga) at the time of inference."
This might be so:
by the etymological derivation "that which is connected" (*saṃbadhyate*), the relation (*saṃbandha*) is the inferential mark (*liṅga*).

Therefore, the establishment of the object to be inferred (*anumeya*) occurs from a single [perceptible] reason (*hetu*) that is inseparably connected (*avinābhūta*) with it, such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

And thus, since the cognition arises from a mark whose invariable concomitance has been grasped, it is established that [the cognition] is "presently perceptual"; to this he says: "Nor is there any other way.
Even under this interpretation, the word "from one" (*ekasmāt*) is redundant.
For, invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is defined as the mere presence of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
Or [is it] the perfection of all forms?
In that case, in the first alternative, let there be no "non-erroneous contradictory" (viruddhāvyabhicārī) reason; however, the reason would be one whose object is sublated (bādhitaviṣaya).

In the second case, however, it is not possible for a reason that is endowed with all the required characteristics to be a "non-erroneous contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*); thus, the phrase "from one [reason]" is superfluous.
Therefore, it was rightly stated: "And there is no other alternative.
He states the fault of the definition—namely, its lack of pervasiveness—with the words: "And by means of form," etc.
First of all, there is no identity between these two, because they are apprehended by different sense organs and are cognized by different cognitions;
nor is any relationship perceived between these two, which do not possess the nature of one another.

Furthermore, it should be understood that even in the theory of momentary transformation (*pratikṣaṇapariṇāmavāda*), there is no relationship whatsoever between the bowl and the jujube fruits and so forth.
He raises an objection with "Now [if you say]...
(*atha*), and he refutes it with "That too... (*so 'pi*).
For in the established doctrines of either the Sāṃkhyas or the Buddhists, there exists no relation called "inherence" (samavāya),
nor does there exist any substance that serves as its substratum. Nor does there exist any substance that serves as its substratum.
Therefore, the meaning is that there would be a contradiction of one's own doctrine.

If it were argued that because color and the other [sensory objects] are derived from primordial matter (pradhāna), primordial matter is their single substratum, and thus wherever there is color, there is touch, [the author] says: "Wherever there is color... and so forth.
Why? Because it is nowhere [stated] so.
For the *pradhāna* is not the substratum of the effects; rather, it is maintained that these [effects] have the *pradhāna* as their very essence.
And thus, the [notion] that "it is here or there" is untenable;
nor has it been stated that there is identity [between the two].
The point is that difference and non-difference cannot coexist in one and the same thing due to their mutual contradiction.
He raises an objection with the words "paraspara" (mutually).

For just as the parts of a stool, though distinct and not arranged in a vertical sequence, do not fall because they support one another, so too color and touch support each other; this is the meaning.
He refutes [this]: even if there were a state of mutual support elsewhere, as in the case of a chair and its parts, that is not so for color and touch.
Why? Because "touch is not in color."
The parts of a chair, whose weights are counteracted by the distinctions of their mutual conjunctions, remain stationary and are designated as such because they serve as mutual supports.
However, the meaning is that the stability of form, touch, and so forth is not caused by one another; rather, it is caused by the purpose of the Puruṣa, characterized by experience and liberation.
By this, the sevenfold relationship of the Sāṅkhyas is refuted.
The remainder is easily understood. //5//
Comparison is the means of establishing what is to be proven through its similarity to something well-known.

In the *Vibhāga-sūtra*, because comparison (*upamāna*) is mentioned immediately after inference (*anumāna*), and because its definition follows the order of their enumeration, the author states the definition of comparison immediately after the definition of inference: "Now, comparison" (*athopamānam*), as stated in the *Bhāṣya*.
He recites the *sūtra*: "Comparison is the means of establishing that which is to be established through well-known similarity.
Here too, the word "from which" (*yataḥ*) must be supplied.
*Siddhi* means accomplishment;
this has been explained by the author of the *Bhāṣya*:
"by what is well-known," that is, by what is established.
Because of the commonality (*sādharmya*) or similarity (*sāmānya*) of the *gavaya* with the cow;
and by one who asserts that this commonality is a "similarity" (*sāmānya*), it is implied that there exists no separate category of reality called "likeness" (*sādṛśya*) distinct from commonality.
Furthermore, since a commonality that is not well-known is insufficient for establishing what is to be proven, the establishment of that commonality must also be observed.
And that [knowledge] arises from the authoritative statement (āptavākya): "As is a cow, so is a gavaya.
This is what was stated: "as is a cow.

The explanation of the terms *sādhya* (the probandum) and *sādhana* (the means of proof) is as follows: comparison (*upamāna*) is the communication of the object to be made known—a physical entity possessing the specific universal of *gavayatva* (cowness-in-a-gavaya) and perceived through direct perception as being similar to a cow—by way of its being denotable by the word "gavaya."

For a person, through perception aided by the recollection of the analogical statement (*atideśavākya*), cognizes that the individual (*piṇḍa*) is denotable by the word "gavaya" based on the similarity to a cow residing in the gavaya; thus, it is said that the operation of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is "making known" (*prajñāpana*).
Regarding this, the author of the *Vārttika* first states the intended meaning of the Sūtra: "The meaning of the Sūtra is as before."
The meaning is the exclusion of both similar and dissimilar classes.

If it were merely stated as "the proving of what is to be proven" (*sādhyasādhanam*), there would be the undesirable consequence [of including] perception and other means of proof, as well as the means for achieving pleasure and pain;
therefore, it is said "by means of a well-known similarity" (*prasiddhasādharmyāt*).

Although the term *upamāna*— when it is stated that "analogy is a well-known similarity"— acquires the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*) due to its grammatical coordination with the word *upamāna* which denotes a specific means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),

nevertheless, the inclusion of the words "that which is to be established" (*sādhya*) and "the means of establishing it" (*sādhana*) is for the purpose of excluding fallacious analogies (*tadābhāsa*).
By this, the fallacious form of analogy is set aside.
He analyzes the meaning of the individual components [of the compound] with the words "prasiddha" and so forth.

The author of the Vārttika has shown the possibility of two types of *bahuvrīhi* compounds, but he did not reject the third type of compound (the instrumental *tatpuruṣa*) favored by the author of the Bhāṣya.

For the author of the Bhāṣya has stated that the cognition of the *gavaya* as possessing a name is the result, which is expressed by the terms "the goal" (*sādhya*) and "the means" (*sādhana*), because it implies the operation of the person being prompted.

Subsequently, he has separately stated the operation of the prompter, namely the act of instruction, saying: "The purpose of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) consists in the cognition of the relationship between the name and the named."

The author of the Vārttika explains this very point by way of the categories of the "probandum" (sādhya) and the "means of proof" (sādhana): the purpose of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is the cognition of the relationship between the name and [the object] designated by it;
by the word "probandum," the relationship with the name is expressed; its "means of proof" is its establishment, that is, its cognition.
Surely, let this person perceive the gavaya as being endowed with similarity to a cow;
but from what source does the understanding of the relationship between the name and its referent arise?
For it is not the case that whoever perceives something as similar to another [automatically understands the linguistic connection].
Intending to convey that he understands even the name of that [object], he asks: "What is meant by this? The answer is: "Through scripture.
That is, memory arises from a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) deposited by the experience of scripture.
This is what is meant:

it is not only the cognition of similarity that is the cause for understanding the connection with a name, but rather [that cognition] in dependence upon the recollection of the meaning of the scripture.
Now, one might ask: "If there has been no experience of the scripture, how can there be memory? To this he says: "For when by this...

In the phrase "due to similarity with a well-known object" (*prasiddhasādharmyāt*), "well-knownness" (*prasiddhi*) is twofold: that consisting of hearing (*śrutamayī*) and that consisting of perception (*pratyakṣamayī*).
That consisting of hearing is, for example, "As is a cow, so is a *gavaya*."
And there is that which consists of perception, such as: "This object is of such a kind, characterized by its similarity to a cow.
In this case, the well-known fact consisting of perception—dependent upon the memory produced by traditional scripture—is the cause for understanding the connection with the name.

Although it is possible to understand from the statement "As is a cow, so is a gavaya" that the word *gavaya* is the name for what is similar to a cow, [it is still necessary to rely on the perceptual identification].
Indeed, the act of naming does not occur solely through perception; for that [act] takes place with respect to an object distinguished from those of its own class.
And if that [distinction] is likewise understood by another means of valid cognition as well, [then the name is applied].
Who could prevent the act of naming there?

For the individual body (*piṇḍa*) characterized by its similarity to a cow, which is referred to by the pronoun "that" (*yaḥ*), can be understood as distinct from jars and other things of a different genus, as well as from buffaloes and others of the same genus; thus, it is possible to cognize it as a *gavaya*.

Nevertheless, as long as this person does not apply the name to the related object once it has been directly perceived as "this is a gavaya," that cognizer, whose mind is wandering, remains anxiously awaiting the perception [of the object], thinking, "Will I indeed see such a body where I shall understand the name 'gavaya'? Nor is he able, by means of the sentence alone, to understand that "this object, which possesses the genus of *gavayatva* similar to a cow and has not yet been perceived, is called a gavaya."
And this [cognition] cannot arise from perception alone without the aid of a statement.

Therefore, one must accept that this means of valid cognition called analogy (*upamāna*) is indeed something distinct from both scripture (*āgama*) and perception (*pratyakṣa*), consisting of a cognition of similarity accompanied by the recollection of the scriptural statement.
Now, suppose a person from the North has said in disparagement of a camel:
"Fie upon the camel—its neck is exceedingly long and crooked, its lips hang down, it feeds on harsh and sharp thorns, its limbs are arranged in a loathsome manner; it is the lowest of animals!
Having heard this, a person from the South travels to the Northern region, and upon perceiving such a creature, he recognizes, "This must surely be that camel."
Among these, what then is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
It is not, first of all, analogy (*upamāna*), because of the absence of similarity;
nor is a fifth means of valid cognition accepted.

If it is argued that a statement intended for censure is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the camel's suchness, because one thing cannot be understood from a word whose purpose lies elsewhere—
then what is the recourse in a case where the sentence does indeed culminate in establishing that very nature?

Now, even in that case, if such a camel is recognized through direct perception as being understood from scripture, its status as the denotatum of the word "camel" is understood— despite the scripture previously referring to such a camel— merely through usage, by means of inference:
for whatever word is employed for a certain object when no other mode of application exists, that word is its denotator.
Just as the word "cow" is applied to the universal "cowness," and this [word] is applied in such a manner,
therefore it is the designator of that [object].
Thus, this denotative power of it, which was already inferred prior to the application [of the word], is merely remembered at the time of direct perception.
This is the same in the case of the sentence of comparison as well; for there too, the object possessing similarity, understood from the sentence, is recognized through direct perception.
And since the denotative power of the word "gavaya," inferred through application, is remembered, no further result remains for which analogy (upamāna) would be a means of valid cognition.
To this it is replied:

First of all, this word "gavaya" is not a direct designator of the individual object, like words such as "space" (*ākāśa*) and so forth; rather, the ultimate truth is that it applies to the individual by taking "gavaya-ness" (*gavayatva*) as its basis.

Nor is "gavayaness" understood from the sentence "as is a cow, so is a gavaya," for this word *gavaya* does not convey that [meaning] when its relation [to the object] is unknown. If, however, that [gavayaness] were understood first, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*) regarding the cognition of the relation.
Furthermore, the nature of the *gavaya* is not indicated by its similarity to a cow;
for one who has never previously perceived the nature of the *gavaya*, its connection with similarity to a cow has not been seen.
And that which has not had its connection observed cannot serve as an indicator.
For a staff whose connection to a person has not been perceived is not capable of indicating that person.

Therefore, since the related property of *gavayatva* (the state of being a *gavaya*) is not perceived in any way, how could there be a determination of the relationship between the signified and the signifier (*vācyavācaka-sambandha*) from either verbal testimony or inference?
And how much less, then, could there be a recollection of that relationship?

However, when the individual object (*piṇḍa*) possessing the specific universal (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*) of "gavaya-ness" is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the comprehension of the relationship is logical; for the relatum, "gavaya-ness," is perceptible, and the meaning of the sentence is already remembered.
Nevertheless, is it the individual object possessing the genus (*jāti*) of "gavaya-ness" that is denoted?
If it is asked, "Why is there a principle of determination (*vinigamanā*) that [the word 'gavaya'] denotes something possessing similarity to a cow?"—the answer is:

the perception of the similarity to a cow in a physical object (*piṇḍa*) that possesses the genus *gavayatva*, acting as an auxiliary to the recollection of the sentence-meaning and aided by reasoning (*tarka*), is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for denoting *gavayatva*.

And the reasoning (*tarka*) is as follows: if one were to assume that the term denotes a physical object qualified by similarity to a cow, there would be the consequence of conceptual complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*). For, in the case of denoting a physical object qualified by similarity, [the following would apply]:
It must be understood that a similarity which is not itself perceived does not qualify the individual object;
nor can that [similarity] be comprehended through anything other than a word, and thus the word's status as its denoter must be postulated.
Furthermore, a similarity that is not itself qualified cannot establish the application of the term "gavaya" to a specific individual.
The claim that [the word 'gavaya'] applies to anything on account of its similarity to something else must also be qualified by "to a cow";

furthermore, since the nature of being a cow (*gotva*) cannot be understood from any other source, that too would have to be denoted by the word 'gavaya'—thus there is the fault of conceptual complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*).
However, when the term denotes an individual possessing the universal of *gavayatva*, there is simplicity; therefore, he accepts that [definition].

Furthermore, since the mention of "similarity" (*sādharmya*) is intended as an illustration for any property (*dharma*) whatsoever, even the cognition of the name "camel" resulting from comparison is indeed [a form of] analogy; thus, there is no lack of pervasion [in the definition].
Nor is there the acceptance of a fifth means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For this very reason, after providing many examples, the venerable author of the Commentary (*Bhāṣyakāra*) said:
In this way, other objects of comparison in the world should also be understood;
therefore, everything is consistent.

Not knowing that such is the fruit of comparison—that is, the knowledge of an object qualified by similarity—and being mistaken in thinking that the fruit of comparison is [merely] the knowledge of an object qualified by similarity, the Venerable Dignāga objects with the words "perception" (*pratyakṣa*).
He asks: "How so? The answer is: "When... (*yadā tāvat*).
And this is an elliptical expression for "he perceives both by means of direct perception";
for when he perceives a single gavaya by means of direct perception, [he subsequently recognizes the cow].
And when one remembers the cow, even then the similarity to a cow residing in the gavaya is indeed perceptible; however,
the cow itself is not perceptible.

If it is argued that [the cow] is not perceived because it is not present to the senses, then, alas! What kind of similarity do you intend, O long-lived one, which is not perceived when the cow itself is not perceived?
[It would be] an abundance of common features existing in one genus that belong to another genus.
As they have said:
"Similarity is said to be the occurrence of numerous commonalities of qualities, parts, and actions within different primary universals."
If this is so, then have you now resolved to assert that the universal of "ear-ness" (*karṇatva*) is distinct due to the differences between the ears of a cow and a gavaya? Therefore,

just as for one who has perceived "cowness" (*gotva*) in a brindled cow, when [that same nature] is recognized in a healthy cow as "this is that very same thing," it is understood as "this is precisely that."

Thus, here too, there is no additional result [from the cognition]; therefore, it is well said that analogy does not differ from perception or from verbal testimony, as its result—the cognition of similarity—is not distinct from them. [The author] exposes the error of the Venerable [Dignāga] with the words "a cow," etc.
The meaning is that the existence of the gavaya is qualified by similarity. He recalls the actual state of affairs, saying "gavaya," and concludes with "therefore."

The formal argument (prayoga), however, is as follows: comparison (upamāna) is a means of valid cognition distinct from perception and the others, because it produces a cognition that is distinct from the cognitions produced by them.
If, however, it were not distinct from them, it would not produce a valid cognition distinct from them; and the same would apply to those [cognitions] themselves.
But this is not the case.
Therefore, it is so. //6//
Verbal testimony is the instruction of a reliable person.
"Now, 'Word' (śabda)" is the commentary.

Since "Word" is mentioned immediately after "Comparison" (upamāna), the meaning is that the definition of Word follows the definition of Comparison. He recites the defining sūtra: "Word is the instruction of a reliable person" (āptopadeśaḥ śabdaḥ).
In this context, "word" (*śabda*) is the term to be defined (*lakṣya*);
"instruction by a reliable person" (*āptopadeśa*) is the definition (*lakṣaṇa*).
That which is called "instruction" (*upadeśa*)—because one is instructed by means of it—is either the knowledge of a sentence, or the knowledge of its meaning, as it is being expressed.

In that regard, on the view that the validity belongs to the knowledge of the sentence, the result is the knowledge of its meaning, while the recollection of word-meanings and so forth are the intermediate procedural steps (*itikartavyatā*).
On the other hand, on the view that the validity belongs to the knowledge of that meaning, the result is the cognition of avoidance (*hāna*) and so forth.
Although "injunction" (*vidhi*), "instruction" (*upadeśa*), and "impulsion" (*pravartana*) are synonymous,
and although this [injunction] exceeds mere commands (*ājñā*) and requests (*adhyeṣaṇā*) by enjoining activity or cessation for the sake of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*),
for those two [commands and requests] enjoin activity and cessation for the sake of the enjoiner (*niyoktṛ*).

Nevertheless, because terms such as *paropaniṣad* and others pervade [the meaning of] the true reality (*bhūtārtha*), the word "instruction" (*upadeśa*) must be explained with the intention of referring merely to speech that possesses a purpose for another;
even though a statement such as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" does not function in certain cases [to produce direct realization].
Or, even if it turns a person away from something,
it is still called "instruction" (upadeśa) because it declares what is beneficial for the person;
yet, even so, there is over-extension (ativyāpti).
Since even the sentences for the veneration of caityas (*caityavandanā*) possess this same characteristic, it is said: "by the authoritative" (*āpta*).

The word is the instruction of authoritative persons—whether sages (*ṛṣi*), noble ones (*ārya*), or barbarians (*mleccha*)—and not that of non-authoritative persons such as the Buddha, the Bull, and others, who are created by illusion and delusion and who propound the doctrine of the momentariness and selflessness of all phenomena, which contradicts valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The author of the Vārttika states this very point: "It is not mere sound"—this is the meaning of the sūtra.

The commentary, which focuses on the definition of an authoritative person (*āpta*) as found in the Sūtra, states: "An authoritative person (*āpta*) is indeed one who has directly perceived the *dharma*.

He is so called because he has directly perceived—that is, determined by means of a most firm instrument of knowledge—the *dharmas*, which are entities whose purpose is the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful.
Nevertheless, even though he knows the truth, if he does not teach it out of a lack of compassion or out of indolence,"
Lest one who teaches erroneously out of stinginess (matsaritā) be considered an authoritative person (āpta), he says: "Impelled by the desire to communicate the object exactly as it was perceived.
By the phrase "exactly as it was perceived," teaching erroneously out of stinginess is excluded;
by the phrase "by the desire to communicate," lack of compassion and the desire for one's own self-interest are refuted.

"Engaged" means having exerted effort; thus, there is no lack of diligence. Nevertheless, one might fall into the error of being [merely] an "attainer" due to a lack of proficiency in the articulatory points (*sthāna*) and organs (*karaṇa*), which results in an inability to produce the phonemes (*varṇa*);
therefore, he says—"the instructor" (*upadeṣṭā*).
The meaning is that he possesses proficiency in the points of articulation and the organs of speech.
Regarding the term *āpta*, having extracted the base (*prakṛti*) from the combination of base and suffix (*samudāya*), he states its meaning: "direct realization" (*sākṣātkaraṇa*).
By this, the aforementioned perfection of qualities is indicated.
He states the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*): "by that" (*tayā*).
He states the pervasiveness of the definition of an authoritative person (*āpta*) with the word "seer" (*ṛṣi*). A seer is so called because of his vision;
he is one who has directly perceived all objects of knowledge existing in the three periods of time, like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of his hand.
The middle world is called "Ārya" because it has moved far away from sins;
the "Mleccha" is well known.

For even Mlecchas situated along the road are considered trustworthy by others when they point out the way to travelers whose belongings have been stolen, as they lack any visible motive [to deceive]. Thus, it is stated that the definition of a trustworthy person (*āpta*) given by others is non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*).
It comes to be.
He restates this commentary in order to raise an objection: "The authoritative person (āpta), indeed...
He raises the objection: "Heaven...
Having raised the objection against the commentary, the objector resolves the Sūtra with the words: "Therefore..."
"Valid" (*āpta*) means "attained" (*prāpta*), that is to say, "appropriate" (*yukta*).

The Vedic instruction, which is not of human origin and concerns such matters as heaven, the unseen force (*apūrva*), and deities, is appropriate—that is, established—by virtue of its being free from defects once its intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) has been proven.
And the worldly [instruction] of the Āryas and Mlecchas, which is based on other means of valid cognition, is likewise appropriate.
But in the absence of another means of knowledge, [the claim that the Veda is] unauthored is illogical.
He provides the answer: "We do not say so.
That the Vedas are of human origin will be established in the second chapter.

Therefore, the meaning is that the commentary by the author of the Bhāṣya provides the correct explanation: "instruction by a reliable person" (āptopadeśa) means the instruction of a reliable person (āpta) himself.
He asks: "But who [is it]?
For there is indeed a logical argument regarding the imperceptibility of heaven and so forth:
the intuition of a yogin does not have heaven and so forth as its object, because it is a form of perception, just like the perception of people such as ourselves; this is the intended meaning.
The reply is: we state the logical argument (*nyāya*).
He states it as follows: "Because they possess both generality and particularity, some [objects] are perceptible.
Here, whatever reason (*hetu*) is established within the subject (*pakṣa*), [that is the one to be considered].
That [perception] must be included within the subject (*pakṣa*).
Since yogic perception is established by the very same means of valid cognition that establishes it, its having heaven and so forth as its objects is also established;
therefore, the Mīmāṃsakas' inference—which contradicts the means of valid cognition that apprehends the subject—is not even capable of arising, let alone subverting it.
But if perception born of yoga (*yogaja-pratyakṣa*) is unestablished, then the reason is a fallacy characterized by an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*).
The underlying intention is that for us, however, there are many correct principles of reasoning (*nyāya*).
He challenges the reason "impermanence" by stating, "it is unestablished."
He refutes this, saying "no.
Regarding the phrase "and [if] the apūrva were eternal," there are three possible alternatives here.
Is this single apūrva common to all persons, or is it uncommon?
Even if it is uncommon, is there a distinct apūrva for each individual person?
Or is it manifold for each individual person?
Regarding this, he refutes the first alternative with the words: "If it were common [to all].
For an ordinary person never perceives anything that is unprecedented.
The meaning is that yogis perceive [the body] even when it is unmanifest.
He refutes the second alternative with the words "by this, for each person," etc.;
"exaltation" (utkarṣa) means abundance, which is to say, the accumulation of parts.
He raises an objection: "By means of the manifester.
Even a single thing is seen to possess excellence or deficiency due to the difference in its manifesters.
For example, just as a large face appears on a great surface of a mirror, yet that very same face appears minute within the pupil—this is the sense.
He refutes this with the following intention: "For it is not one [and the same]."
The skeptic reveals his own intention with the words, "But if...
He refutes it according to his own view by saying, "We say it is not seen.
The skeptic asks, "What then is that, if it is not seen?"
In that regard, if it is not seen as distinct,
there is no seeing.
What, then, is that?
As for the appearance that "the perception of difference [arises] through difference," he states his own intention: "it is a false cognition. We do not deny the perception of difference.

However, [it refers to] ultimate difference. The point is that a fabricated, unprecedented difference is not capable of producing an ultimate effect. Or, "the agency of increase and decrease" refers to the object; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
He sets forth the third alternative: "it is manifold for each individual.
He refutes it with: "it is not ceased," and then:
"at a later time."

By means of the performance of the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), that *apūrva* is manifested at its own time and rendered ready to bestow its fruit; for manifestation occurs simultaneously with the manifesting agent, as is observed in the case of lamps and similar objects.
Nevertheless, the meaning is that it does not yield its fruit as long as the activity has not ceased;
however, once the activity has ceased, it yields the fruit.
He refutes this with the words "asatī" (non-existent).
For that effect, although it existed previously, did not produce its result because the final action and the manifestation produced by it had not yet arisen.
But once the action or the manifestation has arisen, why does it not produce [the result]?
For there is no utility whatsoever for the destruction of an action;
therefore, even against your will, you must admit that it is only a non-existent action that possesses the capacity to manifest [the result] and the capacity to assist [it].
The meaning is that both of these are equally problematic.
Furthermore, if an action manifests something that is non-existent, then since non-existence is easily found everywhere, nothing new would ever be manifested.
The "destruction of action" means the destruction of effort.

In this context, Dignāga, unable to tolerate verbal testimony as a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), challenges its definition by analyzing it: "The instruction of a reliable person" (*āptopadeśa*).
First of all, the ascertainment of one thing from another cannot occur without a connection, for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Furthermore, the word is not identical in nature to the object.
Nor is it caused by the object,
because that [word] arises from the mere desire to speak of a person even in the absence of an object;
therefore, the determination of the object does not come directly from the word.
But through its effect, which is the desire to speak, one may infer that desire to speak;
and that [desire] is preceded by an intention regarding an object.
Furthermore, that intention has its origin in the mind alone.
The other, however, is rooted in valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
In that regard, one who intends to express an object ascertained by valid cognition and articulates it exactly as intended is an authoritative person (*āpta*).
From his speech, which is the effect, the speaker’s intention—the cause—is inferred;
and the cause of that intention is the cognition of the object.
Thus, because the cognition of the object is the effect of the object, this is the process of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇagati*).
In that context, by the act of "instruction" (*upadeśa*) in the phrase "the instruction of a reliable person" (*āptopadeśa*), instructors are brought to mind.

Since they are generally seen to be deceptive, the inclusion of the term "reliable" (*āpta*) serves to indicate their non-deceptiveness. If it were argued that this is for the purpose of ensuring a definitive determination of the object from such instruction, he says: "If [it were said] 'of the reliable ones'... (*yadyāptānām*).
The meaning is "of the instructors. He refutes this [opponent's] position: "From that inference.
The reliability of the instructor is inferential.
The word of such a person is indeed inference for the sake of ascertaining the meaning.
For instance, whatever word is spoken by a faultless being is all meaningful,
just like the Buddha’s teaching concerning subjects such as momentariness and selflessness.
And thus, this teaching under discussion is [analogous];
as it was stated by the Bhadanta:
"Because of its commonality with the non-deceptiveness of authoritative speech, it possesses the nature of inference."
Thus he sets forth the second alternative: "Now, the object exists in that manner.
For here, by the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) "that which is taught is instruction" (*upadiśyate ity upadeśaḥ*), the object (*artha*) is what is being spoken of.
"Āpta" means one who has attained [the truth]; that from which such instruction is obtained is so described.

This is what is meant: since one who acts after understanding an object through a word attains that very object, that word—being the instruction of a reliable person (āpta)—is a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
And thus, whatever object is indicated by a word, [one attains it].
By its attainment, suchness (tathatā) is revealed; thus it is said: "Now, the state of being as-it-is of the object. He refutes this with: "That too..."
He clarifies that very point with the words "for when" (yadā hi).
For one who determines the true nature of an object through its attainment (*āpti*) cannot determine it as being unperceived;
and since perception generally occurs through direct sensory experience (*pratyakṣa*), it is said to be "by means of direct perception."
He refutes this very point, saying "no.
The meaning of the sūtra is that a word does not cause the cognition of an object by virtue of being accompanied by reliability (*āptatva*);
nor is the reality of the word's object established through the attainment of that object.
To the question "What then [is the case]? he says: "But rather...
The phrase "connected with or disconnected from the senses" means those things previously perceived;
as it has been stated: "That [inference] is of two kinds, through the distinction between the perceived and the unperceived."
This is what is meant:
by this sutra, it is not being established as the meaning of the scripture that non-contradiction has "being spoken by a reliable person" as its cause;
nor is it being established as the meaning of the scripture that the suchness of the object [is proven] by means of the scripture.
Nor is scripture (āgama) distinct from perception and inference;
rather, it has been stated that "instruction" (upadeśa) is verbal testimony (śabda).
And the term "instruction" is a word denoting an agent (kāraka).
It is called *upadeśa* because by means of it a purposeful object is taught (*upadiśyate*) or made known (*jñāpyate*).
Nevertheless, since even the instruction found in works such as the *Vārttika* would then be considered *śabda*, it is specified that it must be "from a reliable person" (*āpta*).
Thus, by the very term "instruction," it is stated that the fruit of *āgama* (testimony) is the comprehension of the meaning of the sentence.

This has been stated as follows: that cognition which occurs with the mental mention of the word—through the intermediate operation of recollecting the object from the word—with the specific mental mention "I understand the object from the word itself," is the meaning of scripture (*āgama*), that is, its result.
Furthermore, the quality of being authoritative (*āptatva*) does not cause one to understand the meaning of the sentence; rather, it establishes the non-deviation (*avyabhicāritā*) of the scripture.
Nor is it the case that the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is understood from that very source from which the validity (*prāmāṇya*) is apprehended.

And this being the case, since the comprehension of the objects of perception and other means of knowledge would arise from inference alone—which is the cause for the cognition of their validity—it follows that perception and the others would lack the status of valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇya*).
This being so, what [other] inference could even determine the validity of an inference?

Nor is the word of a trustworthy person (*āptavākya*), though it is something to be accomplished, anything other than inference with respect to its object, since it functions by way of inferring the speaker’s cognition.
But it is not correct to say that it does not cause the object to be known;
for if it did not cause the object to be known, it would only infer the mere cognition, and in that case, there would be no establishment of the specific object.
Furthermore, there is no distinction whatsoever in cognition other than its object;
therefore, in order to qualify the speaker’s cognition, the understanding of the sentence-meaning must first be sought from the word alone.

Thus, the inference of the speaker’s cognition—which was previously thought to serve the purpose of apprehending the meaning—is rendered unnecessary, as its utility lies solely in the cognition of [the word's] validity (*prāmāṇya*).

Nor is inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) alone the relation [in question], such that there would be no relationship of signifier and signified between word and object due to their lack of such a connection;
for it will be stated that a conventional (*sāṅketika*) relation does exist between these two.
Furthermore, inseparable connection alone is not the factor that constitutes comprehension.
It has been stated that the eyes and other sense organs, although observed to deviate with respect to specific objects such as blue and so forth, are nonetheless the means for cognizing them.
Therefore, words, having been assigned conventional designations, cause their own respective meanings to be recollected;
and when accompanied by expectancy, semantic competency, and contiguity, they bring about the cognition of the sentence-meaning, even though that meaning has never been perceived before.
They do not even wait for the apprehension of a concomitance; thus, they remain far removed from inference.
How this is so has been stated briefly in the *Uddesa*.
And this has been established in the *Tattvabindu*;
therefore, everything is clear. //7//
It is of two kinds, because its objects are either perceived or unperceived.
He states the purport of the sūtra—"It is of two kinds because its objects are seen and unseen"—as being for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtham*). He analyzes it as "in many ways" (*anekadhā*).
According to the view of the Bhāṣya, he explains "because its objects are seen and unseen" as "perceptible" (*pratyakṣa*), etc.

The relationship between heaven, sacrifice, and so forth—which are the exclusive objects of verbal testimony whose validity is inferred from the mark (*liṅga*) of being composed by a reliable person (*āpta*)—is within the scope of inference.
As the author of the Bhāṣya said:
"That which is understood as being in the other world is an object that is not [otherwise] perceived."
"Even that which has an unperceived object is a means of valid cognition because its object is inferred.
Therefore, that scripture whose object is perceived is "thus" (tathā);
the other is likewise.
Having thus explained it according to the opinion of the Bhāṣya, he explains it according to his own view with the words "by the difference of the speaker" (*vaktṛbhedena*).

One who has seen the object is a speaker who has "seen the object" (*dṛṣṭārtha*); likewise, one by whom the unseen object has been inferred is [a speaker] "who has inferred the object" (*adṛṣṭārtha*).
