In this context, those who have perceived the object are the sages and people like ourselves;
those who have inferred the object are likewise only people like ourselves.

Even so, in order to establish the twofold nature of verbal testimony, [the author] adds the term "speaker" so that the reason does not fail to reside in the subject (*apakṣadharmatā*), stating: "because they are spoken by speakers of both perceived and unperceived objects."
An author whose scripture has an invisible purpose is described as such. He states its meaning by saying, "He does not engage in dispute based on direct perception.
The remainder is easily understood.
"He would not consider the authority of those statements that have been observed.
Regarding the word "he":
the commentary explains that this refers to a remote nihilist (*nāstika*). This is the construction of the *bhāṣya*.
The remainder, however, will be explained in the Parīkṣāparvan. //8//
NyS 1.1.9: The objects of valid cognition (prameya) are the self, body, sense organs, objects, intellect, mind, activity, defects, rebirth, fruit, suffering, and liberation.
In this context, the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is that which exists as something to be abandoned or accepted and is sought to be understood by one desiring liberation.
And its comprehension depends upon the specific means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by which it has been examined.
Furthermore, the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) of this [object] consists in the specific means of valid cognition.

Furthermore, it is not possible to introduce the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the self (*ātman*) and so forth without first defining the intermediate general categories of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the rest, because that [cognition of the self] is a particular instance of the general categories such as perception.
Therefore, the introduction of that [self-cognition] follows immediately after the definitions of perception and the other means of valid cognition.
Since that which has not been examined is insufficient for the determination of truth, an examination will be undertaken;
and since doubt and the other categories are the prerequisites for that examination, it is appropriate that their definitions follow later.

Therefore, here, in order to introduce the aphorism that enumerates the divisions of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) for the purpose of defining them, the author of the Commentary (*bhāṣyakāra*) asks: "But what, then, is accomplished by this means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?"

The singular number is used with reference to the genus (*jāti*), because in the present context of the object of knowledge (*prameya*), the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are employed according to their respective functions.
Having cited this commentary (*bhāṣya*), the author of the *Vārttika* raises an objection: "But what [is the purpose]? etc.
The capacity of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consists in their being necessarily concomitant with the object of cognition (*prameya*). He responds: "No.
By the capacity inherent in the definitions of perception and the other means of cognition, the mere existence of the object of cognition is established.

However, since that which remains to be explained—the object of cognition (*prameya*)—is not yet established, there is a question regarding it. Furthermore, that specific distinction has not been shown as it truly is;
and this alone is the meaning of the Sūtra.
The meaning is that those for whom liberation and saṃsāra arise through the knowledge of reality and the lack of reality are exactly this many; they are neither fewer nor more.
He extends the arrangement established for the first sūtra [to this case] with the words "here too.
Not grasping the meaning already stated, he raises an objection with the words "both" and "of direction, etc."
Because space, time, and atoms are not mentioned among [the categories of] substances;
[as in the example] "the tree stands.
The word "iti" has the sense of "and so forth," by which [one understands] "he sees the tree," and so on.

Expressions such as "he sees the moon by means of a tree" are to be understood in this way. [The author] provides the resolution: "No, because of a failure to understand the meaning of the Sūtra," for the term *prameya* (the object of cognition) does not apply to every possible object of cognition (*prameyamātra*).

However, the meaning is that since that which is known in its true nature as the means to liberation is precisely that [self] and nothing else— namely, the self and so forth— the exclusion of connection with anything else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*) is logical.
He states, "it is indeed an object of knowledge" (*prameyameva*), showing that there is no fault even in the case of the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*).
[Objection: "In this view, there would never be the status of being a means of valid cognition (pramāṇatā); thus, there is a fault. To this, he says: "What is meant by this?
It is not the state of being an object of knowledge (prameyatva) for every person that is enjoined here;
rather, it is enjoined specifically for the learned seeker of liberation (mokṣamāṇa).
The phrase "is restated" (*anūdyate*) shows that the injunction gains strength by being rooted in another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
He concludes with "therefore" (*tasmāt*).
To demonstrate his own skill, he proposes an alternative resolution while conceding the point, saying "having granted" (*upetya*).
Space and time possess the quality of being formative factors for activity, as in the injunction:
"One should eat food facing the east."
One should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva on ground sloping toward the east.
One should sacrifice with the Paurṇamāsī [offering] on the full moon day.
On the new moon day, one should sacrifice with the Amāvāsyā [offering].
Because of such scriptural statements as these,
he says— "But this is not [the case]"— to show that this is merely a skillful means (*kauśalamātra*) and not the actual resolution (*samādhāna*).
He explains this by saying, "because of the prescription of what has already been prescribed."

The meaning is that it is enjoined by the force of the prescription of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). He says "and by the first" to show that it is not only implied by the prescription of the means of valid cognition, but is also obtained from the term "object of valid cognition" (*prameya*) found in the very first sūtra.
And regarding this matter, he states the author of the Sūtra’s agreement with the words: "and this meaning.
The commentary says: [he is] the seer of every means of pleasure and pain, and the experiencer of all pleasure and pain.
Since he knows all the means for happiness and suffering, and all happiness and suffering themselves,
he is therefore omniscient.
And since one does not know these [objects] without having attained them, he says: "experiencing all" (*sarvānubhāvī*).
"Experience" (*anubhava*) means attainment (*prāpti*).
This was stated for the purpose of generating dispassion (*vairāgya*).
The same should be understood for what follows as well.
This is the distinction regarding the self: that it is to be abandoned in its conditioned form, yet to be accepted in its state of absolute isolation (kaivalya).
The body and so forth are indeed to be abandoned,
whereas liberation (apavarga) alone is to be attained.
That which has no prior body is "unprecedented" (apūrva) with respect to its body.
He refutes that with the words "not this of him.

That which has no subsequent body—that is, for the Self who is ignorant of the reality of the object of knowledge (*prameya-tattva*), there exists no further body—is "without a subsequent" (*anuttara*).
If even that is not denied, [then...]
[The objection is raised: "No," because of the implication [of the word 'no'].
But surely, just as there is no beginning for the preceding bodies, so too there would be no end for the subsequent ones;
and if that were so, the activities of those seeking liberation and the scriptures intended for that purpose would result in being purposeless. To this, he says: "Of the subsequent ones."
The meaning is "from the realization of the true nature of the object of knowledge" (*prameyatattvāvagamāt*).

Now, one might ask: when "suffering" (*duḥkha*) alone is to be indicated, does the mention of suffering by itself exclude pleasure (*sukha*)? If so, would that not contradict experience? To this, he says: "Not this... (*nedam iti*).
The author of the Vārttika explains this very commentary through objection and resolution: "Furthermore, pleasure... [is not perceived] from anything other than the words "self" and so forth;
rather, it is from these very [words] "self" and so forth, because it is perceived individually as distinct from them.
The explanation of "one becomes disenchanted" is as follows: for one who cultivates that [disenchantment], craving is severed by that very same opposing quality;
by not mentioning pleasure, this indicates its inclusion within the category of suffering.
Thus, the intended meaning is that detachment from pleasure arises for such a person. //9//
Desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain, and cognition are the marks of the self.

Since liberation also has the self as its ultimate purpose, and because the self is the most important among the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), the first sūtra defining the self begins with "desire" (*icchā*) and so forth.
To introduce that [sūtra], the commentary states: "In this regard, the self...

The intention is that the cognition "I," which takes the form of being fair-skinned and so on and manifests as the body, cannot be immediately established as a valid means of knowledge regarding the self, in the same way that the cognition of a jar or similar objects can.
Or [it refers to] the intention regarding a self existing in another body.
In this regard, the author of the Vārttika states the purport of the Sūtra: "samāna... etc.
That which is of the same class [as the self] is the body and so forth.
"Of a different kind" refers to means of valid cognition such as doubt and the like.

While this purpose exists, it follows that there is a further purpose for the scripture; namely, that although the validity of the word is established by the inference based on its being spoken by an authoritative person (*āptoktatva*), it becomes even more firm through this inference which corroborates its meaning. This is the sense.
And he adds another purpose with the words "of the convergence of means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇasaṃplavasya*).
Both instances of the word "or" (*vā*) should be understood as having the sense of "and" (*ca*) in the sense of conjunction (*anvācaya*).

Thus, by this Vārttika, the Bhāṣya passage "it is to be understood from inference" is explained; and the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "of whatever kind" (*yajjātīyasya*), which is intent on stating that desire is a mark of the self (*ātmaliṅga*), is also explained.
The phrase "of whatever kind" expresses the recollection of the pervasion (*vyāpti*).
The phrase "seeing that which is of that same kind" constitutes the application (*upanaya*) of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).
Thereupon, having inferred, "Therefore, this is a cause of pleasure," one desires to take it up.

This very desire [for inference] indicates that the apprehension of pervasion, the recollection thereof, the apprehension of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), and the desire for inference have a single agent; for if there were a difference [of agents], such a connection would be impossible due to the absence of recognition (*pratisaṃdhāna*).
This is what was stated by the words "of one" (*ekasya*).
And that which is the single experiencer, rememberer, inferer, and desirer— that is the self (*ātman*).
It cannot be the body alone, because the body itself undergoes change through the distinctions of infancy, childhood, youth, and old age.

It is not the sense faculty (*indriya*), because it would follow that what is grasped by one sense faculty could not be connected with another, such that one could say, "I see that which I previously touched.
Nor is it the mind (*manas*), because the mind is inferred solely as an instrument (*karaṇa*).
For he will state all of this because of the logical possibility of the means of knowledge for a knower.
In this rule, 3/1/17.

It might be argued that even in the absence of a self as a knower, and despite the difference between cognition and other mental states, the establishment of recognition would still be possible through the non-difference of their continuum; to this, he says: "with regard to a restricted object."
The phrase "having a restricted object" refutes the reconnection of distinct cognitions;
and by the inclusion of the word "only" (*mātra*), it refutes a continuum that is distinct from the members of that continuum.
Alternatively, if such a continuum is admitted, then that itself is the self, and thus our desired conclusion is established.

Having restated this commentary (*bhāṣya*), the author of the *Vārttika* states its purport with the words "of whatever kind" (*yajjātīyasya*). Therein he begins the investigation with the word "therein" (*tatra*).
He states the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "how [can there be] desire and so forth? (*katham icchādi*).
He refutes [the objection] with the word "by memory" (*smṛtyā*).
Now, one might ask: what contradiction is there in memory and the other [mental states] having different agents when they have a single object? To this he says: "For not...
He provides an example for the case of having different objects: "For it does not happen that [what is perceived as] color... and so forth.

He provides an example for the state of having diverse causes (*nānānimittatva*): "Nor does it happen," because from whatever cause—that is, from the tactile sense-organ (*tvagindriya*)—I touched a certain touch, from that same cause I see a form with the eye.
He provides an example for the state of having diverse agents (*nānākartṛtva*): "For it does not happen that Devadatta... [is the one who touches and sees].

It has indeed been stated that this very act of recognition establishes the identity of a single agent by means of its exclusion from cases where there is a difference of agents, such as Devadatta and Yajñadatta.
This is untenable,

because since they have different authors, there is the possibility of an extrinsic condition (*upādhi*), resulting in a deficiency in the cognition of an essential connection (*svābhāvikapratibandha*);
for indeed, the cognitions of Devadatta and Yajñadatta possess both different authors and the absence of a causal relationship.

In this regard, one who intends to argue that "recognition" (*pratisandhāna*) is not a valid member of the proof because its negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful—being uncertain whether it is due to the absence of the cause-and-effect relationship or due to having different agents—raises the objection: "Is the recognition absent because of the absence of the cause-and-effect relationship, or because of having different agents? To this, [the author] replies with the hidden intention: "This recognition occurs otherwise," and [the opponent] counters: "Not so, because of plurality."
The challenger says: "It is not an effect.

The respondent, whose intention remains concealed, replies: "That is incorrect," meaning that there is inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) due to the doubtful negative concomitance (*sandigdhavyatirekitā*).
The opponent says: "This is equally true for you as well.
The proponent, with a hidden intention, replies: "Because it is accepted. The opponent says: "No, because there is no proof."
"Unestablished purpose" means having a purpose established otherwise; that is to say, [unestablished] regarding the reason or the statement of the reason.
Now, the respondent reveals his own intention: "No."
This is due to a lack of full understanding of the meaning of the reason (*hetu*).
He analyzes that very point by saying, "it does not exist.
To the question, "What, then, is this specific reason? he replies: "And this reconnection (*pratisaṃdhāna*) has been specified."

This explains it as follows: conjunction (*pratisaṃdhāna*) is the linking together of preceding and succeeding cognitions by means of memory, through their having a single object. For instance, one thinks: "I remember that which was experienced as a cause of pleasure, such as sandalwood or a woman; I now perceive this [object] as belonging to that same class.

By this, [the author] distinguishes [this type of conjunction] from the kind of conjunction characterized by the successive production of another rice seed by a rice sprout, which is based on the necessity of the causal relationship between effect and cause.

[Objection: But surely this memory, which is a synthesis of preceding and succeeding cognitions, will also be possible through the very relation of cause and effect; what need is there for a single agent? To this he says: "And that memory is untenable on your view. [The opponent] asks: "Why?"
The answer: Because what has been experienced by one cause cannot be remembered by another cause.
For it does not happen that "I am touching with the very same tactile organ that eye with which I saw the jar."

Having stated that there is no unification [of cognition] when there is a difference in the causal signs (*nimitta*), he says the same regarding a difference in the objects (*viṣaya*): for there is no recollection by means of one intrinsic nature, such as "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*), of that which was experienced by another intrinsic nature, such as "tree-ness" (*vṛkṣatva*).
Indeed, it does not occur that one thinks, "This very tree is the pot that I saw.
Regarding a difference in the agent (*kartṛ*), he states the absence of unification: for Yajñadatta does not remember what was experienced by another, Devadatta.
For it does not occur that one who was Devadatta and saw [something] is that same person who, as Yajñadatta, sees [it].
Nor can this recognition occur on the basis of the cause-and-effect relationship despite the existence of difference;
for recognition does not occur in cases where the cause-and-effect relationship is most evident, such as between a thread and a cloth, or between a pot and its shards.

If it is argued that the cause for the synthesis [of moments] is the non-apprehension of the difference between those things that are in fact cause and effect— just as one sees it in the case of homogeneous moments, such as "the cloth is the very same as those threads" or "the moment of the potsherd is the very same as the moment of the jar"—
that is not so; for when a single *āmalaka* fruit is removed and another *āmalaka* fruit is placed in that very same spot, a synthesis occurs.
Furthermore, there is no relationship of cause and effect between those two *āmalaka* fruits.

If it is argued that the fact that the preceding and succeeding cognitions share a single object with memory is based on a relationship of cause and effect residing in the agent (*kartṛ*) and not in the action (*karman*), then—alas!—even when the realization of selflessness becomes habitual, there still exists a relationship of cause and effect among the consciousnesses; consequently, the synthesis [of experiences] based upon that would follow as before.
Furthermore, that very view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) is the supreme source of all defects; thus, the effort to realize and internalize selflessness (*nairātmya*) would be in vain.

If, on the other hand, the Tathāgata brings about a connection (*pratisaṃdhāna*) even though it does not exist—just as an actor assumes the role of Rāma for a specific purpose—that [connection] must be based upon the relationship between cause and effect.
How is it non-existent? How is it to be brought forth? Furthermore, if even the relation of cause and effect is a non-entity based solely upon conceptual construction, [how can it be real]?
Therefore, such [a conceptualized entity] cannot truly determine the production of a rice seed;
for a boy who is conceptually identified as fire can never be employed for burning or cooking.
Nor is it correct to say that there is a synthesis [of cognitions] due to the non-apprehension of the difference between conditions.
Because the various functioning consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) that take objects such as form as their domain are perceived even by ordinary people as distinct entities;
because an *ālayavijñāna* separate from the functioning consciousnesses is not apprehended;
and because the view of a self (*sattvadṛṣṭi*) expressed as "I" must have a stable entity as its object when momentariness has been refuted and no subverting evidence exists.

Therefore, because the synthesis (*pratisandhāna*)—characterized by the single-object nature of preceding and succeeding cognitions together with memory—is performed by multiple agents, its absence (*vyatireka*) establishes, in the absence of any limiting conditions (*nirupādhi*), the fact of having a single agent;
and it is established that this single agent is the Self (*ātman*), distinct from the body, the senses, and the intellect.
With this intention it was said: "And there is memory of the aforementioned nature;
therefore, in whichever position memory is possible, in that [position] the connection [of the act with its result] is logical.
The meaning is that this refers to the position of the identity of the agent.
Not understanding the intention, another person objects again, saying "You [say]...
The opponent himself states this in a single sentence: "How?"—the meaning being, "How is it not possible?"

It might be argued that even the mind of a yogin could serve as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the mind of an omniscient one, and thus there would be a reconnection (*pratisandhāna*) [of the continuum] by means of that yogin’s mind; therefore, he says: "belonging to which body" (*yatkāya*).
This is what is meant:
The continuum (*santāna*) is the stream of consciousness (*cittapravāha*) existing in the relationship of material cause and its effect (*upādānopādeyabhāva*).
Furthermore, the mind of a yogi is not the material cause of the mind of an omniscient one;
for that [omniscient mind] has [the object] as its objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).
Furthermore, the mention of "the body" is intended to indicate a single continuum;
therefore, it follows that memory is possible even in another birth.
The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin), wishing to instruct this opponent—who is ignorant of our intention—in another way, states that memory would otherwise be untenable: "No."
Because cognitions are unstable,

there is indeed no distinction between that which has not arisen and that which is superimposed without a causal continuity; therefore, one must admit that a previously arisen experience, having deposited a certain latent impression (*vāsanā*), perishes, and by means of that [impression], memory is produced at a later time.
The meaning is that since an unstable cognition cannot be habituated, the self must be accepted as stable.
He states another argument: "And because of the lack of connection.
The meaning is that there is no connection between cognitions that do not exist at the same time.

Again, the opponent objects: "By power (*śakti*). The meaning is this: for us who maintain that all things are momentary (*kṣaṇika*), there is nothing in this world observed to be stable such that it could be perfumed by a perfuming agent. [The author] refutes this under the guise of explaining the introductory statement (*grahaṇakavākya*), saying: "Even so... and so forth. He argues that even if that were the case, it is impossible to perfume something that lacks a connection because it exists at a different time.
The preceding mind, which is the evolving consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*), is of six kinds:
the five cognitions of form and so forth, which are non-conceptual, and the sixth, which is conceptual consciousness.
That which arises together with it, being simultaneous and indistinguishable from it, is called the *ālayavijñāna*.
It is the locus of the notion of "I" and possesses the capacity for memory;
furthermore, that capacity is not distinct from that cognition itself.
Therefore, by some means, with the intention of expressing a distinction, it is said to be "qualified by power.
The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) says: "It has been stated in this regard."
For the stability of entities, established through the common consensus of all people, will indeed be demonstrated by the refutation of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*).
And thus, since it is observed that stable and connected things such as cloth are perfumed by musk and the like, the meaning is that this cannot occur in what is unstable or unconnected.
It might be argued:

"Even though two cognitions are unstable, since they exist simultaneously, there is a connection between them; why then does one cognition not instill a memory in the other cognition that has been perfumed by it? To this, he says:
"And that which..."—the word "and" (api) here refers to what is about to be stated.
[Objection: "But surely, although it might not provide assistance while the mind is present, it will do so when it is future. To this he says: "Nor even... [The opponent] asks: "How?"
The answer begins with "First, the present...
He concludes the subject at hand with "Therefore...";
he states "And for this reason as well" to show that even apart from this, memory does not arise from mere consciousness alone through the relationship of cause and effect in the absence of a self.
Why? Because an entity (bhāva) depends upon an agent of being (bhavitṛ). An entity is a phenomenon characterized by arising;
the agent of being is a phenomenon [that brings about that arising].
Cooking is softening, which is the disjunction of conjunctions.

Although it inheres in the parts of the rice grain, it is said to belong "to the rice grains" because of the metaphorical treatment of the parts and the whole as non-different. Motion is vibration, as in the case of Devadatta acting as the agent.

The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin), having raised the proponent of momentariness (kṣaṇikavādin), refutes him by means of the doctrine of non-momentariness, stating: "It would be without a substratum.

The opponent, with the intention of asserting momentariness, says: "The effect... The proponent of the established doctrine replies with the intention of asserting non-momentariness: "And that is not so."
The relationship of container and contained is observed between two things that exist at the same time,
as in the case of a bowl and a jujube fruit.
For it is only a stable bowl that, by obstructing the gravity of a stable jujube fruit falling due to its own weight and thereby preventing its downward fall, becomes its container.

If it should be argued that memory is not the "being" (bhāva), but rather its "arising" (utpatti) is the being, and that it is not logical for the "becoming entity" (bhavitṛ) to depend on another becoming entity because it would lead to an infinite regress— this is the objection raised in the words "athāpīdam" (but even this...).
He refutes this with the words "and that is not so.
He explains the reason for the contradiction with the words "if...":
why is it contradictory? To this he says: "and its own nature... and so forth.
The meaning of "because" (*yataḥ*) is as follows:
since the nature of arising, when being stated, contradicts [the opponent's] independent [position], therefore there is a contradiction; this is the meaning.
He explains "because it is not accepted" with the words "for you [do not accept this].
He clarifies "because of contradiction" with the words "and if [it were] distinct.
*Tantra* means a treatise (*śāstra*).
He raises an objection with "Now, if... (atheti);
the meaning is that in this way there is neither contradiction nor non-acceptance [of the position].
He refutes it with "What, where? (kiṃ kveti).

He states the essential nature of the designation: "It is memory. Furthermore, even though arising is an entity (*bhāva*), memory is neither [arising] nor an entity, because being an entity is invariably concomitant with being an effect (*kārya*) alone, and memory is an effect.
Nor does there follow an infinite regress, because [the series] is established as being eternal.
Thus, with the intention that for memory, the single, eternal self remains as the possessor of the state, he says: "And when there is origination..."
He concludes the subject under discussion with the words "therefore":
this is established— that memory has a single agent as its author through the preceding and succeeding cognitions, because it is connected with them by virtue of having the same object.
Furthermore, that which has a single agent as its cause is not reconnected at the navel in the same way that Devadatta’s memory is not [reconnected] through the cognitions of Yajñadatta;
and this [memory] is not like that.
Therefore, it is so.

Having thus established the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), he provides proof for this point through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatirekin*) with the words "Or rather" (*atha vā*).

The inclusion of the term "many" (*aneka*) is for the purpose of dispelling the doubt that there might be multiple causes; for indeed, there is a synthesis (*pratisandhāna*) together with the memory: "By that very same [agent] by whom color and the rest were experienced, the odor is perceived"—therefore, in dramatic performance (*abhinaya*), it arises from the practice of Bharata’s doctrine.
This refers to those for whom a convention has been established.
And as it has been stated by others:
"The movement of the creeper-like eyebrow of a dancer is certainly not a single [entity] in the ultimate sense."
Because it is a collection of atoms, its unity is merely conceptualized.
Thus it is said;
regarding this, he replies: because the raising of the eyebrows is a single entity.
The eyebrow is not a collection of atoms, but rather a single composite substance (*avayavidravya*).
And even the act of exhaling directed toward that [object] is but a single action.
Or, let it be that the raising of the eyebrows is merely an aggregate of atoms;
nevertheless, because the aggregate is not distinct from its constituent members, it is nothing but those very atoms.
Furthermore, each of these [cognitions] possesses both unity and commonality among various discerning perceivers who hold the view of Bharata.

Moreover, even for these, there exists—by way of producing non-conceptual cognitions within their own respective domains—the state of being a cause for the subsequent synthesis [of experience] as "by me. Thus, this so-called "unity" is merely imagined.

Having thus stated that desire and the rest are signs of the self by way of synthesis, the author of the Vārttika now states "Or rather," explaining their status as a sign by virtue of being qualities (*guṇatayā*).
The dependence of desire and the other qualities must be established as being like color and so forth.
And that [dependence] is proven by their very impermanence, which distinguishes them from generality, particularity, and inherence;
for no impermanent entity exists independently of a substance.

Therefore, since dependence is established by that very same reason which proves the status of being a quality (*guṇatva*), there is no need for a separate reason to prove dependence; keeping this in mind, the author of the *Vārttika* states, "That too has been stated previously," and thus establishes the status of being a quality by means of the already-established dependence.
Furthermore, this dependence of the impermanent is not established by [the category of] substance (*dravya*).

Since even substance and action, though impermanent, are dependent upon something else, [the author] distinguishes them from desire and so forth by means of their dependence on a substance— a dependence which is established as being impermanent— stating: "Desire and so forth are neither substance nor action,
because they are inherent in a pervasive substance, like sound," and so on.
Although its inherence in a substance is established merely by its impermanence,

nevertheless, since its existence is accounted for by the mere postulation of a substance, and there is a lack of evidence for postulating parts for it, that substance is first established as being partless.
And a partless substance is of two kinds:
It is both all-pervasive and atomic;
yet it is not atomic,
because desire and other qualities are perceived therein.

In some cases [the conjunction] occurs through the action of one of the two, and in others by way of its own nature; since there is no evidence for postulating a motion in that [ether] when such a conjunction is established, its all-pervasiveness is proven.
This is the explanation of the inclusion of the word "etc. (ādi).
By this indirect statement, the eternity and supreme magnitude of the self (ātman) are demonstrated.
He states that everything has been demonstrated by the one who formulated this inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*), saying "by way of generality" (*sāmānyataḥ*).
He brings to light that inference which was previously held in mind— where the dependence of desire and so forth upon a substance was to be proven by means of the reason of impermanence—
and he also combines the reason of being an effect (*kāryatva*), saying "by this."

[Objection: Let there be dependence on a substance; nevertheless, let there be dependence on the body, so that there is no need for a self (ātman) that has never been perceived. To this, he says: "not as long as... [The qualities] are not qualities of earth and the other elements, because that would entail their being common to all persons.
And because it is conceived as the instrument for the production of those [qualities], the mind is not their agent.
Therefore, it is a distinct substance different from the eight substances; in that [substance] reside desire and the other qualities.
And he says that it is established that "that [is] the self" by means of the phrase "because of its negation. //10//
The body is the substratum of movement, the sense organs, and their objects.

Having identified the self, [the author notes] that all the causes of suffering for the self—such as the sense organs and so forth—are, both directly and indirectly, dependent upon the body as their source; thus, the body alone is the primary root cause of this suffering. Consequently, the following sūtra begins with "volitional activity" (*ceṣṭā*) in order to define the body.
To introduce that [topic], the commentary says: "Of that" (tasya). The word "of that" refers to the self (ātmānam).
Experience (bhoga) is the consciousness of pleasure and pain.
The body is the substratum for that [consciousness].
Thus, by this, it is stated that the body is the ultimate cause of the entire accumulation of misfortune;
therefore, it alone should be defined prior to the sense faculties and so forth.

In this context, by virtue of being the locus of activity, the locus of the sense organs, and the locus of objects, the body is distinguished from each of its own kind— namely the self, the sense organs, and so forth— as well as from those of a different kind, such as the means of valid cognition, doubt, and the like.
And how is it that [the body] is the substratum of activity? This refers to the Bhāṣya. He explains its meaning with the words "What, moreover, is...
Activity (ceṣṭā) is functional operation (vyāpāra).
And that [definition] is not a valid definition because it is both over-extensive and under-extensive;
the point is that it exists in trees and the like, yet it is absent in the bodies of frogs and other creatures residing within stones.
The subsequent commentary begins with "that which is desired" (*īpsitam*), etc.
He explains that as follows: "beneficial and harmful" (*hitāhita*), etc.
[This refers to] that which has been employed, meaning that for which effort has been generated.
Furthermore, "activity" (ceṣṭā) is not intended to mean mere activity in general, but rather a specific kind of activity;
and since that [specific activity] does not exist in trees and the like, there is no over-extension [of the definition].
And although such an activity exists in wooden machines and the like,
there is nevertheless no deviation [from the rule] because of the qualification "provided there is no employment by another corporeal being," since those [machines] are employed by a corporeal body.
The point is this: a body that has not been constrained by another material form possesses such functional activity;
for even though the body of a frog situated within a stone lacks that activity at the moment, it possesses the capacity for it, since such activity is observed when the stone is split open.
He explains the commentary on the phrase "how [is it] the substratum of the sense organs" with the word "how.
The point is that if being the substratum of the sense organs were due to being in conjunction with them, then even jars and the like would follow as being bodies,
because they too are in conjunction with the sense organs.
He explains the commentary on the refutation beginning with "yasya" (of whom) as follows: "The body... and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "by this":
since it is logically untenable for them to subsist [in that way], the meaning of "basis" (*āśraya*) for objects must also be explained differently.

Although objects such as odors do not reside in the body by their own nature, nevertheless, they "reside" in it for the sake of their effect or purpose, which is to serve as the cause for the perception of pleasure and so forth; this is the meaning.
By this, the commentary beginning with "yasmin" and so forth has been explained.
He raises an objection: "But how [is it]? He provides the reply: "By means of the universal," and so on.

The capacity that is restricted by specific factors such as hunger—which is introduced by the context—is included under the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "context and so forth. He states another meaning of the word "capacity" (*sāmarthya*): "And capacity...
He also states yet another: "By means of valid cognition... (pramāṇa).
In this regard, in the first position, the word *ceṣṭā* has its primary meaning as a specific kind of activity, such as "vibration" (*spanda*) and so forth.
This very point is demonstrated by the passage beginning with "The world, for its part... and ending with "...and thus this word *ceṣṭā*.
He then explains the second position—that there is an impossibility of a means of valid cognition—with the words "Even though it expresses a universal... (*sāmānyavācyapi*).
"Api" signifies admission;
"pramāṇāsaṃbhavaḥ" means the impossibility of a means of valid cognition; [this is] the non-establishment [of the thesis].
And that [body] is shown by the phrase "not merely action.
Thus, when the term *ceṣṭā* (volitional effort) is explained in this way, there is no undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of jars and the like being considered bodies.

Having thus described, both according to the Bhāṣya and by his own view, that each [of the three]— being the locus of movement (*ceṣṭā*), etc.— is a definition (*lakṣaṇa*) of the body, he refutes the opinion of those who have maintained that all of these together constitute the definition of the body, with the words "by whomsoever... If the first term, "the locus of movement," were the definition...
In that case, there would be a deviation (vyabhicāra) with respect to a pot;
therefore, the second term "indriyāśraya" is included, which means "that which is in contact with the sense organ."

Nevertheless, there is still an inconsistency (vyabhicāra) with that very same jar and so forth, because since the sense organs function by reaching their objects (prāpyakāritva), jars and other such things are also in contact with the sense organs.
Therefore, he says: "having the object as its locus" (arthāśraya).
Even so, the fallacy of deviation remains exactly as it was,

because even jars and the like serve as substrata for objects by virtue of the inherence (*samavāya*) of objects such as color and so forth within them. Now, if "substratum" is intended to mean [inherence] itself, [then the definition is still flawed].
Nevertheless, there is no inherence of the sense organs in the body.
If it is argued that there is no contradiction in the inherence of the olfactory organ because it is composed of earth, we say no;
for, since it inheres in the parts of the body, it does not inhere in the body as a whole.
If the nose-tip itself were the olfactory organ,
or if its substrate were beyond the reach of the senses, even so, the body would not be inherent in it.
Otherwise, because its activity would be partly perceptible and partly imperceptible, it would follow that the body is imperceptible, like the conjunction between a wind and a tree.
Furthermore, if the status of being a "body" consists in the inherence of movement, sense organs, and objects, then alas!
since all of these exist in the atoms which are the inherent causes of the sense organs, it would follow that those atoms too are bodies; thus he says: "all... (samasta-).

It might be argued: "Even in your own view, there is a deviation [from the rule] in the case of the sense organs such as the eye, because they too serve as the substratum for the aforementioned activity. To this, he says: "But just as... (yathā tu).
The qualification "provided there is no application by another corporeal [entity]" has been specified;
however, since the eyes and other [senses] are applied to the body by means of a corporeal [action] such as opening, there is no over-extension [of the definition].
But the ear is not at all a substratum for effort.
Thus it is established that one becomes disenchanted by contemplating this body as a mere sign. //11//
NyS 1.1.12: The sense organs—the olfactory, gustatory, visual, tactile, and auditory—are derived from the elements.

Because the sense organs (indriya) are distinguished from objects and other factors by their quality of being "conduits" (upanāyaka), the definition of the sense organs is stated before that of objects and the rest.

Furthermore, the author of the Bhāṣya states that it is not possible to provide a specific definition (viśeṣalakṣaṇa) without first establishing a general definition (sāmānyalakṣaṇa); thus, he first provides the general definition of the sense organs useful for the purpose of detachment (nirveda): "They are the means of enjoyment" (bhogasādhanāni).

By this, the general definition is indicated: "A sense organ is that which, being conjoined with the body, is distinct from the agent (kāraka) and the object (doṣa), and is a direct instrument of cognition."

While it should have been stated that "the sense organ is the means for direct perception," the description of it as "the means for experience" is intended for the purpose of inducing world-weariness (*nirveda*).
Furthermore, the nose and other organs are means for experience only through a mediated succession, because the mind alone is the direct means for that;
for the direct apprehension of pleasure and pain constitutes experience.
To the [deities] of the nose—12.
In this context, "the faculties" (*indriyāṇi*) is the designation of the subject to be defined, meaning the nose and the others.
He states that these five have exactly five characteristics—namely, the "characteristic sūtras. These are sūtras in the sense of being introductory.
The meaning is that when the sūtras are being examined:
those of the same class as the nose and so forth are the tongue and so forth, because they have restricted objects;
whereas those of a different class are the mind and so forth, because they have all things as their objects.
He states the doubt to be refuted by the commentary beginning with "jighrati" (one smells), etc., as follows:
"by way of enumeration," meaning by way of the general enumeration of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and so forth.
For it is the definition that is to be enjoined.
The object of reference (lakṣya) is that which is intended to be pointed out;
for that which is already known is pointed out,
while that which is unknown is enjoined.

Furthermore, it is not possible for a single thing to be both known and unknown simultaneously, nor can it possess the status of both the characterized (lakṣya) and the characteristic (lakṣaṇa); such is the sense [of the objection].
He refutes this: "This is not so, as was stated" is the meaning.
Why? Because they exist as instruments (*karaṇa*), since the nose and the other [senses] are characterized by the apprehension of their own respective objects.
This is what is meant:

because the sense-faculties (*indriya*) are beyond the reach of the senses themselves (*atīndriya*), they must always be inferred solely by virtue of being the instruments for the perception of their own respective objects.

Therefore, the very fact of being the means for the apprehension of their respective objects is the definition (*lakṣaṇa*), by virtue of its exclusion of both similar and dissimilar classes. However, the olfactory nature (*ghrāṇatva*) and so forth, which are inherent in that same object, are the definienda (*lakṣya*).

And in this context, words such as "nose" (*ghrāṇa*) and so on—just like the word "lotus-born" (*paṅkaja*) and others—sometimes function by taking the meaning of their constituent parts as their basis.
In some cases, [words] apply to a general-particular (sāmānya-viśeṣa),
because it is impossible to abandon the perceived connection between the meanings of the parts when there is no subverting factor (bādhaka).

However, in the case of words such as *aśvakarṇa*, which denote a specific type of tree, the meaning of the parts is abandoned due to the subverting factor of the impossibility of [an actual] horse's ear.

Furthermore, since terms such as "nose" (*ghrāṇa*) are not applied to contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) and the like—even though those are the means for perceiving odors and so forth, which constitute the meaning of the word's components—the cause for the application of terms such as "nose" is precisely the generic property of being a nose (*ghrāṇatva*) as conjoined with the meaning of its components.

Thus, the term "nose" itself indicates the property of being a nose and so forth; this is what is meant by the expression "pointing out through indication" (*lakṣaṇanirdeśa*). And this has been indicated by the [sūtra] phrase "the sense-faculties" (*indriyāṇi*).
However, that very [definition] is intended to convey the meaning of its constituent parts; thus, the specification of the definition is "the olfactory organ" (*ghrāṇa*) and so forth.
Nor is there any deviation [from the definition] regarding contact (*saṃnikarṣa*), which is the means for perceiving odor;
for the property of being the means for perceiving odor belongs to that which possesses the general characteristics of a sense faculty (*indriya*), and not to contact.
Thus, by this [commentary], the Bhāṣya beginning with "it smells" (jighrati) and ending with "characterized by the apprehension of its own object" has been explained.
By the inclusion of the term "etymological definition" (nirvacana), the mere ground for the application of a word is expressed;
by that, the word "skin" (tvak) is also included.
Furthermore, the designation [of "tongue" and so forth] is applied metaphorically to that sense organ located in the skin, which serves as the means for perceiving touch.
The commentary (*bhāṣya*) beginning with "Regarding the phrase 'from the elements' (*bhūtebhyaḥ*)," which is intended to explain the purport of that portion of the aphorism (*sūtra*), states:
"Of those having diverse material causes," and so forth.
The author of the *Vārttika* explains that [portion] as follows: "Regarding the phrase 'from the elements' (*bhūtebhyaḥ*)."

He asks: "But what [is it]? The answer: "The state of being the means for perceiving the specific quality of the element. For it is by the sense of smell alone that the specific quality of earth, which is odor, is perceived, and not by the sense of taste or others.
In this way, it is by the sense of taste alone that the specific quality of sweetness belonging to water is perceived,
and not by the sense of smell or others;
likewise, it is by the eye alone that the white and luminous form of fire is perceived.
In this way, the touch of air is neither hot nor cold and is not produced by heat;
likewise, sound belongs to space only through the ear—such indeed is the rule.
And here the formal argument (prayoga) is as follows: the perception of odor is accomplished by an instrument, because it is an action, like the action of cutting.
Thus, that [perception] is produced by an instrument distinct from the causes of other actions.

Because it is an effect while not following the positive and negative concomitance of that [specific] action; for whatever is an effect that does not follow the positive and negative concomitance of the performance of a particular action is all produced by an instrument other than the instrument of that action.

Just as the action of weaving cloth and so forth is produced by instruments such as the loom, which are distinct from the instruments such as the wheel and staff used for the action of making a jar; and this [action] is likewise;
therefore, it is so.
And that instrument is the olfactory organ, which is distinct from the eye and the other senses.
It is a substance, because it is the substratum of conjunction, like a jar.
And that [smell] belongs to earth, because, while being a substance, it is the manifestor of smell alone among [the qualities] such as color and so forth, just like another earthly object.
The same should be applied to the sense of taste and the others as well.

This has been stated: whatever kind of sense organ there is—whether it be earthen (*pārthiva*) or consisting of water (*pārthasīya*)—the specific quality (*guṇaviśeṣa*) of that earth or water is either odor or a particular taste such as sweet.
Therefore, earth is distinguished from water and the other elements, or water is distinguished from earth and the others;
that which is the cause for the mutual exclusion of the elements is perceived by that very same sense organ and not by another.
Furthermore, the tongue does not perceive the variety of tastes belonging to earth in the same way it perceives those of water; therefore, it is not composed of earth.
If that were the case, odor would also be perceived by it.
Thus, the restriction that "each specific sense organ [perceives its own object]" determines the particularity of the qualities.
But these are not the sense-faculties (*indriya*).

And in this context, having intended to express some kind of distinction of the auditory faculty— which is space— by means of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of its conjunction with the ear-cavity (*karṇaśaṣkulī*), the meaning of the phrase "from the elements" (*bhūtebhyaḥ*) is to be explained as follows.
By this, indeed, that which the Sāṃkhyas assert— namely, that "the sense organs are derived from the ego" (ahaṃkārika)—
is refuted.
He states the reason for this refutation in the compound word *aikātmye*.

According to the established doctrine (rāddhānta) of the Sāṃkhyas, the effect is of the same nature as its cause; and since that cause of the sense organs is indeed the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra), there would be a single essence—that is, a single causality.
Consequently, there would be no fixed rule regarding the unity of the nose and the other senses, as they would all share that same single essence.
He analyzes this as follows: "If, however... He raises an objection: "A single...
He analyzes further: "Now..."
The meaning is that there is one thing to be cooked, one conjunction with fire, and one heat.
He refutes this by saying, "We do not say so.
Even though heat is a common cause, [it does not establish identity].

Nevertheless, in the production of a fragrance or other quality, because the preceding destructions of the fragrance and so forth—which serve as the efficient causes—are distinct, there arises a diversity of effects based on that diversity of causes.

This is what was stated: "The intrinsic particularity (*svagato viśeṣaḥ*) of those preceding forms and so forth is their destruction"—this is the meaning. Now, one might ask: why is the universal (*sāmānya*) such as "form-ness" (*rūpatva*) itself not considered an intrinsic particularity? To this he says: "And having done so... (*evaṃ ca kṛtvā*).

The sense is that if universals such as "color-ness" (rūpatva) remain in their original state, there can be no distinction such as "more cooked" or "most cooked"; however, in the case of destructions (pradhvaṃsa), it is impossible for them to be "small," "greater," or "total," because they are [by nature] non-existent. He raises a further objection: "A single action... (ekaṃ karma).
He refutes this with "no" (na).
The sense is that an inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) depends upon proximity to its own substratum. He raises an objection with "if, then" (yadi tarhi).
"Loss of characteristics" means, likewise, the loss of its defining marks.
He refutes this, saying "no";
the meaning is that there is no other subsequent cause in the form of a positive entity.
But the absence of conjunction indeed depends upon the production of a subsequent conjunction.
He concludes: "Therefore... //12//
NyS 1.1.13: Earth, water, fire, air, and ether are the elements.
However, the characteristic of the elements should be understood as being the nature of the sense faculties. //13//
Smell, taste, color, touch, and sound are the qualities of earth and the other elements; they are the objects of those [senses].
The author of the Bhāṣya introduces the definition of *artha* (the object/purpose), which follows in sequence, with the words "But these...
(*ime tu*). By the word "but" (*tu*), he distinguishes [them] from the mere object (*artha-mātra*).
Those things which, when cultivated as objects of the senses, serve as means for attaining the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*)— [End of sentence fragment]
But those which are made objects of false knowledge (mithyājñāna) are the causes of saṃsāra; this is the meaning of "these [are they]."
The Gandharvas... // 14 //

In this context, the objects recalled by the order of the enumeration are to be understood as the "objects of definition" (lakṣya); their "definition" (lakṣaṇa) consists of those [sūtras] beginning with "tad-artha.
The word "tat" refers back to the sense organs (indriya) that were just defined immediately prior.
These are the objects of those sense-faculties.
The definition of objects is that they are apprehended by the sense-faculties.
Since the definition is fully established by this much alone, the subsequent statement—"the qualities of earth and so forth"—is made out of friendliness for the sake of detailed classification.
Earth, water, fire, as well as qualities (guṇas), properties (dharmas) such as number, action, and so forth—

even when these have been understood through their distinct divisions— this mention of "earth and the rest" is made out of friendship for the purpose of making known the restriction of the sense organs to their respective objects. The commentary stating "of earth and the rest" is not intended to indicate that it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*).
Rather, it is merely a designation of their objects;
that is, "according to their application.

This means that, in their respective order, from earth up to air, the qualities beginning with odor and ending with touch are applied according to the restriction of four, three, two, and one respectively.
The meaning is that sound exists only in space (*ākāśa*).
He explains the defining term "having that as their object" with the words "of the sense-faculties" (*indriyāṇām*):
[this refers] to the order in which the olfactory faculty and the others are recited in the Sūtra on the Faculties, and to the order in which odor and the others are presented here.
The meaning is "without transgressing that.

Here, the author of the Vārttika, having raised a doubt due to the appearance of several possible compound types in the expression *pṛthivyādiguṇāḥ*, determines it to be a *dvandva* compound—namely, *pṛthivyādiguṇāḥ*.
A locative (*saptamī*) compound is not shown here because it would have the same meaning as a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) compound.

[Objection: But surely a *bahuvrīhi* compound may occur through grammatical non-co-referentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), as in the case of *kaṇṭhekāla* ("the one with a black throat"). [The meaning would be: "those from which the qualities of earth and so forth—namely smell and the rest—arise. For instance, smells and other qualities residing in atoms initiate smells and other qualities in the composite whole (*avayavin*), and sound residing in space produces a sound of the same class in space. To this, he replies: "And not otherwise."

The sense is that, by virtue of an indicative mark (*jñāpaka*), a *bahuvrīhi* compound is sometimes formed even from words with different loci (*vyadhikaraṇa*). However, what is established by such an indicative mark does not apply everywhere.

Furthermore, the demonstration that smell and the other qualities are the causes of earth and the other elements is of no use in certain contexts, such as the contemplation of revulsion (*nirveda*). This is the intended meaning.
Any other compound, such as a *karmadhāraya* and so forth; he implies the exclusion of the *dvandva* by saying "not a *dvandva*"; he provides the resolution: "No."
Regarding the phrase "of both as well":
by the inclusion of "earth and so forth" (pṛthivyādi).
If, by the word "and so forth" (ādi), wind and the others were to be included, [then the following would apply].
The definition "having that as their object" would be under-extended (*avyāpaka*), because those [objects] lack the status of being objects of the external sense-faculties; this is the meaning.
By the inclusion of the term "qualities" (*guṇa*), the word "all" intends to include both those that are dependent (*āśrita*) and those that are not dependent (*anāśrita*).
Because the word "quality" (guṇa) denotes a property (dharma);
the particularity (viśeṣa), moreover, consists of lines, sub-lines, and so forth, but not the ultimate one (antyaviśeṣa),
because that is beyond the reach of the senses.

And it should be inferred that these [objects], as appropriate, serve as the causes for passion and dispassion, being the respective objects of false knowledge and right knowledge. An objection is raised: "What about fragrance? He replies:
"The aphorism need not be made so concise."
The meaning is that a separate enumeration of smell and the other [objects] must be made.
He states the restriction: "the sense organs. Therein, among those that are unrestricted, [he specifies].

The meanings are as follows: earth, water, and fire are perceptible by two sense organs; the remaining collection of qualities, beginning with number and ending with particularity (*viśeṣa*), is not perceptible by two sense organs;
likewise, [the universal] is perceptible by all sense organs.
Here, he sets forth the Buddhist position with the words "by seeing and touching.
He states the objection to that with the word "he":
[the object] is apprehended as having color-form (rūpa) as its objective support either by self-cognition (svasaṃvedana) or by mental cognition (mānasa-jñāna).

The meaning is that just as a cognition is experienced as qualified by color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth, so too it is experienced as qualified by a jar (*ghaṭa*) and so forth, which are distinct from color-form and the rest.
To this, the opponent says: "From color-form and so forth, thus arranged..."
He indicates the aspect as "thus" (tathā).
"Arrangement" (sanniveśa) means a specific configuration.
It is the atoms of form and so forth themselves, arisen in such-and-such a manner and distinguished by a single function such as carrying water, that are called a "jar."
However, the designation "form" (rūpa) and so forth is applied by way of association with [the whole], such as a jar.
As it has been said: "Even when one speaks of a 'jar,' it is simply the form and other [qualities] that perform a single purposeful action which are so designated. [The author] refutes this: No.
Regarding the phrase "the meaning of the aspect" (*ākārārtha*):

because the object is eternally connected with its corresponding word-meaning, just as [one understands] "a jar," so too is the meaning understood as "form and the other [sensory objects] are arranged in such a way."
The meaning is: "by way of that jar-form" means "by way of similarity to a jar. And thus there is a refutation.
He states another refutation: "and if [it were] merely color and so forth."
First of all, a single moment of form and so forth is not the pot,
because it would follow that there could be no application of that term to a subsequent moment.
Therefore:
The meaning is that if one intends only form and so forth without intending their distinctions, then this objection applies. He raises an objection: "Because of the distinction in configuration.
[This means: just as objects such as form are experienced according to their configurations, [so too are they perceived].
The meaning is that the cognitions of jars and so forth arise from those [atoms] arranged in such a manner.
He refutes this, saying: "This is not so.
If [the whole] were something other [than the atoms], it would be merely a difference in designation, namely, that it is called the "composite" (avayavin).
If there were non-difference [between the pot and its cognition], the designation would be purposeless.
He raises an objection: "The cognitions of pots and so forth.

Because they cannot withstand analysis as being either one or many, pots and the like are indeed non-existent; they merely appear in conceptual cognitions produced by the beginningless latencies of conceptual construction (*vikalpavāsanā*).
By the word "sound" (śabda), he indicates conceptual construction (vikalpa)—that is, [he means] "by the power of the latent impression of sound.
He refutes this, saying: "That is incorrect.
The seed of false cognition is the object that is the domain of correct cognition.
The meaning is that if one accepts [the former view] in some respect, there is a loss of the intended object.

However, he who speaks by transcending worldly conventions says: "A false cognition that has a beginning takes correct knowledge as its cause, whereas this [false cognition] is, moreover, beginningless."
A stream of false cognitions arises from each preceding false cognition;
[the opponent might argue] that there is no need for right knowledge in this matter.
To that, he replies: "And these are false cognitions."

The meaning is that the whole (avayavin) is not distinct from its parts, such as color and so forth. The opponent, however, states the proof for this non-distinction: "It is not the case that [it does not exist]," for there is no such thing as "soup" (yūṣa) apart from the meat and water.
Nor is there such a thing as a "row" apart from the bamboo trees themselves.

He refutes [the argument], saying: "This is not a valid reason," with regard to those things that have attained the state of jars and so forth in your own system. The triple world consists of the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); within the realm of desire, there is the atom (*aṇu*) composed of eight substances (*aṣṭadravyaka*) which is devoid of sound.
In that regard, the nature of the desire realm has been explained:
"In the desire realm,
a [sensory] atom consists of eight substances."
Form, taste, odor, and tangibility are four substances;
earth, water, fire, and air are four [others].
The word "substance" (dravya) denotes a real entity (vastu).
Therefore, there is the traditional teaching (āgama) that "an atom consists of eight substances.
This would be contradicted if one does not accept earth and the other elements as being distinct from visible form and the rest.
Now, if out of impudence it is argued: "Of earth and the others..."
And thus, because the number eight is established as being conventional (saṃvṛta), there is no contradiction with scripture; this is the intended meaning.
The response is: "Even so" (tathāpi).
Let it be that they do not exist in reality (vastutas).
Since both [the parts and the whole] would likewise be merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*), he says: "of that which is being aggregated" (*saṃhanyamānasya*).
For whatever is dependent upon something else cannot be logically accepted once the existence of that [basis] is denied;
the meaning is that conjunction cannot be logically accepted in the absence of those things that are being conjoined.
Nor is there conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*),
for that conceals the nature of another with its own nature; and in the absence of that which is being concealed, there is no composite.
Nor are they being combined; the sense is: what could this [nature] conceal by way of its own essential form?

Thus, having demonstrated the fault of contradiction in the argument "because there is no cognition of that [the probans] when that [the object] is not apprehended," he states— "when that is not apprehended"— to show that, upon examining its own capacity, the statement of the reason does not express the intended mark (liṅga), but rather possesses an unrelated meaning.
This is indeed what is intended here.

[The opponent argues: "Earth and the other [elements] are non-different from color and the other [sensory qualities], because when color and the others are not perceived, there is no cognition of earth and the others.
To this we reply: that cannot be stated by means of the principle that "when X is not perceived, there is no cognition of Y."
In the phrase "non-apprehension of that" (*tadagraha*), the word "that" (*tat*) refers to the primary subject;
since earth and the other elements are the subjects (*dharmin*), they alone are what must be referred to.
Consequently, the meaning would be: "because there is an absence of the cognition of earth and so forth when earth and so forth are not apprehended."
And thus, the non-difference of their form and so forth, which was asserted by you, would not be established; therefore, [your argument] is incoherent.

Alternatively, if form and so forth are made the subject of the proposition (*pakṣa*), even then [the reason] would be "because in the absence of the apprehension of form and so forth, there is an absence of the cognition of form and so forth."
Nevertheless, since the intended meaning of the proposition is not established, the point is that it is incoherent.
He states—“In this way, ‘mere form and so forth’”—that the same undesirable consequence applies even when the proposition is formulated with different words.
He states the fault in the proposition—“And in all cases”—as follows.

The meaning is that there is a contradiction in terms of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the number "plurality," which is restricted to a manifold of objects related to a single referent, and the number "oneness," which is restricted to a non-differentiated single object.
He raises the objection that this is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with the words "But surely" (*nanu*).
He refutes it: "That is not so."
"Because it is not accepted"— this is the same proof for the property (*dharma*). There are five precepts (*yamas*).
The observances (niyamas) are five.
For the student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and the ascetic alike, these ten constitute the means for accomplishing dharma.
That they serve as the means for accomplishing dharma for all four stages of life (cāturāśramya) is stated by the case ending inherent in the word "prakṛti."
However, a case-ending (*vibhakti*) following a nominal stem (*prakṛti*) that has entered into its own inherent form expresses only the number "plurality" as inherent in the meaning of that stem;
for even when stems have the same meaning, there is a difference in the capacity of the suffix following it due to the difference in the form of the stems.
For example, although the words *āpaḥ* and *toya* have the same meaning, the case-ending following the word *toya* in the expression *toyāni* expresses only the plurality inherent in *toya*.
The term "waters" does not refer to those actually residing in water, but rather to those connected with it;
and those connected with it are its constituent parts.
Alternatively, since there are many forms and so forth contained therein, the use of the plural number is justified even for a single drop of water; thus, "the waters" [is said].
Nor is it correct to say that this is not so because common people do not cease from their usage even when crying out with beating breasts;
for the world merely employs conventional expressions and does not engage in analytical discernment.
However, those who investigate, following that [method], do indeed discern [the distinction].
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of rendering the formulation of definitions for perception and so forth useless.
By this, cases such as "dārāḥ" (wife/wives) and "ṣaṇṇagarī" (the six cities) are also explained.
The term *ṣāṅguṇya* refers to the sixfold policy (*ṣaḍguṇa*), wherein the single function of the six qualities is the accomplishment of the king's objectives.
Similarly, regarding the term *vaiśeṣika*, it should be understood that the single function of the *viśeṣas* (particularities) is the exclusion of things from those of the same or different classes.
He states the fallacy of the reason (*hetudoṣa*) as follows: "even if unestablished" (*asiddho 'pi*).
The color of crystal is white;
however, due to its association with indigo dye, that [white color] is overwhelmed and is not perceived,
while the crystal itself is perceived.
Furthermore, it will be explained in the third [chapter] that there is no production of blue characterized as a crystal;
therefore, the meaning is that the reason (hetu) is unestablished (asiddha).
He states that the example is also deficient in the property to be proven (sādhyavikala) with the words "And this which...
[referring to] the parts of a mass of roasted meat in oil or ghee, which have produced qualities born of cooking (pākaja),
when they come into contact with another substance, namely water, and qualities born of cooking arise once again.
And this does not happen all at once;
therefore it was said: "when there is assistance from a specific time.
And that [assistance] is indeed a particular conjunction between the water and the meat.
But a composite whole [consisting] of two heterogeneous [substances] is not possible, because [heterogeneous substances] do not produce [a single effect].
Nor is it logical to claim that a substance of the class *yūṣa* (soup) joined with water is of the same class as milk;
for even in the absence of water, when there is solidity, the cognition and designation of "milk" would remain exactly as they were.

But in this case, since there is no cognition or designation of "soup" with respect to the hardness [of the meat], it is logical that the soup of water and meat is merely a specific kind of conjunction (*saṃyoga-bheda*).
And that [conjunction] is established by experience as distinct from the conjuncts.
Likewise, the number "plurality" is established by experience as distinct from the objects numbered.
In this manner, it should be explained in each respective case;
one should understand that [the term] "beginningless and endless" refers to those things whose composite parts have not been initiated.

Furthermore, since the establishment of one's own position does not follow merely from pointing out defects in the opponent's proof, he asks the proponent for his proof: "Now, what is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for a substance (*dravya*) that is a distinct entity from color and the other [sensory qualities]?"

Since this other person, although perceiving through direct perception that substance is an entity distinct from color and the rest, does not employ such conventional usage because he suffers from the delirium of confusion induced by the habituation to his own philosophical tenets,
he is therefore brought to such usage by means of this inference.
For indeed, among all ordinary people and investigators alike, there exists the designation "the colors and so forth of the sandalwood," just as one says "the water-pot of the Brahmin."
And in that case, the opponent accepts the perception of form and so forth, as well as the perception of sandalwood;
otherwise, since there would be no cognition of it, one need only have stated "because of the absence of that cognition. Why then does he say "because of the non-apprehension of that"?
From this we understand that he intends the cognition of sandalwood to occur when there is the apprehension of form and so forth.
Nor is it logical to claim that this [cognition] is merely born of the mind and is of the nature of memory;
for it has already been established during the explanation of the term "determinate" (*vyavasāyātmaka*) that this conceptual cognition is produced by the sense organs.
Furthermore, the arguments intended to refute its status as a substance will be refuted in the section on examination (*parīkṣā*).
Therefore, the perceptibility of sandalwood is established.
This very sandalwood is distinct from the color-form (rūpa) and other qualities that are the objects of dispute,
because it is itself perceived and is designated by all those things that are perceived.

Intellect (*buddhi*) is indeed a transformation of the three qualities (*traiguṇya*); and since the three qualities are insentient, the intellect is itself insentient. It undergoes modification into the form of objects solely through the channel of the senses.

Due to its proximity to that [intellect], the intellect—resembling a magnet—attracts the reflection of that [object] and, as it were, attains the nature of consciousness; thus, it cognizes the object which has been transformed into the form of the object.

This very principle of the intellect, being insentient by nature, does not shine by itself— like the lunar orb— but shines through the falling of the shadow of the solar orb of consciousness.
And it is said that "it illuminates objects";

while it is secondary in relation to the body and so forth.

by this, it is stated that all things such as the body, which arise [with birth], are denoted by the word "suffering."
Furthermore, "fearlessness" refers to the absence of fear of saṃsāra,
because the scripture repeatedly declares that "Brahman is indeed fearlessness."
But as for those who say that Brahman itself undergoes transformation into the form of the manifold diversity of names and forms, he says in response: "undecaying" (ajara).

The author of the Vārttika explains this Bhāṣya with the words "by that" (*tena*).

Thus, from the scriptural teaching of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), bliss has the nature of Brahman; and since Brahman is eternal by virtue of that [coreferentiality], bliss too is eternal—this is the meaning.
Furthermore, the genitive case in the word "of the Self" (*ātmanaḥ*) should be understood as being like [the expression] "the head of Rāhu."

If, however, in the state of liberation (*mukti*), it were to produce the cognition of pleasure independently of that [merit], [then...]

and since the Dharma was relied upon by him at that time, he relies on the Dharma alone even in the state of liberation.
The only distinction is that this [knowledge] is born of yoga (*yogaja*).
And thus, there is no consequence of [the cognition] being a consciousness of form and so forth. He raises an objection: "This [cognition] is eternal.
He refutes it: "Because of connection."

Now, one might object: "Just as the experience of pleasure is to be abandoned in your view, so too will [the seeker] strive in our view to abandon the experience of pleasure. To this he says: "And this is not pleasure.
For in our view, it is precisely for the sake of abandoning suffering that the pleasure attached to it is to be abandoned.
The meaning is that eternal happiness, being entirely free from all suffering, cannot possibly be something desired to be abandoned for the sake of eliminating suffering.

Not only is there no obstructiveness on the part of the body and so forth due to their being favorable [to pleasure], but rather they must be postulated as existing even in the state of liberation; thus he says: "The body and so forth are eternal."
Having restated the opponent's statement—"It has been said that [the self does not exist] because there is a lack of means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), and that is not so"—[the author replies:
For it is by means of scripture (śāstra) that people are to be incited toward the means of attaining liberation;
and those who are not yet engaged [in such practice] must be incited to engage.
And one who desires a desired object engages in its means; happiness is the desired object. The meaning is that liberation consists of happiness.
He refutes [the objection] by stating that this worldly activity is a cause for doubt because of its uncertainty: "No, [it is not so], because of activity."
This might be the case:
when the primary sense is impossible, a secondary sense is resorted to;
and the word "pleasure" (sukha) is primary in the sense of pleasure itself.
But [the term "bliss"] is used figuratively with respect to the cessation of suffering.
Therefore, since liberation is indeed eternal bliss, he says: "If, however...
*Saṃcakṣāṇakaḥ* refers to a yogi engaged in discriminative discernment (*saṃkhyāna*).
Dharma and adharma are, first of all, real in the self, and not merely imagined through ignorance;
and these two can be exhausted by experience when one has become free from passion and unattached.
But it is not in the case of attachment;
for one who is attached, while experiencing each object as it is acquired and taking up each as it is discarded, would not be liberated from saṃsāra.

Therefore, this passion is known as a bond; and the activity based upon it must be avoided. Otherwise, this demoness of craving, pampered by the conviction of eternal happiness, will find its opportunity even within the pleasures of the sensory objects.
Since it would incite a person toward things that are near at hand and thereby cast liberation far away for him, not even the slightest opportunity must be given to this [objection].

Therefore, the sense is that it is logical that the scriptural text teaching eternal bliss is figurative (*bhāktī*) with respect to the absolute cessation of suffering. He raises an objection: "Even though... and so forth.
Just as with passion, one must not allow hatred to gain ground;
yet you have given it its opportunity, and thus the fault is equal.
He refutes this: No.
Because it is not contrary [to desire].

For example, the attainment of eternal happiness, such as liberation, is accompanied by attachment that is not contrary [to desire] and is thus not contrary; however, the absolute abandonment of suffering is not like that, as it is followed by an aversion toward suffering.
Aversion (*dveṣa*), anger (*krodha*), and pride (*mānya*) are not different in meaning.
