For that [fire] is of the nature of a flame,
whereas detachment is not so;
for it is a condition of sufficiency, meaning the removal of suffering without opposition.

By this, the collection of commentaries beginning with "In liberation, eternal happiness of the self is manifested" and ending with "When that [defilement] has been abandoned, his attachment to eternal happiness does not become an obstacle" is to be understood as explained.
The meaning of the commentary beginning with "If it were so... is as follows:

Thus, for one seeking liberation through dispassion, even if activity has commenced, whether eternal bliss belongs to the liberated one or not— let it be so or let it not be— on both these views, the attainment of liberation is not called into question for one who is free from passion while engaged in activity.
The meaning is that he does not become doubtful.
He presents the liberation of the nihilists (vaināśika) as follows: "the mind is liberated.
For it is the transmigrating being who is liberated;
passion and the like are its causes.
Furthermore, if the self were eternal, passion and the other afflictions would not be able to bring about saṃsāra;
for since that which is eternal is unchangeable, it remains in its original state, and thus there can be nothing to be added or removed.
As they have said:
What effect do rain and sun have on the sky? Their effect is seen upon leather.
If the self were like leather, it would be impermanent; if it were like the sky, it would be devoid of effects.
Thus,
the meaning is that it is logical that the mind (*citta*) is subject to cyclic existence (*saṃsārin*) due to the power of passion and so forth, and is liberated through separation from them.
The "destiny" (gati) refers to birth among the classes of gods, humans, and so forth; it is the arising therein.
He refutes this as follows: "No, because it is without effort."
Because the mind is momentary,
its purpose is solely birth and destruction;
for since "another birth" is indeed destruction, there can be nothing to be added or removed in a moment that is indivisible.
And the meaning is that [the effort] is useless because it would destroy its own natural flow (*svarasa-bhaṅgitvāt*).
He raises an objection: "Of the continuum" (*santateḥ*). Indeed, the continuum of cognitions is beginningless and consists of a stream of cause and effect.
And that [suffering] ceases for one whose web of afflictions (*kleśa*) along with their latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) has been uprooted by the direct realization of the self (*ātmasākṣātkāra*).
The meaning is that this very cessation consists in the non-arising of future moments of consciousness belonging to that same continuum.
He refutes [this view]: "No."
Because that is impossible:
it is not possible for what has arisen not to arise,
nor is it possible to bring about the cessation of the continuum.
Because a final moment is logically untenable.
For does that final moment initiate something or not? If it initiates something, it is not "final," and thus there would be no cessation of the stream of cause and effect.
Since the "stream" is the continuum (*santāna*), there is no cessation of the continuum. If there were no commencement [of the stream], it would be non-existent due to its lack of efficacy;
consequently, all preceding moments would also be non-existent—such is the sense of the question, "Whose destruction [is there]?"
He raises an objection: "the non-arising of the future.
The implication is that, if this were so, the final moment would be established because it performs a causal function characterized by the non-arising of the future.
He refutes this: "the future..."
The meaning is that prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) is beginningless. He asks: "In that case, of what [is it the negation]?
The implication is that since that which is eternal cannot be assisted, there is no absence of something to be removed.
The answer is: "That which...
Just as the capacity of a non-momentary entity to receive assistance will be demonstrated in the refutation of momentariness (*kṣaṇabhaṅgabhaṅga*), this is established. //22//

NyS 1.1.23: Doubt is a deliberation requiring specific distinguishing characteristics, arising from the perception of common or multiple properties, from conflicting testimony, and from the lack of a settled determination regarding perception or non-perception.
The commentary, beginning with "Now, this [is] possessed of its proper place," is intent on introducing the definition of doubt.
Its meaning is as follows:
"place" (sthāna) refers to sequence (krama).
"Tadvataḥ" means "at this time," that is, "now. In some recensions, the reading is "sthānavata eva tarhi" (only for one who possesses a [specific] position).
In that case, at the time of the enumeration, what is the position—
that is, the sequence— of doubt, which follows the objects of cognition (*prameya*) in the enumeration and follows the definition of the objects of cognition in the definition? This is the meaning.
The author of the Vārttika explains this as "the object of knowledge" (prameya).
He clarifies this very point with the word "yati.
The term *sthāna* (position) has been explained by the mention of sequence (*krama*).
And the meaning of the suffix -mat is included by the mention of "attainment" (prāpti).
Equanimity—this is it.
And here, "deliberation" (*vimarśa*) means "doubt" (*saṃśaya*); this is the general definition of doubt.
In that context, "doubt" is the designation of the object to be defined (*lakṣya*), and "deliberation" is the defining term (*lakṣaṇa*).
Doubt (*vimarśa*) is the deliberation upon contradictory and manifold objects regarding a single substratum (*dharmī*),
a cognition in the form "what indeed [could it be]?
By this, doubt is distinguished from heterogeneous factors such as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and from homogeneous factors such as error (*viparyaya*).

The three [terms] beginning with "samāna" (common), however, are the specific definitions (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*). In these cases, the phrase "doubt is a deliberation" (*vimarśaḥ saṃśayaḥ*) is to be supplied.
Here, "a distinguished deliberation" (*viśiṣṭo 'vamarśo vimarśaviśiṣṭaḥ*) is the term defining the object (*lakṣyapada*), meaning doubt is a deliberation characterized by its distinction.
"Because of the occurrence of common properties, because of the occurrence of multiple properties, and because of conflicting testimony"—these three are each characterized by the remaining terms.
Thus the author of the *Vārttika* says: "In that regard, 'common'...
By this, those who assert that [the types of *sādhāraṇa*] are fivefold are refuted; for it is indeed only threefold.

He explains the Bhāṣya—which provides the general definition of doubt as "that knowledge which is non-determinative is doubt"—with the words: "In that regard, regarding the nature of the object... and "...the cognition is of a non-determinative nature.
The objection and its resolution have already been explained in the very first Sūtra.
The explanation is understood by accepting that the word *pratyaya* signifies certainty (*niścaya*).
However, in the ultimate sense, the word *pratyaya* is a synonym for cognition (*jñāna*). Since the nature of cognition exists even in doubt and other such states, there is no contradiction.
He explains "because of the occurrence of common properties" with the word "common.
He raises an objection by means of an alternative analysis with the words "but what," and asks "why?"
"Do not entertain doubt regarding the substance;
the meaning of the question is: why does it not produce [the effect] when it is indeed a quality? He provides the answer: "No."

Regarding the term "common" (*sādhāraṇa*): just as the dimension (*parimāṇa*) of a post and a person arises from a difference in number, accumulation, and size, such is the dimension of this substance also present before one.
Therefore, the meaning is that it is because a subject (dharmin) possessing the property of similar magnitude is established.

The point is that although the connection with common properties such as largeness and length exists, it is not a cause for doubt; for even when those [properties] are connected, no doubt arises if there is no similarity.
This might be so:
"upapatti" means existence.
And a similar property is not a cause for doubt merely by virtue of its existence.
Nevertheless, it has been apprehended;
yet, since there is no word here denoting apprehension, he says: "Its occurrence is determination" (*tasyopapattir adhyavasāyaḥ*).
Although this word *upapatti* denotes existence (*sattā*) and refers to that [existence],...
Nevertheless, from the co-occurrence with other words, it is understood that even when denoting mere existence, its apprehension is intended to be expressed.

The grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is justified by the intention to express non-difference between the object and the subject of cognition; thus, "apprehension" (*upalabdhi*) [is used].
He asks: "Why? (*kasmāt*).
The meaning is: since the employment of words is under our own control, why should we employ something that is non-expressive?
The answer is: "even though it is not stated.
By the expression "expectation of a qualification" (*viśeṣāpekṣā*), the expectation for a qualification is expressed.
And although the word *apekṣā* (expectation) refers to desire (*icchā*), it here refers to the desire to grasp (*jighṛkṣā*) due to the force of the sentence;
moreover, that [desire] is not the cause of doubt.
Because it exists when there is doubt regarding that [object],

therefore, here, by means of a desire for distinction characterized by the expectation of a specific quality, non-apprehension (agrahaṇa) is to be defined as occurring when there is recollection due to the similarity between the two specific qualities and the object present before one;
just as the word "Ganges" indicates only the bank with which it is connected.
But it does not mean merely the shore.
With this very intention, the author of the Bhāṣya will say: "dependent on the recollection of a particular.
Therefore, by the prohibition of grasping a particular, the grasping of a universal is permitted; such is the meaning.
He states another alternative explanation with the words "Or else" (*atha vā*).

It might be argued: the word *upapatti* denotes both existence (*sattā*) and apprehension (*upalabdhi*); so, what is the reason for deciding between these? To this he says: "But that which... (*yaḥ punar iti*).
Now, one might object: "Has it not been stated that non-existence (abhāva) is the objective support (ālambana) of a means of valid cognition?
Therefore, how is there no contradiction? To this it is said: "independent" (svatantra).

Alternatively, although this word *upapatti* denotes existence (*sattā*), it indicates the apprehension (upalabdhi) whose object is its own denotation; thus he says: "by the word ‘object’" (viṣaya-śabdena).
And he says "it is worldly" (laukikam) to show that this definition is not unworldly;
and it has already been stated previously how smoke is not a cause by its mere existence.
He presents the supplementary argument of the "partialists" (ekadeśin) with the words "avyavaccheda" (non-exclusion).
They indeed believe that even a property which serves as the cause for exclusion is common [to both].
For example, "producedness" (kṛtakatva) is common to the subject of the thesis (sādhyadharmin), namely sound, and to the subject of the example (dṛṣṭāntadharmin), such as a jar.
And this [reason] is not a cause for doubt regarding permanence or impermanence;
rather, it excludes the non-connection with impermanence from the subject of the thesis (sādhyadharmin).
Therefore, the meaning is that one should state: "because it is a cause of non-exclusion."
He refutes this very point that must be stated with the words "not common" (*na samāna*).
For a common property (*dharma*) requires a correlative—by whom [is it common]?
And by the word "doubt" (*saṃśaya*), which presents its own object, those two mutually contradictory [properties] are presented.
Therefore, it is understood that [the property] is common to those two.
Consequently, while it is intended to reside in that specific class, it is understood as residing in a different class altogether;
and such is not the case with "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*).
Therefore, one should not say "because it is not a cause of exclusion.
The meaning is that similarity, which is the referent of the word "common" (*samāna*), does not exist there.
Regarding this very point, he connects the two words beginning with "perception" (*upalabdhi*) by way of a preliminary objection: "This is common (*sādhāraṇa*)."
Perception and non-perception do not remain fixed [in their application].

The non-perception of [features such as] a head and hands, and the perception of [features such as] curvature and hollows, constitute the subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) for [the claim that] this is a person;
for that [evidence] establishes that "this is indeed a person," or—
It is established either as "this-ness" or by the negation of "this-ness";
for example, "This is not a person" is established as non-"this-ness."
The absence of that [determination] is non-ascertainment (*avyavasthā*).
By this, the absence of both proving and subverting means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is shown.
Furthermore, by the phrase "and when there is a desire for a specific [attribute]," the recollection of a specific [attribute] is shown.
He determines that everything is preceded by reflection, asking: "What is this?
In that regard, he states the fault in accepting [the word] as a single term: "If it were 'samāna'...
The "particularity" (viśeṣa) refers to the head, hands, and so forth.

For by this [definition], a person is distinguished from a post; thus, even for that which has not been perceived as a universal, there exists in some cases an unsettled state regarding perception and non-perception,
as in the case of the seventh taste or the tenth substance.
For in that case, there exists neither a validating nor a subverting means of valid cognition (pramāṇa),
nor is there doubt; for [the definition of doubt] extends only so far as "that which depends on a distinguishing feature" (viśeṣāpekṣa).
For example, having seen an elephant, one remembers its related post and the elephant-driver, and one does not have any doubt regarding them.
He states the fault in the apprehension of two-footed beings: "In this way, when things are equal," and so forth.

For one traveling on a boat, even when seeing an object at a distance that possesses both height and circumference, and even though there is an absence of any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) to confirm or refute [its specific nature], one does not hesitate as to whether it is a mountain or an elephant, due to the absence of recollection of its specific characteristics.

Thus, because of the lack of a fixed determination regarding perception and non-perception, when the two terms "dependent on a specific feature" (*viśeṣāpekṣa*) are prescribed, doubt would arise even when a substratum possessing similar properties is not being perceived, provided that a specific feature is being remembered from something else. For at that time, there is indeed a recollection of the specific feature and an absence of both a proving and a subverting means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Indeed, when a common property is not perceived, it is impossible to apprehend the curved hollows and such, or the head, hands, and so forth, belonging to that subject (dharmin).
This is the case when this observer [perceives them]— that is,
when this observer [sees them] amidst the Malaya breezes, which are gentle and swaying with a graceful dance produced by the breaking forth of tender sprouts.

Having experienced the mango trees, which have commenced a concert enchanting with the lute-like warbling of swarms of bees intoxicated by honey and delighted by the branches, and where the fifth note is played upon the lute-like throats of flocks of male cuckoos in rut, one who stands at a distance then experiences that which possesses qualities similar to an elephant.
At that time, he possesses the apprehension of common properties and the recollection of specific features such as the trunk and the tree;
however, because there is an absence of both proving and subverting evidence (*sādhaka-bādhaka-pramāṇa*), he does not doubt.
The dependence upon only a few individuals constitutes the limited scope (*alpaviṣayatva*) of a particular such as "cooperation" (*sahakāratva*).

On the other hand, the extensive pervasion (*bahuvyāpitva*) of features such as height and girth constitutes its great scope (*mahāviṣayatva*). Furthermore, the consideration of multiple objects should be understood as the consideration of contradictory objects.
By this, the commentary beginning with "of the post and the person" and so forth has been explained.
"Seeing" is the explanation of the logical justification (*upapatti*).
"Desiring to know the specific difference" is the explanation of "having regard for the specific difference."
The phrase "What indeed? (*kiṃ svid iti*) is an elaboration on deliberation (*vimarśa*).
This may be so:
that the desire to know (*bubhutsā*) occurs at a time subsequent to doubt (*saṃśaya*).
To the question, "How can one who desires to know be in doubt?", the Commentator stated:
"The two are similar.

The meaning is that by the word *viśeṣāpekṣā* (expectation of a distinguishing feature), which denotes desire, the recollection of a [previously perceived] object whose specific qualities are not being grasped is indicated.

Thus, it is established that when there is no occurrence of either proving or disproving evidence, this perception of a common property— existing in a single moment as a non-perishing state together with the memory of a specific property in a state of perishing— is the cause of doubtful cognition.
He applies this [explanation] also to the inclusion of the three terms [in the definition], namely "from the occurrence of multiple properties" and "from conflicting testimony," by saying "by this."
It should be understood that the first two and the subsequent two are each unified by way of their respective pairs.

In order to adopt the commentary of the Bhāṣyakāra on the phrase "because of the production from multiple factors" (anekadharmopapatteḥ), [the author] sets forth and refutes the interpretation of a partial exponent (ekadeśin) with the words "aneka... Sound is indeed produced by conjunction (saṃyoga). For being produced by conjunction is common to substances, qualities, and actions; it exists in the case of a substance as an effect, in qualities such as color (rūpa), and in actions such as bodily movement. Thus, it is shared by substances, qualities, and actions alike.
Therefore, a property belonging to multiple things has its purpose fulfilled.
Likewise, even though a property residing in a word is manifold, it is through its very commonality that it becomes a cause for doubt regarding substancehood and so forth among the three categories;
thus, "being produced by conjunction" (saṃyogajatva), which is common to all [categories], is distinguished from existence (sattva) and the rest.

The meaning is that the absence of qualities in qualities and actions, as well as the momentariness of substances, qualities, and actions, has already been established through the occurrence of common properties;
thus, [the author] asks: "Now... (atha).
The answer provided by the commentator’s explanation is: "It is uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*).
He asks again: "How so?
The meaning is that by the word "compound term" (*samāsapada*), its constituent part, the word "multiple" (*aneka*), is indicated; that is, by the word "multiple" occurring within the compound.
The answer: "Equal."
This is what is meant:

since this [definition] distinguishes its own substratum from many things— both those of the same and different classes— it is called a "definition" (lakṣaṇa) figuratively, because it has as its cause the exclusion [of others] based on multiple points of departure (apādāna).
Thus, this commentary—"the manifold, both of the same class and of different classes"—is explained by supplying the word "distinction" (*viśeṣa*) from the phrase "therefore, a distinction.
The explanation of the supplied word "distinction" is that it is a "distinguishing property" (*viśeṣaka-dharma*).
However, the genitive case in "of that manifold" (*tasyānekasya*) is used with the intention of expressing a general relationship.
He states another seed for the definition: "And of that which is manifold" (*tasya cānekasya*).
The meaning is that by the word "manifold" (*aneka*), two properties (*dharmau*) are indicated through the relationship of the sublated and the sublator (*nivartyanivartaka*).
Thus, by this, "manifold" refers to both what is of the same class and what is of a different class, even without the need for ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*).
It has been explained that [the term] refers to its being a negator of dharma;
however, one should not entertain a misconception regarding the compound here,
for the author of the Vārttika will demonstrate that it is a *bahuvrīhi* in this very context.

Thus, by the presentation of these two types of seeds—namely, the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and the seed (*bīja*)—the summary statement (*grahaṇakavākya*) "an uncommon property" (*asādhāraṇo dharmaḥ*) has been explained.

He now explains the term "multiple properties" (*anekadharma*) in another way: "one and many," etc. That which is both one and many is "the manifold" (*aneka*); a property that is the cause of the cognition of that manifold is a "multiple property" (*anekadharma*). The meaning is: it is the cause of the cognition of both difference and non-difference.

The state of being produced by disjunction (*vibhāgajatva*) is the cause for the cognition of non-difference among those sounds produced by disjunction, and it is the cause for the cognition of their difference from others.
This is what [the author] says: "Because they are produced by disjunction, this cognition arises that this collection of sounds produced by disjunction is one."
And this [latter] is other than that, being manifold and distinct.
In this regard, that very dharma which is the cause of a single cognition is non-differentiation (*abheda*), while that which is the cause of manifold cognitions is differentiation (*viśeṣa*).
Furthermore, the singular number is used with the intention of referring to the genus (*jāti*).

For the property "Being" (*sat*) and so forth is the cause of the cognition of non-difference among substances, qualities, and actions, and it distinguishes the word from [the categories of] generality (*sāmānya*) and the rest.

This is what he says: since this cognition arises from "Being" and so forth, "this is one"; and since this cognition arises from being produced by disjunction (*vibhāga-ja*) and so forth, "this is many."
Therefore, it is established that [the object] is both one and many.
"Many" means that which is the cause of those [multiple] cognitions; it is called "many" by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*).
This is the explanation of what was stated.
He provides an example here, saying "for instance" (*yathā*).

It is stated that [the object] is "from generality, particularity, and inherence" (*sāmānyaviśeṣasamavāyebhyaḥ*) for the purpose of demonstrating a doubt whose objects are the three alternatives beginning with substantiality (*dravyatva*).
"Real, eternal, possessing substance, being an effect, being a cause, and possessing generality and particularity"—this is the non-distinction among substances, qualities, and motions.
By this [word] "separate" (nirbhakta), the meaning is that which is distinguished or set apart from the "existent" (sat) and so forth.
This might be so:

that which is observed to be concomitant with something else, when seen in some instance, causes that thing to be remembered; and by not establishing a connection even with its opposite, it becomes a cause of doubt, just like a common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*).

But the uncommon property, namely being produced by disjunction (*vibhāgajatva*), is not observed anywhere—neither in sound, nor in earth and the other elements, nor in actions such as upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*), nor in qualities such as odor. Therefore, how could it cause one to remember [other instances]?
Or, if it did not cause one to remember, how could it generate doubt regarding them?

Consequently, this [uncommon property] would merely produce a desire to know (*jijñāsā*) in the form "What might this be?", rather than generating a doubt in the form "Is this or that?". To address this, he says: "For not... (*na hi*).
Why is it not observed? To this he says: "Because it is impossible in all cases.

For birth through the disintegration of substance and so forth is not possible, because [birth] does not conform to the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) of that [disintegration]; such is the meaning.

Is it not the case that for this very reason it was stated that [the property of] being produced by disjunction is not a cause of doubt? To this, he says: "The state of being produced by disjunction causes doubt because it is excluded from everything else.
The meaning is this:
although the state of being produced by disjunction is not observed anywhere among substances and so forth, [it nevertheless causes doubt].

Nevertheless, since its exclusion from each [of the other categories] is observed in substance and so forth individually, sound—which possesses the non-specificity (aviśeṣa) of existence and the like by virtue of being produced by disjunction—serves as a cause of doubt through its uncommon property (asādhāraṇadharma), reminding one of each category by way of exclusion: "Being excluded from substance and action, is it a quality? Being excluded from quality and action, is it a substance? Being excluded from quality and substance, is it an action? Thus it becomes a cause for uncertainty.
He explains: "Is it not so? and so forth.
This is the intended meaning:
when a bamboo stalk is being split, there is motion in the two halves of the bamboo,
and from that, their mutual disjunction occurs.
Therefore, this disjunction, which consists in the separation of the portion of space occupied by the bamboo segments,
is produced by disjunction and not by the action of the bamboo segments themselves.

For the action in a constituent part is pervaded by the production of a disjunction that does not oppose the conjunction initiating a substance, as is seen in the case of the petals of a blooming lotus bud, which produces the disjunction of the portion of space occupied by its own parts.
It is observed that in each case there is no blooming lotus other than the one that was closed;
for it is recognized as being identical in reality, just like a palm with fingers contracted and then extended.
If even the action of splitting bamboo were of that same nature, then it too must necessarily produce a disjunction that is not counteracted by the conjunction initiating a substance;
and in that case, the effect-substance would not perish.
Therefore, the disjunction of the space [occupied by] the bamboo segments cannot be produced by this [action].
Nor is any other cause for it possible.

Consequently, the disjunction between the two segments produced by the action of the bamboo segments—which is inherent in the same object as its effect—must be accepted as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of the disjunction from the spatial point occupied and delimited by those [segments].
"The reason is thus established.

[The author] refutes this: for one who does not accept the production of disjunction from disjunction (*vibhāgaja-vibhāga*), this very state of being produced by disjunction (*vibhāgajatva*) serves as a cause for doubt. Furthermore, on what basis is it understood that the motion in the parts of a lotus petal produces two disjunctions?
If it is argued that there is no evidence for postulating a sequence of two divisions,
alas, the same applies to the two divisions of the bamboo segments.
But has it not been stated that action must be the producer of a division that is not the counter-correlative of the conjunction that originated the substance?

And thus, there would be no destruction of the substance. Now, why does the opposite not occur? [The answer is: only the action of the two bamboo-splits produces the two disjunctions, whereas the action of the parts of the lotus-petal produces only the disjunction of its own parts.
However, the disjunction of space from those parts is produced by the disjunction of the parts themselves.

If, on the other hand, the motion in the part of the lotus petal were the producer of both [the disjunction of the parts and the disjunction from space], then the motion in the bamboo splinter alone would produce the disjunction that is the opposite of the conjunction initiating the substance.
Furthermore, the simultaneous determination of the two types of disjunction in either case, as well as the absence of evidence for a sequential order, are equal.

Therefore, due to the doubt regarding the capacity to produce the disjunction of the parts of a lotus petal, the relationship of pervader and pervaded (vyāpyavyāpakabhāva) cannot be definitively established.
However, because of the difference in action, there would be a difference in the disjunction—the effect—which arises from a difference in its own cause.
Although one [conjunction] is the counter-positive of the conjunction that initiates a substance while the other is not,
nevertheless this distinction must be admitted regarding action: namely, that one produces a single disjunction, whereas the other produces two disjunctions.
Therefore, by the force of this example, the establishment of disjunction produced by disjunction is not achieved.
When, immediately following the action of a finger, the disjunction of the finger-tree and the disjunction of the hand-tree, as well as the disjunctions of the body-trees, are observed,
let the action residing in the finger effect that disjunction of the finger-tree.
However, it is not capable of producing the disjunction from the hand-tree,
because that [disjunction] inheres in its own substrate (the tree),
and because motion is determined to have the capacity to produce only an effect that inheres in its own substrate.

Therefore, since a disjunction from a tree cannot occur directly from that hand, it causes a disjunction from the tree [occurring] in the finger and so forth by means of a proximity characterized by inherence in a single effect; with reference to the proof of such a "disjunction-born disjunction," he says:
"But as for that which... Or, let there be a disjunction born of disjunction.

Nevertheless, since such "being produced by disjunction" (vibhāgajatva) is indeed an uncommon [property], he says: "Or let there be for that [sound]—even for that which has admitted disjunction—the uncommon and specific quality of being produced by disjunction.
He indicates this very point with the words "produced by disjunction" (vibhāgaja).
For when a bamboo stalk is being split, in the production of sound, the mutual disjunction of the two halves of the bamboo is the efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa).
The portion of space enclosed by the bamboo slivers is its non-inherent cause;

however, the conjunction between the bamboo slivers and space cannot be the non-inherent cause, as is the case with the conjunction between the drum and space. For the formal argument (prayoga) is as follows:
This sound, which has as its cause the disjunction of bamboo leaves, is produced by a non-inherent cause that belongs to the same genus as its efficient cause,
because it is a sound produced by a cause unique to it.
Whatever sound arises from a specific uncommon cause, all such sounds are produced by a non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa) belonging to that same class;
for example, a sound caused by the conjunction of a drum and a stick has the conjunction of the drum and space as its non-inherent cause.
And so it is with this;
therefore, it is "thus.

Thus, in this manner, sound is produced by the disjunction of the space within the bamboo segments, which arises from the disjunction of the bamboo segments themselves and acts as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*).
Thus, sound has as its non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa) a disjunction produced by a disjunction;

and although this [definition] applies to the disjunction of the body and space— which has as its non-inherent cause the disjunction of the hand and space, which in turn was produced by the disjunction of the finger and space—

nevertheless, the reason "because it is produced by a disjunction" (vibhāgajatvāt), as indicated by the author of the Bhāṣya, is formulated as "because it has as its non-inherent cause a disjunction produced by a disjunction of the causes alone" (kāraṇamātravibhāgajavibhāgāsamavāyikāraṇakatvāt).
Furthermore, the disjunction of the body from space is not preceded by the disjunction of a finger from space in that manner;
for that [latter] is preceded by the disjunction of a cause from a non-cause,
rather than being preceded merely by the disjunction of a cause.
This has been stated: sound has disjunction produced by disjunction as its non-inherent cause; it is not any other category of entity.

One might object: "It is observed that what is seen in association (sahacarita) causes recollection and thus becomes a cause for doubt regarding specific instances; however, that which is excluded (vyāvṛtta) cannot do so, because it lacks such association with them. To dispel this doubt, the author of the Bhāṣya offers the following answer: "Among those of the same class" (*tulyajātīyeṣu*).
For even though the uncommon [reason] (*asādhāraṇa*) is capable of causing recollection by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), [the point remains as stated].
Nevertheless, that which was stated in the Bhāṣya has also been stated: indeed,
that which is endowed with the nature of existence and so forth, and possesses specific qualities, is excluded from both those of its own class and those of a different class,
just like the substance earth.
A substance-class is distinguished by its possession of odor from other substances such as earth and so forth, as well as from heterogeneous qualities and actions;
likewise, color is a quality by virtue of being color,
and throwing upward is an action by virtue of being throwing upward.

Such a sound, being endowed with properties such as existence (*sat*) and so forth, is distinguished from both homogeneous and heterogeneous categories by its quality of being produced through disjunction (*vibhāgaja*).
Therefore, the doubt arises whether it is a substance (*dravya*), a quality (*guṇa*), or an action (*karman*).
According to the previous explanation, it was stated that the uncommon property (*asādhāraṇadharma*) is indicated by the word "many" (*aneka*).

Now, by examining the word *samāna* (common), he states that even a multi-word compound functions through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the sense of the "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*): "Or because the common property (*samānadharma*) is useful as a cause of doubt.
For the common [property], by way of being the counter-correlate (*pratigogitā*), brings the uncommon [property] to mind.
In that context, there is both the common and the uncommon property, which are conveyed by the word *samāna* through its primary and secondary meanings (*śruti* and *artha*).
The construction is: "because the common [term] is employed as a cause of doubt.
He asks: "Why?
The sense is: "Since the use of words is within our own control, why should we employ something that is non-expressive?"
The answer is: "It is not so.

For a unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*) is a cause of doubt by way of negative concomitance (*vyatirekamukhena*), and that [negative concomitance] is established through exclusion from multiple [instances].

And since that [definition] depends on multiple words with secondary (lakṣaṇika) meanings and cannot be obtained from a single word, the inclusion of words with secondary meanings is for a specific purpose.
Furthermore, this very definition is described through the analysis of the compound *anekadharma* as "a property excluded from many" (*anekasmād vyāvṛtto dharmaḥ*).
He states the following merely as an additional point: "or there is brevity."
Thinking that exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is the operative factor when an uncommon [property] serves as a cause for doubt, he raises an objection: "If it were manifold... He answers: "This is not a fault.
For indeed, deviation (*vyabhicāra*) and non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) are the operative factors for doubt and certainty, respectively.
The meaning is that it is not merely positive and negative concomitance. He raises an objection: "If, then...
For the deviation of a reason consists precisely in its being common to both similar and dissimilar instances.
If it is the cause of doubt, then alas!
Since the mere occurrence of a common characteristic (*samānadharmopapatti*) alone is the cause of doubt everywhere, the inclusion of the term "multiple" (*aneka*) is redundant; this is the meaning.
He refutes [the objection] with the words "True.
For the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of a reason consists in its being common to both similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and dissimilar instances (*asapakṣa*),
and that [deviation] is the cause of doubt.

Nevertheless, the meaning is that both are employed simply because the positive concomitance (anvaya) of one is common [to others], while the negative concomitance (vyatireka) of the other is [also common].
Having thus explained his own position on the grounds that "many properties arise," he introduces the refutation of the opponent's explanation with the words: "No. One [proponent] asserts:

"Sound is eternal because it is audible, like the nature of sound (*śabdatva*). This is a non-deviant reason endowed with the five characteristics (*pañcarūpopapanna*). Another asserts: "Sound is non-eternal because it is produced, like a jar. This too is [a reason] endowed with the five characteristics.
"An inconclusive reason"— this he refutes with "that is incorrect. The meaning is that [the two reasons] are not non-inconclusive and endowed with the five characteristics.
Nor is this application [of the reason] by the opponent even logical.
The meaning of the word "contradictory" (*viruddha*) is "having a contradictory object" (*viruddhārtha*);
the sense is that their own natures (*svarūpa*) are contradictory, meaning they exist as mutual absences of one another.
"It arises from the perception of a specific feature.
For indeed, the non-perception of a specific feature is the producer of doubt, while the perception of a specific feature is its remover.

The meaning is this: if, according to your view, [the doubt] were produced from that which causes its cessation—namely, from the perception of a distinguishing feature (*viśeṣadarśana*) generated by a non-deviant cause—then its cessation would not occur.

Furthermore, he states that it is not the case that when something possesses the capacity to cause cessation, it simultaneously possesses the capacity to produce [the doubt]: "For when there is the perception of a distinguishing feature... and so forth.
It might be argued as follows:
perception itself—known as recognition (pratyabhijñā) in the form "this is that very same letter *ga*"—apprehends the stability of the sound;
and since it remains stable for that duration, who could destroy it afterwards?
Thinking that [the opponent] might thus determine eternality, he says: "This matter is not the object of perception;
for only that perception which is established as non-erroneous (ananyathāsiddha) is the remover of doubt, such as the perception of heat in the case of fire."
The meaning is this: however, because it can also arise through similarity, this [perception] is itself doubtful and thus not capable of eliminating doubt.
Let it not be the object of perception; yet it may be the object of scripture (āgama).

Indeed, a momentary sound is not capable of conveying meaning, because since it does not persist through the time of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is impossible to establish a linguistic convention (*samaya*) for it, and thus the comprehension of meaning is untenable.
Therefore, even if the scripture does not explicitly state "I am eternal," [the meaning follows].
Nevertheless, by producing the cognition of an object through a known connection, it implies its own permanence and thus becomes an object of permanence;
as they have said:
"But it must be permanent, because perception exists for the sake of another."
To this he says: "It is not the object of scripture.

Although the individual phonemes are momentary, nevertheless—just as individual cows and the like are capable of being the objects of convention when qualified by their respective universals and particulars such as "cowness"—the phonemes are likewise capable of being the objects of convention when qualified by [their respective] universals such as "phoneme-ness" (*varṇatva*). Thus, the meaning is that scripture does not necessitate [the existence of] permanence.

"Let it be; what is the harm to us?"—the meaning is that for people such as ourselves, the doubt regarding the existence or non-existence of the deer on the far side of the moon can never be dispelled.
Why is it not refuted?
The meaning is that since "producedness" is observed in a sound whose status as permanent or impermanent is doubtful, it is not inherently connected with impermanence;
and thus, it is not capable of proving the impermanence of cognition and so forth.
This applies to all [such cases].
The meaning is: "being produced," "necessarily following upon effort," "varying according to the difference in conditions," and so forth.
And [it refers to] "all inference.
Furthermore, if the logical reason (hetu) possesses even these five characteristics, [then it is valid].
The meaning is that since all inference would have doubt as its cause, all of it would be invalid.
The Nihilists (Vaināśikas) say, "Because [an eternal thing] is impossible";
[the reply is: no, because they do not understand sublation (*bādhā*).
The meaning is: because there is no cognition of an object that obstructs [it]. "Possessing resistance" (sapratighatva) means being an obstacle to the arising of another in its own location.
For in the Sautrāntika system, form (rūpa) is held to be both possessing resistance and corporeal (mūrta).

The verbal designation "it is indeed eternal" or "it is indeed non-eternal" would not be tenable, nor would the verbal designation "it is indeed a post" or "it is indeed a person. [The opponent] objects: "It will not be so."
The meaning is: "Let there be no verbal expression.
He refutes this, saying: "It is contradictory.
He states the same point in a single passage, beginning with: "But surely..."

Thus, it has been stated that there is no coexistence (*samavāya*) of two reasons possessing five forms in a single instance. However, if one were to admit the possibility of two reasons—each lacking the form of being "unopposed" (*asatpratipakṣa*)—occurring together in one place, and thus maintain that they constitute a cause for doubt, [the author] raises an objection with this intention: "Now, [regarding] the state of being produced... and so forth.
He refutes this with the words "even so" (*tathāpi*):
[the first reason] is countered by a valid counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*) individually, whereas the two combined are over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇa*).
The meaning is that such [a reason] is not seen elsewhere.

With the intention of asking, "In that case, is 'being produced' (kṛtakatva) now no longer a proof for the non-eternality of sound because it is counterbalanced (satpratipakṣa), and thus much would be contradicted?", he asks: "But when they are of such a nature..."
The answer is: "In that case, of those two.

Now, one might object: since "being produced" (kṛtakatva) is the probandum and "audibility" (śrāvaṇatva) is already established, let the inference of impermanence—which occurs later, has a probandum as its constituent part, and has its object sublated—be the one that is annulled by the inference of permanence, which occurs first and has an established constituent part. To this [the author replies]:
He says: "And an effort being made...

[means that] although audibility (*śravaṇatva*) is established, it cannot serve as a proof for permanence because it is inconclusive (*savyabhicāra*), since it is common to other non-eternal properties such as being inferable (*anumānasikatā*) and so forth.
However, producedness (*kṛtakatva*) possesses the fivefold form (*pāñcarūpya*).
The meaning is that the sublation of permanence by valid cognition will be demonstrated.

The explanation of the term *vipratipatteḥ* is as follows: although *vipratipattiḥ* literally means a contradictory cognition (*jñāna*), nevertheless, because such a cognition residing in the minds of the proponent and the opponent is entirely beyond perception, it cannot logically serve as a cause for doubt; therefore, the meaning is that it indicates its own effect, namely, public discourse (*pravāda*).

In this context, the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra), considering that the non-ascertainment of perception and the non-ascertainment of non-perception are distinct causes of doubt, stated— "the former [is] common and manifold," etc.— in order to avoid the charge of redundancy with the phrase "from the occurrence of a common property.
Having introduced that, the Vārttikakāra refutes it with the words "therein" (*tatra*).

Indeed, it has been stated that doubt does not arise merely upon the perception of common and unique properties, nor even when there is a recollection of specific qualities, provided that neither a proving nor a subverting means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is present.
Therefore, the lack of determination regarding perception and non-perception are not separate causes of doubt.
He also refutes the distinction [between the three types of doubt] with the words "samāne" (when there is similarity).

Now, if there is no difference [between them], then why is it that all three causes of doubt— similarity (*sāmānya*), multiplicity (*aneka*), and contradiction (*vipratipatti*)— are not identical, given that they are all equally located in the cognizer?
And thus, since the separate mention [of the two] would be redundant, he says: "Of the similar and the manifold properties.
He objects again: "This entire thing is indeed a similar property.
This is the underlying intention.
For that which is uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) and has never been seen before anywhere does not even venture to produce doubt;
as for what was described by the author of the Bhāṣya— that being uncommon is a cause of doubt— that is indeed "common" (*samāna*), and not "uncommon."
As they have said:
"A property that is unique [to one thing] and its possession by another is observed;
if that [possession] were intended to be common to all [things], it would be a cause of doubt."
Consequently, it is established that only the common [reason] functions as a cause for doubt.

Furthermore, regarding what the author of the *Vārttika* stated—that the uncommon [reason] (*asādhāraṇa*) is a cause of doubt because it is excluded from all [similar and dissimilar instances]—even there, if the absence of that [uncommon reason], which is common [to both classes], is the cause of doubt, what has happened to the uncommon [reason] itself? As they say:
"If doubt arises from its absence because it is excluded from everything..."
What, then, is the point of that which is unique [to a single object], since its nature consists in not occurring elsewhere?
Thus it is said.
Conflicting cognition (*vipratipatti*), which arises from two contradictory reasons regarding a single object, is also a cause of doubt;
and the coexistence of contradictory reasons is indeed nothing other than the "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) [reason].
Since that [uncommon reason] is included within the "common" (*sādhāraṇa*) [reason], it is well said that all of this is designated as the "property common to both" (*samānadharmatva*).
He refutes this, saying: "No, because of a failure to understand the meaning of the sūtra.

We do not deny that [the causes of doubt] are common to all cases; rather, taking into account only the distinctions of positive and negative concomitance, deviation, and whether the [cause] resides in the speaker, we describe doubt as being of three kinds according to the difference in its causes.
This is the meaning.
The author of the Vārttika, having set forth the opinion of the author of the Bhāṣya, refutes it with the words "others, however" (*apare punar*).
The meaning is that all three [factors], being devoid of any proving or subverting evidence (*sādhaka-bādhaka-pramāṇa*), have been stated not to be causes of doubt.
Furthermore, if these two were causes of doubt independently, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); consequently, people would not act preceded by certainty.
And thus he demonstrates the contradiction with common worldly experience by stating: "because of the twofold nature of apprehension and non-apprehension.

Nor should it be said that there is no confidence or freedom from doubt regarding this [object], nor that there is doubt due to the lack of a settled distinction between apprehension and non-apprehension at the stage prior to repeated practice.
For when one has not reached the stage of repeated practice, even upon perceiving fire from a distance, people do not doubt whether it is "a serpent" (nāga) or "a mountain" (naga);
rather, they doubt whether it is "a cluster of *kiṃśuka* flowers" or "a fire" (*uṣarbudha*).
In that case, the cause—conjoined with other factors—is precisely the occurrence of a common property (*samānadharmopapatti*).
Thus, it has been stated that doubt does not arise from the mere non-perception of the unqualified even without the perception of common characteristics and so forth.
Having analyzed [the opponent's position], he states another refutation with the words "And for those who...

If there is a distinction based on a difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), then doubt is threefold; however, if the distinction is based on a difference in the causes that enter into the causal complex, then it is fivefold.
However, the meaning is that it is of many kinds.

Regarding the phrase "because of the occurrence of common and multiple properties," he raises an objection by taking it as a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound: "Not from the apprehension of a common property.
Then, taking it as a *bahuvrīhi* compound, he provides the resolution: "This is the answer.
Now, [the word] "atha" [is used].

And what is this "distinction" (*viśeṣa*), such that it is called *kiṃviśe�șa*? The meaning is: "that which has a distinction not previously perceived. When there is doubt regarding an individual (*vyakti*) already perceived, the distinctions residing in that [individual] are what one wishes to recall; however, when there is doubt regarding another individual of the same class, those [distinctions] residing in the other [individual] have indeed been perceived by way of the universal (*sāmānya*). Thus, because of the perception of the universal (*sāmānyapratyakṣāt*), that which possesses the universal is itself the "universal" (*sāmānya*).
Just as it was said that "this bridge of dharma is common to kings," so too is the subject (dharmin) described as being both common and perceptible;
the meaning is that its specific characteristics are not established due to the absence of any proving or subverting means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
He presents the definition of doubt as accepted by the Buddhists with the words, "But others...
He refutes it while concealing his intention with the words, "By them also...
Not perceiving this intention, the opponent objects: "If the locus (dharmin)..."
The proponent of the refutation reveals his own intention: "If, first of all," and so forth.
For in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) of the Buddhists, there exists no substratum (*dharmin*) whatsoever for properties (*dharmas*) such as form (*rūpa*) and the like;
consequently, there would be a contradiction with their own tenet.

If, however, he says: "Let there be no contradiction with the established conclusion (siddhānta), for this discussion does not rely upon the treatise," [the author] states another fault even in that case: "of the property and the property-possessor" (dharmadharmiṇoś ca).
And then: "even according to our own method."

The meaning is that it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound containing words expressing common or multiple properties (*samāna-anekadharma-pada*). Furthermore, the word "common" (*sāmānya*) is seen used in the sense of the possessor [of the property], as in: "In the arising of a common object, the division is traditionally held to be equal."
This is the intended meaning.
Furthermore, the designation is redundant;

for even if one accepts the categories of the universal (sāmānya), the particular (viśeṣa), and that which possesses them (tadvat), since the "possessor of those" (tadvat) is not explicitly heard [in the compound], it would be understood that the "particulars" belong to the universal, which is the common property (sādharmya).
The meaning is that it would be a contradictory statement to say that "particulars belong to a universal.
For in the definition of the Vaiśeṣika [system], by the phrase "because particulars are not perceived," the absence of both proving and refuting evidence was shown;
however, in this case, such [evidence] must be stated.
Therefore, he states that the Buddhist definition is deficient with the words "perception," and so forth.

Furthermore, if by the phrase "from the observation of similarity" the Buddhist intends only a deviation from positive concomitance (*anvaya*), then it should have been stated as "from the observation of multiple properties.
Thus, in this way, the general definition is one [and the same].
And it is established that there are three specific characteristics.

Taking these four characteristics as the basis for his investigation, he considers them with the words "If [they were] similar" (*samāna*). If, first of all, while the general definition of doubt (*saṃśaya*) remains established, there are three specific definitions, then the definition of each of those three— once they have been subsumed under the category of doubt— would merely serve to exclude one from the other.
Therefore, one need only state: "because of the occurrence of common and unique properties" and "because of conflicting opinions.
There is no need for anything further here, since the mutual exclusion [of the categories] is established by that much alone.
Therefore, this sūtra is intended solely to state the causes of doubt without regard for their mutual exclusion;
and since there are other causes of doubt as well, those too ought to be mentioned. Indeed, when one doubts regarding one's own tranquility and so forth, [the following applies].

He resolves [the objection] by stating, "Let it be for now," etc., [meaning]: "Whether I am attached or detached when in the presence of sandalwood, women, and so forth"—this doubt of his arises from proximity (*sannikarṣa*) to an internal object such as tranquility (*śama*).
Although the exclusion of those belonging to the same class is established by that much alone, [he says this to show the distinction].

Nevertheless, in order to exclude [the possibility of] determining what is of a different class (*vijātīya*), the general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) must be followed; and since this would result in a cumbersome understanding, it is appropriate to rely on the remaining factors for the sake of brevity. The point is that the contact between the self and the mind (*ātmamanaḥ-saṃnikarṣa*) and so forth are entirely common [to all cognitions] and are not even capable of excluding what is of a different class; therefore, they are not mentioned.
Thus, it has been stated that by determining the causes of doubt, one determines the varieties of doubt as a matter of course.
Now, however, the very nature of doubt itself is being stated as a qualification of its causes; thus he says: "Or, [it is] the indication of its own nature.
Considering that even a person who holds a contrary view must be instructed just like one who is in doubt, he raises an objection: "Like doubt."

One who is mistaken is not a disciple; rather, having led such a person away from mere wrangling and cavil (*jalpa-vitaṇḍā*), one should instruct him while he is still in a state of doubt. With this intention, he replies: "True. //23//
NyS 1.1.24: That object with reference to which one acts is the purpose (prayojana).
The definition of *prayojana* (purpose), which follows in the sequence of the topical outline, is as follows: [it is] that which leads to the attainment of the goal. //2//
In this context, the word "artha" (purpose/object) is intended to include both primary and secondary purposes.
Among these, the primary [purpose] consists of the attainment of happiness and the avoidance of suffering, while the secondary [purpose] consists of the means to achieve them.
Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states: "The object [which]... and so forth.
Here, the explanation of the term *adhikṛtya* is: "having determined" or "having resolved.
Furthermore, the two purposes (*artha*) are the attainment of happiness and the avoidance of suffering.

Furthermore, the attainment of pleasure and the avoidance of pain do not, in their own nature, constitute the objects of engagement or withdrawal; rather, it is shown that they become the objects of a conscious being's engagement only through the engagement with the means to achieve them—this is indicated by the phrase "one performs the means for their attainment and avoidance" because these [means] are the causes of engagement.
Although the attainment and avoidance of pleasure and pain, as well as the means to them, do indeed exist, [it is the means that drive action].
Nevertheless, when understood in a general sense, they are causes for engagement by way of the offering of desire and so forth.
Now, [it may be argued] that the word "adhikṛtya" (with reference to) occurs in the Sūtra,
and "vyavasāya" (determination) occurs in the Bhāṣya.
To the question, "Why then is there no contradiction? he says: "The determination (*vyavasāya*) is the application (*adhikāra*) to the object," and so forth.
The author of the *Vārttika* explains this as follows: "Having made that object the subject of application (*adhikṛtya*)," and "the determination."

He asks: "Of what? [The answer is: It is the resolve regarding the attainment of happiness and the avoidance of suffering that would cause one to engage in that very [object]. Yet these two lack the capacity for such engagement;
nor does a certainty regarding one thing cause one to engage with another.
The meaning is that [otherwise] there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
The reply is: "of the means to pleasure and pain.
And thus, the meaning is that there is a consensus regarding both cognition and practical engagement (*pravṛtti*).
He demonstrates its all-pervasiveness with the words, "by this purpose.
The purpose of the *vitaṇḍā* (cavil) has also been stated in the first sūtra.
The meaning is: "of one who is being questioned and who proceeds [to act]."
He raises an objection with the words "yadi" (if).
That by which something is perceived is a *loka*, meaning a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
"Endowed with that" (*tadanvita*) means produced from that.

The meaning is that such a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does not exist, because it would lead to the consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). He refutes this by stating: "This is an excessive fault."
And how it is that the validity of a means of valid cognition is established by another means of valid cognition without resulting in an infinite regress will be explained in the second [chapter].
Nor is it correct to say that because something is more well-known, its definition need not be formulated.
For how it serves as a means when applied,
where it applies it,
and how it is pervasive— all this must be made known to the investigator.
"Now, as for 'another':
it refers to one who is not authoritative, namely a worldly person,
such as [the claim] that Vaiśravaṇa dwells in every banyan tree."
Thus [the opponent argues]. He refutes this, saying: "We do not understand that," meaning that the purpose is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
As for what was said— that because the purpose is not a constituent part of the reasoning (nyāya), it should not be stated—
that is not correct.
Indeed, we do not say that it is purposeless; nor do we maintain that purpose is merely a subordinate limb (*aṅga*) of reasoning (*nyāya*).
For that which exists for the sake of something other than the person could not be the primary purpose itself.
However, reasoning, while possessing its own purpose, accepts the purposeless reflection concerning that [subject] as a subordinate limb.
This is according to the maxim that "that which is fruitless in the presence of something fruitful is an auxiliary to it.

Therefore, it is established that even though it is not an auxiliary, purpose (*prayojana*) is the root of investigation, just as heaven is the root of the performance of sacrifices and the like, along with their constituent procedures (*itikartavyatā*). //24//
NyS 1.1.25: A corroborative instance (dṛṣṭānta) is that object regarding which there is a consensus of understanding among ordinary people and experts.
He defines the example (dṛṣṭānta), which follows in sequence: "The worldly... [up to] "...the end. //25//
"Example" (dṛṣṭānta) is the designation of the object to be defined; the remainder is the definition.

That object in which [the probandum] is established—either through similarity with the probandum by virtue of possessing its properties, or through dissimilarity with the probandum by virtue of not possessing those properties—is the example.
And thus there is no over-extension [of the definition].
Such a specific qualification is obtained from the sūtra on the example (udāharaṇa).
To the question, "What is this commonality with the world? he says: "Innate" (naisargika).

The excellence of intellect acquired through the study of the treatises is that which pertains to those under training (*vainayika*). Those devoid of this are the worldly persons (*laukika*) who are to be instructed; this is the first point.

Conversely, those who possess both [worldly knowledge and scriptural learning] are the investigators (*parīkṣaka*), who are the instructors; this is what is meant. Furthermore, the plural form is used because of the multiplicity of such discussions.
By this, the proponent and the opponent have been shown; he explains their agreement of intellect with the words "just as that object...
He states the purpose of the definition with the words "by contradiction with the example."

Contradiction of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) means its being contradictory (*viruddhatva*), such as its being devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatva*). "Counter-arguments" (*pratipakṣāḥ*) refers to arguments that establish a counter-position. "Resolution" (*samādhi*) is the refutation of the attribution of non-existent faults.
The *Bhāṣya* states: "An observed instance (lakṣita-dṛṣṭānta) is fit for—and serves—the purpose of defining an example (udāharaṇa-lakṣaṇa).

Regarding this, the author of the *Vārttika*, considering that the specific nature of ordinary people (*laukika*) and experts (*parīkṣaka*) was not intended [to be emphasized], says: "In terms of a commonality of cognition" (*buddhi-sāmyena*).
He states the purpose of this non-intention through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), saying: "And if it is so... (*evañ ca*).
Having set forth the opponent's objection regarding the definition and rejection of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), he refutes it with the words "this is the example.
He states the purpose of the example: "The example is for the sake of understanding similarity.
Then, having repeated those very syllables as they were stated by the objector, he refutes them: "Or else, its purpose is to establish what is not yet established."
The meaning is that the invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) of the probans with the probandum is certainly not established by means of an example as something unestablished. //25//
NyS 1.1.26: A tenet (siddhānta) is the establishment of a position through the acceptance of a system and its constituent parts.

Here, the author of the Bhāṣya explains the intended meaning (*tātparya*) without first stating the general definition of a tenet (*siddhānta*), beginning with the words "Now, as for the tenet" (*atha siddhāntaḥ*).
Regarding that, the author of the Vārttika explains [the phrase] "this is such-and-such" (*idamitthaṃbhūtam*) by saying "the word 'this' refers to the general.

And in the Bhāṣya, the statement "establishment (*saṃsthitiḥ*) is the determination of the state of being such-and-such" means that the establishment is the final completion of an acceptance that began with a general statement, reaching its conclusion through the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) at the level of specific detail.
Regarding this very point, the author of the Vārttika says: "Of this meaning," referring to the Sūtra.
The end of the Tantra. // 26 //
He introduces the meaning of the sūtra with the words "But what [is it]?
and "And for the purpose of the definition";
that is, for the purpose of the general definition (sāmānyalakṣaṇa).
Indeed, it has been stated that without a general characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa), a distinction [between them] is not possible. //26//

NyS 1.1.27: [The term "acknowledgment" (abhyupagama) is used] because it has a different meaning from the categories of "entire treatise" (sarvatantra), "specific treatise" (pratitantra), and "establishment of a topic" (adhikaraṇa).
He provides the explanation: "it is not the work of various seers.

The term *lakṣaṇārthatva* means having the sense of a general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). It is called a *tantra* because by it (*anena*) objects of knowledge (*prameya*) are woven (*tantryante*) or explained (*vyutpādyante*); thus, *tantra* refers to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
That very locus is the basis for those objects which serve as indicators; they are described as such.
"Unscriptural" means lacking authoritative proof. And [this] status of being authoritative is merely based on conceit.
Therefore, there is no consequence of all objects that differ from the established tenets (siddhānta) being considered authoritative.
Having thus explained the general definition, the Commentator recites it;
then, preceded by this very explanation, he recites the aphorism on classification: "The establishment of the meaning of the system" (tantrārthasaṃsthitiḥ).

And by the term "tantra," both the general tantra (*sarvatantra*) and the specific tantra (*pratitantra*) are included, since both are indeed tantras. This is what was meant by the statement: "but because of the division of tantras."
"Apprehension of an object not previously determined" refers to that which is not explicitly mentioned in the treatise, such as the status of the mind as a sense-faculty. //27//
NyS 1.1.28: A tenet that is not contradicted by any system and is accepted within a system is a tenet common to all systems (*sarvatantrasiddhānta*).

"Of all [the senses]... //27//" Although there are disagreements regarding whether the olfactory and other senses are elemental (*bhautika*) or non-elemental (*abhautika*), nevertheless, there is no disagreement regarding their status as sense organs (*indriyatva*). The author of the *Vārttika* explains this with the words "of all."
Here, an objection is raised: "It is not [established] from an example. He replies: "It is distinct.
And this is not a tenet established by all schools (*sarvatantrasiddhānta*).
Because it is ascertained by all [means of knowledge],
namely inference and scripture;
for inference and scripture are based upon the apprehension of a relationship.
And the meaning is that where there is the apprehension of a relation, that is the example (dṛṣṭānta). //28//
A tenet established in one's own school but not established in other schools is a tenet established in a specific school (pratitantrasiddhānta). //29//
NyS 1.1.29: A tenet established in one's own system but not established in other systems is a tenet specific to that particular system (pratitantrasiddhānta).
"Samā-antaḥ" //29// The word *samāna* is a synonym for "one. For the Naiyāyikas, their own system is the *Nyāya-śāstra*, while the systems of others are the *Sāṃkhya* and other treatises.
The consciousness (cetanā) of the self is unsurpassed and immutable; it is not joined with any property characterized by arising or passing away.

Furthermore, "particularity" (viśeṣa)—meaning "excellence" (atiśaya)—is found in the primary constituents such as the body, as well as in their causes: the intellect (mahat), the ego (ahaṅkāra), the five subtle elements (tanmātra), and the gross elements.
The author of the Vārttika explains this sūtra with the words "in a general sense" (sāmānyena).
The restriction is that [this applies] only to the Yogas and only to the Sāṃkhyas. //29//
NyS 1.1.30: That, upon the establishment of which there is the establishment of another topic, is the *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* (a tenet established by the context).
"Upon the establishment of which"— that is, upon the establishment of either the object (*artha*) to be proven (*sādhya*) or the reason (*hetu*). This is a locative of domain (*viṣaya-saptamī*),
and not a locative of cause (*nimitta-saptamī*), because the relationship between cause and effect (*nimitta-naimittika-bhāva*) cannot exist between two things that are both being cognized.
Therefore, when a certain object is being cognized, other objects associated with it are understood as being included within it;
that object, being directly under discussion, serves as the substratum for those associated objects because their establishment depends upon it.
Whether that [object] be the *pakṣa* (the thesis) or the *hetu* (the reason), in this form it is an *adhikaraṇasiddhānta*.
The thesis (*pakṣa*) is as follows: "That which is the subject of dispute has an intelligent cause (*upalabdhimatkāraṇa*), because it is produced (*utpattimattvāt*), like a jar and so forth.

For here, when the state of having an intelligent antecedent belonging to the earth and other elements is being proven by means of their state of being produced, it is established precisely as accompanied by omniscience and other qualities that are necessarily concomitant with its own proof; otherwise, the establishment of having an intelligent antecedent would not occur in this case.
In the Bhāṣya, it is illustrated that when the connection of the reason (hetu) is established, the connection with other related meanings is also established.
To include all such cases, the author of the Vārttika says: "the meaning of the sentence" (vākyārtha).
The meaning is that such a reason and the subject (pakṣa) constitute the meaning of the sentence.
The meaning of the Bhāṣya is that the previously mentioned subject matter, which is directly under discussion, is included within its established conclusion. //30//
NyS 1.1.31: The acceptance of specific characteristics after having accepted [the general] without examination is the *abhyupagamasiddhānta*.
Now follows the sūtra on the tenet of admission (abhyupagamasiddhānta): "That which is accepted [by oneself] is an admitted tenet. //31//
The author of the *Vārttika* explains this: "It was not examined because it was not formulated as a sutra," for that which is formulated as a sutra is generally connected with examination;
since the acceptance of the mind as a sense-organ—even though it was not formulated as such—occurs within the section on the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, this is an *abhyupagama-siddhānta* (a tenet accepted for the sake of argument).
And the sūtra should be formulated in this way: "Because a reason is accepted even though it has not been formally stated in a sūtra, an examination of its specific details is carried out."
Therefore, from the examination of specific points, it is known that even what was not explicitly stated in the sutra was accepted by the author of the sutras;
this acceptance of his is the "accepted tenet" (abhyupagama-siddhānta).
Having thus explained the Sūtra according to his own view, he refutes the commentary of the Bhāṣyakāra with the words "not accepted by the treatise" (śāstrānabhyupagata).

This means not authorized by the treatise that has been accepted as a valid authority (pramāṇa), that is, not dependent upon such valid authority. For the general definition of a tenet (siddhānta) is: "the establishment of an acceptance based on valid authority."

And since an acceptance that is not dependent upon means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does not follow [from reason], such an acceptance cannot constitute a "tenet established by acceptance" (*abhyupagama-siddhānta*); bearing this in mind, [the author] has shown it to be improper, even though it was presented. This is because [such an acceptance] would be improper conduct toward an ignorant person, and because it is impossible for one who relies on valid cognition; the meaning of "impossibility" is that it is improper for an intelligent person to disregard [valid cognition].
Thus, "all of this is a position."

To begin with, the tenets of all systems (*sarvatantra-siddhānta*) and the tenets of specific systems (*pratitantra-siddhānta*) are stated as the subject (*pakṣa*) by their own explicit admission (*svamukhena*).

As for the tenets of a context (*adhikaraṇa-siddhānta*) and the tenets by admission (*abhyupagama-siddhānta*), although they are not explicitly admitted, they must nevertheless be admitted by implication; thus, the meaning is that they are subjects by way of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
Now, if it is the case that a tenet is established as an admission through its validity as a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), [then...]

In that case, since objects that differ from the established tenets would possess the status of being authoritative, it would follow that entities are embraced by contradictory properties; therefore, he says: "because of the conviction regarding that.
This means because of the conviction—that is, the misconception—regarding that [notion] of being an action established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
[The word] "pakṣe" means "in the thesis."

The word *pakṣa* is derived from the root *pac* in the sense of "manifestation. It is a term for the subject (*svārtha*) because it is grasped either as an object (*karman*) or by way of being manifested;
this is according to the etymological derivation: "that by which something is grasped" (*upādīyate 'nena*).
"In the accomplishment of an action" means in the accomplishment of the primary action;

"endowed with a specific action" means endowed with an intermediate operation, for it is by that [intermediate operation] that the diversity of the factors of action (*kāraka*) occurs in relation to the primary action. And as for that "acceptance of the principle":
Just as it is accepted that the means of establishing what is logical is "reasoning" (*nyāya*),
so too it is accepted that the means of establishing the object of cognition (*prameya*) is "valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*).
And when the subject (*dharmin*) is not accepted, its basis cannot be accepted.
Therefore, the meaning is that in both ways there is no denial of the tenets established by all schools (*sarvatantra-siddhānta*).

Now, as for the summary: [it is] by means of the word "position" (*pakṣa*), just as by the word "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*) all things—whether of the same or different classes—are included, their boundaries being delimited by the connection with a staff.

The meaning is that this is also the case with the word "thesis" (*pakṣa*). However, this alternative view has already been implicitly refuted by the statement that [the definition] does not encompass all *sarvatantra-siddhāntas* (tenets common to all systems), and thus it is not refuted separately.

The point is that the word "thesis" functions based on the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of being "manifested," whereas a *sarvatantra-siddhānta* is manifest by its very nature; therefore, such a siddhānta lacks the quality of being manifested.
Regarding the phrase "in the comprehension of the sentence-meaning":
the meaning of the sentence "Fat Devadatta does not eat during the day" is the prohibition of eating during the day.
Therefore, the injunction of eating at night—which is the opposite of that—is *arthāpatti* (presumption), as established in common worldly usage.
And how that is not as it appears to other means of valid cognition will be explained in the second [chapter].
Thus, by this sequence of arguments, the refutations uttered by the Venerable Dignāga have been set aside. //31//
NyS 1.1.32: The members [of a syllogism] are the proposition, the reason, the example, the application, and the conclusion.
Regarding the word *prati*—[the Vārttikakāra] states the purport of the Sūtra: "Of the members [of the syllogism].
Now, one might object: without a general definition of the members, it is impossible to provide their classification and enumeration, as well as their specific definitions.

And this is not a definition of the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) because it is intended for the purpose of division; therefore, he says: "The Sūtra"—meaning that although this [Sūtra] is intended for division, it indicates by implication the definition of the general characteristic of the parts.
For those who follow the science of words (*śābdāḥ*) maintain that even from a sentence whose primary intent lies elsewhere, a meaning that is perceived and required must indeed be accepted.

In that context, the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is understood from the very words that constitute the members (*avayava*). By virtue of being members, their status as a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) is demonstrated; and this unity arises through the cognition of meanings that are mutually non-referential yet capable of being related and required [of one another].

Therefore, the author of the Vārttika has shown by the word "sūtra" that the general definition of the members (*avayava*) such as the proposition (*pratijñā*) and so forth is established precisely as the communication of such a meaning.
He states the intended meaning of the enumeration of the divisions with the words "vibhāga... [etc.].
The mention of "three members" is for the purpose of illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*).
It should also be understood that [the proof] consists of two members.

Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states: "In that case, when it is not yet perceived... This refers to a subject (dharmin) which is known in a general sense, but regarding which there is doubt as to its specific qualification, such as possessing fire.
The ascertainment of the reality of "possessing fire" and so forth is the *pratyaya* (cognition).
