Its purpose (*artha*) or utility is the cognitions of avoidance, acquisition, and indifference.

That which sets it in motion and produces it is the desire to know (*jijñāsā*). This is the proximity (*pratyāsatti*) by way of pursuing the means of cognition; it pertains to the distinction between doubt and the knowledge of reality, but not to their intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*).
Because doubt is separated [from its object] by the desire to know (jijñāsā) which follows immediately after doubt,
the object of knowledge (prameya) is capable [of being known].
In that regard, "attainment" (prāpti) refers to the capacity (śaktatā) of both the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and the knower (pramātṛ).
And that [capacity] is twofold, consisting of its own nature and its auxiliary factors.
The author of the Bhāṣya demonstrates this through the following turn of phrase: "The means of valid cognition are manifested," and "like the thesis and so forth."
Examples by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*);
the description of the counter-position (*pratipakṣa*) is as follows:
"If sound were eternal..."
The permanence of impermanence would not be its opposite in the sense that "it is not created";
therefore, the description of the absence of a reason for it is stated as "and this is not uncreated.
This description is provided for the purpose of permitting the knowledge of reality once that [false] description has been refuted.

Tattvajñāna (knowledge of reality) is that by which reality is known; it is valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For the purpose of authorizing that [cognition], there is the removal of doubt, which has another name, "reasoning" (*tarka*).
For doubt is removed by that [reasoning] through the medium of authorizing valid cognition, acting as its instrumental procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
The author of the Vārttika explains this collection of commentaries by means of a series of questions, beginning with: "But how [is it]?
It is not the case, however, that the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) and so forth, having been understood from words, serve as means of communication to others.
Now, let it be granted that they do not serve as means of communication to others; [nevertheless...]
To the question, "Why do they not themselves serve as their own means of proof? he says: "And because they are already certain.
The meaning is that [the object] is understood—that is, attained—precisely through the means of proof (sādhana), and once attained, it is known.
And "attainability" (śakyaprāpti) means that [the object] is sought after and known.
To the question, "Are then desire to know (jijñāsā) and the others entirely non-factors (anaṅga)? the Commentator replied:
"But within the context (prakaraṇa), desire to know and the others are effective."
Having restated that, he explains: "But in the case of a *prakaraṇa*.
*Prakaraṇa* means the commencement of a discussion (*kathā*).
The meaning is that the members [of the syllogism], such as the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) and so forth, which give rise to that [discussion], are its auxiliary parts (*aṅga*).

Furthermore, these [factors] such as the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) and so forth, once arisen, are the instigators of the treatise by their very nature; they are not, however, instigators through the cognition of themselves, whereby— being objects to be conveyed by words— they would become constituent parts of the treatise, as is the case with the thesis (*pratijñā*) and other members which convey their own respective meanings through the cognition of themselves.
Therefore, the intention is that the employment of words expressive of "desire to know" (*jijñāsā*) and so forth is entirely useless in every respect.
For this very reason, he says: "because it causes another to understand.
The word *tu* (but/however) serves to distinguish [the term] from "desire to know" and the rest.
By the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "even the three-membered [proof]," he includes the negation of the two-membered proof.
In the phrase "of the application and the conclusion," it should be understood that "of the proposition" (*pratijñā*) is also implied. //32//
NyS 1.1.33: The statement of that which is to be proven is the proposition (*pratijñā*).

The *sādhya* (the probandum) is that which is to be known. That by which something is grasped is a "grasper" (*parigraha*); and since it is also a statement (*vacana*), it is called a "grasping statement" (*parigrahavacana*).
An example is: "Sound is impermanent."
Having raised this objection, the author of the *Vārttika* provides the resolution: "Because it is already established.
That which possesses fire does not lack it; thus, there is no non-connection with fire for it at this time.
And when that [subject] is being proven as possessing fire on the mountain, the restriction—characterized by the mutual relation between the qualifier and the qualified—is established by implication.
However, the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) itself is not directly the probandum,

because it is not admitted that the logical mark (*liṅga*) has the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) as its object. Its indication is expressed by the statement of the proposition (*pratijñāvākya*), namely, "it is indicated by this."

Here, the Venerable [Vasubandhu], considering the meaning of the sentence to be the exclusion of connection with anything else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*), challenges the definition of a thesis (*pratijñā*) by means of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) and under-extension (*avyāpti*) with the words "in both" (*ubhaya*).

The meaning is that when both types of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) are applicable, a doubt arises as to which one is being restricted, and thus the question "What is this being restricted? presents itself.
[He says] "the thesis is restricted."
The intention is that the Grammarians hold the view that restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) does not apply elsewhere than where the particle *eva* is employed.
The phrase "because of being excluded" (*vyatirekitvāt*) means "because of deviation" (*vyabhicārāt*). He provides the resolution: "In every sentence... and so forth.
The general rule is that the meaning of a sentence is a relation (saṃsarga);
however, in some cases, there is also the exclusion of connection with others (anyayogavyavaccheda). Thus, when a general term is heard, a restriction (niyama) is understood.
Just as when it is stated that [cognition] "arises from the contact of a sense faculty with its object," both cognition and pleasure (sukha) and so forth are obtained in a general sense;
therein, the mention of "cognition" (jñāna) is not prescriptive,
because it is already obtained.

Therefore, it is understood that the result is the exclusion of pleasure and so forth. However, if one were to disregard our view and apply restriction everywhere, then there would be a contradiction with worldly convention; thus he says: "And in all cases... [sarvatra ca].

Since there is no such restriction anywhere in the world, he says: "And where... He raises an objection: "But surely... The intention is that the meaning of the word *sādhya* (the probandum) is that which has an established counter-position (*siddhapratipakṣa*).
He refutes this, saying: "It is not the meaning of the Sūtra.

The intention is that in all cases of doubt, the principle "the meaning is understood from the commentary" (vyākhyānato 'rthapratipattiḥ) applies. The challenger reveals his own view, saying: "But then..."
The non-indication of what is not to be proven is the non-indication of what is already established. Its cessation is understood from the word "sādhya" (to be proven),
but the meaning is that it is not the object to be made known.
He refutes this with the words "and that which is unprovable.
This would be the case if only what is already established were unprovable;
however, that for which a proof is impossible—that too is unprovable.

And thus, the meaning is that there is an exclusion of such unestablished properties as visibility (*cākṣuṣatva*). He raises an objection again with the words "But then" (*atha punar*): "Being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth is neither unestablished, nor is its probans impossible."
Nor is it the case that [properties] such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) are employed as subordinate members [of the thesis], such that [the subject] would become indefinable; this is the meaning.
He refutes [this objection]: "This is not a fault.
The meaning of the *sūtra* is that it is a statement of the apprehension of a subject (*dharmin*) as qualified by a property (*dharma*) that is capable of being defined.
This, however, is not a statement regarding the apprehension of the mere property (dharma) alone.
This was said by accepting exclusion as the meaning of the word; but in ultimate reality, there is no fixed rule, and in some cases there is association (saṃsarga).
Because there might be an exclusion [of other meanings] in some cases, he says: "And this which...

For this reason as well, there is no possibility of the fallacy of the unestablished (*asiddha*) for the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*); thus he says: "And the statement of the probandum (*sādhya*) is the thesis (*pratijñā*).
Indeed, a tenet (*siddhānta*) is an acceptance that is dependent upon the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, there is no basis in valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for [the properties] such as being visible by the eye;
even the conceit regarding them is removed by sublation (*bādhaka*).

Now, if other doctrines (*siddhānta*)—distinct from those established in all systems (*sarvatantra-siddhānta*)—are to be considered "probanda" (*sādhya*), then since their purpose would already be fulfilled by that very probandum, their separate mention would be useless.
Therefore it was said: "in the state [of disagreement].
This refers to the state of having differing opinions;
however, it has been stated that in all tantras, such disagreement is impossible.
He states another resolution: "jijñāsādi" (beginning with the desire to know).

By the *dhibhāga-sūtra*, the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) and so forth—which are the causes for the commencement of the treatise—are brought to mind as the members of the sentence that must be excluded [as the subject].
Therefore, wherever there is the desire to know and so forth, that is the probandum (*sādhya*).
The meaning is that those [qualities] do not exist in cases such as visibility and so forth, which are sublated by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
He states another solution: "it is worthy of the sense" (*arhatyartha*).
He states another refutation as well: "Or [it refers to] the object and the instrument.

Thus, first of all, by considering the etymological derivation and so forth, it has been stated that there is no possibility of the term *sādhya* applying to the reason (*hetu*) or the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Now, in common worldly usage itself, there are three very clear modes of meaning for words.
He says that there is no need for further subtle investigation here: "Because of the distinction between the unestablished and the established [as the probandum].

It has been stated that the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) are presented as objects (*karman*) so that the fallacy of being unestablished for either one of the two parties might be avoided.
In the phrase "of both sides" (*ubhayapakṣa*), the word *pakṣa* denotes a group or category.
The meaning is that it is accepted by both parties.
He states another resolution with the words "Or rather" (*atha vā*).
This is the section concerning the members (*avayava*) [of a syllogism].
And these [members], having attained the status of a single sentence through the communication of a single primary meaning, possess the nature of constituent parts (*avayava*).
That which they proceed to communicate is the primary object;
and that is the locus (*dharmin*) as qualified by the property (*dharma*) one wishes to establish.
And thus, since they are not capable of directly conveying that [object], they operate toward the proof for its sake.
Therefore, the subject (dharmin) as qualified by the property (dharma) intended to be proven is their primary object;
and since the primary object is the first to appear in the mind, it alone is expressed by the term "probandum" (sādhya).
But the meaning is that the reason and the example are not the primary elements.

Thus, our definition is faultless; however, that very definition which the Venerable One has formulated otherwise by refuting our own with this objection is indeed faulty—this is what he says with the words "And if this... [is not so].
Now, one might object: where the term *sādhya* (the probandum) is already present, the inclusion of the word *iṣṭa* (intended) would be redundant.
But since that [property] does not exist in this [subject], how can the inclusion of the word "desired" (*iṣṭa*) be purposeless? To this he says: "And because of the mention of 'action' (*karman*).
Let there be no term for the probandum (*sādhya*); however, there is the term for the subject (*pakṣa*).

For even that which is being cooked or manifested is indeed something to be accomplished; and that is an object (*karman*), and an object is "that which is desired to be attained"—this is the meaning.
[The opponent] objects: "But what if it is undesired?"
To the objection that "this position is indeed undesirable and thus contradictory," it is said: "it is indeed [unwanted] from the perspective of the meaning.
The meaning is that for one who is engaged in establishing the actual state of things (*vastu-vyavasthāpana*), such a thing is not desired.
While presenting the Buddhist position, [the author] refutes a certain point favored by them in the middle [of the argument]: "It is not audible" (*aśrāvaṇa*).
This has already been explained in the first sūtra.
However, inference [is valid] from the cause (*kāraṇa*) and from transformation (*vikāra*).
This refers to such passages as the above;
for the manifested (vyangya) does not conform to the manifesting cause (vyañjaka-kāraṇa).
Indeed, a jar is not large when the lamp is large, nor small when it is small;
rather, the sound is large when the cause is large.
Therefore, because it is a modification resulting from its cause, sound is an effect.
Just as a composite whole (*avayavin*) produced from large, thick masses is itself large;

by this, the reason—namely, that [the object] varies according to the variation of its cognitions—is indicated, and by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the [reason] regarding sound while it exists is [indicated].
Because there is a fault in [the theory of] manifestation.
These and similar [arguments] are to be understood.

Furthermore, the fault is that, like sacrificial grass (*darbha*) and the like, *ṛc* verses that have been employed [once] cannot be used again because they are "exhausted" (*niriṣṭika*); however, if they were effects, they would be distinct [entities] each time, and thus there would be no such state of being "exhausted"—this is the meaning.
Even though there is scriptural authority for the non-eternality of sound, such as: "He created King Soma; from him the three Vedas were created."
Thus it is said;
nevertheless, there was neither non-existence nor existence, for this was indeed the primordial state according to the sacred tradition.
Thus, even though there is scriptural evidence for eternality, because it lacks certainty, only inference possesses authority in this matter;
and so, there is a contradiction with inference. However, we do not consider contradiction with common consensus (prasiddhi) as distinct from contradiction with a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
He states the lack of understanding: "What is this contradiction with common consensus?
He says in a single passage: "Common consensus refers to perception and the other means of valid cognition," as in the case of [the claim] "The moon is not the hare-marked one."
If the denotability of the word "moon" (śaśin) with respect to the moon is being negated,
then there is a contradiction with inference arising from positive and negative concomitance as understood through worldly linguistic usage.
Alternatively, if it is the status of being an object of conceptual cognition that is being negated, [then...]

Consequently, for you there is a contradiction with the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*), whereas for us there is a contradiction with mental direct perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*); thus, in every respect, establishment does not differ from valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Having thus presented the Buddhist position and refuted the examples cited by them, he concludes the Buddhist position with the words: "etadartha... (for this purpose).
He refutes this as follows: "And this...
For an entity, exactly as it was produced from its own causes, remains precisely that way;
since there is no alteration of its nature, no defect can enter into it.
The words referring to those [objects] are also individually non-defective.

However, that verbal composition— which is human in origin, which superimposes an object seen in one place onto another, and which takes the form of a proposition (*pratijñā*) and so forth, whether through delusion or for the purpose of deceiving others—
is defective when it possesses such qualities as contradiction with one's own words (*svavacanavirodha*).
By means of that [sentence], it is the person who is refuted,
not the meaning nor the words.
The denial of its own meaning, the contradiction with one's own statement, or the fault of the agent— whether it be error or deception— is metaphorically attributed to the action.

Furthermore, there is neither error nor deception regarding the action, because those two—being based on a divergence of intention—are attributes of the person; since the action sublates only the object [of the intention], it is said that "by means of the action" one understands the person's intention.
He raises an objection: "Now, regarding the thesis... He then refutes this by way of an over-extension: "This is not tenable, because [the definition] begins with 'the reason' (*hetu*) and so forth.
Furthermore, the refutations (*dūṣaṇa*) consist in the pointing out of deficiencies, the omission of members, and the manifestation of the presence of faults in subsequent parts.

A reason (*hetu*) endowed with the three characteristics (*trairūpya*) is complete. If it lacks any one of those three characteristics, it is deficient; such a reason is either unestablished (*asiddha*), contradictory (*viruddha*), or inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). This is the fault of deficiency in the reason.
Furthermore, there are faults of the members [of the syllogism], such as faults of the proposition (*pratijñādoṣa*), including contradictions with one's own words and so forth.

A fault of the reason (*hetudoṣa*) consists of [fallacies] such as being unestablished (*asiddhatva*); likewise, a fault of the example (*udāharaṇadoṣa*) consists of [defects] such as being devoid of the probandum (*sādhyavikalatva*).
A fault of the response (*uttaradoṣa*) is a futile rejoinder (*jāti*), such as the "equivalence by reaching" (*prāptisama*) or the "equivalence by non-reaching" (*aprāptisama*).
Its "rejection" (*ākṣepa*) means its taking up, its adoption, that is to say, its acceptance.
The "state" (bhāva) refers to [faults] such as lack of ingenuity (apratibhā);
for that is the intention of either the proponent or the opponent.
The "expositions" (udbhāvanāni) of that [intention] are called "refutations" (dūṣaṇāni).
For there is no metaphorical designation when [the primary sense] is possible.
Indeed, if the faults residing in the thesis, when pointed out as such, did not bring about the defeat of the proponent, then—
because they would be purposeless in that context— they could be metaphorically attributed to the thesis itself due to their impossibility there.
However, they are able to refute the disputant by means of the refutations contained within the proposition itself.
Thus, this is the occurrence of the faults of the proposition within the proposition.
But why, then, is [the term] "those situated on the bed" (*mañcasthāḥ*) not employed in this way?
To this, it has been said: "It is an explanation of sentences employed in common worldly usage.
No; the meaning is that worldly usage is beginningless, and thus it is neither to be enjoined nor to be questioned.
It might be argued as follows:

the inclusion of the term "intended" (*iṣṭa*) is for the purpose of ensuring that the probandum (*sādhya*)—even if not explicitly stated in the words—is nonetheless encompassed by the [proponent's] intention, as in the case of the argument, "The eyes and so forth are for the sake of another.
For in this instance, the mere fact of being for the sake of another (*pārārthya*) is what is established by the words.
And it is not that alone which is to be proven for this [subject], but rather its being for the sake of another (pārārthya).
And he does not state that [alone], lest the reason "because of being a composite" (saṃghātatvāt) be rendered inconclusive (ananvaya).
Therefore, he says that the mention of "the desired" (*iṣṭa*) is for the purpose of excluding that [unwanted consequence]: "Now, by the mention of 'the desired'...
He refutes this: "This point is also understood from the proof (*sādhana*) itself;
it is understood from the very employment of the proposition (*pratijñā*)."
This is the intended meaning:
for the indicators of speech are the intentions of the speaker;
and that which is the ultimate purpose of a statement is the meaning of that statement.
And its *tātparya* (intended meaning) resides sometimes in the expressed (*vācya*) and sometimes in the indicated (*lakṣya*); thus, this entire [meaning] constitutes the meaning of the statement.
But how can that which is not of such a nature be the meaning of a statement?
And how is it to be understood that it is pervaded by the intention of the speaker?
Furthermore, the thesis (pakṣa) is not denotable by the word "pratijñā" anywhere,
precisely because it is to be indicated (lakṣya) as the meaning of a sentence. Thus, the cessation of the undesired is the desired [result].

Even when its means are being sought, that [desire] is indeed desirable at that time, because effort is preceded by desire and would otherwise be impossible. Now, deliberation (*vicāraṇā*) is doubt (*saṃśaya*).

Therefore, the meaning is that when something is the object of doubt, being desired and being sought after through inquiry, it is precisely the probandum (sādhya), and not the means of proof (sādhana) or anything else.
And the definition of the venerable [Dignāga] regarding another point is:
"The thesis (pakṣa) is that which is intended as the probandum and is not refuted by a contradictory object."
Thus he refutes [the opponent's position] with the words "even so.
For here too, there are four superfluous syllables following the word expressing the probandum (*sādhya*).
Likewise, the thesis (*pakṣa*) is that which is intended to be proven.
In this regard, even in Vasubandhu’s definition, the inclusion of the terms "not having a contradictory meaning" (*viruddhārtha*) and "not being refuted" (*anirākṛta*) need not be made.

What is meant is this: it is not only to us that these terms "having a contradictory meaning" and "not being refuted" appear superfluous; they appear so to our fellow adherents of the same school as well.
Because it has not been accepted by them, for this very reason it must be stated thus: "the thesis is that which is intended to be proven.
Even here, although the expression "to prove" (sādhayitum) is the same for both the operation of the one who employs [the argument] and the one who employs it, [the distinction remains].

Nevertheless, by the use of the suffix *tumun*, it is stated that whoever is the one who establishes [the proof], the proponent (*vādī*), is the very same as the seeker (*eṣitṛ*). It does not mean, however, that the one who enjoins the proponent is the establisher, nor that the proponent is the seeker. And this is said while taking the status of being the seeker to belong certainly to the proponent.

The intention [of the rule] "tattvabhāktayośca" is that when even the status of being the one who causes another to act (*prayojaka*) is transferred to the instigator (*prayojaka*), then there is no remedy even by means of the term "self-grasping" (*svayaṃgrahaṇa*).
An established agent (*siddhaḥ kartā*) is the instigator of that which is to be accomplished (*sādhyasya prayojakaḥ*).
For the proponent [asserts] that this proof is inherent in that which is being proven as it is being established;

however, that which is the instigator even of that [proponent], falling into a third position, is not inherently connected to that proof. Although he who causes another to act is in some sense said to "act" himself through figurative usage (*bhakti*), his status as an agent is merely metaphorical.

And that is incorrect, because [the term "agent"] refers to the primary agent; "primariness" (mukhyatva) consists in being the actual [agent]. He reveals the meaning established by the previous intention with the words "and [after] the suffix tumun."

Regarding this, it was stated by the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) on the occasion of refuting the *abhyupagama-siddhānta* (the doctrine accepted for the sake of argument): "An object that lacks a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*).

For an object that is not contradicted by the treatise (*śāstra*) and is established by a means of valid cognition is indeed scriptural (*śāstrīya*), because it is established by the very means of valid cognition accepted by the treatise; one who explains such an object does not subvert the treatise.

However, one who establishes the eternality of sound while having accepted the Vaiśeṣika system as authoritative is not to be heeded; for he is defeated immediately after the statement of his proposition, before even the reason has been presented, as the assembly and the opponent have already determined the matter. On the other hand, one who merely declares himself a Vaiśeṣika based on the simple study of the Vaiśeṣika treatises, yet puts forward the eternality of sound, is not defeated, because he has not actually accepted the Vaiśeṣika system as authoritative.
Thus:
"And that which is an acceptance without a means of valid cognition (apramāṇaka)"—
it is called an "acceptance" (abhyupagama) because it is accepted (abhyupagamyate).
It should be stated that "the naming of that" is the proposition (*pratijñā*); the meaning is that by mentioning the "probandum" (*sādhya*), there is the advantage of brevity in mentioning it.
As for the venerable Naiyāyika, he concludes his initial position with the words: "Therefore, [it is] devoid of that. //33//
NyS 1.1.34: The reason (hetu) is that which establishes the probandum (sādhya) through its similarity to the example (udāharaṇa).

Demonstrating the intermediate connection, he also shows that the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) is a constituent part of the proof (*sādhana*), by saying: "of the reason (*hetu*) which has reached its proper occasion.
The occasion for the statement of the reason follows immediately after the proposition.
For indeed, it is with a view toward the instruction of others that discerning persons utter speech.

And one should inform others only of that which they wish to know; for when this is so, the other person is informed by one who expresses what is required. Indeed, one who, being asked about mango trees, speaks of *kovidāra* trees, does not have words worthy of attention from the questioner.
And how can one whose words are not worthy of attention be called an instructor?

For example, when a teacher has sent forth the command, "Māṭhara, bring fuel," and this [student] enters the house for that purpose without saying, "Here I am, I shall bring it," then the teacher becomes angry with him, saying: "Ah, you wretched disciple, you mere reciter of the Veda, Māṭhara! Do you disregard me?"

Thus, for one who desires to know that sound is impermanent, if one does not state "sound is impermanent," but instead says something such as "because it is produced," or "whatever is produced is impermanent," or "and sound is produced"— all of this is disregarded by the listener because, at first glance, it is perceived as an unrelated statement.
And thus, one who is not attentive is unable to understand. If it is argued that the statement, "Whatever is produced is impermanent, like a jar;

and sound is produced," determines the impermanence of sound through the very force of the meaning (*arthasāmarthya*) even without explicit mention, and that attention is therefore required here—[we reply: no.
Because it would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence:
for if there is attention, then there is certainty regarding the object; and from that certainty, attention [arises].

Furthermore, if the assembly and the opponent were to wait for this statement [of the proponent] as a means of establishing a connection— acting as if they had accepted the proponent as an authority— then in that case, they would not even require the reason (*hetu*) and so forth,
since the determination of the meaning would follow from that statement alone.
When it is stated that "sound is impermanent," and the question "Why? arises, the reason "because it is produced" presents itself.
Thus, both in the formal application of the five-membered syllogism and according to its definition, the occasion for the reason occurs immediately after the proposition (*pratijñā*).
Therefore, since the reason has reached its proper occasion, the aphorism defining its specific characteristics follows by way of first stating its general characteristic.
"Udā-tuḥ" (34). It is called a *sūtra* because it indicates both [the definition and the example] through its word and its meaning.

Here, "hetu" (reason) is the designation of the thing to be defined (*lakṣya*). And that, as stated in the section on the enumeration of divisions, is a constituent part of a sentence, consisting of a verbal expression.

Regarding its general definition, although the phrase "the means of proving" (*sādhanam*)—derived from the etymology "that by which something is proved"—denotes an object such as "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) that has entered into a state of subservience to another (the probandum), nevertheless, because it is impossible for that [object] to share the same grammatical locus (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the statement [itself], it indicates the statement "producedness, etc. as the actual subject matter.
Furthermore, if the statement itself were called the "reason" (*hetu*), then when it is uttered together with the probandum, it would become a "thesis" (*pratijñā*).
If it were stated merely as "speech," there would be over-extension; however, with the inclusion of the term "metaphorical" (upacāra), there is no such contingency anywhere.
Even in the case of an "introduction" (upanaya), it is not understood as a means (sādhana) by virtue of being an auxiliary to another;

rather, because the meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadikārtha) is primary, it is self-contained (svaniṣṭha). Thus, there is no over-extension (prasaṅga) to that case either. Furthermore, fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) are excluded by the very term "means" (sādhana), since they are not true means.
And precisely because it is a member (*avayava*) of a logical statement (*nyāyavākya*), there is no over-extension (*prasaṅga*) to the word itself.
Thus, the exclusion of both similar and dissimilar classes is established as the general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
And this [definition] pertains to the object (*artha*).
The specific definition, however, is that which is derived from the sacred scriptures (śrauta). Although the term "reason" (hetu) is a general one,
it should nevertheless be understood as referring specifically to the reason characterized by both positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatirekin), on account of the context.
By that [statement], "the reason" is the indication of the definiendum;
the remainder, however, is the definition.
The author of the Bhāṣya explains this with the words "by way of an example.
The explanation of the term *sādharmya* is "from similarity" (*sāmānyāt*).
The explanation of the terms *sādhya* and *sādhana* is "of the property to be proven" (*sādhyasya dharmasya*).

Regarding the phrase "of the probandum" (*sādhyasya*), it is stated "of the property" (*dharmasya*) so that the cognition might not be restricted to the locus (*dharmin*) alone; the meaning is "of the locus accompanied by its property.
He clarifies this very point by saying, "by connecting it to the probandum" (*sādhye pratisandhāya*).

By the phrase "from the similarity with the example of the probandum," the positive concomitance (*anvaya*), the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), and the positive and negative concomitances along with the property of being a feature of the subject are shown. Furthermore, by the mention of "probandum" in the expression "the proof of the probandum," the conditions of having an unsublated object and not being countered by an opposing argument (*asatpratipakṣatva*) are indicated, because that which is the opposite of these is unfit to be a means of proof.
The author of the Vārttika explains this by means of an example:
"That property which exists in the probandum, such as smoke and so forth, exists in exactly that same way in the example.
It is called an *udāharaṇa* (example) because it is illustrated (*udāhriyate*); it is the subject of the instance (*dṛṣṭāntadharmī*), and not that very [probandum] itself.
Why? Because it is the property of another.
If, then, the property of one thing does not reside in another, how is there similarity?

Since that [similarity] is opposed to being either identical or different, he says: "Rather, it is said to be 'that very same thing' because it is similar to it, just as one says, 'he eats those very same śali rice grains' or 'those very same partridges. By this, the commentary's statement "on account of its similarity" (sāmānyāt) has been explained.
He states the purpose of including the term "example" (udāharaṇa): "If, however...

Since mere similarity (sādharmyamātratva) exists both in the contradictory (viruddha) and the over-exclusive (asādhāraṇa) fallacies as well as in the inconclusive (savyabhicāra), their statements too would constitute a valid reason (hetu).
This is undesirable because they are each, according to their nature, common (sādhāraṇa) [to both the similar and dissimilar instances]. This is the meaning.
[Objection: "But even so, since there is similarity with the example even in the case of the 'deviant' (savyabhicāra), how is that excluded? To this he says: "By the word 'example'.
The meaning is that when a specific rule is prescribed, the exclusion of the remainder is established by implication.
He states another alternative: "Or by means of restriction" (avadhāraṇena).

Since the phrase "due to similarity" (sādharmyāt) implies that by way of this qualification all possible similarities would be obtained, the similarity with the example (udāharaṇasādharmya) is already included; thus, the explicit formulation [of the definition] is purposeless. Being a restrictive exclusion (parisaṃkhyā), it serves only for the sake of determination (avadhāraṇa). To illuminate this, the particle *eva*—in the expression "similarity alone" (sādharmyameva)—should be construed with the word "probandum" (sādhya).
By this, he will dispel the objection that the reason is unestablished with respect to a portion of the probandum.
He asks: "Of what, then? The answer is: "Of what other [thing]?"
Regarding this very point, he states two reasons: "because it is the subject under discussion and because of its proximity.
For here, the probandum (*sādhya*) is indeed the subject under discussion and the primary element, since the constituent members [of the syllogism] proceed with that as their objective.
Since the term "the proof of the probandum" (*sādhyasādhana*) brings [the probandum] into proximity, he clarifies that very second restriction with the words "here too.
He states the meaning of the *Bhāṣya*— "having connected it with the probandum"— with the words "by means of the probandum and the example," and "two."
The meaning is: "pervading the similar instances" (sapakṣa) and "not pervading them.
And "of the inconclusive" (anaikāntika) means:
of both the common (sādhāraṇa) and the uncommon (asādhāraṇa).
"By being cultivated in this way" means by being thoroughly meditated upon. "Not excessively attached" means...
The meaning is that the definition of a fallacious reason (hetvābhāsa) is merely restrictive (parisaṃkhyāyaka), not prescriptive (vidhāyaka).
It is said that the Venerable [Dignāga] refuted this definition of the reason (*hetu*): "If the proof (*sādhana*) is similarity (*sādharmya*), it is not a member of the statement;
for the meaning (*artha*) is not a member of the five-membered syllogistic statement.

Whether there is an absolute non-difference between the proof and the similarity, or some degree of difference by way of the relation of universal and particular, in either case, there is no fifth [member]."
Because [if it were a substance], the nominative case would result from coreferentiality with the means (*sādhana*);
and because, in the case of absolute non-difference, one of the two terms would not be employed.
If, however, it is a sentence, then the ablative case is justified.
For the proof (*sādhana*) consists of the form of a sentence because it arises from the meaning through similarity; therefore,
that [sentence] would be the qualificand (*viśeṣya*),
for it is not the case that the sentence itself arises from the meaning.
But rather, it is also [the speaker's] intention to speak and so forth.
It is not the qualificand; why? Because, being a means of proof, it is impossible [to be the qualificand].
There is also no possibility of [citing] the arising of the object, such as knowledge or the desire to speak, because these are not the means of proof;
for even in that case, there is a twofold fault: is it a means of proof directly or indirectly?

If it is by way of a succession, then the speaker’s cognition would be directly produced from the similarity [of the example], and the reason (*hetu*) would be that which indirectly serves as the means for the listener’s cognition of the probandum (*sādhyavijñāna*).
Alternatively, if it is a direct means, [then...]

In that case, the listener’s cognition, being produced through a causal chain from similarity (*sādharmya*), would be the direct means of proof (*sādhana*) and thus the logical reason (*hetu*). However, in the present context, [the reason] is subject to the possibility of being something else.
If, however, because the five-membered syllogism is the subject under discussion, there is an exclusion of [the reason as] cognition and so forth, [then the following applies].
Nevertheless, there is the possibility of [the reason] occurring elsewhere,
because the application (upanaya) also arises from similarity.
If it is argued that there is sublation by means of the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa), no, because conceptual construction (vikalpa) and so forth are possible.
Therefore, even in that case, the genitive case ending is unnecessary;
one should simply state "the reason is the similarity" (*sādharmya-hetuḥ*).
Now, he sets forth this refutation by Dignāga: "Because of similarity with the example" (*udāharaṇasādharmyāt*).
The meaning is that this constitutes a refutation if it is claimed that the means of proof (*sādhana*) is simply the similarity (*sādharmya*) consisting of the object itself.
However, if, on the other hand, it is claimed that the means of proof is a universal (*sāmānya*) which is the very same objective similarity as the object itself, [then there is no fault].
Regarding this, he says: "Now, however...
This very point was stated by the Venerable One: "The fifth [case] is not [applicable]."
But others explain this otherwise; thus he says, "Others, however.

The intention is that there is no such thing as a universal (sāmānya) apart from the particular (viśeṣa), because the universal is merely a conceptual construction (kalpanāmātra), whereas difference (bheda) has a real entity as its substratum (vastvadhiṣṭhāna).
He states another fault: "sādhyasādhaneti" (regarding the probandum and the probans).

For when the so-called probandum and probans do not exist as something distinct from the similarity of the example (*udāharaṇasādharmya*), but only the mere word remains, then [the probandum] must be qualified by that similarity of the example through its being the denotable object (*abhidheyatva*).

And thus, there is a contradiction with the statement that "the proposition (pratijñā) is the indication of the probandum (sādhya)," for by this [definition], the proposition is characterized as a component (avayava) consisting of speech; and a thing becomes a component only in relation to a collection of parts, such as the reason (hetu) and so forth.
Furthermore, a collection consisting of both the denoter and the denoted is not observed;
therefore, because such a collection does not exist, neither of the two can possess the status of being a part.
This has been stated [in the verse]: "nor is it a part of the sentence.
Since this definition has already been refuted by us while explaining it, it does not require another refutation; thus he says: "In that case, however...
It has been explained how, in the proximity of the word *hetu* (reason), the word *sādhana* (means of proof) functions as a synonym for the word *hetu*.

Nor does there follow the contingency of an application (upanaya), because that [application] has as its primary object only the meaning of the nominal stem and thus does not reveal the state of being a reason (hetubhāva).
Here he raises an objection: "Of the similarity" (*sādharmyasya*).

The meaning is that because the similarity—which is the mark (*liṅga*) expressed by terms such as the reason "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*)—is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) and so forth, it requires a qualification in the example; however, this is not the case for the statement of the reason itself, such as "because it is produced," which is expressed by the terms "probandum" (*sādhya*) and "probans" (*sādhana*).
This was stated by the Venerable [Bhadanta]: "In that case as well, the qualification is useless even in the statement"—that is, even in the verbal expression.
He refutes this as follows: "of speech" (vacasaḥ).
Even speech occurs in both ways according to different philosophical systems; for example, for the Mīmāṃsakas, speech is eternal.
According to the Vaiśeṣikas, [sound] is impermanent;
for some, sound is formless (amūrta), while for others, it is material (mūrta).
As they say:
"The wind attains the state of sound."
He says "and it is seen" to show that the particle *iti* indicates the individual distinction of all words.
He states the contradiction with his own conduct by saying "himself," and [he uses the term] "not accepted."
That reason for which no distinct counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is accepted—such as "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) when proving impermanence—is described in that way.

He refutes [the opponent's position] by saying "even that which," referring to what the Venerable One has accepted, namely that there are sixty [reasons]. This is because the application of grammatical case-terminations depends upon the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*).

The state of being related as a *kāraka* (participant in an action) is what must be indicated by implication (*lakṣaṇīya*), because the state of being related is inherently pregnant with the relationship between an action and its factors;
it is not, however, the case that the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) or the ablative of cause (*hetu-pañcamī*) constitutes a *kāraka*-case ending.

In this context, the author of the Commentary has cited a pure statement of the reason—namely, "because it possesses the property of arising"—and, in order to demonstrate that this [reason] arises from similarity with the example (*udāharaṇasādharmya*), he has also shown the example: "it is observed that whatever possesses the property of arising is impermanent."

In that context, the author of the Bhāṣya has cited a pure statement of the reason (*hetu*). Having completed it with the word "proposition" (*pratijñā*), the author of the Vārttika says: "The example.
Here he asks: "But what [is the purpose]?"

Is impermanence the destruction of an existent thing, or its connection with that [destruction]? Both of these are untenable, for there can be no relationship whatsoever between the existent and the non-existent.
Because they do not exist at the same time,

there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇya*) in the statement "therefore sound is impermanent. Furthermore, as for the non-existence of sound after it has come into being, [it would likewise be impossible].
That [non-existence] does not belong to the pot;
for there is no such universal as "the state of non-existence" by which the example would not be deficient in the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*).

Furthermore, no other entity called "similarity" (sādṛśya) distinct from the universal (sāmānya) is observed or accepted. Therefore, the intended meaning is that this "impermanence" (anityatva), which is merely a conceptual construct, is what is to be proven (sādhya). The reply for those of subtle intellect is: that which possesses impermanence is impermanent.
He asks according to his own intention with the word "Now" (*atha*).
He reveals the intention of the respondent with the words "both ends" (*ubhayānta*).

Although it would have been sufficient to say "the future end" (*aparānta*), by using the term "both ends," he demonstrates that the inclusion of the "past end" (*pūrvānta*) shows the absolute proximity of the reason—namely, "having an origin"—which is necessary for its inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).
And being a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) is the state of being a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇatva*), not that of being a primary qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*).
And this is possible for the "other end" (*aparānta*), which, although existing at a different time and though connected [to the action], resides in the intellect by way of opposition.
And thus, whatever existence belongs to a pot delimited by its posterior limit (the moment of destruction), that very same existence belongs to sound delimited by its posterior limit as well.
Likewise, the inherence of existence is also common to both that pot and that sound.

Furthermore, the state of being contradictory and the state of occurring subsequently are the specific characteristics of destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) as distinguished from mere non-existence (*abhāvamātra*).
He asks: "Now, regarding 'origination'...

First of all, origination is not a property (*dharma*) of that which has already originated, because it would entail the logical consequence of [repeatedly] applying the suffix *-ti* (i.e., the notion that "it originates again").
Nor can that which is unarisen and non-existent possess the status of a subject (*dharmin*); such is the intended meaning.
To one of hidden intelligence, the answer is given: "Arising.
Then, intending the aforementioned point, he asks again: "What, then, is this [arising]?"

The reply: The negation of the absolute non-existence of an existent qualified by "non-existent" means that the term "non-existent" expresses prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), and the status of being a qualifier for prior non-existence is merely figurative (*upalakṣaṇatva*).
And that [status] is stated even for something belonging to a different time, simply by virtue of its presence in the intellect.

By the phrase "of that which exists as qualified by non-existence," merely through this much, the connection with existence—or existence itself—is shown for that which was previously delimited by its prior limit; or rather, its arising is indicated as its qualification.
Furthermore, its nature is stated in order to characterize its arising: such a thing, like space, does not have absolute possibility, nor, like a sky-flower, does it have absolute non-existence.
Furthermore, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) and the indicated (*upalakṣya*) because of the intended non-difference between them.
Nor does it follow that the notion "it is arising" would apply to an entity that has already attained its arising;

for in common worldly usage, this term is seen to be applied to the parts of that [entity] which are currently undergoing arising—parts that possess a temporal sequence (prior and posterior) acquired through the penetration of an activity conducive to their production.

Therefore, by means of the existence of a thing delimited by its prior limit, or by a relation thereto, either the existence of that very same thing delimited by its subsequent limit, or a relation thereto, is made known; thus everything is satisfactory. But surely the author of the Bhāṣya will explain "origination" as the meaning of the sentence "having not been, it comes to be," whereas you, however, explain origination as the meaning of the sentence "the absolute negation of the non-existence of an existent qualified by non-existence."
Therefore, as to why there is no contradiction, he says: "The meaning of the sentence" (*vākyārtha*).
That very same meaning which was accepted and admitted by the author of the *Bhāṣya* as the meaning of the word "origination" (*utpatti*) is the very one we also accept.

The meaning is that origination is not the negation of an absolute non-existence; rather, it has been stated that it is either the existence of that which already exists as a particularized entity, or its connection with that [existence]. //34//
Likewise, [the same applies] by way of dissimilarity.
He introduces another sutra: "Is it merely this much?

and likewise: "T //35 //" Here, if it were said that [the reason] is "due to dissimilarity" (*vaidharmya*), then when "horseness" is being proved by means of "hornedness" by taking all things possessing manes and so forth as the subject (*pakṣa*), the reason would possess dissimilarity with the subject; therefore, he says: "Dissimilarity by way of the example."
The meaning is "by way of the counter-example" (*vipakṣa*).

Nevertheless, when one takes the mere body as the subject (*pakṣa*) and proves its possession of a self (*sātmakatva*) by means of its having breath and so forth, then that [reason] would also be a valid reason because it possesses dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) with the example; therefore, he says "even so" (*evam api*).
Nor does this entail the presence [of the reason] in the similar instances (sapakṣa), because there is no similar instance;
and because the restriction is justified by its pervasion with existence in the subject (pakṣa).

Nevertheless, there would be an inclusion of the inconclusive (anaikāntika) reason that possesses both positive and negative concomitance (anvayavyatirekin), which pervades only a portion of the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa).

For example: "Sound is impermanent because it has the property of being produced" and "Sound is impermanent because it is corporeal. To this he says: "And by means of the example of dissimilarity alone"—the meaning is "by means of the example of the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa)."
He presents the example given by the author of the Bhāṣya: "Sound is non-eternal.
The construction is: "That which is eternal is observed to have the property of being unproduced."
He refutes this with the words "And this...

[etacceti]. One might argue that even if there is no difference based on a mere difference in formulation (*prayoga*), there will be a difference based on a difference in the example (*udāharaṇa*); therefore, he says: "And because of a mere difference in the example."
Having refuted this example provided by the author of the Bhāṣya, he states his own example: "But the example," and so forth.

By means of "breath" (prāṇa) and the rest, he indicates its own causes, such as effort (prayatna) and desire (icchā)—the construction being applied in reverse order as follows: "Whatever is admitted by both parties to be soulless, such as a jar and the like, all that is observed to be devoid of breath and the rest."

The meaning is that it is devoid of causes such as vital breath (prāṇa) and causes such as desire (icchā). Therefore, "this is not [that]" means it is not devoid of the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) of desire and so forth.
The meaning is that that which is the inherent cause of desire and so forth, distinct from earth and the other [elements], and the ninth among substances, is called the "self" (ātman).

He shows that this positive-negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) and its distinction [from others] possess the status of being well-known in another system by using the name established in that other system: "this is the avīta."
That which has been reached from here in various ways is *vīta*;
since it pervades the subject (*pakṣa*), it is either pervasive or non-pervasive with respect to the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).
Therefore, that which is other than this is *avīta*.
With a hidden intention, he asks: "But how [is this]?
The answer from one with a hidden intention is: "Now, that which is admitted...
The meaning is that just as the *vīta* (direct) syllogism possesses the capacity to determine an object, so too does the *avīta* (indirect) syllogism.
The questioner reveals his own intention with the word "from positive concomitance" (*anvayāt*).

For a reason (*hetu*) that has grasped its inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) with the property to be proven (*sādhya*) is the determiner of that [property]; and that inseparable connection is observed only when the presence of both the reason and the property to be proven is seen in the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmī*).
Furthermore, possession of a self (sātmakatva) is not observed anywhere;
therefore, how could there be an observation of the inseparable connection (avinābhāva) of the state of possessing breath and so forth with that?
Or, if such an observation were made, it would not be *avīta*, but rather *vīta*—this is the meaning.
The respondent asks the questioner: "Now, what about 'knowability'?
The questioner says: "Because of deviation. The respondent says: "In that case, there is no positive concomitance (anvaya)."
He states this very point in a single sentence: "If [it is argued]...
Thus, the respondent has revealed his own intention.
He asks: "How?"
Regarding the non-deviation of the negative-only (vyatirekin) inference, he states its non-deviation with the words "as far as" (*yāvat*).
Here too, the construction is to be applied by transposition: "As far as something is soulless (*nirātmaka*), all that is observed to be devoid of breath and so forth."
Because the opposite of the probandum is pervaded [by the absence of the reason],
and when the pervader ceases, the pervaded also ceases—
just as the state of being a *śiṃśapā* ceases when the state of being a tree ceases— from a mountain region consisting of a single rock that is perceived from afar; such is the meaning.

If, however, it is argued as follows: "Let the lack of validity and so forth [of the reason] be withdrawn, since the possession of breath and so forth is perceived through valid means (*pramāṇa*) in the living body; let 'selflessness' (*nairātmya*) not be withdrawn. Therefore, because of this deviation (*vyabhicāra*), it is not a valid reason"—this is the objection introduced by the words "if, however" (*atha punar*).
He refutes it with the words "it is not right to say thus."
When the living body is the subject of proof, is there a deviation (vyabhicāra) due to the certainty of selflessness (nairātmya), or due to doubt regarding it?
If it is due to certainty,
what is the use of citing a case of deviation?
The meaning is that since the reason is refuted precisely by the fact that its object is sublated,
if it were instead [refuted] due to doubt, then even a positive (anvayin) reason would not be a valid reason, which would entail the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of all inference.
He raises an objection: "If it is argued that this leads to the undesirable consequence [of everything] being of the nature of all things?
He refutes it: "No, because an alternative [explanation] is untenable."
He analyzes the statement expressing doubt with the words "If... [yadīti]:
First of all, this so-called self (ātman) has not been perceived anywhere by means of a valid means of cognition (pramāṇa), such that its negation could be understood as selflessness (nairātmya).
Or, if that [self] were perceived, what would be the use of this fallacious construction?
Therefore, having postulated a self that lacks any basis in valid cognition, one must grasp the pervasion of its negation by the absence of breath and so forth in objects such as jars;
then, through the cessation of the pervader—the absence of breath and so forth—in a living body, the cessation of the pervaded—selflessness—is established, whereby the self is understood.
And this being the case, since the treasury of conceptual constructions (*kalpanā*) is immeasurable, whatever is imagined is easily found to be absent in things such as a jar;

thus, because non-possession of breath and so forth is pervaded [by the absence of a self], the cessation of that pervader—non-possession of breath and so forth—in a living body would entail the presence of a self, just as it entails the presence of all imagined entities such as *Ḍittha* and others at all times. This is the meaning.
He analyzes the refuting statement: "And that is not so.
Why? Because an alternative is untenable.
He proposes the alternatives: "What [is it]?"
This is the meaning:
since the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth exist or do not exist in accordance with the presence or absence of desire and the like, they are effects of desire and the like;
and since it is established that these are non-momentary, an effect must depend upon an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), and thus there must be an inherent cause for desire and the like.
Because it is an effect, like a jar;

and since the status of being an inherent cause has been denied to the body, the sense organs, and so forth, that substance which remains as the inherent cause of desire and the rest is designated as the *ātman*, the *kṣetrajña*, and the *jīva*.

Therefore, even though this [soul] is not specifically understood, since it has been determined in its general form as the inherent cause of desire and so forth, its absence in objects such as jars—which are devoid of breath and the like—is capable of being apprehended.
This very same meaning is also expressed by the term "soulless" (*nirātmaka*).

By means of this absence of the effect characterized by breath and so forth, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the absence of the cause characterized by soullessness in the jar and other such things is established.

Thus, since this absence of the effect in a living body, as a pervader, upon its own cessation, ceases by taking with it the absence of its cause which is pervaded by it, it is established that there is a cause of breath in the living body, and that is the self (*ātman*).
And if persons such as Ḍittha and others are also of such a nature, [then they too must possess that cause].
At that time, the other names of the self do not signify different entities;
for names are dependent upon worldly convention, not dependent upon one's own will.
"Avadhāritakāryaḥ" refers to one for whom the effects—such as desire and the like—are determined to be characterized by the vital breaths (prāṇas) and so forth;
"sa eva svabhāvaḥ" means that he has that very [nature] as his essential character. This is what is meant.

In general, first of all, by means of the reason consisting of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—namely, that desire and so forth are effects—it is inferred that they possess an inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*).
Furthermore, the absence of a cause for desire and so forth in things such as jars is established for both parties.

For even those who advocate the doctrine of selflessness (*nairātmyavādin*), whether they assert that cognition (*buddhi*) or the non-difference of the elements (*bhūta-prakṛti*) is the cause of desire and so forth, [admit this absence].
They, too, do not maintain that [selfhood] exists in jars and the like.
Therefore, jars and so forth are established for both parties as being devoid of self (nairātmya).
And since the absence of effects such as desire is pervaded by selflessness in those cases, [the argument holds].
Thus, this absence of the effect in a living body, by its own exclusion, excludes the absence of the cause.
And why should the cause not be inferred from the effect itself in a living body; what is the use of a negative inference (vyatirekin)?
It must be said that one who is being accomplished by way of the straight path—who indeed would accomplish him by a crooked path?
For it has been stated that [the effect] is established from the mere cause.
If it is argued that the specific [cause] is established by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*)?
It has been stated that this very [reason] is the one characterized by negative concomitance (vyatirekin).
For if desire and the like were to have earth and so forth as their inherent causes (samavāyikāraṇa), they would necessarily follow [as being present] even in jars and the like.

Therefore, since the absence of effects such as desire in jars and the like is seen to be pervaded by the absence of a cause distinct from the eight substances, [it follows that] desire and the like [must have such a distinct cause].
Observed in the body, these qualities, by negating their own pervasion, establish a ninth substance through the negation of any cause other than the eight pervasive substances;
nor is cognition itself their inherent cause.
Because it is a fixed rule that only a substance (*dravya*) can be an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), and because cognition (*buddhi*) is not a substance;
and just as the specific transformation of the elements (*bhūta*) is not the cause, so too will be demonstrated in the third [chapter].

If it is argued that, since the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with a self is established through the example of a house and so forth by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), this is not a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*).

We do not deny that there is an essential connection (*svābhāvikapratibandha*) with the probandum in the case of a reason possessing both positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatirekin*); rather, we refute its connection by way of affirmation due to the absence of similar instances (*sapakṣa*).
It is precisely for this much that it differs from the purely positive (*anvayin*) reason.
Furthermore, the subject (*pakṣa*) itself is not the similar instance (*sapakṣa*),

because that which has its specific property sought to be known is distinct from that which already possesses that specific property. Moreover, in the case of bodies and so forth, the very negation of selflessness constitutes the existence of a self.
Because the negation of a non-existent thing is characterized by the existence [of its opposite],
and because the absence of a similar instance (*sapakṣa*) cannot even be designated by "selflessness" (*nairātmya*), how could it be designated by the negation of selflessness?
For it has been stated that what is non-existent cannot function as a locus (*adhikaraṇa*).
By this, that which has been stated by others is refuted: "If the reason were non-deviating from the similar class (sapakṣa), it would therefore be positive (anvayin);
if it were neither positive nor negative, then [the argument] 'that which is without self is not possessed of a self' [would fail]."
Thus, this has been refuted by the aforementioned;
and this has been made clear by us through the establishment of the positive concomitant reason (*anvayihetu*).
Therefore, everything is perfectly clear.
Thinking that the negative-only (vyatirekin) [reason] possesses probative force merely by virtue of its exclusion from the counter-example, he objects: "If, then...
He replies: "No, because of a failure to understand the meaning of the reason."
The capacity to prove [a conclusion] does not reside in mere dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*),
but rather in that which is non-deviant (*avyabhicārin*); the meaning here is that such non-deviance is absent in this case.

One might object: "Let it be granted that 'possessing odor' is not a valid reason because it deviates in its negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*), since, like 'non-eternal' and so forth, it is absent from eternal things as well; however, in this case, [the property] exists only in the subject (*pakṣa*) and not in either the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) or the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*). Since there is no deviation in its negative concomitance for that [reason], why is it not a valid reason? Thus he raises the objection with the words: "But as for that which... (*yaḥ punar iti*).
He refutes this, saying: "True.
A property of exclusion (*vyatirekadharma*) cannot exist in the absence of exclusion, because it has already been stated that what is non-existent cannot function as a locus (*adhikaraṇa*).
He shows another counter-example with the words "by this" (*etena*). This means:

by this [fact], namely, due to the absence of exclusion from that [subject] because of the non-existence of a dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*). He raises an objection with the words: "that which is a part of the subject" (*pakṣaikadeśa*).

For if a reason that subsists in only a portion of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśavṛtti*) were not a negative reason (*vyatirekin*) due to the absence of a counter-example (*vipakṣa*), then it would follow that even a reason subsisting in only a portion of the subject could be a [valid] reason, provided it possesses exclusion from the counter-example (*vipakṣanivṛtti*).
The intended meaning is that its very dissimilarity to the example (*udāharaṇavaidharmya*) indeed constitutes the definition of a negative reason.
He refutes it: "This too is not a valid reason; why?
Because it is contradicted by the meaning of the Sūtra.
He demonstrates this by first citing the reading of the Sūtra, saying: "The meaning of the Sūtra..."
And here, that which excludes the fallacious negative-only (vyatirekin) reason—namely, one that subsists in only a portion of the subject—is shown first by the restriction [of the definition].
It is stated that "the dissimilarity is by the example alone, not by the non-example nor even by the subject";
however, for this [other type], it is said "even by the subject," meaning that even a negative-only reason is not a valid logical mark (*hetu*).
The meaning of the Sūtra, however, is not that it refers exclusively to dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).

For if that were the case, there would be the exclusion of all merely erratic reasons (*savyabhicāra*), but not of those that subsist in only a portion of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśavṛtti*); such is the sense.
Now he introduces the definition of the reason (*hetu*) according to Vāsubandhu in order to refute it: "Others [hold] that the reason is a distinction from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*).
He explains this with the words "others, however," and "in the refutation of mere similarity."
Regarding the refutation of any similarity whatsoever:
first, in the refutation of similarity with the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), there is the inclusion of what is intended;
however, when there is a refutation of similarity with the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and so forth, [the same applies].
Then, there is the inclusion of the undesirable, the contradictory, and so forth;
and this is an illustration,
meaning the inclusion of both the desirable and the undesirable.
It should also be understood as the "renunciation of what is desired," and that [renunciation] has many subdivisions;
for even when there is a distinction from the similar class (*sapakṣa*), there is also a distinction from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*).

Even when there is a distinction from the similar class (*pakṣa*), there are two possible modes: either a distinction from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) or a distinction from the dissimilar class alone.
Among these, in the case of the first two modes, there would follow, respectively, the fallacy of the reason being either "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) or "unestablished" (*asiddha*).
In order to exclude that [misconception], it is restricted by the words "only from the counter-example" (*vipakṣād eva*).
To introduce the second restriction, he says: "And regarding the restriction.
By this restriction, "only from the counter-example," the specific qualification is established.
It is not the case that it is non-opposite (*avipakṣa*).

Since this [reason] extends to both the specific and the non-specific, there would follow the undesirable consequence that even a reason which exists in only a portion of the opposite class (*vipakṣaikadeśavṛtti*)—provided it is common to both the subject (*pakṣa*) and similar instances (*sapakṣa*)—would be a valid reason.
To exclude that, the second restriction is stated: "only the specific" (*viśeṣa eva*).
He summarizes: "Thus, in this way."

He refutes that very [reason] by way of its being non-pervasive: "It is true that it is one," and so forth. Here he raises an objection: "Because of the exclusion of [the reason] residing in only a portion of the counter-example.
By the restriction "only a specific [property]," the [fallacy of] residing in only a portion of the counter-example—such as the reason "this is a cow because it has horns"—is excluded.

Therefore, since this restriction [of the definition] must hold true, it is precisely the restriction "only from the dissimilar instance" (*vipakṣāt eva*) that must be established. And thus, it is stated that only that which is a unique property (*viśeṣa*) of the dissimilar instance alone is the logical reason (*hetu*); whereas that which is a unique property of the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) is not a logical reason.
Just as the argument "this is a horse because it has horns" is refuted as a reason because it is a specific property (viśeṣa) of the similar instances (sapakṣa),

that which exists in only a portion of the similar instances— such as "being produced immediately after an effort"— is not merely a specific property of the similar instances, but is also a general property (sāmānya).
The meaning is that its status as a non-reason has not been established; therefore, it is indeed a reason. He refutes this with the words "If this were so.

If even that which is a specific property of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), such as "being produced immediately after effort," were a reason residing in only a portion of the similar instances, [then the definition would be too broad].

This being the case, the restriction "only from the dissimilar instances" (*vipakṣād eva*) would be contradicted. He raises an objection with "Now [if]... (*atha*). It is not merely this much that is restricted—namely, "only from the dissimilar instances"—such that a reason like "being produced by effort" (*prayatnāntarīyakatva*), which exists in only a portion of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), would fail to be a valid reason.
However, when it is argued that "only that which is a specific property (viśeṣa) is the reason," it is restricted by the rule "only from the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa).

By this, the status of being a reason for a specific property that is accompanied by such a restriction and yet occurs in the dissimilar instances is negated; for example: "This is a horse, because it has horns.
On the other hand, that which is both a specific and a non-specific property in the similar instances (sapakṣa) is a reason.
Even though it is its cause, it is not invalidated by the restriction "only from the dissimilar instances" (vipakṣāt eva).

And although, even in this case, the status of being a logical reason (hetutva) for that which occurs in only a portion of the similar instances (sapakṣaikadeśavṛtti) is not explicitly heard [in the definition],
nevertheless, because it is not prohibited by the restrictive phrase "only from the dissimilar instances," it is indeed accepted.
And by that meaning which has not been heard, [the word] becomes meaningful; the sense is that it serves as a restriction (avadhāraṇa).
He refutes this with the words "and thus":

just as the status of being a reason (hetutva) for that which subsists in only one part of what is similar [to the subject] is accepted by implication because it is not prohibited, so too would it be for that which subsists in only one part of the subject (pakṣaikadeśavṛtti); the meaning is that such a thing would also be a valid reason.
He objects again: "This is not a fault.

The meaning is: when there is the restriction that, given the presence of the property in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), the [reason] must reside in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) alone and exclude the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) alone, how could there be the possibility of it residing in only a portion of the subject?
For that [reason] would then lack the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*apakṣadharmatva*).
He refutes [the objection] with the words, "by the phrase 'that property which belongs to the subject'.
The opponent says, "It need not be so.
To refute this, he analyzes the restrictive emphasis by asking, "But what then?"

He first adopts the first alternative—"let it be so"—and then refutes even this by means of a dilemma: "But what [is the purpose] of this? In the view that the connection between capacity and purpose is for the sake of making known a possibility, the purpose is the cessation of non-knowing.

In the case of the position that [the term] excludes what is impossible (*asaṃbhavanivṛtti*), the result is the exclusion of absolute non-connection (*atyantāyogavyāvṛtti*), as in "the lotus is indeed blue. He refutes this by considering both cases, stating: "in either way... (*ubhayathāpi*).
He states another argument with the words "And not...
The meaning is that absolute non-connection is what is negated, but not mere non-connection.
He raises an objection with "Now [if...
(*atha*). For the particle *eva* (only/just), when conjoined with a qualifier, excludes non-connection (*ayoga-vyavaccheda*), as in the example: "Caitra is indeed an archer."
If the reason (*hetu*) is a qualification, then it is indeed not a property of the subject (*apakṣadharma*).
Therefore, the meaning is that the exclusion [of the reason] from occurring in only a part of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśavṛtti*) is established.
He refutes this, saying: "True."
The remainder has already been largely explained in the Sūtra on Inference (Anumāna-sūtra), and thus it is not explained here.

And when [the definition] "the reason is that which is distinguished from the counter-example (vipakṣa)" refers to the Sautrāntika position, then, since the definition is being examined with respect to the subject (lakṣya) in the case of the reason "impermanence," the meaning of the term "counter-example" must be stated. Now, one might object: "But isn't the 'eternal' the counter-example? To this he says: "For it is not [the case that the reason exists] in what is non-existent."
The meaning is that what is devoid of any designation cannot be designated.

Nor can it possess the status of an ablative (*apādāna*) or the status of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), such that either the fifth (*pañcamī*) or seventh (*saptamī*) case-ending would be employed; thus he says, "And not being non-existent...

Furthermore, since there is an absence of exclusion from a non-existent counter-example (*vipakṣa*), there is no distinction [between the two]; thus he says, "And when the counter-example is impossible..."

Regarding the phrase "of the subject alone" (*pakṣasyaiva*): here, the three instances of the particle *eva* indicate independence from other words. If the definition of a reason were simply "a property of the subject alone," then the reason would necessarily be only the "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) one.

If [the definition] were "that which is established only in the similar" (*samāna*), then in the case where "having horns" is to be proven of a horse, the property of "being a cow" and so forth would become a valid reason (*hetu*).

Therefore, these three positions regarding the subject (*pakṣa*) must be rejected. Furthermore, if [the definition were] "a property of the subject that is established in the similar," then a reason that is inconclusive (*savyabhicāra*) would become a valid reason.

If [the definition were] "a property of the subject (pakṣadharma) that does not exist in the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa)," then the inconclusive reason (asādhāraṇahetu) would be a valid reason. And if [it were] "established in the similar instance (samāna) and not existing in the dissimilar instance," then the reason "atoms are impermanent because they are produced" would be a valid reason. Thus, there are three [possible faults].
He states the intended seventh [definition]: "of the subject" (pakṣasya).
The remainder is easily understood.

In this regard, Dignāga [states]: "The property of the subject (pakṣadharma) exists in three ways—being present in the similar class (sapakṣa), being absent, or both; furthermore, each of these is again threefold due to the two possibilities of being present or absent in the dissimilar class (asapakṣa)."

Thus, having shown the nine types of properties of the subject (*pakṣadharma*)—which include both valid reasons and fallacious reasons—it is said: "That which exists in the subject, exists in the similar class (*sajātīya*), and is absent in its absence (*tadatyaya*), is a valid reason (*hetu*). That which is the opposite of this is the contradictory (*viruddha*); the others are determined to be inconclusive."
By this, the distinction between the valid reason (*hetu*) and its fallacious counterpart (*tadābhāsa*) has been shown.
Its meaning is as follows:
that which is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is threefold—being present in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), being absent from them, or both.
Furthermore, because it exists or does not exist in two ways within the dissimilar class (*asapakṣa*), each [of these] becomes threefold.

A property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) that exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) is threefold due to its existence or non-existence in two ways within the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*). A property of the subject that does not exist in the similar class is threefold due to its existence or non-existence in two ways within the dissimilar class.

The property of the subject (pakṣadharma) is threefold because it exists in two ways in the similar class (sapakṣa) and has a twofold status—both existing and non-existing—in the dissimilar class (vipakṣa).
An illustration of this is:
[the properties] being an object of cognition, being produced, being impermanent, being created, being audible, and being born of effort.
Those nine [types of] contact, which arise from impermanent effort, [are applied] to the [objects] beginning with permanence.
