When permanence and so forth are the properties to be proven (*sādhya*), there are nine reasons (*hetu*) and pseudo-reasons (*tadābhāsa*), such as "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and others.
They cite the respective properties to be proven for these, in their proper order, as follows: permanence, impermanence, produced by effort, the middle triad, and eternity.
And [the properties] of being effortless, impermanent, and permanent are [also] proofs for [the existence of God], such as through the property of being knowable and so forth.
Thus, having presented that by which the reason is determined among these reasons and fallacious reasons, the author of the Vārttika explains it with the words "tatra yaḥ" (therein, that which...).
He refutes this with the words "yathāśruti" (according to the literal hearing).
The meaning is that [the definition] is not obtained from merely the statement: "that which exists in the similar class and is of two kinds in its absence."
He objects: "But has it not been said? This was stated by Dignāga:
"Since the property to be proven [is the reason], the reasons and their fallacies are for the most part [based upon it]."
He addresses this [objection] as follows: "This has already been stated.
The meaning is that it is not the case that [the reason] must be a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) alone;
yet, failing to understand this restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), he raises a doubt: "But even so..."
Since the intended restrictive sense is not obtained, he provides the answer: "True, [it follows] from the meaning.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that the pervasion of the subject (*pakṣavyāpakatva*) is understood precisely through the exclusion of the mark's non-residence in the subject (*apakṣadharmatvanivṛtti*), for that which possesses the mere exclusion of non-residence in the subject cannot be non-pervasive? To this he replies: "And by the mere fact of the exclusion of non-residence in the subject..."

The meaning is that by the negation of absolute cessation, there would be mere activity, not an exclusive activity. He raises an objection: "It has not been reached. He replies: "Not so, because of the restriction."

The meaning is that you maintain the restriction [of the word "only"] for the purpose of making known the rule that only the reason and the fallacious reason are properties of the subject (pakṣadharma), and nothing else.
He raises an objection: "Now, [if it is] both...
He refutes it: "Even so, that which exists is of the same class.
This has already been explained for the most part previously.
"In both ways, it should not be stated" means that whether one accepts or does not accept [the definition] "existent and of the same class.
As for what was said, that "existent and of the same class" should not be accepted:
In this regard, he raises an objection: "Now, one might think...
He refutes it: "...the restriction.
If a restriction were appropriate, then an undertaking for the purpose of restriction would be justified.
The meaning is that this very [position] is incorrect.
Regarding the phrase "in the first word":
the meaning is in the word "only" (*eva*) within the expression "the property of the subject alone" (*pakṣasya dharma eva*).
Regarding the phrase "in the case of other [terms]": those two, namely the presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and the absence from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣāsattva*),
are so described because their twofold nature is being refuted therein.
"Existing in the similar class" (*san sajātīye*) means "in every respect" (*sarvathā*).
The meaning is that whether the words "and in two ways in the similar class" (*sajātīye dvedhā ca*) are employed or not employed.

By the phrase "only in the similar class in two ways," the intended meaning is that the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) remains established as the general rule for both the valid reason (*hetu*) and its fallacy (*tadābhāsa*).
He raises an objection: "Now, let it not be so"—the meaning is that there is no restriction that [the object] must be of the same class (*sajātīya*) and twofold (*dvidhā*).
He refutes this: "Even so" (*tathāpi*).
The meaning is that [the term] "twofold" (*dvidhā*) applies to the middle member of the compound *san sajātīye dvidhā*.
Thus, the restriction that [the two types] exist only among those of the same class has been refuted. Now, he raises the second restriction with the words "But if...
and refutes it with "Even so..."
Nevertheless, it follows that even a reason (hetu) that exists in only one part of the subject (pakṣaikadeśavṛtti) would be admissible;
furthermore, if it were not restricted by the condition "only upon the passing away of that," then even an inconclusive (anaikāntika) reason would become valid—this is the fault.
Dignāga’s own definition of the characteristic of a reason in another passage states: "The property of the subject (pakṣadharma) is the property of the object of apprehension;
the reason is that which is pervaded by a portion of that very subject—that is, by the generality of the property to be proven (sādhyadharma)."
Having thus set forth this definition of the reason (*hetu*), he extends the previously mentioned fault to it by saying "by this" (*etena*).
He clarifies that extension itself by saying "non-pervasive, etc. (*avyāpakādi*):
according to the definition as it was heard [literally], even that which does not pervade the subject (*pakṣa*) would be a reason.

By examining the explanation of the phrase "pervaded by a portion of that," the meaning is that [the reason] exists in the similar instances (sapakṣa) and is excluded from the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa).
And thus, the previously mentioned fault follows as a consequence; this is the meaning.
He refutes [this] according to the "lion's glance" (siṃhāvalokita) method: "asaṃstadatyaya iti."
He introduces [the following] to refute the definition of causality held by others, beginning with the words "tādṛg" (such).
He explains this very point with the words "tādṛśa" (of such a kind).
The particle "kila" is used here to express disapproval.
The term "property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*) is a designation for the reason (*hetu*). By this, the meaning is that the reason is one whose nature is manifested by the three characteristics.
He refutes [this] with the words: "That, first of all... (*tat tāvad iti*).
The phrase "even [the reason] such as being audible" means that it has been stated to be an uncommon (asādhāraṇa) [reason]. However,

in the case of that which possesses such an inseparable connection (avinābhāvin), because its existence in the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa) is negated, its existence in the similar instance (sapakṣa) is indeed understood.
If one should think that a specific prohibition has as its scope the permission of the remainder, he says in response: "Let it be for now.
The intention is that since a specific prohibition is logically consistent even when only a portion is permitted, there is no evidence for the permission of everything without exception.
He objects: "But surely [it follows] from the mention of 'demonstration'. He replies: "That is not obtained," for there is no such thing as "being visible to the eye" [in that sense].
The meaning is that for Buddhists, since there is no eternal universal such as "color-ness" (*rūpatva*), visual perceptibility does not occur without impermanence.

However, one might think that because the exclusion of a specific [alternative] implies the admission of the remaining possibility, and because no specific [alternative] is being grasped, the existence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣasattā*) is admitted;
thus, by the word "demonstration," the existence of the reason in the subject is demonstrated. To such a person, he says, "Or, having admitted... (*upetya vā*).
This is easily understood.
Having thus refuted that definition, he refutes its illustration with the words "As for this... The meaning is: regarding this definition of the reason (*hetu*).
Is "being immediately subsequent to effort" (i.e., having effort as its cause) direct or indirect?
Regarding that, he states the refutation of the first alternative with the words "of being immediately subsequent to effort.
Anticipating the second alternative, he refutes it with the word "atha" (now/if).
The meaning is that the mention of "effort" is purposeless.
He refutes [the opponent's position] by analyzing what is expressed by the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), beginning with "And as for this...
[and so on]. Even so, it is due to perception alone;
for in the system of the Knower (*boddhṛ*), there is nothing whatsoever that is perceived which is eternal.
The intention is that by means of this, perception (*upalabdhi*) would be distinguished.
Regarding the phrase "immediately after effort" (*prayatnānantaram*) and "otherwise" (*anyathā*):
the meaning is that whatever is the object of perception, all of that is perceived only through effort—that is, from human activity—and not otherwise.
He raises an objection with "Now [if it be argued]...";
the sense is: "for us Naiyāyikas. He provides the answer with "By you yourself..."

The meaning is that even if you, as a Buddhist, speak while relying upon our own [Mīmāṃsaka] view, the fallacy of inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva) remains exactly as it was, despite the inclusion of the term "effort" (prayatna).
Furthermore, [the reason] is non-pervasive (avyāpaka).
The meaning is that the *ṭhātkāra* sound produced by the splitting of bamboo leaves when struck by a forest fire is not the result of the effort of persons such as ourselves.
He raises an objection with "Now [if it be argued]... (*atheti*), meaning that [the sound] consists of phonemes (*varṇa*). He refutes this with "Even in that case" (*tatrāpi*).
Even through a traditional sequence, only the first sound is produced immediately following the effort,
not the second and subsequent ones;
however, if one were to rely on an excessively remote sequence, it would lead to an over-extension of the principle.
The sense is that this is because it is generally easy to find [the reason] here and there. He raises an objection with the words "Now, as for that which...
The distinction (*viśeṣa*)—namely, being produced immediately after an effort—is a qualification of the subject (*dharmin*).
The meaning is that "being produced immediately after an effort" and "generality" (*sāmānya*) are the logical reason (*hetu*).
He refutes this with the words: "Even so, it is something else.
For you [the Vaiśeṣikas] do not have a real entity called "generality" existing apart from the particular (*viśeṣa*), like we [Buddhists] do, which could serve as the reason.
The meaning is that what is superimposed by conceptual construction cannot be the cause of right knowledge, nor is even conceptual construction possible for that which is absolutely non-existent.
Having thus refuted that example, he refutes by extension the opponents’ analysis of examples with the words "as for what was also said.
The meaning is: that [non-entity] is indeed non-existent, devoid of all causal capacity, and does not possess the properties of being dependent or independent, or having existence or non-existence;
however, something eternal does exist.
The connection with dharma is indeed possible for him;
however, even for him, "not being immediately subsequent to effort" is not what is denoted by the suffix -tva, for birth is what is expressed by that suffix,
and that [birth] must be qualified either by effort or by something other than effort.
But for that which has no birth at all, that qualification is cast far away; this is the meaning. By this, non-existence (abhāva) as it is conceived by the Naiyāyikas is also explained.

For even in that case, since there is no birth—meaning that what was previously non-existent has no connection (*samavāya*) with its own cause—the application of those qualifiers is impossible; this is the meaning.
He concludes the subject under discussion: "Thus, in this way" (verse 35).
NyS 1.1.36: An example (udāharaṇa) is an instance which, by virtue of its similarity to the subject of proof (sādhya), possesses the properties of that [subject].
When the reason (*hetu*) has been stated, it does not remain established as a reason unless it is pervaded by the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*);

and since the demonstration of this pervasion (*vyāpti*) cannot occur without an example (*udāharaṇa*), he states the definition of the example, which follows in sequence immediately after the definition of the reason: "The example... (36).
It has been shown that by this [definition], the general definition of an example (*udāharaṇa*)—namely, "it is a sūtra"—is also indicated.
He states the intended meaning of this: "of this," etc.;
for an example in the form of an object (*artharūpa*) cannot constitute the essential definition of an example in the form of a verbal expression (*vacanātmaka*).

Therefore, with the intention that [the example] possesses the character of a definition and the property of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) by virtue of indicating its own designating statement, it is said: "the indication of the example.
By this, the example is distinguished from similar items such as the thesis (*pratijñā*) and so forth, as well as from dissimilar items such as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth.
The commentary states: "similarity with the probandum," and so on.
Its meaning is as follows:
there is a similarity of the example, such as a cooking pot and so forth, with the subject (*dharmin*) to be proven, namely "sound."
The property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is the logical reason (*hetu*).
For it is common to both the sound to be proven as impermanent and the example, such as a cooking pot;
therefore, by virtue of that causal factor which acts as the motivator, [the conclusion follows].
"Belonging to that property" (*taddharmabhāvī*) means: whatever other property belongs to that very sound which is the subject of proof (*sādhya*),
by which the sound is intended to be qualified as impermanent—
that impermanence is "that property" (*taddharma*).
That very state is "tadbhāva. One who possesses that is "taddharmabhāvī," meaning, for instance, that a pot or similar object possesses the property of impermanence.
Therefore, an example (*udāharaṇa*) is a statement concerning that [subject] which is characterized by such an illustration.
In this regard, the author of the *Vārttika*, while explaining the words of the *Sūtra*, effectively explains the *Bhāṣya* as well: "The probandum," etc.

He also applies the explanation of the phrase "due to similarity with the example" (*udāharaṇasādharmyāt*) to the expression "due to similarity with the probandum" (*sādhyasādharmyāt*), stating: "In this case too," etc.
By the word "probandum" (*sādhya*) itself, the similarity of the example consists in its being produced (*kṛtakatva*).
It is not by means of an unprovable counter-example (*vipakṣa*) such as space (*ākāśa*) or other eternal things, for from those [examples] "the state of being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is excluded;
and thus, that which is "erroneous" (*savyabhicāra*) is excluded.

The phrase "only similarity" (sādharmyam eva) excludes the fallacy of partial non-establishment (bhāgāsiddha). For that which possesses the existence of real properties due to its similarity to the probandum (sādhya) is this example (dṛṣṭānta), namely the illustration (udāharaṇa).
Before the sentence is finished, he asks—while it is still only half-spoken—"From what?

The point is that since the example possesses a twofold restriction—namely, that by virtue of its similarity to the probandum (sādhya-sādharmya) it must necessarily possess that property—the meaning of the term "possessing that property" (taddharmabhāvī) is already understood. This is the intended sense.
The answer is: "It does not exist either.
For example, when sound is to be proven eternal, because of the similarity of action with the probandum—sound—in terms of being incorporeal, action does not possess that property;
the meaning is that it is not eternal.
By the very restriction "only by the probandum," this example is refuted.
Here, the dark complexion of a teacher and his pupil, or the state of being Maitra’s son, and so forth, are to be cited as examples of relations based on adventitious conditions (*upādhi*).
However, since a specific definition depends upon a general definition within the definition of a logical reason (*hetu*), there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*).
And here, by the inclusion of the phrase "similarity with the probandum" (sādhyasādharmya), it is stated that an example lacking the probans (sādhana) does not qualify as an example;
for instance, "Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal, like an atom.
Furthermore, by the phrase "possessing the property of that" (taddharmabhāvī), examples lacking the probandum (sādhya) are excluded.
For example: "Sound is eternal because it possesses form, like an action.
By this, that which lacks both [the property of the subject and the probandum] is also refuted.
For example: "Sound is eternal because it is formless, like a pot."

By the inclusion of the fifth [case-ending], it is shown that only that statement in which "the possession of that property" (*taddharmabhāvitva*)—which is employed through similarity with the probandum (*sādhyasādharmya*)—is demonstrated is the example (*udāharaṇa*), and nothing else.

Furthermore, "being the employer" (*prayojakatva*) refers to the essential connection of the reason (*hetu*) with the similarity to the probandum, which is to say its state of being the pervaded (*vyāpyatva*);
whereas "being the employed" (*prayojyatva*) refers precisely to the pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*) of the similarity to the probandum.

By this, it is stated that [the fallacies of] the non-demonstration of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and the demonstration of a perverted positive concomitance do not qualify as examples [of valid inference].
For instance: "Sound is impermanent because it is produced, like a cloth."
"Whatever is impermanent, all that possesses origination, just like a jar.

With the intention that the general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is also indicated by this through the power of the etymological explanation (*samākhyā-nirvacana*), the author of the *Bhāṣya* provides an etymological derivation (*nirukti*) of the term *samākhyā*.
The author of the *Vārttika* demonstrates it as follows: "That by which something is illustrated (*udāhriyate*) [is called an example]."
He raises an objection with "But surely... and answers with "This is not a fault.
The meaning is that [the word] functions as either a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) or an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the statement.
Furthermore, the phrase "being denoted" is intended as an indicator of the act of denotation (*abhidhāna*), not as referring to the object denoted (*abhidheya*);
for otherwise, the fault of lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*asāmānādhikaraṇya*) would remain unavoidable.
The commentary beginning with "tasya dharmaḥ" (its property) is intended to explain the portion of the Sūtra "taddharmabhāvī" (that which comes into being as its property).
Here, the word "uttaram" (the answer) contains a hidden intention.
Having restated this commentary, he explains it: "tasya dharmaḥ" (its property).
"His dharma is that dharma"— for thus the dharma is mentioned separately by virtue of its being related [to him].
And it is not the case that the dharma itself is the dharma,
nor is another dharma the dharma.

"But rather, the meaning is 'of the subject' (*dharmin*). Having thus stated the inconsistency in the Bhāṣyakāra’s [position], the Vārttikakāra states his own [view]: "And the property (*dharma*) is what is to be proven.
By this, he points out the contradiction with the definitions of the reason (*hetu*), the example (*udāharaṇa*), and the application (*upanaya*).

The commentary states: "By virtue of similarity with the probandum, because it possesses the property of being subject to origination"; he explains this as "of that subject (dharmin). [It means] "it comes to possess that property."
That is untenable;

for it is not the case that the impermanence of a pot or similar object arises from its being produced, in the same way that a sprout arises from a seed. Therefore, it is said: "it comes into being" (bhavati) means "it exists" (vidyate). //36//
Or, by the reversal of that, it is the opposite.
The definition of the example by way of dissimilarity (vaidharmyodāharaṇa) is as follows: [it is] that which is devoid of it. // 37 //

Having continued [the previous discussion], he recites the Sūtra together with its commentary: "And an example which, by virtue of being dissimilar to the probandum (*sādhyavaidharmya*), does not possess that property (*ataddharmabhāvī*) is the 'illustration' (*udāharaṇa*).

This means that because the example, such as a jar, is dissimilar to the living body—the subject whose property is to be proven (*sādhya*)—insofar as it lacks the similarity (*sādharmya*) of possessing a self (*sātmakatva*).
"That property" (*taddharma*) refers to the possession of breath and so forth, which is the property of the living body, the very subject of the probandum.
That very state is the existence of that property; one who possesses it is "possessing that property. One who does not possess that property is "not possessing that property" (*ataddharmabhāvī*).
This means that a jar and the like are devoid of breath and so forth.
What is intended is this: in cases such as a jar, the absence of the probans (sādhana-dharma) is necessitated by the absence of the property to be proven (sādhya-dharma).
That jar and so forth are the example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*);
the word [or statement] concerning that is the "illustration" (*udāharaṇa*).
Furthermore, the word "or" (*vā*) found in the Sūtra should be understood as serving the purpose of conjunction (*samuccaye*).
"Because the example of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) has as its object the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
Here, the author of the *Bhāṣya* has cited the same example of the positive-negative (*anvaya-vyatirekin*) inference that was previously mentioned in the preceding sutra;
furthermore, he has stated that the absence of the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*) is necessitated by the absence of the probans (*sādhana-dharma*).
And that is incorrect;
for even when the reason possesses both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatirekin*), an example based on similarity (*sādharmya*) alone is appropriate,
because the cognition of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) is preceded by it, and it is improper to establish a matter through a circuitous route when it can be established by a direct path.
The relationship of pervaded and pervader that exists between two positive entities (bhāva) should be understood as being reversed in the case of their respective absences (abhāva).

Otherwise, [the author] would consider that a reason existing only in a portion of the similar instances (sapakṣa) would not be a valid reason; thus, with this in mind, the author of the Vārttika says: "The example is in the case of a non-reductive (avīta) reason."
And that has been stated by us while correlating it with the Sūtra.

Wishing to demonstrate that the criticism of the non-scriptural (anārṣa) recension of the Sūtra by those who are like teachers (ācāryadeśīya) does not apply to our own scriptural (ārṣa) recension of the Sūtra, he states the reading and the intention of those like teachers, beginning with "But others [say]... For in the scriptural recension, because of the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) of the example— which is of the nature of an object— with the illustration which is of the nature of a word, there would be identity [between them].
But when the reading is "dṛṣṭāntasyodāharaṇam" (the illustration of the example), then this fault does not arise;
and [this is] the refutation of others.
Just as there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the example and its illustration,

so too it is with the state of being endowed with that property (*taddharmabhāvitva*), which consists in the nature of the object; however, coreferentiality is equally present even in the case of the example by virtue of its being characterized by the expression of its own object.

"Therefore, let it be the reading of the Ṛṣis (ārṣa) itself. Even regarding this reading of the Ṛṣis, he sets forth the objection raised by the opponent with the words "In this case too," etc.; the particle *kila* is used here in a mocking sense.
The word *bhāvī* is derived from the root *bhū* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) followed by the suffix *ṇini* in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*).
Thus, its meaning is "one who habitually performs that [act].
Since no other activity is possible apart from making known [the object], it possesses the capacity for communication (*gamakatva*).
And since that [universal] is non-different from all its constituent parts, it need not be mentioned because it is common to them all; this is the meaning.
He refutes this very point by way of concession: "This is not... and so forth.
But others, having raised a dilemma regarding the phrase "one who possesses that quality" (*taddharmabhāvī*), offer a refutation; thus he says, "But others...
In that regard, they state the refutation for the first alternative: "If that were so...
[and] "This is not the meaning of the Sūtra, because it applies to all its constituent parts (*sarvāvayavasādhāraṇyāt*)."
Therefore, this [explanation]—that "one whose nature is to cultivate that dharma"—is of no consequence.
Regarding the second alternative, they state the refutation: "But as in the case of the 'staff-bearer' (daṇḍin)...
A qualification is meaningful only when there is both possibility and deviation [of the general term from the qualified].

The meaning is not "merely by possibility. He refutes this objection of the opponents by resorting to the logic of the "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*): "It need not be stated," meaning that a qualifier is significant when there is both the possibility [of its application] and the potential for deviation [from the object to be qualified].
"Not in a bahuvrīhi" [means]:
the suffix *ini* is employed precisely because one intends to express a meaning external to the constituent members (*anyapadārtha*).
And since that [external meaning] is already obtained through the bahuvrīhi compound itself, the purpose of using *ini* is exhausted; such is the meaning.
If it is out of friendship, for that very reason he says "then necessarily" (*athāvaśyam*), thereby following up on the future grasping as another purpose: "they exist" (*santi*).

And regarding this, it was stated that Vasubandhu has incorrectly formulated the three members beginning with the proposition (pratijñā) according to the definition of Akṣapāda; [the author] refutes that by saying "tadetasmin" and so forth.
Having thus established the definition of the example (*udāharaṇa*), he sets forth and explains the definition of others in order to refute it: "Just as that which is established...
and "And just as that very same [subject] is qualified by being differentiated according to the difference in conditions (*pratyaya*)," where "condition" means the cause (*kāraṇa*).
This possession of both the probandum and the probans in the example is non-pervasive within the Buddhist tenet system,
because the examples such as a cooking pot lack the possession of the probandum and probans in the form of "producedness" and "impermanence.
For, according to the Buddhist tenet system, the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) of the pot is its "producedness," and its subsequent absence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) is its "impermanence."
And he refutes [the opponent's position] by stating, "Even though it is throbbing here," because both [properties] do not exist in the pot, since they are contradictory to its very nature.
By the word "etena" (by this), it is indicated as an illustration (*nidarśana*), in the sense of "that by which something is illustrated in this or that."

The requirement that the reason must be concomitant with the probandum and absent when the probandum is absent has already been refuted; for it is shown to be non-pervasive, since [the reason] "being produced" is not found in a pot in the case of "impermanence.
However, in our own system, it has been stated in the *Hetulakṣaṇasūtra* how those two [reasons] are indeed possible in pots and the like.
In the commentary, "to be experienced by those appearing as scholars" means "to be experienced by eminent scholars. //37//
The application (upanaya) is the restatement of the subject of the thesis (sādhya) as "similar" or "not similar," depending on the example.

In one's own realization [of the inference], immediately after the recollection of the pervasion (*vyāpti*), there arises the knowledge of "reflection" (*parāmarśa*)—either in the form "and this [subject] is so," or "it is not so"—because the statement of the example (*udāharaṇa*) serves to establish that pervasion, and because it is a rule that the application (*upanaya*) of the reason within the knowledge of reflection must be preceded by the example.
Immediately after the example, he defines the application: "The example... which... (38).

The author of the Bhāṣya explains the term *apekṣāpada* as "dependent on the example" (*udāharaṇatantra*). It means being under the influence of the example; for that which is brought under control is called *vaśa*.

The meaning of "vaśin" (the controller) in the example is "vaśya" (the controlled). He explains this very same state of the object (*karman*) by extracting its essential nature: "vaśa" means capacity (*sāmarthya*).
The meaning is that there is a connection with the application (*upanaya*) by means of the result of the example (*udāharaṇa*) which has been brought under control.
He distinguishes the scope of "being so" (*tathātva*) and "not being so" (*atathātva*) [in the application] by saying: "endowed with similarity to the probandum" (*sādhyasādharmyayukta*).
But surely, the application is the restatement of the reason (*hetu*), not of the probandum (*sādhya*)?
And thus, the application of the probandum would be untenable; therefore, it is said: "the production-character of the word, which is the probandum.
The meaning is that the probandum is applied by virtue of possessing a reason whose pervasion has been established through the example, and not by its own nature.
Here too, the general definition is that the application (upanaya) is an application that depends upon the example.
It should be understood that "thus" and "not thus" refer to the specific characteristic (viśeṣalakṣaṇa) in relation to the general characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa).

On this point, some say that since the probandum (*sādhya*) is established by the statement of the reason (*hetu*) alone together with the example (*udāharaṇa*), the application (*upanaya*) is not a constituent part of the proof.
To refute that, the author of the *Vārttika* says: "‘As... so’ is for the sake of reflection (*pratibimbana*).
He analyzes this very point by means of a question: “But what [is its purpose]? etc.

Therefore, since this [reasoning] serves as a means for others to arrive at an indeterminate understanding due to their being either learned or unlearned, others must be instructed according to one's own realization.

Furthermore, since one's own cognition of the object to be inferred is preceded by the consideration of the logical mark (*liṅgaparāmarśa*) arising immediately after the recollection of the pervasion (*vyāpti*), others are instructed in that very same way.
Thus, it is established that the application (*upanaya*)—which is the cause of the cognition of the consideration—is purposeful.

And it is not the case that the cognition of the object of inference follows the positive and negative concomitance of the consideration of the logical mark (*liṅgaparāmarśa*) in the same way that it follows the consumption of curd and so forth, such that an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) might be urged.

He states another purpose for the application (upanaya): "or its occurrence in the probandum. He raises an objection: "But surely... Although "being produced" was stated as a means of proof (sādhana), [it is not yet established as such].

The sense is this: since immediately after the thesis (*pratijñā*) the proponent requires only the means of proof (*sādhana*), nevertheless, that [means] is not unestablished (*asiddha*) therein, as it stands as the very proof; thus, by its own efficacy, it implies its own establishment. He refutes this, saying: "It is not stated."
The proponents of verbal testimony (śābdas) maintain that "whatever a word aims at, that is the meaning of the word.

And since [the reason] "because it is produced" aims at being a means of proof (*sādhanatva*), [the example] follows by implication (*sāmarthyāt*). However, in the case of an implied [reason], even the example need not be stated.

Since even this [reason] is implied by the power of the proof (*sādhana*), and because that which is not pervaded cannot function as a proof, the application of a reason such as "knowability" (*prameyatva*)—which, though of that same nature, is used under the delusion that it serves as a proof for the eternality of sound—is equivalent to the case of an unestablished (*asiddha*) reason. Therefore, just as there is the employment of an example (*udāharaṇa*) to demonstrate pervasion, the employment of the application (*upanaya*) is also appropriate in order to establish the established nature of the reason; thus, this is elegant. //38//
NyS 1.1.39: The conclusion (nigamana) is the restatement of the proposition (pratijñā) following the indication of the reason (hetu).
The commentary on the definition of the conclusion (*nigamana*) begins with the words "Furthermore, of the two-fold...

This means that the definition of the conclusion is common to both types of reasons (*hetu*), examples (*udāharaṇa*), and applications (*upanaya*), whether they are based on similarity (*sādharmya*) or dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).
[The word] "therefore" (*tasmāt*) [is used]. //39// The application of the reason... [ends here].

Because of the statement of the reason, there is a restatement of the proposition that "sound is impermanent," which is caused by that [reason]. And although the conclusion (*nigamana*) is the statement of what is already established,
while the proposition (*pratijñā*) is the statement of what is yet to be proven, [the two differ in this way].

Nevertheless, since that very thing which was the probandum (*sādhya*) in the proposition (*pratijñā*) is the established (*siddha*) in the conclusion (*nigamana*), the conclusion is figuratively designated as the "proposition" by virtue of having the same object, based on its reliance upon that single entity possessing distinct states.
In this way, even the repetition [of the initial statement] is justified.
The author of the Commentary explains this as "stated by way of similarity" (*sādharmya-ukta*). He elucidates it with the words "they are concluded" (*nigamyante*).
He states the formal application (*prayoga*) of both similarity and dissimilarity, beginning from the proposition (*pratijñā*) up to the conclusion (*nigamana*), with the word "therein" (*tatra*).

Here, just as in the first sūtra, he states the possibility [of the means of knowledge] in order to praise the supreme logic regarding the respective parts, saying: "And in the collection of parts," and "of the authoritative instruction": "In the beginning, my dear, this was indeed Being alone."

This is because such authoritative instruction (*āptopadeśa*) as "thus," and so forth, is corroborated by perception and inference. Now, one might ask: why is the thesis (*pratijñā*) itself not considered authoritative instruction? What is the point of its being the subject matter of another means of knowledge (*āgama*)? To this, he says: "And [the word] 'of one who is not a seer' (*anṛṣeśca*)."
Inference is the cause. It might be argued:
"The second observation of the mark is the cause."

And that is not an inference, because there is no such [correspondence] for the third instance, namely the observation of the mark (liṅga) regarding the subject of the application (upanaya); therefore, he says: "In the example" (udāharaṇe), meaning in the substratum of the example (dṛṣṭāntadharmi).
Having clearly perceived—that is, having correctly seen—the necessary connection between the probandum and the probans, [the cognition arises] from the apprehension of the logical mark.

This is what is meant: although all three observations of the mark (*liṅga*), together with the recollection [of the pervasion], constitute inference, nevertheless, even in the case of the middle observation of the mark—which is but one part of that [process]—the designation "inference" is applied by metaphorically treating the part as the whole.
An example of the object of perception (*pratyakṣa*) follows.
Why? Because the unperceived object to be inferred in the subject of the thesis (sādhyadharmin) is established through a connection with a perceived example.
The point is that if perception were not accepted as the foundation, the unperceived would not be established due to a lack of systematic order.
He sets forth the purpose of the treatise: "Of all [the members]," etc.

The single object of the members beginning with the proposition and ending with the application is either the mark (liṅga) which is essentially connected [to the probandum] or the object of inference (anumeya); the comprehension of that [is the purpose].
In that [conclusion], the demonstration of capacity is the *nigamana* (conclusion).
By this, the unity of purpose is shown.
And the purpose is twofold.
In that regard, the intermediate [result] is the cognition of the logical mark (liṅga) which is intrinsically connected [to the probandum],
and the ultimate [result] is the cognition of the probandum (sādhya).

Now, he demonstrates the state of expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*) regarding the division [of the sentence] with the words "mutual connection" (*itaretarābhisaṃbandha*). By means of the result, which is the connection, he indicates the expectancy with the words "in its absence.
For the word of the proposition (*pratijñāpada*) is the primary element.

For it is only at a subsequent time, when there is a requirement for a proof (*sādhana*), that the word "reason" (*hetu*) proceeds by depending upon the proposition (*pratijñā*); it is not the case that there is an expectation for a reason from the very beginning. We have already established this in our exposition of the definition of the reason. He demonstrates the expectation [for a reason] in the absence of the word "reason" with the words: "if the reason were absent."
He states the requirement for the absence of an example: "if the example is absent.

He also states the requirement for the absence of the application (upanaya): "and without the application. He further states the requirement for the absence of the conclusion (nigamana): "and in the absence of the conclusion."

Although the individual purpose of each member [of the syllogism] has already been stated, the author of the Bhāṣya demonstrates it again for the benefit of the students, beginning with "Now" (*atha*).
He shows the purpose of the effort to set forth the five members with the words "And not in this" (*na caitasyām*).
To the question "But how does it proceed?", he says: "Without having established" (*avyavasthāpya*).
But since there is no occasion for a universal once [the object] has been established, he says: "For when [it] is established... and so forth.
On this point, some say that the conclusion (*nigamana*) is not a member of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*). Why? Because its purpose has already been fulfilled by the proposition (*pratijñā*).
To refute that view, the author of the *Vārttika* demonstrates that the conclusion serves a specific purpose, stating: "of the object which is the subject of the proposition."

Indeed, by means of the four members [of the syllogism], three or two forms of the reason are established, but not its "uncontradicted object" (*abādhitaviṣayatva*) or "absence of a counter-argument" (*asatpratipakṣitatva*).
Whether there be five or four forms, the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) of the reason is fully completed.
Therefore, the conclusion (*nigamana*) is intended to indicate the two characteristics of having a non-sublated object and being unopposed by a counter-argument.
This is what was stated: "for the purpose of negating the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the opposite.
For if there were sublation or a counter-argument, there would be the undesirable consequence of the opposite of the probandum (*sādhya*).

Thus, when this subject matter of the proposition has been established through the justification of its constituent parts, which are rooted in all valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it is refuted by the conclusion (*nigamana*) through the restatement of the matter to be proven;
for the matter is not established by the statement of the proposition alone, since that is directed toward what remains to be proved.
Nor can there be establishment through implication from something else, because that would entail the futility of employing words such as "reason" (*hetu*) and so forth,
since everything could be implied by the thesis (*pratijñā*) alone.
Therefore, the conclusion (*nigamana*) is for the purpose of demonstrating the two-fold nature [of the proof].

And just as we have demonstrated in the first aphorism that these two forms are distinct from the three-fold criteria [of a valid reason], so too will the remainder be shown regarding fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*). Thus,
within the meaning of this aphorism, there is no room for an opponent who considers the conclusion (*nigamana*) in a thesis to be redundant.
But one who might think that the statement of what is already established cannot be the conclusion (*nigamana*) without the establishment of the inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*) of the reason,
and that the establishment of the inseparable relation does not occur without the five features (*pāñcarūpya*),
yet that its establishment occurs through the conclusion— [we reply: the conclusion is not the statement of what is already established.

However, since even that [statement] is indeed the indication of the probandum (*sādhya*), the statement of others is introduced with the desire to refute its defects by accepting it for the sake of argument.
He recites the statement of others: "But as for the application (*upanaya*) and the conclusion (*nigamana*)."
He refutes this with the words "First of all, this...

For according to the literal text, he establishes the non-difference between the conclusion (*nigamana*) and the application (*upanaya*), and states the reason for the lack of distinction regarding their meaning: "And thus, this identity of light and darkness has resulted, like the blackness of a crow."
He raises an objection: "Now, [if you say] the reason and the application...
This is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa); one should also understand that the thesis and the conclusion are included.
Regarding the phrase "because there is no difference in meaning," it should be understood as "because the meaning is not distinct.
Such is the intention of the objector in asserting that there is a [logical] connection.
To this, he states the fault: "That [reason] is present in the counter-example (vipakṣa)."
He raises an objection again: "Now, [it might be argued] by virtue of having a single purpose.
He refutes this: "Even so... When it is established that there is a single purpose as the probandum (*sādhya*), there is no contradiction regarding the logical reason (*hetu*).

The meaning is that the reason (*hetu*) does not transcend the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*). "That has been described" means that it has been described how the meaning of the reason is one thing and the meaning of the application (*upanaya*) is another.

By this statement regarding the purpose of the application (upanaya) and the conclusion (nigamana), he says that the opinion of those who claim the argument consists of only three members is also refuted: "pakṣadharmatva... etc.
He first sets forth the objection raised by others through various alternatives: "As for what was said, 'whether it be thus or otherwise'—
for if it were connected with every universal, it would be that very thing,
and not 'thus'."
Otherwise, [the reason] "because sound is produced" [would fail];
for it is not the case that just as a pot is produced,
so too is sound produced.
The meaning is that it would follow as a consequence that there is no difference between the pot and the word "pot.
Therefore, when both the general property (*sāmānya*) and the specific instance (*viśeṣa*) are negated, "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) remains as the general property;
and since that [general property] lacks both the states of being "as it is" (*yathābhāva*) and "otherwise than that" (*tathābhāva*), the reason would simply be "because of being produced."
And thus, he says "by elimination" (*pariśeṣāt*) because the application (*upanaya*), which is the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of the reason, would not otherwise be possible.
He refutes this objection of the opponents by stating, "that too is incorrect.
The phrase "as this, so that" (*yathā tathā*) is a part of the means of comparison (*upamāna*), yet it is figuratively called "comparison" (*upamāna*) itself.
That which has similarity as its object is "that which has similarity as its object" (*upamānārtha*), namely the application (*upanaya*).
Its state is "similarity-ness" (*tattva*); [the word *tasmāt*] refers to that.
Furthermore, that similarity does not function by relying on a relationship of probandum and probans in every respect.

The meaning is as follows: the proof (*sādhana*) of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*), when residing in a pot, does not function by relying on its absolute absence in the subject (*sādhya*)—the sound—which consists in its inherence in a single substrate such as "pot-ness.
For if that were the case, it would follow that sound and the pot are non-different; thus, the expression "just as... so" (*yathā tathā*) would be impossible.

Therefore, by excluding other modes [of being] present in the pot, and by virtue of the commonality of the mere universal of "being produced," the application of the analogy "just as... so" is established.

But even so, one might object that in the case of sound there would be only the generality of being produced (*kṛtakatvasāmānyamātra*), and not its specific mode of existence; and thus, as has been stated, there would be no distinction from the [mere] reason (*hetu*). To this, he says: "But the generality of being produced... and so forth.
For the universal of cowness (*gotvasāmānya*) never exists in isolation from the presence of a brindled cow (*śāvaleyasannidhi*); rather, it always exists accompanied by its particularity (*viśeṣa*).
Thus, the meaning is that the state of being "as it is" (the identity of the universal with the particular) is logically established.

By this, he states that "because its purpose has already been fulfilled," even that which others have described— the non-difference of the application (*upanaya*) from the example (*dṛṣṭānta*)— is also refuted;
namely, by this description of its similarity to comparison (*upamāna*).
He analyzes this very point with the words "as for what was said":

the meaning is that there is a great difference between the two, for the *dṛṣṭānta* (example) is the locus for demonstrating pervasion (*vyāpti*), whereas the *upanaya* (application) is the subsumption of the reason—whose pervasion has already been observed—into the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*).
By this, the *nigamana* (conclusion) is also refuted, even though it shares the same referent as the *pratijñā* (thesis), because it serves the purpose of the thesis itself.
Because the thesis (*pratijñā*) has as its purpose the statement of the probandum (*sādhya*), while the conclusion (*nigamana*) has as its purpose the removal of contrary doubt;
thus, by the phrase "by this," it is stated with the intention of expressing only the commonality of their distinct purposes.

In this regard, the author of the Bhāṣya has cited both the *vīta* and *avīta* statements—consisting of five members—as being contained within a single [inference] that possesses both positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatirekin*).
In this regard, there might occasionally be the misconception that, because they are presented as a single example, both sentences are mutually dependent;
to dispel that, he says: "These two..."—the meaning being that it is not the case that "positive" (anvayi) and "negative" (vyatireki) constitute a single sentence. //39//
Tarka (reasoning) is the deliberation for the sake of knowing the truth regarding an object whose true nature is unknown, based on the logical possibility of the reasons [for its being so].
Here, the commentary is intended to introduce the definition of reasoning (tarka): "From this point forward," according to the sequence of the enumeration;
[this refers to] that which is without reasoning (avitarka).

//40// He states the sequence of the operation of reasoning (*tarka*): "When the true nature of an object is not being cognized. Although inquiry (*jijñāsā*) occurs only after doubt (*saṃśaya*), nevertheless, doubt may also occur even subsequent to inquiry; it is this latter type that is intended here.
Because it is a constituent factor for the operation of reasoning (*tarka*).

For, by means of reasoning—also known as *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum)—one of two positions must be negated so that the other may be accepted as an object of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus, due to its proximity to the object [of inquiry], doubt (*saṃśaya*) serves as a constituent factor for the operation of reasoning.

He explains [the term] "by way of the occurrence of the cause" as follows: "In this [case], a cause—that is, a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)—is possible. Here, the explanation of the word "cause" is "means of valid cognition," and the explanation of "occurrence" is "is possible."
The explanation of authorization:
"It is thus, and not otherwise."
This is what is meant:

with regard to an object for which a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is about to operate, that pramāṇa does not yet function as long as there is a suspicion of its opposite; rather, it functions only when the suspicion of the opposite is removed by demonstrating the undesirable consequences [of such a doubt].
And it is explained that the very removal of that [doubt] is the logical justification (*upapatti*) for the possibility of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding its own object.

When the object has been purified by that justification—which serves as a procedural requirement (*itikartavyatā*) by permitting the scope of the means of valid cognition—the means of valid cognition proceeds without obstruction.
Furthermore, one should not say: "Let justification alone be the cause of certainty; what is the use of a means of valid cognition?"

Because an independent proof (*upapatti*) cannot be established by itself due to its lack of a locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*), it has been demonstrated in the first aphorism that such a proof cannot lead to certainty on its own.
He states the illustration: "The example" (*nidarśanam*).

By the passage beginning with "of one's own performed action" and ending with "the cause of the previous," *saṃsāra* is shown. By the passage beginning with "the subsequent" and ending with "liberation" (*apavarga*), *apavarga* is shown.

Therefore, for the proponent and the opponent who both desire liberation from saṃsāra, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) operating upon the subject of the self’s permanence is assisted by this reasoning (*tarka*). Furthermore, the non-acceptance of the opposite of the object of a means of valid cognition is itself the acceptance of that very object,
because the opposite is directly averted through the consequence of an undesirable outcome (*aniṣṭaprasakti*).
For this very reason, the author of the Bhāṣya concluded at the end: "Where one perceives a cause to be untenable, one does not accept that [object]."

Now, if reasoning (*tarka*) has such a form as "this is so, not otherwise," how then is it for the sake of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), and not the knowledge of reality itself? To this he asks: "How then? (*kathaṃ punar iti*).
He refutes this, saying: "Because there is no restriction.
Since it is ascertained through synonyms, an absolute difference has been stated. [The term] *bhāvitāt* means from that which has been reflected upon (*cintitāt*).
"Therefore, from the clear [cognition], that is, from the stainless"—by this he refutes the independence of *tarka* (reasoning), [meaning] "by the force of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
This might be the case: if *tarka* were not a means for establishing the ascertainment of reality, but rather valid cognition itself.
"Alas, sir! For what reason, then, was it said that 'in debate, one employs means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and reasoning (tarka)'? To this he replies: "This is that reasoning.
This is said with the intention of referring to specific instances [of reasoning].
The meaning is: one who connects the means of valid cognition by dispelling doubts regarding errors concerning the objects of those means of valid cognition.
The author of the Vārttika states the intended meaning of the Sūtra: "Of this" (asya).
It is distinguished from that which is of the same class, such as doubt and the like, and from that which is of a different class, such as desire and the like.
Although doubt and the desire to know also operate upon an object whose true nature is not yet known, nevertheless, they do so "not through the application of reasons"; thus, these two are excluded.
He explains "true nature" (tattva) as follows: "Just as..."
The meaning is that "reality" (*tattva*) refers to an unerring nature that is distinguished from both similar and dissimilar classes.
He raises an objection: "But why [is this so]?"—the sense being that there is no word here that prescribes the cognition of a universal (*sāmānya*).
He refutes [the objection] with the words "not having its reality known.
The meaning is that the negation of a specific case implies the admission of the remainder.
He reflects: "this is a compound [meaning] 'one whose reality is not known'."
He determines— by means of a genitive analysis—
that it is logical and appropriate; however,
the meaning is that it is not appropriate by means of a instrumental analysis.
The proponent of doubt says: "Because there is no specific reason.
The sense is that this is stated merely as a proposition (*pratijñā*)—it is claimed to be logical—but no actual reason (*hetu*) is being adduced here.
He states the reason for its being logical: "It is logical because of the capacity to grasp an object.
Another objects: "Even without grasping an object.
For it is by means of the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) that cognition (*jñāna*) is defined, not by the knower (*jñātṛ*).
"Because it is common to that" means "because it has the capacity [to denote it].
He offers a rebuttal while concealing his intention: "Even so...
Accepting a different intention on his part, he raises an objection: "Let there be no compound."
The respondent says, "It is indeed so.
Thinking that his own intention has not yet been revealed by this [statement], the opponent challenges him again with the words, "Even if it is not stated.

He then discloses his own intention by first stating the rebuttal to what was said: "Because it has already been stated here" and "because it would follow that nothing at all could be expressed"—this is the disclosure of his own intention.
This is what is meant:

since there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) if that which is established by implication were not explicitly stated, doubt regarding the definition cannot be dispelled by relying on implication alone; therefore, the term "object" (*artha*) must be included in order to dispel that [doubt].
To this, the opponent objects: "The phrase 'whose true nature is unknown' (*avijñātatattva*) need not be stated."
For once reality has been known, there can be no desire for the knowledge of reality;
therefore, the sense is that [the person] is one whose reality is not yet known. He recalls the response spoken with a hidden intention: "In this regard, it has already been said."
Not understanding the intended meaning, the opponent says, "Let it not be so," meaning that tarka should be nothing more than mere conjecture (ūha).
The respondent reveals his own intention, saying, "It does not become wisdom."

Although in our own system desire to hear (*śuśrūṣā*) and so forth are not qualities of the intellect (*buddhi*), because the principle of the intellect (*buddhitattva*) itself does not exist [for us], nevertheless, even these are called qualities of the intellect according to the intention of the Sāṃkhya.
This is what is meant:
If it were merely stated that "tarka is ūha," or if it were simply defined as "tarka is ūha for the sake of knowing reality" (tattvajñāna),

then even after reality has been known, that ūha which arises— consisting of a re-evaluation of what was previously experienced— for the sake of further knowing reality would also have to be considered tarka.
Therefore, the meaning is that one must state "whose true nature is unknown.

Although this meaning is indeed understood from the phrase "due to the logical possibility of the cause," nevertheless, such a character of the logical possibility of the cause itself does not occur without the inclusion of the term "whose true nature is unknown."
For instance, even though reasoning (*ūha*) has the nature of discerning what has been apprehended, it arises through the logical possibility (*upapatti*) or occurrence (*saṃbhava*) of a cause;
for when a cause is present, the effect cannot be absent.
However, this [reasoning] does not have its true nature unapprehended; therefore, it is distinguished from that [other type].

And that being the case, even a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would become reasoning (*tarka*). Therefore, it was said: "by the occurrence of a reason. Once this has been stated, one proceeds to investigate the purpose.
However, it should not be thought that the author of the Sūtras here shows a preference for brevity.
He objects: "There is the use of the genitive case.
He replies: "Not so, because it is not a case of transposing the case endings," as is seen elsewhere in the aphorisms of Kaṇabhuj.
One who has fallen into error asks: "Why?
The questioner himself states [the objection] in a single sentence: "If [it were] by way of reversal.
He provides the reply: "It is not the case that it is not logical."
This is for the purpose of making known, in particular, that which has been understood in a general sense.
The particulars are eternity and so forth, which inhere [in the subject], and fire and so forth, which are conjoined with smoke and so forth.
The rest is easy to understand.
He explains: "Reasoning [arises] from doubt and resolution.
Some proponents of a particular school of tenets say that reasoning (*tarka*) is inference (*anumāna*).
Others, however, describe inference itself—when it depends upon logical justification and anticipates the undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭaprasaṅga*) in the case of the opposite—as reasoning.
Regarding that, he first addresses the challenger with the words "As for what...
The meaning is that [the person] is "overwhelmed" (ākṣipta), meaning his heart is overwhelmed; he does not, however, cognize the actual nature of the conceptual cognition (tarka-pratyaya).
"From the perception of a specific feature" means that certainty arises from the perception of a specific feature through a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and not through reasoning (*tarka*),
because reasoning is merely an authorization for that [knowledge]. Having refuted the objector, he refutes the proponent of a partial view with the words "by this."
If one has fallen away from doubt but has not yet attained certainty, then its nature must be stated; thus he asks: "What, then?
The answer is: "It would be..."
The meaning is: "the admission of the object of the means of valid cognition.
He refutes the second proponent, the *ekadeśin*, with the words "by whomsoever... Here, "reasoning" (*yukti*) refers to the establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And the cognition arising from that is precisely *tarka* (reasoning);
and you state that it is inference (*anumāna*).
However, for us, the point is that there is merely a difference in nomenclature, namely that it is called *tarka*.
He raises an objection with "Now" (*atha*).
He refutes it with "Inference" (*anumāna*).
Since no logical reasoning (*yukti*) other than reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) and demonstration (*upapatti*) can be defined, the meaning of "dependence" (*apekṣā*) must be stated.
The point is that without something to be depended upon, dependence itself cannot be established.

Now, one might object: "Whatever reasoning an inference requires for the apprehension of its own object, that very reasoning will be the requisite dependence for the inference. To this, he says: "And in the apprehension of its own object... [and so forth].
He raises an objection with "Now [if]... (atha).
He refutes it with "Even so... (evam api).
If inference depends upon perception and scripture regarding origination...

It should not be said that [inference] depends on reasoning (*yukti*), because it is impossible to qualify all inference as being non-deviant (*avyabhicārin*) by virtue of its being of such a nature; this is the intended meaning.
He raises an objection again: "Now, regarding inference... (*athānumānasya*).
He refutes this with the words "tatrāpi" (even there).
Even in this case, reasoning (*tarka*) would not be a distinct category [of valid cognition]. The sense is that such a variety of inference must be included within valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) itself.
He provides the proof for the stated point with the words "it would be. The meaning is that the cognition "it would be" is a cognition of ascertainment.
He raises an objection with the words "inference."

The contrapositive (*viparyaya*), which results in an undesired consequence (*aniṣṭaprasaṅga*), is the negative concomitance (*vyatireki*) as a logical mark (*liṅga*). Since that [mark] does not function as a mark when the relationship [between the mark and the probandum] has not been grasped, it follows that because it depends on the recollection of the relationship between the mark and the marked (*liṅgaliṅgisaṃbandha*), it is indeed inference (*anumāna*), as in the case of the undesirable consequence of being devoid of breath and so forth. He refutes this by saying, "It is not *tarka*."

It is appropriate [to speak of the perception of the probans] in a negative inference (*vyatirekin*), because the probans-property (*sādhanadharma*), namely "possessing breath and so forth," is observed in the subject (*dharmin*) of a living body; however, it is not the case here that the probans-property "origination" exists in the subject "self"—such that, upon its observation, there would arise a recollection of the relationship between the mark and the marked when the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is awakened. This is the meaning.
Not only is the *prasaṅgasādhana* unestablished with respect to the subject (*sādhyadharmin*), but the reason (*hetu*) in a *prasaṅga* resides only in something else;
however, an inference does not proceed from a property that resides in something else.
Therefore, he states that its distinction from inference is clear by saying "and inference" (*anumānaṃ ca*). This is the explanation of the *Bhāṣya*: "This is that" (*so 'yam iti*) //40//
NyS 1.1.41: Ascertainment is the determination of the truth after having deliberated through the proponent's position and the opponent's counter-position.
This is not the definition of mere ascertainment (*nirṇaya*) alone, but rather of the purpose of investigation (*parīkṣā*).

And that specific kind of ascertainment is based upon the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) assisted by reasoning (*tarka*) arising immediately after deliberation (*vimarśa*); thus, it pertains exclusively to the domain of reasoning.

To show that the definition of the distinction between *nirṇaya* (ascertainment) is not non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*) in that context, the author of the Bhāṣya introduces the definition of *nirṇaya*: "And in this subject matter of *tarka*..."

Having reflected—[on the following]: //42// Here, since the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the counter-thesis (*pratipakṣa*) function as the objects [of proof], they cannot be the means for establishing a definitive conclusion (*nirṇaya*). Therefore, by way of this logical inconsistency, it must be understood that "proof" (*sādhana*) and "refutation" (*upālambha*)—as found in the aphorism on debate (*vāda-sūtra*)—are what must be characterized. Thus, the author of the Commentary (*bhāṣyakṛt*) first analyzes those two: "Proof" (*sthāpanā*) is the means of establishment;
"refutation" (*pratiṣedha*) is the critique of that means of establishment.
He states the relationship based on their defining characteristics: "those two, the proof and the refutation.
Although the refutation does not depend upon the counter-position [as its object], nevertheless, because it proceeds with that as its aim, it is said to be dependent upon it.
He states the purpose obtainable by employing a word in its secondary (lakṣaṇika) sense, thereby bypassing the employment of the primary (mukhya) sense: "intermingled" (*vyatiṣaktau*).

He states that the state of terminating with the determination of one or the other is obtained through the force of the inclusion of the word "meaning" (*artha*): "proceeding with their respective adjuncts" (*anubandhena pravartamānau*).
This will become clear in the Vārttika.

He demonstrates that very mutual connection between the proof (*sādhana*) and the refutation (*upālambha*) by saying, "of one of those two. The meaning is: the determination of the object—which is either the thesis (*pakṣa*) or the counter-thesis (*pratipakṣa*)—of whichever proof or refutation remains established.

Here, one objects with the words "this is not so" due to a misconception regarding debate, thinking that doubt exists because of the employment of the proponent's and opponent's positions (*pakṣa-pratipakṣa*).
"One" refers to the proponent (*vādī*);
he establishes the matter asserted by means of a reason (*hetu*).

The negation of the second opponent—that is, the refutation of the reason stated by the proponent—is what is meant by "refuting the refutation. [The proponent] "rescues" it, meaning he renders the refutation a mere semblance of a refutation.
However, the second opponent negates the status of the reason stated by the proponent as being a valid establishing reason (*sthāpanāhetu*).
And the reason for refuting the objection raised by the opponent against that very proponent is also brought forward by the opponent himself.
Whether it be the reason or the censure of either the proponent or the opponent, it ceases;
when that has ceased, one remains alone.
Therefore, the determination of the matter is not [effected] by both;
consequently, it is incorrect to say that it is [effected] by the proponent's position and the opponent's counter-position.
To begin with, the proponent and the opponent do not exist in a state of doubt or regarding a matter already resolved, for they only engage when their positions are certain.
Having accepted [the objection], he refutes it with the words "by both":
for the proponent, there is the possibility of a proof (*sādhana*) and the impossibility of a censure (*upālambha*) by the opponent;
likewise, for the opponent, there is the possibility of a proof and the impossibility of a censure by the proponent.
"Having reflected" means having performed reflection (*vimarśa*).
Although reflection is not something to be adopted [as a result], it is said to be "pervaded by action" (*kṛtivyāpya*) because it is an effect.
He states the purpose of employing the word "having reflected" as follows: "This very [is it]."
"Having illuminated" means having made [the object] a focus by way of a restrictive rule (*niyama*).
He states the counter-example (*vyatireka*) for the phrase "residing in a single substratum" (*ekadharmisthayoḥ*) with the words "as in the case of that which possesses action" (*yathā kriyāvat*).

He states the counter-example for the phrase "of two contradictory [properties]" (*viruddhayoḥ*) by way of a difference in time with the words "and residing in a single substratum" (*ekadharmisthayośca*).
He states that this definition does not apply to mere ascertainment (*nirṇaya*) alone, but rather to the object of investigation: "And this is not [mere] ascertainment.
The construction is as follows: the definition consisting merely of "ascertainment is the determination of an object" applies to perception produced by the contact of the sense organ with its object.
He reveals the position held in his heart: "In the treatise (*śāstra*) and in debate (*vāda*)."

For there is no deliberation required when determining the connection between the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices with their results such as heaven— since this is to be established through scripture (āgama)—
nor is there deliberation in the forms of debate (vāda), sophistry (jalpa), or cavil (vitaṇḍā),
because those activities proceed only between a proponent and an opponent who already possess certainty. This is the meaning.
The Vārttika states: "The relationship and the purpose are as before.
The relationship is characterized by the sequence following *tarka* according to the order of enumeration;
and the purpose is the objective.
The meaning is "exclusion from those of the same and different classes.
The rest has been understood through the explanation of the Bhāṣya.
Now, let it be granted that the means of proof (sādhana), as indicated by the word *pakṣa*, functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the ascertainment (*nirṇaya*).

However, since that refutation, which is characterized by its counter-position (*pratipakṣa*), does not possess direct probative force, he says: "And from the counter-position. The meaning is that its status as a reason (*hetutva*) is through a mediated succession (*pāramparyeṇa*).
"By means of the position and the counter-position" means by means of the proof (*sādhana*) and the refutation (*dūṣaṇa*).
Desiring to explain the definition, he raises the question: "But where [is this]?
Here, the first alternative is that it is "only by means of the thesis and the counter-thesis";
for in that case, since the restrictive particle *eva* is used, there would be a restriction of the determination to what is other than that.

The second alternative is that it is indeed the final determination (*nirṇaya*); for in that case, there is a restriction [implied] by the phrase "by means of the proponent's and opponent's positions" (*pakṣapratipakṣābhyām*).
And the third is that it must be preceded by deliberation (*vimṛśya*).
Even then, there is a restrictive rule regarding determination (*nirṇaya*).
In that regard, he challenges the first alternative with the words "if, having deliberated" (*yadi vimṛśya*).

In that alternative, determination would not proceed elsewhere by overstepping the deliberation between the proponent's and opponent's positions; thus, perception (*pratyakṣa*) as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would not have determination as its result.
The meaning is that since there is neither a thesis nor a counter-thesis there, nor even a deliberation, the definition of perception is not contradicted.
He introduces the third alternative with the words "by this."
The meaning is "by way of contradiction.
Regarding the second alternative, he states the refutation: "Now, if [it is argued that] the thesis...
In that case, because there is no certainty regarding the conclusion, both the thesis and the counter-thesis, as well as their absence—these two together [would follow].
The conclusion (*nirṇaya*) obtains by having that [reasoning] as its basis;
thus, the meaning is that the definition is non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*). He offers a solution by relying on the first alternative: "in the domain of reasoning" (*tarkaviṣaye*).
The meaning is that this definition does not apply to determination in general, but rather to a specific kind of determination.
"Not determination" means not mere determination.
Now, what is meant by "of the determination"? The meaning is "of determination in general. And "by the means of knowledge individually" refers to perception and so forth;
and "by the means of knowledge collectively" means by the establishment of proofs, the refutation [of objections], and the resolution [of difficulties].
In debate, the final determination (*nirṇaya*) arises from the proponent's position (*pakṣa*) and the opponent's counter-position (*pratipakṣa*), but not from mere deliberation (*vimarśa*).
In a formal treatise (*śāstra*), however, there is only final determination; the meaning is that no means of proof other than those contained within the treatise itself is relied upon therein.
Regarding the phrase "by means of the thesis and the counter-thesis":
for in a definition (*lakṣaṇā*), that by which something is defined is also brought to mind as its delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*).
Consequently, through that [delimiting factor], there arises a restriction of the thing being defined.
Just as in the expression "the cowherd settlement on the Gaṅgā," it is only the bank connected to the Gaṅgā that is associated with the cowherd settlement,
and not the bank of the ocean as well.
He objects: "The word 'object' (artha)...
He replies: "No, not so.
When the word "object" is employed, its conceptual nature is negated.
And since that which is non-imagined cannot possess contradictory properties, there can be no determination of one side or the other.
He explains the objection in the Bhāṣya beginning with "This is not [established] by means of the thesis and the counter-thesis" with the words "by means of the thesis and the counter-thesis.
He explains the reply in the Bhāṣya beginning with "By both of them" with the words "He says: 'By both of them indeed'."
He asks: "In this [case]," where the first is the proof (*sādhana*) and the second is the refutation (*dūṣaṇa*).
The third resolution:
the answer is "everywhere.
This means that sometimes it occurs in the first, sometimes in the second, and sometimes in the third.
He states that the third [alternative] is indeed necessary, saying "or else" (*atha vā*).
Regarding both alternatives, there is the question: "How so? The answer is: "First of all, one... (*eka-stāvat*).
Having refuted that proof of the proponent by means of a refutation, the opponent states the proof for his own position;
the "first" refers to the proponent.
Some maintain that ascertainment (*nirṇaya*) is nothing but inference (*anumāna*). For instance, the third observation of the mark (*liṅga*), which is the result of perception, is ascertainment;
and since that very [observation] is inference, the meaning is that ascertainment does not exceed [the scope of] inference.

He refutes this: "It is not the case that [all] determination is inference. For if mere determination were called inference, then it would not be the case that all of it depends upon the recollection of the relationship between the mark (liṅga) and the marked (liṅgin).

If, however, the consideration of the mark (*liṅgaparāmarśa*) is the definitive conclusion (*nirṇaya*), and that [conclusion] requires dependence upon the relationship between the mark and the marked (*liṅgaliṅgisambandha*), then he says: "Because it is the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphalatvāt*).
A particular that is pervaded by a universal ceases when the universal ceases.

It is like the state of being a *śiṃśapā* [tree] existing through the exclusion of the state of being a tree. Furthermore, since the status of being an instrument of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does not exist within the result—namely, the determination (*nirṇaya*) which is the nature of valid cognition—it follows that inference is not a specific instance of that [result];
this is the meaning.

He states that determination (*nirṇaya*) differs from inference (*anumāna*) for this reason as well: "Determination pertains only to its own object. For determination does not extend beyond the object that serves as the basis for its cognition by virtue of being a determination;
inference, however, applies both to that [object] and elsewhere.
This is because when the inferable fire itself is delimited as something to be avoided and so forth by the inferential cognition of fire.
But when fire is inferred by means of the cognition of smoke, then it must be understood that [the rule] applies elsewhere as well.
Thus ends the first Āhnika of the first Adhyāya in the *Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā* composed by Vācaspatimiśra. *Nyāyasūtra* 1.2.1:

Debate (*vāda*) is the adoption of a thesis and its counter-thesis, employing means of valid knowledge and reasoning, free from contradiction with established tenets, and consisting of the five members.
May you, whose intellects are exceedingly skillful and gentle, grasp the true meanings of these words without envy,
just as the gods do the meanings of the speech of Vācaspati.
The commentary, intended to introduce the sūtra concerning the definition of debate (vāda) which follows in the sequence of the topical outline, states: "There are three types of discourse.
This is incorrect, because works such as the *Bṛhatkathā* do not fall within these three types of discourse.

Furthermore, there is no occasion for the definition of specific characteristics (viśeṣalakṣaṇa) without first stating the general characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa), and since debate (vāda) and the like are specific types of discourse (kathā), the author of the Vārttika says: "There are three types of discourse.
This is not a restriction to discourse in general, such that [the rule would exclude] the *Bṛhatkathā* and similar works.
It would not be "non-discourse" (akathātva); rather, that which resides in an investigation involving multiple speakers is the subject of investigation (vicāravastu).
In other words, discourse (kathā) is a composition of sentences that serves as the object of investigation.
The rule for this *kathā* (debate) is that it consists of exactly three [parts].

Thus, it should be understood that the general definition—that a *kathā* is a composition of sentences concerning an object of investigation with multiple speakers—is indicated by the phrase "the adoption of a position and a counter-position" (*pakṣapratipakṣaparigraha*) from the Sūtra; this is also stated implicitly.
The phrase "the object which is investigated" is merely a designation for the meaning; it is not an elaboration of the term "the object of investigation.
He states who the persons qualified for debate and so forth are: "In that regard, by the teacher and others," and so on.
