He states the reason for the immediate sequence of the definition of debate: "In that regard, according to the order of enumeration."
Regarding the term "sūtra":
it is stated that by this, the general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is also indicated.
He explains the commentary beginning with "residing in a single substratum" (*ekādhikaraṇastha*), starting with "the sun," etc., by means of a question—"Which ones?"—as follows:
He analyzes [the phrase] "the two properties of the object" as follows: "the two properties of the object.
Here, the word *dharma* (property) refers to a specific attribute;
since that [specific attribute] is not determined, what is stated is the determination of the object in its general form.
This is what he says: "of the object in its generality.
The meaning is that even though they are not contradictory, they do not necessitate an investigation in this manner.
He states the intended meaning of the phrase "attainment through the means of valid cognition and reasoning" as follows: "of this..."
By this, the commentary beginning with "its qualification" and so forth has been explained.
Although there is indeed the adoption of a thesis and a counter-thesis even in the case of *vitaṇḍā* (cavil), [the distinction remains].

Nevertheless, there is no establishment of a counter-position because that [vitaṇḍā] lacks a formal proof. And although in *jalpa* (disputation) there is indeed the establishment of both a position and a counter-position, nevertheless, the proof and refutation are not carried out through members [of a syllogism] rooted in valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and through reasoning (*tarka*). Thus, by the inclusion of the phrase "proof and refutation based on valid cognition and reasoning," *jalpa* and *vitaṇḍā* are excluded.
And how this is so will be demonstrated further below.
He raises an objection: "But how [can it be established] by means of reasoning (*tarka*)? He provides the answer: "We do not say so.

Since reasoning, which takes the form of a procedural method (*itikartavyatā*), assists the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the members [of the syllogism], being rooted in the means of valid cognition, are also rooted in reasoning.

And thus, the meaning is that the state of being a cause for proof and refutation is established for reasoning (*tarka*) as well. He objects by means of an alternative analysis: "In this [reasoning], there is both proof and refutation."
For it is the proof and refutation directed toward another that are intended [to be stated], and these two do not consist of formal means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and reasoning (*tarka*),
because those two serve as causes for one's own comprehension.
The meaning is "of the meaning of the parts," that is, of the meaning of the words constituting the parts.
Even though both [interpretations] are accepted,
he first provides a resolution by adopting the position that the suffix [-ana] has an instrumental sense (karaṇasādhana)— namely, "No."
"Because it has another purpose" means "because it serves a different objective.
But when [the two terms] function as abstract nouns (*bhāvasādhana*), he then asks: "Now, these two..."

The meaning of the objection is as follows: the question is posed by one who has fallen into error; it is neither a censure directed at the counter-position (*pratipakṣa*) nor a censure directed at its proof (*sādhana*), because those two entities, having arisen from their own causes, always possess that very nature and thus cannot be the locus for a censure consisting of human attributes.
He confirms it, saying "it is thus":

the subject (*dharmin*) as qualified by its property (*dharma*)— whether it be the thesis (*pakṣa*) or the counter-thesis (*pratipakṣa*)— is the object (*karman*), and that [object] is the domain (*viṣaya*).
Whether that substratum (dharmin) possesses suchness or non-suchness is its actual state; however, the object of the instrument is exclusively the action.
And in that regard, both the object and the instrument must be capable, not incapable.
But when a person applies himself to another object, he renders [the original task] incapable;
this is a fault of the person, not of the action or the instrument.

Just as when a person brandishes a sharp sword in the sky, the fault lies with the person and not with the sky— which is incapable of producing sound— nor with the sharp sword itself, which is incapable of cutting wood; therefore, the censure directed at the means of proof is merely figurative, not primary.
However, it belongs primarily to the person (puruṣa) alone;
it is designated as "of the person" by way of the statement (vacana).
It is figuratively attributed to the statement, but not to the position (pakṣa), because it is not pointed out by way of the position; thus it is established.
He demonstrates how this meaning is obtained from the words of the Sūtra by means of a series of questions, beginning with: "But how?"

Regarding what was stated—that the inclusion of "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) and "refutation by means of reasoning" (*tarka-sādhanopālambha*) is for the purpose of distinguishing *vāda* from *jalpa* and *vitaṇḍā*—he asks about the manner [of that distinction] with the word "Now" (*atha*).
The questioner himself says: "But even this... (*nanvidamapi*).
The answer is: "It is not the same.

He states the restriction: "Vāda is that which consists precisely of the establishment [of one's own position] and the refutation [of the opponent's position] by means of valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) and critical reasoning (tarka)."
By the word "only" (*eva*),
the status of debate as consisting of the means of proof and refutation through quibbles (*chala*) and so forth is excluded;
thus, it is distinguished from *jalpa* (wrangling) and *vitaṇḍā* (cavil).
This is what is meant:

let the members [of the syllogism] be, in ultimate reality, either rooted in valid cognition supported by reasoning or not; however, let the intention of the proponent and the opponent be that the members are rooted in valid cognition.

By this much alone, debate possesses the character of employing means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and reasoning (*tarka*) for proof and refutation, because, as a discourse of those free from passion (*vītarāga*), it culminates in the ascertainment of reality (*tattvanirṇaya*).

However, in the case of wrangling (*jalpa*) and cavil (*vitaṇḍā*), even a learned opponent may counter with quibbles (*chala*) and the like, since they are rooted in what is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa-mūla*), due to the certain defeat [of the proponent].

By one who desires victory and wishes that "there may indeed be doubt," we shall explain in the definition of *jalpa* how its exposition in this treatise is not inconsistent with reality and how it accords with the conduct of the virtuous.
The commentary beginning with "Because of the application of points of defeat in debate" is untenable.

Since a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) is already obtained in debate (*vāda*) by the very mention of "objection" (*upālambha*), the author of the *Vārttika* says: "quibble and futile rejoinder" (*chalajāti*).
The intended meaning is that [the term "objection"] would not be mentioned if this were not the case.
He objects: "It is collective.

If the purpose of mentioning "objection" (*upālambha*) is to establish it as a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), then, alas, there would be no distinction between a debate (*jalpa*) and a formal discussion (*vāda*).
The meaning is that it has been accomplished by the two subsequent words.
He refutes this, saying: "Not by the two subsequent ones.
*Niyama* here means *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification).
Thus, by this, the commentary stating "for the purpose of permitting something" has been explained;
it is not in contradiction with the established tenet (siddhānta).
Having presented the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on this point, he refutes it with the words "it is said that [the phrase] 'not contrary to the established doctrine' (*siddhāntāviruddhaḥ*).
When the interpretation of the *bhāṣya* has been refuted, he asks and then explains according to his own view: "Now, what is this word?"
He asks: "But why?
The answer is: "By means of the teacher and so forth.
Indeed, the manifestation of a lack of ingenuity (*apratibhā*) and other such faults is not appropriate for the realization of reality.

Although an excess [of arguments], even if it does not directly obstruct the comprehension of reality, nevertheless, when pursuing that [excess], the opponent's intellect becomes confused and is unable to comprehend reality; thus, even an excess serves as a cause for the obstruction of the comprehension of reality.
Therefore, by using the phrase "one who desires to know reality," he excludes the desire for victory (*jigīṣutā*).
For there is no possibility of a desire to conquer (jigīṣā) regarding teachers and the like;
thus, the fruit is threefold.
The three fruits are: the realization of a truth not previously understood, the removal of doubt, and the confirmation of what has been determined.
But when there is an adversary, it is not *vāda* (debate), but rather *jalpa* (wrangling) or *vitaṇḍā* (cavil). [The author] objects: "By the words 'means of valid cognition and reasoning'..."

The meaning is that if proof and refutation were possible regarding a single object by means of ultimate valid cognition accompanied by reasoning, then at one time a single entity would result in being embraced by contradictory properties.
He refutes this, saying: "This is not a fault."

In debate, the intention of the proponent and the opponent is regulated by their commitment to valid cognition; they must employ means of proof and refutation based on such valid cognition, not based on what lacks validity as in the case of *jalpa* and *vitaṇḍā*.
However, the actual nature of the object (*vastu*) is not thereby regulated.
Thus,
in debate, even the employment of quibbles (*chala*) and the like without prior intention may occur;
and these must be pointed out [as fallacies] only so long as their non-pointing out would obstruct the comprehension of the truth.
However, that which, even if not pointed out, does not obstruct the comprehension of reality, need not be pointed out even if it has been employed [by the opponent].
This will be demonstrated more thoroughly in the fifth chapter.
He extends the method stated for the proof (*sādhana*) to the refutation (*dūṣaṇa*) as well: "The refutation is also thus.
Since the previous purpose has been established, the author of the Commentary (*bhāṣyakāra*) introduces another purpose: "In the members [of the syllogism]," etc.

For indeed, being endowed with the five members and the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), along with the reasoning (*tarka*) that supports them, does not occur without [the aforementioned conditions].

Precisely because it is endowed with five members, once valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and reasoning (*tarka*) have been obtained, the mention of "proof and refutation" (*sādhanopālambha*) must necessarily be made in order to indicate their mutual connection;
otherwise, one person, remaining in his own place, might simply employ a five-membered statement regarding the impermanence of sound.
Furthermore, another person might employ an identical statement regarding the eternality of sound; thus, that too would result in being considered a "vāda" (debate).

The point is that the inclusion of the terms *pramāṇa* (means of valid cognition) and *tarka* (reasoning) is intended to specify the [proper] means of proof (*sādhana*) and the refutation (*upālambha*). There is also another purpose.
He adds: "Even without [the other members]," and thus the position that the debate consists of five members is one alternative;
[the other is] that it consists of proof and refutation through means of valid cognition and reasoning (*pramāṇa-tarka*).
And thus, "the second" is the meaning. He cites another purpose: "quibbles and futile rejoinders," so that it may not be understood as mere contentious debate (*jalpa*).

The meaning is that he should not be known as one devoid of the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) occurring in formal debate (*vāda*). To the question, "What is the purpose served by knowing those? he says: "by means of quibbles (*chala*), futile rejoinders (*jāti*), and points of defeat.
Defeat occurs in formal debate, not in contentious discussion (*jalpa*).
One might think that defeat occurring in *jalpa* (disputatious debate) is not part of *vāda* (discussion).
However, it is indeed accepted that defeat occurring even in *vāda* is present in *jalpa*.
This desired point is obtained through the inclusion of "proof" (*pramāṇa*) and "reasoning" (*tarka*), which serves to expand the scope of the text.
This is the meaning.

Having thus explained his own preferred definition of debate (*vāda*), he introduces the definition of Vasubandhu in order to refute it: "But others [say]... The meaning is that debate is speech for the purpose of establishing one's own position and refuting the position of the opponent.
He refutes this with the words: "And here..."
He analyzes the first reason with the words "these two":
the former position is untenable, whereas the latter position is tenable; such is the meaning.

Alternatively, for a single word—that is, a single subject (*dharmin*)—which is connected with multiple qualifiers such as "eternal" and "non-eternal," there is the designation by multiple words due to the difference in the speaker’s intention;
this means the designation by both its own word and other words.
This very point is being considered: what constitutes that "appropriation" (*svīkaraṇa*)? It is not [the case that it is merely the word itself].

The meaning is this: ownership (*svatva*) consists in the fitness for being employed at will in purposeful actions (*arthakriyā*) appropriate to oneself, such as those regarding land, wealth, and so forth; this [fitness] is possible in the case of sound and the like when they are asserted to be impermanent and so on, even though they have been acquired. An objection is raised: "Ownership is the state of being the cause for the arising of the notion 'mine' (*mama*)," [to which it is replied: "It is not the cause."
Regarding the claim that "it is ownerlessness," he refutes it with the words "as for what was specified":
the cause of the cognition "this is mine" is precisely the fitness for being employed according to one's will, and nothing else.
The meaning is that this [beneficial agency] does not belong to the author of the treatise with respect to the word, which has been proposed as being eternal and so forth.
Furthermore, existence is pervaded by beneficial agency, since it is observed to be so in the case of cows, jars, and the like;

thus, beneficial agency, when it is excluded from the subject (pakṣa), also excludes its own pervaded property, existence, just as "being a tree" excludes "being a śiṃśapā. This is what he says: "And whatever belongs to whom... and so on.
He entertains a second objection: "It must be established" (sādhanīyā).
He refutes it: "Oh, the meaning of the word! (aho śabdārtha iti).
The meaning is that the qualifying term (viśeṣaṇapada) does not possess a meaning distinct from the qualified term (viśeṣyapada).
Furthermore, does this qualifying term establish the qualified object— which was previously extended in a general sense— within a specific instance, or not?
If you say it does establish it,
then the word "one's own position" (svapakṣa) would not have the meaning of merely that which is to be proven.
He says that the qualification would not be useless: "And this [qualification] is for the purpose of exclusion.
Now, although the word to be qualified (*viśeṣya*) refers to a particular (*viśeṣa*) due to its connection with a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), it is nonetheless a general term (*sāmānyaśabda*).
And then, [the opponent] objects that one is able to express an identical meaning, saying: "Even general terms... [The author] replies: "Those are not general terms," and further:
"Moreover, the thesis is yet to be proven."
Since a clear understanding arises through the presentation of an example, the logical (*yukta*) [reason] is also introduced for the purpose of demonstrating what is illogical (*ayukta*).

One raises the objection: "If the refutation (*dūṣaṇa*) is not connected with the thesis (*pakṣa*), then what is its object?"—this is expressed by the words "Now, of the refutation... The answer is: "Of something... (*kasyacit*).
The "subsequent fault" (uttaradoṣa) is the pointing out of a [logical] genus (jāti). They are called "objections" (ākṣepa) because they are cast forth (ākṣipyante).
What are those factors?
They are lack of ingenuity (*apratibhā*), distraction (*vikṣepa*), and so forth.
These are not connected with either one's own position or the opponent's position, nor are they connected with the formal proof (*sthāpanā*).
He objects: "That is true. He replies: "It has been explained. One does not accept a departure from the primary meaning of a word without a specific purpose.
The meaning is that this verse indeed belongs to you.
Furthermore, if it is a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), then for the sake of brevity, let the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) be formulated in this way; thus he says: "If, however... (*yadi ca*).
He raises an objection with "Now, if...
and refutes it with "In its own nature..."
The meaning is "primarily. He raises an objection: "Even by means of establishment. He replies: "There is no fault."

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that only a refutation (dūṣaṇa) is connected [to the word], and since the phrase 'for the sake of non-establishment' (asiddhyartha) expresses only a refutation, how is a specific distinction obtained? To this, he says: "Even when there is a mention of the general."
He introduces the third alternative in order to refute it, stating: "The words 'self' and 'other'...
He refutes this as well by pointing out its contradiction with another sūtra, saying: "Even this is not tenable."
Since the terms "one's own" and "the other's" are connected with proof and refutation respectively,

it is indeed established by rule in the Sūtra that there is proof regarding one's own position and refutation regarding the position of the other; and thus, in the subsequent position, [the former] is to be refuted.
The meaning is as follows: just as [the position] is to be refuted by the proponent of the counter-argument (*uttarapakṣavādin*),
so too would the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)— being thus established— have to be established rather than refuted by the proponent of the counter-argument.

Furthermore, he states that there would be the fallacy of a reversal— namely, the proving of an untenable prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the refutation of a tenable rejoinder (*uttarapakṣa*)— because the proponent of the rejoinder’s own position is distinct from the untenable prima facie position; the meaning is that it is tenable.
It is neither the meaning of the word nor the meaning of the constituent parts;
by this, it is meant that there would be a contradiction with the designation of the rules for other sūtras.
It has been explained that [the opponent's view] is to be rejected. To refute the sixth alternative, he introduces it with the words, "This is one and the same.
He then refutes it: "It is reasonable that one thing should have multiple qualifiers."
He recalls [the previous argument] to explain the second reason presented: "samāsa" etc.
He says "bhedācca" with the intention that not only is the qualifier not apprehended as having its own meaning distinct from the qualificand, but it is also not differentiated from anything else.
He objects: "Even though there is no difference.
This means that the army is not only non-different from its qualifier, the lord, but also from others—namely, the elephant-riders, cavalry, charioteers, and infantry.
The same applies to the beverage (*pānaka*).
It is not only from its constituent parts, such as cumin and so forth, but also from others, such as fruits and water;
he refutes this, saying: "And that is not so."
Having set aside what was said, he suspects: "Now, you might think it is for its own sake.
He refutes this by reminding him of what was already stated: "That is not so.
And by this very [argument], the *karmadhāraya* and *bahuvrīhi* [compounds are also refuted].
He says "even by this" (apītyāha)—by this [reasoning].
Furthermore, he who has his own position (svapakṣa) to be established is described as such;
and thus, it would pertain to the subject of the establisher (sādhayitṛ), as he says: "and pertaining to the subject of the establisher."
Now, it might be argued: "Granted that the word itself may not have as its object something fit for arbitrary application, yet it will certainly have as its object the thing to be proven."
And as for the objection regarding how the compound is formed, he raises the question: "But surely...
He recalls the fault stated regarding the position of the genitive compound: "it is not possible.

Furthermore, if there is a distinction between [this] position and his own position, there is a contradiction with another sūtra; or if there is no distinction, there is a contradiction within this very [sūtra].
Thus he says: "And because of contradiction."

Furthermore, he states that between a sentence and a compound, the compound is superior due to its brevity, saying: "Let it be for now. This is because the compound is not [merely] "capable" (*samartha*).

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of establishment and non-establishment" (*siddhyasiddhyartham*), this compound does not mean "for the purpose of connecting each of one's own position and the opponent's position"; rather, the meaning is that there is the establishment of something and the non-establishment of something else.

He refutes [the objection]: "If, due to incapacity, the compound is not established for the sake of proving or disproving"—then [the response is] "even in the case of a compound. The meaning of "even in the case of a compound" is: even when the compound is used for the sake of proving one's own position and disproving the opponent's position.

He demonstrates through an objection and its resolution that there is no contingency of using either the singular or the plural number due to a lack of semantic capacity—this is shown by the words "ekavacana" (singular) and so forth. He demonstrates through an objection and its resolution that even though the rule for compound formation is non-eternal (*anitya*), the compound itself is superior to the analytical statement (*vigraha*)—this is shown by the words "anitya" (non-eternal) and so forth. [The opponent asks: "Let there be this prolixity; even so, what is the fault? To this, he replies: "evamapi ko doṣaḥ" (even so, what is the fault?).
He says: "And for the sake of understanding the meaning.
To achieve swift accomplishment by means of a concise method, a verbose exposition is useless.
As they say:
If one should find honey right here at home, why would one go to the mountain?
When the desired object is already accomplished, what wise person would exert effort?
Thus, because the employment of meaningless expressions would be disregarded by students, it would not constitute a *śāstra* since it would not provide instruction (*aśāsana*) to them;
this is what is meant by the phrase "by way of being a *śāstra*."
He refutes even this [argument] regarding "for the sake of success or failure," stating that "even this [claim] 'for the sake of success or failure' is not tenable.
"Tat na tāvat" means "among those two";
"establishing the locus of authority" (adhikāraṇapratyāyanam) means "establishing [the matter] for the judges" (prāśnikapratyāyanam).

To the question "From what is it contradicted?", he says: "And these which... Here, the particle *ca* is used in the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*); it functions as an ablative, meaning that the thesis (*pakṣa*) is contradicted.
He objects: "This is not [the case].
The meaning is that "success" (siddhi) refers to knowledge; its "subject" (pakṣa) is the object, while the "basis" (āśraya) consists of the judges (prāśnikas).
He refutes [the opponent's position] by means of a conceptual analysis, stating: "This is not tenable.

First of all, it is not possible within the Buddhist tenet-system for cognition to be both the subject of the thesis and the locus of the debate, because cognition lacks a substratum (*anādhāratvāt*).
And because the relationship between the subject and the object is not ultimately real, there must be another way of establishing [the self].
In this regard, the following question arises: "What then?"
Through the establishment of the connection [with valid cognition],
the thesis becomes established; the establishment of the connection with the means of valid cognition is itself the suchness of the object.
However, the conviction of the judges (*prāśnika*) arises regarding that [matter].
Therefore, it is not the case that the non-establishment of the thesis (*pakṣāsiddhi*) consists in the conviction of the judges; thus, there is a contradiction.

Since that object exists in such a way, the communication of the locus (*adhikaraṇapratyāyana*) occurs because of its being so; thus he anticipates the second alternative: "Now, [if you say] it is unestablished (*asiddha*)."

As long as the proof (sādhana) has not been employed within the scope of the thesis (pakṣa), if the determination of the locus (adhikaraṇapratyāyana) were already present, then since the determination of the locus would exist prior to the employment of the proof, the debate would be futile;
the employment of proofs and refutations (dūṣaṇa) would be purposeless. He states another refutation: "of the thesis" (pakṣasya).
The meaning is that for people like us today, there can be no transgression of the primary sense of a word through the employment of non-expressive terms without a specific purpose.
As they have said:
"Since the employment of words rests with us, why should we employ what is non-expressive?"
This might be the case:
although one ought to say "those on the beds are crying out," the metaphorical usage "the beds are crying out" is observed even without a specific purpose; therefore, he says:
"but because of the impossibility of [such] valid cognition."
The construction is: "But [it is] also because of the impossibility of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Now, one might object: "In this case as well, even without a purpose, a metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) will occur based on the mere impossibility of a means of valid cognition, just as in the expression 'the beds are crying'. To this he says: "As used in the world. Just like the meaning of words used in the world, metaphorical usage is also worldly; it cannot be refuted by the absence of a purpose, for the world is not to be questioned.
With the intention that our contemporary usage cannot be questioned for lack of purpose, he says: "And this is not worldly."
"But others," however,
[hold that] non-establishment (*asiddhi*) is not the state of being an object of refutation— which would mean it could not be connected with the thesis (*pakṣa*)— but rather, it is ignorance.
The meaning is that since this [definition] refers exclusively to the subject (pakṣa), there is no deviation from the primary sense.
Regarding this as well, he states the aforementioned undesirable consequence (prasaṅga): "If that...

Therefore, by one who accepts [the definition] "of the subject," both the knowledge and non-knowledge of proof and non-proof must be admitted to reside in the properties of the subject (pakṣadharma) alone.
Since, because of their being properties of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), it follows that the subject is either established or unestablished;
[the opponent] says "let it be so," to which [the author] replies: "this being the case."
The point is that, according to the Buddhist tenet, it is simply not possible for knowledge to have a seer as its substratum or as its object. He raises an objection: "Let it not be so.
Indeed, there exists the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), depending upon which all six types of active consciousnesses arise.
Therefore, the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is the seer;
success and failure reside only in that [consciousness].
If it is argued that this is not so because the subject (pakṣa) has that [consciousness] as its object, and for that [subject] as well—
What, then, is this state of being an object (*viṣayabhāva*)?
If it is said to be "being its cause," then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the eyes and other causes of cognition would also be objects.
Furthermore, it would follow that what is non-existent and lacks a cause could not be an object.
If it is argued that being an object consists in being made manifest by cognition— no, [that is not correct].

Since cognition does not produce illumination regarding an object, it is established that cognition— which does not inhere in that [object] and for which that [object] is not its own object— resides solely in the perceiver.
[The author] refutes this with the words "even so" (*tathāpi*).
Again, he raises an objection: "Now, 'in such and such ways' means the application of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
He refutes this with: "Even so.
One desiring to know the truth asks: "But who are these?"
He provides the following answer out of friendship: "The properties of the object," and so forth.

Although the application or non-application of the means of valid cognition pertains to both the object of cognition and the cognizer, [the former] is intended here because agency is untenable in the absence of a connection with the instrument of proof (*sādhana*).

Nevertheless, because the object of cognition (*prameya*) is primary, it is with respect to that very object that the designation and the cognition occur; thus, manifestation (*vyakti*) and non-manifestation (*avyakti*) are said to be properties of the object of cognition, and not properties of the cognizer (*pramātṛ*).
Regarding the phrase "for the sake of success or failure" (*siddhyasiddhyartham*), the word "purpose" (*artha*) is inappropriate [in this context].
Why? Because no other alternative is possible.
He states the alternative: "The word 'object' (artha), indeed...
In this sūtra, since the word 'object' cannot possibly mean wealth, a cause, and so forth, only three [meanings] remain; thus it was said that it functions in three ways.
There are four types of statements: the proof (*sādhana*), the fallacy of proof (*sādhanābhāsa*), the refutation (*dūṣaṇa*), and the fallacy of refutation (*dūṣaṇābhāsa*).
He rejects the first alternative with the words "that is not so" (*tan na tāvat*);
the word "that" (*tat*) means "among those [four]."

In another treatise, the word *artha* was explained in the *uddeśa* as being intended to include the four types of statements by way of the qualification "proper" (*yukta*) and "improper" (*ayukta*). However, the inclusion of the four types of statements does not occur when qualifying them as "proper" and "improper," because a thesis (*pakṣa*) associated with a fallacious proof (*sādhanābhāsa*) lacks propriety, and a counter-thesis (*pratipakṣa*) associated with a fallacious refutation (*dūṣaṇābhāsa*) lacks impropriety—this is the meaning. Now, he raises an objection: "But what if... [suggesting that] it is not a connection with proof and so forth, but rather the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) itself, independent of proof, which constitutes propriety and impropriety. Thus he asks: "But then again... (*atha punar iti*).
He refutes this with the words "even so" (tathāpi).
To the question "Whence is the contradiction? he says: "For not... (na hi).
If accomplishment (*siddhi*) is understood as cognition (*pratīti*), even so, that which is to be cognized (*pratyāyyā*) is not possible.
Or is it the instrument (*karaṇa*)?
Nevertheless, the meaning is that there is a contradiction, because the performance of an action is not possible.
Anticipating the second alternative, he refutes it with the words: "Now, [if you say] for the sake of a purpose.
"Purpose" (prayojana) means the effect (kārya).
Therefore, that [cognition] cannot arise from a fallacious cause;
for a firefly, even when perceived as "fire," does not burn or cook.
Anticipating a third objection, he refutes it with the words "Now, as for the subject matter. Here, "the author" refers to the author of the Sūtras.
"In this way, however":
if this were the case, then the words "success" (*siddhi*) and "non-success" (*asiddhi*) would constitute a formal debate (*vāda*).
Now, it might be argued that even things such as wealth and its causes are denotable by the word "object" (*artha*).
To the question "Why are these not included here?", he says: "In that Sūtra,
no other object for the word 'artha' is possible."

The meaning is that neither the establishment [of a position], nor wealth, nor the proof of one's own side or the opponent's side, nor even their cessation, is possible. Furthermore, he states that under the view where "speech" (*vacana*) is the qualifier, there would be a contradiction with one's own treatise: "Speech for the sake of establishing or disproving [a point] is debate" (*vāda*).
Regarding the phrase "by one who speaks thus":
this previous sūtra is the refutation of the Naiyāyika's reason, while the present one is the response.
He summarizes: "Thus, in this way.
*Tantra* refers to the treatise (*śāstra*). They contradict both the treatise and the world.

The meaning is as follows: because of the employment of non-expressive words; because it results in the loss of the status of a "debater" for one who utters fallacious proofs and refutations—despite being established by worldly convention as a debater; and because the words "established" (*siddhi*) and "unestablished" (*asiddhi*) are intended to establish the status of being a debate (*vāda*).
Having thus refuted the *sūtra*, he refutes the *vṛtti* with the words "And just as...
[and] "of his own position... (*svasya pakṣasya*).
Of one's own position;

for apart from the position, there can exist no other object of proof— whether it be the knowledge supported by that position or something else— that is denoted by the term "establishment" (*siddhi*).

Since knowledge—whether by being based on a person or by not being based on anything at all—cannot logically serve as the locus of the thesis (*pakṣa*), whereas the thesis itself may indeed have some kind of relationship [with the person], such as it may be; this is the meaning. In the phrase "by those means of proof and refutations" (*sādhanadūṣaṇaiḥ*), the means of proof and refutation are mentioned separately.

The terms "proper" (*yukta*) and "improper" (*ayukta*) refer to their respective states of being proper or improper by means of proofs (*sādhana*) and refutations (*dūṣaṇa*). The meaning is that an object (*karman*) cannot itself function as an instrument (*karaṇa*).

Furthermore, he says— "and by the words 'proper' and 'improper'"— because if there were no distinction between what is proper and improper, your terms for proof (*sādhana*) and refutation (*dūṣaṇa*) would be meaningless, as their purpose is already served by the very apprehension of what is proper and improper. Now, if these are not synonyms...
Rather, there is a relationship of general and particular:
"proper" and "improper" constitute the general, while "proof" and "refutation" constitute the particular; thus he raises an objection with the words, "Now, you might think."
He refutes [this] with the words "not the first.
Since there is deviation from both [possibilities], the term "by lotuses" was stated because one may choose either the qualifier-qualified relationship or its reverse.
Anticipating the second alternative, he refutes it with the words "if [you say] 'conjunction'..."
The meaning is that, for Buddhists, there is indeed no such thing as "yoga" consisting of the operation of means and ends, or the operation of the refutable and the refutation.
Furthermore, even conventional yoga—since its definition depends upon the knowledge of the means and the end—is not defined when the end is not yet defined;

and since definition is a form of ascertainment (*nirṇaya*), the ascertainment of the end must occur prior to the definition of yoga. Thus, the definition of yoga is rendered useless for the purpose of ascertaining the end.

He states that there is a contradiction in saying that "the locus is made known by means of the instrument [of proof] through its being appropriate or inappropriate," for he says: "by the means" (*sādhanena*);
[that is, the locus] comes to be or is known.
Anticipating a third alternative, he refutes it with the words "atha padārthasya" (now, of the object).

The statement that "the demonstration of the locus [is by means of] what is appropriate or inappropriate" indicates that appropriateness and inappropriateness function as the instrument (*karaṇa*); however, this is not possible under the view that they are either the state of being such (*tathātva*) or the state of not being such (*atathātva*), because in those cases they would be the object (*karman*).

This is what was stated: "They [the objects] are that which is to be excluded (*vyavacchedya*) and that which is to be determined (*paricchedya*), but not the means for the exclusion or the determination."
He refutes [the view] that "it is the communication of the subject matter" with the words "adhikaraṇa... [i.e., *adhikaraṇapratyāyanam iti*].
[The opponent states: "The connection with the treatise is for the sake of the purpose.
He raises an objection: "Because it is for the sake of communicating to the judges (*prāśnika*)."
Someone asks the challenger: "What is the reason?
[The challenger replies: "Because it makes that known."
The respondent’s reply is: "It is said that the opponent...
The proponent says: "...does not comprehend even an existing object."

The meaning is that it is simply not possible for one who is endowed with internal capacity, who is concentrated, and who employs the complete application of the means of knowledge, not to apprehend an existing object.
If, even by such an apprehender, that object were apprehended otherwise, how could it be said to be "as it is"? To this he says: "And how... [and so forth].
He raises an objection: "Even if one proceeds out of a desire to conquer.
"Kāmakāraḥ" means permission. He refutes it: "Nevertheless... (tathāpi).
The statement "one who is practicing does not practice" is a contradiction.

Furthermore, this negation of knowledge—"one does not practice"—is not a debate for victory (jigīṣā), because it is a discourse concerning one free from passion (vītarāga-kathā); such is the intended meaning.
And as for the statement "because of convincing the judges":
it is well said that one person understands by means of an instrument belonging to another.
"Belonging to another object" (anyaviṣayasya) means "residing in another" (anyāśritasya).
And this is not a restrictive rule;
that is to say, there is no requirement to formally appoint the judges (*prāśnika*) in a debate, nor is there a prohibition against accepting those who happen to arrive by chance.
Intending that debate (*vāda*) is not distinct from wrangling (*jalpa*) and cavil (*vitaṇḍā*), he raises an objection: "But when this is not...
He offers a rebuttal while not accepting the point held in his own mind: "True.
He reveals his own intention: "Not threefold..."
He refutes [the opponent's position] by stating: "Not because it is denied by you alone.
He refutes [the claim that there are only three types of inference] by stating: "Even that which... on the grounds that the threefold division is not accepted.
He introduces the following [point] in order to refute what was stated in the *Vṛtti* regarding the establishment of the subject (*pakṣa*), saying: "And as for what was said...
[meaning] "not at will, that is, without a purpose."
The construction is: "even without a purpose" and "due to the impossibility of a means of valid cognition.
He states in the *Vṛtti* the refutation mentioned in the *Sūtra*: "the statement for that purpose is for the sake of establishing or not establishing"—this is the meaning.
He refutes the *adhikaraṇa* [section] with the words: "the *adhikaraṇa*."
For it is not the case that [the burden of proof] rests upon the judges in a debate;
for first of all, there are no judges at all in a debate, even granting that they exist.

Regarding the phrase "it has been said," he raises an objection: "because they are the substratum of the communication. The meaning is that "establishment" (siddhi) refers to the act of communication (pratyāyana), and the "arbiters" (prāśnikāḥ) are the substrata of that.
He refutes [this] with "no.
He raises an objection with "in that," meaning:
when the audience has been assembled by fate.
He refutes this with "no.
For a cause is not something that happens by mere chance;
the underlying idea is that even a donkey should not be considered a cause of smoke.

He objects: "If there are no adjudicators (prāśnika), then it is not a formal debate (vāda). What is the examination of the debate between those two, the proponent and the opponent, and of whom? And where does that examination of their debate take place?
For in the absence of adjudicators, there would be a lack of knowledge regarding the debate, its examination, and its locus; such is the meaning.
He refutes this with the words "by the means of proof" (*sādhanena*).

For it is only the proponent and the opponent, being free from passion, who are capable of both understanding the nature of the debate and examining it; so what need is there for the members of the assembly (*prāśnikas*) here?
The nature of debate consists in the application of proof, which has the thesis as its object, and the application of refutation, which has the establishment [of the thesis] as its object.
Thorough examination is the complete knowledge of proofs, refutations, and their fallacies.
For that purpose—that is, for the sake of examination—the qualification (*adhikāra*) in that debate belongs only to the proponent and the opponent who are free from passion (*vītarāga*).
This is the answer to the question "Where is this?
Therefore, the meaning of the locative case (*saptamī-artha*) is the sense of locus (*adhikaraṇa*), which amounts to saying it refers to the arbiter (*prāśnika*) as intended by the opponent.
The meaning is that this [defeat] does not occur for the proponent and the opponent when both are free from passion (*vītarāga*) until the conclusion of the discussion.

Regarding that which was raised in the *Vṛtti*— namely, that if debate (*vāda*) is defined as speech for the sake of establishing or disproving [a point], then it would follow that it applies to the pleasant or unpleasant speech of judges and opponents, as well as to the idle chatter of the streets— he says "even that" (*yadapi*), meaning that this objection is utterly baseless. For pleasant or unpleasant speech does not, either directly or indirectly, have the purpose of establishing or disproving [a point].
Nor is there a connection with the qualification of being correct or incorrect regarding proof and refutation;
therefore, one who speaks in such a manner is not worthy of a reply,
for [one does not argue] with a madman.
If someone who is not insane were to give an answer, or were to speak at all, he too would be insane.
This has been stated: "given with one's own hand.
One [instance] refers to success or failure in the past;
the other refers to what is appropriate or inappropriate.
Since this objection is irrelevant to both [positions], if an answer must certainly be given, then it should rather be stated in this way; thus he says: "If, however... (yadi tu).
This subtle analysis was made here by others; following upon that, the author of the Vārttika has also composed it. //1//

NyS 1.2.2: Debate (jalpa) is the employment of means for establishing one's own position and refuting the opponent's, characterized by the use of equivocation, futile rejoinders, and points of defeat, as previously described.
In accordance with the order of the topical outline (*uddeśakrama*), he defines *jalpa* (wrangling) immediately after the definition of *vāda* (debate): "Wrangling is as follows... (2).

In this case as well, the meaning of the sūtra is that *jalpa* (disputation) is distinguished from its own kind, namely *vāda* (discussion) and *vitaṇḍā* (cavil), as well as from those of a different kind, such as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth.
He explains the term "endowed with what has been stated" (*yathoktopapanna*) by saying "all of it. An objection is raised: "It is not correct to say 'endowed with what has been stated'."

Because the restriction of points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) and the restriction of the intention to employ means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and reasoning (*tarka*) for proof and refutation are absent in debate (*jalpa*), or else, if they were present, it would follow that there is no difference between discussion (*vāda*) and debate (*jalpa*), and furthermore,
it would entail the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) since the definition of discussion would then over-extend to include debate.
The meaning is that the claim "it is endowed with what has been stated" is untenable.
He refutes this, saying: "This is not a fault," because what was merely stated here is possible due to the possibility of its fitness (*yogyatā*).
It is understood, however, that the restriction (niyama) is not one obtained by implication from what was not explicitly stated;

for this is not apprehended merely by hearing the words of the sūtra, but rather, once its meaning has been understood and its establishment from other sources is found to exist, it is then inferred. Thus, the phrase "establishment and refutation through means of valid cognition and reasoning" (pramāṇatarkasādhanopālambha) is extended [by analogy].
This statement is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*).

Therefore, it is established that there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the entire definition—including "the employment of means of valid cognition and reasoning, the refutation [of the opponent], being endowed with the five members, and the undertaking of a thesis and its counter-thesis"—with the exception of the specific terms for debate (*vāda*); however, the restrictive rule (*niyama*) regarding the purpose does not apply here.
"Of the mere definition" means of that which has been merely stated;
it does not mean of the object, nor of the word to be defined.
On this very point, he provides an example: "as elsewhere in the Vaiśeṣika system."
The phrase "not for the purpose of restriction" is an illustration;
it should also be understood that the restriction of intention is not obtainable from the words "means of valid cognition," "reasoning," "proof," or "refutation."
He states another alternative with the words "or else" (atha vā):
just as a chariot joined with oxen is called a "go-ratha" (ox-chariot), this is an instance of the elision of the word "joined" (yukta).
The phrase "for [the rule] regarding the two restrictive purposes" is also an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa), just as before.

Thinking that the author of the Bhāṣya, while reciting the definition of debate (vāda) here, has also extended the restriction (niyama), the opponent raises an objection: "Now, the Bhāṣya... and so forth.
He refutes this with the words "not there.
The meaning is that from the sequence of recitation which conforms to the definition of *jalpa*, only the essential nature of the object is perceived, but not the actual object itself.
The meaning is that it was stated merely as it arose [in the context].

Here, the author of the Bhāṣya, having raised the objection that quibbles (*chala*) and so forth cannot be constituent parts of a proof because they serve the purpose of refutation, has demonstrated that they do possess the status of being constituent parts because they protect one's own position by means of destroying the opponent's position.

The author of the Vārttika raises this objection: "By means of quibbles (chala), futile rejoinders (jāti), and points of defeat (nigrahasthāna). To the question, "Are even the points of defeat improper? And is this not possible? he replies: "First, as for the quibble..."
The intention is that the points of defeat (nigrahasthāna) which have arisen incidentally [in the discussion] are to be applied to the two types of fallacies (chalajāti).
He anticipates the resolution stated in the Bhāṣya: "If it is argued that they are constituent parts (aṅga)."
He refutes this with the words "this too":
for even by a thousand blind men, a house cannot be protected from thieves; such is the meaning.
When this has been raised as an objection, a bystander asks: "Then for what purpose [are they stated]?
The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) replies: "[They are stated] by way of proof" (*sādhanena*).
First, in the case of formal debate (*vāda*), although [these statements] are not capable of refuting the proof, [they serve another purpose].
Nevertheless, one who does not know their true nature proceeds, being presented with and deluded by the thought, "I shall refute the proof by means of these.
Therefore, the meaning is that in debate (*vāda*), these are employed through error.
However, where one proceeds knowing their true nature, that is not *vāda*.
But is it *jalpa* (disputatious debate) or *vitaṇḍā* (cavil)? He says: "In which these... [are employed].
Now, one might object: since *jalpa* and *vitaṇḍā* involve formal application, would they not then constitute a member of the proof (*sādhana*)? To this [he replies]:...
He says: "But not...

[The opponent asks: "Well then, if these are neither a means of proof (*sādhana*) nor a member of the proof (*aṅga*), why is there their employment in debate (*jalpa*) and destructive criticism (*vitaṇḍā*)?"
To this he says: "And when a valid proof has been adduced.

When a valid proof has been adduced by the proponent (*vādin*), the opponent (*prativādin*)—desiring victory and with his intellect confounded, failing to immediately grasp the ultimate reply—employs quibbles (*chala*) and the like.
For what purpose? To this [he replies]:
He says: "Sometimes.
This refers to by some means or other through the application [of the mantra].
In this manner, it is for the purpose of protecting the reality (tattva).
This is not improper conduct;
nor is it inconsistent with the treatises that the exposition of *chala* (equivocation) and other such categories is taught,
nor does it entail the consequence of using terms such as "box" or "slap."
"In verbal combat,
there is no application of those [means]" means that one does not sublate the other at that very moment; this is the meaning.
"Roṣa" is easily understood. //2//
That same [vitaṇḍā] is a destructive criticism (vitaṇḍā) when it is devoid of the establishment of a counter-position.
In accordance with the order of the enumeration, he states the definition of *vitaṇḍā* immediately after *jalpa*: "That is *vitaṇḍā*. (3)
In relation to the position of the proponent (*pūrvavādin*), the opponent’s own position is the counter-position (*pratipakṣa*).
The establishment of that [position] is the proof (*sādhana*).
One who is deficient in that [proof] is [said to be defeated].
Thus, by this [statement], he distinguishes it from mere verbalization (jalpa).
The author of the Commentary says this very thing: "That is verbalization."
Thus,
by means of the refutation of the opponent's position, the respondent does not establish one of those two as his own thesis.
This is what is meant by "by means of the refutation of the opponent's position."
The meaning is: by way of negating its establishment.
This might be so:
just as the opponent's position [is established] in relation to the proponent's position.

Since a counter-position is likewise a position for the proponent (vādipakṣa) in relation to the position of the opponent (prativādipakṣa), it would follow that *vitaṇḍā* is the absence of establishing both positions.
To this, the author of the Vārttika says: "Devoid of the establishment of a counter-position," meaning devoid of the establishment of the second position.
For if there is an absence of the establishment [of a position] by the proponent of the first position, what is the point of the caviller?
Is it struck down? And yet, the position cannot be struck down.

Therefore, since there is a formal presentation (*sthāpanā*) for the proponent of the first position, it follows by implication that it is the second position alone which is devoid of a formal presentation; thus, [the objection] is logical.
Herein lies the statement of the objection (*codyabhāṣya*).
"In that case, let it be so.

The point is that in the absence of a formal presentation (*sthāpanā*), there can be no "probandum" (*sthāpya*) thesis (*pakṣa*); for otherwise, a thesis would not possess the status of being a thesis.
He addresses this [objection] with the words, "Indeed, that which...

For even a caviller (*vaitaṇḍika*), though not establishing his own position, strikes down the establishment of the opponent's position with the thought that, by the method of exhaustion (*pāriśeṣya*), his own position will thereby be established.

Therefore, his statement—characterized by the refutation of the opponent's position—is figuratively called a "position" (*pakṣa*), because it serves as the cause for the establishment of a position through the refutation of the opponent's position by means of the method of exhaustion.
Therefore, the caviller (vaitaṇḍika) does have a position;
however, his establishment [of a position] is nothing other than the refutation of the opponent's position.
Thus, he does possess a position.

And there is no establishment of a formal thesis (*pakṣasthāpanā*). This is what was stated: "One does not establish anything by asserting a thesis for the sake of another. However, the status of being a thesis exists merely by virtue of its fitness (*yogyatāmātreṇa*).
But not by way of being established.
The author of the Vārttika states "apare tu" to explain the meaning of the Bhāṣya's "astu tarhi":
the sense is that one must say, "therefore, *vitaṇḍā* is [a debate] devoid of a counter-position.
He refutes this, saying, "and this is improper."
First of all, it is not the case that "being a thesis" (*pakṣatā*), characterized by the fitness for being established even when not yet being established, is untenable; therefore,
since a caviller (*vaitaṇḍika*) accepts nothing other than refutation,
it must be said that he has no thesis because of his lack of acceptance.

The sense is that there is a logical consequence (*prasaṅga*) that if one accepts the fourfold goal (*caturvarga*), there is a contradiction, and if one does not accept it, one is neither a worldly person nor an investigator.
This refers to the proponent’s lack of understanding of the true state of affairs and the respondent’s [misconception] of himself.
As for the one who thinks that even if the fourfold goal is accepted, one should simply say "this is *vitaṇḍā* (destructive criticism) alone" for the sake of brevity—
Having set forth that view, he refutes it by demonstrating an over-extension of the argument—this is the meaning of the phrase "merely a refutation.
The sense is that this is understood from the very power of the etymological explanation (*nirvacana*) of the designation (*samākhyā*).
He concludes with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*).
Thus, by this, the commentary beginning with "yad vai khalu" has been explained according to its meaning. //3//
NS 1.2.4: Fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) are the erratic, the contradictory, the equal to the point at issue, the identical with the probandum, and the mistimed.

In accordance with the order of the topical outline (*uddeśakrama*), after *vitandā*, the fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are to be defined. Regarding these, there is a sūtra intended to provide their classification and enumeration while implying their general definition: "Those [reasons] which possess a similar counter-reason... (NS 1.2.6).

The author of the Vārttika recites this sūtra, providing its commentary and establishing the general definition by means of its etymological explanation: "[They are so called] because they lack the definition of a valid reason.
He then asks: "But what [is that definition]?"
The point is that similarity does not arise merely from one thing being different from another; otherwise, it would follow that everything is similar to everything else.
The response is: "It is a mere proposition."

Having stated the general [definition] pertaining to the means of application (*prayoga*), he states that which pertains to the object of application (*prayojya*) with the words "anyatama" (one or another).

Even though the conditions of having an unsublated object (*abādhitaviṣayatā*) and being unopposed (*asatpratipakṣatva*) are present, it should be understood that the mention of the three characteristics (*trailakṣaṇya*) and their opposites (*vailakṣaṇya*) is made without intending to include them [in the definition]. The rest is not obscure.

He calculates six hundred and seventy: therein, regarding the "pervader of the probandum" (*sādhyavyāpaka*), within this group of sixteen, there are two sets of sixteen due to the distinction between properties that pervade the probandum and those that reside in only one part of the probandum; [furthermore,] these are divided by the distinctions of the unestablished qualifier (*viśeṣaṇāsiddha*) and the unestablished qualificand (*viśeṣyāsiddha*).
Sixty-four.
Thus, from the distinction between capable and incapable [terms] and between qualifiers and qualificands, there are sixty-four.
Thus, this [number] is one hundred twenty-eight, which, together with the previous three sixteen-verse sections, totals one hundred seventy-six.
He provides examples of the specific properties that pervade the objects to be established (sādhya), beginning with the word "tatra" (in that regard).
The first and second [reasons] are common (sādhāraṇa) due to their pervading or not pervading the counter-examples (vipakṣa).
The third is a positive-negative (anvaya-vyatirekin) reason that indeed pervades both the probandum and its like.
The fourth and fifth are contradictory (viruddha) fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) due to their pervading or not pervading the counter-examples.
He shows that [reason] which does not occur in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) by saying "like a dyad" (*dvyaṇukavat*).

The sixth type, which lacks both similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and counter-examples (*vipakṣa*), is the "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*); for this very reason, he says "like a jar and so forth" (*ghaṭādivat*).

The seventh and eighth [reasons] are common [inconclusive] due to their pervading or not pervading the counter-examples (*vipakṣa*). The ninth, however, being present in only a portion of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), is indeed a reason that possesses both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatirekī*). The tenth and eleventh are reasons possessing positive concomitance (*anvayin*), due to their pervading or not pervading the similar instances.
The twelfth, however, is the uncommon [reason], for which no counter-example exists.
The thirteenth and fourteenth, on the other hand, are contradictory reasons because they lack similar instances and either pervade or do not pervade the counter-examples.
The fifteenth is likewise a purely negative reason (*vyatirekin*).
The sixteenth, however, is the uncommon [reason], which lacks both similar instances (sapakṣa) and dissimilar instances (vipakṣa).

If it were to be proven that speech and mind are perceptible by external instruments (*bāhyakaraṇapratyakṣa*), then non-eternality would not pervade the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), because it is absent from universals (*sāmānya*) which are perceptible by external instruments.
Therefore, he qualifies the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) as "possessing universals and particulars" (*sāmānyaviśeṣavat*).
"Form and consciousness are impermanent because they are immaterial.

Here, immateriality is the pervader (*vyāpaka*) of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), namely the aggregates of feeling, perception, and mental formations, which—being distinct from the aggregates of form and consciousness—are themselves impermanent.
To demonstrate that immateriality exists in only one part of that class [of similar instances], the example "like form, etc. is first presented as that in which it does not exist.
In the argument "Sound is impermanent because it is inaudible," [the reason] does not apply to the eternality of sound;
[this is] the meaning of the term "sound."
Thus, "sound" is the subject (*dharmin*);
"an object" is the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*),
meaning one of the categories of substance, quality, or action.
If it were said, "because it is not graspable by the ear," then [the reason] would also apply to dissimilar instances (vipakṣa) such as universals (sāmānya) and other non-entities;
therefore, it is stated: "because it possesses a universal that is not graspable by the ear."
The analysis of the compound is: "that which is not graspable by the ear and which possesses generality.

Now, one might object that visibility resides in the counter-example, because inherence—which is itself non-dependent—is visible; therefore, it is stated: "in the view of the followers of Ulūka (the Vaiśeṣikas)."
Regarding the phrase "a difference in tenets," this refers to the Sautrāntikas.
An example of an incapable qualificand is: "because of being knowable, while being produced."
An example of an ineffective qualification is: "because it is produced, while being knowable.

The meaning is that "produced-ness" (*kṛtakatva*) alone is indeed capable of proving impermanence when that is the probandum (*sādhya*), whereas "knowability" (*prameyatva*) is dependent on something else and thus ineffective.
Thus, by means of the sixteenfold [classification] of the three [types of reasons], there are forty-eight reasons and fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*). However,

when the sixteenfold [classification] of the two [types of reasons] is divided according to the distinction between pervading and non-pervading [reasons], it includes cases where both [the reason and the example] are agreed upon by both parties through the non-establishment of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*),
as well as cases where both are agreed upon by both parties through the incapacity of the qualifier and the qualified, and through the doubt regarding the qualifier and the qualified.
When that is modified by the triad of sixty-four, it becomes one hundred and ninety-two.

By means of the two sets of sixty-four—due to being unestablished for the proponent, unestablished for the opponent, and doubtful for both or either—one further set of one hundred and twenty-eight arises.
This very point was indicated by the author of the Vārttika with the phrase "unestablished for either."
Thirty minus two makes thirty-two; this is stated through some etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*).

Furthermore, by means of the distinction between pervasive and non-pervasive [qualifiers], qualifiers and qualificands in different substrata (*vyadhikaraṇa*), doubtful qualifiers and qualificands in different substrata, and incapable qualifiers and qualificands, there is another one hundred and ninety-eight [types] through three sets of sixty-four.

Thus, when both the locus (*āśraya*) and the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya*) are unestablished, there are one hundred and twenty-eight [fallacies] due to the non-establishment of either both or one of the two positions.
Here too, "thirty-two" is to be explained as before;
in this context, only one side is intended, not the distinction between proponent (*vādin*) and opponent (*prativādin*).

Furthermore, those [reasons] whose substratum is unestablished (*aprasiddhāśraya*)— as before, divided by the distinctions of having different loci (*vyadhikaraṇa*), doubtful qualifier and qualified (*sandigdhaviśeṣaṇaviśeṣya*), and incapable qualifier and qualified (*asamarthaviśeṣaṇaviśeṣya*)— amount to three hundred and ninety-four when added to the sixty-four. Thus, the three hundred and eighty-four resulting from the two preceding sets of three hundred and ninety-four, when combined with the two hundred and twenty-eight and the one hundred and ninety-two, total eight hundred and thirty-two.
It becomes a modification; the forty-eight primary elements are to be introduced later. Thus, both the substratum and the qualified object remain unestablished.
He provides an example: "The place possesses fire because it possesses smoke.
For it was stated previously that the place is not what is to be proven as possessing fire, but rather the specific instance of smoke itself.
He states an example of a reason where the locus is unestablished for one of the two parties: "The self exists, because it possesses qualities such as desire."
The fallacies of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*) and the unestablished qualifier (*viśeṣaṇāsiddha*), among others, should also be inferred.
Here are examples of the unqualifiedly incapable (*asamartha*), the non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*), and the unestablished qualifier (*asiddhaviśeṣaṇa*):
they are both incapable and non-pervasive.
The analysis [of the compound] is: "and they are unestablished due to having different loci" (*vyadhikaraṇatayā asiddhāḥ*).

In the argument, "Sound is impermanent because it is produced, provided that it follows immediately upon effort," the quality of following immediately upon effort is ineffective with respect to impermanence by virtue of the capacity of the qualificandum, which is simply the state of being produced;
furthermore, it is non-pervasive because it does not pervade the sounds of thunderclouds.

Furthermore, it is unestablished due to a difference in locus; for the state of being immediately preceded by effort exists only in the case of the action of the abdominal air upon the palate and so forth,
but not even in the case of the first sound,
let alone in that which inheres in the auditory organ.
Thus,

"because it is produced and because it follows immediately upon effort" should be seen as examples of [reasons] that are ineffective (*asamartha*), non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*), unestablished (*asiddha*), and have unestablished qualificands (*asiddhaviśeṣya*).

By way of elaboration, he provides examples for all [fallacies] except for "unestablished" (*asiddha*): examples of those where the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) or the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is either non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*) or ineffective (*asamartha*). "Sound is impermanent because it is perceived as varying according to the variation of its cognition.
Here, the property of being "perceived" (*upalabhyamānatva*) is ineffective because it is inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*), since it exists even in permanent things.
However, the qualification "varying according to the variation of its cause" (*kāraṇabhedabheditva*) alone is effective, as it is not inconclusive.
An example of [reasons] whose qualificands reside in entirely different loci is:

"Pradhāna exists, because we observe a commonality among the various differentiated things—such as cows, jars, and so forth—in their consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion. For this observation of commonality has the differentiated things as its locus, not Pradhāna as its locus.

"Having a different locus" (*vyadhikaraṇa*) means that the qualifier has a different locus [from the qualified]. An example of qualifiers that have exclusively different loci is as follows: color, taste, smell, touch, and sound.

These are entirely distinct in meaning from the word "sandalwood. This is because, given the impossibility of a whole being identical with its parts, the objects such as color and so forth, as well as the words for those objects, are designated by that word "sandalwood."

The meaning is that the phrase "the color and so forth of sandalwood" involves an impossibility of relation between the whole and its parts, and that the designation [of the whole] within the colors and so forth occurs through words such as "color" and so on; thus, it is a qualifier with a different grammatical locus (*vyadhikaraṇa*).
By this detailed exposition, one hundred and thirty-two [objections] have been demonstrated.

Now, in order to demonstrate the interval of one hundred and ninety-two [examples], he provides an illustration: "An example of that which is otherwise established (*anyathāsiddha*) is: 'Sound is eternal because of repetition' (*abhyāsāt*).
This repetition of action will be shown in the second [section] to be compatible even with the non-eternality of sound.

Following the logic of the lion’s backward glance (*siṃhāvalokita*), he provides examples where the qualifier and the subject reside in different loci (*vyadhikaraṇa-viśeṣya*) and where the qualifier is doubtful (*sandigdha-viśeṣaṇa*), stating: "Doubtful and unestablished" (*sandigdhāprasiddha*).
The word "qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇa*) is used by way of *tantra* (simultaneous application) as both the qualifier and the qualified, functioning as the object (*karman*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*).
Therefore, the meaning is that this is an example of those [reasons] for which the qualifier is doubtful and the qualified is unestablished due to being in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇa*).
For instance: "The place possesses fire because, while possessing smoke, it is illuminating," when the existence of smoke and so forth is itself doubted.
The property of possessing smoke is a doubtful qualifier,
and the property of being illuminating is a dislocated (vyadhikaraṇa) qualificand;
for that [latter] is indeed a property of fire, not of the place.
He shows examples of those [reasons] whose qualifiers are unestablished (*aprasiddha*) and whose qualificands are doubtful (*sandigdha*), by means of the phrase "by way of reversal.
It should also be understood that "unestablished" applies here as well.
For example: "The place possesses fire, because it possesses smoke while being luminous."
Now, in order to demonstrate the interval of one hundred and ninety-two [cases], he constructs the arrangement of the grounds with the words "In this way" (*evam*).

Those thirty-two [reasons] which were doubtful or unestablished (*asiddha*), divided into the categories of the pervasive (*vyāpaka*) and the non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*), become sixty-four through the distinction of being unestablished for both [parties] or for either one. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Having reached the state of sixty-four... (*te catuḥṣaṣṭitām āpannāḥ*).

As before, by means of the distinctions of having different substrata (*vyadhikaraṇa*), doubtful qualifier and qualified (*sandigdha-viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya*), and incapable qualifier and qualified (*asamartha-viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya*), there are three sets of sixty-four; thus, one hundred and ninety-two.

Furthermore, by means of the distinctions of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*), having different substrata, doubtful qualifier and qualified, and incapable qualifier and qualified, there are another one hundred and ninety-two.
Having relied upon these three hundred and eighty-four [cases] as being doubtful-unestablished (*sandigdhāsiddha*),

he speaks further by relying on another two hundred and ninety-eight cases as being otherwise-established (*anyathāsiddha*): "In this way, the divisions of the otherwise-established are to be understood."

For even the classification of the "otherwise established" (*anyathāsiddha*) consists of sixty-four types, arising from the distinctions between qualifiers and qualificands that reside in different loci (*vyadhikaraṇa*), those involving doubtful qualifiers and qualificands, and those involving ineffective qualifiers and qualificands;
and furthermore, that...

Thus, the "otherwise established" (anyathāsiddha) fallacy consists of three sets of sixty-four types— namely, those based on the unestablished locus (āśrayāsiddha), the non-co-referential qualifier (vyadhikaraṇaviśeṣaṇa), and the non-co-referential qualificand (vyadhikaraṇaviśeṣya)— along with the doubtful, the ineffective qualifier, and the ineffective qualificand; this results in a total of three hundred eighty-four.
He states another one hundred and ninety-two pairs as well: "In this way, there are those with contradictory qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) and those with contradictory qualificands (*viśeṣya*).

For those with contradictory qualifiers and qualificands are further divided into: those with non-co-referential (*vyadhikaraṇa*) qualifiers and qualificands, those with doubtful qualifiers and qualificands, and those with ineffective qualifiers and qualificands; and [again] through the divisions of those with unestablished substrates (*āśrayāsiddha*), non-co-referential qualifiers and qualificands, doubtful qualifiers and qualificands, and ineffective qualifiers and qualificands, they amount to three hundred and eighty-four.
Thus, by these three sets of eighty-four [verses] totaling three hundred, there are one thousand one hundred fifty-two;
and with eight hundred thirty-two, there is one thousand nine hundred eighty-four.
Thus, by adding the forty-eight that constitute the original [text], the total condensed sum becomes two thousand thirty-two.
That is not so, because of non-existence.
The coexistence of five or four forms is what constitutes non-deviation;
and that is not possible for two contradictory [forms] within a single object.
The meaning is that, ultimately, there is an absence of any form [of evidence] that lacks a counter-position (*asatpratipakṣa*).
Regarding "the five reasons":
the positive concomitant (*anvayin*) is of two kinds, according to whether it pervades the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) or does not pervade them.

There is one purely negative (vyatirekin) reason, and the positive-negative (anvayavyatirekin) reason is also twofold— based on whether it pervades or does not pervade the similar instances (sapakṣa)— thus there are five types of reasons.
Due to the combination of these five reasons with themselves and with others, there are twenty-five combinations.
A similar [reason] is positive for a positive [inference],
negative for a negative [inference], and both positive and negative for a positive-and-negative [inference].
And that which is dissimilar in form (asarūpa), such as the negative concomitance (vyatireka) and so forth, [is related] to the positive concomitance (anvaya) and so forth;
by means of that, there is a logical connection (pratibandha).
This is what is meant:

"In each of the [five types], such as the positive concomitant (anvayin) and so forth, there are five reasons—both similar and dissimilar—that act as obstructors; thus, by five sets of five, there are twenty-five non-erroneous contradictories (viruddhāvyabhicārin).
He raises an objection: "By their very definition..."
He refutes [the objection] by stating: "It is not meaningless.
For a word is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding that which it intends to convey;

and since the definition-sūtra is intended to exclude both similar and dissimilar classes, it is a means of valid cognition precisely with respect to that, but not with respect to the total number [of definitions], because it does not intend to convey that.
And this [object] is not a [real] object of cognition, because even though it exists, its non-perception is possible due to its lack of utility, just like any other non-object of cognition. // 4 //
The inconclusive [reason] is that which deviates.

Thus, having shown the classification whose general definition is implied by the sense, the author of the Commentary introduces the specific definition: "Among those fallacious reasons, the non-contradictory... (NS 1.2.5).

In this context, the terms *anaikāntika* (inconclusive) and *savyabhicāra* (deviant) are synonyms; however, depending on the difference between persons, they function as the definiendum (*lakṣya*) and the definition (*lakṣaṇa*).

For one to whom the meaning of the term *anaikāntika* is unfamiliar while the meaning of the term *savyabhicāra* is well-known, the designation of the definiendum is given as "the inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*).

"Savyabhicāra" is the definition. However, for one to whom the term "savyabhicāra" is unfamiliar while the term "anaikāntika" is well-known, the indication of the definiendum is given as "savyabhicāra," [which is synonymous with] "anaikāntika."
Such is the definition.
Regarding that, having accepted the term "savyabhicāra" (inconclusive) as part of the definition, the author of the Bhāṣya says: "vyabhicāra" is non-settlement in one [locus].
This is what is meant:
by the power of its etymological definition, the term *savyabhicāra* (deviant) constitutes the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
In the view that the term *anaikāntika* (inconclusive) is the defining characteristic, the author of the Bhāṣya stated: "Even impermanence is one extreme," and so forth.
The author of the *Vārttika* explains this with the intention of a *paryudāsa* (exclusion): "That which is restricted to one end (*anta*) is 'conclusive' (*aikāntika*).

It is not that the reason (*hetu*) itself is conclusive, such that by excluding it, all fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) would be subsumed under a single category, thereby contradicting the *sūtra* on their classification;
rather, that which is restricted to one end is conclusive.

The opposite of that is the "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*), which is "uncertain" (*aniyata*) because it applies to both permanence and impermanence, as well as to both positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). In other words, it belongs to both sides. The intention is that fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) such as the "contradictory" (*viruddha*) and so forth are not of this nature. Thus, since it has been established that the inconclusive is the "deviant" (*savyabhicāra*), he asks: "But what [is it]?"
The answer is: "That which is to be proven and that which belongs to its class.
Since this deviation (vyabhicāra) is already understood, one might ask how it can be designated by the term "inconclusive" (anaikāntika); to this, he says: "In all other cases, this [is so]."
However, since there is no end or exclusion for the category of the object of knowledge (*prameya*), which pervades everything, it was therefore stated: "except for the object of knowledge."
Here, he sets forth the objection formulated by the Buddhists through conceptual construction: "It is inconclusive" (anaikāntika).
What, then, is this?
It is the conclusive reason (*aikāntika-hetu*).
The meaning is that everything other than that is merely a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*).
He refutes the second alternative with the words "atha prasajyet" (then it would follow that...). Even so, the absence of the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*);
yet, this is not a case of deviation (*savyabhicāra*).

The meaning is that positive entities (*bhāva*) alone—whether characterized by deviation or non-deviation—are applicable, whereas these do not apply to a non-entity (*abhāva*), which is devoid of all designations.
He refutes this Buddhist objection, stating: "This is not the position of relative negation (*paryudāsa*).
