Indeed, the position of relative negation is both our preferred view and the more logically tenable one.

This is the resolution offered by one who intends to say: "Since this [opponent] refutes everything by resorting solely to his fondness for *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (non-presuppositional negation), we shall likewise speak everywhere while accepting that very same [negation].
However, the author of the Vārttika does not intend *prasajya-pratiṣedha* even in cases such as "non-Brāhmaṇa" (*abrāhmaṇa*).
However, it is indeed an exclusion (*paryudāsa*);
yet, having granted that [it is a negation], even there one speaks of a non-implicative negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*).
For even a non-implicative negation (prasajya-pratiṣedha) is not a mere nothing; rather, its meaning is that it is a certain entity itself, qualified by the absence of some other entity.
Regarding this, the commentary states: "The illustration [of similarity] is: 'Sound is eternal because it is intangible.
He provides an example by way of dissimilarity: '[That which is] tangible [is] non-eternal.'"
The construction is: "A jar is seen to possess tangibility.

He states the deviation from the method of difference (*vaidharmya-vyabhicāra*) because the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader is reversed in the case of dissimilarity: "In the example, the two properties—possessing tangibility and impermanence—are not apprehended as being in the relationship of the probans and the probandum."
For it is not the case that everything which is impermanent possesses tangibility, because this would be contradicted by [qualities such as] cognition and so forth;
furthermore, although there is similarity with these [same examples], the contradiction will be stated later,
and thus it is not mentioned here.
Now, one might argue: "Let it not be that 'eternality' is the probandum;
rather, let 'intangible-ness' itself be the probandum for eternality.
To this, he says: "And the atom possesses tangibility and is eternal."

Nevertheless, the point is that the dissimilarity (vaidharmya)—namely, "that which is not tangible is not eternal"—is subject to deviation, because even an atom (aṇu), though possessing tangibility, is eternal. He states the deviation from similarity (sādharmya) with the words: "and in the case of the self (ātman) etc."

In this context, the author of the Vārttika determines the nature of the reason "being intangible" by means of a question: "What, then, is that intangibility? The meaning is "distinctness from sound. Alternatively, it is inherence qualified by existence (*sattā*).
Alternatively, existence (sattā) is qualified by inherence (samavāya), meaning this is established through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).
He states "vākyārthe" etc., [meaning]: the use of a word for the sake of the sentence-meaning is non-tangential (asparśa), just like the word "śrotriya."
He raises an objection regarding the position that "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*) is the definition: "Atideśa," etc.
For if it were stated in some section of the treatise that [the reason] is inconclusive, [then the objection would hold].

The meaning is this: by overstepping its proper scope, the [definition] being extended here—its form already known—would characterize "inconclusive" (savyabhicāra) fallacies; however, there is no mention of it anywhere in the section of this treatise [dealing with fallacies].
He refutes this, saying: "Not so."
The meaning is that it has already been stated as being well-known in the world (*lokaprasiddha*).

Thinking that the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reason is necessarily restricted to both extremes only through positive concomitance (*anvaya*), he raises an objection: "Because it is not all-pervasive (*avyāpaka*)."
He refutes this, saying "no.
Regarding the term "exclusion" (*vyāvṛtti*): in some cases, positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is necessarily bound by both limits.
"In some cases" means "of the negative concomitance. He introduces the opinion of some with the words "others, however";
he refutes it with the words "by them, however."
A deviation in the definition does not follow from a deviation in the example, because they are distinct.
For indeed, investigators do not rely upon the example, but rather upon the definition; such is the meaning. // 5 //
NyS 1.2.6: Having accepted a tenet, that which contradicts it is the "contradictory" (viruddha) [reason].
Siddhā—ddhaḥ // 6 //
He asks: "Of what [reason] is this the sūtra?
Indeed, a non-conscious reason does not accept a tenet;
and that which does accept it is conscious, yet such a conscious being is not endowed with any of the characteristics of a reason. Therefore, it is not a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*).

The sense is that since a "position" (*pakṣa*) is not the same as a "tenet" (*siddhānta*), that which contradicts it would not be [considered] a "contradictory" (*viruddha*) [reason]. The answer is: a "contradictory" reason is that which contradicts an accepted meaning; the person's acceptance is figuratively attributed to the reason by means of the reason itself. Furthermore, the word "tenet" (*siddhānta*) is employed with the intention of referring merely to the object of that acceptance, and not to the tenet [itself].

This is what is intended here. Therefore, since "accepted" (*abhyupagata*) refers to the object of one's own commitment (*abhyupagama*), that which contradicts it is subsumed as a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*); and it is thereby stated that the "contradictory of the particular" (*viśeṣaviruddha*) is not a fallacious reason.
For a particular is not the object of one's commitment.

The meaning is that this is certainly not within the scope of the proposition itself, but rather it follows as a consequence of the establishment of the proposition's meaning; thus, it is not within the scope of what is explicitly accepted.
He states the fruit of such an explanation of the sūtra with the words "And thus" (*evaṃ ca*).
The meaning is that, without such an explanation, [the position] would be either unspoken or contradicted;
or else, it would be sublated by what has been accepted.
"Thus," meaning either by way of its own nature or as a logical reason (*hetu*).
By this, the commentary beginning with "it contradicts that" (*tadanena taṃ viruṇaddhi*) has been explained. He raises an objection: "But if it is so... (*nanvevam iti*).
If it is argued that [the reason] is contradictory (viruddha) because it subverts its own status as a valid reason,
then alas!

The *savyabhicāra* (inconclusive) and other such fallacies are also contradictory (*viruddha*), for their status as valid reasons is likewise sublated; or, if they were not so sublated, they would not be fallacious reasons— this is the intended meaning.
He refutes this: "It is true that there is only one.
Although they are equal in being thus non-contradictory, the number five is intended by a desire to express internal subdivisions.

Just as, for example, although the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and so forth are equal in being objects of knowledge (*prameya*), the number sixteen is established by a desire to express the internal subdivisions of the means of knowledge, the objects of knowledge, and so on.
Or, just as a specific kind of grass is designated by the term "tṛṇolapa" due to its uniqueness,
so too is a specific type of contradictory [reason].
The meaning is that this very [reason], being inconclusive and so forth, is denoted by such terms as "contradictory-inconclusive" (viruddhānaikāntika) and the like.
The commentary on the example here states: "For instance, 'this is that modification' (*vikāra*).
The modifications consist of the intellect (*mahat*), the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the eleven sense organs, and the gross elements.
Their manifestation is the transformation (*pariṇāma*) of their properties (*dharma*), characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and states (*avasthā*).
Therefore, it is called "destruction" (apāya).
The reason for this is stated as: "because of the negation of permanence."
The explanation of this is as follows: "A modification that is eternal is not tenable.
Even when a modification has departed [from its substrate], it still exists, because destruction is denied.

Thus, this reason—"because of the denial of eternality"—is contradicted by one's own established doctrine (svasiddhānta), namely, that "even when a modification has departed from its manifestation, it still exists."
He analyzes this very point by means of a question, beginning with "How so? and so forth.

The meaning is that, intending to show that [the opponent's position] contradicts the established doctrine (siddhānta) because contradiction necessarily involves two parties, he states that "it subverts the established doctrine.
He explains this very commentary with the words "An example," and so on.

Now, one who asserts that the reason "because of the prohibition of permanence" is contradictory to the established doctrine (siddhānta) by means of the prohibition of destruction, incurs a contradiction with the scripture (*śāstra*).
And since a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) designated as "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*) is not [simply] contradictory, he says: "These two statements contradict each other's meaning.
For a reason becomes "mistimed" when it is sublated by a more firmly established means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Just as the argument that "liquor should be drunk by a Brahmin because it is a liquid substance, like milk" is fallacious—since it is taught:
"Liquor is to be known as threefold: that made from molasses, that made from flour, and that made from honey;
as one is, so are all; it must not be drunk by those who proclaim the Veda."
By such extremely firm scriptures as these, [the opponent's position] becomes a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) due to being "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*).
However, in the case of the statement under discussion, because the meanings are mutually contradictory, neither finds a firm footing;
yet one cannot be sublated by the other, since both possess equal strength. Therefore, the meaning is that this is not a "mistimed" fallacy.
He states another interpretation: "Or there is a contradiction between the proposition and the reason.
This proposition, namely, "this modification departs from the manifest," is contradicted by the reason, "because of the negation of permanence.
[It means that] it departs from mere manifestation.
However, the meaning of the proposition is that "it does not perish"; this has been explained by the statement, "even when departed, it exists, because perishing is denied.
Likewise, the proposition that "it departs from manifestation" asserts the permanence of the modification; this becomes contradictory with the reason "because permanence is denied.
The phrase "by his own established tenet" means "by his own position."
And regarding this point, the commentary (*bhāṣya*) is easy to understand.
Here, the author of the *Vārttika* raises an objection: "But surely, there is a contradiction with the thesis (*pratijñā-virodha*)."
The contradiction between the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*) is what is meant by "contradiction of the proposition" (*pratijñāvirodha*).
He refutes this, saying: "This is not a fault."

The inclusion of "contradiction of the thesis" (*pratijñāvirodha*) among the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) is intended to show that contradiction is based on the thesis; however, when that same contradiction is intended to be based on the reason (*hetu*), it is included within the fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*). When one speaks of a "contradiction of the reason by the thesis," the intention is that the reason is unestablished for at least one party, and thus the thesis possesses equal force.
But when the reason is established for both [parties], then it is the reason that contradicts the proposition. He concludes: "Therefore... (ataḥ).
This is an example of a contradictory reason (*hetu*).
Contradiction consists in being contradictory.
The fact that sound possesses the property of arising, as established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), subverts the thesis of its permanence.
This is the meaning.

By way of digression, he provides an example of the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) consisting of the contradiction between the two members of the proposition (*pratijñā*), which is distinct from a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*), by stating: "of the contradiction of the proposition."
And this contradiction will be demonstrated in the third chapter;

it is called a "guṇa" (excellence) because it serves as an illustration of the contradiction between a proposition and a reason when they possess equal strength, due to the reason being unestablished for one of the two parties.
The example of contradiction with the reason is: "No single entity exists.
For since the property of having an origin (*utpattimattva*) can be established even if it is unestablished for one of the two parties, it contradicts the meaning of the thesis (*pratijñārtha*).

The meaning is that the distinction lies simply in this: while the opponent asserts that the term for "existence" (bhāva) is applied to a collection (*samūha*), which is a point established for both parties, [the proponent] contradicts the very meaning of the thesis (*pratijñārtha*) by that much. // 6 //

NyS 1.2.7: That [reason] for which there is deliberation regarding the subject matter, and which is adduced for the sake of a definitive conclusion, is the "equal-to-the-subject" (prakaraṇasama) fallacy.
Because of this—*maḥ* // 7 // The author of the Bhāṣya states the meaning of the word *prakaraṇa* as "the two bases of inquiry" (*vimarśādhiṣṭhānau*).
*Vimarśa* means doubt;
these are its two objects.
"Unascertained" means not yet determined;
for it is precisely such [unascertained matters] that are denoted by the terms "proposition" (pakṣa) and "counter-proposition" (pratipakṣa).
It is called a "treatise" (prakaraṇa) based on this etymological derivation: that which is "practiced" (prakriyate), meaning it is undertaken as the object of proof (sādhya).

He explains *cintā* (reflection): Reflection upon that subject (*prakaraṇa*) is the investigation (*samīkṣaṇa*), the deliberation (*ālocana*), or the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) starting from the stage of inquiry (*vimarśa*) until the attainment of certainty (*nirṇaya*).
That [desire to know] is indeed produced by the non-perception of the true nature [of the object].
For one who perceives either eternal properties inseparable from eternity or non-eternal properties inseparable from non-eternity does not doubt or desire to know [the object] therein.

That very same non-perception of eternal properties, or non-perception of non-eternal properties, when adduced by a disputant for the sake of a conclusion due to a variety of underlying intentions, is the *prakaraṇasama* fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*).

Why? Because it is equal with respect to both sides; just as there is a non-perception of non-eternal properties in the case of the position of eternality, so too is there a non-perception of eternal properties in the case of the position of non-eternality.
Thus, this is equal for both sides because it intends merely the non-perception of the true nature [of the subject].
The meaning is that the *prakaraṇasama* [reason], like the context itself, is non-conclusive; furthermore,
this term *prakaraṇasama* is used merely as a conventional designation for its etymological basis.
The basis for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*), however, is the state of having a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣatva*);
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*) would be considered a "neutralized" reason (*prakaraṇasama*).
By the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) "that by which something is made known," it is called an "illustration" (*nidarśana*).

The phrase "where it is equal" excludes the suspicion of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) regarding this counter-balanced reason (*satpratipakṣa*); that is, it is "equal to doubt" because it is non-conclusive.
This is what is meant:

For there is no non-perception of a property of the eternal in a case where the eternal is established for both parties, by which [reason] it would be inconclusive; nor is there a non-perception of a property of the non-eternal in a case where the non-eternal is accepted by both, by which it would be inconclusive.
Rather, these two are [rendered inconclusive] precisely through their being counter-arguments to one another (*satpratipakṣatā*).
Regarding the phrase "the state of being a fallacy of the reason" (*hetvābhāsatva*):

since the author of the Sūtras stated that "it is because of this that there is deliberation on the matter," the author of the Vārttika demonstrates the meaning of the word "because" (*yasmāt*) by first posing the question: "Why? (*kasmāt*).
He teaches the causality [of this] by way of the non-perception of reality through the method of exclusion (*vyatireka*), beginning with the words "since" (*yasmāt*).
The phrase "for this very reason" (*ata eva*) means "because of the non-perception of reality. He raises an objection with the words "but surely this... (*nanv ayam*).
For a "treatise" (*prakaraṇa*) consists of the thesis and the counter-thesis;
these two are what are to be proven (*sādhya*). That which is equal to those two is "equal to the thing to be proven" (*sādhyasama*).
And thus, the meaning is that *prakaraṇasama* need not be taught separately from the *sādhyasama* fallacy.
He refutes this by stating: "It is not undistinguished."

Although the term *prakaraṇasama* (the "equal-to-the-issue") has, by etymological derivation, the same meaning as "not distinct from the probandum" (*sādhyāviśiṣṭa*), nevertheless its actual basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is the state of having a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣatva*).
Nor is that [state] unestablished in itself.
For the sense is that it is easily attained because of the absence of apprehension.
Having restated the opponent's view, he refutes it by pointing out an over-extension: "But those who [say] 'because it is a cause of doubt'... He objects: "It is a collection.
That in the presence of which something necessarily occurs is the cause.
And since it occurs when there is a collection, but not in each individual member, the sense is that no single [member] is the cause.
He refutes this with the words: "The collection is the cause."
For a collection of things that are not causes themselves cannot constitute a cause, as this would lead to an over-extension of the principle;
nor can there be a distinctness in a collection for one who does not perceive a distinctness in the individual members of that collection.
Therefore, it is only the members of the collection, existing in mutual conjunction, that constitute the cause.
And thus, it is logically established that perception can be a cause of doubt.
Furthermore, it is not the case that whatever, when present, necessarily brings about an effect is its cause.
However, we shall explain in the *Lakṣaṇabhaṅgabhaṅga* that [the definition] holds only when [the cause] exists, and not when it does not exist.
Now, one might object that the non-perception of both properties is common to both sides and is therefore indeed inconclusive; to this he says: "In the case of the non-perception of both properties.
Here, the non-perception of both properties is not the reason, but rather the non-perception of one property.
And this [reason] is not common to both sides;
rather, it means it is the counter-position to that.

Because it is impossible to state [the reason] as being "equal to the point at issue" (*prakaraṇasama*) due to the non-perception of any distinction between the two, he refutes another example of the *prakaraṇasama* by stating: "But as for being other than the body..."
It is said that others offer the following example: "The self is eternal because it is distinct from the body, like space."
In that regard, when one perceives the self as distinct from the body and realizes its reality as permanence,
one does not then proceed to investigate that permanence.
However, when one does not perceive that reality of permanence— even while perceiving the self's distinction from the body— one then proceeds [to investigate].

Therefore, it is the non-perception of the true nature [of the self] through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) alone that initiates the deliberation on the subject (*prakaraṇacintā*), and not the distinctness from the body.
Consequently, this is not an example of the "neutralized" (*prakaraṇasama*) fallacy;
rather, it is simply the non-perception of the true nature.
For this reason as well, he states that this is not an example of the *prakaraṇasama* [fallacy]: "And being other than the body is inconclusive.
He concludes: "Therefore, this is neither the meaning of the sūtra nor the subject matter of the sūtra."
In this manner, other examples of counter-balanced arguments (*satpratipakṣa*) should also be inferred. // 7 //
NS 1.2.8: That which is not distinct from the probandum, because it is itself yet to be proven, is "equal to the probandum" (sādhyasama).
*sādhyā-maḥ* // 7 // Here, *sādhyasama* is the designation of the term to be defined (*lakṣya-nirdeśa*);
*sādhyāviśiṣṭa* is the definition (*lakṣaṇa*).

Thus, by this [definition], there is a comprehensive inclusion of the unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*), the unestablished in part (*ekadeśāsiddha*), the unestablished in its locus (*āśrayāsiddha*), and the unestablished otherwise (*anyathāsiddha*),

because they are indistinguishable from the probandum (*sādhya*) due to their lack of establishment. And although it would have been sufficient here to say that the unestablished is "equal to the probandum" (*sādhyasama*), the use of the term "indistinguishable from the probandum" (*sādhyāviśiṣṭa*) is for the purpose of making known that even the "unestablished for one of the two parties" (*anyatarāsiddha*) is not a valid reason prior to its establishment.

Otherwise, there would be the misconception that the "unestablished-for-one-of-the-two" (anyatarāsiddha) is actually nothing but the "absolutely unestablished" (atyantāsiddha), which is identical to the "unestablished-as-the-probandum" (sādhyasama), because the former is sometimes established; however,
even that [anyatarāsiddha] is included within the category of what is not distinct from the probandum.
[Objection: But in that case, because it is non-different from the probandum (*sādhya*), it would be unestablished for one of the two parties (*anyatarāsiddha*) alone, and not the others;
for there is no lack of non-difference from the probandum in those [other cases] due to their being unestablished. To this [the author replies]:
The author of the Sūtras has stated that it is "because it is yet to be proven" (sādhyatvāt).
For if that which is to be proven were not unestablished, it would cease to be "that which is to be proven," since what is already established is certainly not proven.
Therefore, because it is yet to be proven, it is unestablished;
and since this applies to some at all times and to others only occasionally, it is common to all [cases], and thus there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*).

Nor is there an over-extension (*atiprasakti*) or over-pervasion (*ativyāpti*) regarding the state of being the probandum (*sādhyatva*), because the specific definition of that [fallacy] depends upon the general definition of a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*). This is the meaning of the Sūtra. Furthermore, the phrase *sādhanīyatvāt* found in the Bhāṣya is an explanation of *na sādhyatvāt*.
Rather, it is intended to show that the possession of motion is unestablished.
Here the author of the Vārttika explains the meaning of the sūtra: "that which is not distinct from the probandum.
He says this so that there may be no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to the probandum.

His intention is that since this definition applies when the general definition of a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) is present—namely, being a property of the subject (*sādhanadharma*)—there is no deviation.

In this context, the author of the Bhāṣya has provided a common example for those [fallacies] that are unestablished in their essential nature (svarūpāsiddha), unestablished in their locus (āśrayāsiddha), and unestablished otherwise (anyathāsiddha): "Shadow is a substance, because it possesses motion.
The author of the Vārttika analyzes that [example]:
"Shadow is a substance..."
Here, he first states the lack of essential proof (*svarūpāsiddhatā*) with the words "just as" (*yathaiva*).

To introduce the lack of proof regarding the locus (*āśrayāsiddhatā*), he establishes the possession of motion in shadow by means of a five-membered syllogism, stating "the state of possessing motion.
He then declares the lack of proof regarding the locus with the words "not, because of the lack of proof regarding the locus" (*nāśrayāsiddhatvāt*).

Since a shadow is indeed real, for one who infers its possession of motion from its observation in another location, that observation in another location is "unestablished with respect to the locus" (*āśrayāsiddha*), because its substratum is unestablished.
This is what was stated: "when [the shadow] exists, there is an absence of substance."
The meaning is that "being" (sattva) exists;
however, shadow is not included within [the categories of] generality, particularity, or inherence, because it lacks permanence.
Nor is it action, because it lacks the status of being a non-inherent cause of conjunction and disjunction.
It is not a quality because it does not inhere in a substance;
nor is it a quality of the mind, space, or time,
because the qualities of those are imperceptible.
Nor is it a quality of the self, because it is perceptible by the external sense faculties;
nor is it a quality of space or air, because their qualities are not visible to the eye.
Nor does it belong to fire, because of its opposition to fire and because no other quality concomitant with it is perceived;
for the same reason, it does not belong to earth or water either.
Moreover, its quality, which is visual, cannot be perceived without light;
yet it is claimed that shadow is perceived in the absence of that [light], but not when it is present— this is a contradiction.
Nor is it a substance;
for that would have to be one of the [four] beginning with earth, or else a tenth [substance] distinct from them. It is not.
It is not tenable that it be one or another [of those], because its qualities are not perceived; nor is it logical that it be something else possessing form.
Since it is impossible for that non-substance (adravya) to be perceptible—
because, being intangible, it lacks cohesion and thus lacks the state of being composed of multiple substances—
it is established that shadow is indeed the absence of light, and not a real entity.

As for one who thinks: "Let it be that the shadow is not a real entity; let it be a mere absence of light (*bhābhāva*). Nevertheless, there is no fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*), because the perception [of the shadow] in another location has precisely the absence of light as its locus"—to him, the author replies by showing that even if this is granted, the reason is superfluous (*anyathāsiddha*) and thus equivalent to the probandum (*sādhyasama*). He says "even if granted" (*abhyupetya*);
for it was established in the definition of inference that the natural (*svābhāvika*) relation of the reason with the probandum is a constituent of inference, and not a conditional (*aupādhika*) one.
Thus, this pseudo-reason (*hetvābhāsa*) is an "otherwise-established" (*anyathāsiddha*) adventitious relation (*aupādhikasambandha*).
This non-establishment (*asiddhi*) of the reason is twofold: by way of its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*) and by way of being a reason (*hetutvena*).
It is also twofold by way of its own nature.
And [it is invalid] because of the lack of establishment of its own locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*).

Nor does this mean that the "inconclusive" (*savyabhicāra*) and other fallacies are included within the "unestablished" (*asiddha*) simply because their status as valid reasons is unestablished; for they are distinct from it due to their specific qualifiers, such as being inconclusive.

However, the "otherwise established" (*anyathāsiddha*), which cannot serve as a qualifier for those [other fallacies], is included within the "equal to the probandum" (*sādhyasama*) merely because its status as a valid reason is unestablished.
Thus everything is clear. He summarizes: "This is that.
These varieties of the unestablished (asiddha) are to be understood even in the case of different examples.
For example, "Sound is eternal because it is visible" is unestablished in itself (*svarūpāsiddha*);
"God is not the creator of the body, the world, and so forth, because he is bodiless" is unestablished in its locus (*āśrayāsiddha*).
The argument that "he is dark-skinned because he is the son of Maitra, like the group of sons of Maitra who are seen [to be dark]" is *anyathāsiddha* (established otherwise);
for the difference in complexion is established otherwise as being caused by differences in the digestion of food and drink.
By the word "also" (*api*) in the *Bhāṣya*, it is indicated that this [reason] is also *asiddha* (unestablished).
It is indicated that [the reason] is unestablished because the shadow of the substratum also exists.
In this regard, the Venerable One has refuted this by imagining another example that possesses the same characteristics as the probandum (*sādhyasama*);
for it is said that his [original] example was:
"It is eternal."
"Sound is [non-eternal] because it lacks tangibility, like cognition"—
having refuted this by showing that it is unestablished (*asiddha*) in all three ways, the Bhadanta raised the following doubt:

"If a reason is called a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) when its example is not distinct from the probandum (*sādhyāviśiṣṭa*), then [this reason] is unestablished because the example, cognition, is not established as eternal."
Having raised this objection, [the opponent's position] was refuted on the grounds that it lacks the status of a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
The author of the *Vārttika* refutes all of this by rejecting it—stating "sound is eternal.
To the question, "If this is not the example, what then is the example, or what is the meaning of the sūtra?", he says: "But as we [have explained]..."
The meaning is that this is the fault stated by the Venerable One.
Why? To this he says: the Venerable One has not understood the meaning of the Sūtra;
for by this [definition], that which is deviant (savyabhicāra) is not characterized, such that "not being tangible" (asparśavattva) would serve as an example of something deviant for it.
However, [the reason] is "equal to the probandum" (sādhyasama).
Nor has the literal meaning been understood through the refutation of the *vyadhikaraṇa-bahuvrīhi* compound.

Furthermore, by treating the pseudo-example "like cognition" (*buddhivat*) as a pseudo-reason (*hetvābhāsa*), the Venerable Master has demonstrated that he understands both pseudo-reasons and pseudo-examples; this is the meaning. // 8 //
NyS 1.2.9: A reason stated when the time has passed is "mistimed" (kālātīta).
"Kālātītaḥ" (9). Here, "kālātīta" is the designation of the term to be defined (*lakṣya*), while "kālātyayāpadiṣṭa" is the definition (*lakṣaṇa*).
For the time [of the statement] of a reason (*hetu*) or a probans (*apadeśa*) is characterized by the presence of doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhya*).
As they have said:
"Reasoning does not proceed regarding what is unperceived or what is already certain, but rather regarding what is doubtful."
Others also say:
"Because the statement of a reason occurs when there is doubt."
And where there is contradiction with perception, inference, or scripture—
such as "fire is not hot because it is a substance," "sound is not audible because it is a quality," and "the human skull is pure because it is a part of a living being."

All of that, by means of a contrary determination based on a valid means of knowledge, passes beyond the time characterized by doubt; thus, being designated as such because of the lapse of that time, it is called "kālātīta" (the "missed-timely").
And so it has been illustrated:

As for the statement, "That which contradicts perception and scripture is a fallacy of reasoning (*nyāyābhāsa*)," here the author of the *Vārttika* has resolved the Buddhist objection that sublation (*bādha*) and invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) cannot coexist. This being established, the author of the *Bhāṣya* explains the Sūtra as being consistent with both his own and other schools' views: "By 'lapse of time' (*kālātyaya*)—that is, by the lapse of the time of doubt—is characterized the object of the reason being stated, of which only a portion [is valid]."
For the subject qualified by the property is the object indicated by the reason; indeed,
it is pervaded by the reason,
and a portion of that [subject] is the property to be proven (sādhyadharma).
For that subject (dharmin) has had its time of doubt bypassed by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) which establishes a property contrary to it;
such a reason is "indicated as having passed the [proper] time" (kālātyayāpadiṣṭa), or "one whose time has elapsed" (kālātīta)—
this is the meaning according to his own view.

And since this has already been cited previously, it is not cited here for fear of redundancy. Furthermore, according to the opponent's view, a reason is "vitiated by lapse of time" (kālātyaya) when one part of its objective form— that is to say, a specific qualification of the reason— is [already superseded].
The construction is: "that is [the fallacy] called *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*. He states an illustration according to the view of the opponent itself, saying: "the illustration."
And since "permanence" (nityatva) here is intended merely as continued existence, there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) by means of examples such as jars, which are manifested by contact with light.

Having thus presented this five-membered syllogism, he declares that the reason—specifically the one part of it, the qualifier "contact"—is a fallacious reason (hetvābhāsa) because the time for its manifestation has passed, stating: "This is not a valid reason."

Furthermore, since this fallacy of the reason (hetvābhāsa) due to the unestablished qualification is in fact identical to the "equal to the probandum" (sādhyasama), it need not be mentioned separately; thus, this fault was not pointed out by the author of the Bhāṣya in its full detail.
Furthermore, as for the Venerable One’s explanation regarding the "mistimed" (kālātīta) reason: the time for a reason is immediately after the proposition;
a reason stated subsequently, having passed beyond that [time], becomes mistimed.
For example: "Sound is impermanent..."

When it has been stated, "like a jar and so forth," and one is questioned as to why [it is so], one states the reason, "because of being produced" (*kṛtakatvāt*); this is a "mistimed" (*kālātīta*) reason. And it is refuted by him [the opponent] in this way: "Is this question of the opponent directed at the proponent when he is already free from doubt?"
Or is it when it is expectant?
If it is non-expectant, then its defeat-ground (*nigrahasthāna*) is simply deficiency (*nyūna*), not a fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*), because that [reason] was not employed.
For either a valid reason (*hetu*) or its fallacy (*tadābhāsa*) must be formally adduced,
not one that is not adduced.
Now, if the opponent’s question is raised while the proponent is still in the midst of an expectation for further argument, [the debate remains incomplete].

Nevertheless, even if this reason is employed later, it remains a valid reason; for at that time, it is neither not invariably concomitant with its own probandum, nor is it a non-property of the subject (*apakṣadharma*).
Therefore, there is no such thing as a "fallacious reason" (hetvābhāsa) that transcends time;
this is the refutation of the Venerable One (Bhadanta).
He refutes [the objection] by not accepting this explanation, stating: "But as for the statement that consists of a reversal of the members...
He asks for the reason for not accepting it: "Why? The answer is: "Of which..."
The "connection with the meaning" (*arthasaṃbandha*) is the connection by virtue of the capacity of the meaning.
Furthermore, he says "of the parts," etc., to show that [the connection] is not accepted even because of tautology (*paunaruktya*).
The Vārttika, beginning with "of that which is being pointed out" and ending with "is stated again," has been explained by the very explanation of the Bhāṣya.
He raises an objection: "Because [the object] is denoted once it has been made equal."
The meaning is this:
this is not a point of defeat (nigrahasthāna) consisting of "premature statement" (aprāptakāla),
but rather it is simply a fallacy of the reason (hetvābhāsa).

This is indeed called the "reversal of the members" (avayavaviparyāsa), wherein a proponent employs the proposition (*pratijñā*), the example (*udāharaṇa*), and so forth by means of a single continuous discourse, and only afterwards employs the reason (*hetu*); however, this [case] occurs when,
having employed the proposition and the example, he has ceased and is subsequently questioned by the opponent.
He employs a reason;
therefore,
when the subject has been made equal by the refutation of the charge of deficiency.

If it is argued that this is a *hetvābhāsa* (fallacious reason) called "mistimed" (*kālātīta*)— because the reason is stated after the [thesis] has already been reduced to the status of a mere *pakṣa* (the subject of proof) and displaced from the state of being established,
and not because it is "untimely" (*aprāptakāla*) as a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*)— then [the response follows].
He refutes this with the words "by what?
If the thesis has been leveled by the statement of a reason through [the charge of] deficiency, what is the incapacity of the reason here?
For one thing is not rendered faulty by the defect of another; such is the meaning.
The opponent, being suspicious, says: "This belongs to him.
[The proponent] refutes it: "This is not so.
If one who has been defeated by way of deficiency is to be defeated later by means of a subsequent statement, then let the proponent alone be defeated, and not the other.

The meaning is that since this [reason] was stated later by you, it is capable of being refuted; therefore, it is not a fallacious reason (hetvābhāsa) merely because it was stated after [the opponent's position] has been established. He concludes the refutation of both [positions] with the words "Therefore" (tasmāt). // 9 //
Quibble (chala) is the subversion of a statement by means of an alternative interpretation of its meaning.

In accordance with the order of the enumeration, since *chala* (quibble) was enumerated immediately after the fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), the author of the Bhāṣya states that the definition of *chala* also follows immediately after the definition of the fallacious reasons: "Now, quibble (*chala*) is speech... (NS 1.2.10). It is the conceptualization (*kalpanā*) of a meaning contrary to the meaning intended by the speaker.
That itself is the justification for that [omission].
Now, as to why an example is not provided for the general definition of *chala*—as one might be for other definitions—he says: "Not in the general definition."
Every example possesses both the universal and the particular;
the meaning is that since a universal devoid of particulars does not exist, it is impossible to provide an example of a universal alone.
As for the phrase "but in the case of division":
"Vibhāga" means that which is being analyzed; it is the specific characteristic.
In this regard, there are examples. // 10 //
That [quibble] is of three kinds: quibble regarding speech (*vākchala*), quibble regarding a general term (*sāmānyacchala*), and quibble regarding metaphorical usage (*upacāracchala*).

Having stated the general definition of *chala*, he introduces the sūtra on classification (*vibhāga*)—which serves as the definition for its specific types—in order to state those specific definitions and first to exclude [the notions of] too few or too many categories: "And the classification...
Here, "classification" (*vibhāga*) refers to the sūtra by which [the subject] is classified.
That is three times eleven. // 11 //
Quibble regarding speech (*vākchala*) is the imagining of another meaning for a statement whose meaning has been expressed without qualification, based on the speaker's intention.
And therein he introduces the specific definition:
among those quibbles (*chala*), the quibble regarding words (*vākchala*) is defined as follows—[it is] "unrestricted" (avi-).
In one instance, the analysis of the compound is: "he has a new blanket" (*navaḥ kambalo 'sya*).
The distinction lies in the analysis [of the compound] as "one who has nine blankets" (*nava-kambala*) in one case and "elsewhere" (*aparatra*) in the other.
He explains the etymology of *vākchala* (verbal quibble): "quibble regarding speech" means a quibble when speech is the cause (*nimitta*).
The meaning is that in both cases, such as "nine blankets" (*navakambala*), the speech is the same, serving as the causal basis.
It has been stated that this *chala* (quibble) is to be employed in debate (*jalpa*) at the stage of defeat;
it has also been stated that its function is the interrogation (*paryanuyoga*) of the opponent's statement.
Therefore, in this regard, as to how the interrogation is to be conducted:
The author of the Commentary (Bhāṣyakāra) demonstrates this for the benefit of his students: "This is the counter-argument.
The meaning is that when both meanings are possible, it is improper to abandon the meaning of the term that is possible and instead imagine a meaning of the term that is impossible.
Now, one might ask: how does the speaker also cause the understanding of a specific meaning by means of a common word?
And if he does not cause such understanding, how can he be called an "informant"? To this, he says: "And because it is well-known.
He states the nature of the relationship: it is the restriction between the signifier and the signified.
"This very word has this very meaning"— in that regard, the person's injunction is of such a form as: "From this [word], this alone is to be understood."
To the question, "What follows if this is so?", he says: "And they have been previously employed.
To the further question, "Even so, what of it?", he says: "And the employment..."
He applies this arrangement of the stages to the present context: "In that case, it is for the sake of understanding the meaning.
What is meant is this:
at the time of establishing a convention, or in the linguistic usage of elders, no word makes a particular object known by seizing it directly like a horn; rather, [it does so through a process].
By means of the universal, assisted by context, purpose, and so forth, the word functions with respect to the particular.
Therefore, it is not the fault of the speaker that he does not convey the particular through words for particulars;
rather, it is the fault of the convention that the words operate upon the universal while setting aside the particular.
Therefore, it is established that the user is not at fault when he causes understanding according to convention.
He demonstrates this very capacity [of words] with the statement: "In whatever meaning there is an injunction of action..."

It might be argued as follows: it is not correct to say that "an object is denoted without distinction," for the word *navakambala* does not denote some object without distinction independently of context and so forth, unlike words such as *go* (cow). Indeed, there exists no common property (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*)—such as "cowness" (*gotva*) in the case of Bāhuleya and other cows—which subsists both in a specific number and in novelty, which the word could thus denote. Therefore...
The author of the Vārttika says: "When there is a general hearing" (*sāmānyaśruti*).
"Abhihiti" means that which is expressed, namely, its utterance.
The word "samāna" (common) does not mean identity of meaning; rather, it means generality (*sāmānya*).
The noun-phrase "horse" (*aśva*) is the designator of "horseness" (*aśvatva*);
when the verbal phrase "horse" is employed while facing someone, [it functions as such].

Then it is understood that "you have grown. He objects: "Without distinction," meaning that a word, being identical [in form], produces doubt regarding its referent, but does not denote a specific meaning.

He refutes [the objection] with the words "not from context and so forth. The meaning is that there is a doubt regarding the sense, as in the case of "The white one runs," where one wonders whether it is a dog that is running very fast, or a leper who is washing himself.
He states the purpose of the term "artha" [in the sūtra] as follows: "The mention of 'artha'...
When a word is heard without qualification, there arises the postulation of another meaning [other than its primary one].
The meaning is "not sound.
He explains the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "the counter-argument against this" and so forth by saying "of that," which is easy to understand. // 12 //
NyS 1.2.13: Quibble regarding the general (*sāmānyacchala*) is the imagining of an impossible meaning due to the connection with an overly general sense of a possible meaning.
Enough with this arising. // 13 //

When there is a prohibition based on the assumption of an impossible meaning— by connecting the most general property of "brahminhood" found in an outcast brahmin (*vrātya*) with the excellence of knowledge and conduct, which belongs specifically to a particular type of brahmin— this is *sāmānyacchala* (quibble regarding the general).

"Aha! This brahmin is indeed endowed with knowledge and conduct"—this statement was spoken by one who granted [the claim] for the sake of praise, implying that the perfection of knowledge and conduct is possible in a brahmin;
yet even this sentence is merely for the sake of praise, and it does not mean that his possession of knowledge and conduct is due to the cause of his being a brahmin.

Regarding the term "intended" (*vivakṣita*): in this case, the opponent, having superimposed upon it an unintended meaning of the reason (*hetu*), refutes the statement; thus, this is a "quibble regarding the general" (*sāmānyacchala*).
It is a restatement of the subject matter (*viṣayānuvāda*).
Thus,
the meaning is that this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the Brahminhood which is the object of the accomplishment (*saṃpad*).
Of what? Of a person for whom the cause is not intended to be expressed.
The author of the Vārttika explains this with the words "of the universal" (sāmānyasya);
the meaning is that the universal is understood as having its intended object [already] apprehended.
The remainder is easily understood. //13//
NyS 1.2.14: When there is an instruction based on a distinction of properties, the denial of the actual existence of the object is quibble regarding metaphorical usage (*upacāra-chala*).
The path of Dharma. //14// The property of sound is its usage; its "alternative" (vikalpa) refers to its twofold nature. Usage is of two kinds.
It is both primary and secondary;
therein, the primary is the general rule, while the secondary arises from some exception to it.
It is figurative. Regarding this, the author of the Bhāṣya says: "The rule that a word used in its primary sense [denotes its object] is the general principle (*autsargika-dharma*).
Is this [the case] here alone?"

He says "no"—the term *vikalpa* means twofoldness. What is this second [type]? To this he says: the application elsewhere of a general rule (*utsarga*) that has been observed in one context, due to some exception (*apavāda*). Thus, when there is an instruction in a sentence by means of such a fixed alternative of properties (*dharmavikalpa*), [the following applies].
It is designated by this [term] according to its etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*).

In that regard, when there is an intention to speak figuratively (*bhākta-vivakṣā*), as in the case of "the platforms are crying out," there is a negation [of the literal meaning] due to the non-existence of the actual object.
He states that very existence of the object: "The men on the platform are shouting, but the platforms themselves do not shout.
According to the view of the Vārttika, however, it should be explained as a negation of the very existence of the object.

Now, if it were the case that what is seen in one place is applied elsewhere, then alas, everything would be applied everywhere! To this he says: "Metaphorical application (*upacāra*) has its meaning established (*nītārtha*), i.e., its referent brought forward (*prāpitārtha*) by means of a cause such as association (*sahacaraṇa*) and so forth."
The application elsewhere of what has been seen in another place occurs precisely because of a connection;
thus, there is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
This means it does not occur by mere whim (chandataḥ), nor by deception (chadmanā).
Now, if an explanation were possible even through a figurative sense, then nothing at all spoken by a mere chatterer would be faulty.
Since everything can be established in some way as being figurative, he says: "of that which is primary.
While it would have been sufficient to say merely "of the figurative," the inclusion of the word "primary" is for the purpose of obtaining an example by virtue of its being an established fact.
A metaphorical usage (upacāra) must be one established in common worldly practice, not something unprecedented, unless there is a specific purpose;
and this metaphorical usage, namely "the platforms are crying out," is indeed established in common worldly practice.
The *vārttika* devoted to the explanation of the *sūtra* is [referred to] by the term "instruction on the conceptualization of dharmas" found within the *sūtra*.

The expression "the application (*prayoga*) of a word is a *dharma*" is stated in two ways; he states this twofold nature as follows: "it is the primary [meaning]. Thus, this is the conventional usage of the signifier (*abhidhāna*) and the signified (*abhidheya*).
The denoter is the word; the denoted is that which is to be understood. And that [denoted] is in some cases the expressed meaning (vācya).
In some cases, the meaning is that [the term] is used in a figurative sense. // 14 //
NyS 1.2.15: Figurative quibble is merely verbal quibble, because there is no difference between them.

Because the section on examination (*parīkṣāparvan*) is imminent, for that purpose, in the section on characteristics (*lakṣaṇaparvan*) as well, the author of the aphorisms examines the concealed characteristic (*channalakṣaṇa*) [in the following]: "Speech... (Sūtra 1.1.15).
The construction is as follows: having assumed that a word for a quality which actually has the sense of a location (*sthāna*) is itself a word for the primary object (*pradhāna*).

For just as in the case of the word *vākśvala*, the word *nava*—which has the new meaning [of nine]—is conceived as a numerical difference, so it is here as well; such is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). // 15 //
No, because that [quality] is a different entity from that [substance].
The sūtra of the established conclusion: "Not so"—16.

The meaning is that this [fallacy] is a "verbal quibble" (*vākchala*) because it consists in the postulation of a different meaning for the negation of the actual existence of an object based on a deceptive usage (*upacāracchale*).
The author of the *Vārttika* states the intent of the Sūtra regarding the term "because there is no distinction" (*aviśeṣāt*) as follows: [it refers to] the object to be enjoined.
In the expression "the beds cry out" (*mañcāḥ krośanti*), the act of crying out is what is being enjoined, while "the beds" is merely restated;
for this very reason...
But regarding the quality (*guṇa*), there is the postulation of another meaning;
thus, in the case of "the platforms" (*mañcāḥ*), this [word] is secondary (*bhākta*) as it refers to something non-primary by way of being restated (*anūdyatayā*),
but not [in the sense that they are actually] crying out.
According to the principle that "the primary meaning of a word does not extend beyond its injunction," it is the very act of crying out that is prohibited here as it is being enjoined.

It is not by means of a deceptive statement such as "the beds are crying," nor in the sentence "Devadatta has a new blanket," where Devadatta is the subject (anūdyamāna) and a blanket qualified by novelty is the predicate (vidheya).
In that case, the existence of the entity to be predicated— the blanket— is not being negated.
However, the established conclusion is that there is a great difference [between the two views], because [in the former case] there is a multiplicity of parts within that single entity. // 16 //
Or, if there were no distinction [between types of quibble], it would follow that all quibbles would be one and the same, on account of some common property.

[The opponent says: "Not so, sir. [The author replies: Because of some similarity, if there is an absence of three, then there follows the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the absence of even two, which has been accepted.
For one who says "yes" [to this], there follows the undesirable consequence of the destruction of all distinctions by virtue of their being real entities (*vastutva*).
The *Bhāṣya* and *Vārttika* on this point have meanings that are not obscure. // 17 //
NyS 1.2.18: A futile rejoinder (jāti) is an opposition based on similarity or dissimilarity.

In accordance with the order of the enumeration, the author of the Bhāṣya states the sequence of the definitions of the *jātis*—that is, after the definition of *chala* (sophistry)—as follows: "The proof...
(verse 18). "Pratyavasthāna" means standing in opposition;
if that were the case, it would follow as an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that both *chala* and a valid refutation (*samyagdūṣaṇa*) would also be *jātis*.

Therefore it was said: "by means of similarity and dissimilarity. Now, similarity and dissimilarity do not exist in the case of quibbling (*chala*), nor does a valid refutation arise from mere similarity and dissimilarity alone.
"Rather, it is from the application [of a reason]";
for when a reason or a fallacy thereof is employed, the consequence that arises is a *jāti* (futile rejoinder).
Indeed, in the context of debate (*jalpa*), when the authority of the Vedas is challenged by atheists using fallacious reasons against a learned person, [this is where *jāti* occurs].

Furthermore, when a valid rejoinder does not suddenly occur to him, one should employ a *jāti* (futile rejoinder) even by way of its formal class, so that those who are lords and supporters of the people do not entertain the notion that the Vedas lack authority;
otherwise, there would be a ruin for the subjects who follow the conduct of the Lord.
In some cases, however, the employment of a *jāti* may occur even unintentionally, whether regarding a true reason (*hetu*) or a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*).
By the phrase "an object being born," the etymological basis for the term *jāti* (genus/class) is shown.
The author of the Vārttika explains this as follows: "by way of similarity"—just as when there is a thesis (*pakṣa*), there is a counter-thesis (*pratipakṣa*).
Thus, when there is a formal establishment [of a position], there is a counter-position.
However, the meaning of the Sūtra is to be understood according to the literal text, and not by way of similarity with the examples as explained in the Bhāṣya.
If this is so, then how is the Bhāṣya to be understood?
To this he says: "For the sake of illustration.
This also applies to the phrase "or by way of dissimilarity" (vaidharmyeṇa).
The meaning is that this is cited for the sake of illustration according to the scripture (*yathāśruti*), and not according to the commentary (*yathābhāṣyam*).
He elaborates upon this explanation by first posing a question regarding its merits: "For what purpose is this? (verse 18).
Misconception and lack of comprehension are points of defeat.

[The opponent asks: "How is it that a misconception (*vipratipatti*)—which is either a cognition of a subtle object in a distorted way or a cognition of a gross object that is contemptible—is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*)? To this, [the author] says: "one who misapprehends" (*vipratipadyamāna*).

He states the lack of comprehension (*apratipatti*). Regarding the phrase "the object of the undertaking" (*ārambhaviṣaya*), one might ask: since it would have been more concise to say "misconception and lack of comprehension" (*vipratipatty-apratipattī*) using a compound, why was a non-compound used? To this he replies: "And because of the non-compound. The meaning is that there are other points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) in debate (*jalpa*) besides misconception and lack of comprehension—namely, "excess of reason and example"—and these are also included by means of the expansion of the text.
Regarding the commentary beginning with "non-commencement in the sphere of commencement," he explains it as follows: "the non-cognition of the subsequent [aim] for one's own or another's benefit.
Indeed, there are two ways in which non-commencement occurs in the sphere of commencement.

One either does not comprehend a refutation stated by another, or a probans, or a reason for contradiction; this is "non-comprehension of the response" regarding the argument of another. The mention of "response" (uttara) here also indicates the "probans" (sādhana). However, "non-comprehension of the response" regarding one's own case occurs when, having comprehended the probans and the reason for contradiction belonging to the opponent, one fails to comprehend one's own response in order to refute them.
This is the meaning.

He objects: "When a means of proof (sādhana) is employed by oneself and is in fact capable [of establishing the point], how can there be non-comprehension or misconception? This is how it should be understood."
He refutes this with the words "even then":

the meaning is that the cognition of a capable means of proof (*samarthasādhanajñāna*) constitutes the apprehension of the proof (*sādhanapratipatti*), not the mere cognition of the proof (*sādhanamātrajñāna*). // 19 //
NyS 1.2.20: From its various classifications, there arises a multiplicity of *jātis* (futile rejoinders) and *nigrahasthānas* (points of defeat).
In order to introduce another sūtra, the author of the commentary (bhāṣyakāra) says: "But what [is the difference]?
Although there is indeed a distinction between examples based on similarity (sādharmya) and dissimilarity (vaidharmya), [the following is stated].
Nevertheless, non-difference was stated with the intention of referring to the non-difference of their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
That is its nature. "Various conceptual constructions" (*nānā-kalpa*) refers to them in terms of their essential form (*svarūpataḥ*).
"Various" means by way of their types;
"according to their characteristics" means according to their intrinsic natures.
The author of the Vārttika summarizes the meaning of the chapter, stating: "The proposition of the system.

This refers to the aphorism (sūtra) which states that the attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) results from the knowledge of the true nature of the categories beginning with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For the scripture itself states that the knowledge of reality consists of [the following]:
"Samsara is the cycle of suffering, birth, activity, defects, and false knowledge."
And the cessation of that [pain] occurs through consciousness; when each subsequent [element] is removed, the one immediately preceding it ceases to exist, which constitutes liberation (*apavarga*).
Therefore, that which was the enumeration by means of the sutra beginning with "the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*), etc., [is established].
The second sutra consists of its surrounding context; the summary is given by means of two [verses]. The remainder is easily understood. // 20 //
Thus ends the second daily lesson of the first chapter in the *Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā* composed by Vācaspatimiśra.
The first chapter is completed. *Oṃ*.
In the *Nyāyavārtikatātparyaṭīkā*, the second chapter begins.

The author of the Vārttika states, "And of this [treatise], it is threefold," expressing the doubt that must be refuted by the Bhāṣya's statement, "Now follows the examination of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth.

He argues that since the statement regarding the examination applies to those things that have a fixed position and a fixed sequence, it is logical that the means of valid cognition alone is what is being examined.
Why was the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) not examined here at the outset? Rather, he says "having bypassed those" because it is doubt itself that is being examined.
He states the meaning of the Bhāṣya—"Why is there this difference in order?"—as follows:
"Because it is a subordinate member of the investigation (parīkṣā).
For it was the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that was defined first, in accordance with the order of the enumeration (*uddeśa*).
However, doubt has no utility whatsoever regarding the definition [of a category].
Since all investigation consists in deliberation, doubt necessarily precedes it in the sequence of the stages of investigation;
just as one says, "He performs the agnihotra sacrifice."
In the statement "he cooks gruel," the cooking of the gruel occurs prior to the Agnihotra sacrifice because it serves as a means for that sacrifice;
furthermore, since it is the *definition* of doubt (*saṃśaya-lakṣaṇa*) that is being examined here, rather than doubt itself, there is no infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
He explains:
"But has it not been said?
This investigation, however, pertains to the treatise (*śāstra*).
And since that [ascertainment] is not necessarily preceded by doubt, there is no sequential order of meaning; thus, the order of enunciation (*uddeśakrama*) need not be subverted—this is the meaning.
He replies: "True, there is no such rule regarding ascertainment.
Not every ascertainment is preceded by doubt.
Every deliberation (*vicāra*) is preceded by doubt;
since there is deliberation in both scriptural study and debate, it too must be preceded by doubt.
Furthermore, the absence of inquiry in the scripture pertains to the learned teacher and the opponent, not to those being instructed.
Therefore, it is established that even in the treatise (*śāstra*), investigation is preceded by deliberation. "Doubt" (*saṃśīti*) is the etymological derivation of "uncertainty" (*saṃśaya*);
its meaning is that one does not ascertain [the object]. (182/2)
NyS 2.1.1: Doubt does not arise from the ascertainment of common or multiple properties, nor from the ascertainment of one of the two properties.
Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that, just as the meaning of the definition was previously determined, so too is the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) baseless?
To this he says: "Of that, according to the literal hearing [of the text].
For the meaning to be established through investigation is understood directly from the words of the definition by means of the commentary; such is the sense.
The phrase "these two are similar" indicates direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*).
For one who directly perceives both a post and a person, as well as some common property belonging to them, cannot be in doubt; this is the meaning.
[This is so] because [the cognition] consists of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*).
Certainty does not produce uncertainty,
because an effect must conform to its cause; thus,
the phrase "not from the determination of a common property alone" is intended as an illustration of all the causes mentioned in the definition of doubt.
"And because they exist in a single substratum" means that the height and girth of a post are not the very same as those of a person. // 1 //
NyS 2.1.2: And because of disagreement, lack of consensus, and misconception.
And because there is agreement even in the face of disagreement.
And because non-determination is determined within a self that is not itself determined.
And because there is agreement even in the face of disagreement, the meaning is that there is no such thing as disagreement due to a contradiction in essential nature. // 2-4 //
Likewise, there would be perpetual doubt, because of the constant occurrence of its properties.

Likewise, "extreme doubt" refers to the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) of one who, through another term, does not perceive a qualification of the occurrence of common properties and so forth. // 5 //

NyS 2.1.6: Precisely from the aforementioned determination, when there is a dependence on its specific qualities, there arises doubt; neither is there an absence of doubt, nor is there perpetual doubt.
He states the established conclusion: "The answer to this is as follows" (Sūtra 6). Or rather: [as stated in] Sūtra 6.

If the cause of doubt were stated to be the perception of common properties and so forth without qualification, then because that [cause] does not exist later, one would not doubt even before; thus there would be no doubt at all. Or, because it exists before, one would not cease to doubt later either.
Therefore, the meaning is that this unqualified state is not the cause of doubt, and thus there is neither an absence of doubt nor an absolute state of doubt.
"By this" means by the employment of the word *samāna*;
for it was explained previously that the word *samāna* has the meaning of "similar.
As for this [objection] regarding the absence of similarity (*sārūpyābhāvāt*)... (184)
7) Regarding "of determination and doubt, which are cause and effect":
the meaning is that the non-determination of the specific characteristic is common to both.
However, the similarity mentioned by the author of the Bhāṣya should not be understood in that way.
For if the production of cause and effect were similarity, that [definition] would be both over-extensive and under-extensive;
because even eternal things possess causality.
Therefore, the word "similarity" is not a designation for similarity itself.
Rather, he says "because of the existence of the cause" in order to demonstrate the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) between cause and effect.
This has already been refuted by the fact that reality is not apprehended precisely because of non-determination (*anavadhāraṇa*).
Even in the case of two counter-balanced reasons (*satpratipakṣa*), since they are not observed together elsewhere, they are included within the "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) fallacy;
however, the intention is that they constitute separate fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) when each is intended individually.

Nor does doubt arise from non-determination alone; the meaning is that this [non-determination] is not an independent cause, but rather functions as an accessory through the occurrence of common characteristics and so forth. As for what was said regarding "disagreement":
There is disagreement with respect to the object, but agreement with respect to its essential nature;
this should also be understood to apply to cases where there is no such fixed distinction. // 6 //
Where there is doubt, there is this successive application of further questions.
"Whose [is this]? is the question regarding the purport of this sūtra. The answer is "by oneself.

Since all investigations are preceded by doubt, one who desires to investigate should not refute the causes that give rise to doubt; rather, when such a doubt has been raised by others, [one should address it].
It is to be resolved by the aforementioned causes of resolution.
The meaning of "vathohitvā" in the Bhāṣya is "even that which was stated"; the meaning is "in the discourse of the treatise characterized as a formal debate (vāda). // 7 //
NyS 2.1.8: Perception and the other means of knowledge are not valid, because they cannot be established in any of the three periods of time.
For if the means of valid cognition were established prior [to the object], perception would not arise from the contact of the sense organ with its object.
Now follows the commentary beginning with "The examination of the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇaparīkṣā*).
For, by the sequence according to the subject matter (*ārtha*) stated in the examination of doubt (*saṃśayaparīkṣā*), the order of the enumeration (*uddeśakrama*) was set aside;
however, in the case of the means of valid cognition and the others, there is no reason for such a setting aside.
In accordance with the order of the topical outline (*uddeśa*), the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) themselves were examined prior to the objects of cognition (*prameya*) and so forth;
therein, first, was the examination of the general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of the means of valid cognition.
Because the specific definitions are preceded by that [general definition].

In this context, the general definition is that "pramāṇa is the means of apprehension"; and since that quality of being a means of apprehension belongs only to perception and the other [means of knowledge], it is said, "of perception and the others."
The author of the Vārttika states this:
"Now then," etc.; he asks concerning that which is to be examined.
What, then, is the case for these [proponents]? All disputants must accept means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in order to establish their own tenets,
because in their absence, such establishment would be impossible.
But he who possesses not even his own position is neither a worldly person nor an investigator; thus, like a madman, he is to be disregarded.
Therefore, the point is that since the existence of all living beings is established, the general nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) need not be investigated.
The reply is as follows: first, there is "possibility" (*saṃbhava*). Since investigation does not occur without doubt, he states the seed of doubt.
"Of the existent and the non-existent":
he states the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa).
"Having dispelled doubt": [this is the response].

This is the intention of the Mādhyamika opponent here: although for me, who maintains that the universe cannot withstand analysis, there is no such thing as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that can withstand analysis,
nevertheless, even those very means of valid cognition established in the world, when examined by those same means of valid cognition, do not withstand analysis.
Thus, it is the fault of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that they dissolve through their own internal contradiction; it is not my fault.
For knowledge is the means of valid cognition, and by its connection with that, the object becomes both the "object of cognition" (*prameya*) and the "referent" (*artha*).

If, therefore, the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) arises prior to the object of cognition (prameya), then that object would not exist prior to the means of valid cognition; this would contradict the sūtra beginning with "indriyārtha... (NS 1.1.4). // 8–9 //
If [the means of valid cognition] were established subsequently, there would be no establishment of the objects of valid cognition from those means of valid cognition.
Now, regarding the claim that the object of cognition (*prameya*) comes first and the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) comes later, he says:
"later.
Although the essential nature (*svarūpa*) [of an object] does not depend upon the means of cognition, [the subsequent determination of it does].

Nevertheless, its status as an object of cognition (prameyatva) is dependent upon that [cognition]; and if that too were not prior to the means of cognition, it would not be contingent upon the application of a means of cognition—this is the meaning. This very point has been stated in the phrase "the designation of an object of cognition" (prameyasaṃjñā). // 10 //
NyS 2.1.11: If [cognitions] were established as simultaneous, there would be an absence of sequential occurrence among cognitions, because each is restricted to its own respective object.
If they were simultaneous, there would be a contradiction with observed facts and a contradiction with the Sūtra.

The formal argument, however, is as follows: perception and the other means of knowledge should not be treated as valid means of cognition, because they do not bring about the comprehension of an object even across the three periods of time.
Whatever is not thus [established] is not treated as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
such as a rabbit's horn;
and this is likewise, therefore it is so.
Having thus presented the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa), he states the established conclusion (siddhānta):
"The resolution here [is as follows].

The meaning of this is the demonstration that the reason [adduced]—namely, that the commentary beginning with "because of the cause of perception" (upalabdhi-hetoḥ) and so forth—is unestablished (asiddha), since it does not convey a meaningful sense even in the three periods of time.
The author of the Vārttika himself states the refutation of this inference:
"And [the claim] that perception and the other means of knowledge are invalid.
Indeed, it is only when an inference has established its own nature that it can bring about the invalidity of perception and the other means of knowledge.
However, it does not lack an intrinsic nature;

rather, since its very acquisition of an intrinsic nature is impossible due to the contradiction with its own thesis, how could it be possible to establish their lack of authority? This is the intended meaning.
If the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) do not establish an object, then they would not even be "perception" and so forth;
for indeed, it is not the case that perception and the rest exist as such without being established by a means of valid cognition— this is the meaning.

Furthermore, he states that these [means of knowledge] do not possess the capacity to accomplish a purpose, nor are they even within the scope of words such as "perception" which denote both the general and the particular;
thus he asks, "And how else?
Moreover, the negation of their validity does not imply the non-existence of the means of knowledge, such as perception and the rest.
For by the expression "the boy who does not have a water-pot," the boy himself is not negated; rather,
what is [negated] is his attribute of being connected with a water-pot.

And because of this, he says "and because of the negation of dharma," [meaning] that the non-existence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), which was intended by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*), would not [otherwise] be established;
thus he raises an objection.
Now, regarding the argument "because an entity lacks independence," he refutes it with the words "even so."
The term "being negated" (*pratiṣidhyamāna*) is used when only the mother is to be expressed; "being enjoined" (*vidhīyamāna*) is for the sake of providing an illustration.
By this, [the case of] the meaning of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is explained.

The meaning is that "the category of validity" (prāmāṇyapadārtha) is intended. And since the reason (hetu), as it was literally stated, is misplaced (vyadhikaraṇa), he says: "And this reason... which follows.

He explains the commentary beginning with "But as for that... and so forth: "As for this [statement], 'by means of a valid cognition' (pramāṇena), it is the possibility of perception and the other [means of knowledge] that is being negated."
The meaning is that it is a statement of a causal reason when perception and the other means of knowledge are absent.
He says that it makes known the established impossibility of perception and the others:
"Now, the impossibility is made known."
"For there is no cessation of what is non-existent" (189/3); the meaning is that a non-existent pot is not brought to cessation by the stroke of a mallet. // 11 //
NyS 2.1.12: Since [the relation] is not established across the three times, the negation is untenable.
He explains:
"Because the three times are not established, the negation is untenable"— by stating this very thing, he provides the rebuttal.
"This is not a fault" means that while your statement contradicts your own tenets, this statement of ours does not contradict our own tenets;
furthermore, there is no logical principle whatsoever for the negation of subjects (dharmins).
(190/1) Inference is not capable of negating a subject (*dharmī*), because the reason (*hetu*) suffers from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*); this is the meaning.

Furthermore, for one who rejects all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in general, the two statements "perception and the others are invalid" and "perception and the others are valid" cannot withstand scrutiny regarding whether their meanings are different or identical; thus he says:
"One should state it exactly thus: 'the non-validity of perception and the other means of knowledge,' because of the brevity resulting from the non-employment of the two negative particles."
Regarding the phrase "or [it is] by way of dissimilarity":
when one intends to express its incapacity even while the jar exists, saying "the jar does not exist" or "it is not capable of fetching water," then it is understood.
This is a refutation of what is accepted in other systems. Whatever kind of authority is accepted in another system, that very kind is here being rejected.
For example, the existence of *pradhāna*—which is defined as the cause of the world consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion—is denied when it is stated that "the *pradhāna* does not exist."
Nor is it the cause of the world,
because that [cause] is accepted as being of a different nature.
"How so?"— this is the challenge regarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
"Whose? is the objection regarding the object of instruction; "Who? is the objection regarding the instructor.
He analyzes the objection regarding the object of instruction.
Regarding the term "one who has not entered" (*apratipanna*),
he analyzes the rejection of the proponent;
[he then states] "and one who has entered" (*pratipanna*).
What is the subject to be established? What is it that is being established? // 12 //
And because all means of valid cognition are denied, the denial itself is untenable.

The point is that if an example is to be employed, it cannot be employed if it has not been ascertained by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). He states that it is not only impossible [to employ], but also useless, with the words: "And of perception and the rest."

"By all means of valid cognition" (sarvaiḥ pramāṇaiḥ) means that it becomes contradicted— that is, opposed— by those means of valid cognition whose objects are examples and so forth; the meaning is that it becomes a fallacy of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇābhāsa) because its object is sublated.
And he states that it is contradictory, saying:
"having accepted the established tenet" (*siddhāntam abhyupetya*).
