The term "of the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇānām*) refers to the [five] members [of a syllogism].
"Avoiding" refers to an undertaking that is the opposite of avoidance; the meaning is "taking up. // 13 //
Or, if that [scripture] is authoritative, there is no sublation of all means of valid cognition.
"By that very authority" means this:

if the Mādhyamika were to say, "Perception and the other means of knowledge lack authority because they are not established in the three times," [one would reply] that the means of knowledge which depend upon the components of one's own statement are established according to worldly convention.
"By means of those [means of knowledge] established without being investigated, the validity of others is negated.
To this, it is said:

"Or, if their validity—that is, the validity of perception and so forth which depend upon parts—is accepted, there is no negation of all means of knowledge, because validity is admitted only for those things that depend upon parts."
Furthermore, what is this "established without investigation"?
Does it mean being unable to withstand investigation, or rather, being beyond the scope of doubt because it is established for all people?
In this regard, it is well said that in the first alternative, because [the cognition] is itself defective due to being unable to withstand critical examination, it subverts the validity of others.
Therefore, the second alternative is correct;
and thus, there is no universal validity [of all cognitions], because validity belongs to that [cognition] alone.
Regarding this, the commentary states:

"The prefix *vi-* here, in the sense of 'agreement,' permits the meaning of the word 'negation' (*pratiṣedha*) so as to express a specific distinction; however, it does not have a meaning distinct from that, nor does it signify contradiction.
This is what was meant by [the statement] "not in the case of contradiction" (*na vyāghāte*).

Why? Because there is no objective referent (*arthābhāvāt*). For it was previously stated that if the validity of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) relied upon the constituent parts of one's own statement were established, there would be a contradiction with the negation of all means of knowledge; thus, that negation would be inconsistent with what preceded. Furthermore, it is impossible [to negate them], because there is no objective referent.
This is the meaning.
The author of the Vārttika explains this as follows:
the prefix *vi-* is used here in the sense of a specific negation.
To say "specifically" (*viśeṣeṇa*) all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are negated is equivalent to saying there is a "contradiction" (*vipratiṣedha*),
because the prefix *vi-* implies the admission of the meaning of the word "negation" (*pratiṣedha*).
By the phrase "therefore, there is no negation of all means of valid cognition," what is stated together with the word *vipada*?
This is what is meant: "some.
Having examined the means of valid cognition as they depend upon their parts, he now examines the whole.
Thus it is said: // 14 //
And there is no negation of [the existence of the cause] in the three times; for its establishment is like the establishment of a musical instrument from the sound [it produces].

Thus, although the author of the Sūtras has refuted the [opponent's] objection regarding the impossibility of the three times (*traikālya*), he has nonetheless established that there is a contradiction with the means of valid cognition (*apramāṇavirodha*) due to the symmetry [of the argument]. Now, he recites the Sūtra intended to point out the [reason's] lack of establishment (*asiddhatā*): "Because of the non-establishment of the three times" (Sūtra 15). He introduces the reading of this Sūtra as follows:
"For what purpose? means:
if the meaning of this sūtra has already been stated independently, then the recitation of the sūtra is superfluous.
"He avoids [the objection] by saying 'as previously stated'":

the meaning is that this recitation of the sūtra is our own, for the purpose of making it known that what we have said is not something contrary to the sūtra, but rather the very meaning of the sūtra itself.

The term "without restriction" (*aniyama*) negates that which is a restriction— namely, that [negation] occurs only before, only after, or simultaneously. Indeed, this word *khalu* has the sense of "because."
Because the seer [Kātyāyana] perceives that there is no fixed rule,
he shows that the recitation of the Sūtra is intended to indicate the origin of that Vārttika;
why then, bypassing the order of recitation, is this [Vārttika] placed right there?
It should also be considered why that commentary was not stated right here; he answers:
"Because there is no distinction."

Now, as to how a sound inherent within the cavity of the ear causes one to perceive a musical instrument with which it is not connected, he says: "That which [exists] in the sounds of the lute and the flute... and so forth.

This sound is the subject (*dharmin*); "being preceded by a sound produced by the contact of a lute and fingers" is the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), because it possesses a unique characteristic that is caused by that [contact].
"Just like the sound characterized by the previously perceived sign of a lute"— this is what is meant by "having the lute as its cause. "From the sight of smoke."
For it is smoke as qualified by fire through conjunction that is inferred, not [fire] as a cause, because the appearance of "it exists" as something present would otherwise be untenable. // 15 //
And knowability is like the validity of a scale.
Furthermore, that which is projected and is indeterminate is not ultimately real— just as, for example, the nature of a snake superimposed upon a rope;
for at that very time, one person conceives of that same rope as a snake, while another conceives of it as a rope.
At one time he conceives of that very thing as a snake, and subsequently he conceives of it as a rope;
likewise is the relationship between the means of knowledge and the object of knowledge, and therefore it does not exist in the ultimate sense.
In this regard, the following sūtra is stated:
"And the scale is an object of knowledge, just like the means of valid cognition" (Sūtra 16). He provides its application as follows:
"Valid cognition" and "the object of valid cognition"—
this is the intended meaning [of the following]:

when the theories of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) and transformation (*pariṇāma*) have been refuted, a stable entity produced from its own causes, upon entering into a connection with various other entities through proximity to them, undergoes those respective cognitions and designations when it possesses those respective properties.
He asks in order to demonstrate the absorption (*samāveśa*): "But when... (193/1). The answer is: "Then, by means of the sign (*nimitta*)."
And for the purpose of making known the object itself, the Sūtra states: "The scale is also the object of cognition, like the validity [of the weight].

It is not only the scale that serves as the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the total weight; rather, when there arises a doubt concerning its own validity, then the scale is also the object of cognition (*prameya*), by means of another scale that has been tested and whose status as a valid means of cognition is established, such as gold and so forth.
Like validity (*prāmāṇya*).

Just as the balance is both the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the object of cognition (*prameya*) regarding validity, so too all other means of valid cognition are objects of cognition with respect to validity; this is the meaning.
Thus the author of the Bhāṣya says:
Thus, without exception and in its entirety,
this is the meaning of the tantra;
it is the meaning of the treatise.
Thus [it is said].

In some cases, there is a coexistence of the states of being the knower (*pramātṛtva*), the object of knowledge (*prameyatva*), and the means of knowledge (*pramāṇatva*), as for example in the case of the Self (*ātman*).
For that [Self] is indeed the knower, and when it is being cognized, it is the object of knowledge.
However, that which has been cognized by it serves as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the inference of other qualities residing therein.

Furthermore, in some cases—such as in the case of the intellect (*buddhi*)—there is a coalescence of the status of being a means of valid cognition, the status of being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*), and the status of being a result; in other cases, however, there is a coalescence of the status of being a means of valid cognition and the status of being an object of cognition.

—as in the case of *saṃśatha* and so forth. This is the pervasion of the meaning of the *tantra* by means of [the principle of] simultaneous occurrence (*samāveśa*). And thus, there are words denoting the factors of action (*kāraka*).
Here, having completed [the citation], the author of the Vārttika explains:
"And just as 'pramāṇa' [is used]... for as many [as there are]."
Wherever there are causes (nimitta), there is the necessary occurrence of their corresponding effects (naimittika); this is the rule (niyama).
Regarding the statement in the Bhāṣya that "the tree is the agent (kartṛ) in its own state because of its independence (svātantrya)," the author of the Vārttika asks about that independence:
What, then, is independence?
It is the state of not being employed by other causal factors;
[that is, this instigator is not [employed] by other causal factors].

The status of being an instigator (*prayojakatva*) is said to be the independence (*svātantrya*) of the agent (*kartṛ*) over other causal factors (*kāraka*). However, the point here is that because other causal factors are absent, such independence does not exist. The subsequent [point] is the lack of dependence on other causal factors.

The meaning is that while something dependent on other factors may be intended to have some degree of independence by virtue of being the instigator (*prayojaka*), that which is independent of them possesses absolute independence.
This is the case when this word *sthiti* (staying) is understood as a negation of motion (*gati*).
To the extent that it is said "he does not go," to that same extent it is said "he stands.

And here, since the negation is defined in dependence upon that which is to be negated, its temporal sequence is merely a conditional attribute (upādhi); for a temporal sequence is not possible for the negation in its own essential nature.
When it is said that "it denotes existence," the meaning is that it denotes the generality of being (*sattāsāmānya*).
There is the view that [the cause] manifests [the effect].

For when a tree possesses magnitude and possesses color, its manifestation of existence (*sattā*) consists simply in the inherence (*samavāya*) of existence; and in that case, the meaning is that it is independent [of anything else].
The influence of the connection with a house is the attainment of that connection, which is inherence (*samavāya*).
The action directed toward that object is the effort that restrains motion; for by means of that effort, it remains stationary.
The expression "the jar is in the house" is a figurative usage;

likewise, even when this [term] is used in the sense of "unbroken," here too, the negation's state of being such is conditioned solely by the prior and posterior sequence of that which is to be negated.

Alternatively, even in the case of the word "tiṣṭhati" (he stands), let there be a dependence on another factor due to some intended meaning; nevertheless, its independence exists precisely by virtue of being the prompter (*prayojaka*) of that [action], as he says:
"with respect to the aggregate."
A collection of parts is a whole (samudāya), and a single portion thereof is a part (avayava).
In the word "dhriyate," the suffix *lakāra* denotes the agent.
Alternatively, stability is the state of being the object of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*).
Even while that [stability] exists, he states that there is independence (*svātantrya*) by virtue of being the motivator (*prayojaka*), despite the dependence upon other causal factors,
with the words "prior and posterior" (*pūrvāpara*).

The Nihilist (Vaināśika) teaches as follows: "First there are various conditions possessing multiple aspects; then there is the subsequent experience of the substratum (dharmin) which is the locus of those [aspects];
then there is memory;
and then there is the synthesis (pratisandhāna)."
"Regarding the wheel": the meaning is that this very rotation of the wheel which occurs through conjunction with the staff continues even when that conjunction with the staff has ceased.
He refutes this by saying, "not by means of a valid cognition."

The meaning is that as long as there is no powerful subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), it is impossible for recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) to be false; however, in the case of [the perception of] flames and the like, such a subversion exists.
Furthermore, he states that if all cognitions of synthesis (*pratisandhāna*) were false, then a cognition of synthesis could not possibly be false, because of the absence of its cause (*bīja*).
"And false cognitions. The Nihilist asks: "Now, what about yours?"

One who speaks thus, not accepting direct perception as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), cannot be enlightened by that [perception alone]; therefore, he states inference as a valid means of knowledge.
This has been explained under the definition of the self (*ātman*) with the word "form" (*rūpa*).
(195/4) He states another inference:
"kārayiṣyati" (he will cause to be made).
"Experiencing the time of the effect" means the arrival at the time of the effect.
The nihilist raises an objection:
"Without a substratum.
This means: having depended upon a prior state, [and] having undergone transformation.
He refutes this, saying "no.

For it is established by experience that the substratum and the supported exist at the same time; therefore, by means of that substratum as the cause, the effect must persist until the moment of its own completion.
However, the fact that an effect lacks a substratum is not within the scope of direct experience;
rather, it must be established through reasoning, and that reasoning is untenable due to the absence of an illustrative example.
Nor can direct experience be denied merely because of a disagreement [with one's own view],
and the proofs for momentary destruction will be refuted later.
For if the fact that form and the other [sensory objects] possess a substratum were denied, it would contradict your own accepted position.
The elements (*bhūta*) are earth and so forth, while the derivative matter (*bhautika*) consists of form and so forth;
[the author] states this to show the contradiction with another accepted position.
Regarding what was stated by you:
not only is the state of being dependent (*āśritatva*) of form and so forth accepted by you, but it is also logically established;
thus he says, "and because of the absence of dependence" (*anāśritatvāt*).
He asks:
what is the meaning of the term *kāraka* in the context of the object (*karman*)?
It is the meaning of the word *kāraka*.

For that which is a *kāraka* (agentive factor) is so by virtue of being the cause (*nimitta*) of an action; however, that which is merely the object (*vyāpya*) of the action itself is not the cause of the action, and thus it is not a *kāraka*.
And how can that which is not a *kāraka* be an *object* (*karman*)?
The sense is that the designation "object" (*karmasaṃjñā*) is governed by the heading (*adhikāra*) concerning *kārakas*.
The answer is that it is the state of being the object of an action (*kriyāviṣayatva*).
The state of being an object (*karmatva*) consists in possessing the fruit of an action that does not inhere in the self (*anātmasamaveta*).
For, by means of an action inhering in Devadatta—namely, the action characterized as seeing—an experience having the tree as its object is produced.
And it has been stated in the *Pramāṇalakṣaṇa* that this alone constitutes the objectivity of an experience toward its referent, namely, that its determination is dependent upon the referent.

Therefore, since an object of action exists prior to the action itself, its status as a *kāraka* (participant in an action) is logical. In this way, the status of being an object (*karman*) is established for both the modified (*vikārya*) and the attained (*prāpya*) objects; however, although a word-base (*pada*) and the like, which are produced (*nirvartya*), do not exist prior to the action, [their status as an object is still justified].

Nevertheless, because those constituent threads exist prior [to the cloth], it is appropriate to use the expression "he makes a cloth" by metaphorically attributing the status of the cloth to them for the sake of that [cloth].
For the author will state in the *Sahacaraṇādi-sūtra*: "in the case of vīraṇa grass intended for a mat.
By this definition of the object (*karman*), one does not [transgress] here.
Expressions such as "going to the village, he approaches the roots of the trees" should also be understood as being included [in this category].
Just as in the case of "Caitra goes to the city," the reaching (*prāpti*) is inherent in the city;

Thus, even in the case of [an action] inherent in Caitra, so that Caitra—who possesses the fruit produced by the action—does not become the object (*karman*), it is stated [in the definition] that [the object] must not be inherent in the self (*anātmamaveta*). Furthermore, regarding the mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*) whose object is the self, although the self does not have the status of an object, nevertheless the act of cognition (*jñānakriyā*) is indeed transitive (*sakarmika*), because some property of the self other than the self itself appears as its object; thus, everything is clear.

"The tree becomes the recipient (*sampradāna*)"— the sense is that, according to Pāṇini’s grammatical rules and in accordance with common usage, this term "recipient" is not an etymological designation (*anvartha-saṃjñā*).
The phrase "the cause for the obstruction of heaviness" refers to the intention behind the example under discussion.

And thus, since qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth are also understood to possess the state of being supported (*ādheyatva*), their status as that which is supported by substances (*dravya*) and the like is established.
Therefore, what was stated by the Mādhyamika—that the causal agent (*kāraka*) does not have the nature of a substance—is precisely what we also accept;
however, with the intention of not tolerating a conceptualized (*kālpnika*) causal agent, the author of the Commentary (*bhāṣyakāra*) has spoken [as follows].
And this being so,
it is not merely an action;
that is, it is not merely an intermediate action.
"That which is the means for the principal action, being connected with specific intermediate actions"—
having restated this, the author of the Vārttika explains it with the words "And this being so."
Thus, by this, the general definition of a *kāraka* has been stated.

As for the commentary (*bhāṣya*) intended to provide the specific definition—namely, "that which is independent and is the means of accomplishing an action"—he explains it [as follows]: "But when there is a specific [distinction]..."
Thus [it is said].
This might be the case:
let there be only this much—that it is the means for accomplishing an action.
Or, [if one objects] that it is because both [the action and its qualification] have been mentioned,
he says:
"and of every causal factor" (sarvasya ca kārakasya).
If only the intermediate action were mentioned, then since everyone would be the agent of that [intermediate action], there would be no diversity among the factors of action (*kāraka*).
Furthermore, if only the principal action were taken up, there could be no diversity therein without the intermediate operations of all [the agents]. Therefore, the mention of both is purposeful.
Thus he explains the commentary [bhāṣya] "in this way, by way of its characteristics" and "and thus the treatise [śāstra]."
He teaches;
that is to say,
he refutes.
"It is not from power," he says; then he teaches again:
"It is from power."
He avoids [this objection], saying: "This is not a fault.
But surely cognition (*buddhi*) and the others are also causes for the manifestation of capacity (*śakti*), and yet these are not of the nature of action (*kriyā*).
But since [the word] consists of qualities (guṇa),
it was stated by the word "action" (kriyā);
its meaning is power (sāmarthya).
For one who is weak does not employ a means even though he knows it, just as a blunted axe-bearer does not use an axe with his hand;
therefore, the term "kāraka" (agent/cause) is primary in relation to capacity, action, and their connection.
"But it is figurative in the case of mere power" (śaktimātre tu gauṇaḥ);
he thus applies [this principle] to the subject at hand.
And this [word] is a term denoting an agent.

(198/5) NyS 2.1.17: Since [the means of knowledge] are established by means of a means of knowledge, it follows that there must be the establishment of means of knowledge by another means of knowledge.
Now, having raised an objection against the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by way of another method, they are resolved:
"O sir, there exist words denoting agents.
Here, these conceptual constructions (*kalpa*) arise as disturbances.
Is the apprehension of perception and the other [means of knowledge] established by means of proof or without means of proof?
Even if it is with means of proof, is it by these very same perceptions and so forth, or by another means of knowledge?
And even if it is by these, is it by that very same individual instance of perception?

Now, if it is argued that one individual instance [is related] to another individual instance, then, if a further means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is admitted for that, there would be a contradiction with the Sūtra on "differentiation" (vibhāga),
and there would also be the consequence of an infinite regress.
In that regard, if one perception and so forth were to be apprehended by another perception and so forth, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress.
If, however, it were apprehended by that very same individual [perception], there would be the contradiction of something acting upon itself;
for indeed, a blade cannot be cut by that very same blade.
Therefore, the apprehension of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not established by a means;
if this is so, then what is the use of means of valid cognition as the instruments for establishing objects of cognition (*prameya*)?
Let the apprehension of objects of cognition likewise be without means, just like the means themselves. This is the prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*).

The establishment of valid cognition does not occur without a means of proof, nor is there an admission of a means of cognition other than perception and the rest, which would contradict the aphorism on their classification.
Nor is it maintained that the very same individual instance is apprehended by itself,
which would entail the contradiction of something acting upon itself.
Rather, we maintain that the apprehension of one thing belonging to the class of perception, etc., by another belonging to the same class of perception,

etc., occurs; and there is no infinite regress, because there exists certain means of valid cognition which, through their own cognition, serve as causes for the cognition of something else, such as smoke and the like.
Furthermore, there may be some means of cognition that is itself unknown, such as the eye and so forth;
in that case, while the eye and others depend upon their own prior cognition, the eye and others are themselves means of cognition independent of cognition—so where is the infinite regress?

Moreover, that [unknown means] can also be known through the desire to know (*bubhutsā*), and since that desire occurs only occasionally and in certain places, it cannot be argued that an infinite regress results from the need for another means of knowledge for its sake.

In the case of objects that are perceptible, since activity occurs even from doubt, its validity is easily known through the efficacy of that activity; whereas in the case of imperceptible objects, its validity can be known by means of the similarity of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) whose authority has been ascertained through the efficacy of activity—this was demonstrated in the first sūtra.

Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the apprehension of perception and the other means of knowledge occurs through perception and the others themselves, and thus there is no infinite regress.
The commentary: "Bho" is an address of invitation.
But from what [source] does it derive its status as a cause of apprehension? To this he says: "And because they are cognizable," where "and" (ca) functions as a reason.
To the question "From what [source] does it have the status of being an object of apprehension?", he says: "My cognition is perceptual. (17)
Or rather, from the cessation of that [doubt], there is the establishment of the object of cognition, just as there is the establishment of the means of valid cognition.
Not so, because its establishment is like the establishment of the illumination of a lamp.

The Bhāṣya states: "Because perception exists when there is the presence or absence of a lamp, and because [perception] occurs for both the knower and the mind"; the author of the Vārttika explains this as follows:
And this is not an absolute rule;
the terms "knower" and "known" are intended with reference to an object of action.
For the activity of cognition does not inhere in anything other [than the self], such that it would constitute an object (*karman*) for the self; rather, it resides solely within the knower.
Indeed, it has been stated that an object is that which possesses the fruit of an action inhering in something else.
Therefore, pleasure and the like, being attributes of the self, function as objects here.
The self, however, possesses luminosity;
it is with a specific intention that its state of being knowable is predicated therein.
As for the mind, although it is both the instrument and the object with respect to its own cognition, [it is not so in the case of the self].
Nevertheless, there is no contradiction regarding its own operation upon itself;

for if the cognition were the instrument [of its own cognition], then the fallacy of self-dependence would follow. However, it is by its very existence that cognition serves as the instrument for [the production of] knowledge.
Furthermore, its cognition is one thing and its existence another; the act of cognizing does not inhere in that [existence],
but rather in the self.

Therefore, it is not a fault that the mind is both an object of knowledge and an instrument of cognition. However, certain teachers who follow the tradition of the Master (Ācāryadeśīya) maintain that just as the light of a lamp does not require another light to illuminate it, so too there may be things that exist without depending on other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
He replies to them:
"Because cessation is observed in some cases and non-cessation is observed in others, there is inconclusiveness. (NyS 2.1.19)
In some cases, there is no [intermediate state] (Sūtra 19).
Just as this consequence—the consequence that means of valid cognition would be independent [of other means]—is intended for this purpose:
since a lamp is seen to be an illuminator without depending on another lamp, the means of valid cognition will be established as independent of other means of valid cognition, like light;
it is for this reason that the consequence is employed.

It is also to be accepted for the purpose that the objects of cognition (*prameya*) themselves will be established independently; and thus, the meaning is that there is no lack of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Having thus stated the consequence of the non-existence of means of valid cognition by resorting to the example of a lamp, he says the following regarding the adoption of examples such as a pot, which shows that even a means of valid cognition requires another means of valid cognition:
Regarding the phrase "just as the apprehension of the form of a pot and so forth," the author of the Vārttika explains this Bhāṣya as follows:

just as the light of a lamp does not depend on another of its own kind, so too the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) do not depend on another of their own kind; however, it is not the case that just as the form of a pot and so forth depends on a means of valid cognition, so too the means of valid cognition themselves depend on a means of valid cognition.
Furthermore, why is it that the form of a pot and so forth depends upon a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? To this he says:
"And in the manifestation of the form of a pot and so forth...
(200/18). The meaning is that it is established in the world that the light of a lamp is the means of valid cognition in that regard.
Why are the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) not like the form of a pot?
The meaning is that those [means of cognition] too should be illuminated by another means of cognition.

Thus, by this example of the lamp, it has been stated that there is no restrictive reason for [the claim] that independence belongs to the lamp-example whereas dependence belongs to the pot-example and so forth.
He states the absence of any other restrictive cause:
"And this is the example of the light of a lamp."

For just as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are independent according to the analogy of a lamp, why, by that very same analogy, are the objects of cognition (*prameya*) not also [independent]?
And from that, it would follow as a consequence that there is an absence of means of valid cognition.
For there is no restrictive reason to maintain that the lamp is an illustration only for the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and not for the objects of cognition (*prameya*).

By this, the commentary stating "just as in the case of the reductio ad absurdum" has been explained. By the statement "let the illumination of the lamp be the illustration," the restriction that "this alone is the illustration and not that one" is refuted.

However, by means of the previous lamp-example, the restriction that there is indeed independence and not dependence as in the case of the pot-example has been refuted; thus, this is not a redundant statement.
It is possible to state the restriction that the lamp-example is subsumed under reasons such as "being illuminating" and so forth.
Yet, when "being illuminating" is to be proven as being independent of another of its own kind, it must be subjected to critical analysis.
Is it something that is absolutely of the same class (*atyantasajātīya*) or merely of the same class (*sajātīyamātra*)?
If it is absolutely of the same class, then there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*),
for the eye and other sense organs do not require another eye or organ to apprehend themselves.
Now, if it is somehow argued that there is a homogeneous instance, even light possesses dependence upon that [the eye],
since it too depends on the eye and so forth; consequently, the example is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyahīna*).

Furthermore, the reason is contradictory because even the cognition of an object is not grasped by that very cognition of the object, but rather by a cognition whose object is that [first] cognition; thus, it is not of an absolutely similar kind.
With this intention, the author of the Vārttika stated that "this fault of inconclusiveness does not occur.
The meaning is, however, that another fault does indeed arise.
As for the other text, however, since its meaning has already been established by us while demonstrating our own tenet (*siddhānta*), it has not been commented upon;
[this was done] with a touch of irony, lest one should fall into an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). // 19 //
NyS 2.1.20: The definition of perception is untenable because it is stated incompletely.
Pratyātma (Sūtra 20).
By this sūtra, either the definition of perception or the essential nature of perception is stated, but not the cause of perception; thus he says:
"As for this which is called by you the 'definition of perception'..."
The meaning is "the cause of direct perception. When the cause exists, the effect—namely, cognition—is characterized. He raises the second alternative with the word "atha" (now/if).
"Not in either way" means that the position regarding the characteristic (*lakṣaṇapakṣa*) alone is intended as the established tenet (*siddhānta*);
the acceptance of the position regarding the cause (*kāraṇapakṣa*) is to be understood as a bold assertion (*prauḍhivāda*).
The uncommon cause that pervades all perception is determined [to be the sense-object contact].
For there is no other such cause for perception as either the contact between the self and the mind or the contact between the sense organ and the mind;
because the former is common [to other types of cognition] and the latter is non-pervasive.
He states another [possible] solution with the words "or by way of the object," ending with "the contact of the mind is also a cause. // 20 //
NyS 2.1.21: Perception does not arise in the absence of contact between the self and the mind.
Thus, having stated the essence of the established doctrine, the author of the Bhāṣya explains [the matter] without even citing the sūtra beginning with "na ātmamanasoḥ," stating:
"nor [is there contact] when the substance is not conjoined."
For every collection of causes requires mutual conjunction for the production of an effect;
otherwise, the effect would arise from causes situated anywhere at all. Therefore, even by way of its own nature, the mind must produce the effect while being connected [to the object].
And the relation between the self and the mind is precisely conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
Or, let it be that cognition is produced by conjunction;
why then does it not arise from the conjunction of the object, the sense organ, and the self?
To the objection that [cognition] is produced by the conjunction with the mind,
he says:
"in the contact with the mind."
Therefore, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the contact between the self and the mind must also be stated.
This very point was already commented upon by the author of the *Bhāṣya* prior to the recitation of the sūtra beginning with "na ātma-manasoḥ saṃnikarṣāt.
Having repeated that *Bhāṣya*, the author of the *Vārttika* recites the sūtra of the prima facie position.
There is no self-subsistence. (Sūtra 21)
He states the meaning of the sūtra:
"of the self and the mind.
Not tolerating even a moment's duration for the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa), the author of the Vārttika recalls the stated refutation of it.
It is not said. (203/2) // 21 //
NyS 2.1.22: By this same reasoning, the same undesirable consequence applies to direction, space, time, and ether as well.

Thus, when the prima facie position has been established by these two sūtras, a bystander, thinking that the causality of the contact between sense-faculties and objects and so forth has been stated here merely by way of affirmation, objects as follows:
"And when there is the sense-faculty and the object... (1).
The meaning is that mere existence does not constitute causality, as this would result in even space and other such entities being causes;
therefore, it is not logical for the conjunction of the self and the mind, nor the conjunction of the sense organ and the self, to be considered the cause in such a manner.
It refutes [the opponent's view] by stating,
"even in the absence of a causal relationship.
The determination of causality does not arise from mere positive concomitance (*anvaya*) alone.
Furthermore, [causality] is established through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka); however,
there is no negative concomitance regarding space and so forth,
since their proximity is unavoidable due to their eternity and omnipresence.
The conjunction of the self and the mind, which resides within the body endowed with sense organs, has its causal efficacy ascertained through positive and negative concomitance;

for knowledge does not arise in one who is asleep. Furthermore, even when there is contact between a sense organ and its object, if that object is too distant or obstructed, knowledge is not produced.

However, in the absence of contact between the sense-faculties and the mind, cognitions do not arise simultaneously; therefore, there is no over-extension of the principle to space and other such entities.
The author of the Vārttika explains this as follows:

"Those who describe the nature of a cause based on the principle that 'when [the cause] exists, [the effect] exists'—whether they be proponents of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) or those of the established conclusion (siddhāntin)—and who state that 'when [the cause] does not exist, [the effect] does not exist,' have arrived at a negative concomitance (vyatireka) by mere chance; it is not, however, the logically necessary factor.
To them, a bystander says:"
Regarding the phrase "of those [colors], direction and place," and "just as the lunar form":

although heat exists there in that fire as well, nevertheless, because it is utterly overwhelmed and thus incapable of performing its own characteristic causal function (*arthakriyā*), it is as good as non-existent; this is the meaning. // 22 //
NyS 2.1.23: Since the self has cognition as its mark, there is no non-inclusion [of it].
When the partisan has been thus refuted, the proponent says, "If it is so";
the respondent replies: "If it is so," [the proponent] says; the respondent says: (204/2) [as follows].
"It is not to be added," [concerning] the basis of knowledge (jñānādhiṣṭhāna) (Sūtra 23).
Here, the fact that cognition is an inferential mark of the self is stated:
cognition is, first of all, an effect because it is impermanent, like a jar.
And that...
In some cases, [the subject] is established as being produced because it is an effect, like a jar.
Furthermore, that [subject] does not reside in earth and so forth, because it is perceived by mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*).
On the other hand, whatever resides in earth and so forth is either cognizable by another type of perception or is simply imperceptible.
Furthermore, cognition does not reside in a substratum other than the eight substances;
and its substratum must belong to the category of substance,
because it is an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), like space.
And its omnipresence has been stated by us in the definition of the Self;
therefore, knowledge belongs to the class of qualities, because, while being an effect, it inheres in an omnipresent substance, just like sound.
Since the question and answer are thus established, they must be explained as they appear in the Vārttika:
"Because of inherence in the self" (ātmasamavāyāt) means that, while being an effect, it inheres in an all-pervading substance.
He says: "Let it be said that the inherence in an omnipresent substance is unestablished;
[it is not so], for it is not a quality of earth and the other elements, because it is self-cognizable.
The meaning is: because it is cognizable through mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*).
That which is connected to both self and other should be understood as cognizable by another perception;
otherwise, there would be a deviation [in the inference] due to qualities such as duality (dvitva) belonging to earth and so forth.
Therefore, the self has cognition as its inferential mark (liṅga).
However, that [self], being unconnected, does not produce cognition;
for if it were eternal, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of cognition arising at all times.
Therefore, it follows by implication that it depends upon a particular conjunction that occurs only occasionally.
The author of the Sūtra did not state "the conjunction of the self and the mind.
To show that this [conjunction] is a conclusion reached through bold assertion (prauḍhivāda), he recalls the supreme conclusion already stated;
and it has been said in this regard: // 23 //
And because their non-simultaneity is the mark [of the mind], the mind does not [exist as a single entity].
"Having another purpose" means for the sake of demonstrating the nature of the mind as an object of cognition (*prameya*).
It is logical that even something intended for another purpose can illuminate that [specific] purpose.
The indicative mark (*liṅga*): for such is this indicative mark that it establishes the mind as the cause of cognition even for [cognitions] directed toward other objects.
Indeed, cognition is not independent, such that it would not depend upon the mind as its own cause.
Nor is the eye and so forth independent in the production of cognition, such that it would not be the instrument (*karaṇa*) for mental cognition; thus he says:
"Not the eye and so forth.
Therefore, because [the self] has reached the object, there is a conjunction with the self.
And the conjunction of the sense-organ with the mind has not been mentioned by the author of the Sūtras. // 24 //
And because the contact between the sense organ and the object is the cause of perception, it is mentioned by its own specific term.
He explains:
"Then why [is it not so]?
The sense is that even when there is contact between the sense faculty and its object, attainment (*prāpti*) is in fact no different [from non-contact].
He avoids this [objection]:
for if one were to state everything as "perception," perception itself would not be defined; therefore, something must be stated for the sake of its definition.
In that case, it is precisely the contact between the sense organ and the object (*indriyārthasannikarṣa*) that must be stated.
The ultimate resolution is that [the definition applies] because it pervades all direct perception, whereas the other two do not, due to being either under-pervasive or over-pervasive. // 25 //
And because [the perception of objects] by those whose minds are asleep or distracted is caused by the contact between the sense organs and their objects.
"Suṣuptat" (Sūtra 26). The remainder of the sūtra is "due to the arising of knowledge.
Having made a resolution—that is, having formed a mental intention—such as, "I shall wake up at midnight after having fallen asleep at dusk," [one wakes up].
He awakens precisely at midnight.
"Knowledge upon awakening" means that when there is awakening—that is, the cessation of sleep—there is the cognition of the touch of a substance; this is the meaning of "knowledge upon awakening."
He explains [the phrase] "of those whose minds are asleep" as follows: "Indeed, at one time this [mind] engages with another object. (26)
And by means of these, there is the designation of specific cognitions.
And there is another reason for its predominance:
"And by those [qualities], of the atoms" (Sūtra 27).
He demonstrates that knowledge is designated by means of the sense faculties through both a distributive and a collective compound.
He states "the olfactory" (*ghrāṇa*) because that knowledge is designated according to the number of the sense faculty and its object.

Regarding the term "indriya" (the sense organ): the Vārttika states, "and that which is uncommon [is the cause]. The intention is that even the directions and so forth, by qualifying an effect through specificities such as "easternness" which are themselves conceptually constructed based on limiting adjuncts (upādhi), are indeed uncommon [causes]. // 27 //
NyS 2.1.28: It is not a valid reason because it is contradictory.
By this continuous argument, it is established that the contact between the sense organ and its object alone is the cause of cognition,
and not the contact between the self and the mind.
Thinking that he has stated here that the cause of cognition is the contact between the sense faculty and the mind, [the opponent] objects as follows.
They both spoke (Sūtra 28).
Not so, because of the intensity of a particular object.
The sūtra of refutation.
Not [the case] when there is an object (sūtra 29).
The meaning is that by this [statement], only the primacy of the contact between the sense organ and its object is expressed;
however, it is not asserted that the conjunction of the self and the mind, or the conjunction of the sense organ and the mind, is not a cause. Thus, there is no contradiction. He asks:
Regarding the phrase "in the absence of intention and resolve":
effort is resolve;
intention is desire.
The answer is:
"Just as... [the opponent objects:
But has it not been understood that this [karma] is the cause of birth, lifespan, and experience?
But it does not [mean] that it is also the impeller of the mind; therefore, he says:
"for when the mind is not being impelled by that [karman].
For experience is the primary purpose of the unseen force (adṛṣṭa), and as an inseparable concomitant of that, it projects birth and lifespan.
Experience (*bhoga*) consists in the direct perception of pleasure and pain related to oneself, and the body is the locus of that experience.

Furthermore, the mind, when not yet reached [by the senses], cannot produce knowledge— which is the cause of those two, as well as the experience itself and its objects, namely pleasure and pain— within that [body].
Surely, one must speak of an unseen cause (*adṛṣṭa*) as the cause of the mental action (*manaskarma*) for the sake of attaining that [result];
otherwise, this [unseen cause] would not be the cause of all substances, qualities, and actions.
Lest it be thought that it does not serve all purposes, he says:
"And it must be sought by him" refers to the qualification of the atoms, namely, the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*). "Because of contradiction" is a sūtra of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).
The author of the Vārttika states its intended meaning: "By this... (206/7).
Now, one might object: does not this set of three sūtras state that the contact between the sense faculty and its object is the primary factor?
However, he does not deny that another conjunction can be a cause;
therefore, he says: "This, indeed... and so forth.
The meaning is that the opponent's misconception is that causality is being negated;
[this would result in] a contradiction with what is observed.
Thus,
the meaning is that non-simultaneity has been observed, and there is a contradiction of that.
The remainder, however, has been explained by the commentary on the Bhāṣya. // 29 //
Nyāyasūtra 2.1.30: Perception and inference [are not the means of knowing dharma], because perception arises from the apprehension of a single part [of an object].
Regarding the phrase "henceforth, now":
for there is no such thing as a "whole" (*avayavin*) that exists as a distinct entity apart from its parts; rather, it is the parts themselves that are ultimately real (*paramārthasat*).
Furthermore, by grasping a few of its constituent parts and inferring the other parts associated with them,

this cognition of a "tree"— which arises through synthesis— would have those very parts as its objective support and would thus be an inference. Consequently, because perception would be included within inference,
the exclusion of numbers fewer or greater than two [from the categories] in the Sūtra on their classification would be untenable.
This is the meaning. He refutes [this view], stating:
"No, because conceptual alternatives are untenable according to their possible occurrence."
For a single part is the locus of the whole; it is called a "single part" (*ekadeśa*) because it is both one and a part.
The meaning is: since a location (*deśa*) is a substratum (*ādhāra*) and there is no composite whole (*avayavin*) to be supported (*ādheya*), how can it be a substratum?
Alternatively, he speaks of skill in words and meanings;
that is to say, skill regarding either the word or its referent.
First, he states the lack of skill regarding the object:
"In what is not to be done" (*akārye*).
Regarding a single effect, there exists a mutual proximity among its causes for the purpose of producing that one effect.
Just as there is a proximity among clay, the staff, the wheel, and the string when a jar is to be produced,
so too is there a mutual proximity among effects born from a single causal complex,
such as form, taste, odor, and touch.
Or [the relationship] between cause and effect, such as that between fire and smoke;
however, for those things which possess neither the state of being cause and effect, nor the state of having a single effect, nor the state of having a single cause—
The meaning is: from what source does their proximity possess such a fixed rule? He states their lack of skill regarding words:
"And not mutually," and so forth.
The possessor of parts (the whole) requires one part in relation to another part;
therefore, the parts become mutual benefactors of one another.
However, in the absence of the whole, they would not be mutual benefactors—this is the meaning of the question, "How [then] could there be parts?"
And it is not the case that there is no synthesis with what is not a tree;
for, having perceived a healthy cow, a synthesis as "cow" is observed in the case of a brindled cow, but having perceived a horse, a synthesis as "cow" is not observed in the case of another horse.
For what reason?
Because those two do not possess the nature of a cow;
likewise, because the near and far parts do not possess the nature of a tree, [the whole] is a tree.
The meaning is that there would be no such synthesis.

If it were argued: "Let there be no apprehension of the subject (*dharmin*) in the form of the tree; rather, having first inferred the specific tree as the subject through its front part, one will subsequently synthesize [the perception]," [then the following applies:]
He says:
"Nor is it inference.
To the question "Why?", he says:
Regarding the term "inference" (anumāna):
this inferrer does not first perceive fire and then, through inference, apprehend fire as the qualifier of smoke and subsequently synthesize them, thinking, "This is smoke and this is fire.
Nor is it the case that there is synthesis first and inference later; therefore, he says:

"And it is not for the sake of reconnection" means that since fire is already known at the very moment of reconnection, the thought "there must be fire here" would be rendered useless by inference; this is the meaning.
He says this while conceding the point.
"And even by way of connection" means:
furthermore, how can that which consists of a front part be a possessor of parts? It is not a part-possessor, but rather it is simply a part itself.
To the question "Why does it not see?", he says:
"The near part and the far part are not joined.
For they would be mutually connected only through their inherence in a single composite whole (*ekāvayavin*).
The meaning is that neither does the whole exist, nor are they conjoined, because conjunction has already been refuted by the method used to refute the whole.
He asks:
"But how so? The answer is:
"Always by means of its near side."

It has already been stated that there is no relation whatsoever. Even granting that [relation], the reply is as follows: the meaning is that even though the two are related, that relation is impossible to apprehend.
The statement "they are indeed related" is merely a concession (*abhyupagamavāda*).
As for what was said regarding [the cognition] being "born from the synthesis of conditions":
it was stated previously that even when a tree exists, the cognition of a "tree" is not born from the synthesis of its parts, because the parts themselves are not the tree.
But now, because the tree is not present [as a whole], there is no such synthesis as "the tree is in its parts"; thus, there is no tautology.

Furthermore, regarding the cognitions "color has been perceived by me" and "taste," it is that very same perceiver who is colored by the cognition of taste who is likewise colored by the cognition of color.
This is the meaning:
because a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which determines an object exactly as it is.
For example, even though inference is erroneous, it does not fail to be a means of valid cognition by virtue of its connection with the object.
Thus it was shown in the first chapter:
when there is the theory of misapprehension (*atasmims-tad-khyāti*), error occurs by following the lead of the primary cause (*pradhāna*).
And that has been established in the first chapter [by the statement]:
"Not so, because the word does not denote the object.
But what, then, is the meaning of this word "tathā" (so/likewise)?
Is it the form of the atoms, or their contiguity, or a distinction in conjunction, or a distinction in production?
If it were merely form, then since that exists in jars and other things as well, the cognition of a "tree" would arise there too.
Now, if it is a distinction of form, [then...]
In another moment, it would be treeless;
for that previous form does not exist [then].
If you argue that continuity exists [there], then that [continuity] also exists in the case of jars and other such things.
Nor is there any [conjunction] anywhere, because of the intervention of atoms of odor, taste, color, and touch;
since conjunction is not accepted by you, how can there be its distinction?
Even the differentiation of the arising of atoms is merely form;
for there is no arising of them whatsoever that exists apart from the atoms themselves,
and form has already been analyzed above.

For if a real arrangement of parts were observed anywhere as the cause for the application of terms such as "prior" and "posterior," then the meaning of the word [tathā] would be understood accordingly;
however, for you, this is not real anywhere,
because atoms, being substantially existent, are partless— this is the meaning.
Mistakenly thinking that even with respect to the subject (*dharmin*) in the case of *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* there is no perception (*pratyakṣa*), he asks:
"Of *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*? The answer follows.
"This is the distinction":
when two [factors] are established through perception, the *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* [inference] operates;
but when three [factors] are established through perception, it is *pratyakṣatodṛṣṭa*—this is the distinction.

Since everything is beyond direct perception (*apratyakṣa*), the cognition of a "tree" is not derived from perception; nor is it from inference, whether from what is seen in a specific instance (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*) or otherwise—so he says: "But in your position... (verse 30).
Not so, because even that which is not [otherwise] perceived is apprehended by perception.
Not so (Sūtra 31). Perception does not possess the nature of inference.
Why?

Because even as much of the class of objects as constitutes a single part is grasped by perception; that is, even regarding the reason proposed here—that "there is apprehension because of the grasping of a single part"—that much is also [established] by perception.
Otherwise, because there would be no apprehension of a single part (*ekadeśa*), inference could not arise;
or, if that part were apprehended by another inference, it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Therefore, since the claim that "inference is as much as is perceived through direct perception" is based on the reason that "no apprehension of a single part is found," this proposition is sublated by that very reason.

If the apprehension of a single part is not admitted by perception, then because no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is applicable there, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished; this is the meaning of the phrase "this is a rope caught at both ends.

To the objection that the reason is not unestablished because the apprehension of a single part occurs through inference (*anumāna*), the author of the *Bhāṣya* says: "And there is no apprehension of a single part... [and so forth].
Inference is the act of inferring.
[The opponent argues that] it cannot be brought about or performed because of the absence of a cause, which would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress.
The author of the Vārttika explains this sūtra as follows:

"And this [position] is contradictory. Now, one might object: "Even if only a single part is perceived, that much alone would be perceptible, but it would not follow that the whole is perceptible. To this, [the author replies: "Therefore..."
He said:
"It is not asserted that 'everything' is thus;
rather, it is asserted that it is 'without variety.'"
For inference has three types [of objects] which perception does not possess; and because its object pertains to the three times,
this indicates that inference concerns objects beyond the reach of the senses (*parokṣārtha*).
Perception, however, has as its object that which is not beyond the senses;
therefore, there is a distinction [between inference and perception]—this is the meaning.

Furthermore, although the cognition consisting of the consideration of the mark (liṅgaparāmarśa) is a means of valid cognition whose fruit is perception, it possesses the assistance of the recollection of the relationship between the mark and the marked (liṅga-liṅgisambandha) in its production.

But this is not the case for the means of valid cognition that is perception; therefore, the meaning is that perception does not depend on the recollection of the relationship between the mark (liṅga) and the marked (liṅgin), whether in its own arising or in its effect.
He explains the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "And otherwise... by saying "For this reason also."
He states the meaning of the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "But this is not inference" as follows:
"By the sense organ," etc.;
for perception of an object arises from its connection with the sense organ.
But inference is not like this; such is the meaning. // 31 //
Nor is there perception of only one part [of an object] because of the real existence of the whole.
Furthermore, you, who maintain that the whole (*avayavin*) does not exist, have stated that the cognition of a tree is inferential based on the perception of only a single part;

however, this is not merely the perception of a single part, but rather the establishment of both that [part] and its concomitant whole, which has reached the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*).
Thus he says: "And there is no perception of a single part."
Having restated this commentary (*bhāṣya*), the author of the *Vārttika* explains it with the words "And not... (*na ca*). Here, the following is the introductory objection (*deśyabhāṣya*):
"If it is argued that [the definition] does not apply because it does not grasp the whole (*akṛtsnagrahaṇāt*)."
"The later commentary [states] 'not by way of cause';
this is an explanation of the point to be shown.
And [it states] 'nor are there parts'."
For you have resorted to the apprehension of the whole (avayavin) precisely to avoid the apprehension of only a part;
yet by this much, the apprehension of the whole is not possible, such that there would be an avoidance of the apprehension of only a part.
Indeed, when the whole is apprehended, all the parts are not thereby apprehended.
Nor is it a whole (avayavin), because even when its front portion is perceived, the middle and rear portions situated behind it are not perceived; such is the meaning of the *deśya* commentary.
The author of the *Vārttika* explains this very commentary as follows:
There is no perception of a whole (*avayavin*). For that which indeed exists in many things must exist either in each individually or in their aggregate,
as for example, the quality of the throat of the *kalaṃviṅka* bird.
Or [it may be] by way of a single part, as a garland-thread is [related] to its flowers;
nor is there any other mode besides these two,
since the negation of one of them is necessarily concomitant with the affirmation of the other.
It is like the case of permanence and impermanence.
Furthermore, it is not possible for that very same thing to be fully present in one place while also being present elsewhere;
for if that were so, there would be no such thing as "full presence" (kṛtsnasamāpti).
Therefore, it should also be observed that what is seen in one part is not the whole; thus, it follows that there are only parts.
For [the whole] does not exist apart from its causes.
For if it were to have other parts within those [parts],
then there would follow the consequence of an infinite regress by virtue of having to postulate yet further parts within those parts as well;
such is the meaning.
The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) himself states the non-occurrence of the action (*kriyātipatti*) by means of a question:
"Now, if it is being perceived... The entire subsequent commentary, beginning with "Indeed, [it is] thus," is intended to explain the following portion of the *Bhāṣya*.
Because it forms a single continuous work, the Bhāṣya begins with the address "But you, sir," and so forth;
the author of the Vārttika explains this as follows:
"In one [work]," etc.
This is the underlying intention: as for the claim that it is observed [the thread] exists in its entirety within each individual flower, that is untenable;
for if the parts of the thread exist in the flowers, what has come of the thread as a whole?
For it has been stated that when one thing exists, another does not exist; nor,
in the absence of the whole (*avayavin*), can this sūtra— namely, "the whole exists by means of its parts"— be valid.
Now, let it not be that the thread itself is the whole; rather, we say that its parts reside in the flower.
This being the case, it is not a single thing that exists in many places by way of its parts, but rather it is the many [parts] that exist in the many [places].
And thus, it is effectively stated that a single thread-atom resides within a single flower-atom;
yet this "residing" (vṛtti) is not something distinct from the two atoms themselves, since it is only because they exist that one says "it resides.
Therefore, there is only uninterrupted arising.
Thus, the occurrence [of a whole] in two atoms should be designated as such;
however, there is no occurrence whatsoever that exists as a real entity distinct from the nature of the atoms themselves.
And in this way, the explanation that "occurrence" means the complete presence of the whole in each [part], like the color of a sparrow's throat, is also refuted.
And thus, because there is no such occurrence [of the thread], the statement that "it exists either partially or in its entirety" is empty.

However, if one accepts occurrence according to worldly cognition, the aphorism states: "The thread does not exist in the flowers partially; rather, it is the parts of the thread and the thread itself that exist in the flowers"—this is the worldly experience.
In that case, the presence of the thread in the flowers is neither by way of a single part nor by way of its entirety,
but rather by way of its own nature;
likewise, the presence of the whole in its parts is only by way of its own nature.

However, there is this distinction: regarding the subsistence of a thread in flowers, there are both parts and the form of the thread itself that subsist in the flowers; whereas regarding the subsistence of a whole in its own parts, there are no further constituent parts [of the whole], so the whole subsists therein by way of its mere form alone.
Therefore, nothing is observed to subsist anywhere either in its entirety or in part; thus, the pervasion of those two [part and whole] with respect to subsistence is unestablished.

It is the form (*rūpa*) alone that possesses pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*), and since that [pervasiveness] also exists in the whole (*avayavin*), the non-perception of the pervader is unestablished; thus it is proven that there is neither the occurrence nor the non-occurrence of the whole within its parts.
Furthermore, as for how the terms "entirety" (*kṛtsna*) and "part" (*ekadeśa*) do not apply to the nature of the whole, this has been stated by the author of the *Vārttika*.

The phrase "it does not exist in one part, nor does it exist in its entirety, and yet it exists" is a manner of expression; the construction here is that whatever object exists in a certain way, it is designated as such in this context. "Because of contradiction by both ways" means that there is a contradiction in a single entity existing in multiple locations, whether by way of one part or in its entirety.
For it is only that property which, when being conceptualized, does not subvert the substratum (dharmin) that is subject to conceptualization;
for example, "Is sound eternal or non-eternal?
However, that conceptualization of a property which subverts the very substratum that serves as its locus is not logically tenable as a conceptualization of a property.

Because it is untenable due to the unestablished nature of its locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*). The following is stated as a factual reality: whatever exists is entirely partless, just like consciousness (*vijñāna*).
The statement "it is determined by the experience of blue and so forth" is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), because the world, being partless, is pervaded by mere existence.
For indeed, the existence of a single entity is pervaded by the non-association with contradictory properties.

And its opposite—the conjunction of contradictory properties—entails that if blue and other such qualities possess parts, it would result in a contradiction; by negating its own opposite (the non-conjunction of contradictory properties), it also negates existence (*sattva*), which is pervaded by that [conjunction]. For instance, when the hand and so forth move, the whole (*avayavin*) situated therein must also move. Consequently, that whole, which remains in an undifferentiated state across parts such as the shanks, would be perceived as moving; yet it is not so perceived. Therefore, that...
Thus, at that time, there would be a conjunction of contradictory properties, namely "it vibrates" and "it does not vibrate.
Alternatively, even if the parts are vibrating, if the whole inhering in them does not vibrate,
then it would follow that the moving and the non-moving are established as separate entities, like cloth and water.
If, upon the obscuration of one part, the whole situated in that particular part were obscured, it would follow that the whole situated in other parts would also be obscured,
because there is no difference [between the parts and the whole].
Nor would it be seen as complete, since there would be no obstruction anywhere for it.
If it is argued that the obstruction belongs to the part and not to the whole because they are distinct—
and that when one thing is obstructed, another does not become obstructed, lest there be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga)— we say no.
Even if one part is covered, since the whole (avayavin) remains uncovered, it follows that it would be perceived in its entirety, just as before.

If it is argued that the whole is not apprehended because the perception of the whole occurs through the perception of its parts, and thus the whole cannot be known when its parts are not seen— this is not so, for the argument does not withstand scrutiny.

Is the cognition of the whole (avayavin) by way of perceiving all its parts, or by way of perceiving only a few parts? In the former case, the whole would never be perceived at all; for one who is not omniscient is incapable of perceiving every single part.

Because the near part is separated from the middle and far parts, if the whole were manifested by the perception of only a few parts, then even when only a few parts are seen, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of perceiving the whole, just as one perceives many parts [when they are fully visible].

Furthermore, if one part is dyed red, the whole situated in that part would also be red; since it is non-different from its other parts, there would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving the redness in those other parts as well.
Or, if there were coloring of only a single part, the form of the whole (avayavin) situated therein would be seen as uncolored;
this, then, is the conjunction of contradictory properties (viruddhadharmasaṃsarga).

With this intention, the author of the Vārttika indicates all instances of the association with contradictory properties by means of the association with the properties of apprehension and non-apprehension; that is,
he refutes them by means of the phrase "apprehension and non-apprehension."
"Not a difference.
First, this must be addressed here: if the blue perceived in experience is being proven to be partless, [then...]
Consequently, this results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
For even for us, a specific color such as blue is not itself possessed of parts, because it is a quality (*guṇa*).
If it is argued that the jar is the substratum of that [color], [we reply: ...
Now, one might object: even in the case of what is called a "jar," it is actually only color, smell, taste, and touch that perform causal functions and are designated as such;
and since these are qualities, they are indeed partless, and there is no such thing as a substratum for them at all.

Now, if one takes as the subject a substance established by the opponent— which is the substratum of color and the like— and proves its partlessness through its existence as established by that very opponent, he demonstrates his own status as a great logician by proving what is unestablished through what is [already] established.
For a subject and a property to be proven are not fit for communicating to another if they are not themselves apprehended.
As they have said:

"Even in the case where that which is unestablished for the opponent is stated to be established for oneself, a remedy might exist there; but what action can be taken regarding that which is unestablished for oneself?"
Thus [it is said].
Nor can this [consequence] apply even in the case of a *prasaṅga* proof;
nor by virtue of having parts (*sāvayavatva*).
Because there is no contradiction;
nor is there any subverting proof for a single entity possessing contradictory properties.
For instance, there is no such proof regarding the simultaneous perception and non-perception of a single whole (avayavin).
Even when its parts are covered, [the whole] is perceived precisely because some of its parts remain present.
Nor is it correct to argue that the whole is not perceived because, unlike when many parts are perceived, such grossness (sthūlatva) does not appear when only a few parts are perceived.

For magnitude (*parimāṇa*) is a specific dimension (*bhedo hi sthaulyam*), which is a property of the whole (*avayavidharma*); and when such [magnitude] does not appear, the whole does not appear, because it is distinct from that [magnitude].
Therefore, the apprehension of the whole occurs through mere contact with the sense faculty (*indriyasannikarṣamātrāt*).
The perception of differences in magnitude arises from the contact of the sense organ with the object, the sense organ with the parts of the object,

the sense organ with the parts of the object, and the sense organ with the parts of the object; thus, due to the diversity of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), the perception and non-perception of both the whole and its distinct magnitudes are logically established.
By this it is stated that even when the front part is grasped, the non-grasping of the middle part does not in any way entail a contradiction;
nor indeed does the movement of a part imply the movement of the whole, such that there would be the undesirable consequence of movement in other parts as well,
because the part and the whole are distinct.

If it is argued that this being the case would entail the consequence of separate existence (*yutasiddhi*), what then is this "separate existence"? Is it the difference between the part and the whole?
Or rather, is it the existence of that which is unrelated?
If there is a distinction [between them],
that is indeed accepted by us.
Now, if it is argued that there is existence of the unconnected [whole], even though it possesses a separate motion, this is not the case for the whole;
for the time of its being produced and the time of its becoming connected are one and the same.

For instance, there is no whole that exists unconnected with its parts; nor is there anything possessing a genus that exists unconnected with that genus; nor do quality and action exist unconnected with a substance.
Nor is it the case that a particular property (*viśeṣa*) is unconnected to a substance.

However, as for those who assert that non-attainment (*aprāpti*) and conjunction (*saṃyoga*) constitute separate establishment (*yutasiddhi*), they must state the reason why there is no conjunction between a part (*avayava*) and its whole (*avayavin*).
If it is argued that this is because they are not established as separate entities (ayutasiddhi), we say no; for that very [state] is not sought after as a form of conjunction (asaṃyoga).
Furthermore, the state of being colored and uncolored does not belong to a single composite whole (avayavin).
This is precisely because that [cloth] is not red;
whereas the safflower in conjunction with it is red,
and that [safflower] is distinct from the cloth which is not red.
The notion that "the cloth is red" is an error; however, it need not follow from this error that [redness] exists everywhere,

because that [redness] has its cause in conjunction with saffron (mahārajana), because that [conjunction] resides only in the cloth, and because the cloth does not exist everywhere without distinction.
If the cloth were not in conjunction with anything at all, it would follow that there is a distinction between its being conjoined and its being unconjoined;
for it is not logically tenable that the very same thing, at the very same time, and in the very same place, both exists and does not exist.
Therefore, it follows that the cloth which is not conjoined is distinct from the cloth which is conjoined.
To this it is replied:
such, at least, is the understanding of the object of cognition.
Existence and non-existence consist in mutual exclusion: the cessation of existence is itself non-existence,
and the cessation of non-existence is itself existence.
The cessation of those two is not something other than existence and non-existence;
therefore, it is never possible for these two to have a mutual identity, because such is not observed.
Likewise, their unity or plurality as substrata must be established according to what is observed.
Just as, for that very crow, when it is present in the palace, at that same time it is absent [elsewhere];

and likewise, this jar is black, yet that same jar later becomes non-black through contact with fire; furthermore, whatever difference in its dimension there may be perishes when the jar itself perishes.
In that case, even when a *kiṅkacva* atom reaches a state of aggregation, it is not destroyed. Thus,

just as the diversity of perceptions is established based on the diversity of objects of cognition (*prameya*) as it is accepted [by you], so too must the existence and non-existence of that very conjunction be established at that same time,
for it is observed to be exactly so.
For indeed, when the nature of a perceived object is apprehended through its dissimilarity to another perceived object, it is impossible to deny it;
otherwise, there would be the denial of one perceived form by means of its dissimilarity to another perceived object, as there is no distinction between them.

Therefore, since the diversity of objects of knowledge is established in accordance with perception, for those who maintain that [form] exists, conjunction, sound, cognition, and so forth, both exist and do not exist at that very place and at that very time.
In this case, it is maintained that these [qualities] have non-pervasive occurrence (*avyāpyavṛttitva*).

However, in the case of color and so forth, it is not observed that there is both existence and non-existence at that very same place at that very same time; thus it is established that for those qualities which have pervasive occurrence (*vyāpyavṛttitva*), existence and non-existence are contradictory when simultaneous in one location. Therefore, there is no contradiction between being red and being non-red in one place, because they are observed together.
Furthermore, that which exists in multiple locations is manifold;
and since the whole (*avayavin*) is admitted to exist in multiple locations, this is a *prasaṅga-sādhana* based on a reason of essential nature (*svabhāva-hetu*).
[The consequence is: because of the absence of manifoldness, there is an absence of existing in multiple locations.
Thus, [you claim] that the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) and its contrapositive (*viparyaya*) constitute a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).

To this we reply: since there is no contradiction between being one and subsisting in many, the pervasion of manifoldness is not established; therefore, neither the reductio nor its contrapositive is valid.
Just as when blue is being determined, its absence is excluded— otherwise, blue would not be determined—
so too does perception, which determines blue, exclude yellow, which is invariably concomitant with that absence.
Likewise, when the connection with one part is perceived while the whole is being delimited, the absence of that [connection] is excluded;
and since the connections with other parts are invariably concomitant with that absence, they too must be excluded.

If they were not excluded, the absence of those [connections] would not be excluded; consequently, it would result in the absurdity that the very same thing both exists and does not exist in that place at that very time.
If it is argued that this constitutes a contradiction between existing as one and existing as many,
then indeed it is logical that when a positive entity is delimited, its absence is thereby excluded.
Because the exclusion of its absence has the characteristic of being a determination of existence;
for indeed, according to you, there is no such thing as the absence of existence that is distinct from existence itself.
But why then are other existences excluded?
If it is argued that this is because of the invariable concomitance with the absence of that [other],
then from what source does this invariable concomitance between the presence and absence of other entities arise?
If it is argued that it is because blue is never perceived as being identical in nature with yellow and other such entities;

In that case, where a single entity residing in one part is seen to have identity with other parts as well, there is no invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) between its connection with one part and its absence in the connection with other parts;
therefore, there is no contradiction between being one and residing in many.
Furthermore, how can a single cognition be connected with multiple factors, such as form, the eye, light, and mental attention?
Whether it is being connected or not, there is no such relation called "the causal relationship" that exists in reality;
how can one thing exist dependently?
If it is argued that it is merely a matter of arising [in dependence],
