then why does visual consciousness arise only in dependence upon visible form (*rūpa*) and not also from taste (*rasa*) and so forth?
If it is argued that its very nature (*svabhāva*) is such that it arises only in dependence upon those [visible forms] and not from donkeys and the like, [we reply:]...
"Alas, sir! How can a single entity arise depending on causes that are distinct in their own-nature (*svabhāva*)?
What is the contradiction here? For there is no identity (*tādātmya*) between cause and effect such that the effect would have to conform to the own-nature of the cause. [If this is argued, we reply:
"In that case, is there likewise no difference between the parts and the whole, or between inherence (*samavāya*) and those two?"
The same resolution applies whether one argues that there would be a difference between the parts and the whole, or a difference within the inherent relation (*samavāya*) itself.
Therefore, whatever proof we shall state regarding the whole will, in the absence of a subverting argument, establish the whole without obstruction; thus it is proven.
Furthermore, regarding one who thinks that the "whole" (avayavin) is merely the collection of its parts, the author of the Commentary says:
"Because it is not the entirety of the constituents," and so forth.
This is easy to understand. // 32 //
Nyāyasūtra 2.1.33: Because it is the object of proof, there is doubt regarding the whole.
That which is to be proven is [the subject] (Sūtra 33).

The very fact that the whole (*avayavin*) is unestablished for the opponent constitutes its status as the probandum (*sādhyatva*). Indeed, he [the author] thought thus: "The determination of objects is grounded in cognition;
only that which is an object of that cognition is established by it."
That alone is the object which imparts its form to this [cognition].
Nor do we perceive a cognition that bears the form of a composite whole (avayavin) distinct from the atoms of color and so forth produced in immediate succession;
rather, [we perceive] a cognition bearing the form of those atoms of color and so forth produced in immediate succession.

And although grossness does not exist in each individual atom, nevertheless, as a property of appearance—just like plurality and so forth—it is not able to establish a single composite whole (*avayavin*).
As they say: "This [proponent] is a buyer who refuses to pay the price; he offers a form to cognition and yet wishes to claim the status of being directly perceived for the composite whole."
Thus, since the existence of a whole (*avayavin*) is unestablished for the opponent, there is a disagreement;
the meaning is that, in the absence of both proof and refutation, doubt arises.

Considering that being the probandum (*sādhyatva*) in its own nature is not a cause for doubt, the author of the Bhāṣya says: "And this being so. This means: "this being the case that [the reason] is unestablished for the opponent (*parāsiddhatve*)."

Taking the sūtra exactly as it is heard—"because it is that which is to be proven"—the author of the Vārttika raises an objection by means of an alternative analysis: "What, then, is the case here? [He asks:
"For what reason should there be an *abhyanujñāna*—that is, an acceptance—of that subject (*dharmin*)?"
The meaning is that for every reason [adduced], the locus is unestablished (*āśrayāsiddhi*).
Now, as for the term "non-exclusion" (*avyatireka*):

The meaning is that while the substratum (dharmin) itself exists, the property (dharma) consisting in its non-difference from its parts is what is to be proven (*sādhya*). This is because [the status of being a part] depends upon the whole (*avayavin*);
for it is only in relation to a cloth that threads become its parts.
Indeed, it is not the case that threads situated within a basket for discarded things are called "parts" (avayava);
nor is it because of the genitive case [that they are so called].
Threads are the parts of a cloth.
Thus, there is no genitive [case];
and so, in the absence of the qualification "of the cloth," the mere state of being a part would be the reason,
and that is contradictory.
This is the meaning.
"Being a part by way of not being a different entity" is the illustration of this;
for example, "the thread is not [a part] of the thread."
But when the sense of the genitive (ṣaṣṭhy-artha) is absent, the subsequent example applies;
it states that "the threads possess the state of being woven into a cloth.
The meaning is that this is because the word *tat* (that) refers back to the primary subject.
Regarding the phrase "of the word *avayava*":

previously, without intending to express causality, it was stated by taking the word *avayava* merely as a relative term denoting what precedes and follows; now, however, it is stated with the intention of expressing causality—thus there is no redundancy.
He explains:
"By no means," meaning that what is non-existent cannot be produced or brought into being;
and for us, who are proponents of the theory that the effect pre-exists (satkāryavādins), such a thing does not exist. This is the meaning.
He refutes this as follows:

For the cognition of the form of a cloth does not have the mere threads as its object, because that would entail the absurd consequence [of such a cognition] even when the threads are situated in a basket or a box.
Nor does it have the difference in the dimensions of the threads as its object, because those [dimensions] exist even previously;
or else, if they did not exist, it would follow that the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (satkāryavāda) would be contradicted.
Since that very non-existent thing arises,
one must— even against one's will— admit that the cognition "this is something else on these threads" is a false cognition;
and thus, the refutation follows.

"And [the fallacy] 'a part of the thesis' (pratijñaikadeśa)" means when conjunction alone is made the subject of the proposition (pakṣa). "Those very same [reasons]" refers to those [previously mentioned reasons].
The meaning is that these very [causes] are proximate because momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) and transformation (*pariṇāma*) have been refuted.
For example, it is like saying "the staff and so forth are multiple causes";
the staff, loom, and so forth are the multiple causes for effects such as pots and cloth.
"Dependent on other causes such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*)," etc.:
"conjunction" is the first among those other causes, such as the potter, the weaver, and so forth; these are the "other causes.
This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the qualities [of the members] are not included in the referent (*atadguṇasaṃvijñāna*).
Just as in the case of "citrā-guḥ" (the brindled cow),
there is no fault because the very thing to be proven serves as the example;
thus one determines it after due reflection.
We, however, say that disjunction is produced.
Since conjunction has action as its cause and not non-action,
and since it is established that [disjunction] is the effect of action just like conjunction, it follows that disjunction performs nothing more than the removal of the obstructing factor.
Thus it is established;
or, for example, conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is a common effect-substance (*sādhāraṇakāryadravya*).
For when a cloth is torn apart, there remain those constituent parts whose conjunctions constitute the common effect known as "cloth."

Regarding that common effect-substance, namely the cloth, and its non-inherent causes—the conjunctions—after the destruction of some of these, when half a cloth is produced, the disjunction produced by action (karman) among those independent factors functions solely toward the destruction of the common effect such as the cloth by way of destroying certain conjunctions; it does not mean that conjunction is the cause for producing the half-cloth in dependence upon disjunction. This is the meaning.
"Indeed, not without a means of valid cognition" (pramāṇa);
the meaning is that even false cognition (mithyājñāna) is preceded by a means of valid cognition, because erroneous manifestation (viparītakhyāti) is preceded by correct cognition (samyagjñāna).

"By those contemplating the stability of the tree" means by those contemplating the stability— that is, the persistence— of the tree, which is the single object of preceding and succeeding cognitions.
"The non-perception of difference" (224).

9) The non-perception of a difference in form: just as a jar and a cloth, being distinct forms, are seen as different, it is not so with the part and the whole, nor with the inherence and the inherent; such is the meaning.
Since this application (*upanaya*) is: "The threads are parts and the cloth is the whole," whereas previously only the phrase "the parts" was made the reason (*hetu*).
Now, however, [the statement] "the parts and the whole" is not a tautology.
"The meaning of 'part' is different" means that the referent of the word "part" is distinct from the whole.
This is the meaning:
the meaning of the word "part" (pradeśa) is something other than the possessor of the part;
that is, it is the state of being the object of designation for that word "part."
For the threads (*tantavaḥ*) have been made the subject (*pakṣīkṛtāḥ*), and thus they must be referred to by the pronoun "that" (*tat*) which functions as the reason (*hetu*).

Consequently, the meaning is that the state of being the object of designation belongs to the location of the threads (*tantupradeśasya*) and not to the threads themselves; therefore, the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*).
As for the phrase "because it arises from them" (*tebhyastūtpatteḥ*), this is an elaboration of the imagined reason: "the cloth arises from the threads."
"Because of contradiction by both" (22/9) means [contradiction] by acceptance, not by non-acceptance. "In another substance," etc.
Exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) is the delimitation of the locus of the arising of a distinct substance;

the meaning is that, for example, the locus of the arising of a jar is different from the locus of the arising of a cloth. [This occurs] through the distinction of properties such as individual instances (*vyakti*) and so forth.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), manifestation (*āvirbhāva*), configuration (*saṃsthāna*), and so forth are meant;
and since these did not exist prior to the operation of the cause, their birth (*janma*) as well is "unprecedented" (*apūrva*). This is the meaning.
For example, from a wheel and other such [causes]... (228)
4) This means "from the parts of a chariot.
Regarding the phrase "consisting of atoms of the Himavat":
the mention of "atoms" (paramāṇu) is for the purpose of indicating subtle substances in general.
Furthermore, there is no possibility of production [of a composite] other than from an atom (paramāṇu) or a dyad (dvyaṇuka).
Moreover, the atom under dispute does not initiate a large substance, because it is an atom, just like an atom that initiates a dyad.
And because of its lack of largeness, an atom of the Himalayas would not be perceptible.
Therefore, from the conjunction of the two conjoined snowflakes with the Himalayas, a composite substance is produced, and its largeness arises from the largeness of its parts;
thus, it possesses visibility.
Likewise, [a composite substance arises] from the conjunction of water droplets released from a cloud with curd.
The production of a distinct substance must be admitted,
lest existence (bhāva) be imperceptible;
here, "existence" (bhāva) means being (sattā).

Now, one might object: "Just as conjunction, whose determination depends upon the determination of the two conjoined things, is not perceived when even one of those two is imperceptible, so too the whole would not be perceptible if its parts were imperceptible. To this, he says:
"And this position [is not tenable]."
For it is logical that a conjunction, whose own definition depends on the definition of the things being conjoined, cannot be defined when those things are not defined; however,
a whole (avayavin) does not have its definition dependent on the definition of its parts (avayava), such that it could not be defined when they are not defined,
because a triad (tryaṇuka) is perceived even when its parts are not grasped.
The meaning is that, in this way, although the parts of the elephant, the forest tree, and so forth are not apprehended by one who is fleeing, they are nonetheless apprehended;
nor does there exist any distinction caused by that [non-apprehension].
The meaning is that there is no difference [between the two views] based on whether there is apprehension or non-apprehension;
for the sense faculty does not manifest an object in one way for the Sāṃkhya as something subtle,
and in another way for the Naiyāyika as something gross.
Because it is non-conceptual and because it abides in a state of uniformity;
[it is so] because it would contradict the means of valid cognition known as direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*).
For the ultimate cause of the great elements (*mahābhūta*) is atoms (*paramāṇu*), which are extremely subtle; since they are not objects of direct perception...

The meaning is that my perception, which is accessible through mental after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) and has an extremely subtle object, exists; thus, the non-existence [of such perception] in the self would contradict perception through the mental contact (*manas-sannikarṣa*) characterized as "conjoined with the qualified" (*saṃyukta-viśeṣaṇa*).
"But some," [it is said]. For that very triad (tryaṇuka) which you call visible and whose parts are themselves visible, we call the atom (paramāṇu);
for there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for the postulation of parts beyond that—this is the sense.
It is divided [into its components] for the sake of determining its nature as a *trasareṇu*.
Its non-perception when rubbed by the tips of fingers is also possible due to its subtlety;
the point is that this dust particle is perceived only in some way when situated within the rays of the sun through a lattice, and not otherwise.
The phrase "being a substance" (dravyatve sati) excludes generality (sāmānya) and inherence (samavāya).
The term "external" (bāhya) excludes the self (ātman).
And [the addition of] "because of impermanence" (anityatvāt ca) [excludes the other categories].

Because [if atoms had parts], it would follow that Mount Meru and a mustard seed would have identical dimensions due to having infinite constituent parts; therefore, one must postulate that the fundamental cause of the great elements (*mahābhūta*) is partless. Furthermore, no substance devoid of parts perishes, just like space and so forth; thus, while atoms (*paramāṇu*) are eternal, triads (*trasareṇu*) are impermanent.
If it is asked why the atom itself is not impermanent, he says:
"Endowed with generality and particularity" means "of those that are aggregated";
it means that an atom is an aggregation of form and so forth.
Nor is there a negation of the non-aggregated;
for if there were no negation, those very atoms would remain non-aggregated.
This is the intended meaning:
since this [whole] is both conjoined with and divided from another whole, there is no distinction [between them].
Just as the absence of conjunction and non-attainment is excluded from what is distinct, so too is it excluded from what is non-distinct.
The meaning is that a particular thread cannot be reached by that very same thread.
There is no conjunction of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*; rather, there is some kind of natural distinction in their transformation (*pariṇati*) through which they act in combination.
[The phrase] "because no effect of another weight is perceived" means...

The meaning is that because of the weight of the parts, there is another weight belonging to the whole; since its effect—a specific degree of downward inclination—is not perceived, [the reason] is unestablished.
It is true that the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) has been demonstrated.
The meaning is that by the non-apprehension of the effect, there is an absence of the effect; consequently, there is an absence of the heaviness of the cause.
Thus, the form and other qualities residing in the effect, which were to be negated, become admitted.
Nevertheless, as to why there is a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), he says:
"The causes are color and so forth" (*kāraṇarūpādayaḥ*). The word *ca* functions as a conjunction (*hetu*).
By this, the apprehension of form and so forth in an effect is refuted as being something to be negated.
For when the effect itself—namely, form and so forth—does not exist, then for what reason would the apprehension of form and so forth therein be negated? This is the meaning.
As in the case of "an effect consisting of another form and so forth."
The effect of the color and other qualities belonging to the parts is the manifestation of color through the formation [of those qualities], and thus the whole (avayavin) becomes visible;
such is the presentation or establishment [of the argument].
Even though this lack of a specific downward bending is located in a different locus from the scale...

No; nevertheless, its connection with the scale is not perceived through verbal testimony, but rather it is merely stated that it is connected with a specific downward bending. This is what is meant by "this is that."
(235/2) "First of all, it is unestablished"—this is the refutation of the partial proponent (ekadeśin). He now refutes that very refutation of the partial proponent:
"Because its possession [of the property] is not perceived."
He states the refutation of the ultimate position:
"This too... [refers to the following].
A scale does not produce any specific downward bending in atoms that are endowed with mere heaviness.

Regarding the phrase "the collection of substances" (dravyasamāhāra): it means the collection of causal and resultant substances, that is to say, the collection of clay particles, clay powder, gravel, potsherds, and the jar.

[Objection: But surely the aggregate (*samāhāra*) is the cause of the jar, and that [aggregate] is nothing other than the heaviness (*gurutva*) of the cognate parts; to this he says: "And not... (236.3). As for those who say that the entire collection of effects, beginning with the lump of clay and ending with the jar, inheres (*samavaiti*) in the atoms themselves—they indeed [proceed] starting from the lump of clay and continuing through the powder of the clay.
Thus, he introduces the view of certain [others] in order to refute that opinion by way of a consequential argument (*prasaṅga*).
"But some... and so forth.
He refutes them with this [argument]:
"Gravity follows that which falls."

And it should not be said that, just as jars and other objects have illumination dependent on a lamp while the lamp itself does not have illumination dependent on a lamp— because its own power precludes any connection with darkness— likewise, jars and other objects have falling dependent on gravity, whereas gravity is the cause of falling for both itself and others without depending on any other gravity.
For when a lamp illuminates itself, nothing else is required;
the lamp is of the same nature as jars and other objects insofar as they require illumination.
However, there is this distinction in the nature of the eye: that while it requires a lamp to illuminate a jar or similar object, it does not require another lamp to illuminate the lamp itself.
Therefore, a lamp does not possess the status of both object and instrument with respect to itself;
however, gravity is the instrument for the action of falling belonging to a substance,
for by it the substance is caused to fall.

However, if the action of falling were the instrument for that which has already occurred (the falling), then that very same action would be both the object and the instrument, which is a contradiction regarding its own self.
Furthermore, it has been established that when the Self is to be manifested within itself, it possesses only the status of agent and not the status of object.
Therefore, it is proven that qualities and so forth, which are the subjects of dispute, do not fall, because they belong to a category other than substance, just like gravity.
The proponent says:
Furthermore, this stated reason is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Color and so forth do not possess the nature of conjunction, because they are qualities, like conjunction itself; since there is no perception [of conjunction] in color and so forth when it has not been attained, the delusion of attainment regarding color and so forth is caused by the non-perception [of conjunction], while the cognition of attainment regarding substances [arises from actual contact].
"Thus" is the definitive conclusion. With this intention, he concludes:
"Therefore, it is established."
The remainder has a meaning that is not obscure. // 33 //
NyS 2.1.34: There would be no perception of anything at all, because the composite whole (avayavin) is not established.
Regarding the sūtra "Because of the non-apprehension of everything" (Sū.

34): it might be argued that just as the opponent does not accept the whole (avayavin), he likewise does not accept qualities, actions, and so forth; therefore, how can this undesirable consequence—that there would be no apprehension of anything at all for the opponent—be established? To this, he says: "This is the sūtra."
For even one who does not accept qualities, actions, and so forth, cannot deny the cognition of them;
there exists among both worldly people and investigators a cognition of substances, qualities, actions, and so on, which is impossible to deny.
Furthermore, its status as perception has been established in the definition of perception (*pratyakṣa-lakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, the proofs that refute the existence of a composite substance (*avayavidravya*) have already been rejected above. Thus, since there is no subverting evidence and because it is perceived together with its qualities (*guṇa*) and other attributes, it cannot be denied; this is the meaning of the section. // 34 //
And because holding and drawing [the breath] are possible.
And [the word] *dhāra* [is used in the sense of "bearing" or "supporting"] (Sūtra 35).
These two, maintenance and attraction, establish the existence of a whole (avayavin) such as a cow or a jar that is currently perceived;
for they are not observed in partless things like consciousness or space, nor in a part, nor in an atom.
This argument proceeds as follows:
This whole (avayavin), such as a cow or a jar, which is being perceived and is the subject of dispute as being a collection of atoms,
is not a non-whole, because it would follow that holding and pulling [the object] would be impossible.
Whichever thing is without parts, in each case holding and pulling occur, as in the case of consciousness and so forth;
and since this [cow, jar, etc. is not like that, it is therefore not partless.
Thus, there is no contradiction.
The fault characterized by deviation is contradiction (*virodha*).
The meaning is that those [parts] belong to the whole (*avayavin*) individually;
however, in an aggregate of atoms (*paramāṇu-samūha*), even individually, the atoms are not wholes.
"Because there is no specific reason [for such a distinction].

For a specific reason would indeed exist if, in some case—such as consciousness, space, or the like—the aforementioned characteristics of "collection" (saṃgraha) or its status as the cause of holding and drawing forth were observed to occur in the absence of a whole (avayavin).
Yet that is not observed; for wood, grass, stones, and so forth, each individually [lacks such properties].
This is the meaning. It might be argued:
"Even though they are equal in being wholes, why is it that holding and pulling occur in one case and not in the other? To this, he says:
Regarding the phrase "a heap of dust":

the meaning is that just as there is a specific cause for something despite its being equal insofar as it is merely an aggregate, so too is it the same in the case of being equal insofar as it is a whole (*avayavin*).
A specific relation belonging to that which coexists with it is produced by moisture and fluidity.
Therefore, the commentator’s refutation of the Sūtra should be understood as being directed against the views of another school. // 35 //
If it is argued that the perception [of atoms] is like that of an army or a forest,
we say no, because atoms are beyond the reach of the senses.
Now,

regarding the term "positive" (anvayi) and the term "positive-negative" (anvaya-vyatireki): [the former refers to a reason that exists only in the similar class, while the latter refers to one that exists in both the similar and dissimilar classes].
The cognition "this is a cloth" is a single cognition because it has a single object; the cognition "threads" is a manifold cognition because it has multiple objects.
This is due to the fact that their objects are either combined or uncombined.
Because a single cognition has an unaggregated object, whereas multiple cognitions have an aggregated object;
from this apprehension, the following sūtra [is stated].
Regarding the [sūtra] on the name "army" (sū.
36): it is stated as follows: "An army and a forest are indeed nothing but a plurality.
However, for one who considers that the designations "army" and "forest" are for the sake of producing a cognition [of those things], [the sūtra teaches] the number of plurality.

He says this in response to one who is not satisfied [with the previous argument], thinking: "How could such a cause possibly exist, since this sensory cognition—which arises suddenly as a single, comprehensive apprehension of a grove, even though the oneness is not grasped in each individual tree and no such cognition has arisen regarding them—is produced? In that case, because multiplicity cannot arise due to the absence of its cause, it cannot have multiplicity as its objective referent. [The author] replies to him:
And regarding the cognition of non-difference:
even with respect to those things whose forms are being perceived, a false cognition of difference arises due to some cause when their distinctness is not being perceived.
The intended meaning is, however, that this does not apply when things are entirely unperceivable.
To one who thinks that there is nothing whatsoever in the world accepted by both parties as being a single entity, he says: "There is no one."
This might be the case:
from a distance, wood, clods of earth, grass, stones, and so forth, are not perceived individually when separated;
however, their collection is seen.

Nor do they initiate a distinct substance because of their heterogeneity; otherwise, atoms would each be individually perceptible. Yet, even without initiating another effect, their aggregate is perceived. To address this, he says:
"And [the argument] of the non-perception of that which is being perceived."

Even when those very atoms are combined, they are not perceived in that form which constitutes their fitness for apprehension; however, because atoms are extremely subtle, they are not fit for apprehension by their own nature, and thus even when combined they certainly cannot be perceived.
Indeed, even when combined, masses of air never become objects of visual perception.
The point is that even the "greatness" (*mahattva*) of entities consists in their essential fitness for apprehension.
Consequently, there is a great contradiction in asserting that those very same things are both perceptible by the senses and imperceptible.

On this point, the author of the *Vārttika* said: "What contradiction is there if many [atoms], having attained excellence (*atiśaya*), were individually the cause of cognition, provided they are not distinct from one another, as is the case with the sense organs and so forth?"
This too has been refuted by the author of the *Vārttika* himself when he stated that "no distinction arises [in the atoms].
Indeed, for the establishment of the stability of entities, there is no other excellence (*atiśaya*) in atoms than the production of a composite substance (*avayavin*).
Nor is it the case that the atoms, having acquired some adventitious quality, produce a gross cognition (*sthūlabuddhi*) through that very [quality] which generates the composite.
It is now established that [the object] belongs to the possessor of parts (the whole). For whatever appears in cognition is its objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).

And this [cognition] does not have mutually distinct, most subtle atoms as its objective support; for if that were the case, it would follow that because of the difference in grossness, it could not be "one."
Nor is this cognition conceptual, because it possesses a clear manifestation (*spaṣṭapratibhāsatva*).
Nor is its clarity a property conditioned by non-conceptuality, since it is not apprehended even by non-conceptual [cognition].
Furthermore, solidity is not a property of the manifestation itself.
The apprehension by a single cognition of atoms situated in various directions and locations as being continuous constitutes "grossness" (*sthaulya*).
Indeed, such a state of the atoms existing at the moment of their appearance is called a property of appearance (*pratibhāsa-dharma*).
And thus, this experience is indeed correct;

for it is not the case that these atoms do not exist, nor that they do not arise in immediate succession, nor that they do not differ according to direction and location, nor that they do not manifest within a single cognition.
Therefore, what here could be otherwise?
As it has been said:
"And that perception is not erroneous, because it apprehends various entities by its own nature;
it is not a different kind of apprehension of the conventional, nor is the apprehension of an entity an error."
Thus it is said.
In this regard, first of all, because they are separated by atoms of odor, color, taste, and touch—just like sesame seeds and rice grains—there is no contiguity among them.

Therefore, due to the non-perception of the intervening spaces and because the atoms of form and so forth possess both intervals and multiplicity, this cognition is a false cognition, similar to the perception of a single dense forest from a distance.
And it is not logical to say that something is false when there is no sublation; the absence of sublation has already been stated,
and the stability of entities will be established [later].
"Therefore, this too is incorrect"—
this is the meaning of the commentary: "This very point is what is being examined."

The intended meaning is that for one who denies the existence of a whole (*avayavin*) everywhere and asserts that there is merely a collection of atoms (*paramāṇu*) beyond the reach of the senses, there can be no supporting example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāva*), because even the components of an army or a forest— such as elephants or safflower— are themselves merely collections of atoms beyond the reach of the senses.

If it is argued that [the example] is "seen," the meaning is that since the components of an army or a forest cannot be denied on the grounds of being perceived, the illustrative instance (nidarśana) is established.
He refutes it, saying: "And that is not so.
If what is perceived is not to be denied, then since the whole (avayavin) is also perceived, it too should not be denied.

Now, if this [example] is rejected after being examined, then the parts of an army or a forest must also be rejected; thus, there is an absence of a valid example because it is equal to the point to be proven (*sādhyasamatvāt*). This is the meaning of the *Bhāṣya*. As for the *Vārttika*: "And this which [occurs] in regard to many things..."—the non-existent particularity is the nature of silver in mother-of-pearl; the perception of that [particularity] occurs in places such as the marketplace; and the door to that [perception] is the latent impression (*saṃskāra*).
Therefore, that perception by which the property of "silver-ness"—which is superimposed upon the mother-of-pearl and is contrary to it—is produced is so described;
the state of being that is its "tattā" (that-ness), belonging to the perception of the common feature (*sāmānyadarśana*).

The distinction is this: comparison (*upamāna*) itself is [the means] when the difference is obscured, whereas that which is known through the explicit mention of difference is figurative (*aupamika*); this is the definition of the knowledge of a name (*saṃjñājñāna*) as an example of the figurative.

As in the case of "the young boy is a lion. [Objection: But even this is merely figurative because the difference [between the boy and the lion] has been concealed. To this, he says: "A lion-like lion."
This is the meaning:
from the word *siṃha* (lion), which serves as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), when the suffix *kvip* is applied according to the rule "after all nominal stems,
[the suffix *kvip* is added] in the sense of behaving like [something]," and subsequently the agentive suffix *ap* is added, the word *siṃha* comes to signify the object of comparison.
He explains the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "And if atoms were of diverse nature," etc., with the words:
"Even false cognitions...
and "But in the absence of that..."
But in the absence of a primary substance (pradhāna), there are merely false cognitions regarding jars and the like;
that is, [they exist] in atoms when they are accumulated.

Even for those who maintain that the jar is a composite whole (avayavin), an accumulation of atoms must be admitted; and even for those for whom no composite whole exists, an accumulation of atoms must likewise be admitted. Thus, this accumulation is agreed upon by both parties.
This is the meaning:
they too are indeed composite.

For the Vaibhāṣikas, who are followers of the Vātsīputrīyas, maintain that even cloth and the like, as well as sound and so forth, arise from a collection of primary elements (bhūta) and derivative matter (bhautika); therefore, in their view, sound and the rest do not possess primary oneness, since number is a quality and [oneness] cannot reside in qualities.
Because [the term] does not apply to sound and so forth,
but rather is merely figurative,
he says:
Regarding the phrase "and a single cognition of sound and so forth," he raises an objection with the word "everywhere" (sarvatra) and then refutes it.
Regarding the phrase "not two" (*na dve*):

if oneness were merely the cessation of conjunction through the negation of duality—such that because conjunction is excluded, oneness is simply the locus of that exclusion—then there would be no doubt as to whether [the object] is one or many; nor would the statement "it is indeed one" serve as a definitive conclusion (*niyama*) in that context.
In the sense of "going" or "attaining," he suspects [an objection] in every case.
He refutes [the opponent] by stating,
"Not one," in this context;
this is the underlying intention.

In the absence of duality and so forth, there would be mere conjunction (*samuccaya*) alone; however, there would be no internal differentiation among those conjunctions. Consequently, since the conjunction of unity accompanied by non-conjunction—namely, "not one"—would already be established, there would be no doubt [regarding its existence]. But this must be stated here: [The original Sanskrit text continues: dvitvādīnāmabhāve samuccayamātraṃ syāt / na tu samuccayānāmavāntarabhedaḥ tathā ca naikamityasamuccayasahitaikatvasamuccayaḥ prāpta eveti na saṃśayaḥ syāt / idaṃ tviha vaktavyam /

If duality and so forth do not exist in sound and the like, how can there be the linguistic usage of "duality" and so on? If you say it is metaphorical (*bhākta*), what is the basis for that metaphor?

If it is merely a collection (*samuccaya*), how can there be the restriction "two"? If you say it is because of a specific kind of collection, has it not been stated that for this [collection], there is no differentiation by nature?
Furthermore, duality does not exist here such that it could qualify [the collection]; thus, even against one's will, an internal differentiation among collections must be admitted as inherent.
And thus, let that very [cognition] itself be the object of doubt; enough with [discussing] duality and so forth in relation to a substance.

Therefore, it must be understood that the venerable cognition alone is our refuge in the apprehension of real entities; it is the establisher of duality and the like by apprehending them as distinct from conjunction and other such categories, and the manner of following that [cognition] has been set forth by the author of the Vārttika with great abundance of reasoning.

Furthermore, for one who does not acknowledge the unity that is being experienced nor the duality and so forth that are being experienced—indeed, for such a person who denies experience, there would be no substratum for unity due to the absence of all limits;

thus, of what could there be a collection (samuccaya) such as duality? And in the absence of such a collection, of what would there be the non-existence [of which] would constitute unity? To this, he says:

Regarding the phrase "yaḥ punar" (as for that person who...): moreover, he states "ekatva-dvitvādīṃśca" (and unity, duality, etc. to show that even this figurative usage would not be possible for one who does not accept primary [entities] such as unity and so forth.
He explains the commentary by restating it:
"And among those, thus," [and] "because there is no determination of their number. (246.2)

The determination of a specific measure (*iyattā*) is an object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); however, in the case of those things that possess the dimension of the "infinitely great" (*paramamahat*), even though their measure is not determined through direct perception, they are not "without dimension" (*aparimāṇa*). This is because, since space (*ākāśa*) and other such entities are substances (*dravya*), their dimension is inferred, just as one says, "it has a large dimension. For instance, people in the world designate the dimension of an *āmalaka* fruit as larger than the dimension of a *kuvala* fruit.
For example, as in the case of saying "the āmalaka fruit is larger than the kuvala fruit.
Furthermore, there can be no conjunction of dimension with dimension,
because that would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress.
Therefore, this designation "the Great" (*mahat*) regarding magnitude is figurative (*bhākta*).

In that [sound], the word "that" (*tat*) possesses the word "Great" figuratively because it is a quality, just as magnitude is a quality; and the fact that sound is a quality has been established in the definition of inference (*anumāna-lakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, since the figurative is preceded by the primary, there must be some primary magnitude [for sound]; and it is established that, in the absence of any sublation, this [quality] is primary in a substance (*dravya*).
"Not because it is the object of the notion of 'great'";
this means that [the status of being a whole] does not arise from that alone, but rather from that which is uncontradicted and not otherwise established;
he states this very point with the words "but rather," and so forth.
By this, the non-otherwise-establishment of the cognition of "large" with respect to a substance is demonstrated;
likewise for the cognitions of "one," "large," and so forth.
The remainder [of the sentence] is: "by relying on a single aggregate."

"And a collection [is established] through the reaching of another collection. For when the constituent members of a collection, though distinct, are unified by reaching, they become a single collection; at that time, another collection is also reached by yet another collection as a single collection. And it is not the case that a single thing is not reached by its own self—for indeed, that very fingertip is not reached by that same fingertip. Therefore, the claim that there is no reaching between two collections is incorrect; this is the meaning.
He objects: "Birth does not exist at all.
This is the underlying intention.
There is no such thing as a "universal" (*sāmānya*) existing as a real entity whose basis could be followed as a real thing.
For it must reside either in that particular cluster [of individuals] or everywhere.

If it were everywhere, it would follow that everything would be a cow; for just as Śābaleya and others are indeed cows because of their connection with "cowness" (*gotva*), so too the entire universe would follow as being a cow, since it is connected to that [universal].
Now, if it were to exist only in some individual bodies (*piṇḍa*), then it must be explained: when an individual body is produced in a certain place, from where does its "cowness" (*gotva*) come?

It cannot be that it existed there even before the production of the body, nor can it have come from another body, because [cowness] is inactive and because it would entail the consequence of abandoning the other body.

Nor is it produced at the very moment the body is being born, for that would result in its being impermanent; furthermore, since the other body would possess the nature of not being born while this one is born, they would be distinct due to the imposition of contradictory properties, and thus the consequence would follow that it is not a universal (*sāmānya*).
Therefore, fearing this great calamity, one should rely on the conventional general [nature] alone, and not on the ultimate;
thus he refutes [the objection] with the words, "of the specific genus."
(249/2) Although the persistence of a causal condition (*pratyaya*) is indeed perceptible, it is nevertheless stated as a logical mark (*liṅga*) for one who is in disagreement.

For there exist certain entities which, despite being co-existent, are not mutually connected; such as the smell, taste, color, and touch existing at the same time, or the many cognitions of others existing simultaneously yet remaining unconnected, as well as space, time, ether, and the self, which all exist together.
Even for the Vaiśeṣikas, the locations [of universals] are mutually unconnected; likewise, the universal, though unrelated to anything, abides together with all [its instances].
However, it is only with its individual manifestations (*vyakti*) that it is ultimately connected.
Thus, wherever the individuals arise, both the universal and inherence (*samavāya*) exist there, even though they are themselves unconnected [to those places].
The very birth of these [universals] constitutes their delimitation by generality and inherence;
and since that [birth] cannot be further questioned regarding its own cause,
those who know the nature of things as established by valid cognition do not fear this objection.
Furthermore, other objections against this [view] have been refuted by the explanation regarding the composite whole (*avayavin*).
In that case, it follows that the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of the universal (*jāti*) is merely [the individual].
Whatever things manifest a universal such as "treeness" and so forth, each of those is distinct from one another as individual instances (*vyakti*) of trees and the like.
Just as the *kiṃśuka*, *aśoka*, *campaka*, and other trees are distinct, so too would its front part, middle part, and back part be distinct [if it were merely a collection of parts].
However, this fault does not apply when there is a whole (*avayavin*) that arises;
for that is recognized as such by virtue of being common to all its constituent parts.
Nor should it be argued that, in this way, there would likewise be as many wholes as there are parts; for that single whole is recognized as common to all its parts,
whereas one part is not recognized within another part.
If these were the causes for the manifestation of trees, it would follow that there are multiple trees; furthermore,
the claim that "it is the most inferior aggregate" involves a contradiction.

The meaning is: "because there is no diminution in relation to that which is being assembled. He states the formal argument (*prayoga*) for one who, like a Sāṃkhya, considers the whole (*avayavin*) to be non-different from its parts:
"it is a different object" (*arthāntaram*).
The capacity for covering belongs to the cloth, whereas the capacity for producing the cloth belongs to the threads.
Regarding the forms of the threads and the cloth:

the form of the threads consists of blue, yellow, red, and so forth, while the form of the cloth is variegated (*citra*). In this regard, the threads are the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of the blue and other colors, but the cloth is the inherent cause of the variegated color.
Thus, even though the yarns and the cloth are of the same nature (*sāvarṇya*), some distinction must be inferred.

This possession of distinction consists in being perceived as non-co-referential (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*); by that, their having different causes is established; and by that, their having different inherent causes (*bhinnasamavāyikāraṇatva*) is proven. Therefore, there is neither the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) nor the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*).
However, having set forth and refuted the opinion of those who, having apprehended the thesis and the reason in a different manner, have criticized them, he says:
"But some... and so on.
Inference is not a valid means of knowledge because it is fallible due to [the presence of] obstructions, damage, and similarity.
"Now, inference [is discussed]," says the Bhāṣya. Regarding this, the author of the Vārttika explains the meaning of the word "now" (*idānīm*): "Now, that which has reached its proper occasion."
The meaning is that the very sequence of the enumeration (*uddeśa*) constitutes the relationship between the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) and the examination (*parīkṣā*).
[Sūtra 37: *rodha-ṇam*].
The *Apramāṇada-vyākhyānabhāṣya* states "even once" (*ekadāpi*).
This means that which establishes [the definition] is what determines it.

Since a definition is intended for the definiendum (*lakṣya*), if there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the definiendum that possesses the definition, the definition itself becomes invalidated by its lack of being a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇatva*). This is the meaning.
The *vātika* [type of inference].

Regarding the examples starting with "as before" (*pūrvavat*), here, in the two examples of *śeṣavat*—namely, the swelling of a river and the cry of a peacock—the movement of ants carrying their eggs is not the effect of rain that is about to fall soon after; for that which has not yet come into being cannot be a cause.
[This refers to] that which has already arisen.
Furthermore, crookedness and so forth are not produced by a future death; for if that were the case, even a son would be the cause of his father. Thus, everything is clarified.
Let the determination of the relationship between cause and effect remain a worldly convention.

Indeed, a preceding existence that is governed by a rule establishes causality, and a subsequent existence that is likewise governed by a rule establishes effectness; for instance, the crookedness of the body and so forth are not the causes of death, yet they lead one to infer death through this proximity, namely, that they are the prior effects of that which is the cause of death.
Furthermore, the movement of ants with their eggs is not the cause of rain, because its causal efficacy is unperceived;
for rain occurs even in the absence of such movement.

Rather, the movement of ants with their eggs is a prior effect of the agitation of the great elements (*mahābhūta-saṃkṣobha*), which is the root cause of rain. Indeed, when being boiled by the subterranean heat, the ants carry their own eggs situated in the earth to a higher level.

Therefore, when inferers, having inferred the cause of rain from the movement of ant-eggs, infer the effect—namely, rain—from that cause of rain, then it is an example of *pūrvavat* (inference based on what has been previously perceived).

However, if they do so without understanding the relationship of cause and effect, then it should be considered an example of *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* (inference based on general observation), due to the absence of the causal relation.
This is by way of illustrating an instance where the example deviates [from the rule].
The meaning is that the definition is refuted by means of refuting the object of definition (the *lakṣya*).

For there is no proof whatsoever for the deviation of the inference itself—which is used to establish the invalidity of inference on the grounds of its own definition involving deviation—[if that inference were itself deviant]. // 37 //
[The definition of inference] is not [invalidated] by partial apprehension, fear, or similarity, because these are distinct entities.
In the commentary, the phrase "consisting mostly of ants" (*pipīlikāprāyasya*) is used; here, the word *prāya* signifies continuity (*prabandha*). // 38 //
NyS 2.1.39: There is no such thing as a present [action], because for one who is falling, only the past and the future times of the fall are logically possible.

Thus, having examined the definition of inference by means of an investigation into that very definition, the author of the Bhāṣya now introduces an examination of inference through an examination of its object, stating:
"it has objects belonging to the three times.

Regarding this, the author of the Vārttika observes that while the present time is being examined, it cannot yet be established as such until time itself is established; therefore, he examines the essential nature of time.
In that context, "firstly" refers to the three causes [of non-apprehension]. Regarding "by way of three causes":
the deficiency of other causes, the unsuitability of the object, or the absence of the object—these are the three causes of non-apprehension.

Now, [it might be argued] that "even dharma does not exist. The meaning is this: for a cause that has the nature of an existent entity cannot have a non-existent thing as its locus; however, there is no contradiction in a cause that has the nature of a non-existent thing having a non-existent thing as its locus.
He avoids [this objection], for the purpose of the proof is lost.

For an "absence" (abhāva) that is intended by the opponent—being devoid of all causal capacity—cannot serve as a means of proof for anything. However, the "absence" intended by us is dependent on another; it exists precisely as the locus of absence, not as a non-locus.
Nor does it mean that [time] has non-existence as its locus; such is the meaning.
Having thus stated the absence of subverting evidence regarding time, he states the proving evidence:
"prior, posterior," and so forth.
When two persons are themselves present, situated in indefinite directions or in the same direction, and either spatially near and far from each other or far and near— such as a youth and an elder—
wherein the elder has a birth separated by a great multitude of accumulated past actions consisting of the rising and setting of the sun inferred from the various bodily states [of his life],

and the youth has a birth separated by a small number of accumulated past actions consisting of the rising and setting of the sun inferred from the various bodily states [of his life], [the observer takes] the youth as the limit for the elder.

Having formed a cognition of remoteness, there arises in dependence upon that [cognition] the production of "priority" (*paratva*) in the older person through its conjunction with a greater interval of time characterized by more numerous sunrises and sunsets. Likewise, having made the younger person the limit (*avadhi*), there arises in dependence upon that [cognition] a cognition of proximity in the younger person; in dependence upon that [cognition], there is the production of "posteriority" (*aparatva*) in the younger person, who has an interval of birth separated by fewer sunrises and sunsets, taking the older person as the limit.

Having performed a remote action, a cognition arises; depending upon that [cognition], the production of "remoteness" (paratva) and "nearness" (aparatva) occurs in cows and other objects through a portion of time characterized by a greater accumulation of the rising and setting of the sun.
Furthermore, the perceptibility of both those [qualities] and the conjunction with the mass of time is not established in common worldly experience.

These two qualities, priority (*paratva*) and posteriority (*aparatva*), when produced from the conjunction of time and a corporeal object (*piṇḍa*), indicate that the Self is characterized by time as its cause, by virtue of being their effect.

If it is argued that priority and posteriority will arise from the corporeal object itself—qualified by the smallness or greatness of the accumulation of actions consisting of the rising and setting of the sun—and that there is therefore no need for a separate substance called "time," we reply:
no, because the action inherent in the sun has no connection with the corporeal object.
Its relation with all-pervading time is through inherence in a conjoined entity (*saṃyuktasamavāya*),
whereas even though space is all-pervading, it is not capable of accounting for the distinction between priority and posteriority,
because it lacks differentiation by its own nature.

Furthermore, space and the self, being devoid of [limited] manifestation, are not the cause of the confusion between the remote and the near, because they possess unique qualities, like earth and the other elements.

Therefore, when seeking the causes for the confusion between the remote and the near, those two—space and time—are designated as substances because they lack dependence on anything else, just like space. In this same way, the cognitions of simultaneity, non-simultaneity, long duration, and brevity [are explained].

Furthermore, time cannot be the mark [of these], for these [phenomena] cannot belong either to the action or to its factors; even when those [action and factors] exist, [these phenomena] occur only occasionally.
Now, one might object: "But this time is also eternal; even while it exists, why are these [phenomena] occasional? How, then, can time not be their cause? To this we reply: [it is not].

If it should be argued: actions delimited by time connected with the movement of a single sun are simultaneous; actions delimited by time connected with the movements of many suns are successive; thus, an action connected with time delimited by a greater number of movements of many suns is the object of the cognition "long" (*ciram*);
and an action connected with time delimited by a smaller number of movements of many suns is the object of the cognition "quick" (*kṣipram*).
In that case, the movement of the sun is delimited by time.
But surely this [movement] will delimit the action directly;
and thus, cognitions such as "simultaneous" and so forth will arise.

Therefore, since there is no connection between the movement of the sun and [the ether] through actions, it is impossible for that [movement] to be its delimiting factor; nor can space and so forth serve as its delimiting factor by way of being connected to it.
For instance, space and the like are not the causes of the cognitions of simultaneity and so forth regarding action, because they possess unique qualities, just like a jar.
Thus, cognitions such as simultaneity and so forth do not have space as their cause, because they do not depend on the restriction of spatial location,
just like priority and posteriority produced by the conjunction of time with a substance.

Therefore, there exists between the movement of the sun and the movement of Devadatta and others a relationship characterized by inherence in what is conjoined (saṃyuktasamavāya) with all-pervading time.
And by this [argument], there is a relation even between two movements;
for it is possible to perceive the movement of Devadatta and others as delimited by the movement of the sun, without depending on a relation with time.

Just as from the word "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*), one perceives a person delimited by a staff, and subsequently—due to the impossibility of that perception otherwise—the specific conjunction between the staff and the person is understood, but not preceded by a cognition of a [prior] relation.
There is the cognition of "the man with the staff.

Similarly, having grasped priority and posteriority—which are based on the conjunction of time and a material object—time is inferred; however, that cognition [of time] does not precede the cognition of those [qualities]. Since it is established as being formless, time is not perceptible, but is rather inferable from priority, posteriority, and so forth.
Therefore, it has been well said: "and of the cognitions such as 'other' (para)," and "in dependence upon the distinction between cause and effect."

Time, though unitary, is the cause of the notions of priority and posteriority regarding effects and their cognitions; it does so by depending on a specific causal factor—the conjunction of a mass of time delimited by a greater or lesser number of past solar movements—and by means of producing the qualities characterized as priority and posteriority.
Thus, time is manifested by its causes, for it is logical that it serves as the manifestor of these [qualities] once it has been produced.
But it is not manifested by action, because, being something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), it is unestablished and thus lacks the status of being a cause for manifestation.

Furthermore, since one perceives only the past and the future, inference regarding the three times is impossible due to the absence of the present. Moreover, the establishment of these two through mutual dependence—like that of father and son, like priority and posteriority, or like short and long—is possible even without [the present].
"The present time" is the prima facie position (pūrva-pakṣa). // 39 //
NyS 2.1.40: There is likewise the non-existence of those two [past and future], because they depend upon the present.
Because there are three [types]—(Sūtra 40).
Time does not possess the nature of being past and so forth as something manifested by its causes (*kāraka*), because those two [the cause and the time] remain in their original state.
Rather, it is manifested by action (*kriyā*). Indeed, depending upon that [action], this [time] proceeds and apprehends the past, future, and present; it is not otherwise.
For when a person apprehends a fruit as qualified by the action of falling currently in progress, he then designates it: "The fruit falls."
And since its pastness and futureness reside in that [gravity], it follows that the fruit has fallen or will fall.

Nor is present falling unestablished, such that it would not manifest time—[for it does manifest time] because those two [past and future states] remain as they are; rather, it is manifested by action.
If that [action] were non-existent, of what would gravity be the cause, of what would the fruit be the agent, and of what would contact with the ground be the effect?

Nor is the establishment of "remoteness," "nearness," and so forth dependent upon mutual relation. What then? Nearness is dependent on the cognition of proximity, while remoteness is dependent on the cognition of distance. Furthermore, proximity consists in the conjunctions being delimited by a lower number, whereas distance consists in their being delimited by a higher number.

In this way, even shortness and length, which are distinctions of dimension, are not mutually dependent, nor are father and son; these have been explained by the analysis of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*).
Therefore, since the past and the future depend upon the present, while the present does not depend upon them, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the three times exist. // 40 //
The establishment of the past and the future through mutual dependence is not possible.
The commentary [begins] with "Now, moreover" (*athāpi*).
It indicates the doubt: "Why do the past and the future not exist in mutual dependence on one another, rather than depending on the present?
To refute that, the Sūtra states: "Not so, because of non-perception" (*nātītāddhiḥ*, Sūtra 41).
The meaning of the Sūtra is that because establishment occurs through mutual dependence, there is no present; yet that very [dependence] does not exist.
The question is: "By what reasoning? The answer is: "In what manner (kalpena) or by what mode (prakāreṇa) is the past [established]?"
Thus, by this, the implication of the nature of the past [is established] in the absence of the present.
Having admitted that shortness, length, and so forth are established through mutual dependence, he says:
"That is not tenable, because there is no specific cause."
From the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), however, even things such as shortness and length are not established through mutual dependence; thus,
the author of the *Vārttika* states his own reasoning:
Moreover, if the present time were not admitted, [the expression] "of one falling" would be impossible. (255/6) // 41 //
NyS 2.1.42: If the present did not exist, there would be no apprehension of anything at all, because perception would be impossible.
The commentary is intended to introduce the sūtra that is about to be stated:
"And this [present time] is manifested by the existence of the object.

Its meaning is as follows: the present time is not manifested solely by actions such as falling; rather, it is manifested by the "existence of the object" (*arthasadbhāva*), which is to say, the being of the object (*sattā*), namely, the action of "being" (*astikriyā*).
By this, another time [the present] is indicated.
This is what is meant: actions such as falling and so forth both cease and continue within the present.
The action of "being" (asti-kriyā), however, pervades all of the present.
Thus, in the absence of the present qualified by the action of being, there would be no apprehension of anything at all, because direct perception would be impossible.
Nor can that which is non-existent be its [the present's] definition, for it is non-real (asad).
Furthermore, one who denies the existence of the present does not admit that anything exists as being present.
Regarding this, the author of the Vārttika asks:
"But how [is this so]?"
The point is that not all perception has a present object, because there is also yogic perception of the past and the future. The response begins with "yasmāt" (because):
we do not say that perception is untenable due to having the past and future as its objects, but rather that it is untenable due to having the past and future as its substrata.

It should be understood that the commentary also implies that in the absence of the present, [the following] would not be tenable: that conjunction is the cause of perception; that the jar and so forth, which are the objects of our perception and exist [in the present], constitute the means of valid cognition (pratyakṣa-pramāṇa); and that all this would be without a basis. // 42 //
But because both "having been done" and "that which is to be done" are possible, there is apprehension in both ways.
Regarding this, the author of the Vārttika introduces and explains the commentary (*bhāṣya*), which states that "that which exists in both ways is apprehended," by saying:
"And being established, it is divided into two kinds;
in some cases, it is manifested by action alone."
Just as in the case of "it exists," [existence] is in some instances manifested by a continuum of activity, as in "it falls" or "it cuts. (256)
3) For here, a sequence of prior and posterior is perceived;
yet there can be no sequence of prior and posterior for a single action— such as cooking or cutting— that perishes at every moment.

Thus [it is said]. However, the continuity of karma must be admitted; and that too does not exist without a single unifying factor. Therefore, the author of the Bhāṣya stated: "A single purposeful action is what constitutes the continuity of action."
The meaning is that they are delimited by a single purpose.

In this regard, let it be that the acts of placing [the pot] on the fire and so forth constitute the meaning of the root *pac* (to cook), as the author of the Mahābhāṣya has said: "That which is preceded by the intention for that [result], whether it be an instigation or a request, all of that is included within the meaning of *pac*."
Alternatively, if the meaning of this [verb] is simply the transformation (*parāvṛtti*) of form and so forth, then the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha*) is as follows:
let all this, beginning with the exhortation (*adhyeṣaṇā*), be the expression of *bhāvanā*; in either case, there is no impairment whatsoever to our philosophical position.

It distinguishes [the action] from the future by means of the term "not beginning" (*anārambha*). The meaning is that "non-beginning" (*anārambha*) is not intended here as a mere non-performance (*ananuṣṭhāna*), just as it is understood in the case of the expression "he will cook" (*pakṣyati*).
It excludes [the action] from the past;
the meaning is that "cessation" is not what is intended to be expressed, as in the case of [the form] *apākṣīt*.
This refers to the intention to express the commencement of a continuum (*saṃtāna*).
There is no contradiction here, for "commencement" (ārambha) is defined as the desire to act (cikīrṣā).
Having thus stated the existence of the action in the present, he expresses the present state of the factor of action (kāraka) as manifested through its connection with that [action], namely:
"that which is being cut."
It is not "being performed" (*kriyamāṇa*);
the meaning is that it is present by virtue of its connection with a present action, but not by way of its own intrinsic nature (*svarūpataḥ*).
And when that factor of action (*kāraka*) is related to a present action, its being past or future is dependent upon [the action] without regard for [its own] pastness or futurity.
The manifestation of the action and also of the agent is the manifestation of their being;
and this twofold nature is caused by that—intending to demonstrate this, he introduces the aphorism:
"When that [action] is being performed."
*kṛta-ṇam* (Sūtra 43). Commentary:
"He cooks" (*pacati*) refers to a continuum of action (*kriyā-saṃtāna*) that has been commenced by the undertaking of a desired result.
He states the nature of this continuum of action for the purpose of its utility in the non-contact (*asaṃpṛkta*) [of the agent] which will be discussed hereafter.
Regarding the phrase "therein" (*tatra*): it refers to the continuum of action (*kriyā-saṃtāna*).

As for the statement "it does not exist," since one understands there too a relation of priority and posteriority, [the action] is indeed conjoined with the past and the future; therefore, the author of the Vārttika says:
For here, by the term "alone" (*kevala*),
the contact [of the senses] is not real, but due to the power of words.
But the actual state of being present is for this very reason stated as "mere" and "pure";
due to the power of words, there is no real contact.
But its actual state of being present is for this very reason stated as "mere" and "pure";
these synonymous terms demonstrate an absolute absence of contact.
If primary presentness were not admitted in any case, then even the figurative use of the term "present," which is based upon that [primary sense], would not occur; therefore, he says:
"And the world [uses it] otherwise. (43)
NS 2.1.44: Comparison is not established because of absolute, general, or partial similarity.
Excessive intensity (of the breath) [is a fault] (Sūtra 44).

Just as with a cow, so too with a gavaya—this perception of similarity, assisted by the recollection of the meaning of the analogical statement (*atideśavākya*), is the means of knowledge (*upamāna*) that establishes the relationship between a name and the object named, namely, "This is a gavaya. However, this is not tenable, because the alternatives do not hold. Is it "just as a cow..."?
Thus, if an absolute similarity with a cow were intended, then the gavaya would simply be another cow.
Regarding this, the author of the Bhāṣya says: "And it is not the case that 'as a cow is so is a gavaya'"; the word *ca* (and) is used in the sense of "because."
Therefore, the meaning of the sentence "as is a cow, so is a gavaya" would be "as is a cow, so is a cow. Even through the similarity of a cow, the comparison of a gavaya is not established;
for since even a buffalo possesses a considerable degree of similarity with a cow, it would follow that it too would be designated as a "gavaya."
This is what he says:
"For it does not happen that [the gavaya] is like the ox, just as [it is said] 'the buffalo is like the ox';
rather, [the gavaya] is like the ox."

The meaning of this statement is as follows: just as [the comparison] "a buffalo is like an ox" does not occur because there is no similarity in every respect, so too a comparison based on partial similarity is not valid; for a comparison based on only a single part is untenable, as it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
This is what he says: "For everything is not comparable with everything; for if that were the case, it would follow that even Mount Sumeru could be compared with a mustard seed. (44)
Since the establishment of analogy (*upamāna*) occurs through a well-known similarity, the aforementioned defects do not apply.
Establishment [of the truth] (Sūtra 45).
For a sentence conveys its own meaning by depending on context and other factors, not in isolation.
By virtue of that [context], in some cases absolute similarity is understood, in some cases majority similarity, and in some cases partial similarity.
Thus, in this instance, with respect to a person who has already perceived a buffalo and so forth, the sentence "As is a cow, so is a gavaya" is uttered.
Then, understanding that similarity is intended once again for the purpose of excluding buffaloes and the like, and recollecting the meaning of the sentence, one—

though seeing the similarity of the cow in buffaloes and other animals in the forest— does not apply the name "gavaya" to them; rather, one applies that name only to the gavaya, which possesses that similarity.

However, the ultimate point is that for one who has not perceived a buffalo and so forth, this sentence does not function as an analogy at all. Furthermore, just as extended application statements (*atideśavākya*) operate by relying on similarity—whether absolute, general, or partial—due to the force of context and other factors, so too has it been stated by the author of the *Vārttika*:

"The Bhāṣya passage beginning with *na sādharmyasya* etc., negates a restriction; an extended application statement does not operate by relying solely on the totality of similarity, nor solely on its deficiency."
What then? It means "having pointed out" by relying on the relationship between the probandum and the probans through the reason of well-known similarity.
This is what is being said:

there is no fixed rule; rather, in some cases, the statement of extended application (*atideśavākya*) proceeds by relying on some form of similarity, and that [similarity] is to be inferred from the context and so forth.
And the *Vārttika* statement, "because it is not admitted," intends precisely a restriction;
its meaning is that [the second] action occurs only through that very [first] action. // 45 //
Because the unperceived is established through perception.
From the counter-argument (Sūtra 46).
For example, the sentence "as is a cow, so is a gavaya" establishes through perception the perception of the gavaya by means of the [already perceived] cow.
Indeed, when one who has heard the sentence perceives the gavaya through direct perception, he does not apprehend anything additional to the comprehension of the meaning of the sentence.
Even the relationship between the name and the named is understood by him solely from that which was expressed [by the sentence].

Therefore, since the perception of the gavaya—qualified by the name "gavaya"—is achieved through the perception of the cow by means of direct perception, [the opponent argues that] analogy is merely inference; such is the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa). // 46 //
NyS_2.1.47: We do not see the purpose of comparison as a means of valid cognition when the gavaya is not perceived.
But the established conclusion is as follows: (Sūtra 47).
For "gavayatva" (the state of being a gavaya) is the designatum, and it is not understood from the sentence "as a cow is so is a gavaya"; rather, it is the similarity of some [animal] to a cow.
Furthermore, the word "gavaya" occurring in the sentence is not its denoter,
because at that time its relationship [with the object] has not been grasped;
nor is similarity the bearer of the name.
Therefore, since the nature of being a *gavaya* is indeed perceived, the determination of the relationship between the name and the named is the actual purpose of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
This has been established in the definition of analogy (*upamāna*).
Consequently, the *gavaya*, though perceived, is cognized through the [previously] unperceived cow.
The meaning is "it is established.
The proponent of the prima facie view says:
"If you, the proponent of the established conclusion, think that analogy is for the sake of another, that is not so."
Why?

Because it also produces a determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*) in oneself. For it would be for the sake of another only if the statement "as is a cow, so is a gavaya" were to produce a determinative cognition solely in the other; however, since it produces a determinative cognition in the speaker as well, the meaning is that it is for one's own sake too.
The author of the Bhāṣya demonstrates this very point: "O sir, there indeed arises a determination from the sentence even for the speaker himself.
The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) says:
The prohibition of the comparison does not apply to the speaker who utters it; that is, the comparison does not fail to exist for the speaker who utters it.
Why? To this he says: "Because of the well-known similarity" (prasiddhasādharmyāt). // 47 //
Because the establishment of analogy results from the application of the word "so" (tathā), there is no lack of distinction [between inference and analogy].
The Vārttika, however, states that there is a distinction between analogy (*upamāna*) and inference (*anumāna*) on the grounds of its being for the sake of another (*parārthatva*), saying:
"And because it is for the sake of another" (258.19).
Now, one might object: "Analogy is the cognition of similarity, and this [cognition] is not for the sake of another"; to this, he replies:
For it is not as in the case of [the cognition] "this is a cow.
If it is argued that it must therefore be a sentence itself, he says: "For it is not scripture... etc.

He states, "Therefore, just as... under the guise of a summary, that the probandum is established for inference and comparison even when they are distinct by this much alone. The rest is not obscure. // 48 //
NyS 2.1.49: Verbal testimony is inference, because an object [known through it] is inferable due to its non-perception.

For here, the author of the Sūtras first examined the inclusion [of word] within inference; however, since that inclusion is not tenable for something whose status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has not yet been examined, the author of the Vārttika first examines its status as a means of valid cognition.
His objection is: "Word is not a means of valid cognition" (259).

8) That in the presence of which valid cognition (*pramā*) necessarily arises and does not fail to arise is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because that which is most effective in accomplishing [an action] is the instrument (*karaṇa*). However, even when the word exists, if valid cognition does not arise, it undermines its status as an effective agent.
This is also due to the absence of an object (*viṣaya*).

For validity is pervaded by the possession of an object; that [possession of an object], being excluded from verbal cognition, also excludes validity, just as the exclusion of a tree excludes its pervaded property, *śiṃśapā*-ness.
And the object is of two kinds: perceptible and imperceptible.
Of these, the former is the object of the means of knowledge that is perception.

And that which is imperceptible must be understood from a mark (liṅga) that is invariably concomitant with it; for if one did not depend upon such a mark, then because there would be no distinction regarding the lack of connection, everything could be known from everything.
Thus, every cognition of an imperceptible object is pervaded by inference.
Furthermore, there exists no category other than the perceptible and the imperceptible;
therefore, because of the absence of an object [to be cognized], verbal testimony lacks authority. As for the argument that it is "the means of valid cognition of truth":
That is not so;
because it is unestablished.
It is not mere sound that is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), but rather [sound] for which the relationship [with its object] has been apprehended and is being remembered.

The meaning is this: it is not the case that there is no valid cognition (*pramā*) when such a word exists; rather, that [word] for which there is no valid cognition when it exists is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is because it does not produce the cognition of "large" (*mahat*).

For the dimension of "largeness" (*mahattva-parimāṇa*) is a qualifier of that which is large; it is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to the qualified object, "the large," when it is itself unknown.

Thus, examining the distinction of verbal testimony (*śabda*) from inference (*anumāna*)—since the status of verbal testimony as a means of valid cognition has already been established—the proponent of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣin*) argues:
"Verbal testimony is inference..."
Thus:
"Because it is a word" (Sūtra 49).

That knowledge which arises subsequent to perception and has as its object a thing not apprehended by perception is inference (*anumāna*); for example, the knowledge of fire from smoke, and likewise the knowledge of [the object] from a word. Therefore, it is inference—this is the meaning.
(NyS 2.1.50) Because apprehension does not function in two ways.
And because of the connection.

The meaning is that [perception] possesses a non-dual mode of operation and is devoid of a distinction of types, whereas perception and inference possess a distinction of types because they respectively apprehend what is non-mediately evident and what is mediately evident. // 50–51 //
NyS 2.1.52: Through the power of the instruction of a reliable person, there arises a correct comprehension of the meaning from the word.
He begins the exposition of the nature of the final doctrine with the words "As for that which...
By this, [it is meant] because of the deviation [of the reason] in cases such as doubt and so forth.
For those [words] also have the three times as their object.
While the mere occurrence of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) exists even in the case of perception,
