the knowledge of positive and negative concomitance that serves as a factor for communication is of one kind in the case of verbal testimony and of another kind in the case of inference.

For that [inference] depends upon the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) in the case of inference, whereas in the case of verbal testimony (*śabda*), it does not depend upon that; regarding this point, there is the aphorism:

"An authoritative person (*āpta*) is one who... (Sūtra 52). For that which has never been perceived before—such as heaven, the unseen merit (*apūrva*), or the deities—is of the nature of the meaning of a sentence. To illustrate: "That which is unmixed with suffering, not followed by anything unpleasant... and so forth.
And that happiness brought about by desire is the locus of the word *svarga* (heaven). Thus, heaven is the meaning of the sentence;
the same applies to the *apūrva* (unseen potency) as well.

The meaning of the sentence is that [dharma] is indeed a specific quality of the person (puruṣaviśeṣaguṇa) that persists over time, serves as the cause for heaven, hell, and so forth, and is opposed by its own effect;
the same applies to the deity as well.
For she too—being the recipient of hymns and oblations, and possessing a body endowed with a thousand eyes and other attributes—is nothing but the meaning of the sentence.
This [self] is not an object of perception and other means of knowledge for people like us, apart from verbal testimony;
nor can an unapprehended logical mark (liṅga) function toward it;
and a relation cannot be apprehended when the related term is unapprehended.
Although the word (*pada*) requires the cognition of the connection between word-meanings (*padārtha*),
and although the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is simply the word-meaning itself as qualified by other word-meanings—

even those [proponents] who maintain that at the beginning of creation, the understanding of the sentence-meaning proceeds by way of the recollection of word-meanings without depending on the grasping of the connection (*saṅgati*).

They establish the sentence-meaning of "heaven" by referring to a type of pleasure well-known in their own world, and they represent that which is denoted by the word "heaven" as being distinguished by the very absences of pain and so forth established in that world; they do not make a sentence-meaning out of something that is not the meaning of a word, nor is the word "heaven" used for the sentence-meaning, just as in the expression "one who has studied the Veda is a *śrotriya*."

Just as the eyes and other sense organs function toward objects such as form (*rūpa*) without having previously grasped a conventional relation (*saṅgati*), so too words—even those that depend on the prior grasp of word-meaning relations—do not require the grasp of a relation for the cognition of the sentence-meaning.

This is because the status of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatva*) is manifested by the effect itself; furthermore, we observe the effect of cognizing the sentence-meaning arising from distinct words even when they do not depend on the grasp of a relation.

Therefore, neither the word nor its meaning is a logical mark (*liṅga*) for the cognition of the sentence-meaning, because it does not depend on the grasp of a relation therein, just like the eye and other organs in the cognition of form and so forth.

It might be argued as follows: let it be that there is no inference based on what is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣatodṛṣṭa*) regarding the meaning of a sentence; however, there will be an inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*).

Even though the words lack the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*apakṣadharmatva*) when the sentence-meaning is the probandum, and even though the word-meanings recalled by the words are deviant, nevertheless, the word-meanings—when qualified by expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), compatibility (*yogyatā*), and contiguity (*āsatti*)—[constitute the middle term].
The indicator will be the relation [itself].

For instance, the word-meanings recalled by words such as "that which is not with suffering" and so forth, being established in a relationship of subordinate and primary status, possess a connection; because they are recalled by words while possessing expectancy, semantic competency, and contiguity, just like the word-meanings recalled by the words "bring the cow."
Furthermore, the distinction in a relation consists solely in the things being related; there is no distinction whatsoever that exists by its own nature (*ājānataḥ*).

And since those things being related are merely recalled by the words, the attainment of the specific relation occurs [through them]. Thus it is established that the meaning of a sentence is precisely that [relation], and therefore the meaning of a sentence is inferential (*ānumānika*).

In the case of the sentence "Bring the cow" (*gām abhyāja*), the fact that the word-meanings possess a mutual relation is understood from the cognition of the relation between word-meanings, which is inferred from the activity of the elder person who acts immediately after hearing the sentence.
This [position] is not tenable;

for it is the words themselves—having the recollection of word-meanings as their intermediate operation—that constitute the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with respect to the cognition of the sentence-meaning, by virtue of being the instrument (*karaṇa*).
Furthermore, because those [individual word-meanings] lack the property of being attributes of a subject (*apakṣadharmatā*), it is impossible for them to function as logical marks (*liṅga*).

If, however, words were to terminate their operation solely upon the individual word-meanings and not be directed toward the cognition of the sentence-meaning, then there would be no mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) among the word-meanings; and in the absence of expectancy, the sentence-meaning could not be cognized, even if proximity (*sannidhi*) and compatibility (*yogyatā*) were present. Indeed, word-meanings do not combine merely through proximity and compatibility without expectancy, as in the case of [the disconnected utterance]: "This—comes."
In the sentence "The king’s son, the man—let him be removed," the king, having no further expectancy due to his connection with the son, is not connected with the man.
Furthermore, there can be no expectancy among the word-meanings recalled by the words unless the words themselves are directed toward the cognition of the sentence-meaning.

For it is not the case that whatever does not exist without something else necessarily expects that thing; otherwise, a factor of action (*kāraka*) would expect a verb, or a substance (*dravya*) would expect a quality (*guṇa*), and in that case, the sentence "the cloth exists" (*paṭo bhavati*) would not be free from expectancy.

Because a substance such as a cloth requires a quality [to complete its meaning], the phrase "the cloth becomes" from the sentence "the cloth becomes red" is invalid on its own, as it remains expectant (sākāṅkṣa). For the sentence "the cloth becomes" would remain expectant by taking up any quality whatsoever; however, when the phrase "the cloth becomes red" is used, it is no longer expectant once any specific quality has been grasped. Thus, the part of the sentence "the cloth becomes red" [is valid only when completed].
Having projected a quality, [the word] becomes independent; such being the case in this division, there would be a syntactical split (vākyabheda) due to that independence.
Furthermore, the sentence "red" (raktaḥ), having projected some qualified substrate and some action, would be satisfied.

Nor is it logical to say that there is no implication when a specific distinction is observed; for if there were a single syntactical unity, there would be no implication upon the observation of a distinction, and if there were no implication, there would be a single syntactical unity— thus resulting in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).

Therefore, we consider it logical that the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) of word-meanings consists precisely in their non-termination [as isolated meanings], due to their being recalled by a collection of words uttered in proximity with the intent of conveying the meaning of a sentence.
Thus, the mere statement "the cloth exists" (*paṭo bhavati*) is self-sufficient and satisfies its requirement by implying some quality or other;

however, in the case of "the red cloth exists" (*raktaḥ paṭo bhavati*), because of the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of the word "red" as well, it is directed toward the relation [of the cloth] with that [quality].

Since redness cannot be established without its connection to a cloth or the like, and cloths and the like cannot be established without their connection to redness, they come into mutual relation; thus, syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) is proven.

Therefore, it is the words themselves that, by means of the recollection of word-meanings, indicate (*lakṣayanti*) their connection as the authority (*pramāṇa*) for the sentence-meaning. And because these [words] do not reside in a subject (*apakṣadharmatva*), they do not possess the nature of a logical mark (*liṅga*).
It might be argued as follows:

"This particular collection of words possesses a connection between the word-meanings it causes to be remembered, because, while possessing expectancy and so forth, it is a collection of words, like the sequence of words 'Bring the cow' (gām abhyāja).
This is not correct.
Because it would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).
For an object that serves as the *karma*-factor must be established as a distinct entity from the cloth in reality to serve as the basis for the fruit characterized by cognition.

Just as the possession of fire belongs to smoke or the conjunction with fire belongs to a mountain, so too [the cloth] possesses [the property of being an object]; however, its being the generator of the cognition of fire is not what constitutes its "possession" [of fire].
For that [fire-possessing nature] is manifested by the result; it cannot be postulated as long as the result has not yet arisen.

And thus, if the fire-possessing nature exists when the result arises, then the arising of the result occurs in the action when there is that possession [of fire]; this results in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).
For there is no identity between the result and the action.
For the tree itself does not become the act of cutting.
Therefore, in this case, the fact that words possess a state of association—that is, their capacity to generate the cognition of that [meaning]—cannot be established by inference.
For it has been stated that the capacity of smoke to generate the cognition of fire is not something to be established by inference.
Furthermore, the capacity of these [words] to produce recollection is postulated for the purpose of conveying the meaning of the sentence; it does not reveal any other distinct relation.

Thus it is established that words are not a logical mark (*liṅga*) for the cognition of the sentence-meaning, because they lack the property of being a predicate of the subject (*apakṣadharmatva*), just like the mind.
Moreover, investigators follow only worldly objects; they do not resort to something non-worldly merely out of deference to definitions of their own making.

Furthermore, people do not understand the meaning of a sentence from words by imagining a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) through some kind of affliction; rather, they understand it from those words themselves as independent entities. Thus, the distinction of the word as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) from inference is established.
As for being "spoken by a reliable person" (*āptoktatva*), this is merely an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the validity of a Vedic injunction that teaches [matters such as] heaven and so forth.
And it does not follow from this alone that its object becomes inferential.
For the object of a perception whose validity has been inferred through the efficacy of its successful activity (*pravṛttisāmarthya*) does not thereby become inferential.

Indeed, a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has an object in the form of a thing (*artha*), whereas its validity (*prāmāṇya*)—insofar as it consists in the efficacy of activity or being the word of a reliable person—is the object [of inference].

This being the case, it should be understood that the author of the Bhāṣya and the author of the Vārttika have merely presented the points regarding reliance on the words of an authoritative person (*āpta*) and non-reliance as a mere supplementary elaboration, serving as the cause for the distinction between verbal testimony (*śabda*) and inference (*anumāna*).
By this explanation of the difference in their operation, the claim that there is no difference in their mode of operation is refuted.
Having restated what was said by the opponent—that "verbal testimony is inference because comprehension arises from a relation"—he proceeds to refute it.

As for the phrase "that which is this," the commentary states, "of that which is qualified by the genitive [case] in the form 'this belongs to that'"; its explanation is "the relationship between the signifier and the signified.

For the relationship between word and object must be either innate, characterized by identity (*tādātmya*), characterized by the state of being the signified and the signifier (*pratyāyyapratyāyakabhāva*), or characterized by reaching (*prāpti*).
In this context, identity (*tādātmya*) has already been refuted by the term "indescribable" (*avyapadeśya*) found in the definition of perception.

Furthermore, the innate relationship between the signifier and the signified (*autpattikaḥ pratyāyyapratyāyakabhāvaḥ*) will be refuted later on by means of the refutation of the "attainment" (*prāpti*) between word and object.
Therefore, the author of the Bhāṣya refutes attainment with the words: "But [the relation] characterized by attainment... (*prāptilakṣaṇas tu*).

For the contact (*prāpti*) between two things perceivable by a single sense-organ is perceptual, as in the case of two fingers; however, there is no such single-sense-perceivability for word and object. Therefore, the meaning is that the contact between these two [word and object] is not accessible through perception, like that between air and a tree.

[Objection: But surely the object of a word is indeed perceivable by the same sense-organ [as the word]; why then is the word not perceived by that [same] sense-organ? Since the object has passed beyond the state of being a sensory object (*viṣayabhāva*) for the word, [the author] says:
"And there exists [cognition] even when the object is beyond the senses."

The term *atīndriya* (beyond the senses) is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning that which transcends the sense-organ that perceives sound, yet is perceived by the sense-organ alone, and is also the object [of that perception].
This has been explained by the *vārttika* "tadetat yasmācchabdasya" (NyS 2.1.53).
Furthermore, because filling, burning, and splitting are not perceived, there is no connection [between sound and its cause].
He explains the Bhāṣya beginning with "And in the case of the characteristic of attainment," etc., [stating]:
"Not even by means of inference. This concludes the section.
"It reaches" means "it goes.
If it were coming, things such as sweetmeats would be perceived; however, they are not perceived. Therefore, the meaning of words does not come [from elsewhere].
Consequently, under this view, worldly linguistic usage (*lokavyavahāra*) would be cut off by the word.

Now, regarding the phrase "the sound": first of all, motion is not possible for a quality such as sound; therefore, one must say that this sound arrives at a location by way of a continuous series (saṃtāna), and in that case, its eternity would be contradicted—this is the meaning. [The opponent] objects:
Now,
"it comes into being" (bhavati) means "it exists" (vidyate). The meaning of "becoming" (bhava) is coming into existence after not having existed.
Thinking thus, he treats [the other] with contempt and remains constant; such is the doubt, and the one who suspects states his own intention.
Now, [the opponent] objects, "If it does not come," [the author] refutes this by saying,
"Not for all purposes."
The intention is that things occupying the same location and perceptible by the same sense organ have never been observed to be manifested by distinct manifestors.
The perception of the substratum is the cause of manifestation for a universal,
but there is no such perception of a substratum for sound from which sound might be manifested.
On the contrary, the substratum itself should be manifested by the word alone.
And in that case, since the word would be dependent on its meaning and yet be manifested by the palate and other organs even without reaching [the object], the aforementioned fault would ensue.
Furthermore, he states that the operation of the word upon its meaning is not within the scope of experience.
Nor does it function upon the literal meaning;
for one will understand [the intended sense] through the offense—
this refers to the traditional authority of the *Nirukta* and other such works.
The answer is: "This is that very same [thing].
This means that while works such as the *Nirukta* serve to establish the connection with the meaning, it is precisely that [connection] which is being investigated. // 53 //
There is no refutation [of our position] because of the established usage of words and their meanings.
The proponent of the prima facie view says: "Regarding the word and its meaning... (Verse 54).
NyS 2.1.55: No, because the comprehension of the meaning of a word is based on convention.

The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin) says: "No, because it is conventional," meaning that it is a formal agreement regarding the restriction between the signifier and the signified.

The restriction between the signifier and the signified is such that the word "cow" has as its object only that which possesses a dewlap and so forth, and the word "horse" has as its object only that which possesses a mane and so forth. The meaning is that at the beginning of creation, the Blessed Lord Parameśvara enjoined that "this is the convention for this [object]"; this is what is meant by *samaya* (convention).
When that [word] has been employed and cognized, the determination of the word's meaning occurs; moreover,
this is unavoidable even for the proponent of the theory of the relation [between word and meaning].

Even those Mīmāṃsakas or Grammarians who maintain that the relationship between word and meaning is innate—for them too, a word is not a signifier by its mere existence, but only when it is known; and for this knowledge, the only means is convention (*saṃketa*), such as "this is the designator of this" or "from this, this is to be understood. Furthermore, the linguistic usage of elders regarding words like "cow" and so forth is preceded by convention, just like words such as "Devadatta."
Thus,
let there simply be convention; enough with this inherent relation.
The meaning is that the application, comprehension, and linguistic usage [of words] are established by that alone.

Now, one might object: "In this way, a convention (*samaya*) cannot be established for certain words if they lack an inherent connection with their objects; for one would have to point out an object and say, 'This is what should be understood from this word.
And such a pointing-out is not possible for certain words if an inherent connection does not exist."
If the capacity to denote were dependent upon convention, then since no one has established a convention for all [words], what could be designated by what?
Therefore, the very act of establishing a convention demonstrates that words possess an inherent relationship; thus, he says:
"And because they are apprehended as being employed [in usage]."

For the convention regarding the meanings of words such as "cow" and others, which was established by the Supreme Lord at the beginning of creation, can now be grasped even by children who do not know the relationship [between word and meaning], through words being employed in the usage of elders.

To explain: immediately after hearing the speech of an elder, a child infers a cognition as the cause of another elder’s comprehension of activity, cessation, fear, sorrow, joy, and so forth, by observing that elder's engagement in those states.
And when that [meaning], whether real or unreal, occurs immediately after hearing a sentence even though other objects are present,

he understands that the cause is the hearing of the sentence; and by observing the arising and ceasing of the cognition of those respective meanings through the insertion and deletion of the constituent words,
he postulates that those specific words are the denoters of those respective meanings.
The same should be understood regarding the constituent parts of words, such as the *prakṛti* (base) and so forth.

This usage by the elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*) is the means for contemporary people to grasp the linguistic convention (*saṃketa*). However, for the great seers (*maharṣi*), deities, and others existing at the beginning of creation—who are endowed with an excellence of merit, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty—this [convention] was easily established by the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) through his grace.
In this way, the convention can be established;
and through the usage thereof, the convention is easily grasped even by people such as ourselves (and for us, it has been transmitted through a succession of usage).
The apprehension of a convention does not depend upon the recollection of a [permanent] relationship,
because unhesitating linguistic usage is established through the mere tradition of authoritative persons;
for this very reason, the author of the Bhāṣya says, "of worldly people."
It might be argued as follows:
if the relationship between words and their meanings is conventional rather than inherent, then grammar—which is intended to distinguish between correct and incorrect forms—is rendered useless;
for that whose denotative capacity is inherent is correct, while the other is incorrect.
But since all practitioners, whether virtuous or non-virtuous, are equal in terms of belonging to a convention (*samaya*), he says:
"And this is for the sake of observing the convention.
The meaning is: for the sake of observing the convention of the Supreme Lord (*pārameśvara-samaya*).

And thus, it is established that grammar is meaningful for the purpose of distinguishing those words which have been assigned by the Supreme Lord to a particular meaning as being correct (*sādhu*) in that context and incorrect (*asādhu*) elsewhere. The "husk of meaning" (*arthatuṣa*) refers to a mere fragment of the husk consisting of meaning; the sense is that such a thing does not exist, for the connection characterized by attainment has been merely imagined by others.

And thus it is established that, because there is no inherent connection (*svābhāvikasambandha*), the assertion of an inherent connection is improper for the purpose of establishing the inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*) required for inference to be non-different from perception.
In the *Vārttika*, [it asks]: "But from where does this convention (*samaya*) arise?
The implication is that if not even a single word had a well-known relationship [to its object], then a convention would be impossible to comprehend.
"Superior" means through the knowledge of words (*pada*).
By the etymology "that by which a word is known—that is, derived (*vyutpādyate*)"—the meaning is that it is grammar (*vyākaraṇa*).

Now, one might object: "How can someone who does not know the conventional relationship (*saṅgati*) of all words understand the convention (*samaya*) from grammar alone, even though it consists merely of words? To this, he says:
"And from the world" means that one should understand the conventional usage established by elders and, through grammar, discern the distinction between correct and incorrect forms.
He analyzes this as follows:
This is that very treatise. // 55 //
And because there is no fixed rule regarding specific classes of beings.

Thus, since the establishment of the relationship between word and meaning is possible through a convention that is directly perceived and proven for both parties, it has been stated that it is not reasonable to postulate an inherently natural (*svābhāvika*) connection that is entirely imperceptible. Now, [the author] says [the following] to show that this inherent connection is even untenable: *Jāti-t* (Sūtra 56). For an inherently natural connection belongs to a particular word with a particular meaning, and not to every word with every meaning.
If that were the case, there would be no established convention for the meaning of words;
and if so, there would be no fixed rule for sages, Aryans, and Mlecchas.
For instance, the word *yava* is used by Aryans to refer to the long-awned grain (*dīrghaśūka*).
For by the word "yava," those [Aryas] understand the long-awned grain (dīrghaśūka), whereas the Mlecchas understand it as the *priyaṅgu* plant.
Similarly, the seers (*ṛṣis*) employ the word "trivṛt" to refer to a group of nine hymn-verses (*stotrīyā*),
while the Aryas employ it for a specific kind of creeper.
There would be no restriction regarding the nature of this [connection] if the relation were inherent;
for light, which is inherently connected with color, cannot— even by a thousand artisans— be made connected with taste and so forth.
From that [connection], the aesthetic flavors (rasa) and so forth would be understood;
nor is an inherent relation manifested there by means of convention, for it is only that which already exists that is manifested, not that which does not exist.
Indeed, a lamp is not capable of manifesting a jar where that jar does not exist;
this lack of restriction is consistent with [the manifestation] being occasional, because it depends upon the will of a person,
and that will is itself unrestricted.
But it is not by way of an intrinsic nature (*svābhāvika*).
Nor should it be said that all words are by their very nature connected to all meanings, and are merely restricted by convention (*saṃketa*),
because there is a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*) for this.
Furthermore, since the cognition of a difference in meaning can be accounted for even by a difference in convention (*saṃketa*) based on a difference in genus (*jāti*), one might object:
"But for Mlecchas living in the land of the Āryas—who have established conventions determined by Ārya usage—there is no lack of restriction. To this, the author of the *Vārttika* says (265.2):
"By the word 'particular genus' (*jātiviśeṣaśabdena*). // 56 //
NyS 2.1.57: Its lack of authority [is established] due to the defects of falsehood, contradiction, and tautology.
[The suffixes] *taddhita* [are applied] after those [stems] (Sūtra 57).

Thinking that if verbal testimony were included within inference, its validity might occasionally arise from its inseparable connection with the object, whereas if it were excluded from it, its lack of validity would be easily established, the proponent (pūrvapakṣin) states its invalidity immediately after enumerating the varieties of inference. The author of the Vārttika explains the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "tasya" [of that].

The word "that" (*tad*) refers to the Veda, because it is the subject under discussion; for in this treatise, which is devoted solely to the attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), the demonstration of the authority of the Veda is undertaken as being inseparable from that [attainment]. Thus, the meaning of the word "subject" (*adhikṛta*) is the Veda.
It might be argued: "Untruthfulness" and "lack of authority" are synonyms; therefore, the reason (*hetu*) is identical to the meaning of the thesis (*pratijñā*). To this [we reply]:
He said:
"Invalidity is the state of not making an object known.
'Of the object' means of the non-erroneous object."

For rites such as the *putrakāmeṣṭi* and the *kārīrī* have results pertaining to this world (*aihika*) and not results pertaining to the next world (*āmuṣmika*), because their fruit is desired by the conscious agent precisely as something belonging to this life, and because that fruit is fit for enjoyment within this very body.
Alternatively, there is an impossibility [of coexistence] between two sentences or two words due to their presenting contradictory meanings.

Regarding this, the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) stated that there is a contradiction with the censure of the injunctions concerning the *uditahoma* and other rites; however, the Vārttikakāra speaks further, desiring to elaborate on this point.

Regarding the term *agnihotra*: because the times for the oblation, such as sunrise and so forth, are prohibited by way of censure, one might ask: "Will not midday, afternoon, and evening be the times for the oblation? To this, he says:
"And not another" means that for all of them as well, the time [of the reason] is one in which it has already arisen (*uditakāla*). However,

regarding one who is not satisfied by the contradiction in the statement that "the time immediately following the arising is called the time of having arisen, and thus there is another time," he states the contradiction in another way.
Regarding the phrase "at sunrise and before sunrise":

with reference to the fire-oblation named Agnihotra, which is enjoined by the originative injunction "he performs the Agnihotra," one sentence prescribes the time of sunrise as an attribute of that rite,
another prescribes the time of before sunrise, and yet another prescribes the time when the night has passed (samayādhyuṣita).
Furthermore, it is not possible to perform only a single oblation at each respective time;
nor is it logical that there should be a repetition of the primary oblation merely in accordance with the qualities of the time.
Moreover, no repetition of the oblation is heard in the scriptural injunctions concerning the *coditā* and other such verses.
Therefore, because of this mutual contradiction, it is more appropriate to conclude that [the Veda] lacks authority altogether.
Now, one might object: "But these qualities, such as being false and so forth, do not pervade all Vedic sentences."
Since [the reason] would thus be a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) due to being partially unestablished (*bhāgāsiddha*),
he says:
"as an example."

The formal argument here is as follows: "The statements concerning the performance of the *putrakāmeṣṭi* sacrifice are not authoritative, because they are false and so forth, like statements regarding momentariness.
Likewise, "the remaining Vedic statements are not authoritative, because they are Vedic statements, like the statement regarding the *putrakāmeṣṭi* sacrifice."
Having stated that the probandum is a paryudāsa (presuppositional negation) by means of that very reason, he states that the probandum is a prasajyapratiṣedha (absolute negation):
"or [the case] of sentences such as the Agnihotra," etc. That other sentence is "one desiring a son," and so forth. // 57 //
NyS 2.1.58: [The non-arising of knowledge] is not [due to the excellence of the means], but rather due to a deficiency in the object, the agent, or the instrument.
Having thus stated the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), he begins the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) by first refuting the claim of its being unreal: "Not so... (Sūtra 58).
The meaning is that since the non-appearance of the result can be accounted for otherwise, it does not prove falsity; therefore, falsity remains unestablished as the reason.
It might be argued: "Since the sacrifice is prescribed by scripture, it establishes [the desired end] independently;
what could defects in the ritual or the agent do to it? To this, he says:
"By way of the sacrifice being the instrument (*karaṇa*)," [it means]:
the unseen cause is not alone; rather, it has a seen co-operative cause (*sahakārin*).
Therefore, the non-occurrence of the fruit is logically established due to a deficiency in the seen [factors]. This is the meaning.
He states the agent to be depended upon as "the parents";
he states the instrument as "by means of sacrifice."
He states the action:
"the two being conjoined," as the commentary says, "they are indeed supported by desire."
"Samīhā" refers to the performance of its constituent acts, such as the offering of fuel (samidh) and so forth; "bhreṣa" means its failure, that is to say, its non-performance.
"The ignorant person is the performer"—for it is the learned person who has the entitlement [to perform the rite], by virtue of their competence.

For this very reason, women, Śūdras, and animals—who lack the capacity—have no entitlement [to knowledge]. Furthermore, even a learned man who has committed an act such as the killing of a Brahmin, which causes the loss of the duties of the twice-born, is shown to be incapable of escaping the fruit of that committed act because of the deficiency in his agency; thus it says, "one who does what is foul."
A person who performs blameworthy or censurable actions is called an *ācaraṇa*. An oblation (*havis*) that is unrefined, unpurified, or unsprinkled is likewise [blameworthy].
"Defiled" means contaminated by dogs, cats, and the like.
"Mantras deficient" means lacking in their specific sequence. "Dakṣiṇā ill-gotten" means obtained through improper means, such as acting as a messenger, gambling, or being overly eager for gain.
The *anvāhārya* refers to the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).

It is given in an amount less than that, yet sufficient such that a person is not satisfied; and that human food is censured because it is unwholesome due to its state of being worn out. "False union" refers to acts such as a man acting like a woman toward one's mother.
Various disorders of the womb are causes for the obstruction of the birth of a son,
because the seed— consisting of blood and semen— is impaired, whereby the birth of a son does not occur;
it is like improper churning, whereby fire is not produced.
Regarding the deficiency of the ritual action and the deficiency of the performer, the author of the Vārttika says:
"Likewise, [it is due to] the desire and the one who accomplishes it," and "due to the lack of efficacy of the mantras."
This means [the efficacy] of rituals such as the performance of mantras and so forth, or rites like the *putrakāmeṣṭi* (the sacrifice for one desiring a son).

Now, if the sacrifice were not an independent means, then the parents themselves—when properly united—would be the progenitors of the son; what, then, would be the use of the *putrakāmeṣṭi* in this matter?
For this very reason, the birth of a son is possible even for Mlecchas and others; therefore, he says:
"Because of being its cooperative cause.

(267/6) This status as a cooperative cause of the desired [result] is not to be understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), but rather is to be understood through scripture (*āgama*).

The birth of sons among Mlecchas and others must be understood through the authority of scripture (*āgama*) as resulting from unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) acquired in previous lives. Furthermore, the non-arising of a result when there is a deficiency in the agent or the ritual action—which is otherwise visible—indicates that an unseen factor (*adṛṣṭa*) must be taken into account.
By this, it is also indicated that sacrifices such as the *putrakāmeṣṭi* have results that are not necessarily fixed.
Thus, it is established that even when there is no deficiency in the agent, the instrument, or the action itself, the non-arising of the fruit may occur due to the obstruction by another karma.
However, in the case of rites such as the *kārīrī* which yield results in this life, the remedy for the non-arising of the fruit is a deficiency in the means (*sādhana*).
[The opponent objects: "If it is argued that [the Veda] is not a valid means of knowledge because it is untrue..."
The meaning is that there is no fault in stating [the qualities] separately after they have already been employed as qualifiers of the subject (*dharmī*).
The response is: "What is this?

[The opponent asks: "But surely, the non-communicative nature of the meaning was what was proposed; and since this very thing is the reason for its being false, there is no difference in meaning between the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*)."
Therefore, he says: "And [the state of] being unreal," etc. (58).
NyS 2.1.59: Because a fault is stated regarding the difference in time, even after having accepted [the argument].
Regarding the claim that there is mutual contradiction among such statements as "one should offer when the sun has risen," he replies with the words "ubhaya" (both).

The meaning is that in sentences intended as injunctions (*vidhi*), since neither of the two sentence-meanings is negated by any single sentence, their validity is not otherwise [compromised]. Thus, they do not lack authority.

Even though a single oblation (*homa*) cannot be performed by combining [multiple options] at each respective time, it may nevertheless be performed by way of option (*vikalpa*), for option is frequently observed even in the world.

Indeed, a fixed entity (*vastu*) is not subject to option; however, regarding an action to be accomplished in the future, there is no contradiction among injunctions and prohibitions as options, because its essential nature has not yet been established.
Thus, the meaning of the sentence is not that [the action] must necessarily be performed.
Thus,
the meaning of that statement is that it should not be performed;
or else, it may be undertaken out of desire.
The meaning is that it would be postulated as having mutually contradictory meanings.
Or, "stated": that which is stated by this sentence through its own inherent capacity is apprehended and restated by the investigators, [in the form]: "This is what was stated by this sentence."
He determines [the meaning]. There is a reading in some places: "it is stated," or "it is a restatement of what has been prescribed."
The meaning is that since the oblation has already been enjoined, this is a restatement (anuvāda) for the purpose of prescribing a specific time;

it is more reasonable that it is a restatement of what is already enjoined in order to prescribe a specific time, rather than that its purpose should be construed as a prohibition of other times. // 59 //
And because the justification for restatement is established.

The eleven *sāmidhenī* verses are recited in their original form; by repeating the first and last of these three times, the mantra fulfills its purpose, thereby achieving the state of having fifteen verses, which serves a specific function. // 60 //
Thus, having set aside the reasons for the invalidity of the Veda, the author of the Sūtras must state the reasons for the possibility of its validity;
therefore, the author of the Vārttika first states the reasons for the possibility of validity being intrinsic (*svataḥ*) itself,
beginning with the words "pūtra-kāmeṣṭi."
And because the division of sentences is understood through the mention of "meaning" (artha).
Because of the application of speech to injunctions, explanatory passages (arthavāda), and restatements (anuvāda).
He introduces the scriptural reason [with the words] "all together" (samastāni). // 61–62 //
NyS 2.1.63: An injunction is that which prescribes.
An injunction is that which prescribes (sūtra 63).
Its explanation is the statement "that which is the word" (*vākya*).
An instigator (*codaka*) is that which sets [an action] in motion.
In this context, immediately after hearing an instruction such as "one who desires health should eat wholesome food," [the inclination to] eat wholesome food [arises].

Observing an elderly person being prompted to act, a child infers the causal cognition that motivates that activity; [he reasons]: "This person's engagement was preceded by a motivating cognition, because it is an independent action, like my own engagement. Thus, this learner, desiring to acquire linguistic proficiency, infers the very motivating knowledge established for himself.
It is not something previously unperceived; for when a cause of activity already established in itself has been perceived, it is not logical to assume the existence of an unseen factor (*adṛṣṭa*).

Nor does this [word] convey a notion of an *apūrva*—which is a mere instigator of activity independent of the word, its operation, the person’s intention, or any other condition—as something that instigates activity within itself, such that even a suspicion of their being instigators might arise regarding them.
If it is argued that the cognition of an effect (kārya) regarding objects such as drinking milk is what prompts this [child] to act, then what is this "effect"?
If it is said to be human effort (puruṣaprayatna), namely volitional action (kṛti), and its being the object of that [action]— then [we reply]:

Now, "action" (*kṛti*) is a mental activity; that which is conditioned by it—the task (*kārya*)—is either the object of that activity or its fruit, since a person's activity is directed toward a fruit.
The cognition of that [task] is the cause of activity.
In that case, it follows that the cognition of activity is the cause of activity.
Nor is [the Veda] non-compliant or untrustworthy;
nor is there a lack of understanding regarding our engagement with its injunctions for those of us who are learned, such that we would not act upon them.
Furthermore, this engagement—another name for which is effort—originates from desire and aversion; in the absence of these causes, it cannot arise from the mere cognition of the injunction itself.
Nor is it correct to say that desire and aversion alone are the causes of activity directed toward the object indicated by the logical mark (liṅgin),
for that [mark] must indeed be accepted as having the indicated object as its domain insofar as it prompts activity through its own cognition.
But it is not by its own existence that sound is an indicator, because it does not produce [the cognition] and because it is not a producer;
nor do desire and aversion set one in motion through their own cognition, such that they would depend upon sound for the sake of cognition regarding the impulse to act.
Rather, they exist [as motivators] by their very presence; therefore, that alone is what is to be indicated by the logical mark (liṅga) and so forth.

Truth produces knowledge, desire, and aversion; therein, that which is known as being naturally beautiful produces desire in the self. Likewise, its means, when known as such through its connection with the fruit, produces desire in the self.
Therefore, only two things remain: either the fruit or its means.
Among these, although the fruit is [desirable] in itself...

Even though [the fruit] is the object of desire and so forth, a desire directed toward that [fruit] cannot impel one toward it, because it is unfit for such activity due to its being unsuitable as an object of volitional effort (*pravṛtti*).

Nor can a desire whose scope is not the fruit produce an effort—which is its own effect—toward something else that is its means; for cause and effect must coincide in their object through the unity of the effort.

Furthermore, it is not the case that the means is not desired simply because of its connection with that [fruit], such that one would have to postulate that the desire for the fruit itself is the cause for generating an effort directed toward the means.
As they have said: "To desire one thing and do another is a contradiction.
Therefore, even though the fruit is desired, it does not incite activity toward itself through its own cognition, because it lacks the status of being an object of activity.
However, we consider it logical that the means to that [fruit] does incite activity through its own cognition, because it is both an object of activity and something desired.

However, in the case of infants, the cognition that breast-milk and such things are a means to what is desired arises through the persistence of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) in a previous birth; for those who have thus developed a recollection of pervasion, this is indeed an inference born from the cognition of a mark (*liṅga*) consisting in its belonging to that same class.
This point will be demonstrated in the section beginning with "because of the connection with the recollection of a previously perceived [pervasion].

For this very reason, while explaining the definition of purpose (*prayojana*), the author of the Vārttika stated: "Having cognized 'this is a means to happiness,' one exerts oneself to obtain happiness; and having understood 'this is a means to suffering'..."
For the sake of the destruction of suffering...

Therefore, the child who is learning [the language] understands that "being a desired means" (*apekṣitopāyatā*), which is established within itself as an instigation (*pravartanā*), is the cause of activity even for an elder.
And since this [instigation] arises immediately after hearing the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, he determines it to be the meaning of the optative suffix and the like.

Moreover, being merely a desired means is not the cause of activity; for instance, the *Kārīrī* sacrifice performed by a patron (*yajamāna*) is a desired means for farmers, yet they do not engage in it because it is already accomplished [for them].
Therefore, it must be accepted that being the means desired by the agent is the cause of activity;
and agency does not exist in what is already established.
As the Blessed One has said:
Jaimini [states]:
"The fruit of the scripture belongs to the performer, because that is its defining characteristic."

In the world, action alone is observed to be the required means, and thus it is the meaning of words; accordingly, even Vedic injunctions such as "one desiring heaven should perform the Agnihotra" express only action as the required means. And this action, although perishing immediately, becomes capable of producing a result that occurs after a long time by means of an intermediate operation known as the *apūrva* (unseen potency), just as a sowing performed in the summer season results in a harvest in the winter season.
It is not necessary to postulate that the "unprecedented" (apūrva) possesses the status of a required means here.

Or, even if that [unprecedented] were indeed the cause for engaging in activity as a required means, nevertheless, since the word "injunction" (vidhi) shares the common attribute of being characterized by the agent's requirement of a means, it functions toward an action in some cases and toward the unprecedented in others due to its connection with that single attribute; thus, there is no impairment of our view.

Thus, having become proficient in the act of instruction—which consists of the person to be enjoined, the purpose, and the action—upon observing those very same words being employed in acts such as commanding for a specific purpose, he also understands that they possess the capacity to express entreaty and permission.
However, sentences such as "The Agnihotra [should be performed]," which denote the person to be enjoined, the purpose, and the action, constitute instruction alone.
Therefore, although command, entreaty, invitation, and instruction are all forms of injunction (*vidhi*), here it is instruction that is intended by the term "injunction."
Therefore, it has been well said that "an injunction is that which prescribes";
the meaning is that it makes known the status of being a means sought by the agent.
Having restated the Bhāṣya—"An injunction (vidhi), however, is a mandate (niyoga) or a permission (anujñā)"—he explains it.
Regarding the phrase "But it is an injunction" (269/11):

this sentence, "One desiring heaven should offer the Agnihotra," which is characterized by its capacity to impel one who has not yet acted, is an injunction because it makes known that [the act] is a means sought by the agent; that very injunction permits the activity directed toward obtaining the substances and other requirements for that [act].

This is what is meant: those rules regarding the acquisition of wealth for a Brāhmaṇa—such as "by means of receiving gifts" and so forth—are intended for the human goal (puruṣārtha) of restriction when Brāhmaṇas, who are already engaged in acquiring wealth out of passion, employ various worldly means; they do not serve the purpose of the sacrifice (kratvartha). However, the sacrificial injunctions which take wealth as their means merely restate these [rules] and culminate in them.

Furthermore, people do not employ the acquisition of wealth or its restriction as a human goal (puruṣārtha) in itself; rather, they merely grant permission [for it], because that [acquisition] is already employed for the sake of other goals.

Therefore, it is established that the very same sentence concerning the Agnihotra and other rites is an injunction (vidhi) when the Agnihotra and so forth are not otherwise established, whereas it is a permission (anujñā) when the means [of performance] are established by another source. In the case of conjunction, the word "or" (vā) is used. // 63 //
Praise, censure, the deeds of others, and ancient legends constitute *arthavāda* (explanatory or corroborative statements).
Praise has two functions: it serves as an auxiliary for engaging in a duty through an injunction, and it acts as an auxiliary when engagement is to be performed.
Men, knowing that [the act] is praiseworthy, engage themselves all the more; and that engagement produces merit (*dharma*) for one who possesses faith (*śraddhā*), not for one who lacks it.
Thus it is heard in scripture: "Whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*), that alone becomes more powerful for him."
In that context, he states that [the praise] functions as a cooperative cause for the activity [of the injunction],
saying "being praised.
He states that it functions as a cooperative cause for the action of the injunction.
And [it is] "that which sets [the ritual] in motion.
How are the *arthavāda*s concerning the deeds of others (*parakṛti*) and ancient history (*purākalpa*) [to be understood]?

Because of the hearing of a connection between the Caraka and the Adhvaryu priests, there arises the non-attainment of a different sequence for the offering of the omentum (*vapā-homa*) and the sprinkling of the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya-abhighāraṇa*).

The sense is this: why should a *parakṛti* statement— which prescribes something as a quality of a particular person— not likewise be a *purākalpa* statement that prescribes it as a duty for persons of the present time, given that it is heard as being connected to a person of a former time through its association with the *bahiṣpavamāna*, the *soma*, and the *stoma* mantras?
The answer is: because of the connection with some injunction as a supplement to the statements of praise and censure.
For there is no direct scriptural statement of an injunction (*vidhiśruti*) in these sentences which express already established facts.
In this regard, should an unexpressed injunction be postulated, or should there be syntactic unity with an already perceived injunction?

Here, because of the parsimony of postulation (*kalpanālāghava*), syntactic unity with the perceived injunction alone is superior—the sense being that in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) two things must be postulated: the postulation of an injunction and the postulation of its syntactic unity; whereas in the latter [the final view], only syntactic unity needs to be postulated.

Furthermore, because praise and blame are not perceived as more clearly manifest in the cases of "the deeds of others" (parakṛti) and "ancient accounts" (purākalpa), they are presented separately from [ordinary] praise and blame. // 64 //
NyS 2.1.65: Anuvāda (reiteration) is the restatement of that which has been enjoined by a vidhi (injunction).
The discourse on injunction (sūtra 65).
Having set aside what has been prescribed, praise is expressed as if it were censure;
for example, the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) "he who sacrifices with the horse-sacrifice" is attached to the injunction "one should sacrifice with the horse-sacrifice.
For what purpose? To praise.

"He crosses over death, he crosses over evil"—this is the praise (*stuti*). "One should offer when the sun has risen" is the injunction (*vidhi*), and "because he offers when the sun has risen" is its explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
For what purpose? To censure;
for "the dark one indeed devours his offering" is the censure (*nindā*).
He states another purpose:
"Or else, it is stated as a supplement to the injunction (*vidhiśeṣa*).
For example, by means of originative injunctions (*utpattivākya*) such as "The cake on eight potsherds for Agni comes into being," the six [offerings] beginning with the Āgneya are [established].

The sacrifices connected with the times of the full moon and the new moon have been enjoined; these injunctions, consisting in the form of being means to a desired end, are dependent because they do not attain a desired object within their own sentences.
Likewise, the originative injunctions for the *āghāra* libations and so forth, which are unconnected to specific times, are likewise dependent on a desired end. In that regard:

The statement, "He who, knowing thus, sacrifices at the full moon; he who, knowing thus, sacrifices at the new moon," is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the Āgneya and other rites that were originally produced in connection with specific times. For what purpose? It is for the purpose of establishing a restriction regarding the relationship with the desired result (*iṣṭa*), which was required by the original productive injunctions (*utpatti-vidhi*) such as "the cake on eight potsherds for Agni. This ensures that the connection with the fruit—expressed in the injunction "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa"—belongs only to these six rites, the Āgneya and others, which were restated as being produced in connection with specific times, and not to the Āghāra and other subsidiary acts.
This is for the purpose of [excluding] those things that have arisen without connection to time.

Therefore, it is established that the substratum and so forth are determined to be subsidiaries of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices by the principle: "In the proximity of that which has a fruit, that which lacks a fruit is a subsidiary to it."
Thus, this rule regarding the connection with the fruit is a supplement to the injunction; the meaning is that it is a restatement for that purpose.
In this way, the oblation enjoined by the statement "one performs the Agnihotra" is restated.
For what purpose? For the purpose of enjoining specific qualities such as curd and so forth.

In cases such as "He offers with curd" and "He offers with milk," this injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) is a supplement to the primary injunction; thus, he states another purpose for the restatement (*anuvāda*),
namely that it serves to provide the meaning immediately following what has been enjoined.
Just as the Soma sacrifice is prescribed after performing the New and Full Moon sacrifices, according to the rule: "Having sacrificed with the Darśapūrṇamāsa, one should sacrifice with Soma";
and likewise: "The Adhvaryu, having initiated the Gṛhapati, initiates the Brahman"—validity ought to exist because the meaning is grasped through such distinct divisions.
The meaning is that validity comes into being. // 65 //
There is no distinction between a restatement and a tautology, because both result in the repetition of words.
Not so, because of the lack of repetition (Sūtra 66). The prima facie view [of Sūtra 66] belongs to one who does not understand the purpose of restatement as stated in the Bhāṣya. 66.
As in the instruction to move more quickly, there is no difference [in the result] due to practice.
Regarding the Vārttika on sūtra 67, "śīghra-ṣaḥ," it says: "As for example, when it is said, 'Go quickly,' [the response] 'Go even more quickly' is not a tautology.
(270/5) Just as when one says, "Go quickly," the statement "Go more quickly" is not redundant.

Because the excellence of the action is perceived from the repetition [of the word *tarapa*], and because the excellence of the action is perceived through the practice of saying "go faster and faster," whereas it is not understood when [the word] is uttered only once, this repetition is purposeful for the excellence of the action.

The meaning is that even the excellence of the adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*) is indeed the excellence of the action itself. It has been established, therefore, that in the expression "go faster and faster," there is a distinction in the repetition due to the perception of excellence. This constitutes a specific instance of a restatement (*anuvāda*).
He explains what the distinction is in cases such as *pacati pacati* ("he cooks, he cooks"): "But what is this distinction that occurs in cases such as *pacati pacati*?"
And it cannot be that the speaker has one cognition while the listener has another, such that— due to this discrepancy— one might assume the listener’s cognition is erroneous;
thus he says, "And as for the listener," and likewise,
"so too for the other."
Just as in expressions such as "every village is delightful," and so forth. // 67 //
And its authority is like the authority of the Mantras and Ayurveda, because of the authority of the trustworthy person.
The commentary, which is intent on introducing the immediately following sūtra, asks: "What, moreover, does it negate?
Having restated that, he explains it with the words:
"What, moreover..."
The answer is "no.
He asks: "What is the reason?"
"Just as the answer [is not established] without a means of proof," he asks again:
"From what, then, [does it arise]?"
The answer is: by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). He asks: what is that valid cognition?
In that regard, first, he states the proof for the possibility of the Veda's authority:
"the possession of a division of meaning.
However, this is not a proof for the authority of the Veda, because [non-Vedic] scriptures composed by those who are enlightened or unenlightened also possess a division of meaning.
Because it is inconclusive.
However, the authority for the validity of the Vedas is stated in the Sūtra: "From the Mantras" (Sūtra 68).
The word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of drawing forward the previous reason; that is,
it serves to draw forward the quality of having a distinct meaning, which was the reason for the possibility of its being authoritative in the preceding case.
For a position that is possible is established by a reason, but not one that is impossible.
As they have said: "A position that is possible within the thesis may be proven by a reason;
there is no protection for it by means of reasons, [for] that which is destroyed as soon as it arises..."
Thus he explains the Sūtra: "Just like the sentences of the Mantras and Āyurveda.

The excellence of the Person—the Blessed One, the author of the Veda—consists in his having directly perceived what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, the compassion for living beings that is the cause thereof, the desire to communicate things as they truly are, and proficiency in the instruments [of expression].
For it is by these very qualities that this Person is distinguished from other persons who are non-reliable authorities (anāpta).
The phrase "by means of threefold qualification" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa); impairment of the sense organs should also be understood as included.
This is the intended meaning here:
various classes of living beings are observed to possess infinite internal distinctions of pleasure and pain.
Furthermore, it will be explained in the third [chapter] that this diversity is not inherent;
nor is it based solely on visible causes, because such causes are observed to be fallible.
Therefore, the unseen (adṛṣṭa) acting as an auxiliary to the visible is the cause of this diversity, and it is designated as "the unprecedented" (apūrva), as well as "dharma" and "adharma."
And it has been established that this [knowledge] is directly perceived by someone such as Manu and others.

Therefore, the agent of the effects characterized by the body, the world, and so forth— who is capable of their creation, who knows the true nature of all things, who is untouched by afflictions, karma, its results, or latent dispositions, and who is supremely compassionate— is inferred from those very effects, namely the body, the world, and the like.
The fourth [point] will be established later.

Seeing these living beings who do not know the means for attaining what is beneficial and avoiding what is harmful to themselves, and moreover observing them being scorched by the fire of manifold sufferings, how could he not feel compassion?
Or, if he were feeling compassion, knowing the reality of the means for avoiding the harmful and attaining the beneficial, how could he not teach it, or how could he teach otherwise?
Therefore, having created the earth and so forth, this supremely compassionate one must teach the means for those four classes of beings to attain what is beneficial and avoid what is harmful;
for he ought not to remain without having taught them.

The instruction of this one who is like a father to all creatures, which pertains to the domain of gods, sages, and humans, must be respectfully accepted by the four castes (*cāturvarṇya*) and the four stages of life (*cāturāśramya*).
It must also be retained for the purpose of practicing the means to attain what is beneficial and avoid what is harmful.

Therefore, it is established that the scripture which establishes the system of conduct for the castes and stages of life and is embraced by great men is authoritative because it was composed by him [the Buddha], being the word of a reliable person (*āpta*), just like the statements of the *Mantra* and *Āyurveda*.
What is this scripture spoken by a reliable person (*āptokta*)? Are they the scriptures of the Śākya mendicants, the Digambaras, the Saṃsāramocakas, and so forth, or are they the Vedas?

In that regard, it is quite clear from tradition that the founders of the scriptures of the Śākyas and others were the Buddha, Ṛṣabha, and so on; however, there is no such recollection of an Īśvara possessing the aforementioned characteristics as their author.
Furthermore, these individuals such as the son of Śuddhodana and others are not the creators of the body, the world, and so forth, by virtue of which they could be determined to be omniscient.

It might be possible for them to attain omniscience through the practice of those means; however, mere possibility does not justify confidence in the scriptures composed by them on the part of discerning people. Furthermore, their scriptures are not the cause for the established order of conduct regarding the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*). Indeed, these [Buddhists] do not ordain for living beings the rites beginning with the consecration ceremony (*niṣeka*) and ending at the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*).

For even those who have accepted the Buddhist and other scriptures as authoritative do not act in worldly affairs solely on the basis of such scriptures, independent of the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, *Itihāsa*, and *Purāṇa*.
Moreover, even they, asserting that this [world] is veiled by *āvaraṇa*, follow only the Vedas and other scriptures in their worldly conduct.

Therefore, let there be a tradition regarding the Vedas that they were created by a creator who is the fashioner of the universe, or let there not; we nevertheless perceive that these [Vedas] alone were composed by Īśvara.

For these [texts] are not remembered as having other authors, like the sentences concerning the worship of shrines (*caitya-vandana*) and so forth; nor is any other scripture seen to be remembered as being composed by Īśvara, which, while sustaining the course of worldly life, is accepted by the great multitude of people;
and it has already been stated that Īśvara cannot remain without teaching.

Therefore, because of the remaining evidence of that [authorship], we understand that the Vedas themselves— which sustain the entire course of worldly life and teach the means for attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful— are composed by Īśvara;
for it is precisely for this reason that they have been diligently received and preserved by those of the three higher castes until the present day.

And for the preservation of that purpose, the lineages of great seers composed the Vedas, their auxiliary branches (aṅga), the secondary branches (upāṅga), the Itihāsas, the Purāṇas, and the Dharmaśāstras.
However, the words of the Buddha and others do not sustain the course of worldly life;
nor is there a lack of disagreement among worldly people regarding them.
Furthermore, even though it is said that there is no disagreement regarding conventional (sāṃvṛtta) matters, their actual practice does not correspond to that meaning.

Therefore, because they have been adopted by certain outcasts and the like—those lowest of men who are akin to beasts—there is no possibility that these [texts] were spoken by authoritative persons (āpta).
Nor is it correct to claim that these possess authority based on being rooted in the Veda, as is the case with the statements of Manu and others.

This is because the inferential mark (liṅga) consisting of the commonality among students, teachers, and practitioners—which establishes that [the Smṛtis] are rooted in the Veda—is absent in the words of the Buddha and others, as it is in the case of the Smṛtis and the Vedas;
furthermore, due to doubt regarding their omniscience, there is no certainty that they are rooted in direct experience (anubhava).

Moreover, since the authority of the Mantras and Āyurveda is inferred from the efficacy of their application, they authorize Vedic rites such as those for pacification (śāntika) and prosperity (pauṣṭika).

Furthermore, since at the commencement of treatments such as elixirs (rasāyana), there is the instruction of expiatory rites (prāyaścitta) like the Cāndrāyaṇa as prescribed by the Vedas, it is thereby accepted even by Āyurveda—composed by a trustworthy person—that the authority of the Vedas is established.
Thus, it is proven that the Vedas, being composed by a trustworthy person, are a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
The corroboration found in cases such as the Kārīrī sacrifice is merely a secondary reinforcement.
Intending precisely this, the author of the Vārttika states the formal argument (*prayoga*): "The Vedic sentences are a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
He then states another formal argument:
"By virtue of having a single author" means:
the sentences of the Mantras and Āyurveda have an omniscient being as their author, because, while being accepted by the great masses of people, they set forth matters that are not worldly.

As for those [texts] which do not have an omniscient being as their precursor, they do not possess such characteristics, just like the sentences of the Vātaputrīyas; this is a negative (vyatireka) reason.
And just as the words of the Buddha and others, though they concern the supramundane, are not accepted by the great multitude, so it has been stated immediately prior. Furthermore,

although the words of the *mantras* and *Āyurveda* possess the capacity for successful application, no one who is not omniscient— even in a thousand human lifetimes— is capable of [knowing] those various medicinal plants, the specific variations in their combinations, and the distinctions between the insertion and extraction of each respective syllable.
First, one must establish positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).
Nor can "not being for the first time" (anidamprathamatā) serve as a solution to that [problem], because such a state is impossible at the beginning of a creation.
Furthermore, both the creation and the great dissolution will be established through inference and scripture; thus, everything is entirely satisfactory.

Thus, since it is established that [the Vedas] are preceded by an omniscient being, their authority as the word of a reliable person (*āptoktatva*) is proven—just like the worldly sentence "one who desires rice should cook.

If they were not eternal, how could they be authoritative? For if they were non-eternal, there would be a suspicion of error due to the diverse intentions of human beings, and such a suspicion could not be dispelled.

Therefore, the meaning is that it is precisely the authorlessness (*apauruṣeyatva*) which establishes the authority of the Veda by removing the defects inherent in human beings. The subsequent phrase "because of being a communicator" means that even though [the Veda] is non-eternal, it is determinative because it is spoken by a reliable person (*āpta*).
"Ke cit tu" means:
that which performs a purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) characterized by validity is a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*);
however, since there is no purposeful action for that which is eternal, it is therefore not a valid means of cognition—this is the meaning.
He refutes it;
we see, however, that this is not correct.
The intention is that we shall explain in the third chapter how even an eternal entity can possess causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
Furthermore, the phrase "and the self" is intended merely to indicate its status as a cause of valid cognition (*pramā*), and does not imply that it is an instrument (*karaṇa*).
This refers to the word "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*).

In this case as well, it should be understood that the intention is not to express [the atom] as an instrument (*karaṇa*), but rather merely to express it as a cause of valid cognition (*pramāṇahetu*).
"By way of establishing other things" means by way of establishing other properties residing in the atoms themselves, such as corporeality (*mūrtatva*) and so forth.
Thus, having refuted the view of the proponents of a single position, he states his own position:
"Therefore," and "And that [is so] because cyclic existence is beginningless."
(273/17) Although phonemes, words, and sentences differ with each utterance,

the meaning is that it is possible to grasp the convention for the phonemes such as *ga*, which are delimited by universals such as *gatva*, and for the collections of those [phonemes] which constitute sentences, by means of individual instances such as the *śābaleya* cow, which are likewise delimited by universals such as *gotva*.
Regarding the phrase "at the beginning of a Manvantara":
the sense is that during the great dissolution (mahāpralaya), however, the Lord (Īśvara) compiles the Vedas and indeed initiates the tradition at the start of creation.
The remainder of the Bhāṣya and the Vārttika have meanings that are not obscure. // 68 //
Thus ends the first Āhnika of the second Adhyāya in the *Nyāyavārtikatātparyaṭīkā* composed by the venerable Vācaspati Miśra.
*** *Examination of the Tetrad* ***
NyS 2.2.1: Nor is there a fourfold [number of means of valid cognition], because tradition, presumptive testimony, probability, and non-existence are also means of valid cognition.
"It is not according to reality," says the Bhāṣya.
"That which is the non-distinctive enumeration of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) is not according to reality.
The author of the Vārttika explains this as follows: "Perception... and so forth.
Having thus explained the sūtra according to the opinion of the Bhāṣya— that it is a refutation of one who is deluded— the author explains it by another method as well:
"Or rather, the section [of the Bhāṣya] is for the purpose of removing doubt,
while the sūtra is for the purpose of raising doubt."
It is not possible to determine that there are exactly four [means of valid cognition]. Why?
Because of the validity of tradition (aitihya), presumption (arthāpatti), probability (saṃbhava), and non-existence (abhāva).
The meaning of the sūtra is that these are accepted by others as means of knowledge, whereas for us, they remain objects of doubt.
He states another intended meaning:
"vidhi" etc.
In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the enumeration of divisions is intended to imply a prohibition of others, the enumeration of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would be incorrect.
This was explained previously;

however, the present undertaking is devoted to the injunction regarding perception and the other [means of knowledge], namely: "Perception, inference, comparison, and word are the means of valid cognition" (*pratyakṣānumānopamānaśabdāḥ pramāṇāni*).
This statement was made with the intention of adopting the position that the exclusion of additional [means] is obtained through the force of the context (*arthāt*), and thus there is no tautology.
He states another intended meaning with the words "of those possessing defects" (doṣavatām).
He states yet another intended meaning with the words "in perception and so forth" (pratyakṣādiṣu).

The meaning is that the correspondence between the subject matter and the enumeration of the divisions is established by the fact that this treatise is primarily concerned with inclusion (antarbhāva).
He explains:
"Because it is established.

The meaning is that it is not necessarily the case that everything which is merely indicated by the author of the Sūtra must be formally demonstrated by the author of the Bhāṣya and others, since its demonstration is already accomplished by them as well.
He does not avoid [the objection] regarding the purpose of restriction, namely the exclusion of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

That which can be understood even without being explicitly stated through mere indication is not mentioned by the author of the Sūtras; and that which, though indicated, remains as if concealed, must indeed be clarified by the author of the Sūtras.
For there is no certainty in such cases that the commentators and others speak only of what we intend and nothing else—this is the sense.
"What is implied here by the sense? is the question. "It exists when [the conditions] are present" is the answer.
This is because of the mention of the opposite.

Because of the apprehension of that which has been approached as being opposed to the falling of water, there is the apprehension of its opposite— the conjunction of wind and cloud— which is indeed contrary to falling; for this very thing, called the means of knowledge known as non-existence (abhāva), is what is cognized when, despite the rising of clouds, there is no falling of water, [and thus one infers] the conjunction of wind and cloud.
He states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words "these very [means of knowledge].

Now, one might object: "This object will exist as something beyond the scope of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) defined above, and other means of knowledge such as *aitihya* (tradition) and so forth will operate upon it. To this he replies:
"And because of the absence of an object."
He objects: "But [the number] differs because of the difference in purpose.
He refutes this by showing that it leads to an over-extension:
"In that case, there would be eight [categories]."

There do not exist such general and specific purposes by which the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇas*), being purposeful, would be mutually distinguished; rather, it must be said that they are distinguished merely by their difference [in number].
And thus, by over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), there would be an exclusion of the number eight—this is the meaning.
Now, as for the phrase "by a generality of objects" (*viṣayasāmānyena*).
The phrase "because of being form" (rūpatvāt) means that the generality of the object (viṣayasāmānya) is non-different from its own respective particulars; it is their oneness (ekatva).
The refutation begins with the words "In that case, it is not logical."

The meaning is that it is not correct to deny the number four, because there are four objects—generalities and particulars—consisting of one which has the nature of being without adjuncts (*nirupādhāna-svarūpa*), and three which have the adjuncts of pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*), possession (*anvitattva*), and nameability (*saṃjñitva*). // 1 //

NyS 2.2.2: There is no refutation [of our position], because oral tradition (*aitihya*) is not distinct from verbal testimony (*śabda*), and because presumption (*arthāpatti*), possibility (*saṃbhava*), and absence (*abhāva*) are not distinct from inference (*anumāna*).
"If these... means:

if tradition (*aitihya*) and the other such things were valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it must be stated where they are included—within perception (*pratyakṣa*) or elsewhere. [But they are not,] for they are not valid means of knowledge.
It was stated that [itineraries and the like] are "means of valid cognition" because they are not included within other means of valid cognition.

Indeed, regarding *aitihya*—which is a succession of reports whose original speaker has not been specified—if a trustworthy author is not ascertained, then it is not a means of valid cognition at all; this is the sense in which it was so stated. However, if it is understood as a succession of syllables, then there is the instruction of a trustworthy person (*āptopadeśa*) therein.
Thus, it does not deviate from the definition of a word; this is what was stated by the phrase "because they possess the same characteristic.
He asks: "In what way is it presumptive testimony (arthāpatti)?"
(276/1) "When clouds are absent, rain does not occur; when they are present, it does occur"—how is this *arthāpatti* (presumption) subsumed under inference (*anumāna*)?
The answer is: "Of the two."
He states an example here: "wherever... wherever.
He points out that the example is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*).
Regarding the phrase "but one":

if it is determined that there is a prohibition of a specific time in the sense that "one does not eat only during the day," then it would follow that there is a prescription of another time in the sense that "one eats at night"; however, there is no determination of a specific time, but rather [the meaning is] simply that "one does not eat during the day."
Because the eating at night is implied through the negation of the negation of other activities such as sitting and so forth that are distinct from the activity of eating;
for when the single [proposition] "he does not eat during the day" is established, there would be the negation of another action, namely, "he eats at night."
And since there is no prior occasion for the prohibition, it should not be stated that "he eats at night";
this is what he refutes by saying,
"But this is not correct."
For prohibitions are preceded by the possibility of what they negate.
In this case, neither for one who is eating nor for one who is not eating is the absence of some other action established such that it could be prohibited by saying "he does not eat at all.
Indeed, no one exists who eats and yet does not look.
