Because even such actions as "existence" (asti) and so forth ultimately involve activity;

for one who is already engaged in an action might at times fail to perform another action, but how much more so one who is not so engaged? For he indeed performs other actions without being distracted by them—this is the meaning.
He concludes with the words "therefore" (tasmāt).
The negation of time means the negation of the statement "he eats only during the day."
The sense is that there can be no negation because it is impossible for the cessation of the prohibition of another action to occur, and because [the object] has not been previously established.
Regarding the phrase "prohibition of another action," the word *antara* signifies a distinction.
The meaning is that there is a negation of the specific interval in the act of eating—an interval devoid of any other action—such that he is indeed eating;
this is called "inference from general observation" (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*).
That is, where there is no relationship of effect and cause serving as the signified and the signifier, that is *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*. // 2 //
NyS 2.2.3: Presumption (arthāpatti) is not a means of valid cognition because it is inconclusive.

The statement "these are true" means this: these means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), such as tradition (aitihya) and the rest, are indeed true; however, they are not a separate means of valid cognition distinct from inference (anumāna) and the others. They are by no means a separate means of valid cognition apart from inference and so forth.
Thus it has been stated;
the intention is not that we do not accept their status as valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), but rather [the objection concerns something else].
The *Vārttika* says "of presumption-only" (*arthāpattimātrasya*).
(277/2) Because the presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) such as "he does not eat divine [food]" is not conclusive. // 3 //
NyS 2.2.4: [The fallacy arises] from the misconception of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) where there is no actual presumptive testimony.
Having refuted [the opponent's position] according to his own view, he states the refutation based on the Sūtra: "As for what you said...
This does not mean that rain necessarily occurs when clouds exist, such that a deviation [of the rule] could be pointed out; rather, it means that rain does not occur when they are absent.
And thus, there is no deviation; this is the meaning. // 4 //
And the invalidity of the negation [of inference] is due to its being inconclusive (anaikāntika).

But if, having assumed another object from that object where the presumption (arthāpatti) is certain, one were to point out its uncertainty, then—having assumed another object of the negation, namely the existence of the presumption, as the object of that negation—we are able to say that the negation lacks authority; and thus, because the negation lacks authority, the presumption does not lack authority. So he says.
Prati-t (Sūtra 5): For an absolute negation would indeed occur only if [the argument] were to negate both the validity and the existence of presumption (*arthāpatti*).
However, it cannot negate its existence because of its inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*).
For that which is inconclusive is not necessarily non-existent, since properties such as "knowability" (*prameyatva*) exist even though they are inconclusive when used to prove eternality.
Because the distinction [of existence] arises from presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
(278/1) The distinction is the validity [of the cognition] arising from presumptive testimony; for mere presumptive testimony is not existence itself. // 5 //
Or, if that [inference] is authoritative, then presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) is not authoritative.
If the proponent thinks that there is no inconclusiveness regarding the negation of its being a means of valid cognition, then it follows:
"Its validity... (Sūtra 6).

The meaning is that he states that "misapprehension" (*vipratipatti*) or "non-apprehension" (*apratipatti*) constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). Furthermore, as for the *arthāpatti* (presumption) cited by the author of the *Mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya*—namely, the postulation of Caitra’s presence outside based on seeing the absence of the living Caitra from his house—that too is nothing but inference (*anumāna*). For when a person who exists is not in one place, he is in another; or when a non-pervasive entity is in one place, he is not in another. This is precisely how the universal concomitance (*vyāpti*) is grasped within one's own body.
It is easy [to understand].
Thus, the perception of his existence outside is an inference based on the mark (liṅga) of the perception of his absence from the house while he exists.

Nor can his absence from the house be denied by his existence, such that the absence from the house would be unestablished; nor can his existence be denied, such that existence itself—being untenable otherwise—would not establish its own locus outside.
For instance, either mere existence is contradicted by Caitra’s absence from the house, or Caitra’s existence in the house [is contradicted].
First of all, there is no contradiction between existence anywhere whatsoever and non-existence in the house, because they do not share the same objective domain (*viṣaya*).
Even the implication of a specific location, such as the house, through a general location is merely optional (*pākṣika*).

If it is argued that there is a contradiction because the two have the same object, we say no; for that which is ascertained by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) cannot be sublated by that which is merely doubtful.

Nor is it logical that the non-existence, once ascertained by a means of valid cognition, should—while subverting its partial existence in the house—also be able to subvert its [overall] existence or remove its state of being doubtful.

Because existence in the house is precluded by the absence [of the person] delimited by the house due to their mutual contradiction, but mere existence is not [precluded], since that [mere existence] is indifferent to that [absence].
Therefore, it is logical that the existence of the living person outside is inferred by means of the established absence from the house.

By this, the view that the scope of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) consists in the removal of the contradiction between two contradictory means of valid cognition through the determination of their respective objects is refuted.
Because there is no contradiction between the delimited and the undelimited,
it is established that presumption (arthāpatti) is not a distinct means of valid cognition from inference. // 6 //
NyS 2.2.7: Non-existence is not a means of valid cognition, because its object of cognition is not established.
"Because of the non-establishment [of the object of knowledge] from the absence [of the means of knowledge]" (Sūtra 6). Knowledge of an absence is not a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*),
because the object of knowledge— the absence— is not established.
The prima facie argument is that what is devoid of all designations (*sarvopākhyārahita*) certainly does not become an object of valid cognition;
rather, this conventional usage of "non-existence" among worldly people is merely conceptual (*kālpnika*). // 7 //

NyS 2.2.8: The establishment of those [objects] not characterized by definition occurs because those not characterized by definition are characterized by the absence of definition in those that have been characterized.
He states the established conclusion:
"The non-existence [is] more extensive.
The cognition and linguistic usage of non-existence, which are common to all people, cannot be merely conceptual.

Furthermore, it has been stated during the demonstration of *viparītakhyāti* that even conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is incapable of taking as its object that which is devoid of all descriptive designations (*sarvopākhyārahita*).
Moreover, during the occasion of refuting the doctrine of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), its possessibility of such designations will be established.
Therefore, because this [perception] possesses validity, its inclusion within the category of valid cognition is appropriate.
The author of the Vārttika explains all of this:
"Non-existence is not a means of valid cognition," thereby refuting what was previously stated.
And who says this?

For it is non-existence (*abhāva*) that is called the object of cognition (*prameya*), not the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) in its own form; rather, it is the apprehension (*pratipatti*) having that as its object.
And that [apprehension] is the fruit of perception (*pratyakṣa*); it is the means of cognition in the cognition of appropriation and so forth, as will be explained further on.

Regarding the absence of rain, it has been stated that there is an inference based on the conjunction of wind and clouds; having understood [the situation], one brings [the water]. (279/4) One brings [it] after having understood it as something to be brought, being delimited by the qualifier "absence of [rain's] characteristic."

This is what is meant: the cognition of the absence of a characteristic, by producing a conviction regarding the specific cloth, becomes a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) because it is the most effective instrument (sādhakatama). // 8 //
NyS 2.2.9: If it is argued that non-existence cannot exist in the absence of an object, we say no, because another definition [of non-existence] is possible.
Because of non-existence. (Sūtra 9)

The prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) belongs to one who considers that non-existence is nothing other than destruction (pradhvaṃsa), because its definition is dependent upon existence and it is preceded by existence; for non-existence is preceded by existence,
and there is no other kind of non-existence.
"Not due to non-cognition":
for perception as a means of valid cognition establishes the absence of an object of cognition;
and that [capacity] is the same in the case of prior non-existence as it is in the case of destruction.
For worldly people indeed perceive the absence of milk in curd, just as they perceive the absence of curd in milk.
But surely the Sūtra speaks of the occurrence—the existence—of those things whose nature is the absence of characteristics in other clothes;
you do not, however, speak of the perception of non-existence. Therefore, how is there no contradiction? To this he says:
Therefore, the meaning of the Sūtra has been stated; the meaning of the Sūtra has been explained by way of its contrapositive (vyatireka). For this very reason, the author of the Bhāṣya says:
"Not so in the case of uncharacterized things.
For by the non-perception of a characteristic, the absence of a characteristic is indeed indicated. // 9 //
NyS 2.2.10: Because that [non-existence] is established, it is not a reason with respect to those things that have not been characterized.
Regarding the phrase "those which [exist] among the characterized": there is nothing among the characterized that lacks them; and as for those that do exist, their non-existence is contradicted.
What is meant is this: wherever the characteristics exist, the non-existence of those [characteristics] therein is contradicted.

And where [an entity] does not exist, even there non-existence is untenable; for since its determination is dependent upon that [entity], it cannot be determined in the absence of it. He refutes this, saying: "No, because of a lack of understanding."

The meaning is this: non-existence (abhāva) is defined in dependence upon the knowledge of an existent thing (bhāva), but it is not defined in dependence upon the [prior] existent thing itself; furthermore, even prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) can be defined by means of the knowledge of a future existent or by the knowledge of an existent located elsewhere, and thus there is no such thing as the "non-existence of prior non-existence."
No, because the establishment [of the object] depends on its being situated according to its defining characteristics.
And because non-existence prior to origination is logically established.
Regarding the phrase "non-existence is twofold" (*abhāvadvaitam*):

this refers back to the present context; it is presented as an exposition of antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) in response to one who maintains the doctrine of mere destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*). However, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*), non-existence is first of all twofold: non-existence as identity (*tādātmyābhāva*) and non-existence as relation (*saṃsargābhāva*). Furthermore, non-existence as relation is threefold, distinguished by the categories of antecedent, destructive, and absolute non-existence.
Thus, there are four kinds of non-existence (*abhāva*).
Non-existence [is defined] by means of an unreal object;
and "because it is not established, it is not a reason among those that are uncharacterized"—both of these are sūtras on quibbling (*chala*).

(280/3) Whatever is a non-existence (*abhāva*), all of it exists when there is a real object (*satyārtha*), as in the case of destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*); yet, such is not the case for the non-existence of a definition (*lakṣaṇābhāva*).
This is a "quibble regarding the general" (*sāmānyacchala*). 10.
"But 'because of its establishment' is a quibble regarding words (vākchala); for its meaning is: 'How is it that those very definitions which exist do not [exist]? " // 11-12 //
Because it has a beginning, because it is perceptible by the senses, and because it is treated as something produced.

Thus, having introduced the examination of verbal testimony (*śabda*) and having examined its validity, the enumeration of its divisions was examined; now, proceeding with the remainder of the examination of verbal testimony, he says:
"Verbal testimony is the instruction of a reliable person" (*āptopadeśaḥ śabdaḥ*).
He does so while demonstrating the conflicting views that serve as a cause for doubt.
He states the view of the Jaran-Mīmāṃsakas:
"Sound is a quality of space.
For, when the air set in motion by a collision proceeds with its momentum until it reaches the ear, it becomes inherent in that portion of space delimited by the ear-cavity (*karṇaśaṣkulī*).
"Sound is eternal; it is manifested"—this the author of the Vārttika explains with the words, "First of all, some [hold]... and so forth.
Since even that which has a non-perishing substratum is impermanent due to its conjunctions and so forth, he says:
"subsisting in a single substance.
Nevertheless, this [definition] is inconclusive because of the color and other qualities residing in the atoms of earth.
He says:
"And it is a quality of space.

Since the desired conclusion is established by this much alone—that it is a quality of space while being a single substance—it should be understood that the state of having a non-perishing substratum is mentioned for the sake of further elaboration (*prapañca*).
Regarding the phrase "conjunction, disjunction, and sound":

it should be understood that air impelled by the conjunction of a drum and a stick, reaching the space within the ear-cavity, is the manifester of sound; likewise, air impelled by the disjunction of the bamboo slivers is the manifester of sound.
Conjunction and disjunction [produce sound] through a succession of steps,
whereas the articulated sound (nāda) does so directly;
thus he states the Sāṃkhya position.
Regarding the phrase "occurring together with odor and so forth":

sound, which is a modification of earth and other elements produced from a collection of subtle elements (*tanmātra*) derived from the five [subtle elements], exists in things such as cows and jars; however, because it is of the nature of *ahaṃkāra*, it is pervasive in its appropriate location and is perceived only by the auditory organ located at the site of the sense-object.
This is what he says:
"But others [say]...
'due to the impact of a particular primary element.'"
The meaning is "the striking of the drumstick against the drum.
He states the Vaiśeṣika position:
"It is a quality of space."
He states the Buddhist position: "Arising from the agitation of the great elements" (281.2),
[meaning] "not because of a lack of connection."

When an entity exists, it cannot possess prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) or posterior non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), and thus it would follow that it is not impermanent; furthermore, this would lead to the absurd consequence [of impermanence] applying to things that have not yet arisen or those already destroyed.

For there is no coexistence of prior and posterior non-existences; therefore, impermanence would apply to each of them individually. Consequently, it follows that impermanence would apply to an entity that has not yet arisen or one that has already perished.
Nor is this seen or accepted, because impermanence is perceived as a property of an entity (*bhāvadharma*) in the cognition "the pot is impermanent.
Not only is it illogical for there to be impermanence alone according to this [opponent's] position, but the meaning of the genitive case is also absent.
Why is it that the non-existence (*abhāva*) of an entity cannot be its property? To this, he says:
"And it is not the time for the Dharma"— the word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of a reason; this is an objection.
Regarding the word "atha":
the meaning is that since it does not exist prior to being and ceases to exist after having been, its non-existence [is established]; thus, the use of the genitive case is justified.
The reply is: "Even so.
It is true that [the entity] exists and yet does not exist;
however, it is not by means of this [existence] that there is a connection with its non-existence, because they belong to different times.
Therefore, the meaning is that nothing we have stated has been refuted.
He raises an objection regarding contradiction with common worldly usage, saying "the prior non-existence of a jar.

The use of the genitive case here where there is no [actual] relation is figurative (*bhākta*); the meaning of "figurative" is that its determination is dependent upon the existence [of the related entity].
Moreover, a present thing is said to be "permanent," and its state is "permanence" (*nityatā*). To the question, "Even if that be so, what of it?
he says: "And in the present... (*varttamāne ca*).
The meaning is that the suffix *matup* is employed by figuratively attributing a connection to the presence of a necessary destruction, on the grounds that "its destruction will necessarily occur.
[This refers to] "that which has reached the conditions for perception."

For there is no destruction of that which exists, by which a lack of connection for an entity could be taught; rather, just as the manifestation of an existing thing is its birth, so too the absolute disappearance of an existing thing is its destruction, and this is designated as "impermanence. And since this disappearance occurs at the same time as the existence [of the thing], its connection with the existent is logically established—this is the point. Furthermore, since disappearance can occur even in the case of a jar or similar objects, it was stated [in the commentary] that it must have "attained the conditions for perception" (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*).
This refutes that Sāṃkhya doctrine, stating:
"But this is a void assertion.
For since the universe is a modification of the Pradhāna, and a modification is not different from its material cause (prakṛti), [what would there be] of the Pradhāna?
The meaning is that this contradicts the Sāṃkhya tenet, which holds that because consciousness is perceived, there is no such thing as an object that is absolutely unperceived.
Furthermore, just as there is no destruction of what exists, so too there is no birth of what does not exist; and likewise for that in which no particularity has arisen.

The disappearance of the entity is not tenable; and as for the production of a particularity (*viśeṣa*), how can there be the arising of something existent, since the particularity itself was previously non-existent?
Or, if it were already existent, it would follow that it should have been perceived even previously.
As for the phrase "but those who... [the following applies].
The meaning is that impermanence itself is "impermanence," where the suffix *tal* is used in its own sense (*svārthika*). He refutes this:

But this is not tenable: even for Pāṇini, a traditional rule (*smṛti*) that does not contradict valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is a cause for establishing reality, whereas one that contradicts them is not;

and there is indeed a contradiction with valid means of knowledge in the view that suffixes such as *ṭhak* are used in their own sense (*svārthika*). For instance, there would be no co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) of base and suffix, for co-utterance is never observed between two things that have the same meaning—just as one does not say "tree" and "śiṃśapā" [as synonyms], one certainly does not say "tree" and "taru."
The application [of the argument] is as follows:
if it is asked, "How then can there be one, two, or many?", the answer is: no, because the employment of case-endings is for the purpose of expressing specific gender and individuality.
In this way, it should be understood that even in the case of *yāvaka* and other such terms, the exclusion of other contradictory classes (*jātyantara*) is the meaning of the suffix.
And just as they explain the words, saying "that which is barley itself is *yāvaka*," so too has this been stated.
"Even for those whose differences are not perceived, there is a difference through inference.
What is this inference?
The statement "the state of having difference as its object by means of the sixth [case]" intends the suffixes *tva* and *tal*, because permanence and impermanence are the subjects under discussion.

Since the rule "the suffixes *tva* and *tal* express the abstract state (*bhāva*) of that" prescribes the derivation of *tva* and *tal* from a word in the genitive case, it has been stated that inference has everything as its object.
This refers to whether there is dependence on a limit (*avadhi*) or lack thereof.
Existence itself, when dependent upon two limits, is impermanence; and that same existence, when independent of them, is permanence.

Furthermore, the limit is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), not a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*); and it remains an indicator even when occurring at a different time, just as when Devadatta’s mother has died, one says "Yajñadatta is the son of Devadatta," where Devadatta indicates her own son by virtue of being someone who previously existed.
When "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) is [defined as] inherence (*samavāya*), then existence (*sattā*) delimited by both ends is eternity (*nityatā*).

But when origination (*utpatti*) is simply existence delimited by the prior end, then existence delimited by the posterior end is non-eternity (*anityatā*); thus, there is no contradiction with what was stated during the occasion of explaining the definition of the reason (*hetu*).
Inherence is the cause for the acquisition of the self-nature of an effect.
Thus:
the acquisition of its own nature by the effect is its relation to its own cause; the cause of that [acquisition] is inherence (*samavāya*).
For inherence is the state of being inherent; inherence is the state of being an effect qualified by its cause.

The state of having the property of arising in accordance with the distinction between the efficient cause (nimitta) and the instrumental cause (kāraṇa) [is established] by intending not to express the difference between the signifier (gamaka) and the signified (gamya). // 13 //

NyS_2.2.14: [The term "non-eternal" is applied to eternal things] neither because of the eternity of the generality (sāmānya) of the absence of a jar, nor because of the metaphorical application (upacāra) of non-eternality even to eternal things.
NyS 2.2.15: There is no deviation [from the definition] because of the distinction between that which possesses the essence and that which participates in it.
The instrumental causes are the conjunction of the drum and the stick, and so forth;
indeed, it is due to their difference that the sound becomes different.
[The opponent] objects: "By means of conjunction and disjunction..."

For just as a difference [in appearance] is observed due to a difference in causes, so too a difference is observed in the face being manifested by different manifestors such as a gem, a sword, or a mirror; therefore, there is doubt.
First of all, the auditory organ does not travel to the location of the sound, because it is formless (*amūrtatva*).

For the auditory organ (*śrotra*) is the ether (*nabhas*) delimited by the ear-cavity (*karṇaśaṣkulī*); and even though the ear-cavity is material (*mūrta*), it does not travel toward the speaker's mouth, since the ear-cavity situated within the auditory organ is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Therefore, even if [the sound] were to move, the mere ether is not the auditory organ, because of the absence of the ear-cavity as its substrate.
Therefore, it should be understood that this was said with reference to one who thinks that the ear-canal does not move, but rather that the sound produced therein travels through space.
"Due to the inherence of the quality of action" means due to the inherence of impulsion and impact.
This does not mean that it is independent [of all other factors].

Although gravity depends upon the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) for the act of falling, it nevertheless does not depend on any other subsequent efficient cause; this is the meaning of the word "independent" (nirapekṣa).
Even though the removal of an obstacle occurs as a subsequent event, it is nonetheless not a different efficient cause for the obstruction itself.

For when [the obstruction] exists, it does not perform its natural function; moreover, it is not reasonable to postulate that the removal of the obstructer also serves as a cause for that [functioning], because the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) of that [removal] is established otherwise. Thus, the meaning of "independence" (anapekṣā) is that [the capacity] does not depend on any other final cause (nimitta) in the form of a positive entity.

"And because of the absence of an object" (286/3). The capacity for the production of action is the object of action; depending upon that, action occurs. That [capacity] is form (*mūrti*). And this [form], characterized by the dimension of a non-omnipresent substance, does not exist in space and so forth, which are omnipresent.
Therefore, these [latter] do not possess action.
This is the meaning. Therefore, because the final [sound] is extremely weak, it does not initiate another sound; moreover, it does not merely destroy its own cause, the [preceding] sound.
However, even that [sound] is destroyed by its own cause, which is sound; thus, this is the opposition between cause and effect in these two cases.
But the first [sound] is destroyed by the effect itself, whereas for those in the middle, there is no fixed rule.
He raises the view of the old Mīmāṃsakas with the words "if it is argued that it is indeed one.
The meaning is that for them, sound is a single quality of the ether (nabhas) that exists pervading the ether like a substance possessing magnitude.
Having accepted the position that sound is refined (saṃskāra), he states the refutation.
"Not because it would follow that [the sound] would be perceived by all" means:
this is the sense of the question "Why not?
[The reason is: "Because sound subsists in space."

The meaning is that because space is omnipresent, if it were manifested there, it would be manifested everywhere; thus, its perception would necessarily occur everywhere. Having granted the position that it is manifested in only one part, he says: "And if it were manifested in only one part, there would be no cognition of the object."
Because a task to be accomplished by a series of phonemes cannot be achieved by a single part [of that series],
just as when a word consists of multiple phonemes, the cognition of the meaning does not occur upon the manifestation of only one phoneme.
It might be argued that the phoneme (*varṇa*) is merely a single part (*ekadeśa*), and thus a single part is capable of performing the function accomplished by the phoneme; to this he says:
"All [phonemes] are indeed pervasive (*vyāpaka*).
This being the case, the manifestation of a single part of the phoneme is admitted; therefore, the meaning is that the non-pervasive single part is distinct from the pervasive phoneme.
Now, let it be granted that the cognition of meaning arises from only a single part [of a phoneme]; to this he says:
"In this position, the manifestation of a single part of a phoneme is admitted, yet a single part of a phoneme cannot be defined.
For when a phoneme is uttered with very slight effort, the intellect does not perceive it; or, if it perceives it, it perceives the phoneme itself and never a single part of it. This is the meaning.
Having granted the premise of determination (*nirūpaṇa*), he says:
"And not from what has been determined. [Objection: In that case, let many phonemes (*varṇa*) be manifested; the meaning is understood from their determination. To this, he replies:
Regarding the phrase "by this":

as for the one who thinks that there is no spatial part (*ekadeśa*) of the sound in reality, but rather that the "part" is simply the non-pervasive occurrence (*avyāpyavṛttitva*) of the impression (*saṃskāra*),
[he must consider that] in your own position, the non-pervasive occurrence belongs to the sound itself within the ether (*nabhas*).
Regarding the claim that it is "only one part," he states another fault against that view: "And there would be a cacophony.
If it is argued that only a certain sound manifests only a certain word, and therefore there is no cacophony, he replies to that: "And there would be no restriction."
Since there is a restriction regarding the manifestors even for color, taste, and so forth that occupy the same location, it was stated [in the verse] "of those perceptible by the same sense organ.

Nevertheless, even among things perceptible by the same sense organ, there is no simultaneous manifestation of all those occupying different locations; therefore, it was stated "occupying the same location.
He raises an objection: "If something is the manifestor of another..."

The meaning is this: for the manifesting capacity of manifestors is not perceived as distinct from the manifestation itself, and since that [manifestation] is restricted, the restriction of the manifestors is also established.
He refutes this, saying: "That is not so, because it is not observed.

For in other cases, a lack of restriction is observed between manifestors—whether they be material elements (*bhūta*) or otherwise—and the manifested; thus, here too, it subverts any claim of restriction.

The point is this: since a restriction of causes is observed even in the case of effects that occupy the same location—such as color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth, which are apprehended by the same sense organ, as well as number (*saṃkhyā*) and so forth—it follows that for sounds too, a restriction of production is logically established through a restriction of their causes.

[The opponent] objects, thinking that all things are connected with every universal because there is no obstruction between all entities and the universals, such that "every entity is conjoined with every universal."

Regarding the phrase "possessing a universal" (*sāmānyavat*): the author refutes [the opponent's objection] with the intention that, even though there is no obstruction to all objects, only a certain thing is connected with a certain universal, and not everything with every universal.
He does so by stating, "No, because it is not accepted."

Although for those residing in the same location—such as "sentient being-ness" (*sattvatva*), "human-ness" (*naratva*), and "Brahmin-ness" (*brāhmaṇatva*)—which are perceptible by the same sense organ and whose distinct natures are manifested by their specific configurations, origins, and manifestors, there is a relationship where each is manifested by its own specific manifestor; nevertheless, there is no deviation [from the rule] because they do not occupy the same location.

This is because "sentient being-ness," due to its inherence in all three categories of entities, occupies a larger location, whereas "human-ness" exists among Kṣatriyas and others just as it does among Brahmins.

Because the status of being a Brāhmaṇa excludes that of a Kṣatriya and so forth, and because it exists only among those such as the Kaṭhas, they do not occupy the same location due to their differing numerical extents;
by this, the same principle should be understood regarding the refinement of the auditory organ:
just as a sense organ refined by the act of opening its eyes reveals all its own perceivable objects located in the same place at once, and not only some of them, everything is thus clarified.

Furthermore, he demonstrates this through an objection and its reply by stating "yadi ca" (if, moreover): if all sound were manifested by the conjunction of the palate and other organs, then once that conjunction has ceased, sound should be perceived at a distance, yet it is not so perceived;

however, if it were manifested by a series of air-currents, the very absence of the previously mentioned restriction would be the fault. Thus he shows [the point] by means of an objection and its response.
Furthermore, he demonstrates through a doubt and its resolution that this eternal sound would be either localized or all-pervading, and that there is a fault in both cases, [stating]:
"And when the cause is present" (289/10).
This might be so.
"Let it not be that air (*vāyu*) is the manifestor; for indeed, there are qualities of air called *nāda*s (sounds/noises), and these are the manifestors of this sound. To this, he says:
"And regarding the perception of *nāda*.
For no such thing as *nāda*, a quality of air, is ever perceived.
Even granting this for the sake of argument, we say:

even when sound is perceived, one must admit that where there is air, its quality, *nāda*, must also be present; yet, when a distant person perceives a sound, there is neither air nor its quality, *nāda*, at that location. Furthermore, on this position, the movement of a series of air (*vāyusantāna*) is not accepted.
Since it is observed that sound is perceived by a person standing at a distance, [it might be argued that] the manifesting agent is *nāda* (sound/noise).
It might be thought:

"Let there be no series of air (*vāyu-saṃtāna*), nor let *nāda*, which is a quality of that [air], be the manifestor of the sound; rather, let the conjunctions and disjunctions belonging to the air be the manifestors. To this, he says:
Regarding the phrase "by this":

however, there is one who thinks that it is recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) itself—the venerable [cognition]—that proves the permanence of sound; and for the sake of its consistency, [he argues that] the winds impelled by effort, as they persist for as long as their momentum lasts, reach the ear of the sound—which is either an all-pervading quality (*guṇa*) or a substance (*dravya*).

Alternatively, it is postulated that the manifestors (vyañjakas) are those which produce a refinement (*saṃskāra*) in the specific sound delimited by the auditory organ. Nor is it the case that we have never observed a fixed relationship between a manifestor and the manifested among things occupying the same location and perceptible by the same sense organ; thus, recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) sublates this undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*). Therefore, he says to him: "In this matter, the scope [of your argument] is annulled by that recognition."
Because it is treated as something produced (*kṛtaka*). And here, by this metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), he indicates the cause of that, namely, the cognition of the difference between sounds.
For indeed, among men, there are very clear cognitions of differences in form regarding the phonemes such as *ga* when they are produced from the mouths of parrots, starlings, and humans.
Thus, regarding those things arising from woman and man, and those arising from the distinction between woman and man,

it should not be said that this [nature] is merely adventitious (*aupādhikī*) and not by way of its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*). For if it were adventitious, it would have to be based on experience, as in the case of saying "the young woman is red with saffron."

Or, regarding the domain of arising—as in the case of a reflection in the edge of a sword, in water, or in a luminous surface that is long and dark—the appearance of a face is not yet an object of direct experience;
rather, it occurs for one who knows the limiting conditions (*upādhi*), just as one who knows saffron perceives [the color] as "saffron-red.

Furthermore, even for one who does not know the differences between the parrot and other birds, when a parrot or such is obscured by a screen or curtain, there arises a cognition of a difference in sound, from which one infers: "This is a most beautiful verse uttered by a parrot."
Nor is it possible to establish that [the difference] is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*).
For there is no evidence whatsoever that the difference inherent in the very nature of sound is adventitious, as is the case with a face reflected in a jewel, a mirror, or a sword.
Indeed, it is impossible for reflections of contradictory dimensions to arise within mirrors and the like, which possess contradictory dimensions.
However, in the case of sounds produced from conjunction and disjunction, it is logical that there should be a difference in their form due to the difference in those [causes].
This might be argued:

"Qualities such as intensity and dullness differ, but the sound which is their substratum does not; for one thing cannot be differentiated by the differentiation of another, as that would lead to over-extension."

For a substance is not divided when there is a difference among its qualities—such as color, taste, and so forth—whether they occur simultaneously or successively, nor among its conjunctions and other such properties.
If it is asked: "How can there be a connection with contradictory properties, such as intensity and dullness, occurring non-simultaneously in one and the same sound?

[The answer is: For that very reason, let it be adventitious (*aupādhika*), just as the face, though undivided, appears long, circular, and so on, non-simultaneously in a sword-blade, a mirror, and other surfaces.

To this it is replied: we do not assert a difference in the substratum (*dharmin*) merely on the basis of a difference in attributes (*dharma*); rather, let it be examined whether there is only the manifestation of a difference in attributes, or whether a difference in the substratum itself is also manifested. For even while the manifestation "cow, cow" persists, there is a manifestation among cows that is characterized by differences in their attributes—such as those that are horned, tawny, or pigeon-colored—which apprehends a difference in the substratum. And there is also a manifestation that apprehends only a difference in attributes while perceiving the substratum as non-different, such as in the case of a *śāla-pranthu* (a type of tree).

[He is] one with a broad and expansive chest, long arms, dark as the petal of a blue lotus, lion-like face, a voice deep and sweet like the sound of a fresh rain-cloud, and eyes like those of a cakora bird—a youth of the Kṣatriya caste.

Now, when this parrot, this maina, and humans simultaneously utter the syllable *ga*, there arises a common perception (*prathā*) that penetrates the *ga* sounds—whether they be sharp, dull, nasalized, or otherwise.
Does this single *ga* sound, like the single youth of the Kṣatriya caste, serve as the basis for these multiple attributes? Is it one and the same *ga* sound?

Or what does "various dharmas" mean? Just as one says, "this cow is white" and "this cow is brown," so too you yourselves should understand that "this *ga*-sound is intense," "this *ga*-sound is weak," and "this [sound] is nasalized. Thus, just as the nature of being a cow (*gotva*) persists through various individual cows such as the brown one, so too the universal nature of being a *ga*-sound (*gatva*), while being the object of recognition across the differences of words such as "intense" and "weak," will account for both the persistence of recognition and the manifestation of difference.

Moreover, we infer the mutual difference between the phonemes *ga* on the basis of their association with contradictory properties characterized by simultaneity, intensity, dullness, and so forth—just as one infers the difference between the sun and a firefly.

Nor is it correct to argue that this association with contradictory properties does not reside in the phoneme *ga* itself, but is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*), and that while the adventitious conditions (*upādhi*) differ, the phoneme *ga* does not; for [the properties] do indeed belong to the phoneme.
Because it is impossible to assume that the perceived [quality] inherent in the *ga*-sound is adventitious (*aupādhika*) when there is no subverting evidence,
and because the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is satisfactorily explained as having the generality (*sāmānya*) of *ga*-ness as its object;

furthermore, under the view that it is adventitious, one must maintain that either a property of the contact with the palate and so forth, or a property of the sound impelled by the impact thereof— such as intensity or nasality— is superimposed upon the word-sound (*śabda*).
Furthermore, superimposition is not possible for those who do not know the object of superimposition.
Nor can the property of sounds—or of the conjunctions and disjunctions of the palate and other organs—be perceived by the auditory organ, just like the properties of other things.
Nor are these [sounds or their causes] presented at that time by another means of valid cognition, or remembered, such that they could be superimposed.
Nor does such a diversity of capacity arise in the auditory organ by virtue of the differences in sounds or their refinements,
such that an error would occur even when the superimposed object is not apprehended.

Furthermore, it is not tenable to claim that— like those whose eyes have been smeared with frog-fat— there is a superimposition of a snake upon bamboo stems at the very first contact of the sense organ, even for those who do not perceive or remember [the snake].
This is because all errors are necessarily preceded by the apprehension of the object of superimposition and the locus of superimposition as grasped by a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Following this principle, the error of snakes in bamboo for those whose eyes have been smeared with frog-fat should also be explained accordingly.
For there exists a considerable similarity between the bamboos and the snake; thus, when these [bamboos] are apprehended in that specific form, they are capable of evoking the memory of the snake.

Even so, in cases where others do not experience the error, the cause is the perception of the bamboo-stick itself as distinct from the form of a snake; and the application of frog-fat ointment is merely the cause for the covering of the stick’s appearance as a snake.

Furthermore, it is not an authoritative position that the error arises immediately from the first contact of the sense-organ with the object, because the distinction between moments is difficult to discern.
Nor is it reasonable to say that the error occurs for one who has never before perceived a snake.

Because the possibility of being seized by a snake occurs either in that very birth or in another birth, whereas properties of sound such as nasality (*anunāsikatva*) and so forth cannot be perceived in this birth or even in another birth; therefore, nasality and the like, which are inherent in the phoneme (*varṇa*), are perceived as properties of the phoneme itself and are not adventitious (*aupādhika*). Thus, due to the simultaneous association with contradictory properties, there is mutual difference among the *ga*-sounds and the others.
This is correct;
it was stated with this underlying intention that [the term is used] "by way of metaphorical designation, as if it were something produced.
The author of the Vārttika explains this as follows:
The statement "intense" or "mild" is used as a figurative designation;
by virtue of being objects of sound, it indicates the presence of contradictory properties.
He states other reasons for the non-eternality of sound with the phrase "because of being treated as something produced" (*kṛtakavad-upacārāt*).

Although the refutation of the [genus] *jāti* is established by the mere mention of "possessing a universal" (*sāmānyavat*), the inclusion of the term "particular" (*viśeṣa*) is for the purpose of dispelling the misconception that "similarity" (*sādharmya*) is the same as a "universal" (*sāmānya*).
For that [property], such as being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*) or existence (*sattva*), exists not only in qualities (*guṇa*) but also in universals (*jāti*) and so forth;
however, it is excluded from universals by the word "particular" (*viśeṣa*).
As for the term "of that which is perceptible," this will become clear later on.
He raises the objection regarding the word "intense" (*tīvra*).

The meaning is that the word "intense," whose activity conforms to the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with the property of intensity, cannot denote the substratum (*dharmin*) which is sound; thus, there is an implication of exactly what was stated [previously].
He refutes [the objection] by stating:
"not that which is in grammatical coreferentiality with the word 'word'.
This point will be established in the discussion on whether the referent of a word (*padārtha*) consists of the individual (*vyakti*), the form (*ākṛti*), or the genus (*jāti*).
He raises the objection regarding the manifestor (*vyañjaka*):
Indeed, it is from its own cause—the manifestor—that the cognition of sound arises as either intense or weak.

Therefore, a sound known by an intense cognition appears as if it were intense, and a sound known by a weak cognition appears as if it were weak; however, in its intrinsic nature, it possesses neither intensity nor weakness by which it would be differentiated. This is the meaning.
It refutes [the objection] by saying "it does not hear itself.
Indeed, one thing is overcome by another of the same class, but not that very thing by itself;
for a cloth illuminated by the light of a midday torch does not, by its own nature, overcome its own self while being illuminated by the sharp light of the sun.
In this way, the letter *ga* itself might be overwhelmed by the letter *ga* manifested by a loud sound.

However, if this *ga* manifested by a faint sound were different from the *ga* manifested by a loud sound, then it would be logical for the light of a torch at midday to be overwhelmed by the light of the sun due to its smallness; thus, this remaining point is as stated in the Bhāṣya.

It is true that one thing is overcome by another; nevertheless, there is no multiplicity in the letter *ga*, but rather in the perceptions (*grahaṇa*) of it, and it is between those perceptions that the relationship of the overcome and the overcomer exists, not in the letter *ga* itself—with this intention, he raises the objection:
"the perception."
He refutes [the objection] by stating,
"There is no apprehension of difference.
A distinction in apprehension, which is determined in dependence upon a distinction in objects, cannot be established without a distinction in the objects themselves.

The meaning is that it is not possible to cognize [the object] as having the relationship of the sublated and the sublator unless its distinction has been determined. "There would always be a difference in apprehension" means that if one accepts the observation of a difference in apprehension, one must necessarily accept a difference in the object.
And thus, everything would indeed be distinct, and nothing at all would be non-distinct.
The meaning is that even distinction itself would not exist, because distinction has non-distinction as its basis.
Furthermore, there would be the impossibility of recognition.

The meaning is that at the very moment when the preceding cognition is to be produced and overcome by the subsequent one, it is destroyed by that [subsequent cognition]; moreover, there can be no overcoming of what is non-existent.
He states that even in the Sāṃkhya system, there is no such thing as "overcoming."
"Overpowering":
having seen that the Sāṃkhya has been defeated, the Mīmāṃsaka, thinking "this [objection] does not apply to us," raises a further doubt.
"In all cases" means he refutes [the opponent's view] by saying "no. The Sāṃkhya objects:
If it is argued that [the sound] exists as a continuous series (*saṃtāna*), he refutes this by stating:
"Because the series of sounds is first perceived as being directed toward a distinction in its causes."

(291/8) There is a distinction of causes, such as the drum, the conch, the palate, and so forth. When a sound arises initially in that portion of the auditory space (*ākāśa*) enclosed by the ear-canal which is directed toward those [causes], its perception leads to the inference: "This sound is produced from a conch or other source situated in the eastern or another direction. What is meant is this: for that [sound] which is produced by a series of sounds originating from a conch or similar object located in a specific direction and place...

There exists a certain specific property (*dharmabheda*) of sound that falls within the range of the auditory organ, by virtue of which its origin from a conch shell or other source situated in a particular direction and location is inferred.
Nor is this specific universal (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*) non-existent merely because it is inexpressible;

for the internal distinctions among the specific universals of sweetness in sugarcane, milk, molasses, and so forth—which are perceptible through direct experience—cannot be denied on the grounds of being inexpressible.
And the experience is the same;
therefore, the cognition of direction and location regarding sound is inferential.
As for that which is called the "series of sounds" (śabda-saṃtāna):

It is called a "continuum" (*saṃtāna*) because it extends; the connection is that the initial sound which is produced is what extends. The construction is: "from which cause [the sound] goes toward [the object]. Regarding the term "initial sound":
it is a sound endowed with the portion directed toward that [object].
Having thus stated his own position,
he states the position of others with the words "But some," the ellipsis being "when the speaker is out of sight."

Although even for those born blind, a discrimination of sound from the front, back, or sides may somehow be possible, nevertheless, there is no distinction between the directions of east and west; therefore it was said, "of those born blind.
(Nyāyasūtra 2.2.16): because of the qualification [implied by] the inference of a continuum (*santāna*).
"And this does not exist in the case of non-existence" means that there is neither a connection with existence nor the state of being delimited by both extremes. // 15-16 //
Because the term "part" (pradeśa) is used to designate the substance that is the cause, there is no deviation [of the definition] even in the case of eternal things.
Now, one might object: "If there is no other [intrinsic] pervasiveness, then how do you maintain that some things are pervasive while others are non-pervasive? To this, he says:
"We, however, [define] pervasion as belonging to the nature of the finger" (296.6).
That which, wherever its substratum is perceived, is itself perceived—provided it is a thing capable of being perceived—is pervasive.
Therefore, even though whiteness pervades the crane, it is not perceived when the crane is being perceived in very dim light, due to the absence of [perceptual] capability (*yogyatā*).
He says that such pervasiveness of conjunction and the other [qualities] cannot be established by their being qualities, because it contradicts non-perception;
"but not so for sound and the rest."
The phrase "capable of being perceived" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
And he states in brief his own intended pervasiveness and non-pervasiveness regarding all things:
"of those existing in their collective state."

For entities such as "existence" (*sattā*) and universals such as "cowness" (*gotva*), which reside in a collection [of substrates], are pervasive (*vyāpaka*), because they are perceived even when only one member of that collection is perceived. However, conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and the like, though residing in a collection, are non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*);
for these are not determined in a single member of the collection, but rather only when [the members] are collected together.

Thus, with respect to color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth—which are pervasive because they share a single substrate—and sound, cognition, and so forth—which are non-pervasive—their perception, non-perception, and non-perception constitute their pervasion and non-pervasion.
In the phrase "consisting of a single aggregate" (*ekasamudāyī*), the inclusion of the word "single" (*eka*) is for the purpose of excluding all other aggregates;

however, it is not intended to mean "one" [individual]. Nor is that term used [in that restrictive sense], because by it, the whole (*avayavin*)—which is perceived whether some of its parts are perceived or not—is stated to be pervasive (*vyāpaka*).

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "due to having material form, etc. (*mūrtimattvādibhyaḥ*), qualities such as possessing tangibility (*sparśavattva*) and non-pervasiveness (*avyāpitva*) are included.
The conjunction with the ether of an effect is the subject of dispute.

If merely the conjunction with the ether of an effect is made the subject of the thesis (*pakṣa*), then there exists [the fallacy] of "that which resides in a substance whose substratum is perishing," because of the conjunction [of the atoms].

If it were thus, there would be the fallacy of contradicting one's own tenet (*apasiddhānta*) because [the subject] would exist as long as the substance exists; therefore, it is stated that it is "the object of dispute.
Because of that very reason, it might be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); therefore, it is stated that it is "that which has a substrate not yet destroyed."
Nevertheless, since the conjunction of a cloth with an indigo substance— which persists as long as the substance itself— would constitute an inconclusive case,

it is therefore stated that [the property] must "subsist in a substance possessing action. Here, what is intended to be grasped is the state of possessing an action that is the cause of a specific mutual disjunction.
In some places it is stated: "Space and the other [elements] possess parts (*vibhāgin*), because they are conjoined with substances possessing action, like atoms.

Here, if it were to be proven that space and the others "possess parts," then they would also possess parts by virtue of being conjoined with the self (*ātman*) and so forth; this would constitute an *apasiddhānta* (a deviation from one's own tenets). Therefore, it is specified as "objects of dispute" (*vipratipattiviṣayāḥ*).
From this, the intended meaning—that they possess parts only through conjunction with corporeal (*mūrta*) things—is obtained.
And regarding the fact that conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is non-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*):

indeed, the conjunction of two *āmalaka* fruits, which possess spatial parts (*pradeśavat*), is pervasive; however, since there is a commonality of substances possessing spatial parts even in the case of space (*ākāśa*) and so forth, it is said that "spatial parts" are used figuratively (*upacāra*) for space and the like.
Now, he states the basis for the figurative application of another general property (*sāmānya*): "And of one... and so on.
Just as a single jar, being in conjunction with multiple corporeal substances, possesses spatial divisions, so too is space; this is the meaning.
"In what sense? is the question;
its meaning is as follows:
... there is no deviation [in the definition] because of the distinction between the actual reality and that which participates in it; ...
because of the qualification by the inference of a continuum; ...
because the term "region" (pradeśa) is used to denote the causal substance...
Since the avoidance of inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva) is achieved by the very sūtras [already cited], it is incorrect to say that no sūtra is heard regarding this matter.
The response is: "Space is without parts" (niṣpradeśam ākāśam).
For it is not because the term "part" (pradeśa) refers to a causal substance that the sūtra does not directly state the partlessness of space and the other [substances].
The meaning is "he says.
This being the case, regarding the question posed by the author of the Bhāṣya, the author of the Vārttika states his own answer: "Because it is understood through the sense."
He states another subject regarding the question and answer with the words "the series of sounds" (*śabda-saṃtāna*).

He explains the meaning of the Bhāṣya as follows: the author of the Bhāṣya says that [the Sūtrakāra] does not establish two alternative positions (*pakṣa*). This is because the Sūtrakāra, while explicitly stating the partlessness (*niṣpradeśatva*) of the self and so forth as well as the series of sounds, would thereby establish a position; however, this was not what he intended to express by that [statement].
And the meaning is that the many branches are the perfections of either five or four aspects of inference. // 17 //
NyS 2.2.18: [Sound does not exist previously] because it is not perceived before its utterance, and because no obstruction or other such cause for non-perception is perceived.
Regarding the statement "there is no absence of the cause for non-perception of that which exists":

the word "of that which exists" (*sataḥ*) was stated so that there would be no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) caused by antecedent non-existence (*prāk-abhāva*) and non-existence after destruction (*pradhvaṃsa-abhāva*). // 18 //
NyS 2.2.19: Because that [object] is not perceived due to its non-perception, the existence of an obstruction is established.
In this regard, there are two sūtras by the proponent of [intrinsic] birth: "Because that [obscuration] is not perceived due to its non-perception, the existence of obscuration is established...
First of all, the perception [of obscuration] is not possible because of the non-perception of obscuration, due to the contradiction with the very nature of non-perception."

Therefore, the non-perception of an obstruction must be stated; and when there is an absence of the non-perception of an obstruction, there is the perception of an obstruction, and by that, the existence of the obstruction [is established], because it is impossible for cognition to be without an object (*nirālambana*). NyS 2.2.20: Just as the existence of non-perception follows from non-perception [itself], there is no impossibility of an obstruction merely because it is not perceived.

If, for fear of the previously mentioned fallacy, it is argued that the non-perception of an obstruction exists even though it is not being perceived, then—since such non-perception is inconclusive—it follows that the absence of an obstruction does not [necessarily] follow from its non-perception.
Thus, in this context, the inconclusiveness is demonstrated by two sūtras.
The introductory commentary (*avatārabhāṣya*) on this is as follows: "And this being so, [it is] the reality."

The author of the Vārttika explains this with the words "If it is so" (*evaṃ ceti*). He demonstrates the purport of the two sūtras in one place by means of a question: "What is the meaning of this statement? (*ko 'sya vākyasyeti*).
Here, the proponent [of the established view] says: "What is to be known here? Because it is to be personally realized within oneself" (*pratyātmavedanīyatvāt*).
The proponent says: "This being so.
If the non-perception of an obstruction is perceived by mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*), then there is neither inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) nor the actual existence of an obstruction.
This refers to the subsequent statement.
The meaning is that it is a statement consisting of a futile rejoinder (*jātyuttara*). "There is no arising for this" means that there is no arising even for the two sūtras.

Now, one might object: "Since the occurrence of the obscuration has already been demonstrated by the preceding sūtra itself, what is the purpose of this sūtra, 'on account of non-apprehension'? To this, he replies:
"By way of a concessive statement."

In the previous sūtra, non-existence was stated on the grounds that there is no perception of non-perception; however, here it is said that even from non-perception, [non-existence] does not follow, because there is no non-perception [of that non-perception]. Thus, by means of this [sūtra], the inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva) of the concession is stated;
the meaning is that this sūtra is not meaningless.
The word "even" (*api*) in the Sūtra illuminates the aspect of admission;
this very point is stated by the author of the Bhāṣya:
"Even if you grant this."
Thus, it is established that by means of these two sūtras, the lack of necessity (anaikāntikatva) has been stated. // 19–20 //
NyS 2.2.21: Because non-apprehension consists in the nature of non-perception, it is not a [valid] reason.
The subsequent sūtra for this is:
"But [the word] 'anu' [is used] in the sense of 'tu'" (Sūtra 21).

It is thought that there is no non-apprehension of the proponent of birth and so forth because of the absence of apprehension; however, in that case, the status of being an object within the scope of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whose domain is affirmation would be contradicted in the case of non-apprehension.
But surely there is also the status of being an object within the scope of a means of valid cognition whose domain is negation;

therefore, for one who negates apprehension by means of a valid cognition—the mental [cognition]—the grasping of non-apprehension does not entail contradiction. This, then, is the meaning of the Sūtra.

Because non-apprehension consists in the non-apprehension of an obscuration, and because it consists in the negation of the apprehension of that obscuration, this non-apprehension of its non-apprehension is not a valid reason for establishing the existence of an obscuration; for it is unestablished, since the non-apprehension [of the obscuration] is itself not apprehended in the domain of negation.
The author of the Commentary explains this as follows:

"That which is perceived" means that whatever is perceived by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whose object is an affirmation exists; and that which is not perceived—namely, whatever is perceived by a means of valid cognition whose object is a negation—does not exist.
Therefore, it is established that "non-existent" is that which consists in non-apprehension and is not accessible through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whose object is a negation.

Furthermore, non-apprehension is the absence of apprehension; as such, because it is a non-entity (*abhāva*), it is not apprehended by a means of valid cognition whose object is a positive affirmation (*vidhi*).
The remainder is easy to understand.
The author of the Vārttika states the ultimate purport of this [sūtra]: "by that which is not of such a kind. This means: by a rejoinder that is not a valid rejoinder (jātyuttara).
Regarding the phrase "of such a nature":

for a sound that has been perceived, provided there is no cause for its non-perception, it is not observed before or after its utterance; thus, nothing else—such as the self (*ātman*) and so forth—is seen to possess the same property of being impermanent (*anitya*).

[Objection: "But surely, let there be no sound prior to or after its utterance; even by this much, why is sound not eternal, given its dissimilarity to other eternal things? For the self, space, and so forth, though eternal, do not share all the same properties [as each other], lest there be no distinction between them. To this, he says:
And it is said:
he states the proof for impermanence,
namely, "it is impermanent."

If it were stated merely that "because it is perceptible," there would be a deviation (vyabhicāra) by means of [universals] such as cowness (gotva); therefore, it was said: "given its inherence in a pervasive substance.
Even so, there would still be a deviation by means of the oneness inherent in the self; therefore, it was said:
"given the non-inherence of that which is non-pervasive."

Nevertheless, when it is stated that [the reason] is "because of being incorporeal" (*amūrtatvāt*) in the sense of "inherence in a self," there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to jars and the like, which possess spatial extension (*pradeśavat*), at the first moment; therefore, it is said "always" (*sarvadā*).
Even so, there is a deviation with respect to actions, qualities, and so forth, for their inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) is also spatial extension; therefore, it is said:
"being a substance" (*dravyasya sataḥ*). //21//
Because it is intangible.
NyS 2.2.23: No, because action is impermanent.
NyS 2.2.24: No, because atoms are eternal.

23 // 24 // Having thus stated the proof for his own position (*svapakṣasādhana*) and having presented the proof for the opposing position (*parapakṣasādhana*) which serves as the basis for the misconception, he refutes it with the words "Now,
[regarding] sound" (*atha śabdasya*).

Since a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) has already been established on both sides by means of action (*karman*) which is intangible (*asparśa*), the adducing of a deviation by means of an eternal atom (*nityenāṇunā*) is intended to refute the notion of equal pervasion (*samavyāptikatva*), just as [the example of] being produced (*kṛtakatva*) and impermanence (*anityatva*) [do not imply equal pervasion].
This is to be seen. // 22–24 //
NyS 2.2.25: [The word "existent" is used] because of its being handed over.
That is not a valid reason, because there is no perception of anything intervening between them.
NyS 2.2.27: There is no prohibition [of inference] because of the act of teaching.
NyS 2.2.28: There is no refutation [of the argument] because it is taught as one of the two alternative positions.
NyS_2,2.29: [It arises] from repeated practice.
NyS 2.2.30: It is not so, because even when there is difference, there is a figurative application of the term "repetition."
In that case, the reason is "because it is being handed over" (*sampradānāt*);
the meaning is "because it is being imparted.

Between the giver and the recipient, there exists the act of teaching; for [the Veda] is being imparted by the teacher to the pupil through instruction, just like the arrow and other weapons being imparted by a preceptor learned in the science of archery (*dhanurveda*) to his pupil. (25–30)
NyS 2.2.31: Because that which is different from another is non-different [from it], there is no state of difference.

If there were another name in the world distinct from that [name], then the [opponent's] argument might be shown to be inconclusive by means of the statement, "because of the metaphorical application of habituation despite the difference"; however, since that very thing does not exist, he objects through a quibble regarding words (*vākchala*). This is the sūtra: *anyathā-vādaḥ* (Sūtra 31).
In the absence of that [distinction], there is no non-difference between the two, because they are established in mutual dependence upon one another.
The aphorism providing the solution to that is:
"Because of that" (Sūtra 32).

The meaning is that between those two—identity and difference—the identity [of the effect] is established in dependence upon the other [difference]. Nor can it be non-different from the "other" simply because it is non-different from its own nature; for blue, while non-different from itself, is not thereby non-different from yellow.
For it is an ultimate truth that yellow is indeed one thing and blue another;
this cognition is observed to cease when occurring in a different person.
Indeed, when such a cognition arises for one person, it necessarily does not arise for another person.
Therefore, the non-exclusion of doubt is indeed unestablished.
"This is so" means:

it is true that the perception of a specific feature is the cause for the cessation of that doubt; however, in its absence, it is not possible to prevent the perception of a non-specific feature from being a cause of doubt. This is the meaning.
Furthermore, regarding this [notion] "the word 'cow'":
the cognition having a single form, namely "the word 'cow', the word 'cow'," cannot occur without [an underlying] unity.
Now, [the author] asks: why is it not erroneous? To this he says: "And not of the word 'cow' (*gośabda*).

For if it were erroneous, then the cognition of the object from that word "cow" would be erroneous, just as the inference of fire from a mosquito-wick that has the appearance of smoke superimposed upon it.

Therefore, the meaning is that the non-erroneous cognition of the word "cow" as a single entity indicates its stability. [The author] refutes this with the words "this too," etc. However, it is logical that the non-exclusion of that cognition occurs due to the similarity of its causes; for the cause of the cognition of the word "cow" is its objective support, which is the word "cow. Its commonality consists in *gatva*, *autva*, and *gośabdatva*—that is to say, the universal of being the letter *ga*, the letter *au*, and the word "cow."
Therefore, the exclusion of its cognition is logical, in the form "the word 'cow' is the word 'cow'.

To the question "How so? [it is replied]: the cognition of the cognition of a cow is not excluded from the cognition of a cow; the singular number in the phrase "in the cognition of a cow" (gobuddhau) is intended to refer to the universal (jāti).

For just as the cognition of "cow," although distinct in each individual instance, appears as a continuous manifestation— namely, "the cognition of cow, the cognition of cow"— and thus, being conditioned by the universal *gotva* (cowness), takes as its object the various individual cognitions of "cow" that constitute its own causes; in the same way, the cognition "the word 'cow,' the word 'cow'" is also conditioned by the universal *gośabdatva* (word-cowness) and takes as its objects the various individual utterances of the word "cow," rather than a single, eternal individual entity of the word "cow" that pervades multiple places and times.
And in the phrase "of this cognition of the word 'cow'," the singular number is used for the class (*jāti*).
The persistence of the cognition "the word 'cow', the word 'cow'" is based on a universal (*sāmānya*), because, while being persistent, it is related to the cognition of the word 'cow',
just like the persistent cognition "the cognition of the word 'cow', the cognition of the word 'cow'."

Regarding that person who, though the distinct is non-distinct [to him], desists while not perceiving any distinction at all— it is you yourselves who must be asked whether there exists a distinction for that object or not.
He states the fault in both cases, beginning with "if it exists."
"Consisting of two natures" means being both distinct and non-distinct.
"By virtue of being the object of all persons without exception" [is the meaning].
The meaning is "by way of being the support. // 32 //
NyS 2.2.33: Because no cause of destruction is perceived.
NyS 2.2.34: Since no cause for non-hearing is perceived, there would be the consequence of constant hearing.
"The disjunction of the causal substance. Thus, by means of disjunction, the destruction of the non-inherent cause—the conjunction—is characterized, because it is the effect thereof. // 33-34 //
And since non-apprehension is absent when something is being apprehended, it is not a valid reason.
"Non-indication" means "non-reason.
Regarding the phrase "both":
when one attempts to prove that a camel is a horse because it has horns, then for that [camel], there is neither a horn nor a connection with it.
Just as "hornedness" is unestablished in a camel, so too, when a cause of destruction is not perceived through inference, that non-perception is unestablished.
This is because there is no connection with a horse's horn;
since no connection whatsoever between "horseness" and "hornedness" is established in horses, this inference is fallacious due to contradiction—this is the meaning.

Therefore, the meaning is that just as inference from a contradictory reason is non-existent, so too is it from an unestablished one. [The opponent] objects: "If it is argued that it is like the case of 'being an object' (karmatva)," [the author] refutes this.
And that is not so, because the substratum is impermanent;
the meaning is that the action has the substratum as its basis, and because that [substratum] is impermanent.
We say that the non-hearing of an eternal sound is untenable, because no cause for such non-hearing is possible.

He analyzes the summary statement, "Because its substratum is impermanent," with the words, "Furthermore, as for the state of being an action. The commentary states: "However, conjunction with a resistant substance is the cause of the cessation of the final sound."
Its meaning is as follows:
an obstructing substance such as a wall and its conjunction with space [are the causes].
What is meant is this: space conjoined with a very dense substance does not attain the status of being the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of sound.

Consequently, although sound exists as a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), it does not produce another sound; rather, its own cause perishes because of that [subsequent] cause—this is how it should be understood.
In other cases as well, one should infer that the cause for the destruction of sound is of this very same nature.
Thus [it is said].
Furthermore, he states that sound is impermanent:
"when the bell is being struck with a striker," and so forth.

If the eternal sound were manifested by a manifestor residing in the bell— whether that manifestor functions elsewhere, remains stationary, or operates in a continuous stream— then there would be no difference in the auditory perceptions such as loud, louder, loudest, soft, softer, or softest. Furthermore,
it has been established above that for an eternal sound, there can be neither an inherent difference nor one caused by external conditions (upādhi).

If, however, there were as many eternal sounds as there are degrees of intensity (tāratama) and so forth, then all of them would be perceived simultaneously, because there is no distinction [among them] and their single manifestor is constant.

Even if they exist in a continuous stream (santāna), then all those falling within that stream would be capable [of being manifested], and thus all would be manifested by the very first [manifestation]; for it has been established below that a restriction of manifestors is not logical for things occupying the same location and perceivable by the same sense organ.

However, if sound is the effect, it is logical that because the cause—residing in the bell and proceeding as a continuum—differs through distinctions such as intensity and so forth, there is a difference in the effects;
this is the intended meaning.
[Otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving multiple sounds simultaneously.
The meaning is that there would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving many sounds of varying degrees of intensity.
Furthermore, how could the cause of manifestation residing in the bell be moving elsewhere?
The meaning is that it exists in the ear.
Anticipating a second alternative, he refutes it with the words:
"Or else, [if it were] located elsewhere."

The common worldly cognition is indeed that "this sound belongs to this bell. Now, just as this occurs when the manifester of the sound resides in one particular bell, it would likewise occur in other bells situated near it, since there is no distinction [between them].
Therefore, a restrictive cause must be stated for the sound to reside in only one specific bell.
Thus,
"there being no difference in the words of the Śrutis" means there being no difference in the cognitions of those words.
The doubt is raised that "nāda" refers to a property of air, [and thus] it is a cognition based on delusion (*vyāmoha-pratyaya*).

For just as there is a cognition that a crystal is red when its whiteness is obscured by the application of lac juice upon a crystal gem that is in reality clear and white, so too the properties such as high pitch (*tāratva*) belonging to the manifesting articulation (*abhivyañjaka-vṛtti*) are perceived in the sound (*śabda*) through error; this is the meaning.
He refutes [the objection] with the words, "No, because there is no specific reason [for its falsity].

The meaning is that there is no specific reason for the cognition "this is a sound" to be sublated by a contradicting cognition (bādhaka-pratyaya), such that this cognition would be a false one; for it arises from a valid cause of cognition.
Nor can even an error occur without a seed; however, there is indeed a seed for errors such as [the perception of] length and so forth in the case of sound. Thus he says:
"And if this... Indeed, those things which are long, such as bamboo and the like—whether it be their parts or their accumulation—is an accumulation of homogeneous [parts].
In this case as well, within the continuum of sound produced by unceasing effort and with its causes manifested, there exists an accumulation of homogeneous [moments].
Due to that similarity, it is merely an illusion of length; thus, within the very continuum of sound, it is said to be "high" or "loud.

In that instance too, there is an accumulation of homogeneous [moments] and there is a state of being more distinct; since the loud sound is more distinct and this one is likewise so, it is called "loud."

If it is argued that the objection is equal [to our own], the meaning is as follows: just as in the theory of impermanence, the sound residing within a bell, proceeding in a continuous series (*saṃtāna*), does not produce loud and soft tones simultaneously but rather produces them only in succession, so too one might manifest even eternal sounds in succession. To this, he offers a refutation:
This is not so, because the cause [of that distinction] never exists.

First of all, those who maintain the eternity of sound do not accept a difference in sound based on the distinction between properties such as high pitch (*tāra*) and so forth; and thus, when a single sound—residing in a bell, remaining constant, and manifested through a continuous series—is perceived, an occasional variation in its audition cannot be logically accounted for.
