The meaning is that there is a disparity [between sound and a jar]: since sound is impermanent, when one [instance of] sound is being produced and another [is already present], the distinction between them is possible because they function as a continuum (*saṃtāna*), because they are effects, and because they are occasional;
this is the cause, which means it is the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "depending on the contact with the hand":

from the conjunction of a substance possessing touch and velocity with the bell, there arises motion in the bell; and from the conjunction of that [motion] with the space within the bell, there arises a similar sound—this constitutes one moment of time. That motion, depending on the striking by the hand, produces at the same time as the disjunction a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) called velocity.

When that bell moves, it grasps internal air; the atoms of air conjoined with the bell and its parts constitute the internal air. This grasping occurs because the bell, depending on its own momentum, produces motion in the air through conjunction with it. Then, from that action of the air, the conjunction of the bell and the air—depending on the velocity residing in the air—initiates an action in the bell.
Regarding this, it is said: that [conjunction] is struck by the wind and performs action once again.
Thus, it should be understood that the conjunction of the wind and the bell, depending upon the momentum of the bell, along with the conjunction of the bell and space, initiates sound.
Furthermore, it should be understood that from action arises a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), and from the latent impression, in turn, arise both action and sound.
The rest is easy to understand. // 35 //
NyS 2.2.36: Because of the contact with the hand as a cause, there is no non-perception [of sound] when the sound has ceased.
He teaches that it is "located in the bell.
Indeed, there is no destruction of the effect upon the destruction of the cause.
The meaning is: "Let it not be that the cessation of the pot and so forth occurs even upon the cessation of the potter and so forth.
He refutes this by saying, "We do not say [that]."

Although an effect ceases even when its efficient cause ceases—just as duality and so forth cease due to the destruction of enumerative cognition (apekṣābuddhi)—nevertheless, it should be understood that the resolution [of the objection] is made precisely by accepting that the effect does not cease even when the efficient cause ceases. // 36 //
And because no cause of destruction is perceived, it follows that if [sound] were to persist, it would be eternal.
By means of the "lion's glance" (*siṃhāvalokita*) method, he refutes the previously stated reason:
"vināśeti" (regarding destruction).

Since no cause for the destruction of sound is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), if sound were to persist, it would follow as a logical consequence that sound is eternal because it would continue to be perceived.

For even in that case, a cause of destruction is not perceived by direct perception; thus, by this [argument], the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) of the reason "because no cause of destruction is perceived" has been pointed out. // 37 //
NyS 2.2.38: There is no refutation [of the soul] because it is intangible.
Now the Sāṃkhya objects:
"Of that which has the same substratum as the trembling. A sound that follows after [another] is called an *anunāda*.

Regarding the phrase "for if there were a lack of co-referentiality" (*vaiyadhikaraṇye hi*): if the refinement (*saṃskāra*) were not co-referential with the substance (*dravya*), it would follow that only the refinement itself would be destroyed, but not the sound which is in a different substratum (*vyadhikaraṇa*).

However, if one were to accept the destruction of that which is in a different substratum, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, sound must be accepted as having the same substratum as the refinement in the series of vibrations (*kampasaṃtāna*).

By this, the fact that sound has space as its substratum is refuted; the author of the Vārttika explains this as follows: "It is untenable because it involves a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (vyadhikaraṇatva)."
The subsequent sūtra for this is: "That which is not clearly defined" (Sūtra 38).
It has been established previously that the sense-faculties function by reaching their objects. Sound, however, which resides in its substratum such as a bell, does not reach the ear.
For it would only reach [the ear] if either the bell were to come to the ear-canal (*karṇaśaṣkulī*), or the ear-canal were to go to the bell.
Neither of these two [properties] exists [in the self].
Furthermore, it has been stated that the sense organ derived from ego-consciousness (*ahaṅkārika*) is not all-pervading.

Therefore, it is logical that space—which is the substratum of sound, intangible, and all-pervading—is its support; and that sound, proceeding by way of a continuous series (*saṃtānavṛtti*), reaches the ear. In this manner alone is its being heard possible, and not otherwise.
The author of the Vārttika analyzes this [point] with the words "asparśa" and "yena kenacid."
The meaning is "by a weaker or even the weakest causal term.
The reality is that there is a manifold *saṃskāra* because of the difference in words;

for if one were to postulate a distinction of properties (*dharma*) for a single *saṃskāra*, there would be the consequence of an excessive conceptual burden (*kalpanā-gaurava*), namely: "the *saṃskāra* is one property, and yet there are distinctions of properties."
Therefore, let there be a distinction in the *saṃskāras* (potencies) in place of a distinction in properties (*dharma*); what is the use here of a single property-bearer?

Furthermore, one should not postulate distinctions in properties within the various *saṃskāras*, because since the distinction in effects is established solely from the cause that is the distinction in *saṃskāras*, the postulation of distinctions in properties residing therein is redundant—this is the sense.

Moreover, for that Vaiśeṣika who maintains that there is a single *saṃskāra*, the falling of the arrow would never occur; for the destruction or non-destruction of the *saṃskāra* depends upon its contact with a material substance (*mūrtadravya*).

If it were destructible by the very first conjunction with a corporeal substance, then because of its destruction at that moment, the arrow would fall before it had even traveled the distance it was meant to go. In the second alternative, however, since there would be no cause for the destruction of the momentum (saṃskāra) even though it is produced, it would never fall at all. Furthermore, the formal argument (prayoga) is as follows: the velocity of an arrow and the like is momentary, because it is velocity, just like the velocity residing in a jar and the like.
And because another case-ending occurs within a compound.
[The rule] "vibhāṣā" (sūtra 39).

For the Sāṃkhyas, sound is a collection of form, taste, smell, touch, and sound, which constitutes substances such as the lute, the flute, and the conch. Their view is that sound is manifested only when situated within that collection in its combined state. However, in that collection accepted by the Sāṃkhyas, sound would not be manifested because it arises with distinct grammatical inflections (*vibhakti*). If sound were manifested in the collection, there would also be distinct inflections according to the differences of *ṣaḍja*, *dhaivata*, *gāndhāra*, and so forth.
Furthermore, a subsequent division of that which belongs to the same genus—such as the forms of high (*tāra*) or low (*mandra*) pitch—is not possible;
for no difference between various types of odor and so forth belonging to a single substance, such as a lute, is observed moment by moment.
Therefore, since a different state of division arises, it is not the case that sound is manifested in a composite whole; rather, it is correct to say that the quality of space is produced.
By the very commentary on the Sūtra, the Bhāṣya and the Vārttika have been explained. // 39 //
NyS 2.2.40: There is doubt because of the teaching of both modification and substitution.

Thus, when the Sāṃkhya position—that sound, as inherent in form and other qualities, is manifested—has been refuted, that same Sāṃkhya might counter-argue that, because of the scriptural teaching on the relationship between material cause and modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*) among phonemes, similar to clay or gold, phonemes are "transformative-eternal" (*pariṇāminitya*). To this, [the author] begins an investigation with the words: "And this sound is of two kinds."

Furthermore, since the teaching of modification does not apply to sound (*dhvani*) as such, it cannot establish its transformational eternity; it could only establish it if it applied to the phoneme (*varṇa*) itself, provided there were no doubt.
However, even in that case, there is doubt.
For some explain the teaching of modification in rules such as *iko yaṇ aci*.
Others, however, hold that there is doubt regarding such instruction because of the conflicting interpretations of commentators;
the meaning is that it is not possible to determine the truth without investigation.
In that investigation, one determines that the "instruction of the instruction" (*ādeśopadeśa*) is the reality (*tattva*). Regarding the term "instruction of the instruction":

indeed, when the constituent parts belonging to the class of gold, by abandoning one particular arrangement and attaining another arrangement, become what is called a *rucaka* (necklace) or a *vardhamāna* (earring).
Or rather, they transform in this way;

for indeed, in all those [sounds], there is a persistence of parts belonging to the same class as gold, but we do not perceive any persistence of the letter *i*, or of the part that originates it, in the letter *ya*.
Therefore, because there is no modification [of the original], we determine that this is a substitute (ādeśa). Furthermore, he demonstrates another logical argument for its being a non-modification:
"and of two things having different causes."

If the letter *ya* were a modification of the letter *i*, then those employing the letter *ya* would first employ the letter *i*, which has an open articulatory organ (*vivṛtakaraṇa*), as its cause. However, those intending to employ the letter *ya* employ an articulatory organ that is slightly touched (*īṣatspṛṣṭakaraṇa*) independently of that [letter *i*]. Therefore, we conclude that the letter *ya* is not a modification of the letter *i*. He states another argument:

And regarding the phrase "in the case of non-modification," he states that there is no distinction between the two types of causes— the efficient cause (*kāraka*) and the indicative cause (*jñāpaka*).
The term "in both cases" refers to this.
He states another argument for rebirth with the words "being applied" (*prayujyamāna*).
For just as milk is seen to become curd depending on the ripening of time, so too the vowel *i* does not become the consonant *y*; such is the meaning.

If there is no modification (*vikāra*), how then is the grammatical derivation (*anvākhyāna*) of the word [justified] by the rule *ikaḥ yaṇ aci*? To this he says: "And even in the absence of modification. The meaning is that the sūtra teaches the employment of *yaṇ* in *saṃhitā* when there is the occasion for the employment of *ik*; it does not, however, mean that *yaṇ* is a modification of *ik*.

Now, one might object: "Let there be no modification (*vikāra*); let it be a transformation (*pariṇāma*) or rather a different entity (*arthāntara*), and thus the phonemes will be eternal. To this, he says: "And this is only so much.
Whether it be a transformation or, at first sight, the relation of cause and effect—that is the ultimate meaning.
Neither milk nor its constituent parts ever transform into the form of curd; for the parts do not possess the nature of the whole.
Therefore, the relationship of cause and effect alone is real;
and that [relationship] does not exist between the phonemes, because the *yaṇ*-substitution arises independently of the *ik*.
Therefore, in the context of the application [of phonemes], the statement "the *yaṇ* is employed in *saṃhitā*" is for the purpose of providing a grammatical explanation (*anvākhyāna*).
For this reason as well, he states that this is an instruction regarding a substitute (*ādeśopadeśa*).
Regarding the phrase "to a collection of phonemes" (*varṇasamudāya*):

since a single phoneme is a real entity (*vāstavatva*), a modification (*vikāra*) is sometimes possible for it; however, for that collection which is a mere aggregate (*samāhāramātra*), a modification is not possible.
Therefore, even against one's will, the teaching of a substitute (*ādeśa*) must be stated in that case.
The meaning is that, since the choice has been determined, let it be in even a single letter. // 40 //
NyS 2.2.41: Because there is an increase in the transformation when there is an increase in the primal matter.

For this reason as well, there is no relationship of material cause and modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*). Regarding the phrase "in the increase of the material cause": it is observed that a large mass is produced from large lumps of cotton, whereas one produced from small [lumps] is small; likewise here too, the *y* which is a modification of the long *ī* ought to be a modification of the short *i*.
And there is no distinction; therefore, the meaning is that there is no relationship of original nature and modification. // 41 //
The observation of decrease, equality, and increase among modifications is not a valid reason [for their non-eternality].
The sūtra stating this objection is: "But [the argument is] deficient" (sūtra 41).

For instance, a great *nyagrodha* tree is produced from a tiny *nyagrodha* seed; or, a coconut tree produced from an extremely large coconut seed is small; or, [a tree] produced from coconut seeds that are equal and mutually dependent is equal [in size].
This is the sūtra concerning its accumulation (*pratyācaya*).
Regarding the phrase "of both kinds of reason":

if the proof were [based on] the perception of the deficient, the equal, or the superior, then because both kinds of reason would be absent and a mere example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is not probative, [the argument fails].
And because a counter-example is possible, this constitutes a refutation. // 42 //
Not [is there a single cause], because of the variation in transformations among those whose primordial material causes are not identical.

If the manifestation of the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) fallacy regarding conformity to the nature (*prakṛtyanuvidhāna*) is made by means of the phrase "because of the perception of the lesser, equal, or greater," then the refutation in the context of the critique is: "because there is no variation in the transformation of those whose natures are not identical. The inconclusive fallacy is called "irrelevance" (*asambandhatva*) because, even when there is a state of being lesser, equal, or greater, the conformity to the nature of the transformations does not deviate.
For in this way, suffixes are conceptualized according to their respective stems and conform to the distinctions among those stems;
indeed, a coconut tree never arises from a banyan seed,
yet a banyan tree does arise from a banyan seed.

Thus it is said: what is meant is this—we state that the various modifications conform to the variations of their primary material cause (*prakṛti*), but we do not say that the increase or decrease of the former results from the increase or decrease of the latter, such that one might raise the objection of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*). Therefore, the meaning is that the raising of the charge of inconclusiveness is irrelevant.
"But the letter *y* does not follow the variation of the *i*-vowel," so says the Bhāṣya. Its meaning is: "it does not follow the distinction of the *i*-vowel.
Therefore, the case of a modification of substance (*dravyavikāra*) in states of deficiency, equality, or excess is not an illustration [of this rule]. // 43 //
In the case of a modification of substance, there is an alternative regarding the modification of color, as in the case of inequality.
The aphorism raising this objection is: "It is a modification of substance" (308/1).

Modifications do not necessarily conform to the diversity of their material causes; for even when material causes are identical in being substances, there is a disparity among the modifications. Thus, given the disparity between long and short [causes], there will likewise be a disparity among the modifications.
The meaning is that the inequality of the modifications arises precisely from the equilibrium of the primordial nature (prakṛti). // 44 //
NyS_2.2.45: No, because the properties of modification are not possible [in the case of the soul].
In this regard, there is the aphorism of refutation:
"It is not of the nature of a modification.

Although the material cause (*prakṛti*) possesses substantiality and non-difference, nevertheless, when there is a difference in modifications, it is precisely the difference in the material cause that is required, and not the non-difference of the material cause.

Since it is established that its utility lies in that substance-ness (*dravyatva*) which is the non-different form of those modifications, the resolution [to the objection] is stated as follows: the mention of "in the substance" (*dravye*) is the resolution to the objection [contained in the sūtra stating] "the modification [occurs] in the substance. // 45 //
Because those things that have undergone transformation do not return to their original state.
For this reason as well, he says that there are no modifications of phonemes (*varṇavikāra*). Regarding the word "modification" (*vikāra*):
the meaning is that curd, which is a modification of milk, is never seen to become milk again.
The phrase "because it is not an inference" indicates the absence of any valid means of cognition (pramāṇa). // 46 //
Furthermore, the recurrence [of gold and other substances] is not a valid reason [for their being eternal].
The aphorism states that there is an objection to this regarding gold and other such things;
on the side of the proof, the refutation is that it is fallacious due to deviation. // 47 //
Not so, because those modifications do not deviate from the nature of gold.
He states the fault in the position that [the example] is defective:
"And the application of the example of gold.
For it is as follows:

Those very parts consisting of gold which had attained the state of a *rucaka* (necklace) attain the state of a *vardhamāna* (earring) by abandoning their previous configuration, and then again attain the state of a *rucaka*, because those constituent parts are recognized therein.

However, in this case, no other substratum (*dharmin*) is observed that, while following the letter *i*, would first abandon the state of being *i* and then attain the state of being *ya*; nor is there any substratum that follows both *i* and *ya*. Furthermore, although "phonemic-ness" (*varṇatva*) is common to them, it is not the substratum, but rather a property (*dharma*) itself.
Furthermore, the vowel *ī* cannot be a property (*dharma*) of the consonant *y*, because a property and its possessor (*dharmin*) must exist simultaneously; such is the meaning. // 48 //
Because if it were eternal, there would be no modification; and if it were non-eternal, there would be no persistence.
Now, one might ask: in the usage *dadhy atra*, when does the letter *y* arise and cease?
And likewise, in the usage *dadhi atra*, when does the letter *y* arise and cease? To this, he says: "This [occurs] by separating and then joining."

*Avagraha* means non-composition (*asaṃhitā*). Having pronounced "dadhi atra," it is then pronounced as "dadhyatra"; or, having joined them as "dadhyatra," it is then separated as "dadhi atra"—this is the meaning. // 49 //
NyS_2.2.50: There is no refutation of the modifications of phonemes, because eternal [entities] are beyond the senses and because there is a conceptualization of their properties.
The proponent of the theory of birth (jātivādin) objects:
"First, regarding the position that [universals] are eternal...

Just as some things are beyond the senses despite being eternal—such as atoms, space, and so forth—and some are perceptible by the senses—such as cowness and so forth—even so, despite their eternity, atoms, space, and the like...
The phonemes, which do not themselves exist as either primordial nature (*prakṛti*) or modification (*vikāra*), will nevertheless undergo the state of being both nature and modification;
this means they are eternal.
He states that this is a fallacy consisting of a conceptual construction (*vikalpasama*),
saying "because of contradiction" (*virodhāt*).

Indeed, there is no contradiction whatsoever regarding permanence (*nityatva*) on account of being perceptible by the senses (*aindriyakatva*) or not being perceptible by the senses (*anaindriyakatva*).

However, it exists by way of the relationship between primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and its transformation (*vikāra*); for it is not possible for something to be both an effect and eternal—this is the meaning. // 50 //
And if there were non-duration [of the phonemes], then the perception of their modification would occur just like the perception of the phonemes themselves.
Regarding the position that [sound] is impermanent, the proponent of the theory of production (jātivādin) says:
"And even in the case of non-duration.
The meaning is this: just as phonemes, despite their non-duration, produce a cognition of their own object by coming into contact with the sense organ, so too will they effect a modification.
"This is the fallacy known as *sādharmyasama*," he says,
"because of the lack of connection.
For even though phonemes are momentary, it is logical that they serve as the cause for the cognition of their own objects by persisting for a few moments while being held in mind.

When [a phoneme] remains for a long time and is then joined, or when, having been joined, it remains and is then separated—at that time, because impermanent phonemes do not persist for such a duration, they cannot serve as the cause for perception; thus, the claim that phonemes undergo modification is not equivalent [to the case of other phenomena].
Therefore, the meaning is that since there is no connection, the perception of phonemes is incapable of demonstrating a modification of the phonemes.

Lest it be argued that the perception of the letter may not be directly connected with the modification of the letter due to its opposition to *au*, but rather that—by the exclusion of that [perception] through negative remainder—it will establish the modification, the author says:
"And there is no perception of the letter. (51)

NyS 2.2.52: There is no refutation [of the self's existence], because if it possessed the nature of transformation, it would lack permanence, and because its non-transformation at another time is logically consistent.
Thus, having refuted the futile rejoinder (*jātyuttara*) as soon as it arose, the author of the Bhāṣya recites the Sūtra on this very point:
"Because [the vowel *i*] has the nature of modification.
The Vārttika states: "And because the transformation of the perceived vowel *i* into *y* is untenable."

The meaning is that when, having held [the breath] for a long time, having remained [in that state], and having joined [the breaths], there is no perception of the letter *i* at that time or in that place. // 52 //
Because there is no fixed rule regarding the original forms of the modifications of phonemes.
Furthermore, the transformation of phonemes is untenable because there is no fixed rule regarding their original nature (*prakṛti*). For instance,
a product of the class "curd" arises from something of the class "milk," but conversely, products of the class "milk" are never observed to arise from something of the class "curd."

But here, just as a modification belonging to the class of *yakāra* is seen arising from a cause belonging to the class of *ikāra*, as in *dadhyatra*, so too a modification belonging to the class of *ikāra* is seen arising from a cause belonging to the class of *yakāra*, as in *vyathiḥ sati prasāraṇe*. Therefore, because there is no fixed rule, there is no relationship of original cause (*prakṛti*) and modification (*vikāra*).
This is the meaning. // 53 //
NyS 2.2.54: Since there is a restriction regarding what is unrestricted, there is no such thing as unrestriction.
Here, the quibbler (chhalavādī) objects:
"Because there is restriction where there was no restriction. (54)
NyS 2.2.55: There is no refutation [of our position] because of the contradiction between restriction and non-restriction, and because there is restriction even in the case of non-restriction.
This brings about the status of a quibble (*vākchala*) for this [position], because of the contradiction between restriction and non-restriction;
the meaning is that the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of restriction and non-restriction is contradictory, but not their relationship as container and contained (*ādhārādheyabhāva*). // 55 //

But the modification of phonemes is established through the occurrence of transformation [consisting of] the acquisition of another quality, suppression, decrease, increase, diminution, and conjunction.

Thus, having refuted the relationship of material cause and modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*), he establishes the manifestation of words as modifications under the view of substitution (*ādeśa-pakṣa*).
And this is not a logical possibility of phonetic modification (*varṇa-vikāra*); rather, modification consists in the employment of one [element] in place of another when the latter is not employed.
Thus is the general definition. He states its particulars:
"it is divided."

Regarding the term "upamardde": it is like [the rule] *aster bhūḥ*. In the expression *leśaḥ staḥ*, after the elision of the letter *a* from the root *as*, there is the establishment of the mere letter *s* alone as a fragment (*leśa*), that is, as a single part.
The addition (*āgama*) consists in the augmentation of either the base (*prakṛti*) or the suffix (*pratyaya*).

Here too, since there is no usage of the [element] alone but rather the usage of it as qualified [by the addition], the general definition of modification (*vikāra*) is to be characterized by this much alone.
By this, the Vārttika has also been explained. // 56 //
Those [phonemes], ending in an inflectional suffix, constitute a word.
Thus, having established the impermanence of phonemes through the sequence described above, he defines the word (*pada*) which is useful for the authority of speech (*śabda-prāmāṇya*):
"te vi—idam" (Sūtra 57).
Thus, it is said that some perceive this: phonemes do not convey meanings;
for they would either produce the cognition of recurrence individually—like pegs supporting a shelf—or they would do so when combined—like stones supporting the weight of a cooking pot.
In this regard, the first alternative is not tenable,
because the cognition of the meaning does not arise from each individual phoneme,
and because the utterance of subsequent phonemes would be purposeless.

Nor can they be combined, because when uttered by a single speaker, a combination is impossible due to the necessity of sequential order; and even in the case of utterance by multiple speakers, despite simultaneity, there is no production of the cognition of meaning.

Nor is it correct to say that the cognition of the final phoneme, accompanied by the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of the preceding phonemes in their sequence, is the cause of the cognition of meaning.

For it is observed that a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), which is synonymous with cultivation (*bhāvanā*), possesses no capacity other than generating a memory of the object experienced at the time of its own production.
Indeed, an impression produced by the experience of a cow does not produce a memory of a horse.

Furthermore, this hearing of the final phoneme must either produce the cognition of the meaning by depending on the memory of the conventional designation for its own referent, or it must do so without such dependence.

If that [cognition] were dependent upon it, then at that time the hearing of the final phoneme would have already ceased due to its momentariness; so what need would there be for a recollection of the convention? Furthermore, since the recollection of the convention has not yet occurred at the time of hearing the final phoneme, how could the cognition of the final phoneme depend upon it? If it were independent of the recollection of the convention, it would follow that even one who has never grasped the convention would have a cognition of the meaning upon hearing the word for the first time.
For there is no utility whatsoever in the apprehension of a convention that has been long established and for which memory is not required.
Nor is it logical that the final phoneme, accompanied by the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) called "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*), conveys the meaning;

nor is it reasonable that some other impression produced by the experience of the preceding phonemes acts as a cooperative factor for the cognition of the final phoneme, in the same way that sprinkling and other rites act for rice and the like.
Because it would entail the postulation of numerous unseen factors (*adṛṣṭa*):

first, that very unseen factor itself must be postulated, and then its multiplicity as well. Thus, this cognition of meaning arising from the phonemes being otherwise inexplicable leads to the experience of a *sphoṭa* distinct from them.
For even when the phonemes are distinct, there exists a universal experience common to all people that "this is one sentence" or "this is one word."
Furthermore, that [word or sentence] cannot have multiple phonemes as its objective support (*ālambana*), because multiplicity is contradictory to what is a single entity.
Therefore, it takes as its objective support either a word or a sentence that transcends the individual phonemes.
And while each of the preceding sounds merely causes the essential form (*svarūpa*) to appear, it is the final sound that manifests it clearly.
Furthermore, this twofold manifestation— being clearly or unclearly perceived— is not possible regarding the meaning, because it is restricted to perceptual cognition;
for while such a distinction is logically possible in the case of a word that is directly perceived,

as for the meaning which is understood through the word but is not itself perceptible, there is either its apprehension by another means of knowledge or its non-apprehension, but it does not possess the quality of being clear or unclear.
Furthermore, that which ceases to exist while something else persists must be distinct from it; for example, bracelets, crowns, and so forth [cease] while the gold remains constant.

However, while the phonemes persist, the various word-forms cease; therefore, they too must be distinct from the phonemes. To those who hold this view, he replies: "Words are those [phonemes] ending in inflectional suffixes."
The meaning is that the word (*pada*) consists of nothing other than those very phonemes (*varṇa*), and not some entity called *sphoṭa* distinct from them.
This is the underlying intention here:
first of all, no essence of a word distinct from the phonemes is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

The designation "word" (*pada*), however, is figurative; it refers to those very same many phonemes (*varṇa*) by virtue of their being ascended upon a single recollection, or by virtue of being the cause for the cognition of a single meaning, or by virtue of possessing a state of non-differentiation in their grammatical function (*kāraka*).

Nor is there a mutual dependence in this way—namely, that the comprehension of word-meanings does not occur without the determination of words, nor the determination of words without the comprehension of meanings.

Since phonemes that ascend into a single cognition and memory are easily understood as lacking inherent meaning, and since the apprehension of the convention for those phonemes alone in relation to their own referent is likewise easy, the designation "word" (*pada*) occurs only at a subsequent time. Otherwise, in all words denoting grammatical relations (*kāraka*), a circularity (*itaretarāśrayatva*) would be unavoidable; for grammatical relations have their boundaries defined by the action (*kārya*), and the words for them necessarily follow that [action].

Therefore, the word-soul cannot be perceived through mere conformity with conventional designations, because it does not appear in the auditory cognitions produced by each individual phoneme, nor in the memory-cognition— which arises from the impressions deposited by those [auditory cognitions] and consists of a synthesis of the previously experienced phonemes— since that [memory-cognition] sublates the distinction between the phonemes.
Thus it cannot be said; nor is it logical for that which is partless to possess clarity or lack of clarity, or even a reversal of its parts.
Indeed, that which is entirely unperceived cannot be called "clear," nor can it be the object of a superimposition.
For a mother-of-pearl shell, if not apprehended even in its general form, cannot be the object of the superimposition of silver.
Furthermore, when the word-entity (*padātman*), which is partless, is grasped, nothing remains ungrasped such that, due to its non-grasping, there could be either indistinctness or superimposition.
Nor is it possible for that very same thing to be both grasped and ungrasped by that [cognition] at the same time.
Therefore, the word-entity is not the object of either direct perception or its semblance.
Nor can it be through inference, which arises from a mark that itself produces the cognition of an object, because that would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*).
For a word does not produce the cognition of its object by its mere existence; otherwise, it would cause that cognition eternally due to its own eternity.
Therefore, it must do so through its own cognition.

And that self-cognition [of the word] arises from the cognition of the object; thus, when there is the cognition of the object, there is the cognition of the word, and when there is the cognition of the word, there is the cognition of the object—clearly, this is a case of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*). Nor is it the case that the cognition of the object cannot arise from the phonemes (*varṇa*), for those phonemes, having been previously experienced, when each is experienced and joined by a sequence, ascend into a single unitary cognition (*ekabuddhi*) and are capable of producing the cognition of the object.
Furthermore, there is no lack of distinction among phonemes regarding whether they are without sequence, with sequence, or with a reversed sequence.

Since memory follows the arrangement of previous experience, and since there is a distinction in that arrangement, the occurrence of distinctions [in cognition] is logically established. Furthermore, even though phonemes (varṇas) are identical, a difference in words— such as in the case of *hi* versus *na*— is possible without even postulating the existence of the sphoṭa.
Since the distinction between words follows the distinction in their sequence,
it is not the mere phonemes (varṇa) that produce the cognition of meaning, but rather those phonemes as qualified by a specific sequence— whether deficient or excessive [in length].
Because each such qualification is distinct even when the phonemes themselves are identical, the distinction between words is established.

Therefore, since the production of the cognition of meaning is established by the very letters that are perceived following their perceived sequence, it is not necessary to postulate an unseen entity in the form of *sphoṭa* by way of denying the perceived differences among the letters;
this is proven.
Thus, words are those [letters] ending in inflections.
The *Bhāṣya* states: "They are modified according to their appearance.

This means that they are modified in the form of a mirror through the acquisition of other qualities (*guṇāntarāpatti*) and so forth; "according to appearance" means according to the authority of the evidence (*yathāpramāṇa*), and not by way of a relationship between an original material cause and its modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*), because such a view is sublated by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). — Thus the *Vārttika*.
"In that case, the cognition of meaning would not occur"—
this is the intended argument stated against the proponent of *sphoṭa*.
The answer is: "From the cognition of the final phoneme.
A cognition regarding phonemes is a "cognition of phonemes" (varṇapratyaya).
The "cognition of the final phoneme" (*antyavarṇapratyaya*) is a memory (*smṛti*) that encompasses all the phonemes;
it is "final" because it occurs subsequent to the prior experiences of each individual phoneme.

If this were the case, then even those who have not grasped the linguistic convention (*saṃketa*) would possess such a memory, and it would follow that they too would have a cognition of the meaning; therefore, he says:
"Dependent upon the cognition of the connection with preceding phonemes" means:
the time of grasping the convention is "prior"; the phonemes occurring at that time are "preceding. Their "connection" (*pratisaṃdhāna*) consists in the form:
"These [phonemes] are of such a kind and of such a number, being of the very same class as those for which the convention was previously grasped. That [cognition] itself is precisely what is meant.
The cognition [of meaning] arises from depending upon that [final phoneme].

And since this [cognition] does not exist for those who have not grasped the linguistic convention (*saṃketa*), the meaning is that even though the cognition of the final phoneme exists, it does not cause the meaning to be understood.
A word (*nāman*) is a sound whose form is qualified by its connection with other actions [i.e., verbal roots], which constitute the denotable object (*abhidheya*).
The word *antara* signifies a distinction; the meaning is "due to its connection with a specific action.
This is what is being said: that noun whose denotation does not reach completion without a connection to a specific action is [a verb]; however, although the meaning of a verb—though it may be...
In some cases, it is also connected with an action, as in "he offers while stepping forward" (*abhikrāmaṃ juhoti*) or "he goes after eating" (*bhuktvā vrajati*), and so forth.

Nevertheless, verbs such as *juhoti* ("he offers") and *vrajati* ("he goes") do not reach their full meaning without a connection to an action; rather, they are also connected with those [words] uttered in proximity to them.
However, the meaning of a noun does not reach its full meaning without a principal verb whose meaning consists of a sequence of prior and posterior stages.
For this very reason, they say: "Where no other verb (*kriyāpada*) is heard, there the root *as* (to be) in the present tense (*bhavantī*) should be employed.

Thus, in the Brāhmaṇa texts, expressions such as *abhikrāmam bhoktum bhaktaḥ* ("having stepped forward, he is one who eats")—which depend on conjunctions and the like, and which would remain incomplete without a specific action—are subsumed under the category of nouns (*nāman*). He provides an example of this:
Regarding the example "brāhmaṇa," he states its meaning: it is a collection of action and factors (kāraka) qualified by the number of the factor.
For here, by the word "action" (kriyā), the state of being a Brāhmaṇa—namely, *brāhmaṇatva*—is denoted, because the word "state" (*bhāva*) has the sense of "action."
And there will be a Brahmin who is the agent;
the aggregate of those two—the state of being a Brahmin and the Brahmin—is understood from this nominal word "Brahmin" as qualified by the singular number of the agent, the future Brahmin.
This is the meaning.
He states the definition of the verb (*ākhyāta*):

"A verb is that which expresses the connection with action and time, and in which the action is predominant. The connection of an action with time is its sequential order (*pūrvāparībhāva*). Indeed, because of this connection with time, it is possible for [the word] to express that [action].
By this [definition], he excludes [the category of noun] from such items as *pāka* (cooking);
yet even so, there remains the over-extension [of the definition] to nouns such as *bhuktvā* (having eaten) and *bhoktum* (to eat).

For even in that case, there is a cognition of a collection of action-moments existing in a temporal sequence of prior and posterior; otherwise, there would be no connection with the object [denoted by] "rice" (*odana*).
Therefore it is said that the verb has action as its primary meaning (*kriyāpradhāna*);
for from a finite verb (*ākhyāta*), action is understood as residing in itself, not as dependent on something else.
In cases such as "in order to eat" (*bhoktum*), however, the action is understood because it does not terminate until another action follows at the end;
but in cases such as "he goes" (*vrajati*), this is not so. This, then, is the primacy of the action. By this, all verbal forms—such as *pacati*, *paceta*, *pacyate*, and *sthīyate*—are encompassed.

There is no application [of the term "name"] even to the word *asti* and so forth; for although these resemble nouns and verbs, it should be understood that they function in the sense of *sat* (being) as an established entity, and not in the sense of an action consisting of prior and subsequent stages—
since every word is pervaded by being a name.
(311/6) "Abundance" (*bāhulya*) means for the sake of pervasion (*vyāpti*).

For generally, in a sentence, there are many noun-words (*nāmapada*), whereas the verb (*ākhyāta*) is only one in a single sentence; for if there were a plurality of verbs, there would be a plurality of sentences. [The opponent] challenges the topic by asserting that meaning is not apprehended from words.
For by a word, either a particular (viśeṣa) or a universal (sāmānya) is denoted; therein, he first refutes the denotation of a particular:
"particular" means non-termination, that is, lack of determination.
Having relied upon the expression of a generality, he says "not of a word";
he refutes this by saying "not of a generality.
For it is for the sake of practical communication that elders utter sentences.
But it is not out of mere addiction [to the category of the universal].
Nor is there any worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) that is accomplished by means of a universal; rather, every transaction is accomplished by means of a particular (*viśeṣa*).

Furthermore, a word is not the designator of this [transaction]; rather, the sentence alone is the designator of the sentence-meaning. Thus, this is the occasion for an investigation into the meaning of words (*padārtha*).
This is the sense of the objection. He provides the resolution: "Not so, provided that [the sentence] has a universal as its object.
It was stated previously that there is no such thing as a sentence distinct from the words.

Nor is it logical that the mere sequence of phonemes (*varṇamālā*)—without depending on an intermediate operation of conveying word-meanings (*padārtha*)—should be the cognizer of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*).

For if it were independent of the apprehension of convention (*saṃketa*), there would follow the absurd consequence that even a first-time listener, or one who does not know the convention, would understand the sentence-meaning.

This is because, if dependence on the apprehension of convention is required, it is impossible to apprehend a convention for a sentence due to its infinite variety and lack of invariable concomitance with the sentence-meaning.
Thus, even against one's will, one must admit that words possess a conventional denotation (saṃketa) for their own specific meanings.

Therefore, the general sense is the meaning of words, and we have demonstrated more thoroughly in the *Tattvabindu* how both these words—and their intermediate operations directed toward conveying that [general sense]—function as the conveyors of the sentence-meaning.

The point is this: this cognition of the general sense arising from a word—whether it be "cow" or "horse"—which extends over all cows or all horses, is restricted by the hearing of a particular attribute, such as "white" or "black."
He asks: "But how is this so?
Even [words] such as "stands" or "goes" cannot function with respect to a specific [object] as a word [denoting it], because it is impossible to grasp a relationship [between them].
Therefore, the sense is that these too are denoters of universals (*sāmānyavacana*).
The answer is: "It is not so.

Thus, because it is certain that the word denotes a universal (sāmānya), and because both the form (ākṛti) and the individual (vyakti) are understood from the word, a doubt arises due to the disagreement among disputants as to whether the referent is all three or only one of them.
Which of the three is the meaning? Or is it something else?
Thus far, having ascertained that the word is expressive based on the cognition of the general [meaning], the transition to another consideration was shown.

Now, however, since there is no suspicion at all that the word is expressive based on the cognition of both [the general and the particular], he says "Or let it be," indicating that the transition to another consideration is indeed appropriate.
It acknowledges that which is established by direct experience, namely the action and its means;
the meaning is "the cow is to become. // 57 //
Because of the figurative application [of a word] when an individual, a configuration, and a genus are in proximity, there arises doubt.
The Bhāṣya asks: "Is it any one of these categories, or is it all of them?
To this, the author of the Vārttika states the meaning of "any one."
What is manifestation? // 58 //

NyS 2.2.59: The individual is [the meaning of the word], because the collection of words, abandonment, acquisition, number, increase, decrease, color, compound, and connection are metaphorically applied to the individual.
In this regard, some maintain that by the force of the use of the word "yā" (which) and so forth, the individual (*vyakti*) alone is the meaning of the word.
This might be argued: since the form (*ākṛti*) also differs just like the individual, why does [the word] not become the denoter of the form as well? To this [it is replied]:
He says:
"It is so even for the configuration.
And the universal "cowness" will be the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*); therefore, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Nor is there a denotation of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), because even when it is not explicitly denoted, its status as a delimiting factor for that which is denoted by the word is observed.

For example, in the expression *gārgikayā ślāghate* ("he praises on account of being a descendant of Garga"), the suffix *vuñ*, which is prescribed due to the presence of the adjunct "praising," does not denote the act of praising itself; such is the sense.
No, because that would lead to an infinite regress.
He refutes this proponent of the restriction that [a word] denotes the individual by saying "not by this" (NyS 2.2.61):

"On account of association, location, purpose, function, measure, support, proximity, conjunction, instrument, and sovereignty, [the word for one thing is applied] to a Brāhmaṇa, a bed, a mat, a king, groats, sandalwood, the Gaṅgā, a cart, food, and a person, even when the state of being that [other thing] is absent."
There is also a metaphorical designation for that.

An unperceived limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is not capable of effecting a delimited determination. Furthermore, in the expression *gārgikayā*, although the suffix *vuñ* expresses the adjunct, it is not perceived as such because its meaning is expressed by another word, namely *ślāghate*.
However, where the word *ślāghate* is not employed, the suffix *vuñ*—which denotes the existence [of that adjunct]—is not grammatically correct.
This is the interpretation when the substratum is different and there is no limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).
However, when the substratum is the same—as in the case of "cow" and so forth—the denotability by a word ending in a primary suffix (*pratyaya*) exists precisely with respect to the limiting adjunct;
for example, "the white *dṛtihari*."
For here, since the animal is already understood by the mere expression "Dṛtihari," the word "white" (*śveta*) is employed for the purpose of restricting its specific identity.
Nor is it correct to claim that [the quality] is not denoted because it is understood from usage alone;
for one may justifiably question why there is a restriction on usage for that which does not denote such a qualifying attribute (*upādhi*).
If [words] were not subject to such inquiry, it would follow that all words whatsoever are non-denotative, because worldly usage is beginningless;
for it is precisely from the restriction of usage that the meaning is understood even from them.

If you argue that the restriction of usage is untenable for that which does not convey a meaning, and thus one must accept that wherever there is usage, there is denotative power, then this applies equally to the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) as well.
And thus the venerable Kātyāyana records:
"That which is denoted by the suffix -ant is this word *samāna*.
A *samāna-śabda* is a word in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa-śabda*); that which is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is what is denoted by the word ending in the suffix.
This is the meaning.
Therefore, when there is a restriction to a specific individual (vyakti), the genus (jāti) is incapable of being cognized if it is not itself perceived;

and since there is nothing other than the word "cow" that causes its cognition, it too must be conveyed by that word. Thus it is established that the referent of a word (padārtha) is not merely the individual. // 60 //

Regarding the statement "while the vīraṇa grass is being woven for the sake of a mat," the *Bhāṣya* explains that it is untenable for the mat (*kaṭa*), as a product (*nirvartya*), to function as the object (*karman*), because the designation of "object" falls under the governing rule of *kāraka*s (Pāṇini 1.4.23),
and a *kāraka* is defined by its being the cause of an action.

Furthermore, since an action that is not yet accomplished cannot function as a cause prior [to its occurrence], the word *kaṭa* (mat) must therefore apply to the *vīraṇa* grasses being arranged for the sake of the mat, based solely on their being the cause for that purpose (*tādarthya*).
And indeed, the *vīraṇa* grasses, while being woven, possess the status of a cause by virtue of existing prior to the action of making the mat. // 61 //
The universal form (ākṛti) [is the basis of the word], because the establishment of the existence of individual entities is achieved in dependence upon it.

"If there is no restriction on the individual without the genus, then the genus must be the denotation; alas! since that too must be restricted by the configuration (ākṛti), let the configuration itself be what is denoted"—thus he says, "If, then... (314/9). He refutes this as well.
In this case as well, it is that very same [universal] which is present, and not because of its non-abiding;
for even when manifested by configuration (*saṃsthāna*), the universal is manifested and established through its inherence in a single object.
That [universal], however, being continuous despite the individual instances and configurations from which it differs, is determined by a cognition of non-difference.
The meaning is this: such a thing [the individual] can be made known by a word even without depending on the configuration (saṃsthāna) or the name;

however, the configuration—being distinct from the individual and thus impossible to grasp through convention due to its infinity and variability—cannot be made known by a word unless it depends upon the denotation of a universal (jāti). Therefore, the "form" (ākṛti), which is another name for the configuration, is not the referent of a word.

Nor is the configuration (*ākṛti*) the word-meaning by way of the universal (*jāti*), as is the case with the individual (*vyakti*), because it lacks a connection with the universal; thus he says: "And that which has a connection with the universal... (62).

NyS 2.2.63: Even though [the term "cow"] is associated with both the individual and the form, the universal (jāti) is [the referent] because sprinkling and other such rites would not otherwise apply to a clay cow.
"Let it be, then, that the word-meaning is the universal (jāti) alone; for in its case, the apprehension of the convention is easy because there is no deviation (vyabhicāra).

However, there is deviation in the case of the individual (vyakti) and the configuration (ākṛti). With the intention that the usage of words denoting the universal toward the individual and the configuration will be metaphorical (aupacārika), he says:
"Let it be, then."
The remainder of this has a meaning that is not obscure.
One who asserts that "the one exists in many" should not be questioned on the grounds of contradiction by both [criteria].
(318/13) If a single entity existing in many locations exists in each individual instance by its entire self (*sarvātmanā*), then it follows that what is multiple exists in many locations;
and thus there is a contradiction between the subject (*anuyoga*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

Alternatively, if a single entity existing in many locations exists in each instance only by a part (*ekadeśena*), even so, it is not the case that a single entity exists in many locations; rather, it is the multiple [parts] that exist in many locations, because the parts themselves are multiple.
Thus, this contradiction has been stated on both counts regarding the dispute over the composite whole. (63)
NyS_2.2.64: It is not so, because the manifestation of the universal depends upon the form and the individual.
But the referent of a word is the individual, the configuration, and the genus.

Thus, having refuted the restriction to any one particular designation, he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) regarding the unrestricted designation: "The meaning is the individual" (Sūtra 65).
This is the intended meaning here:

immediately after the utterance of the word "cow," for one who knows the conventional relation (*saṃgati*), there arises a cognition in which the individual (*vyakti*), the configuration (*ākṛti*), and the universal (*jāti*) appear as a single unit; this is not, however, like the case of "a hamlet dwells on the Gaṅgā" or "the Vāhīka is a cow," where [the cognition] occurs subsequent to the apprehension of "Gaṅgā-ness" or "cow-ness."

Just as the bank or a Vāhīka person is understood— either because the connection of that [word] with the sentence-meaning is untenable, or because of its invariable concomitance with it, or through association with a quality indicated by it— so too is the understanding here. Due to the frequency of usage and extreme repetition, the sequence of cognition, though present, is not perceived because of its extreme rapidity.
If it is argued that this is like the piercing of a hundred lotuses by a hundred arrows discharged with extreme rapidity, we say no;
for in the absence of a powerful subverting factor (*bādhaka*), it is impossible to alter the manifestation of non-difference (*abheda*) once it has been established.
If that were the case, non-difference would not be established anywhere at all; and consequently, even difference (*bheda*) would not exist, since difference is dependent upon non-difference.
Moreover, the cognition of form is not devoid of form; and form is the genus of a substance, because a substance is "possessing form" (rūpin) by virtue of being manifested as form.
Nor is there a cognition of that by which something is manifested when that [manifestor] itself is not cognized;
just as there is no apprehension of a cognition without an object.
Therefore, the apprehension of the genus is a part of the apprehension of the substance; it cannot occur in isolation without the apprehension of the substance.

Consequently, because they are the objects of a single apprehension, there is no relationship of "characterized" and "characteristic" between the genus and the individual. Furthermore, that apprehension which arises immediately after the cognition of the word is verbal (śābda).
Nor should it be argued that even though the genus and the individual are the objects of a single apprehension, the genus alone is denoted by the word and not the individual.
Even if there were a single denotation, since the perception of both [meanings] is possible, it is illogical to postulate that both are denoted.
For the capacity of causes is manifested (*vyañgya*) only in the effect (*kārya*), not in what is not an effect;
and the effect is experience (*anubhava*), and that is one.
Thus, there is no postulation of a difference in capacity (*sāmarthya*).

However, by means of that [capacity], it is said that even with respect to the action (*karman*), the word is "capable" (*samartha*) regarding the object; and since the effect and the means are one, the capacity remains one and the same even when the objects differ.
Furthermore, for words whose function depends upon human convention, there is no such thing as "capacity" within the scope of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that could be either one or many.

By this, it is refuted that in the case of conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*), one should postulate a capacity for the individual instance (*vyakti*) in a word whose function is exhausted by denoting the genus (*jāti*);
thus, the claim made by others—that the capacity for the individual instance belongs to the meaning itself since it is not occupied elsewhere—is also rejected.
For indeed, would that meaning cause the cognition of the individual instance while being itself cognized, or while being uncognized?
If that which is unperceived were the signifier, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the individual being understood at all times, because the cause [of its existence] is eternal.

If that which is perceived were the signifier, there is the unavoidable fault of self-dependence (*ātmāśrayatva*), for it has already been stated that the cognition of the individual is not distinct from the cognition of the universal (*jāti*).
Therefore, the aphorism of the Great Sage is correct: "The referent of a word is the individual, the configuration (*ākṛti*), and the universal (*jāti*)."

Now, he introduces another proponent of the theory that the referent of a word is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), stating: "Some say that the individual, the configuration, and the genus are not the word-referent" (321.3).
Then, regarding the phrase "because it subsists in substances and so forth," the intended meaning is that there is no relationship of locus and located between a cow and a horse.
Even the word "existent" (sat) does not denote merely that which possesses a genus (jātimat).
Why? Because it is not independent (asvatantra).
Pots, cloths, and so forth are what possess a genus.
Furthermore, these [particulars] such as "jar" are not cognized from the word "existent" (sat) independently, as is the case with words like "jar";

rather, the cognition of jars and so forth hovers over them upon hearing the word "existent," whereas the word "existent," depending upon words such as "jar," is the cause for the ascertainment of the jar and other particulars.
Therefore...
The meaning is that [the word] is not expressive of the possessor of the property (tadvat), because it is dependent upon words such as "jar" (ghaṭa) and so forth.
Alternatively:
whatever exists here as dependent is not expressive of that [dependent object], just as the words "Gaṅgā," "cow" (go), and so forth are not expressive of the bank or a bull, respectively.
And thus, genus-words [denote] that which possesses the genus;
therefore, they do not denote the possessor of the genus. For they function with respect to the possessor of the genus by depending upon the genus; such is the meaning of "dependence.
Now, why do they not function with respect to the possessor of the genus independently of the genus? To this [it is replied]:
He said:
"And it has been stated in this regard:
'Let it then be metaphorical.'"
Because there is no cognition [of the universal] in that which possesses it [the individual], he says: "And in that which possesses it.

The meaning is this: just as the quality characterized by sovereignty exists in a servant who has conquered [his enemies] and thus the word "master" is applied to him, it is not so with the connection of the genus and the quality to the individual.

Furthermore, a word denoting one thing, while applying to another, first produces a cognition of the former and then applies to the latter; for example, the word "cow," having produced a cognition of a cow, applies to a Vāhīka.
And he says that here the genus-word does not function by deviating from the genus, nor is there a simultaneous figurative application;
for there is an absence of sequential application and because simultaneity is impossible.
He thus refutes the coloring by qualities.
Furthermore, there is the consequence that knowledge would arise as non-corresponding to reality (*ayathārthajñāna*).

Just as there is the cognition "the crystal is blue" due to the coloring by a quality (*guṇoparāga*), so too all verbal cognition would, in the absence of a sublater (*bādhaka*), necessarily be non-corresponding to reality; this is the meaning.
[The author] now refutes the thesis that a single unique particular (*ekasvalakṣaṇa*) is denoted.
Regarding the term "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*),
it should also be understood that this is because it is impossible to establish a convention (*samaya*).
Thus, having raised the proponent of the theory of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha-vādin*), he proceeds to refute him.
Regarding the phrase "here by us":
for us, the individual (*vyakti*), the configuration (*ākṛti*), and the genus (*jāti*)—these three are the word-meanings (*padārtha*).

As for the relationship of subordinate and principal, it occurs only in certain instances; however, when a word denotes an individual possessing a genus, both types of independence [of the other two] are impossible for words.
It is not possible to claim that a word first requires the cognition of the universal (*jāti*) for the sake of producing the cognition of the individual (*vyakti*);
for since both are necessarily cognized in a single act of awareness, a sequence of priority and posteriority is impossible.

Nor can there be independence [of the universal] with respect to particularizing words, because without a word denoting a particular, the cognition of universals would be a mere mental fluctuation, necessitating dependence on particularizing words for their ascertainment.
Because the cognition arising from a genus-word (*jātiśabda*) with respect to its own object does not waver,
its object is merely the individual (*vyakti*) possessing the genus; and since there is no wavering of cognition here,
and the restriction to a specific individual is the object, the non-wavering of cognition therein is not defective.
For from a distance, the object of perception is merely a substance possessing height and circumference, but not specifically whether it is a post or a person.
Nor does the fluctuation of cognition in this case cause any impairment to perception.
Furthermore, on this view, the word for the genus (*jāti*) is not a term for the individual (*vyakti*) or the configuration (*ākṛti*), such that it would have to be considered figurative.

Furthermore, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is not impossible for two words denoting a universal (*jāti*) and an individual (*vyakti*), because coreferentiality with distinct substrata (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) is untenable.
Therefore, everything is clear.

Having thus demonstrated that the objections raised by others do not apply to the doctrine of non-absolutism (*anekāntavāda*), he states the absence of faults by refuting the critical statements (*dūṣaṇavākya*) put forward by others.
Nor are these faults [applicable].

The analysis of the term *sattāśabda* is either "the word for existence" (*sattāyāḥ śabdaḥ*) or "the word whose form is existence" (*sattārūpaḥ śabdaḥ*). In the former case, the word "existence" (*sattāśabda*) is not a denoter of existence.

Thus there is a contradiction (*vyāghāta*). In the latter alternative, there is a contradiction with the statement "it is not the designator of existence" (*na vācakaḥ sattāyāḥ*). By the word "of existence" (*sattāyāḥ*), you designate existence; yet you say that the word "existence" (*sattā-śabda*) is not its designator. Therefore, there is a contradiction. Furthermore, the phrase "the word 'existence'" (*sattā-śabda*) is used for the sake of illustration; it should be understood as meaning "it is not the designator by way of existence."
He raises an objection based on your intention; he refutes it, saying:
"No."
The meaning is this: if you accept our intended point—on the grounds that "acceptance is dependent upon the comprehension of the meaning"—then you must not refute it in that way.
Anticipating the objection, "I intend to refute it, but I do not accept it," he says: "And as for this... (322/4). He refutes this by saying: "That too is not [the case]."

That which is not such [i.e., not a person], namely a post (*sthāṇu*) that is not a person, possesses a superimposed property such as "personhood" through its similarity with persons who are actually such; one who has this [superimposition] is described as "being such. Its primary object is the person; the meaning is that there is a cognition appearing in the form of that [person]. Regarding the phrase "of existence (*sattā*) expressed by the primary means of proof": [it refers to the word expressing the primary means of proving the existence of the object].

The meaning is this: *pradhāna* (the primary) is the means (*sādhana*) by way of being a manifester (*vyañjaka*), and it is a substance (*bhavitṛ-dravya*); indeed, the word *sat* denotes that [substance]. However, the word *mattā* (existence) denotes a state (*bhāva*) that is subordinate to the substance; therefore, it does not stand in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a word denoting a substance. Thus, the coreferentiality of the words *sat* and *dravya* is unestablished. As for what has been stated by some—that "proof" (*siddhi*), which is to say "cognition," would not occur according to your view—that too has been refuted by this establishment of coreferentiality.
It has already been explained that [the opponent's position] is to be refuted.
Regarding the phrase "the linguistic formulation (*vācoyukti*) formulated by oneself":

this means that he negates the specific mode of expression (*vacanavyakti*) formulated by himself concerning words such as "existence" (*sat*), and in that case, we have a "proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhana*).
Thinking that the word *sat* is a generic term (*jātiśabda*) and that its denotation of particulars is not accepted [by the opponent], he raises an objection with the words,
"If, then... The refutation is easy to understand.
Nevertheless, it is neither positive nor negative;
since whatever things are infinite are not denotable by genus-words, there is no corroborative instance, because all particular instances have been made the subject of the proposition.

Nor can it be said that "wherever there is a word denoting a universal (jāti), there is no such infinite extension [of the individual], as in the case of 'cowness' (gotva) and so forth," because in your own view, the universal itself is like a lotus in the sky. This is the intended meaning. He raises an objection with the words "But even so" (athāpi);
the intention is that if that were the case, a positive (anvayin) example would be observed.
He refutes this as well, saying "this also is not [the case]," because it contradicts the employment of a qualification.

The point is that, apart from difference (*bheda*), there exists nothing whatsoever that is substantially real (*vastusat*) from which a qualifier could exclude [other things]. Regarding the phrase "because the status of being a logical reason (*hetubhāva*) is not accepted":
sound is not a logical mark (*liṅga*) in the communication of meaning, such that it would be vitiated by deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

Furthermore, the mere capacity to convey meaning is not vitiated by deviation; for if it were, then even the eyes and other sense organs would follow as being non-conveyors of meaning due to their deviation—since they function with respect to yellow and so forth while deviating from blue and so forth.
The point is that the apprehension of convention is indeed easy, provided that the individual particulars, though subject to deviation, are subsumed under a single universal class (*jāti*).
This is because [the opponent] has denied that words denote individual particulars (*bheda*).
When the denotation of difference has been refuted, the denotation of substance is also refuted, because a substance is itself a form of difference.
Consequently, the term "substance" [in the opponent's argument] involves a contradiction;
this is the meaning.
This has already been answered: because the word "existent" (sat) and the word "substance" (dravya) have the same object.
The meaning is that the object of words such as "existent" is merely a particularity; it is not restricted to the thought that "this alone is it and no other."
The meaning is that substances, qualities, and actions are not implied by the word "existence" (sattā),
because they lack the fitness for grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya).
Because that [result] would be impossible without that [cause],
he says, "it is possible to state," meaning that it is possible to state merely the implication (ākṣepa).

Having asked about the meaning of the word *asat*, he determines— according to the method of the author of the Sūtras— that there are three meanings based on the relationship of subordinate (*guṇa*) and principal (*pradhāna*):
namely, "existent" (*sat*), "this" (*ayam*),
and "produced by an object" (*arthakṛta*).
"Artha" means the purpose; it is produced by that [purpose].
This is what is meant: that which is connected with the purpose is the primary element (pradhāna), while that which serves as the delimiter of the connection to the purpose is a subsidiary (aṅga).
By this [statement], etc.
By means of expressing three meanings:
for indeed, there is no cognition of "owner" with respect to a servant;
rather, the meaning is that it is merely designated as an "owner" because of performing the functional activity of one.
"Here there is neither succession nor simultaneity of cognition.
Succession and simultaneity, which depend upon difference, are not possible in a single, specific cognition of a substance.
By this [it is meant]:
This has been refuted by the statement that since a word denotes a substance qualified by existence (*sattā*), it would follow that an incorrect cognition arises.

For while a cognition of blue might indeed be erroneous in the case of a crystal that is ultimately pure and white, due to the proximity of a blue substance— since in reality the quality of blue does not inhere in it—
the inherence of existence (*sattā-samavāya*) in substances and the like is ultimate.
Thus, the meaning is that the cognition "existent" with respect to substances and so forth is not false.

As for the phrase "for no word [is accepted]," the meaning is that because it is impossible to establish a convention for particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), you do not accept any word whatsoever as being expressive of them.
"And not [of] the genus-word" means that there is an absence of genus (*jāti*). The sense is this:

previously it was stated—taking particulars (*bheda*) as primary—that the genus-word is not the denoter of particulars; but now, by the mere fact of being a "genus-word," its non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*) is established.
"There is no dispute" means that there is no disagreement regarding the non-difference in definition between the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) and the universal (*jāti*). However,
as for the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of words denoting substantial entities (*dravyasat*), it is not contradictory that words do not denote [substantial] entities.

For "substance" (*dravya*) is indeed of a positive nature, and likewise "existent" (*sat*) is also of a positive nature; the two words are the designators of those two [meanings], and it is contradictory for them to have the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) as their referent.
Furthermore, it is not possible for two words that are positive in form to have the exclusion of others as their referent.
Nor is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) even tenable between two words that do not denote distinct particulars.

For two [words] existing with respect to a single object that possesses a differentiated form must be co-referential (samānādhikaraṇa) by virtue of having two distinct causes for their application; if they did not denote difference, they would not apply to one and the same thing.
And if they do not apply [to the same thing], being restricted to distinct causes for their application, they cannot be co-referential—just as the words "cow" and "horse" are not.
This is another contradiction.
"Non-denotation of difference and grammatical coreferentiality"—by this, two contradictions have been stated. Desiring to refute these two contradictions, he raises an objection:
"If it is argued that there is no contradiction because [the relationship] is metaphorical (upacāra)."
He analyzes this by stating, "the words 'substantially existent' (dravyasat) and 'existent' (sat).
By this, the first contradiction is resolved.
The proponent of the second contradiction raises it and then resolves it.
"Those two" means they speak, that is to say, they demonstrate and they determine.
This is the intended meaning here:
for words have conceptual construction as their source and thus adhere only to that which is the domain of conceptual constructions,
because cause and effect are apprehended through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
This fourfold class of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) consists of those that apprehend an existent or non-existent subject (*dharmin*) and an existent or non-existent property (*dharma*).

It includes such [constructions] as "Gaurīśvara," "blue," or "eternal. Furthermore, the object of conceptual construction—which is unified through identity across differences of place, time, and state by means of the recognition "this is that very same thing"—is the domain of words, because it is possible to establish linguistic conventions (*saṅketa*) for words with respect to that [object].

Furthermore, particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are not the object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), because they are not characterized in the same way as the three worlds [are characterized by universals]. Nor does there exist any such thing as a "universal" (*sāmānya*) that could serve as its object.

For this very reason, the particular characteristics themselves do not possess those [universals]; since those universals do not exist, the state of possessing them cannot exist in the particular characteristics either.

Furthermore, even if the universal (*sāmānya*) were an existent entity (*vastusat*), nevertheless, because it is eternal and thus incapable of being assisted [by anything], its subsistence as a substratum for particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) is untenable;
for subsistence as a substratum is indeed nothing other than the state of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*).
For things such as jujube fruits, which possess the property of falling, are rendered non-falling by vessels such as bowls.
Furthermore, since that which is eternal is not produced, it cannot be something to be deposited [in a substratum].

Likewise, "treeness" and "śiṃśapā-ness," being independent universals already understood through their own respective words, would not possess grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), just as in the case of "cow" and "horse.
Moreover, even if one were to grant that an eternal entity can be deposited because it is capable of receiving assistance, this must still be subjected to the following dilemma.
Does that particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) assist both "treeness" and "śiṃśapā-ness" by means of the very same intrinsic nature (svabhāva), or by means of a different intrinsic nature?

For if it were by means of a different intrinsic nature, then because of the difference in intrinsic natures, the particular characteristic that is the substratum of "śiṃśapā-ness" would be one thing and the substratum of "treeness" another; consequently, there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), just as in the case of "cow" and "horse."
Thus,

even if a particular (svalakṣaṇa) assists all universals (sāmānya) by means of a single intrinsic nature (svabhāva), nevertheless, since there is no difference in that intrinsic nature, when a particular possessing a single universal is grasped by a single word or conceptual cognition (vikalpa) from among those universals whose natures depend upon that assistance—

Because all universals (*sāmānya*) have a nature bound to that single benefit, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the conceptual cognitions (*vikalpa*) of "existent," "substance," "earthen," "tree," and "śiṃśapā," as well as their corresponding words, would be synonyms.
As it has been said: "When one [entity] that provides a single benefit is being grasped, no other benefits [from that same source] exist apart from it."
"Those things which are not seen when that [particular] is seen are all grasped when it is grasped.
Therefore, conceptual constructions do not have particulars as their objects in the manner of universals.

By negating that [the object] has as its domain the distinction of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), the view that the domain of cognition consists of the aspect of the apprehended (*grāhyākāra*) is also discarded.
If it is argued that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), while determining its own internal aspect— which is not external— to be external, thus has an external object consisting of its own aspect;

As it has been said: "...activity [occurs] through the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of an object within one's own internal appearance, which is not the actual object. Now, what is this "determination"?
Is it grasping (*grahaṇa*), or rather, is it making (*karaṇa*)?
Furthermore, there is the application (*yojanā*) and the superimposition (*samāropa*).
