In that regard, how could a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) grasp or produce an object that is its own internal appearance yet lacks external reality? Indeed, even by a hundred craftsmen, it is impossible to grasp or produce yellow as blue.
Nor can a conceptual construction join its own form with a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) that has not been grasped.
Furthermore, it has been established that the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not within the range of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Nor does [the cognition] superimpose an object upon its own form when that form is not an object.
First of all, an unapprehended own-form cannot be superimposed; therefore, the apprehension of that form must be sought.
Does one grasp [the object] first and then superimpose [the conceptual construction], or does one grasp it and superimpose it at the very same moment?
The former position is not tenable, for a conceptual cognition, being momentary, cannot perform the two successive acts of grasping and superimposing.

As for the latter position, [it would mean that] the direct perception of the self-awareness of the conceptualization—which has the form of a conceptualization and is the locus of the "I-notion"—[would perceive] that which is not the locus of the "I-notion."

A conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) being superimposed is neither its own object-domain, nor can it be apprehended as undifferentiated, nor can it be apprehended by conceptual cognition as being one with an external particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), because the particular does not appear within itself to conceptual cognition.
Therefore, this object of conceptualization is false (*alīka*), for it is neither cognition, nor a form of cognition, nor is it external.
It must be understood in this way,
as the Venerable Dharmottara has said:
"That form which is delineated by a conceptualizing cognition as being distinct from others is neither [the object of] cognition nor is it external."
Nevertheless, for those who seek it, there would be no outward-directed activity toward an external object based on conceptual cognition alone.
Therefore, their object is a false external thing; its externality consists in the non-apprehension of its difference from the external, and not in the apprehension of its identity with the external.
Because conceptualization is incapable of grasping non-difference with respect to external objects, which are the domain of conceptualization;

therefore, the conceptualizations that arise subsequent to non-conceptual perception do not grasp the difference from the external particular (svalakṣaṇa) presented by that [perception], since they grasp their own object as unreal.
They cause those engaged in worldly transaction who seek [an object] to proceed toward that [object], because they are indirectly connected with it;
thus, through the attainment [of the object], they do not deceive the world.

Furthermore, regarding those objects which are the domains of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), their mutual distinction is not grasped either by those very conceptual constructions themselves nor by other conceptual constructions. Due to this non-apprehension of difference, a person conceives of them as non-different; and because of that non-difference, there arises the state of "ascertainment" (*avamarsa*).
And because of the non-difference of those [cognitions], there is a non-difference of their causes, which are non-conceptual cognitions;

and because of the non-difference of those, there is also a non-difference of the particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), even though they are the objects of non-conceptual cognitions. As it has been said: "Because it is the cause of a single unifying reflective awareness (*ekapratyavamarṣa*), cognition is non-differentiating."
Because they share the status of being the cause of a single cognition, even individual instances are non-different...
Thus it is established that the external object of conceptualizations and words is unreal (*alīka*).

And this [unreal object] consists in the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), because it is common to both existence and non-existence, because it produces a semblance of similarity despite being utterly distinct, and because it is experienced as having that form.
For instance, whatever is common to both existence and non-existence is necessarily of the nature of the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*).
For example, incorporeality (*amūrtatva*) is indeed common to both consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the horn of a hare (*śaśaviṣāṇa*);
likewise, the objects of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), such as jars, cloths, and so forth, which are the subject of dispute, [are also common to both].

Thus, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). For the conceptual object (*vikalpaviṣaya*) such as "cow," which is common to both existence and non-existence—as in the thoughts "the cow exists" and "the cow does not exist"—is of a positive form (*vidhirūpa*). It cannot be connected with the word "does not exist" because it would be a contradiction [if it were non-existent], nor can it be connected with the word "exists" because it would be redundant [if it were already established as existent] like a unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, a cognition that apprehends what is common to both existence and non-existence is neither causeless nor does it have another [external] cause as its basis; for it is impossible for that which has a positive form as its object, or that which has the thing's own nature as its object, or that which falls under the category of a positive attribute, to possess a [positive] causal basis therein.

Therefore, the apprehension of what is common is pervaded by the possession of a causal basis; and since this pervader—the possession of a causal basis—is absent from the counter-example (vipakṣa), its absence implies that the apprehension of what is common is pervaded by having the exclusion of others (anyavyāvṛtti) as its object.
Thus is established the proof of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*).
Furthermore, the similarity among things that are absolutely dissimilar is produced solely by their exclusion from others;
just as cows, horses, buffaloes, and elephants, though absolutely dissimilar, possess similarity through their common exclusion of lions.

And thus, there is a similarity in characteristics (*sālakṣaṇya*) between the external particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is of a positive nature (*vidhirūpa*) and ultimately real (*paramārthasat*), and [the conceptual object], which is not ultimately real (*aparamārthasat*) and is entirely different [from it]; this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). For the external [particular], though of a positive nature, is excluded from non-cows (*agovyāvṛtta*); and if the object of conceptual construction (*vikalpaviṣaya*) is also excluded from non-cows, then there is similarity in characteristics, and not otherwise. And such is the case with their similarity in characteristics.
Since it is pervaded by the possession of a cause, its exclusion from the dissimilar class (vipakṣa) through the non-perception of that [cause] entails its being pervaded by its own probandum;
thus, the necessary connection (pratibandha) is established.
Furthermore, the object of conceptual construction is indeed experienced as having the nature of exclusion (vyāvṛtti).

For instance, if that [cow] does not appear [in consciousness], one instructed to "tie up a cow" might tie up a horse, because the cow would not appear as distinct from the horse. Or, if it does appear, how could there not be an appearance of its exclusion from non-cows?
Therefore, both word and conceptual cognition function through the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) and by means of metaphorical designation (*upacara*).
This very point was stated by the author of the *Vārttika*:
"These two, proceeding in the form of the exclusion of non-existent substances, refer to a single object."
Thus [it is said]:

"For one who determines a single particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), determination (*adhyavasāya*) is said to be the non-apprehension of the object of that determination as distinct from its own particular characteristic.
To this, it is replied:
First, the existence of the genus (*jāti*) has been established; therefore, the individual (*vyakti*) that possesses it is also ultimately real (*paramārthasat*).
Furthermore, the natural relation between the individual and the genus does not depend upon any mutual benefit.
Moreover, we shall demonstrate in the refutation of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) that even an impermanent thing can be the recipient of assistance.

And just as it has been demonstrated on the occasion of defining perception that the apprehension of one limiting adjunct does not entail the apprehension of another limiting adjunct as qualified by it,

so too has it been stated by the author of the Vārttika— while establishing that error is caused by similarity— that the manifestation of something absolutely non-existent or of a non-existent form is not possible;
and this has also been established by us.
Therefore, individuals possessing a genus (jāti) are the domain of conceptual cognitions and words;
the meaning is that the form of those [individuals] as they function is excluded from what does not belong to that genus.
Consequently, because of the cognition of that [form], one who is commanded, "Bind the cow," does not bind horses and the like.
Furthermore, it is not the case that the universal (jāti), which is the referent of a word, cannot be common to both existence and non-existence;

for although it is eternal by its own nature, it becomes common to existence and non-existence—capable of being related to "is" and "is not"—by virtue of having as its substrata infinite individuals scattered across space and time.
For the existence of a universal consists in its connection with a present individual, while its non-existence consists in its connection with past and future individuals.

Because its negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful, it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); furthermore, its commonality to both existence and non-existence is established otherwise (*anyathāsiddha*).

Since a particular (*vyakti*) possessing a universal (*jāti*) is the object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and not a mere fiction (*alīka*), with what real entity could its nature as the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛttirūpatā*) be held to have a similarity?

Furthermore, what similarity can there be between a false entity—which lacks all causal capacity and is utterly dissimilar—and a real particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) that exists as a positive entity? If you say it is "exclusion of others" (*anyavyāvṛtti*), [we reply: Is this exclusion of others the actual nature of the particular, or something else? It cannot be its nature, because a positive form and exclusion are contradictory. Nor can it be something else, for that would entail the consequence that the particular is not a real entity. Thus, the universal would be nothing other than the particular itself. Consequently, the universal would be a real entity, and the particular would be nothing other than the universal. Therefore, the distinction between the two is lost. Furthermore, since the universal would be the very nature of the particular, it would follow that the universal is also perceived at the time the particular is perceived. Thus, the universal would be perceived even when the particular is not being perceived; and since the universal is eternal, it would follow that the particular is also eternal. Moreover, since the universal is unitary, it would follow that the particular is also unitary. And since the universal is manifold, it would follow that the particular is also manifold. Furthermore, since the universal is non-momentary, it would follow that the particular is also non-momentary. For these reasons, the universal is not distinct from the particular. Therefore, the universal is merely a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). Since it is a conceptual construction, it is not a real entity. Because it is not a real entity, it is not capable of producing an effect. Because it cannot produce an effect, it is not a cause. Because it is not a cause, it does not exist. Thus, the universal is non-existent. Since the universal is non-existent, the relation between the universal and the particular is also non-existent. Because that relation is non-existent, the cognition of the universal is also non-existent. Because that cognition is non-existent, the linguistic convention based upon it is also non-existent. Because that convention is non-existent, the application of words is also non-existent. Because that application is non-existent, the activity of people is also non-existent. Because that activity is non-existent, all worldly affairs are non-existent. Therefore, the universal is a mere conceptual construction. Alternatively, if there is no contradiction between affirmation and negation because they are one and the same, then it is pointless to establish that the unreal (alīka) has the nature of exclusion from others (*anyavyāvṛtti*) by means of negation, on the grounds that it resembles a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
If you argue that it is impossible for the unreal to resemble a particular characteristic because the former is insubstantial (*tuccha*) while the latter exists in an affirmative form,
then— alas!— does the particular characteristic itself possess even an insubstantial aspect by virtue of which it could resemble the insubstantial unreal?

If that were so, then this "Beloved of the Gods," who accepts the coexistence of two contradictory natures—the void and the non-void—within a single particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), would indeed be one of praiseworthy intelligence.

Furthermore, the exclusion of other things (*anyavyāvṛtti*), which is not the actual particular characteristic itself, does not make the excluded thing identical in form to that particular characteristic; for if it did, an ass would also have to be identical in form to both an elephant and a mosquito.
Furthermore, you do not accept that exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is a dharma characterized by its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇadharma*).
This might be argued:
even though the specific characteristic is being determined (*adhyavasīyamāna*), it is not ultimately real (*paramārthasat*).
Moreover, even that [cognition] is imagined;
therefore, its nature as both affirmation and negation is not contradictory.

For the superimposition of contradictory properties is contradictory only in the case of a real entity (*vastu*), not in the case of a non-entity (*avastu*). Consequently, by relinquishing its affirmative form and assuming a negative form, its similarity to the unreal (*alīka*) is established.
As it has been said: "That which is perceived and that which is conceptually determined—both of these are exclusions of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*), not the real entity itself.
Now, what is established by the similarity between one unreal thing and another unreal thing, such as a unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*)?

First of all, there can be no activity directed toward that [unreal object], because what is non-existent cannot be the object of activity. Furthermore, for a conceptualization of an existent thing, there is no similarity with what is non-existent; or, if there were similarity with the non-existent, the admission of an unreal particular (alīka-svalakṣaṇa) would be futile.
Now, we do not maintain that there is another unreal particular, but rather that we merely superimpose upon the unreal itself capacities such as burning or cooking.

That is not its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), because, due to its exclusion from everything else and its unsuitability for association with verbal expression, it does not appear in conceptual cognition.
Furthermore, that which is suitable for association with verbal expression and possesses positive concomitance (*anvayin*) is not a specific characteristic.

Therefore, for those seeking such [objects], one superimposes efficacy upon that which lacks efficacy—namely, the form of the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*) belonging to its own positive concomitants.

We consider it logical that worldly conceptual constructions, which engage those who act within the world, do not deceive the world because they lead to the attainment of an efficacious object through a continuous succession of connections.

Now, as for this superimposition of the capacity for causal efficiency upon that [object] which lacks such efficiency— is it due to its similarity to the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of an observed object possessing causal efficiency, or rather due to the power of beginningless latent predispositions (*vāsanā*)?
In that regard, there is no similarity with a universal (anvayin) which lacks all capacity, by means of a particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) that is capable and excluded from everything else;
for it has been stated that if similarity were based on its occurrence elsewhere (anyavṛtti), it would follow [absurdly] that even a positive entity (vidhirūpa) could be similar,
since there is no difference between that [universal] and such [a positive entity].

However, due to the power of beginningless latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), when that [unreal form] is superimposed, even at the very first perception, there would be the undesirable consequence of a person born on a coconut island knowing the capacity for burning, cooking, and so forth in fire.

If it is argued that the superimposition of that unreal form occurs because of the non-apprehension of the difference between the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of fire— which performs burning, cooking, and so forth— and [the unreal object],
then is this while the particular characteristic is being apprehended, or while it is not being apprehended?

It has already been stated that this is not the case when [the object] is being apprehended, because it lacks the status of being an object for conceptual cognition. Furthermore, even though non-conceptual cognition apprehends reality at that time, it does not cause its own object to enter into the conceptual cognition;
for since the latter is distinct from the former, it is ignorant of the former's nature.

In the same way, even conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*) cannot take the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object, despite the succession of the operations of the immediately preceding non-conceptual [cognition].
This is because it has been stated that its object is an appearance capable of being associated with verbal expression.

If it is argued that, because it arises from an immediately preceding non-conceptual condition, it appears as if it had that [particular] as its object through the succession of its operation, even though it does not actually have that as its object; [the response follows:]

This process might occur in the case of objects consisting of the impressions of past experiences; however, it is not possible in the case of [cognitions] that apprehend imperceptible non-existences arising from the impressions of ignorance (*avidyā*).

Furthermore, even in the case of what arises from the impressions of experience, the conceit of its being the object of that [perception] cannot exist merely through its production therein if the object itself does not appear.

For if the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of fire is not grasped, then by failing to perceive its difference [from other things], there would follow the absurd consequence of superimposing the form of the entire triple world, since there would be no restrictive cause.
For at that time, there would be no distinction between the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of fire and anything else in the three worlds insofar as they are not being perceived;

since [the cognition] is restricted by its arising from a non-conceptual perception whose object is the particular characteristic of fire, there could be no restriction such that this [restriction] is absent in conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of *pradhāna*, *Īśvara*, and so forth, which arise from the latencies of ignorance (*avidyāvāsanā*).
Furthermore, it has already been stated that the superimposition of something upon another is impossible through non-perception.

Therefore, the claim that the externality of the unreal is the object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is an empty statement. Furthermore, just like the form of cognition (*jñānākāra*) and the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), the state of being an unreal object of apprehension cannot be the object of conceptual construction. For this [unreal object] is dependent upon conceptualization; it arises as if arisen when conceptualization has arisen, and perishes as if perished when it has ceased. It appears as if divided by the differences of conceptualization, and thus it is impossible to treat it as a single unity.
If it is argued that this is because differences are not disregarded, then what is its reality even when those differences are disregarded?
If you say "yes" [it is real], then...
In that case, it is not imagined.
Is it not true that even its difference is not intrinsic? For an intrinsic entity is consistent with both difference and non-difference, but a false (alīka) entity is not.
Let it be that its difference is not intrinsic; nevertheless, that false entity, which depends upon imagination, must be understood as distinct from that [intrinsic] difference.
Otherwise, it would follow that [the object] is dependent upon that [conceptualization].

For this alone is the "dependence on conceptualization" (kalpanādhīnatva) of that which is conceptually constructed (vikalpita): namely, its conformity to the diversity or non-diversity of conceptualization. If it were dependent upon that [conceptualization], its status as a conceptual construct would be untenable, leading to the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that it is not unreal.

Let it be so; however, its intrinsic multiplicity and unity [cannot be maintained]. But since it cannot be apprehended as one when it conforms to diverse conceptualizations, it must be apprehended as distinct.
Thus it is established that the false external object is beyond the scope of conceptual construction (*vikalpāgocara*),
because it is unfit for association with verbal expression (*abhilāpasaṃsargāyogyatva*), just like the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) of pleasure and so forth.
For it is unfit for association with verbal expression, because it is impossible to establish a linguistic convention (*samaya*) regarding it, just like the characteristics of pleasure and so forth.

Indeed, the capacity for association with verbal expression is pervaded by the state of being capable of convention (*śakyasamayatā*), for otherwise there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Since the false external objecthood—which differs in each conceptual construction—is excluded, it also excludes the capacity for association with verbal expression; thus, the logical connection (*pratibandha*) is established.
Furthermore, this [false object] must either be of the nature of the exclusion of the non-cow (*agovyāvṛtti*), or a property thereof.

If it is argued that [the universal] has the nature of the exclusion of non-cows (*agovyāvṛtti*), that is not established, for it cannot be apprehended in a cow. Furthermore, since the "non-cow" consists of the negation of a cow, it depends upon the establishment of the cow; thus, the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*) is unavoidable. Alternatively, if it is a property of the cow, let it simply be the positive, real entity of "cowness" (*gotva*); let there be the property in a positive form, for what is the use of a false, negative form?

The proof that those properties possess an ontological reality has been refuted, and it has been established that such [a property] is common to both existence and non-existence; yet, fearing excessive detail, we have fallen into even greater prolixity.
Let this suffice as a crushing of the pride of the nihilists.
This is the *Vārttika* providing the resolution to the doubt: "If it is argued that there is no contradiction because [the term] is used figuratively."
"Because the primary [meaning] is impossible":

everywhere, metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) or superimposition (*samāropa*) is observed to be preceded by the primary meaning; however, in your system (*rāddhānta*), there is no primary object of prescription—whether it be a word or a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—since everything has cessation as its domain.

The point is that it has been demonstrated above that a positive injunction (*vidhi*) as an object of determination is not possible. Furthermore, the metaphorical application (*upacāra*) is not tenable in the theory of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), because both terms would then be primary words (*pradhānaśabda*).
For there is no such thing as "lion-ness" (*siṃhatva*) existing in lion individuals that would not also exist in a young boy (*māṇavaka*).

The meaning is that since the exclusion of qualities such as acting with violence is absent in the boy (*māṇavaka*), the word "lion" would apply to the boy in a primary sense alone, just as it does to individual lions.
"Is it white or non-white? means "is it a horse or the like?"
The meaning is as follows: "Agreement" (saṃpratipatti) is the engagement with the object of an injunction based on trust in the one who issues the injunction;
furthermore, you yourselves admit the existence of a whole distinct from its parts, such as the large numbers of armies, forests, and so forth.
Moreover, since exclusion (apoha) is of the nature of an action, its object must be stated.

The meaning is that the object of the action must be stated; [the question is] "how [can there be understanding] from an exclusion whose object is other? That is, how can there be an understanding of a non-cow from an exclusion (*apoha*) whose object is something other than a cow?
Now, [if it is argued]: "it is 'non-cow' (*ago*)."
(330/2) For there is indeed a certain action which has another as its object;
for example, consciousness takes the self or an object as its object—this is the meaning. [The author] refutes this:
"By what [is it that one asks] 'What is a cow?
For the action of sentient beings is preceded by volitional effort (*cetanā*).

And action characterized by exclusion (*apoha*) is of the nature of negation; furthermore, negation is preceded by prior apprehension. The meaning is that non-cowness has not been attributed to a cow by anyone such that a discerning person would exclude it.
And how is it that there is no understanding of a cow?
The meaning is that this negation expressed by the word "non-cow" (agavīti) does not occur without a prior cognition of a cow;
thus, because superimposition is impossible, the comprehension of the object is not tenable.
The meaning is that a cognition of an object whose nature is exclusion (apoha) is not tenable; [the question is:
is exclusion the denotable, or is it the non-denotable?
The meaning is "by means of a word such as *apoha*.
Alternatively, if it is said "it is the denotable," the meaning is that *apoha* itself is denotable in its own form (*svarūpeṇa*), and not by means of another *apoha*.
This might be the case:
if a word does not function by means of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), then how does a single word for "many" apply to specific instances such as "two" and so forth?
For here, there is no universal called "multiplicity" (*anekatva*) existing in the same way that "cowness" (*gotva*) exists; to this, he says:
Furthermore, because this term "many" (*aneka*) has as its object two or more [entities],
when there is a general apprehension— namely, an apprehension of the generality of "number-ness" (*saṃkhyātva*) excluding oneness— one must rely upon a particular [instance].

The meaning is that it is the generality of "number-ness" itself, excluding oneness, which serves as the cause for the apprehension of the particular instances such as "two" and so forth, and not merely the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*).

For, in the absence of a general term—such as a word for "number" that excludes oneness and expresses number in general—the apprehension of a specific [referent] cannot arise from a particular word through the mere exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) alone; this is how the connection should be understood. This same principle applies to words such as "non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇa*) and the like.
In that case as well, the meaning of the word "brāhmaṇa" is simply the universal of masculinity (*puṃstva-sāmānya*),
because it is the primary [meaning] of both the words "blue" and "lotus."

For it is the exclusion of the non-blue and the non-lotus that the words "blue" and "lotus" primarily express; indeed, there is no relationship of qualifier and qualified between these two, because they are not mutually connected—this is the intended meaning.
By this demonstration, according to this established doctrine, that the words "blue" and "lotus" have primary denotation, [the same applies to] the words "king" and "servant."

The meaning is that, since these two have been explained as being primary, even here there is no relationship of the delimited and the delimiter between the exclusion of a non-king and the exclusion of a non-puruṣa, nor is there a relationship of owner and owned;
this applies also to the case of co-referential terms (*samānādhikaraṇa*).
The meaning is that there is no possibility of words and conceptual constructions coming into contact with an entity that exists as ultimate reality. // 65 //
Manifestation (vyakti) is that which is the substratum of specific qualities; it is material form (mūrti).

For where there is a convergence of individual (vyakti), configuration (ākṛti), and genus (jāti), the definition [of substance] is the non-difference consisting in the determination of the individual.
Therefore, there is no fault even if space and so forth are not included, because configuration is absent therein; such is the opinion of the Bhāṣya.
As the author of the Bhāṣya says: "Not every substance is an individual."
Although gravity and the like are general qualities (*sāmānyaguṇa*), they are nevertheless called specific qualities (*guṇaviśeṣa*) because they distinguish themselves from other qualities.
By the term "non-pervasive" (*avyāpin*),
the [possessor of] dimension of an all-pervading substance is excluded.
That whose parts are fused together and joined with one another is "that which has fused parts" (*mūrcchitāvayava*).
The author of the *Vārttika* raises an objection against the *Bhāṣya* passage beginning with "How, moreover...
by stating "because it is already understood."

The intention of the objection is that since the comprehension of the sentence's meaning is preceded by the comprehension of its own form (svarūpa), the comprehension of that form is also established as being inseparable from the former. [The author] refutes this:
It is not so, because even though there are three kinds of causes (nimitta), the purpose [of the question] is to make known their specific distinctions.

That is to say, although there are three kinds of causes for the application of words, its object is precisely their specific distinctions; that which has the making known of those as its aim or purpose is described in that way.

This is what is meant: having established that the distinction [between the two types of objects] has been explained as the state of being denotable for those things being discussed, that very distinction is now being demonstrated. Thus says the Sūtra.
The sense is that it is because it indicates many meanings.
Here, he introduces the explanation of the Bhāṣya:
"it is manifested" (*vyajyate*).
(332/2) He refutes this with the words "But this is not so.

The subject under discussion is that "the individual (vyakti) is the meaning of a word. In that regard, just as the individual is the meaning of a word for a whole (avayavin), so too must the definition be explained for space (ākāśa) and the like, as well as for upward motion (utkṣepaṇa) and so forth, in such a way that everything is included; otherwise, the author of the Sūtras [would be contradicted].
"Kuśanala might [be the author]; for that reason, he says: 'But we say.
Herein is the explanation."
"Manifestation" (*vyakti*) is the designation of the object to be defined; the remainder is the definition.

Regarding the compound "particular qualities" (*guṇaviśeṣāḥ*), there are two ways of analyzing it: first, as *guṇaśca viśeṣaśca* ("quality and particularity"). By this, generic form (*ākṛti*) is excluded, while color and so forth are included.
Nevertheless, manifestations such as upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*) and the like remain unaccounted for.
Thus is the second analysis:
"particularities of qualities" (guṇaviśeṣāḥ) means particularities distinguished from qualities; that is to say, throwing upwards and so forth, which are excluded from [other] qualities.
Nevertheless, since the substance is not included,
he says:
"the basis."

By supplying the word "that" (tat), the meaning is: substance is that which is the substratum of specific qualities. Regarding the phrase "word by word": the words are "quality," "specific," and "substratum."
Alternatively, the words are "the substratum of the specific qualities" (*guṇaviśe�ṣāṇām āśrayaḥ*).

Or else, "the substratum of the specific qualities": here, "qualities" (*guṇāḥ*) refers to form (*rūpa*) and so forth, while "specifics" (*viśeṣāḥ*)—by implication from "than the qualities"—refers to actions (*karmāṇi*).
The compound *teṣām āśrayaḥ* is indeed a dvandva; by implication, the meaning is understood as "of those [qualities and specifics]."
In this context, "mūrcchita" means "mūrchana," which is a connection; and here, that [connection] is inherence (samavāya). // 66 //
The generic form (ākṛti) is that which expresses the characteristic marks of a genus (jāti).
That by which both the genus and the characteristics of the genus are expressed is "form" (ākṛti).
The configuration of the head, hands, and so forth is the form; it expresses the genus, such as "humanity" and the like.

The collection of the head, nose, forehead, and so forth, which is the mark of the genus "humanity," indicates the head; as the *Bhāṣya* states: "By means of the head and the foot, they infer [the presence of] a cow. Although the nature of being a cow (*gotva*) is indeed directly perceived and not manifested by the configuration (*ākṛti*), nevertheless, the statement "they infer" is addressed to those who hold a contrary view; it does not mean that every genus is invariably indicated by its configuration.

For the genus (jāti) found in clay, gold, silver, and so forth, is manifested by specific forms (rūpa-viśeṣa) and not by configuration (ākṛti); whereas the genus of being a Brahmin and the like is manifested by birth (yoni). The genus of ghee, oil, and the like is manifested by smell or taste;

for this very reason, there is no "oil-ness" (tailatva) in mustard seeds and the like, because their manifestors—smell and taste—are absent. The application of the word "oil" to them is merely figurative (bhākta). The genus of milk is likewise manifested by taste alone; for this very reason, curdled milk (āmikṣā) possesses the nature of milk, but whey (vājina) does not, because the particular taste that manifests it is absent in the whey.
And because it exists in the curdled milk (āmikṣā). // 67 //
Genus (jāti) has as its essence the production of similar [cognitions].

"Produced" means that which brings forth; a genus (*jāti*) is that which, being common to diverse things, necessarily produces a uniform cognition. However, it should not be understood that everything which produces a uniform cognition is a genus, because of the deviation [of this definition] in the case of "cooks" (*pācaka*) and the like. Furthermore, this definition should be understood as applying merely by way of distinguishing [the universal] from the individual (*vyakti*) and the configuration (*ākṛti*), but not in every respect.
But for one who, out of impudence, disputes even what is perceptible, he states the following inferences:
"The cognition of recurrence with respect to cows and so forth..."

(333/18) "Designation" (*vyapadeśa*) means the qualification of one relation by another related thing, as in the case where a person is designated by the phrase "the king's. Regarding the statement "the cognition of the persistence of 'cowness' in a cow," previously, only the cognition of persistence was taken as the subject of the argument.
But here, since there is the cognition of the recurrence of "cowness" in a cow, there is no tautology.
Regarding the word "kīrtita" (declared):
just as gender is intended to be expressed because it is internal [to the meaning].
"Elsewhere, the suffix follows the gender of the original term (*yathāliṅgaṃ pratyayaḥ*);
therefore, one should not suspect that the neuter gender [of *napuṃsakam*] would be overridden by the rule *napuṃsakamanapuṃsakena*.
Thus ends the second Āhnika of the second Adhyāya in the *Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā* composed by the venerable Miśra Vācaspati.
The second chapter is completed.
Nyāyasūtra 3.1.1: [The self exists] because by means of both seeing and touching, there is the apprehension of a single object.
Regarding this, the commentary states: "The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have been examined; now the object of valid cognition (*prameya*) is to be examined.

This recapitulation of what has preceded is intended to show that the examination of the means of valid cognition—which has already occurred—is the cause for the examination of the object of valid cognition which is about to occur.
For it is by means of the *pramāṇa* that the *prameya* is examined, and not by anything else.
And that [object], if unexamined, is not capable of serving for the examination of the object of cognition (*prameya*).
Therefore, the examination of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the cause; the examination of the object of cognition possesses that cause.
Why, then, is the object of cognition twelvefold from the very beginning?
Since it is the self alone that is examined and not any other object of cognition, he says:
"And that [is] 'the self and so forth'"; thus, the self is investigated.
For among the objects of cognition, the self alone was first mentioned and defined; therefore, in accordance with that, the self alone is examined first, and not the other objects of cognition.

And although here he proposes an investigation into the self (*ātman*) itself by way of its essential nature (*svarūpa*), nevertheless, since the investigation of the object to be defined (*lakṣya*) occurs through the investigation of its definition (*lakṣaṇa*), it should be understood as an investigation of the definition alone.
How this investigation of the definition of the self is to be conducted will be demonstrated further below.
The author of the Vārttika explains this as follows:
"Because of immediate succession.
But what is the purpose of the examination of the objects of cognition (*prameya*)? For wise people do not examine things without a purpose; therefore, he says:
Regarding the phrase "that which is the object of the conceit of 'I'":
the term "conceit of 'I'" (ahaṅkāra) indicates a false cognition whose objects are the self and so forth.
It was stated in the second aphorism that the perception of the self as non-different from the body and so forth indeed sets the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) in motion;
by this, the purposefulness of the investigation of the objects of cognition (prameya) has been demonstrated.
Here, the author of the Commentary (bhāṣyakāra) has shown doubt, which is the preliminary form of inquiry.
Is the self merely the aggregate of the body, senses, mind, and intellect?
And the cause for this doubt has already been stated regarding designation (*vyapadeśa*).

Even though in the case of a tree and a palace—which are wholes (*avayavin*) and aggregates (*samudāya*) distinct from their parts (*avayava*) and constituents (*samudāyin*)—there is a designation by means of the part and the constituent respectively, nevertheless, the absence of a whole and the nature of an aggregate are not distinct from the parts and the constituents themselves.
An example from the perspective of another who holds this view should be examined.
The author of the Vārttika asks this in order to raise an objection.
"What, then, belongs to this?"— the reply is "What is the body?"—
he objects, "No."

The meaning is that doubt arises from the perception of a subject possessing common properties, and not from its non-perception. He provides the resolution: "It is not [the case] according to the *icchādi-sūtra*."
For it has been shown that desire and the rest are signs of the self because they are effects;

yet, while those very signs demonstrate the desirer, they do not examine him. Thus, an inquiry is appropriate: is the desirer established as distinct from the body and the senses, or rather as non-different from them?

Furthermore, he says "because there is no disagreement" (*avipratipatteśca*) to show that this subject (*dharmin*), denoted by the term "self," is established in all systems (*sarvatantra-siddha*); the dispute among proponents concerns only whether it is distinct from or non-distinct from the body.

[Objection: But surely, since others have put forward proofs for the non-existence of the self—such as its not being produced and so forth—how can there be no disagreement regarding its existence? To this, he replies:
And because there is an absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes non-existence.

He who is in disagreement regarding the subject (*dharmin*) is not a proponent at all; for one who is in disagreement regarding the subject possesses no means of valid cognition whatsoever, since every such [cognition] is unestablished in its basis (*āśrayāsiddhi*) and thus lacks the status of a valid cognition.
Furthermore, since non-existence is defined in dependence upon existence, it cannot be defined as being absolutely non-existent.
Therefore, one who asserts the non-existence of the subject (dharmin) is neither a worldly person nor an investigator;
he should be disregarded like a madman.
[The opponent] now presents a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for those who argue that the subject is unestablished.
"It is not that it does not exist" [is what he] refutes;
therein, [he refutes the view] that "the self does not exist."
Furthermore, others have maintained:
"The referent of a word, established by conceptual construction arising from beginningless predispositions, is a threefold subject (dharmin) based on existence, non-existence, or both."
An example based on existence is "blue"; an example based on non-existence is "the horn of a hare"; an example based on both is "formless.
For consciousness is formless, and so too is the horn of a hare.
When that which is external is to be proven as non-apprehensible, this [reason] is its non-perception.

Thus, because the word is employed, it is not the non-existence of that very thing; this conceptualization of a self does not have an external object as its basis. Just as the conceptualization of blue has an external blue object as its basis, the conceptualization of a self does not have an external object as its basis in that same way.
This is the meaning.
In this regard, you should be asked as follows:
is it merely the external material cause of the conceptualization of a self that is being negated, or is it the external self that serves as the material cause?

In the former case, let there be no proving of what is already established; for what of ours is undermined by the notion that conceptual construction has external blue and so forth as its material cause? But in the latter alternative, where is this external self established, such that its status as the material cause of conceptual construction is being denied?
If it is established somewhere, then there can be no absolute negation of it.

If it is unestablished (*asiddha*), how can there be a negation of that which is not cognized? If you argue that what is cognized is negated with respect to the external world—just as Caitra, who is known to exist, is negated in the house by being found on the square—then even so, he is not negated where he is actually cognized; as you yourselves have stated: "There is no absence of that very thing [where it is perceived] because of the employment of words."

Furthermore, since an external self has not been presented by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), it cannot be negated because there is no possibility [of its existence]. If it is argued that even though it is not presented, it is nonetheless apprehended (*adhyavasita*) and thus indeed possible [to negate], [we reply]: what, then, is this so-called "apprehension" of conceptual construction?

If it is argued that there is an external superimposition—either of the form of the object itself or of something false—upon what is apprehended, which is distinct from the act of apprehension, [we reply:
it is strange to claim that conceptual constructions, which do not have the external as their object, can superimpose the external.
For it has been stated more than once that one who does not know both the locus of superimposition (*āropaviṣaya*) and the thing to be superimposed (*āropyam*) cannot perform a superimposition.
Moreover, just as that which is perceived, though false, cannot be denied precisely because it is being perceived, so too is its externality.

If you argue that it is denied because it is false, then is even that falsity itself real? For you have resolved to deny externality by transgressing that very [falsity]. The apprehension of the distinction of externality and the determination thereof do not entail [the reality of that falsity].
Thus, [the self] is not within the scope of negation.
Nor is it correct to say that the self— which is the cause of cognition and ultimately real— is being negated while being superimposed as something external.
For if consciousness consists of everything, there can be no apprehension of anything external because of the possibility of superimposing it [upon consciousness].

Furthermore, if an absolutely non-existent external object were apprehended as having the nature of consciousness, then what wrong has been done by that which is likewise non-existent—namely, that which lacks the nature of consciousness yet is apprehended by consciousness—such that it should not be its object? Thus, it would follow that the doctrine of consciousness (vijñānavāda) would be utterly abandoned.

Furthermore, this self, which persists through prior and subsequent times, cannot possibly be of the nature of a momentary conceptual construction, such that its form could be negated as being external.
Therefore, it is logical that what is perceived elsewhere is superimposed upon something else and then negated.

And that superimposition arises from its own causes in some cases, while in others it is negated—just as, for example, the cognition of silver produced by a defect in the sense organ is negated with respect to mother-of-pearl by the thought, "This is not silver."
In some cases, however, [the negation] is adventitious (*āhārya*), as in "Caitra is not here.

Therefore, since conceptualization regarding another place, time, or entity, as well as within consciousness, is impossible for that which is absolutely non-existent, such a superimposition (*samāropa*) does not exist at all in the case of the self (*ātman*). If it were to exist, how could there be an absolute negation?
Consequently, there is a contradiction between the two words "self" and "does not exist."
Although the words are "ātma" and "nāsti," nevertheless, by intending the compound "nāsti" as a single word, the use of the dual number in "pade" is justified.
Alternatively, intending that "that by which a meaning is reached (padyate) or understood (gamyate)" is a "pada," even a collection of words is called a "pada."

Although there is a negation of jars and the like in other locations and so forth, nevertheless, this will not apply to the self absolutely; for one negation does not necessarily entail another negation. Therefore, he says: "And all this... [is as follows].

It has been established above that it is impossible to superimpose what has not been experienced; thus, nowhere has it been stated that the self is the substrate for anything else, such as the "lump" (piṇḍa) and so forth.
[The author] asks: "What is this?"
(337/2) The meaning is this: that which does not exist anywhere is absolutely non-existent, and since this [object] is such, it is therefore absolutely non-existent.
The reply is: "It is not that it does not exist.
For the statement "it does not exist anywhere" does not negate the sentence itself in its own form, because it negates only a specific location.
The objector asked:
"What kind of verbal formulation is this?
The respondent replied:
"This is the manner of expression" means this refers to the meaning that is about to be explained;
for that purpose, he says:
Regarding the phrase "as it truly is" (*yathābhūtam*):
the point is that the existence of entities is not pervaded by spatial location, such that the absence of spatial location would necessarily entail the absence of existence.
Nor, moreover, is there a negation of a specific time.
Each individual time that serves as a counter-correlative to another time is a specific temporal division; yet even its negation is inappropriate in the case of the Self.
For time does not serve the purpose of delimitation for the eternal Self in the same way it does for jars and other such things.

Indeed, a jar possessing the absence of destruction (pradhvaṃsābhāva) is said to be "non-existent" [in the past], and likewise a jar possessing prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) is said to be "will exist" [in the future]; however, the Self is not like that.

The past is prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), the future is posterior destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*), and the pot is present; however, the Self (*ātman*) is not like that. Therefore, time does not apply to it for the purpose of delimitation. Time exists as manifested by actions delimited from the past and the future, which belong to those things that are eternally existent—since the Self exists, and space exists—and therefore, because the three times that serve as delimiters do not apply to it, [it is eternal].

There is no negation of the three times. Since it is impossible to negate the present—which is manifested by an action distinct from the past and the future—it is established that there is no negation of time with respect to the self (*ātman*). Regarding the phrase "and the negation of the self": for the word "self" is well-established in the world; indeed, by means of this [word], some object is expressed. That by which no object whatsoever is expressed ought to be considered meaningless (*apārthaka*).
"What similarity can there be between the non-existent and the existent?"—this is the sense [of the objection]:
"In that case, according to your own tenet, even the non-existent object of cognition (*aprameya*) is devoid of all designations (*sarvopākhyārahita*).

Now, if it is argued that the status of being the self (*ātmatva*) is merely imagined in relation to the body and so forth, and that the negation is intended to show that "the body and so forth are not the self," to this he replies:
And [the notions of] "self" and "generality.
Now, regarding "the body and so forth":
first of all, from the ultimate standpoint, the *ahaṃkāra* (I-maker) has the body and so forth as its object, because of such cognitions as "I am fat" and "I am fair."
Having conceptualized this very [aggregation] as "self," one becomes inverted; accordingly, one designates it and engages in conventional usage.
This inversion—[the notion] that "there is no self"—is what is being negated and refuted.
"Thus, regarding the body and so forth":

for one who does not accept the existence of the object upon which the superimposition of "I-ness" (*ahaṃkāra*) rests, such a superimposition is not logically possible; therefore, the meaning is that there is a contradiction in negating that [existence].
Because darkness (*tamas*) is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the four [elements].

Form, taste, smell, and touch—these four, having transformed into the form of jars and so forth—are the material cause of those; it is not *bha*. It is called "material cause" (*upādāna*) because it is that which is taken up (*upādīyate*).
The reading "because it is of a nature to be accepted" (*upādeyarūpatvāt*) found in some versions is quite appropriate;
the meaning is that there is a contradiction with this established doctrine (*siddhānta*) of the Vātsīputrīyas, who are Vaibhāṣikas.
The rest is easy to understand.
Now, as for this "negation of existence" (*bhāvapratiṣedha*):
it is not merely a negation of birth, but rather the meaning is that the existence—the being or ontological reality (*sattā*)—of the self (*ātman*) is negated;
for no property (*dharma*) independent [of the self] is observed other than through inherence (*samavāya*).
A *nikāya* is a collection (*saṃghāta*) of gods, humans, animals, and so forth, existing without any hierarchical superiority or inferiority; the meaning is "by those distinguished from that.
Regarding the phrase "the effect or the cause":

if the horn is a constituent part (*avayava*), then it is the cause; however, if it is not a constituent part because—like hair, nails, and so on—it does not initiate [a new substance], then it is the effect, and thus it arises from that.
Even though this point has already been stated, he speaks again by way of a further inquiry, saying:
"one who says 'this rabbit's horn does not exist'";
[the meaning is that] there is a negation of the universal, which is a negation of the mere connection with a horn.

The negation of specific [attributes] is the negation of the relationship characterized by the nature of cause and effect. "Conforming to the distinctions in the intrinsic nature of the object" means that the mental consciousness of "I" conforms to whatever distinction in the intrinsic nature of its object— the self— there may be, such as the characteristics of being an agent or an enjoyer, as in the cognitions "I know," "I eat," and so forth.

This is what is meant: the nature of the self alone is not the object of self-knowledge; for if that were the case, since the self would lack the possession of a fruit resulting from an action inherent in another, it would lack the status of being an object (*karman*), and consequently, knowledge—which is pervaded by that status—would also necessarily cease to exist. However, when knowledge has the self as its object in the same way it has [its] attributes, then because the attributes possess the possession of a fruit resulting from an action inherent in another, the knowledge that is pervaded by them also ceases.
Since cognition, which has the self and phenomena as its objects, also takes the self as its own domain, it is well said that it conforms to the distinctions in the intrinsic nature of its objects.

Regarding the phrase "having the *ahaṃkāra* as its objective support" (*ālambana*): that by means of which something is apprehended is the "objective support," namely, cognition; and by means of the subject, the *ahaṃkāra*, one perceives the object.
He explains:
"Is it not the case that one thinks, 'I am fair-skinned'?
He refutes this, saying: "We say that it is not so."
We have not stated that mere designation is the proof for the existence of a self distinct from the body and so forth, which would render it inconclusive;
rather, it is direct experience.
And that [experience] does not exist with respect to the body and other such objects of the "this" (idam).

Furthermore, the notion of "I" has as its object that which is undifferentiated from this [body]; however, the body and so forth are made the objects of the "I" either through the elision of the possessive suffix *matup* or through the metaphorical attribution of non-difference.

The expression "my self," on the other hand, is a mere designation; the possessive particle *mama* is not primary there as it is in the case of the body and so forth, because no distinction is perceived therein.
Rather, the sense of "mine-ness" (*mamakāra*) with respect to the self should be understood as being like the expression "the head of Rāhu."
For this very reason, he says: "belonging to me" (*mamapratyaya*);
it is not merely the notion of "mine" (*mamakāra*). Therefore, everything is delightful.
"Contrary apprehension" (*vipratipatti*) means a contradictory cognition, that is to say, a sublated [cognition]. "What is the meaning of 'proof' (*sādhana*)?
asks: what is the meaning of the word *sādhana*?

Now, as for the claim that non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) also does not exist: a property (*dharma*) consisting of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*) is contradictory with non-existence, but one consisting of a negative entity (*asadrūpa*) is not; this is because both share the same nature. [The author] refutes this:
"What is the meaning of the proof for non-apprehension? means: what is the sense of being a means of proof (sādhana) for a non-apprehension that is non-existent and void? [The opponent] objects:
Now, regarding the phrase "of the imagined" (kalpitasya):
the non-apprehension is not a mere void, but rather it is a distinct reality that exists; however, because it has the imagined as its locus, it is not "unestablished in its locus" (āśrayāsiddha).
This [objection] he refutes by means of a dilemma.
"How [can it be] of the imagined?"—

the meaning is that a real non-apprehension (*tāttvikanupalabdhi*), which has ultimate reality as its locus, cannot be a property (*dharma*) of a subject (*dharmin*) that possesses an imagined existence. He raises the second alternative.
Now, with the words "by way of non-existence," he refutes [the objection] by establishing that non-apprehension is proven.

The ultimate existence of that which is imagined through non-existence must be admitted, because it is impossible to imagine non-existence in the absence of existence; and thus, the non-apprehension of a substratum for entities is indeed established in its true sense.

However, for the very purpose of this [non-apprehension], that ultimate non-existence of itself is not established, because you yourselves admit that non-existence is merely conceptual—this is the meaning.
Furthermore, having imagined the self—which is actually non-existent—to be existent, he has resolved to prove its absolute non-existence through non-perception (*anupalabdhi*).
Yet, this is not established for him by means of a non-perception that possesses the same properties (*sadharma*) [as the subject].
For it is never possible to establish the ultimate reality of a post’s nature in a person by means of an imagined property of a post; thus he says:
And for what purpose is this "self" [posited]?
It is because it must be distinct from words such as "form" (rūpa) and so forth.
For if it were said merely that it is because [the self] is a word (*padatvāt*), it would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to words such as "form"; therefore, [the qualification] was stated.
Regarding the phrase "provided that it is other than the words *rūpa* and so forth":

if one were to say simply "because it consists of a single word," it would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to the words *rūpa* and so forth; therefore, it is specified as "provided that it is other than the words *rūpa* and so forth. Nevertheless, this term "form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness" is distinct from the term that denotes form and so forth—namely, the non-compounded term beginning with "form, feeling, perception, consciousness," and so on. It is other than that [non-compounded term].
Because [the reason] is thus inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), he stated "one" (*eka*).

By that, the argument is as follows: whatever single word is distinct from those words denoting form and so forth is the denoter of something distinct from form and so forth, just like the word "pot" (*ghaṭa*); and the word "self" (*ātman*) is likewise; therefore, it too is such.
Regarding the phrase "by this": the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*), which is an undifferentiated cognition of "this," has been explained precisely as being established by the word "self" (*ātman*).
He raises an objection, saying: "It is unestablished."
The meaning is that when one says "jar," it is only form and the other [sensory qualities] delimited by the single function of fetching water that are being designated;
there is no such thing as a "jar" existing apart from form and the rest. [The author] refutes this:
Regarding this, it has been said:
"Because darkness (tamas) is of the nature of that which is to be accepted."
Just as "dāya" (to be given) denotes that which is to be given, so too by the term "upādāya" (having appropriated), that which is to be appropriated is expressed.

Thinking that the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) has stated that [the word] "darkness" possesses an object—that is, it has a referent—the opponent raises this objection: "In the case of the word 'darkness' having an object..."

Even though there is no lack of an object [for cognition] even when its object is a non-entity (*abhāva*), nevertheless, conforming to the conventional conceit of place and time, he avoids [the objection] by stating that there is no further example for the meaning of the Sūtra.

The meaning is this: previously, when it was to be proven that the self does not provide assistance, the absence of an example was stated; now, however, it is being stated again. He points out [the following].
Now, regarding the term "self" (ātman): whatever consists of the nature of phonemes is entirely a subject of impermanence, just like words such as "pot" (ghaṭa) and so forth.
Thus, since [the self] would be impermanent, there would be only the cognition of that [impermanent thing], and not a self; the meaning is that, as a result, this is a negation of the self.
He refutes this as well with the words "even so" (tathāpi).
The meaning is that the word "eternal" (nitya) first denotes eternity; otherwise, there could be no negation of it.
He raises an objection with "atha" (now/if).
To exclude the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), he specifies that the object is "distinct from the body and so forth.
He refutes this with "tathāpi" (even so).

The meaning is that your established doctrine—that there is nothing beyond the five aggregates, beginning with form—is contradicted by the acceptance of something additional to those. "If [the argument were] apart from the intended object" means that for the proponent, the intended object is the fact that the collection of body, sense-faculties, intellect, and sensations exists for the sake of another; for the eyes and so forth exist for the sake of another.

While this is being said, the fact that a composite is for the sake of another—which is established here by the force of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*)—is pervaded by this intended meaning;

however, it is not what is directly intended to be expressed. Likewise, if one objects regarding the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) by superimposing upon the intended meaning that which is merely pervaded by the intention, then all inference would be destroyed. This will be demonstrated more skillfully in the *Īśvarasiddhi*.
Now, it is argued that [the opponent's position] is sublated by inference.

It is both the inference from "being a composite" (saṃghātatva), which— aided by a *tarka* consisting of a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) against the undesired consequence characterized by the established definition— is opposed to the intended thesis of being for the sake of another as a composite, and the inference from the existence of breath and so forth (*prāṇādi-sattva*), which serves as its sublater.

And for the author of the Vārttika, who asserts that "one part [is related] to other parts," it is intended that there is no whole (*avayavin*) because heterogeneous things do not initiate [a composite].
And [this applies] to those things that stand in neither the relation of effect nor cause (*akāryakāraṇabhūta*).
For just as one who has seen a brindled cow (*kālākṣī*) has a recognition (*pratisaṃdhāna*) upon seeing a healthy cow (*svastimatī*), yet there is no relation of cause and effect between these two.

This is the meaning. One's own consciousness (caitanya) belongs to the self because, while possessing independence, it is not fixed [in one specific form], just like the eye and other sense organs. The reason is that that single entity which is perceived as the underlying thread throughout valid cognition, doubt, error, and memory is the conscious one, because, while possessing independence, it is not fixed.
That which is insentient does not abide in independence, just like the eye and other such organs; this is a reason based on dissimilar exclusion (*vyatireka*).
If one were to state merely "because of non-abiding," it would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the mind (*manas*); therefore, it is specified as "while being independent.
Alternatively, he says that there is no need for "non-abiding"—let independence alone suffice as the proof for sentience.
"The self is not insentient," because it is experienced as the thread running through perception, doubt, error, and memory.
He observes:
even an argument that has already been refuted, he brings forward again in another manner and refutes it once more,
as in the case of the proof for the eternity of earth and so forth.
The commentary states that "they have different causes" (bhinnanimittau):
those two whose causes are different sense organs; and "having infinite agents"—meaning having the Self as their sole agent.
"Having the same object"—the meaning is that a single substance is the object. // 1 //
NyS 3.1.2: No, because there is a fixed determination of objects.
The sūtra of the prima facie position: "Not so—because of non-perception" (Sūtra 2).
The meaning is as follows: that whose presence and absence are followed by the presence and absence of cognition is sentient.
Since those [presence and absence] follow the presence and absence of the sense organs, it is the sense organs themselves that are sentient; this is the [opponent's] position.

However, the statement of the established doctrine (*siddhāntabhāṣya*) is not a valid reason because it is doubtful. Positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), when established otherwise than through mere causality, are the means of knowledge for [the existence of] a cause in general, but they do not establish that the agent is sentient or that the instrument is sentient. This is the sense.
NyS 3.1.3: Precisely because of the establishment of that [cognition], the existence of the self is proven; therefore, [the opponent's argument] is not a valid refutation.
And he says that the determination of objects is contradictory because it proves the insentience of the sense organs and so forth:
"As for what was said... [this is] the refutation of that (Sūtra 3).

The explanation of the term "omniscient" (*sarvajña*) is as follows: he is the grasper of all objects; that is, he is the grasper of those objects which belong to all the sense faculties. Since other sense faculties and other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have restricted domains, it is established that even one who perceives only what is proximate is omniscient. In this regard, there is the following proof:
The unique characteristic is called the "mark of recognition" (abhijñāna), and that cannot be denied because it is established by experience.
The construction of the sentence is: "the activity of consciousness is cited as a mark of recognition that cannot be denied."
The meaning is that it has an indefinite sequence and an indefinite order.

Regarding the phrase "a collection of objects consisting of many referents": that collection of objects (*arthajāta*) which has multiple things (*anekapadārtha*) as its referent (*viṣaya*) is described in that way.
In some places, the reading is "the multitude of objects consisting of various categories," which is indeed easy to understand.
As for the phrase "only the generic form" (ākṛtimātram): [it refers to the following].
The meaning is that it is a mere generality.

Thus, this function of consciousness, by excluding itself from the body and so forth, establishes a conscious entity distinct from them; therefore, it is established that the body and so forth cannot be the substratum of desire and the like. // 3 //
Because there is an absence of sin when the body is burned.

The commentator introduces another sutra to show that the self is distinct from the body and so forth, and is not merely the aggregate of the body and its constituents: "Because of the body... (Sūtra 4).
"Because it would follow that there is an absence of sin in the taking of life.

Although this is not an undesirable consequence for those who maintain that consciousness is an emergent property of the elements (*bhūtacaitanika*), it must nevertheless be understood as directed against the Śākyas, for they do indeed accept that sin is produced by the taking of life.
And thus, while it should have been said that "the intellect is not the self," the mention of the body and so forth is made because of the diverse intentions of men.

If someone who maintains that consciousness is derived from the primary elements (*bhūtacaitanika*) should not accept the sin committed by taking life, it should be understood that the refutation against him is for this very purpose.
[Vārttika:
There would be the faults of [sin] accruing to one who did not commit it and of [merit] perishing for one who did.
Thus [it is said]:
the meaning is that for one who has not committed an act of taking life, there would be the arrival of sin, and for one by whom it was committed, there would be its destruction.
It is a general rule that the fruit enjoined by the scripture accrues to the performer; however, where the scripture declares the fruit to belong to another—

as in the case of the Śrāddha, the Vaiśvānara sacrifice, and so forth— let it be that the fruit of the Śrāddha performed by the son goes to the father, or that the fruit of the Jāteṣṭi performed by the father goes to the son.

Cultivation is the formative force (*saṃskāra*) that serves as the cause for mindfulness. Regarding the phrase "by which body": the meaning is that a certain continuum of consciousness, characterized by a particular body, experiences the fruit even when it exists within another body.
"Because of the synthesis of conditions that have a single object.
This has been explained as follows: just as when a dancer moves her brow, many people synthesize [the movement] as one.
"Because [the object] is perceived in all its states."
(352/7) Because the parts of the seed are perceived in all states, whereas they would not be perceived if it were in the state of atoms;
therefore, the parts of the seed being cooked do not become atoms at the time of the arising of the sprout. Rather, the meaning is that the whole (avayavin) itself is what is cooked.

Thinking that the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) has stated that the parts of a seed in the state of atoms are not capable of producing something characterized by a specific genus such as "seed-ness," [the opponent] shows this by saying,
"If, then... [The proponent] refutes this, saying, "Not so, because the answer has already been given by this very [argument]."

In order to characterize those parts of a seed that belong to the same class as seeds for the sake of reconnection (*pratisaṃdhāna*), we have refuted the analysis of seed-parts down to the level of atoms; however, at the commencement of a kalpa, there is no reconnection of atoms. For there is no rule of reconnection such that those very same atoms which began a seed in a previous creation must begin it again now, rather than others.

However, the intention is that [the qualities] also arise from other [causes].
