"He avoids [this objection] because there is no obstruction" means that composite substances possess internal spaces. Now, as to why this penetration of parts does not cause the destruction of the substance, he says:
And if this [world] were to enter into the constituent parts [of the vessel],
then when the vessel is destroyed, the water contained within it would have no place to remain at all.
But if there were an interval, only as much water would vibrate within the vessel as is necessary for the perception of a cold touch to occur externally; and by that measure,

there would be no persistence [of the water] therein due to the ripening of time, whereas in the case of destruction, there would be an immediate cessation of the water contained in the vessel— this is the meaning.
He raises an objection: "There is no equal perception when a substance is concealed behind a crystal vessel.

If it is argued that "the action [of the self] is for the sake of [thinking], 'May I be happy,'" then even though the aggregates (*skandhas*) are perishable, this person—under the influence of the beginningless impressions of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsanā*)—conceives of a single being as the locus of the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) and thinks, "May I be happy; may I not suffer."
The meaning is that [the series] proceeds thirstily.
He refutes this by stating, "Because it has not been experienced.

And just as momentary cognitions, due to their lack of mutual communication, lack the capacity for reconnection (*pratisandhāna*), we have already established this in the section concerning the definition of the self (*ātman*).
It is not the case that [the future] does not arise because of the existence of what has not yet arisen;

rather, it is logical that a moment of cognition, when accompanied by the maturation of the holy life (*brahmacarya*) and so forth, produces a subsequent moment of cognition that is capable, and that [subsequent] moment does not fail to produce another moment of cognition.
Thus, there is no non-arising of the future, and the destruction of an incapable moment occurs by its very nature.
Because it is logically untenable for the arising of an incapable moment to either depend upon or not depend upon auxiliary causes;
how this is so will be demonstrated on the occasion of the refutation of the theory of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*). // 4 //
NyS 3.1.5: Its absence [of smoke] would also occur upon the burning of a living body, because of its permanence.

The nihilist (*vaināśika*), in order to demonstrate the impossibility of both violence and its fruit even within the Sāṃkhya position—just as he did regarding the Naiyāyika position—sets forth the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) concerning the occurrence of violence and its fruit, stating: "But this [is] violence, [arising] from the individual (*vyakti*). (355/7)
The meaning is that only an existing effect is manifested by its cause, but what is non-existent is not produced. [The opponent] refutes this, saying "no.

This threefold transformation—of quality (*dharma*), characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and state (*avasthā*)—is not distinct from the eternal substratum (*dharmī*); thus, the impermanence resulting from transformation is contradicted by the permanence of the substratum.
The meaning is that, if one accepts the impermanence of the substratum (dharmin) in order to avoid contradiction, the faults stated regarding the position of the Vaināśikas would follow.
[Regarding the word] "guṇa": [it means] a quality.

"Rectitude and curvature are indeed qualities that are specific types of accumulation, conjunction, and disjunction; they are experienced as arising and passing away even while the conjunction that initiates the substance remains.
Having thus formulated this refutation of the Naiyāyika position against the Sāṃkhya position, he asks the Naiyāyika: "Now, [regarding] the eternal self...
(356/10). —The Naiyāyika.
He said:
"Pleasure and pain.
The meaning is that pleasure and pain, which are impermanent attributes of the self, are produced by merit and demerit—two impermanent attributes of the self that are distinct from the eternal self.
This is what is meant:
the very conferral of impermanent properties upon the eternal is the benefit [conferred], but not the production of the eternal's own nature, by which it would become impermanent;
and the property is distinct from the substratum, but not identical with the substratum's intrinsic nature.

Just as, despite the lack of distinction in their difference, the causal relationship exists only between fire and smoke and not between fire and a camel due to the necessity of the nature of things (*vastusvabhāva*), so too, despite the lack of distinction in their difference, the relationship of property and its locus (*dharmadharmibhāva*) exists only between the self and merit or demerit, and not between the self and space, or between merit and space. Only a brief indication has been stated here; the detailed exposition, however, is found in the *Kṣaṇabhaṅgabhaṅga* under the heading "not because of inconclusiveness" (*anekāntāt*).

The inconclusiveness [of the reason] was stated on the basis of the firmness of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) held by the opponent which grasps the permanence of atoms; however, it is not the case that in the Buddhist tenet system the atom is permanent.
Therefore, out of dissatisfaction with that [previous argument], he states another proof [for impermanence]:
"And the skin is impermanent."
And because stones and the like, which possess those [parts], persist;
there is no means of valid cognition for destruction when the cause of destruction is absent.

Furthermore, in the case of stones and such, destruction is not perceived prior to the disjunction of parts or the destruction [of the whole]; and the refutation of the theory of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) will be established later—this is the intended meaning.
Regarding those which have begun their activity, it is said that they do not initiate a different substance;
thus, a distinction is stated from the conjunction that initiates a composite whole (*avayavin*).

"And there is an absence of an illustrative example regarding modification" means that there is no modification of the essential nature of the substratum (*dharmin*) which does not perish apart from the arising of a property (*dharma*). He raises an objection with the words, "If it is so..."

The meaning is: if one should suspect that such a modification does not belong to the self—that is, that the modification [of the self] is not like the modification of jars and the like when their blackness ceases and redness arises; [the author] refutes this with the words:
"Even in the case of the self."
The modification is not only something graspable by the external senses; rather, it is merely the arising of another property, and that exists even in the self. // 5 //
Not so, because of the destruction of the effect, its substratum, and its agent.
"Either impairment or destruction.
(358/8) Just as one destroys by striking the body, so too one destroys by uprooting the eye and other faculties.
He asks: "From what [source] is this known?"
The intention of the Nihilist (Vaināśika) is that since injury is impossible by way of its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*), metaphorical injury (*bhāktī hiṃsā*) is not tenable.
The reply is: "Because of the experience of the fruit of injury.

For even according to the Nihilist, since entities (*bhāva*) are subject to instantaneous dissolution (*viśarāru*), injury to their own nature cannot be produced by a cause; rather, it is the production of something distinct [from the previous state].

One should say "harm" (*hiṃsā*) there as well, because the operation of a causal factor is possible; and thus, since harm is metaphorically attributed there too, and since this metaphorical status is no different in both cases, that position which is free from the faults of the loss of what was done (*kṛtahāna*) and the acquisition of what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*) must be accepted.
And that is the position of eternalism (*nityatva*).
Therefore, by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), its establishment [is reached]:
agency (*kartṛtva*) is the inherence (*samavāya*) of knowledge, desire to act (*cikīrṣā*), and effort (*prayatna*).
For one who is ignorant of the means and their operations is not an agent even if desiring to act; likewise, one who is knowledgeable but lacks the desire to act is not an agent.

Likewise, even one who desires to act is not an agent if, due to laziness, they do not exert effort. Regarding the phrase "the inherence of the cognition of pleasure and pain," it should be understood as "one's own pleasure and pain."
For yogins indeed possess direct perception of the pleasure and pain belonging to others, yet they are not experiencers [of those states].
NyS 3.1.7: Because there is recognition by the other [eye] of what was seen by the left [eye].
For this reason as well, the self is distinct from the body and so forth; why?
Because of [the perception of] the left [eye by the right]—(Sūtra 7).
In this context, the Commentator demonstrates that recognition, which is mental and characterized by reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*),
as in the phrase "this very same [object] now.
He states that recognition is a determinate cognition (*vyavasāya*) produced by the external sense organs.
"This very object is that [same] one"—this is the prior reflective awareness (anuvyavasāya) regarding that very [object]. // 7 //
It is not so, because there is a misconception of duality with respect to what is not one, being separated by the nasal bone.
This [objection] he refutes by means of the identity of the eye:
"Not one" (Sūtra 8).
NyS 3.1.9: Because the second does not perish when the first perishes, there is no oneness.
He concentrates on oneness (Sūtra 9).
The meaning is that there is a plurality [of entities] due to the imposition of contradictory properties characterized by destruction and non-destruction. // 9 //
Even when the parts have perished, the whole is still perceived; therefore, [the opponent's reason] is not a valid proof.
The objector says:
"But [the word] 'ava' [is used in this sense] (Sūtra 10)."
NyS 3.1.11: There is no refutation [of our position] because it contradicts the illustrative example.
The respondent said:
"It has been seen—[the rule] 'dṛṣṭādhaḥ' (Sūtra 11)."
He states the third explanation:
"Alternatively, because there is no fixed rule for the destruction of a single [entity].
If [the eye] were a single entity, there would be no fixed rule regarding its destruction.
It is [the destruction] of the left eye alone, not of the right;
for since they are one, it would follow that upon the destruction of the left, the right would also be destroyed.
And yet, this restriction is observed.
Therefore, there are two objects, each with its own distinct obscuration and its own distinct substrate.
Moreover, if the single eye were pressed by the bridge of the nose on the left side, and then pressed again with a finger, it would manifest as if it were one that has become divided.
When [the pressure] is withdrawn by squeezing, those two objects which appeared as distinct are joined together;
likewise, it is said that the nose-tip does not show the object as divided when squeezed, but rather joins them once that [pressure] has ceased:
"And because of the squeezing of one eye."
The meaning is that there is a distinction in the contact with the object due to the distinction in the rays [of light].
The meaning is that there is a contradiction [with this view] by means of the example of the eye being pressed by a finger.
Alternatively, the example is the destruction of one [ray] resulting in the destruction of the other.
"Because of that contradiction.
Indeed, the meaning of the sūtra is: "And because it is seen as being restricted to one side, this is the example."
The author of the Vārttika refutes this section, stating:
"Because it is already established, there is no need to begin [this discussion].
Another kind of conjunction is appropriate within the treatise.
This is the underlying intention:
a one-eyed person, or one whose single eye is covered, does not see in the same way as one with unimpaired faculties.

In that case, if the two eyes—which are distinct due to their being located on the left and right—cannot both be simultaneously presided over by the atomic mind (*manas*), then one or the other must be the object of its presiding.
And thus, since everyone sees with each individual eye, there would be an unequal perception for one whose eyes are unimpaired when one eye is covered.

But this is not the case. For if [the eye] were a single entity, then since it would be governed by the mind wherever it emerges from those two bases, there would be no consequence of a person with impaired vision perceiving [objects] like one with unimpaired vision.
Therefore, the eye is a single [organ] that has multiple bases. Furthermore, this contradicts the context [of the treatise], because [it would entail] more than five sense organs. (360)

And this [co-occurrence] does not refer to the genus (*jāti*) within a single body, because the co-occurrence of the four individual instances of breath and so forth is possible with another individual instance, and not by way of genus; for one does not say, "A Brāhmaṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira have arrived," but rather "A Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya" or "Vasiṣṭha and Yudhiṣṭhira."

Even when one substratum has perished, that which remains unperished serves as a mere condition, just like the cause itself. Nor does it follow that everyone would always and everywhere experience a delusion—such as seeing two moons—due to the pressure on the parts [of the sense organ], for we postulate from the observation of the effect that the cause of delusion is the adventitious pressure and not something innate. // 11 //
NyS 3.1.12: [The existence of the soul is known] from the modification of another sense organ.

Thus, having established the self through direct perception by means of recognition (*pratisandhāna*), he now establishes it through inference, stating: "And this [self] is inferred. For recognition was stated for the sake of one who is in disagreement; however, in the ultimate sense, it should be understood that this [inference] follows from the force of experience (*anubhava*).
The sense organs (indriya) [are established] by means of inference (sūtra 12).

When someone experiences the color or the odor associated with a certain tasted substance, such as sour *cirabilva* fruit, they then recollect the taste associated with it. Having recollected it, they desire it; from that desire, a transformation of the gustatory faculty arises, characterized by the salivation of the teeth.
From seeing this, one's desire is inferred, and from the desire, the recollection [is inferred]. Thus, this recollection occurs even in the absence of a self (*ātman*).
It cannot be that which experiences all the objects of the sense-faculties. // 12 //
NyS 3.1.13: No, because memory has as its object that which is to be remembered.
The sūtra stating this objection is:
"Memory [does not perceive itself]" (Sūtra 13). Memory would have to apprehend itself either as its own cause or as its own object.
It is not [the cause] by way of being its cause, because that [impression] is the cause of the mental formation (saṃskāra);
nor is it so by way of being its object, because its object is that which is to be remembered.
The meaning is that from that which has been remembered, there arises a modification of another sense faculty. // 13 //
NyS 3.1.14: There is no refutation [of the self] because its qualities exist.
Because it is concentrated, then—[the suffix] dhaḥ [is applied]. (Sūtra 14)

Having demonstrated that memory does not arise in the absence of a self, [the author] refutes the opponent's conclusion that memory has only the object to be remembered as its domain and not the self as its domain, by means of the sūtra:
"And because the objects of memory are innumerable" (Sūtra 15).
In all four types of memory produced by mental after-cognitions (*anuvyavasāya*) and their resulting latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), it is not the object alone that is the object of cognition;

rather, knowledge, the knower, and the knowable—all of these—are the objects. In the four statements, in one case knowledge is the action extracted from its factors (*kāraka*), as in "in this [object], my knowledge arose. Although the object is not being perceived at that moment, it is referred to as "in this" because it is brought to mind through memory.

Even when not abstracted from the factors of action (*kāraka*), in one case a cognitive activity (*jñāna-kriyā*) is understood as being primarily the process of becoming (*bhāvanā*) occurring in a temporal sequence, as in: "I have known this object. In another case, however, when the process of knowing is not abstracted from the factors of action, it is primarily the agent (*kartṛ*), as in: "I have known this object.
In yet another case, when the process of knowing is not abstracted from the factors of action, it is primarily the object (*karman*), as in: "This object has been known by me."
"Having the same object" means that the illumination of the cognition, the cognizable, and the cognizer is common [to both].
Thus far, memory has been demonstrated with respect to an object not being currently perceived.
Therefore, after direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), memory (*smṛti*) is demonstrated:
"Now, after direct perception, [there is] the object.
By the term "memory," he refers to recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), because it is brought about by the reflection of memory.

Regarding the phrase "I saw": even when one refers back to the previous object through the perception of that object, let it be granted that there is a conceptualization (*kalpanā*) based on the experience of perceiving that object; but from where does this conceptualization of experience itself arise? To this, he says: "Indeed, [this is not so] when one's own seeing is not cognized."
Rather, the meaning is that both the perception of the object and the perception of that [perception] are indeed cognized.
Why is this so? To this he says:
"I saw this."

The meaning is this: because there arises the recollection, "I saw this," preceded by a prior experience, one must necessarily infer that there was indeed a manifestation of experience in that regard.
For this reason as well, memory is not a quality of the body, because of the recollection in old age of what was experienced in childhood;
for the body of a child is one thing, and the body of an old man is another.
Let alone recognition, even similarity is difficult to discern;
moreover, atoms do not possess consciousness.
For they would either have to cognize individually or collectively.
In the former case, if there were multiple consciousnesses in a single body, there would be no fixed unity;
for it is never observed that multiple conscious beings possess a fixed consensus of will.

But since the atoms, when combined, possess consciousness, and because their combinations vary through the process of inclusion and exclusion, there would be a plurality of conscious entities; consequently, it follows that what is perceived by one cannot be remembered by another.
Therefore, consciousness does not have the body as its substrate. Thus, the author of the Vārttika refutes the verse of the opponents.
By this, the [objection] that "it is neither in the eye nor in form" is refuted;
the meaning is that it is established by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) through the demonstration that the self is the substratum of memory.
In whatever locus that cognition is established, it is contradictory to say that such a locus neither exists nor does not exist.
It might be argued: "This is not a negation of specific attributes, such as 'there is no consciousness in the eye' or 'there is no form';
rather, it is the view of those who believe that consciousness has the eye and so forth as its support that is being negated.
However, the fact that [consciousness] possesses a substratum is not negated because it was never asserted. To this, he says:
"Or of whom?
Furthermore, this verse was intended to express the non-existence of a self, yet it establishes the very existence of a self; thus, he says that it is contrary to what was intended:
"And this [belongs] to consciousness."

Having thus explained the sūtra "from the modification of another sense-organ" according to the opinion of the Bhāṣya, the author of the Vārttika explains it according to his own view with the words "or rather, of one [person]. The sūtra demonstrates once again, by means of the modification of another sense-organ, the very recollection (pratisaṃdhāna) already mentioned; and it shows how this recollection establishes a self that is distinct from the body, the senses, and so forth.
Thus, he states that it has already been explained below:
"By the logic already stated" (12–15).
Not so, because the means for the cognition of the self are present in the mind.
NyS 3.1.16: Since the means of knowledge are established for a knower, there is merely a difference in terminology.
Intellect (*mati*) is knowledge consisting of memory, inference, and so forth.

Although this has its own specific causes such as mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), it must nevertheless necessarily be produced by a sense organ because it is a form of knowledge, just like the cognition of color and other objects.
Since that [cognition] occurs even when the eye and other organs are absent, the intellect is the mind (*manas*), which is distinct from the eye and the other senses.
Thus it is said.
Now, one might object: let the mind be another instrument; however, how can it be an auxiliary to the other sense organs, and how can it be of atomic dimension? To this, he says:
And that is the mark for the non-simultaneity of cognitions. // 15–16 //
And restriction is without inferential proof.

If it is argued in the *Vārttika* that "if all cognition is said to be established by [a sense organ], then it would apply to the mind (*manas*) as well," [the response is: In that case, the mind itself cannot be the instrument, because its own activity toward itself is contradictory. If something other than the mind were the instrument, then another sense organ would have to be employed for the cognition of that [instrument] as well, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

However, if [cognition] is not born from a sense organ, then even in the case of mental cognition (*mati*), the cause is simply the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) and so forth; thus, the mind is rendered superfluous—this is the intended meaning.
He refutes this, saying "it omits":

just as a cause is known by the fact that an effect has been produced through its existence, so too the mind makes itself known by the production of the cognition of the mark of the mind through its own existence; and that cognition of the mind produced from the mark has the existence of the mind as its cause.
Nor is there a contradiction in [the mind] operating upon itself;
for the mind is not the instrument for the existence of the mind, nor is mental cognition the instrument for mental cognition, such that there would be a contradiction in its operation upon itself.
Nor is the mind alone the instrument for its own cognition, whereby both the object and the instrument would reside in one and the same thing.

Rather, the mind accompanied by the cognition of the mark (liṅga) is the instrument for the cognition of the object; its nature as such, however, arises from that accompaniment by the cognition of the mark. Thus, there is no contradiction regarding an action operating upon itself, nor is there the status of both object and instrument belonging to one and the same thing in isolation—this is the intended meaning.

It might be argued: "If the mind, when accompanied by the cognition of a mark (liṅgajñāna), is the instrument, let there be no case of one and the same thing being both the object and the instrument, since it is the object in its own form and the instrument through its association with the cognition of the mark.
But when the mind is grasped by a yogi through direct perception (pratyakṣa), how can there be the state of being both object and instrument for one and the same thing?
To this, he says:
But for whom mental perception exists, [it is as follows]. // 17 //
NyS 3.1.18: [The existence of the self is proved] because a newborn infant experiences joy, fear, and sorrow due to the continuity of memories practiced in a previous life.

Desiring to examine the next world—which serves as the basis for the worldly prosperity and the ultimate liberation that constitute the subject matter of the treatise—the author states the doubt that serves as the ground for such examination:
"But what is this [next world]?
Here, the author of the *Vārttika*, refuting the doubt, challenges the commencement of this new section.
Regarding the phrase "in this matter":

by demonstrating that the self is distinct from the body, the senses, the intellect, and sensations, and by establishing— through the fact of the continuity of a single self— that it persists despite the differences between childhood, youth, adulthood, and old age, he has shown that the self exists after the destruction of the body.

And our purpose is fulfilled by that much; therefore, what remains for which there might be doubt, and on account of which this treatise (*prakaraṇa*) was composed? This is the meaning. He provides the answer:
"It is not without a beginning."

Even though the soul's distinction from the body and so forth has been established, and its persistence through stages such as childhood has been shown, the doubt remains unresolved even today as to whether this self exists throughout the continuum of the body from birth until death, or whether it persists even when the continuum of the body and so forth has ceased; therefore, this section is commenced for the purpose of resolving that doubt. This is the meaning. The commentary states: "Because of the difference of bodies," etc.
The fifth case ending is used in the sense of "in relation to" (*lyablope pañcamī*).
The meaning is that its continued existence is established through the reconnection [of the self] after observing the distinctions between the bodies of childhood, youth, adulthood, and old age.
This is the Vārttika.
Regarding the phrase "upon the attainment of the sought-after object through longing":

although it should have been stated simply as "upon the attainment of the sought-after object," the inclusion of the term "longing" (prārthanā) indicates that it is the most intensely desired [object] that is meant.

It is not that joy arises upon the attainment of anything merely desired, but rather upon the attainment of that which is most intensely desired; therefore, the meaning is "upon the attainment of the sought-after object when there is longing for it."
"Impossibility of avoidance":
by means of the object (*viṣaya*), one indicates the cognition (*buddhi*) which possesses that object.

An undesirable object is death and so forth; its means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is the tiger, snake, and so forth; the "encounter" (*upanipāta*) with it is their presence. When that is present, for one who wishes to abandon the tiger and so forth, the cognition that "this [tiger, etc. cannot be avoided" is fear.
For that [sorrow] arises for someone:

when there is separation from a desired object, sorrow is the longing for its attainment which is impossible to achieve. It is the longing, on the part of that very person, for that which cannot be attained; this is sorrow.

When a desired object cannot be obtained, the longing for it—expressed as "May this happen to me," "May it come to pass"—is such a petition; yet this kind of petition is not grief in its own nature. Therefore, he says:
"when there is separation from a desired object," which means by way of its being unattainable.
This is the meaning:
grief is the cognition that one is unable to obtain what has been separated from, due to the loss of a desired object.
This indicates that for one who grieves, there is the cognition that [the object] is impossible to obtain because it is undeserved.
Regarding the phrase "the cessation of perceptual cognition":
by the term "perceptual," it indicates apprehension in general;
that [cognition] is supported by it, meaning it is supported by memory.

Regarding the phrase "the object of that synthesis" (*tadanusaṃdhānaviṣaya*): "synthesis" (*anusaṃdhāna*) means that which is synthesized; thus, the meaning is "that which is to be synthesized by memory is its object.
Nevertheless, there is no distinction between memory (*smṛti*) and recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
Therefore, he says:
"It has as its object the state of that [object] which is a present, visible object.
For it is observed that a child, though lacking a [conceptual] support, remembers that falling from his mother's lap is a means to an undesirable end, and thus—

The meaning is that, having reflected on the falling [of the child], having understood its nature as a means to an undesirable end, and weeping while tossing the auspicious thread from his mother’s breast, taking hold of her hands with trembling limbs—by this behavior, fear and grief are inferred. // 18 //
NyS 3.1.19: Its modification is like the modifications of opening and closing observed in lotuses and the like.
"Because it is qualified by what is seen" means that the causal relationship, being specified and established by the word "seen," cannot be rejected.
Now, as for the inference of the arising and cessation of the self:

The meaning is as follows: whatever undergoes modification is seen to possess the nature of arising and ceasing, just like a lotus; and since the self likewise undergoes modification, it is therefore impermanent.

If "modification" were merely the production of a property (*dharma*), then that would apply to space (*ākāśa*) and so forth as well, making the reason inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Furthermore, because there is a distinction between the property and the substratum (*dharmin*), the arising and passing away of properties cannot logically belong to the substratum; thus, the inference of impermanence based on modification is not established.
With the intention that there exists an inference for the permanence of our own self, he states an inference for permanence;
[the author] says that this is not tenable,
because [the self] is always formless (*amūrta*).

Even jars and other objects are formless (amūrta) in a single moment; for "form" (mūrti) is a specific dimension (parimāṇaviśeṣa), and qualities do not arise at the same time as the substance. To exclude such [a possibility], the word "always" (sarvadā) was stated.
[This is because] the modifications consisting of the five elements have heat, cold, and rain as their temporal causes.
The modifications of the lotus and other things, which consist of the five elements, are called "modifications of the five-elemental. // 20 //
[The newborn's desire for milk] is due to the longing for breast-milk produced by the habitual practice of seeking food after death [in a previous life].
"In order to make known the specific [nature] of that which has been understood in a general way.

The meaning is this: by means of joy and so forth, mere desire is understood in a general sense, but its specific nature here is stated to be the longing for breast milk and passion (*rāga*). // 21 //
Its approaching [the object] is like the movement of iron toward a magnet.

*aya-ṇam* (Sūtra 22): It is not the mere persistence of previously practiced tendencies (*pūrvābhyasta-saṃskāra*) that is the cause of activity. For instance, in the case of iron being attracted to a magnet, such a tendency is absent.

Furthermore, if a newborn child possessed the persistence of memories from previous practice, then those born blind or deaf would perceive smells and touches experienced in that very life, as well as forms, sounds, and so forth experienced in other lives.
He refutes [the opponent's position] by posing the question:
"What is this? [The response is:
The activity of a conscious being during stages such as youth is caused by the persistence of memories previously cultivated regarding milk and other such things.

Since it is recognized [as being caused by that], even in the state of infancy, the activity of consciousness must necessarily be caused by that very [previous] cause; for, through that cause, an inherent relationship is understood, just as smoke [is understood to relate] to fire.
This being established, wherever the effect of memory is observed, the infant's memory must have only that [specific object] as its domain, and not anything else.

Furthermore, there is no restrictive reason why one who remembers a certain thing must necessarily remember another as well, such that those born blind or deaf could describe specific distinctions of color and so forth; for such a restriction is logically established by the fact that the latent impression (*saṃskāra*), awakened by the ripening of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), is restricted to that [specific object].
Even today, regarding things experienced, it is only some [of them] that the self remembers, not all of them. // 22 //
NyS 3.1.23: No, because there is no activity elsewhere.
And there is no other sign for the desire for breast milk;

"In another place," meaning in a clod of earth or the like.
Because the sixth and seventh case endings have the same meaning [of identity].

This is what is meant: since there is no movement toward the magnet on the part of anything other than the clod of earth and so forth, and since the iron's approach occurs only when there is a cause, this was explained previously.

NyS 3.1.24: Because birth is not observed in one who is free from passion.

"Reflection on objects previously experienced" means that reflection (*cintana*) is a stream of memory (*smṛti-pravāha*) directed toward a single object, uninterrupted by heterogeneous cognitions; and because that [memory] occurs after the initial experience, it is called "reflection" (*anucintana*).
And that [desire] does not occur without memory;

for there is no flow [of consciousness] there without a carrier. That very act of reflection is *saṅkalpa*, meaning a longing for an object previously experienced. "Longing" (*prārthanā*) is *saṅkalpa*, and its meaning is that it has as its object something previously experienced.

Now, one might ask: why does the sensory experience of objects in this very life not become a cause for attachment, when it is accompanied by the cognition that the object is a means to what is desired—as determined through positive and negative concomitance? To this, the author of the *Vārttika* says: "Not in those incapable of cognizing the object.
By this, the *Bhāṣya* passage—"and the previous experience of objects in another birth"—is explained. // 25 //
Regarding this, the *Bhāṣya* states: "This is a restatement of what has been said.
Its meaning is as follows: this objection was previously stated by means of the analogy of the magnet;
nevertheless, its restatement here serves the purpose of providing an illustration.
Previously, the magnet was the illustration; now, however, the form and other qualities of pots and so forth as they are being produced are the illustration. This is the meaning of "for that purpose.
Since the objection is merely a restatement of what has already been raised, the resolution is likewise merely a restatement of what has already been given.
"Because it consists of that, it is attachment.

(370/3) Having provisionally accepted that unseen causes (*adṛṣṭa*) are the cause of attachment and so forth, that [objection] has been refuted; however, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*), the meaning is that attachment exists because it consists of that.

It might be argued: if the arising of passion and so forth results from the continuity of previously practiced memory, then alas, for one who has attained the state of a young camel immediately after a human birth, passion and so forth would correspond only to that [human] state due to its immediate proximity, and not to the state of a camel; for this camel species is separated from him by thousands of births of a different kind. Therefore—
He says:
"And because of the distinction of birth.

Since karma is the awakener of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), by means of an action performed for the sake of the camel species, even the impression of being a camel—which has been separated from it by thousands of births—is awakened, whereas the impression of being a human, though immediately preceding, is not awakened because it has been suppressed by death (*prāyaṇa*); this is the intended meaning.
Is the production [of sound] like the production of a substance possessing qualities? NyS 3.1.25.

[Objection: "But surely, as in the case of the production of a substance possessing qualities," [one might argue]. For this very reason, the answer has already been stated.
Thus [ends the twenty-fifth].
Not so, because passion and the like have conceptualization as their cause.

Moreover, even though they are equal in being human, since we observe differences in the excellence or deficiency of wisdom and intelligence (*prajñā-medhā*), one must postulate practice from previous lives.
For even in the present life, the study of treatises is experienced through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) as increasing the wisdom directed toward their subject matter.

Thus, this extraordinary degree of wisdom and intelligence regarding those subjects in a person who has not practiced the treatises in this life indicates an extraordinary degree of practice from a previous life.
It makes its own cause known;

for it must be understood that the decline of wisdom and intelligence in people occurs because the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) from previous lives have been withered by the intervention of hundreds of births among animals and other such states.
Therefore, this beginningless stream of assuming and discarding various kinds of bodies, which is bound by karma and ignorance, belongs to the eternal self and ends only in liberation (*apavarga*).
Thus it is established. // 26 //
The [substance] is earthen, because other qualities are perceived [in it].

Having indicated the self immediately after [the previous topic], the author of the commentary, wishing to examine the body, states the intermediate connection: "It has been said that the connection of the conscious being with a body is beginningless.
He then states its utility for examination as a means for producing world-weariness (*nirveda*).
"By one's own performed karma":
this expresses a doubt that is the precursor to investigation.
"Is it like the nose and so forth? [he asks].

Proponents of the body have maintained that it consists of one, two, three, four, or five primary elements; this is the alternative regarding its numerical composition (*saṃkhyāvikalpa*). Here, the author of the *Vārttika* states the connection for the independent investigation of the body with the words, "immediately after [the discussion of] the self."

He states the connection according to the view of the Bhāṣya with the words "Or rather" (atha vā). He explains the intended meaning of the intermediate connection with the words "when that is being examined" (tasmin parīkṣyamāṇe).
"The human body is composed of earth because it possesses odor, like an atom of earth.
To the objection that "the cause is not the self of the effect, so how can it be of one nature," he says:

"Of a single nature" means having a single essence (*ekasvabhāva*). The "own-nature" (*svabhāva*) of things that exist is their genus (*jāti*); for it is only when there is a commonality of genus in the inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*) that the effect would belong to that same genus, and not otherwise—this is the meaning. Desiring to demonstrate that the reasons stated by the opponent are otherwise established (*anyathāsiddha*), [Vātsyāyana] first speaks out of a friendly disposition: "But this [earth] is not [composed of] water and so forth," etc. (NyS 3.1.28): "It consists of earth, water, and fire, because of the perception of their qualities."
NyS 3.1.29: [The body is] composed of the four elements because inhalation and exhalation are perceived.
NyS 3.1.30: [It is] composed of the five elements because of [the presence of] odor, moisture, digestion, structural arrangement, and the provision of space.

Having stated that the proofs for the opponent's position are otherwise established (*anyathāsiddha*), the author of the *Vārttika* explains the refutation (*bādhaka*) stated by the author of the *Bhāṣya*, after first restating it.
Thus, this [substance] consists of multiple primary elements (*anekaprakṛti*).

When it is produced from earth and water, it is odorless, because a single causal odor cannot initiate [a new odor]. This is the intended meaning: two atoms of earth and water cannot, first of all, initiate a single dyad (*dvyaṇuka*).
Even if the commencement [of a triad] were possible through its possession of color, taste, and touch, it would entail the undesirable consequence of its lacking smell;

for in this way, the smell inherent in the two earthly atoms, being singular, cannot be a cause of commencement. Nor is it tenable that the commencement of atoms—consisting of two earthly atoms and one aqueous atom—could account for the presence of smell.
Because a plurality of atoms does not initiate [a composite substance].
For instance, three atoms do not initiate an effect-substance (kāryadravya), because, while being atoms, they possess the number "plurality," like the collection of atoms contained within a jar.

If those [parts] were initiators [of the whole], then upon the destruction of the jar, the sequence of shards, gravel, and powder contained within it would not be perceived; furthermore, once it is established that dyads do not initiate heterogeneous [substances], by that very same example, the initiation of heterogeneous [substances] must be denied elsewhere as well. By this, the initiation of a body by large earthy parts together with watery parts is refuted.
"Because it has been ascertained in the subject of the example that heterogeneous [factors] do not produce [an effect].

Thus, by this, the author of the Vārttika has refuted twenty-six alternative theories. Furthermore, he asks: "If, on the other hand, each [factor] were a cause individually, what would then follow? and then says:
Regarding the phrase "if there were a single cause":
if there were one eternal, independent cause, the effect would arise continuously.
A substance perishes either through the destruction of its cause or through its disintegration; however, for an eternal single cause, no destruction exists.
Furthermore, there can be no disjunction [of the whole], because it must reside in a substance that has a second [part];

and since a single [entity] lacks a second, and because there is an absence of a cause for destruction, it follows as a consequence that the produced would be eternal. Thus, the color-form (*rūpa*) in the composite whole (*avayavin*), being solitary and without assistance, does not initiate a color-form; consequently, the composite whole is devoid of color-form. And thus, due to the absence of the conditioning factor of color-form, the composite whole—
The meaning is that it would not be perceived. // 28 // 29 // 30 //
And because of the authority of the sacred revelation (śruti).
The term *spṛti* means origination (*utpatti*).

Scripture (*śruti*) reinforces a meaning already established by logic (*nyāya*), but it does not establish that meaning [de novo], since its occurrence can somehow be explained even by relying on the Sāṃkhya doctrine. // 31 //
NyS 3.1.32: Because it is perceived when the black antelope skin is present, and because it is perceived even apart from it, there is doubt.
In accordance with the order of the enumeration, the author of the Commentary (Bhāṣyakāra) promises an examination of the sense organs immediately after the body:
"Now, therefore, [we shall examine] the sense organs according to the sequence of the objects of knowledge.
In that regard, he states the doubt which is the precursor to the examination.
Are they non-material (avyaktika) or rather material (bhautika)?
This is an illustration;
for even when they are material, is it precisely that black pupil which is perceived that constitutes the sense organ?
Furthermore, one should observe that there is also doubt as to whether its substrate is composed of fire (taijasa);

Among those, the former [doubt] arises from the disagreement between the Sāṃkhyas and the Naiyāyikas.
But the latter [view] belongs to the Buddhists and the Naiyāyikas.
"Unmanifestness" (āvyaktikatva) should be understood as being derived from the *ahaṅkāra* (the principle of ego).
For the Sāṃkhyas maintain that the eleven sense organs are produced from the *ahaṅkāra*, which is a modification (*vikāra*) of the intellect (*buddhi*), specifically from the *vaikārika* aspect.
The state of being unmanifest (*avyaktikatva*) is predicated of the Unmanifest because it is the root cause. He asks about the seed of disagreement:
"From what does the doubt arise? Thus he states the disagreement, [explaining that it arises] from the metaphorical application of the name of the effect to the cause.
The reply is: "Because it exists when the black antelope skin exists.
The Buddhists maintain that the eye is the black antelope skin itself because perception occurs when that skin is present;
however, since it is perceived as distinct from it, the eye must be something other than that, and it is composed of *ahaṃkāra*.

The Sāṃkhyas maintain that [the internal organ] is not composed of the elements (bhautika), because, due to the all-pervasiveness of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), there would be no obstruction; whereas if it were elemental, there would follow the consequence of its being obstructed by other elemental things such as glass or clouds. // 32 //
"Not because of the lack of pervasion by lamps and the like" means that there is no lack of pervasion by a lamp, which is light concentrated in the space occupied by its wick;
for it is the radiance (*prabhā*), spreading out and reaching the object, that illuminates it, whereas the lamp itself does not. This is the meaning.
"If it is argued that this is due to the state of being an object," [the response is:

"That is merely a specific kind of arising, such that even when the moment of the eye and the moment of the object have not reached one another, there exists the relationship of the cognized and the cognizer because of their status as object and subject;
however, this does not occur between things that are obstructed or distant, and thus there is no relationship of the cognized and the cognizer between those two. This is the meaning.
He refutes this, saying: "No, because the answer has already been stated.

The meaning is that the same object cannot be both remote and not a sense-object while being near and a sense-object; thus, for a single thing to simultaneously possess the status of being an object and its absence is illogical. Furthermore, the doctrine of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) will be refuted later.
[Nyāyasūtra 3.1.33: "Because of the perception of both the large and the minute."
Therein, having raised the Sāṃkhya position, he refutes the Buddhist view with the words "non-material" (*abhautikāni*).

By the inclusion of the term "black antelope skin" (*kṛṣṇasāra*), the intended meaning is already grasped; its mention is merely incidental and not what is intended here, because it does not serve as a proof.
The sprout from grain.
"But its non-material nature is due to its pervasiveness" means that,
for example, consciousness and so forth are non-material, yet they grasp both the large and the minute.
He states the refutation according to the view of a certain school:
"Not in the case of lamps and such things belonging to the earth.
[Objection: If cognition is the illumination of both the large and the minute, then why is there no illumination of everything? To this he says:
"Of an object that is exhausted by its own limit."
Nor is it the case that the cognitions of avoidance, acquisition, or indifference are either atomic or large; such is the meaning.
The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) says: "No, because this is the same even in the case of the sense organ.
Thus, when the partial proponent's [argument] has been refuted by the opponent through the demonstration of its lack of exclusivity, the proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntin) says:
"It is unreal in nature and yet all-pervasive"—
thus the Sāṃkhya objects, saying,
"It is a function."
The meaning is that the functions of the sense organs, which are the causes of cognition, are being negated;
and because it would entail the undesirable consequence of simultaneous grasping of multiple objects.

Although, according to the established doctrine of the Sāṃkhya school, the simultaneous arising of multiple cognitions is accepted for one eating a long piece of fried dough, nevertheless, a sequence is also observed in some cases, which [the Sāṃkhya theory] would not allow.

The sense is that if the possessor of the activity (*vṛttimat*) were to persist, then the activity, being non-different from it, would also persist; consequently, there could be no succession of cognitions whose arising depends solely upon those [momentary] activities.

"Both are not accepted" means that the non-difference of the possessor of the activity from the activities is not accepted, nor is the non-difference of the activities from the possessor of the activity accepted. // 33 //
NyS 3.1.34: Its perception occurs due to a specific contact between the rays [of light] and the object.
The Naiyāyika refutes the Sāṃkhya.
[The soul's departure] by means of the rays [of the sun] (Sūtra 34).
If the eye were composed of ego (āhaṅkārika), it would not be obstructed; like light passing through glass or a layer of clouds, it would illuminate even what is screened by a wall.
But this is not the case.

Therefore, it is simply elemental light (tejas) based in the black pupil that perceives an object upon reaching it; however, it does not perceive an object screened by a wall because it does not reach it.
But regarding [objects] separated by glass or a film of cloud, he will state later:
"There is further assistance from the contact of the parts."

[The contact is] of the parts of the sense organ with the parts of the object, of the parts of the sense organ with the whole object, of the parts of the object with the sense organ, and of the sense organ with the whole object. // 34 //
Because that [reason] is not perceived, it is not a valid reason.

"Because of its non-perception": the meaning is that it is not possible to infer something that has not been perceived despite meeting the conditions for perceptibility, because otherwise there would be the unwanted consequence of inferring things such as a human horn. // 35 //
The non-perception by means of direct perception of that which is being inferred is not a valid reason for its non-existence.
The rebuttal is that this does not apply to what is being inferred.

It is true that what has not reached the conditions for perception (*anupalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*) and is thus unperceived cannot be inferred; however, it is not only magnitude (*mahattva*) and so forth that constitute these conditions, but also a specific quality of color (*rūpa-viśeṣa*).
And this specific quality, which is designated as "manifestation" (*udbhava*), does not exist in the eye whose locus is the black pupil (*kṛṣṇasāra*). This is the meaning. // 36 //
Furthermore, there is a difference in the means of apprehension due to the distinction between the properties of substances and qualities.
The meaning of the sūtra is: "Where there is perception, there this [is].

Therefore, among the qualities such as magnitude (*mahattva*) and so forth, the author of the sūtra ought to have mentioned only one; for since the point that "where there is perception, there this is" is established quite spontaneously, the inclusion of multiple [qualities] would be redundant. Consequently, the sūtra is a statement intended to express the suitability for such a possibility.
Now, one might ask: "Since the causes for perceiving magnitude and so forth exist for the visual ray just as they are heard [in scripture], why is this [ray] not perceived? To this, he says:
"Because of the properties of substance and quality. (37)
The arrangement of the sense organs is brought about by karma and is dependent upon the purpose of the person (puruṣa).

If there were the presence of many rays and tactile contact were manifested, the substance would be burned; however, if color-form (*rūpa*) were manifested, then because [the object] is obstructed, the substance ought not to be perceived by the eye that first falls upon it. He raises an objection with the words "Now, if many... (*athāneka*).
The meaning is that this single composite whole of the eye (*nayanāvayavin*) is commenced by various parts of the eyes. He refutes this with the words "if this were so":
if this single composite whole of the eye were commenced by various parts of the eyes, it would be common to both persons whose eyes are complete and those whose eyes are incomplete.
The meaning is that, in this way, the perception would be identical.
Its non-perception is like the non-perception of the light of a torch at midday.
Not so, because it is not perceived even at night.
For that which overpowers something cannot be its manifestor.

(380/17) At night, that which overpowers the light of a clod of earth during the day—how could that very same thing be its manifestor, such that in its absence at night the light of the clod would not be perceived? This is the meaning.
It is understood from the word "api" (also/even).
Thus, the meaning of the Sūtra is that [the practice] is not even at night. // 39–40 //
NyS 3.1.41: Because the perception of an object occurs through the assistance of external light, there is no perception [of it] when it is not manifested.
Regarding this ray of the eye, is it not perceived because of its non-existence, or because of its non-manifestation? To this, the author of the Bhāṣya says:
"And this non-perception is logically established as being due to non-manifestation"; the construction [of the sentence] is thus.
"Due to non-manifestation" means "due to its lack of emergence."
The reason for this is that the perception of an object occurs through the assistance of external light, and the object consists of both its own form and that which is other than itself.

What is meant is this: when something requires the assistance of external light for its perception, its non-perception is due solely to its non-manifestation (*anudbhūti*), and not to its being overwhelmed (*abhibhūti*).
Just as in winter, even this substance whose parts are closely joined [is perceived];

for it is observed that a watery substance, though its parts are closely joined, requires the assistance of external light for the perception of its own object, and the eye likewise requires external light for the perception of its object,
because it does not function in the absence of light.

Therefore, since the perception of an object depends upon external light, it is not cognized because that [light] has not arisen, and not because it is overwhelmed; thus the point at hand is established.
The author of the Vārttika explains this as follows: "Of that which exists... (41).
And because there is suppression [of one sound] even when another is manifested.
Why, then, is it said "of the visual"?
This is the answer:
he states the form of that which is to be overcome.
Regarding the phrase "that which has manifested form" (yad-udbhūta-rūpam),
he states its contrast with that which has unmanifested form by saying "and [that which] has unmanifested form."
He provides an illustration for the absence of suppression when form is unmanifested, stating:
"that which has unmanifested form.
And he provides an illustration for the absence of suppression for that which depends upon the assistance of external light, stating: [the same].
Regarding the statement "and that which depends upon the assistance of external light":

if it were said that the *kṛṣṇasāra* (the pupil) possesses rays, then even the *kṛṣṇasāra* of one with clear vision would have to be established as possessing rays; and such would constitute an abandonment of one's own tenet (*apasiddhānta*).
Therefore, he says:
Regarding the phrase "the object of dispute":
by this, the statement of the thesis (*sādhyanirdeśa*) is that the black pupil (*kṛṣṇasāra*) and its color possess rays, because they are the cause for perception.

If it were stated simply as "because they are the cause for perception," it would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to odors and so forth; therefore, it is specified as "for the perception of color."

The meaning is "the direct perception of form. Nevertheless, because [the reason] would be inconclusive due to [factors such as] sense-object contact (*sannikarṣa*), it is stated: "provided that it possesses substantiality" (*dravyatve sati*).
Nevertheless, because the mind is not invariably [a cause of certainty], it was stated [by the author] that "it is a member of the proof for one who has attained certainty," meaning:
provided that the uncommon [reason] is indeed a member of the proof.
But the mind, being common to all [faculties] and a constituent part of the means of cognition, serves as the instrumental cause for the perception of form.
"Means" (sādhana) refers to the aggregate, and its "constituent part" (aṅga) is a component member.
Or else: [the phrase "atha vā"].

If it were stated that [the reason] is "being a substance while being restricted" and "illuminating an object," it would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the olfactory sense-faculty (*ghrāṇa*) and so forth; therefore, it was said "obstructed by crystal and the like. // 42 //
And because the rays from the eyes of nocturnal creatures are observed.
"The human eye possesses rays" means that it is the cause for the perception of form and so forth; this is stated with restriction, implying "only of form and so forth.
Therefore, there is no inconclusiveness [of the reason] by the mind.
Nevertheless, because there is an inconclusive argument regarding proximity (*sannikarṣa*), it is stated that they have the nature of non-attainment (*aprāpti-svabhāvatva*).
Furthermore, for this reason as well, the sense faculties—the eye, tongue, body, and nose—are composed of the primary elements (*bhautika*); such is the meaning.
Nevertheless, since it is not known what the nature of the auditory faculty is like,
he says:
"The auditory faculty is derived from the primary elements (bhūta)."

If it is argued that [the sense-organ] is the means of manifestation because it illuminates the object, this is inconclusive with respect to the mind (*manas*); therefore, he says "having reached" (*prāpta*).

For there is no reaching of the mind together with color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth; nevertheless, this remains inconclusive with respect to the mind itself, since internal suffering and so forth are manifested by the mind after it has reached them. Therefore...
He says, "externally.
Nevertheless, [the reason] is inconclusive due to contact, the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), and so forth; therefore, he says:
Regarding the phrase "provided it is a substance":
this introduces the objection, "If it is argued that there is a distinction among the sense organs just as there is a distinction among universals (jāti)."
He refutes the mere distinction of properties (*dharmabheda-mātra*), which is untenable.
That distinction of properties—namely, that the eye of a cat possesses rays while that of a human does not—is precisely what is meant by "mere," and that is untenable.
The particle *ca* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*) and its position is displaced.
The construction is: "It is simply untenable.
To the question "Why is it untenable? he states the reason: "Because of the obstruction," and so forth.
For instance, while the presence of smoke exists both on the mountain and in Rasavatī, nevertheless this distinction is not a determinant for its having fire or not having fire.
Thus, the states of being a cat and a human are irrelevant; this is the meaning. // 43 //
NyS 3.1.44: There is apprehension without reaching [the object], because there is perception of things separated by glass, clouds, films, or crystal.
There is no refutation [of the argument] because of the non-perception of things obstructed by a wall.
Because there is no resistance, the occurrence of contact is established.
"Unobstructed" means that this ray, being unobstructed by glass, penetrates through the glass and connects with the object situated inside the glass. (44–46)
Because the rays of the sun are not obstructed even when the object to be burned is separated by a crystal.
The *vārttika* states: "The non-penetration of the parts of a substance whose parts are not rearranged.
This refers to a substance such as a frying pan (*bharjanakapāla*), etc., whose parts are not rearranged through the destruction of the conjunctions that previously initiated the substance.

*Vyūhana* (expansion) is the production of a conjunction that generates another substance; that [expansion] is not performed here. Since the expansion of the parts of a substance—such as a frying pan (*bharjanakapāla*)—which is itself not being expanded, also belongs to the whole (*avayavin*), it is specified as "of that which is not being expanded. This is what is meant: because composite substances possess internal spaces, the fire's entry into them without destroying them is called "non-obstruction.

Alternatively, it is the reaching by the hand or other external organs of a substance such as honey or water situated inside;

"of that whose parts are not being displaced, such as a stick (śalākā), etc.; that is its 'outside'. // 47 //
Not so, because it would entail the mutual transfer of properties.

The meaning is that transparency (*svacchatā*) is the inherence (*samavāya*) of a substance not mixed with other substances.
In this context, he describes the sequence by which the error of a reflected image arises,
starting with the words "in mirrors and so forth."

"Just as the face of a person standing in front is oriented toward the connection with the rays of light from the eyes, so too is this [the reflection]. There is doubt because there is multiplicity when the location is different, and because a whole occupies multiple locations.

he introduces the sūtra preceded by a question, beginning with: "But moreover, they are indeed one."

(eke tu).
(385/13) "And this [explanation] is logically untenable.

For here, according to the literal reading, by means of the locative case denoting cause (*nimitta-saptamī*), it is stated that "difference of place" is the cause of multiplicity, and not the cause of unity.
However, as has been stated, the cause of unity is actually the state of having various places.
"Because the whole occupies multiple locations": the term "whole" (avayavin) indicates oneness,
while "difference of location" refers to the difference of the locus itself.

The compound *nānāsthānatva* has as its referent (*anyapadārtha*) that which possesses various locations; it is "other" because of the difference in location, but the two properties themselves are not directly the cause of doubt. Therefore, one of the two must be stated as being common to both the single and the multiple. In that regard, if it were formulated thus: "Doubt arises from the observation of multiplicity and unity when there is a difference in location," [then the following would apply].

When, through an examination of the meaning of the Sūtra, one does not perceive a difference in location within a single entity, there is no common characteristic [to establish identity]. Indeed, the Sūtra states that while there is oneness, there is multiplicity of locations; it does not state a difference in location. For the author of the Sūtra spoke merely of multiplicity, saying "due to the multiplicity of locations" (*sthānānyatvāt*). Now, since both oneness and multiplicity are observed when there is a multiplicity of locations, a doubt arises.
Thus, he refutes this:

at that time, no substance (*dravya*) occupying multiple locations and being manifold is observed. The sūtra—stating "because the whole (*avayavin*) occupies multiple locations"—asserts unity by virtue of occupying multiple locations, but it does not assert multiplicity either. Furthermore, that which is manifold, such as a jar and so forth, was not described by the author of the sūtra as occupying multiple locations.

However, the author of the Sūtra has stated that there is a difference in location; by the phrase "because of the multiplicity [of atoms] due to the difference in location," he summarizes the refutation.

This doubt is untenable in both ways regarding the sense-faculties: namely, by accepting the Sūtra exactly as it was heard, it is untenable in both respects—both through the difference in location and through the multiplicity of locations. This is the meaning.
Having thus refuted the interpretation of others, he states that the commentator’s own explanation is correct: "But it is appropriate in the case of locations.

The locative case in "sthāneṣu" (in the locations) is used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta-saptamī*). It is therefore appropriate that there should be a doubt regarding the unity or plurality of the sense organs based on the fact that they occupy various locations. For indeed, a single composite substance is observed to occupy various locations, as is a single fruit placed in multiple separate vessels.
He states a doubt concerning the object of the sense-faculties, caused by their being located in various places:
"Are the sense-faculties many and located in various places, or is there one sense-faculty located in various places?
This has been stated by the author of the Bhāṣya: "Many substances are seen to be located in various places, and yet that which is located in various places can also be a single composite whole."
Therefore, there is doubt regarding the sense-faculties because they occupy different locations.
Even in the Sūtra, by the phrase "in the case of different locations," it is precisely the state of having various locations that is indicated; thus, there is no contradiction.
However, he says that the literal meaning [of the words] is not the intended meaning of the Sūtra.
However, in the case of the sense-faculties (*indriya*), it is not possible [to have doubt] because of a difference in location;
nor is it [possible] because of being in different locations.
Rather, the meaning is that the doubt raised by the author of the *Bhāṣya* is more sound precisely because the objects of the sense-faculties are in different locations.
Having thus refuted the seed of doubt stated by others and having shown the seed of doubt according to the Bhāṣyakāra, the Vārttikakāra states the seed of doubt independently:
"Because it is distinct from the body and yet exists, there is doubt. (50–51)
NyS 3.1.52: Because it is not distinct from the skin.
He takes up the prima facie position:
"The skin... (Sūtra 52).
What, then, is non-distinction?
The point is that the eye, when directed toward a jar or similar object, is indeed distinct from the skin. This is the answer.
Regarding the phrase "connection with all substrata," he provides another explanation for the word *avyatireka* from the Sūtra:
"or existence when [the cause] exists."
By this, the commentary (*bhāṣya*)—"and in which [truth] being present"—is explained.
The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of an alternative.
The commentary on the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) states: "not by means of the sense-faculties" (*nendriya*).

Regarding the phrase "contradiction with the world" (*lokavirodha*): that by which something is viewed or known is the "world" (*loka*), meaning valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); thus, the meaning is contradiction with that.

And as for the phrase "by means of multiple non-faculties": the body is composed of earth and is conjoined with other elements; its faculties are located within the body and are pervaded by earth and the other elements. Thus, [the reason] is inconclusive (anaikāntika). [The opponent replies:
"No, because of contradiction."
The purpose is solely to expose the opponent's error; it is not intended that the other sense organs possess the nature of the skin. // 52 //
NyS 3.1.53: No, because objects are not perceived simultaneously.

Having thus stated the established doctrine (siddhānta) according to the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra), he states the established doctrine according to the Sūtra. And the connection with the Sūtra for this established doctrine is as follows:
"Not from the word" (Sūtra 53).
"It is not the case that there is a single sense-organ. Why? "Because objects are not perceived simultaneously.
The author of the Vārttika explains this sūtra from the perspective of the Bhāṣya.
Regarding the statement "of which there is one sense-faculty," he refutes that explanation with the words "not for those [objects] graspable by a single sense-faculty."
Having refuted the commentary on the Bhāṣya, he constructs a framework in order to explain the Sūtra otherwise;
thus speaking, he is called an "advocate of a single sense-faculty" (ekendriyavādin). (388)
5) "Half"—meaning a portion.
Even a single sense organ perceives one half by reaching it, and the other half without reaching it; that is to say, by way of a partial location.
The meaning is that for one who transgresses the nature of an instrument (karaṇadharma), the consequence is the simultaneous perception [of all objects]. // 53 //
And because of contradiction, the skin is not one [single organ].

[The opponent argues: "Since unity has been negated, multiplicity will be established by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*). To this, [the author] says: "An action cannot be without a means" (389/7). And as for how unity [is established], it was stated that the position cannot be refuted.
He asks:
"How then? The answer follows.
"And because of the negation immediately following.

Although the ablative case is not prescribed in grammatical tradition for the use of the word *anantaram* (immediately after), nevertheless, by supplying the word *anya* (other), the ablative is to be explained.
The construction is: "The reason for establishing [the thesis] is other than the negation immediately following."
Alternatively:
a reason based on exclusion (vyatirekī hetuḥ) establishes one of two contradictory [possibilities] by means of the negation of the other.
Just as, by the negation of selflessness, the living body possesses a self. // 54 //
NyS 3.1.55: Because the sense organs and their objects are fivefold.
It introduces the sutra:
"But this is the sutra. This principle has been set forth by me in the form of a sutra through a particular turn of phrase.
This is the meaning. // 55 //
Not so, because there is a multiplicity of objects.
The sūtra of the proponent [of the prima facie view] is:
"Not so—ta-t" (Sūtra 56).

He objects to the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) with the words "not because of contradiction" (na virodhāt). The response of the proponent of the prima facie position is "not because of a lack of proof" (nāsādhanāt). // 56 //
NyS 3.1.57: There is no negation of odors and the like, because they are not distinct from the nature of odor-ness and so forth.
The established conclusion: [Smell is] the object of the sense of smell (NySū 3.1.57). NySū 3.1.58: [Smell is] one, because it does not deviate from being an object [of that sense].
NyS 3.1.59: [The soul is not non-eternal] because of the fivefold nature of cognition, its locus, movement, form, and genus.
"Whose basis is distinct" means it is fixedly distinct.
This is what is being said: for that which manifests visible form, the black antelope alone is the basis, not the ear-canal and so forth; this should be understood in the same way elsewhere as well.

Furthermore, for the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*) who maintains that there is no difference in the substrata (*adhiṣṭhāna*), and likewise no difference in the sense organs (*indriya*) which are based upon those substrata, there is the following consequence:

through the destruction of one substratum, even though the sense organ residing therein is destroyed, another sense organ supported by a different substratum remains. Thus, it is not the case that the destruction of all sense organs—characterized by the destruction of all substrata—occurs simply from the destruction of one substratum.
Likewise, if [the mind] were to abide in a single locus, there would be the defect characterized by the non-abiding of all the sense faculties.
Regarding the desirable, the undesirable, and the neutral:
even that which is neutral possesses the status of a human goal (puruṣārtha) in some manner.
For if a person were to engage in that [action], then a person engaged in fruitless action would suffer;
for the world experiences action as suffering, whereas if it were something to be disregarded, that [suffering] would not occur for him. (58–59)
NyS 3.1.60: Because of the perception of specific qualities of the elements, there is identity [between the body and the elements].
In that regard, the olfactory organ is composed of earth because it invariably manifests odor among color, taste, smell, and touch, just like external earthy substances.
The meaning is that just as chicken droppings and the like, which manifest the scent of musk, are earthy;
nor is there an inconclusiveness [in the reason] due to sunlight.

For heat (*tapas*) does not manifest odor; rather, it is simply that the odor of substances, being overwhelmed by water, is not perceived. Water merely removes [the obstruction], but it does not manifest the odor of the substance.
Therefore, there is no inconclusiveness [in the argument].
Likewise, the sense organ of taste (*rasana*) is composed of water, because among odors and the other [sensory objects], it invariably manifests taste.
Just as one whose mouth is drying up does not experience the taste of a sweetmeat (*modaka*) and the like [due to the lack of moisture],
so too the eye is composed of fire (*taijasa*), because it invariably manifests visible form (*rūpa*) among the group of odor and the other objects, just like a lamp and such.

In this way, the tactile sense organ (*tvagindriya*) is composed of air (*vāyavīya*), because among [the objects] such as odor and so forth, it manifests only touch, just like a fan or a fire-heater which manifest the touch of drops of sweat and water.
The inclusion of the term "restriction" (*niyama*) is for the purpose of excluding the mind (*manas*).
And the term "among" (*madhya*) is for the purpose of establishing a definitive determination (*avadhāraṇa*).
Otherwise, there would be no determination of the nose and the other [faculties] as the manifestors of odor-ness and so forth.
This is what he states:
"The same applies to the remaining [faculties]."

And thus, by the fact that there are only five sense-faculties (*indriya*), it is also indicated that the hands, anus, genitals, and speech are not sense-faculties, because they lack the defining characteristic of a sense-faculty.
For the definition of a sense-faculty is: that which is conjoined with the body, distinct from mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) and defects (*doṣa*), and is a direct means of cognition.
And this [characteristic] does not exist in the hands and so forth.
If it is argued that the definition of the sense organs (*jñānendriya*) is this [absence of such a characteristic],
then alas, another definition for their status as organs (*indriyatva*) must be stated.

If it is argued that the definition is "the sense organ which, depending on the body, performs its own specific function," then the specific functions of these [organs] must be stated. It has been said: "Speech, grasping, movement, excretion, and pleasure are the [functions] of the five."
But surely, taking up, moving about, and excreting can be performed even by those with deformed hands and so forth;

moreover, since there are specific, unique functions such as swallowing and so on for the throat, heart, stomach, and large intestine, it would follow that these too must be considered sense-faculties (*indriya*). Therefore, this [definition] is also quite trivial.
NyS 3.1.61: Among smell, taste, color, touch, and sound, those ending with touch (i.e., smell, taste, color, and touch) belong to earth.
Having excluded each preceding one among water, fire, and air, the subsequent one belongs to space.
Desiring to examine the definition of the object (*artha*) which follows in sequence, he recalls the definition of the object:

"Odors and so forth are the qualities (*guṇa*) of earth and so forth. Although it should have been stated as "defined" (*lakṣita*), the vague expression "indicated" (*uddiṣṭa*) was used because it was mentioned by way of its general category.
In that regard, the *Parīkṣāmukha* states the doubt:
"The enunciation and the injunction. It then describes the nature of the injunction (*niyoga*) and the other categories.
Regarding the term "niyoga" (injunction) therein:

having thus reflected and abandoned both the injunction (*niyoga*) and the conjunction (*samuccaya*), the author resorts to the alternative (*vikalpa*) for the sake of specification by means of these two sūtras; therefore, [the sūtras are:
"smell and so forth" (Sūtra 61) and "water and so forth" (Sūtra 62).
Regarding the phrase "for the sake of specification":
the intended meaning of the two sūtras has been stated; he now clarifies that very point with the words "for the sake of restriction."
In each of the subsequent elements beginning with water, there is a progressive diminution of qualities starting from odor and ending with touch.
For instance, among the four [elements], there is no further emergence of an already diminished odor in water; thus, in fire, which follows water, there is a diminution of taste.
Likewise, since there is no further emergence of the already diminished odor and taste, in wind, which follows fire, there is a diminution of form.
Thus, since there is no further arising of those odors, tastes, and forms that have been attenuated, there is an attenuation of touch in the space following the air.
This is what was meant by the phrase "one by one.
The word *uttara* (following) is not used in the sense of "subsequent" (*anantara*); therefore, even when selecting from among many, its meaning remains as previously stated.
Or, let there be an indication of the suffix *tarap*; even so, there is no fault, as he says: "Let it be.
In some places, the reading is "or *tantra*," as in the Bhāṣya.
The meaning is indeed clear. // 61–62 //
Not so, because not all qualities are perceived.
The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) raises the position of the mandate (niyoga):
"Not from the word" (Sūtra 63).
