The restriction that the sense organs, such as the olfactory organ, manifest their respective objects, such as odor, only from their corresponding material causes, such as earth and so forth, is established only if earth possesses the quality of odor alone and water possesses the quality of taste alone, and so on;
it is not otherwise.
For otherwise, by means of the olfactory organ belonging to earth, taste, color, and touch would also be manifested, since there would be no distinction [between them]. This is the meaning. // 63 //
NyS 3.1.64: Because each subsequent quality exists in addition to the preceding ones, those [qualities] are not perceived in the subsequent [substances].
For the subsequent is indeed pervaded by the preceding.
"viṣṭaṃ ṇa" (Sūtra 65).

Although a relation has two loci, it does not possess the character of being co-present in both [in the same way]. For example, the relation between fire and smoke is such that fire is the pervader (*vyāpaka*): in the presence of smoke, fire must exist and cannot be absent; whereas smoke is the pervaded (*vyāpya*): it exists only where there is fire, and not elsewhere.
In the same way, earth and the other elements are pervaded by water and the others; earth does not exist without water.
Therefore, on earth, qualities such as taste and so forth belonging to water and the other elements are invariably perceived, but the qualities of earth are not perceived within water and the others;
in this way, the qualities of fire and the others in water have been explained.
"Pervasion" (viṣṭatva) means a specific kind of conjunction (saṃyoga-viśeṣa), that is to say, interpenetration (vyāpti).
And this commentary [states], "In the accounts of the creation of the elements":
that is, in the Purāṇas which set forth the creation of the elements; "not now" means not at present, because it is not being experienced. (64–65)
NyS 3.1.66: It is not so, because both the earthy and the watery [substances] are perceptible.
The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) refutes this position of the one who argues for alternatives with the following sūtra: "Not so, because... (Sūtra 66).
For it is held that substance is of three kinds—visible: namely, earthy, watery, and fiery.
Among these, only the fiery substance would be visible because it possesses color;
the others would not, as they lack color.
Nor should it be said that visibility belongs to both the earthy and the watery [substances] because of their inclusion within the category of material substances;
for then it would follow as a consequence that space and air are also visible,
since they too possess light which is endowed with color.

Alternatively, the author of the Bhāṣya states that this is because the various kinds of taste and color associated with earth and water are perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as being both single and manifold;
he says this from the words "Or [the distinction] between two tastes," etc., up to "is not tenable.
He then provides another explanation of this very point.
Regarding the phrase "of the two tangibles":
since the mention of "the earthy and the watery" is intended merely as an illustrative example,
it has also been explained that this applies to the "earthy and the fiery" as well.
He states another explanation:
"Or rather" (*atha vā*).
Since the effect is observed to possess fixed qualities, the cause is also inferred to possess fixed qualities.
Nor is there a universal conjunction by which the quality of one thing would be perceived in another, because we observe both distinction (*viveka*) and non-conjunction (*asaṃsarga*).
He states another explanation:
"And it is seen," etc.
What is the meaning of "conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*)? He says that "injunction" (*niyoga*), however, is without inference (*niranumāna*);
for it is said: "That which is entered into without inference is indeed not through a traditional succession."

The restriction that "fragrance exists only in earth" and so forth has no valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) as its cause, because a subverting means of cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against it has already been stated.
Therefore, the creation of the elements must be explained in some way through figurative usage.
Pervasion is conjunction, and that is common to both [the agent and the object].
When a quality belonging to one thing is perceived in another, is that due to conjunction or rather to pervasion?
If, due to a lack of pervasion, the qualities of fire were not perceived in an iron ball (ayogolaka) that has come into contact with fire—
because there would be no relationship of pervaded and pervader between those two—

and yet the qualities of fire were perceived in smoke hanging in the sky by means of the fire situated on the ground— because there exists a relationship of pervaded and pervader between those two; [then the inference would be valid].

Therefore, conjunction with another [substance] is the cause [of perceptibility], and since that is indistinguishable for both, it follows as an undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that even air conjoined with fire would be visible due to its possession of color. // 66 //
NyS 3.1.67: Due to the progressive excellence of each preceding quality, each respective one becomes predominant.
As previously stated (Sūtra 67).
The commentator explains the meaning of the term "predominance": "the state of being the grasper of objects; the object is smell and so forth.
To the question "From where does that very state of being the grasper of objects arise?", he says:
"From the excellence of the quality (guṇa), that is, from the capacity for its manifestation."

Intending that if preeminence consists in being the grasper of objects, then it would apply to all the sense-faculties alike because they all grasp their respective objects, the author of the Vārttika, unable to accept the commentator’s explanation, asks: "What is this preeminence? (395/8). He then provides the answer according to his own view.

"Because it possesses four qualities," etc. This is what is meant: since the olfactory organ (*ghrāṇa*), being composed of earth, possesses four qualities and is thus predominant over the gustatory organ and the others which are composed of water and so forth, it lacks the absence of odor; for if it were odorless, it would not perceive odor. [Objection: But if that is the case, since the olfactory organ also possesses taste and the other qualities, it should also perceive taste and so forth. Therefore, it is said: "due to the predominance of its own quality."

Even though there is no difference in the combination of all [qualities], the excellence of the sense of smell belongs to odor alone; therefore, it perceives odor alone. Thus, the statement regarding its predominance is intended to exclude the absence of odor, but it is not the case that possessing odor is the cause for the perception of odor; rather, it is established that it is the excellence of the odor [that accounts for this]. Regarding this, the author of the Vārttika asks about the meaning of the term "excellence": "What is the excellence of a quality?"

The "superior capacity" refers to the power of manifesting its own quality (*svaguṇa*). The "own quality" of the olfactory organ (*ghrāṇa*) is odor (*gandha*); even though an odor inherent in sandalwood and the like—which belongs to the same genus [as that of the organ]—is also called "its own," the olfactory organ does not manifest only its own quality. For, by the power of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), there occurs such a specific transformation (*nirmāṇabheda*) in the odor inherent in the olfactory organ itself, whereby it manifests an odor of the same genus inherent in sandalwood and the like, just as it manifests the odor of musk and so forth.
"Odor is inherent in other substances that are earthy.
For this very reason he says: "By whichever quality a substance is excelled, that [quality] becomes preeminent because it manifests its own kind;
[this applies] to that substance," so the remainder [of the sentence].
As for the argument "because it possesses the quality of odor":

the meaning is that the nose manifests odor solely because it possesses the quality of odor alone, and not because of an excellence of odor. For that proponent, there would follow the undesirable consequence of perceiving all qualities of earthy substances whatsoever.
The meaning is that there would be the undesirable consequence [of sound] being perceivable by the sense of smell. // 67 //
But its determination [as such] occurs because of its abundance.
He asks, "Why again? in order to introduce the sūtra, [anticipating the objection]: "But from where does your own [position] derive its establishment?
This is the sūtra [68].
Regarding the phrase "the accomplishment of the goal":
"goal" refers to the aim of human life (*puruṣārtha*).
Regarding the phrase "of that which is divided": [it refers to the division of the *prakṛti*].
Of that which is distinguished from others;
"produced by conditioning" means "produced by the unseen force" (adṛṣṭa). // 68 //
NyS 3.1.69: Because the sense organs exist as entities possessing qualities.
He raises an objection: "But if [it is argued] that 'the odor belongs to the sense organ'... He refutes this.
"By that very [means], there is no grasping of that," because of the rule: "And because there is no grasping of that by that very [means]. (NyS 3.1.70)
He explains this mnemonic verse (*grahaṇakavākya*) along with its supplementary context:
if this [odor] were to grasp its own odor by itself, then that odor of the sense organ would be perceived by you through sight;
however, if it is an odor of the sense organ, then it could not be grasped by the sense organ [of sight].
Why is it that the odor of the sense organ is not perceivable by the senses? To this he says:
"And while perceiving the odor..."
The word "co" (also) has the sense of "because.
Since there is no instrument that establishes the self, it was stated that the mind, like other inferential marks (*liṅga*), is an instrument for the self and not something solitary.

To bring about parity [between the mind and the other organs], the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*) questions the opponent (*pūrvapakṣin*): "Why, then, is this objection not raised?"
The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) says, "It is not objected.

The proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntavādin) says, "The non-perception of its own odor by the nose is equal [to the case of sound]. He establishes this very equality, saying, "This too is not to be stated as an objection. // 70 //
Not so, because sound is perceived as a quality.
Its perception [is established] because of its difference in nature from other substances and qualities.

If it is argued that space and time possess sound as their quality (*śabdaguṇatva*), there is merely a dispute over names. For if space and time possessed sound as their quality, they could not—by virtue of having a unique connection—be the cause of the confusion between "prior" and "posterior," just as the case is with earth and the other elements. Thus, since it is space alone that possesses sound as its quality and is the cause of the cognitions of "prior" and "posterior," there is only a dispute over names.
Space and time, however, must be postulated as the causes of the distinction between "prior" and "posterior"; therefore, the meaning is that they are distinct [from the elements].
Furthermore, for one who accepts space, the rejection of space is untenable because its functional capacity is not perceived.

For the very nature and capacity of the sense organs (*indriya*) consists in the direct perception of form and so forth; this is observed in the substance of the eye and other organs, but not in qualities (*guṇa*) and the like—this is the meaning. // 75 //
Thus ends the first Āhnika of the third Adhyāya in the *Nyāyavārtikatātparyaṭīkā* composed by the venerable Miśra Vācaspati.
[End of] the *Nyāyavārtikatātparyaṭīkā* composed by the venerable Vācaspati Miśra.
The Third Chapter. NyS 3.2.1: Doubt arises because of the similarity between action and space.
The sense organs and their objects have been examined; now follows the sequence of the examination of the intellect (*buddhi*).
"Sequence" (*krama*) refers to the order of presentation.
The recitation of what has already occurred and what is yet to occur is for the purpose of making known the relationship between cause and effect.

The examination of objects and sense-faculties, as well as the examination of cognition (*buddhi*), will become clear precisely within the examination of cognition itself, according to their respective applications.
[The author] now introduces doubt.
Regarding the phrase "of an impossible nature" (anupapannarūpa):
if the doubt concerns an object of cognition that is currently being perceived, it is untenable, because even the Sāṃkhyas accept its impermanence.

If, however, the object is the principle of the Great One (mahattattva) as favored by the Sāṃkhyas, there is disagreement regarding its very existence; how then can there be an investigation into its properties? For properties are considered only when a substratum exists, not when its existence is doubtful.
This is the intended meaning. He resolves [the objection] with the words "in the doctrine of views" (*dṛṣṭipravāda*).

For in the system of the Sāṃkhyas, there is a traditional teaching (*pravāda*) that the internal organ, the Great One (*mahat*), is the intellect (*buddhi*); this treatise is for the purpose of censuring—that is, refuting—that [view].
This is the intended meaning:

here, even by means of this investigation into the permanence or impermanence [of the intellect], that "intellect" (buddhi) postulated by the Sāṃkhyas—which is distinct from the mental modifications—is refuted through a general examination of whether the intellect as such is permanent or impermanent.
For if the intellect were indeed permanent, then [it would remain] beyond the modifications...
The internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) would have to be a principle of "Greatness" (*mahattattva*) distinct from those [mental states] characterized by arising and passing away.

However, if the proofs for permanence—such as recognition (*pratisandhāna*) and so forth—do not suffice to establish the permanence of the intellect (*buddhi*), then it follows that the intellects are merely the mental modifications (*vṛtti*) themselves, and no separate intellectual principle beyond them is established; thus it is proven that "intellect," "apprehension," and "knowledge" are synonymous.
Thus, the definition of the intellect (buddhi) is connected to the definition of its substrate;
otherwise, however, an investigation into permanence and impermanence from the perspective of the primary principle would not be connected with the definition. // 1 //
NyS 3.2.2: Because there is recognition of the object.
And they state the proof:
"Because there is recognition of the object.
For it is said that the possessor of the mental states (*vṛttimān*), in recognizing the object, also recognizes himself.
Furthermore, it is not the conscious self that possesses the modifications, because it is immutable and eternal;
otherwise, being subject to differences between prior and subsequent states, it would not be immutable and eternal.

The point is that it is the intellect (*buddhi*), which is transformatively eternal, that is logically consistent with possessing various modifications characterized by arising and passing away. // 2 //
NyS 3.2.3: It is not a valid reason because it is equivalent to the point to be proven.
The proponent of the final view (siddhāntin) says: "It is not a valid reason because it is equivalent to the point to be proven.

For the functions (vṛttayaḥ) are indeed distinct from that which possesses the functions (vṛttimat); therefore, even if those functions are eternal, the possessor of the functions does not fall away from its immutability (kauṭasthya).
Thus, by means of recognition, it is the Self itself that is eternal due to being recognized, and not the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) known as the intellect (buddhi).
The meaning is that it does not manifest in that recognition;
and because an instrument cannot be the locus of an action.

The instrument (*karaṇa*) is that which does not serve as the substratum for the primary action; and this primary action here is perception (*upalabdhi*). When that which is perceived as the self-subsistent substratum of this [perception] is the agent (*kartṛ*), it is not the instrument.

Thus, through perceptions such as recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), the self (*ātman*) is established as the permanent agent who is the substratum of that [perception], and not as the instrument—this is the meaning.
He raises an objection by referring to the mere expression of "action" (*kriyā*).
He refutes this by relying on the primary action (*pradhānakriyā*) as "it becomes real" (*satyaṃ bhavati*).

Now, if the application of terms such as "agent" (*kartṛ*) occurs when there is a desire to express distinction (*bhedavivakṣā*), and the application of the term "factor of action" (*kāraka*) occurs when there is a desire to express non-distinction (*abhedavivakṣā*), [then what follows?]

If that is so, how then can there be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in such expressions as "the agent is an instrument" or "the factor of action (*kāraka*) is an instrument," given that the intentions of emphasizing difference and non-difference have contradictory meanings?
To this, he says: "By the word 'kāraka' also... (440).

4) There is no intention to express the non-difference of particulars; rather, there is an intention to express the universal. For when one says "it is divided," it is the division [of the universal] that is meant, not the non-division [of the particulars], because the universal is what is being denoted. Thus, a word employed with the intention of expressing a universal attains grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a word denoting its particular, and by taking up a particular excluded from others—such as the ablative (*apādāna*) or other specific *kārakas*—it functions toward that particular. This is because there is no other specific *kāraka*.
Because it is impossible for it to be in grammatical apposition with a word denoting a *kāraka* (participant in an action).
"As before" refers to the definition of the specific types of *kārakas* stated in the second chapter; he thus recalls that [definition].
He objects with the words "if [it is] by another agent.
For indeed, an agent who has been set in motion by the appropriation of instruments appropriates those very instruments;
therefore, its state of not being employed by another is unestablished—this is the meaning.
He avoids [the objection] by saying that [the agent] does not apply himself [to the action], because the fruit is the motivator;
we do not call one who does not apply himself an "agent" (kartṛ), but rather one who is not motivated by any causal factor (kāraka).

And the meaning is that the fruit is not the agent. Having granted for the sake of argument that there is recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), [the author asks]: if this recognition were perceptual (*pratyakṣa*), it would not establish oneness; rather, it would be an inference (*anumāna*). Therefore, as for the claim that "whatever is recognized is one," there is no illustrative example (*nidarśana*) [to prove it].
For its unity is not ascertained from any other source than this recognition;
nor is its multiplicity observed. Thus, because it is uncommon (asādhāraṇa), it is a fallacious reason (hetvābhāsa);
this is the meaning.
Furthermore, once the nature of recognition has been determined, the reason [used by the opponent] is a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) because it proves the non-eternality of cognition;
the rest has been explained by the literal recitation [of the commentary] itself.
We have already examined, in our investigation of the definition of cognition, that there is no difference between consciousness and the determination [of an object]. (3)
NyS 3.2.4: No, because they are not perceived simultaneously.
The meaning of the sūtra is that because the possessor of the modification persists, it would follow that the modification itself must persist. // 4 //
And if there were no recognition, it would follow that [the object] has perished.
NyS 3.2.6: Because they occur successively, there is no simultaneous apprehension.
And there is non-recognition due to the engagement with another object.
NyS 3.2.8: No, because there is no motion.
The opponent’s question, "Why is it not the same for me as well? is answered by the respondent: "Because it is observed that [the result] varies according to the difference in causes.
For when there is a difference in causes, it is observed that a single agent produces multiple effects simultaneously.

According to the Sāṅkhyas, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is both the agent and all-pervading; therefore, the sense organs, presided over by this all-pervading internal organ, would perform their functions simultaneously.

For us, however, because the internal organ is an instrument (*karaṇa*), there is no simultaneous production of effects even when [an object] is perceivable by a single sense organ—this is the distinction.

Regarding the commentary's statement, "And because there is no movement, the non-simultaneous apprehension [of objects] by the all-pervading internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is not inferred by any other mark," [the author] quotes the portion "and because there is no movement for the all-pervading internal organ" and explains its meaning as:
"because there is an absence of going, which has the sense of reaching [a destination]."

Furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the simultaneous arising of cognitions, by which one might accept the simultaneity of cognitions even though it has been refuted. Therefore, if the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) were all-pervading (*vibhu*), the simultaneity of cognitions would necessarily occur; yet this is not observed. Thus, the meaning is that the internal organ is atomic (*aṇu*). [Objection: But when one eats a long *śaṣkulī* (a type of pastry), the simultaneous arising of five cognitions is observed. What is this logical consequence? That if the internal organ were all-pervading, simultaneous arising would follow. To this [the author replies]:...
He said:
"And not when cognitions arise simultaneously.
The meaning is that, due to extreme rapidity, there is the conceit of simultaneous arising, but in reality, simultaneity does not exist there.

He explains the Bhāṣya—“But for whom [it is] the modification [of the intellect], [and not] the possessor of the modification”—which is intent on establishing his own position that it is the person (*puruṣa*) who knows, and not the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Furthermore, there is the Bhāṣya intended to refute the claim made by the Sāṃkhyas—that when the internal organ is occupied with another object, even though there is a connection with the eye and other senses, the absence of knowledge occurs because the modification of the internal organ is what constitutes knowledge—and this is addressed by the passage beginning with “by this, [the case of] occupation with another object... (404.12).
Thus [it is said].
Having restated that, the author of the Vārttika explains it with the words "by this."
Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*):

he states the basis for the negation [expressed by] "no," namely, that "the person (*puruṣa*) knows, not the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). By this reason, the objection that the internal organ is distracted by other objects is refuted.
For he who knows [the Self] becomes attached;

however, it is not the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) that knows, but rather the Person (*puruṣa*). Thus, such attachment belongs to the Person and not to the internal organ. The meaning is that the internal organ’s own kind of attachment is not what is being prohibited. // 8 //
The misconception of its being something else is like the misconception of a different crystal.
Regarding the statement of the objection, "The internal organ is one, yet its modifications are manifold," he explains it as follows:
"The internal organ is one, yet its modifications are manifold"—
this is not so.
One who perceives correctly and knows is a *saṃcakṣāṇaka*, a Sāṃkhya.
For *saṃkhyā* is correct cognition; one who functions by means of that is a Sāṃkhya.

This is what is meant: although the mental modifications (*vṛttayaḥ*) appear to be manifold, this is nonetheless an illusion, because multiplicity is impossible for those [modifications] that are non-different from the single internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

Therefore, just as a single crystal appears to have a diversity that is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*) due to the proximity of various flowers such as the *tāpiccha*, *japā*, or *karṇikāra*, so too the gem-like internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), though transparent, acquires an adventitious plurality when colored by this or that object through the channel of the senses; and it is for this reason that it is designated as "modification" (*vṛtti*), "cognition" (*pratyaya*), and "knowledge" (*jñāna*).
He now refutes this.
"Not because of non-exclusivity" (nānekāntāt).

Even for one who asserts that the distinctions among functions (*vṛtti*) are merely adventitious (*aupādhika*), he must also state that the objects which serve as the conditions (*upādhi*) are inherently distinct.
Thus, since difference is observed in two ways, the example is non-exclusive (*anekānta*); it does not prove a single [undifferentiated] object.
He explains the commentary, "Not so, because of the absence of a reason," by stating, "according to the literal meaning of the Sūtra.
He says, "and because an alternative is untenable," to show that it is not merely a lack of proof [for the opponent], but that there is also a sublation [of their position] here.
With the intention that the establishment of one's own position does not occur through the mere refutation of the opponent's position, he asks:
Now, as for your point "of yours," the reply is:
"by means of the successive order of cognitions.
It might be argued that the cause for the multiplicity of functions [of the mind] would be the conceit of a diversity of cognitions, even though there is a unity [of the mind].
"Unity [belongs] to the mental modes because they are the objects of the conceit of diversity, like a crystal; therefore, there is no lack of a reason. To this, he says:
"And because the conceit of the diversity of cognitions has both a single and multiple objects, how can there be an apprehension of a single or multiple object?"
The conceit of diversity is also non-conclusive, like the previous example, because it is not necessarily [indicative of a cause].
Thus, having refuted the opponent's objection in the interim, he again establishes the difference in functions with the words:
"And this which is undivided..."

If there is no difference in cognitions due to the difference in the adjuncts (*upadhāna*) of objects, then for one who does not perceive [that difference], there would be no difference in cognition regarding a single object, because there is an absence of a difference in the adjuncts of the cognition; this is the meaning.
Someone objects:
"Like a crystal," and so forth.

"It avoids [the objection] because of the perception of continuity" means that even the application of an indigo dye has intervals, which are to be inferred from the direct perception [of the object] as "blue crystal"— this is the intended meaning.
He says the following to show that there is also a difference in cognition for this reason:
And as for the phrase "whose difference in cognition [is absent]":

the difference in the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is to be inferred from the difference in its effect, which is characterized by the cognition; it cannot exist in the absence of a difference in cognition.
He raises the objection that "it is due to the difference in objects.
This is what is meant:
even if the individual distinction among objects were the cause for the distinction between means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [the following would apply].

Alas! Due to its infinity, there would be an infinite variety of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and not just three; therefore, one must admit a subordinate generality (*avāntara-sāmānya*) among objects.
Nor can that [generality] reside solely in the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of objects, because there is an overlap (*saṃplava*) of means of valid cognition even with respect to a single object.

Therefore, objects which possess universals conditioned by differences in their respective causes are established as being threefold, and they likewise establish the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as being threefold.
Furthermore, there are three types of cognitions that conform to the positive and negative concomitance of the three sets of causal complexes (*sāmagrī*).
Thus, because they have three objects, the means of valid cognition are three.
This has been stated as "because of the difference in objects";
[the author] refutes it,
saying "that is not so."

When there is no difference in the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no difference in the three causal complexes (*sāmagrī*), because the conditions (*pratyaya*) that constitute them are not different.
Indeed, without a difference in the conditions, a difference in the causal complex cannot be discerned.

Therefore, even when the causal complex of the conditions is undifferentiated, since no difference in the object is apprehended, neither a difference in the object nor the apprehension of its threefold nature occurs without a difference in the conditions.

If it is suspected that [the distinction] arises from identity with the object, the meaning is that the distinction between cognitions is established because there is no difference between the cognition and the object of cognition. He refutes this:
"No, that is not so.

Furthermore, if there were no difference in the conditions (*pratyaya*), then because there would be an absence of modal variety (*prakāravattva*), there would be a contradiction in the claim that "the person intends (*cetayate*) in the same way that the intellect (*buddhi*) determines (*adhyavasyati*).
Why? Because of the absence of modal variety; for that which possesses modal variety is indeed distinct, whereas that which is non-distinct does not—this is the meaning.

If there were no distinction between the internal instrument, namely the intellect (*buddhi*), and its objective conditions (*pratyaya*), then the intellect would perceive that very condition; thus, there would be a contradiction. // 9 //
Even in the case of a crystal, because there is the arising of successive [moments], and because individual entities are momentary, [the opponent's reason] is not a valid proof.

Thus, having refuted the Sāṃkhya position according to his own view, [the author] sets forth the Buddhist position in order to refute the criticism that Buddhists have leveled against the Sāṃkhya tenets;
the proponent of momentariness (kṣaṇikavādin) says this, not tolerating the misconception of a change in the crystal.
Sphaṭika—however (sūtra 10).
The elderly Buddhists maintain that whatever exists is momentary; just as the body is, so too is the crystal.

For, since one observes the decrease of bulk in the body through the power of temporal maturation, a subtle difference in transformation is inferred at every moment, and this is precisely its destruction in the interim.

Even in the case of things such as crystal, for which no such increase or decrease in bulk is perceived, their production and destruction at every moment are inferred by virtue of their existence, just as in the case of the body.

It might be argued: "When the growth and decay of the body are observed, then its production and destruction will occur; but what is the proof for postulating a continuous stream [of moments] prior to that? To this, he says:
Regarding the phrase "for whatever [object] at every moment" (407/9), the formal argument is as follows: "At every moment, it is different and yet different.

When a cloth comes into contact with substances such as saffron and the like, a specific quality characterized by redness is observed at the end; however, this redness does not exist at every moment. Therefore, it was stated: "provided there is no difference in external conditions."

For the cause of the accumulation of the body is not distinct [from the body itself], just as the daily consumption of food and drink is. Just as external contact with fire, dependent on heat, is the causal condition for the production of cooked results (*pākaja*), whereas for the production of redness in a cloth, the immediate and specific cause is contact with saffron substance—this is the meaning. // 10 //
NyS 3.2.11: Since there is no cause for restriction, everything is permitted as it is observed.
The aphorism on the established conclusion: [The soul is] characterized by constant cognition. (Sūtra 11)
He explains this as follows:
"This [is] accumulation and depletion.

For fire inferred from the sight of smoke does not function [only] in that specific instance; rather, even when smoke is no longer visible, inferents infer fire on another mountain by the mere fact of its being a mountain. This is the meaning.
Regarding the phrase "where apprehension is suspected":
momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) means persisting for only a mere fraction of time devoid of prior and posterior parts.
And since such momentariness is not accepted by the Naiyāyikas anywhere, the meaning is that there is no proving of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
He refutes this, saying:
"It is true. But why is it that momentariness, as we maintain it, is not established, given that one observes a continuous process of accumulation and decay? To this [he replies]:
He said:
"And the observation of the continuity of accumulation and depletion occurs otherwise.
The word "and" (ca) has the sense of a reason.
He raises an objection with the words "it is equal" (408/5).
He refutes it with the words "not because of a lack of proof" (nāsādhanāt);
for there is no proof without a definitive certainty.
Refutation, however, occurs even by producing doubt;
this is the meaning of the distinction between proof and refutation. // 11 //
NyS 3.2.12: [The self is eternal] because causes for its production and destruction are not perceived.
He introduces the subsequent sūtra:
"Now, the proof must necessarily be stated," because [the object] has not yet arisen.
(Sūtra 12)
The causes of arising and destruction are indicators [of duration], and the accumulation and depletion of parts are not tenable in the case of momentariness;
for there can be no conditions for accumulation and depletion in the case of arising and destruction that are without continuity.
This is because the causes of arising and destruction are observed to result from accumulation and depletion.
Furthermore, "increase and decrease" and "the causes of arising and destruction" form a *karmadhāraya* compound.
He states another interpretation of the phrase "because the cause of arising and destruction is perceived":
"Alternatively, [it means] 'the cause'."

The meaning is that it is well-established in the world that an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) exists both prior to the effect and at the time of the effect; however, this is untenable if momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) were true.
"Experiencing at one and the same time" means experience or attainment at the same time; that is, attaining [the two] simultaneously.
One who disregards worldly conventions raises the objection regarding the relation of substratum and superstratum (*ādhārādheyabhāva*).
He refutes [the opponent's position] not because of non-conclusiveness (*anekānta*);
for even in your own system, form (*rūpa*) is resistant (*sapratigha*), is an effect (*kārya*), and has a substratum (*ādhāra*).
However, if you consider that form itself is without a substratum, then you would contradict your own established doctrine (*svasiddhānta-vyākopa*); thus he says.
"Contact and its basis [occur simultaneously], which is a contradiction;
thus, it is established that everything is experienced at one and the same time.
To this, he objects: "The causal relationship is established even for momentary things."
Because it would entail the consequence that the effect has no locus;
for the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is not unestablished even under the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*).

Rather, it is established even in the position of momentariness, because the production of the effect occurs simultaneously with the destruction of the cause; thus, the meaning is that the cause and the effect are simultaneous.
He refutes [this] by saying:
"Not so, because of a failure to understand the meaning of the reason.
By such effort as this, you attempt to establish the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) for momentary things, yet this [relationship] does not exist in the case of non-momentary things.
Furthermore, the relationship between cause and effect would be one of locus and located, yet that is impossible to establish. What indeed is this destruction of the cause?
Is it the absence of the cause, or the presence of a cause of destruction?
In the first case, how could there be simultaneity between the effect and the cause?
Furthermore, even in the case of the subsequent [moment], since there is proximity to a cause of destruction for that which has already arisen, how can there be momentariness for that which exists?
Moreover, there is no simultaneity between the state of being produced (*utpadyamānatā*) and the state of perishing (*vinaśyattā*), because that would contradict experience.
And if the effect were being produced at that very same time, there would be an absence of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), like the left and right horns [of a cow]; such is the sense.
Furthermore, he states that the example is also deficient in the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*) with the words "of the weigher" (*tulādhārasya*).
Regarding those two actions of the parts— the upward and downward movements— there is no causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) between them.

The meaning is that, regarding the action of the whole (*avayavin*), there is neither simultaneity nor a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) because of its unity. As for the statement "rising [occurs] from gravity, effort, and conjunction":

the supporting effort belongs to the holder of the scale; the conjunction dependent upon that [effort] is a conjunction with what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasaṃyoga*); and gravity is the cause residing in other parts conjoined with it, which brings about the rising of the part of the scale.

Even in the case of an atom, when a substance such as gold possessing gravity is being weighed, the conjunction of the rope and the scale, assisted by the conjunctions [of the atoms], is the cause. 12.
The establishment of that [soul] is possible, like the non-perception of the cause for the destruction of milk and like the production of curd.
Non-apprehension is not [the cause], because [the object] is apprehended through its mark (liṅga).
He objects: "It is not that there is no distinction between the sensations of cold and heat.
He replies: "But that [distinction] arises from another cause. He objects again.
It is not logical for there to be an entry of the constituent parts of water and fire; rather,
their own inherent specificities are their "parts," namely earth and so forth,
for these are called "specifics" (viśeṣāḥ) because they are distinguished from one another.
He refutes this,
saying it is not tenable:
if a distinction were based merely on the fact that each moment is different, then even the moments of wood would be perceived as distinct from one another, just like earth, stone, and iron.
For just as iron-moments suddenly differ from wood-moments, so too do other wood-moments differ [from one another].

Therefore, even though they share the quality of being earthy (*pārthivatva*), intrinsic distinctions must be admitted, since a wood-moment is excluded from things such as the earth or stone, yet is not excluded from other wood-moments. It is precisely because of this distinction that [the wood-moment] exists, even if it were not momentary (*akṣaṇikatva*).
Since there is an established progressive distinction among wood, earth, stone, and iron, the postulation of momentariness is futile;
the nature of the elements is not a proof [for momentariness].
This means that it does not establish momentariness.
He states another refutation:
"And this reason is contradictory (viruddha),
because of the observation of successive distinctions."
It is said by you that the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of the elements (*bhūta*) is what distinguishes them from one another: the elements consist of solidity, moisture, heat, and motion.
Solidity is earth; moisture is water; heat is fire; and motion is wind—that is, it possesses movement.

However, if the production [of these qualities] in wood, earth, stone, and iron were admitted, then each would consist of only solidity and heat, being composed of solidity, heat, and motion. Consequently, because of this confusion, there would be a contradiction of the defining characteristics of the elements.
The term "hard" (kaṭhina) indicates solid earth.

He says, "But for our position, there is no contradiction," meaning that it is not only contradicted by the definition of earth and so forth, but also by the previously stated proof of manifoldness through the distinction between cold and hot touch; thus he says: "Furthermore, for whom... [etc.].
"And this is contradictory. He asks: "How so? The answer:
This is because one has accepted a distinction [in that very thing].
The meaning is: by the very same distinction—such as the difference between cold and heat—by which diversity from the previous state was accepted, there is now oneness.
"Having accepted a tenet" means that it is contradictory because it contradicts the matter already accepted by means of the previous reason.
He raises an objection: "Now, you might think that it is not merely a particularity [that is the basis of designation].

The intention is that form (*rūpa*) as a single entity should not be both characterized by resistance (*sapratigha*) and the material cause (*upādāna*), lest there be a plurality within that single form. He refutes this, saying: "This is not the intended meaning."

As for the one who would argue that, upon entering the constituent parts [of water], fire would be perceived like the sensation of heat in hot water, and that its form would likewise be perceived as in the case of a red-hot iron ball (*ayogolaka*), [the author] states the rebuttal against him according to the view of the "Partialists" (*Ekadeśin*):
"There would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of perceiving the form of fire in water. He then refutes that [position].
"No," [he replies].
It is logical that at midday the faint light of a torch is overwhelmed by the intense light of the sun, because it is of the same kind (sajātīya) yet inferior in intensity.
However, the form of water is neither intense nor of the same kind, because its nature is non-existence (abhāva).
The meaning is that light is radiant, and therefore there is no overpowering [of it].
He states the ultimate resolution:
"However, because light is of four kinds."
Light exists in some cases with both visible form and touch manifest, such as the solar radiance during the day in autumn;
in some cases, with both visible form and touch unmanifest, such as the ocular light; and in some cases, with visible form manifest and touch unmanifest.

And just as there is some fire in the light of a lamp whose color and touch are unmanifest, or as there is fire in water, or as there is fire at midnight during the summer heat by which those who are corpulent perspire—
one refutes [the opponent's position] by analyzing the meaning of the proposition according to these possibilities.
Regarding this proposition:
having accepted the present crystal as the subject and taking another past crystal as the object of proof, it is established that "it is other than the present one. [The author] refutes this:
"Such being the case" means:

if the logical mark (*liṅga*) were indicative by virtue of both its own existence and its cognition, then even when there is cognition, because the existence of a past phenomenon does not exist, it would not be indicative; this is the sense.
Furthermore, if the logical mark were said to be indicative by its mere cognition, he states another objection:
"And from the present" means that it perishes by following the destruction of its substrate, which is opposed to it;
the term "opposed" refers to the qualities (guṇas).
For a quality is destroyed by another opposing quality and by the destruction of its substratum;

this is common to all cases. Furthermore, the mention of the "substratum" is an illustration, and by it, one should infer—as far as possible—the destruction [of qualities] through the destruction of their non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) and instrumental causes (*nimittakāraṇa*).
He raises the objection that it is a state of perishing:
"Let the lamp not be the example; however, in a substance that is in a state of perishing, motion arises and ceases immediately after its production. Therefore, such motion will serve as the example.
He refutes this with: "Not [by] motion."

For this doctrine of momentariness is based on the denial of karma; it cannot hold if that [karma] is accepted, because the production of an effect is possible from a stable substance itself when conjoined with adventitious karma. He states another refutation:
And because [it] is not accepted:
for even such action is momentary according to us;
thus, the state of the substance being in the process of destruction and the arising of the action are simultaneous.

This is the destruction of the substance; and since the production of the effect does not occur at the same time as the production of the cause, it is established that action perishes immediately after the destruction of the substance, and thus action persists for two moments. [The opponent] objects:

If it is argued that this is because there is no cause for destruction, the underlying intention [of the objection] is as follows: does this entity arise from its own causes as something perishable or as something imperishable?

If it is perishable, it would not require a cause for its destruction; for blue, once produced from its own causes, does not require a further cause for its blueness, since it possesses that very nature.
Even if it were indestructible, its destruction could not be brought about even by hundreds of causes;
for once blue has arisen, it cannot be turned into yellow even by a hundred craftsmen.
Furthermore, this destruction, when produced by the causes of an entity, must arise as either distinct from or non-distinct from that entity.

If there were non-difference [between existence and non-existence], then this [non-existence] would be nothing other than existence itself; thus, the entity, being destroyed, would still perform its perception and causal functions as before.
Furthermore, when there is a difference in causes between existence and non-existence, non-difference is impossible.

For the cloth arises from specific conjunctions of threads, whereas the non-existence of the cloth results from the disjunction of threads or the destruction of the threads; thus, there is a difference in their causes.
If, however, non-existence were different from existence, let it arise; what would happen to the existence? For when a camel is produced, camels do not cease to exist.
If it is argued that existence is concealed by non-existence, we reply:
no, for if concealment is not distinct from existence, there would follow the same consequence as before, namely, that it would still be perceived and so forth.

Even if there is a transformation, when one thing is concealed and another arises, nothing at all has been produced or destroyed; thus, because the entity remains as it was, the consequence follows that it would be perceived as before.
Furthermore, whatever is certain to occur does not depend on other causes, just as the iron-nature of a sword does not depend on other causes.
And since the destruction of produced entities is certain to occur, this is the perception of a pervasion by the contradictory (viruddhavyāptopalabdhi).

For the perception of "inevitability" (dhruvabhāvitā), which is pervaded by independence from other causes—being the opposite of dependence on other causes that are being negated—is apprehended here; this, being present, establishes independence and thereby rejects dependence on other causes. For those things that depend on other causes are not inevitable, just as the dyeing of cloth and the like, which depend on contact with safflower and so forth, are not necessarily produced.

Therefore, since action is untenable for a conceptualized non-existence that is devoid of all descriptive attributes, the expression "he makes non-existence" is impossible because a connection between the act of making and non-existence cannot be established; thus, the negative particle (*nañ*) has no connection [to the verb], as in the case of "he makes a negation. As it has been said: "... nothing happens to it; it simply does not exist..."
Therefore, because there is no cause for destruction, it is established that an entity perishes at the very moment of its arising; thus, momentary disintegration (kṣaṇabhaṅga) is proven.
He refutes this as follows:
"No, because the alternatives are untenable."

This is the underlying intention: regarding the claim that entities, whether perishable or imperishable, are produced from their own causes as imagined [by others], we ask: what, then, is this "perishability" intended by your venerable self to be? Is it the nature of destruction itself, or is it the fitness for destruction—a form excluded from eternal things?
It cannot be the former alternative, because identity between an entity and its destruction is logically impossible, as they are mutually exclusive.

Moreover, if there were identity (*tādātmya*), then existence (*bhāva*) would persist in the second and subsequent moments just as destruction does; thus, you have effectively established the momentariness of entities while attempting to prove their permanence.

Or, if destruction at the time of the entity were itself of the nature of the entity, the entity would become an absolute non-entity (*atyantābhāva*); thus, the true nature of entities has been perfectly elucidated by you.
Furthermore, it is not tenable to claim that the entity has the property of abiding for a single moment, while destruction occurs in the second and subsequent moments.
Because there is a difference [between them] due to the association with contradictory properties characterized by the delimitation of the first and second characteristics;
however, we accept the second alternative.
But if entities produced from their own causes are thus subject to destruction, [then...]

Alas! Things would indeed be destroyed immediately after their arising; yet they are not so destroyed. Even things like cloth, though subject to destruction, perish either from the destruction of the threads or from the disjunction of the threads, since their birth is dependent upon their own causes. For rice grains do not soften without the specific sequence of the contact between fire and water; nor do pieces of wood split without the blow of an axe, even if they are "fit to be split."
As for one who thinks that only those rice grains are ready to be cooked which have coexisted with fire, water, a pot, and a cook— since chaff appears immediately after them,

whereas it does not appear immediately after others, therefore those others are not ready to be cooked— we shall provide the answer to him by demonstrating the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) of non-momentary things.

Therefore, it is logical that for entities which are perishable, their production from their own causes does not depend upon a cause of destruction. You, however, who assert that nothing other than the entity itself can be its cause, must be questioned: do you favor the non-existence of destruction because it lacks a cause, or do you favor its permanence? Regarding this, the author of the *Vārttika* has stated the direct refutation of your Śākya position: "That which is causeless is twofold: permanent..."
Or [it may be] void, like a hare’s horn and so forth, which is insubstantial (*tuccha*).

For us, however, that insubstantial non-existence (*abhāva*) favored by you is not at all accepted; rather, because what we favor is not accepted by you, you have superimposed the notion "it does not exist" and spoken of it as a single category.
That "the destruction of what has arisen" is common knowledge for all people; however, on your position, the opposite of that would result.
To the objection, "Let there be the co-existence of existence and non-existence; what is the fault?", he says: "And therefore, of entities... [and so forth].

(414/5) He raises an objection with the words, "But [because] of its indestructibility. The meaning is this: the flaw here is that if destruction were causeless, it would result in the failure of the [intended] purpose; however, one cannot accept the causality of destruction—though it is clearly contradicted by more evident means of valid cognition—merely out of fear of such a flaw.
The proponent, with a hidden intention, asks: "How is it that destruction does not perish?
The challenger replies: "Because [those things] have already perished."
The proponent, relying on the Buddhist position, says:
"For there is no such thing as the absence of destruction.

The sense is this: for one for whom even the absence of a cloth is a mere void, what can be said regarding its [the destruction's] absence? For that [absence of destruction] would be even more void than a void.
Adopting his own position, he says:
"Furthermore, destruction has a cause.
The rest is easily understood.

As for the reason that was stated for [non-existence] being causeless—namely, that if non-existence were produced as something distinct from existence, existence would remain in its original state—it is replied to as follows: In the production of non-existence, there is no further cessation of existence; rather, the very production of non-existence is itself its cessation. How could it be so when something else is produced?

Regarding the cessation of one thing [upon the presence of another], the answer here must be stated by means of differences in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*): those things that exist through mutual exclusion are produced from their own respective causes.

For it is not the case that because fire is not the cause of a sprout simply due to its being "other" than it, fire would therefore also not be the cause of ash, since the quality of being "other" is no different in both cases.

However, the justification for the restriction of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) by means of a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*) applies equally to the restriction of existence through mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihārasthitiniyama*). Just as seeds and other factors produce a sprout—even though they do not perform any service toward the prior non-existence of the sprout, which, prior to its arising, is devoid of all capacity—because the very arising of that [sprout] consists in the cessation of its prior non-existence; in the same way, the causes of that non-existence also bring about that non-existence, even though they do nothing toward it in its positive form, provided it is not a positive entity.

If that [effect] were produced by causes for its non-existence, then why does it not perform its own essential function and cognition at the time of its own nature, just as it did previously? Or, if the sprout, once produced, performs cognition and its function just as it did before production, why does it not do so now?
If you argue: "The sprout did not exist prior to its production, therefore it did not act; but having been produced, it exists, and therefore it acts," [we reply:]...
If it is argued: "Indeed, when the entity existed, it then performed [its function]; but now that it has perished, it does not perform it because it no longer exists.

Just as the very arising of an entity is the non-existence of its prior absence, so too the very arising of a non-entity is the non-existence of the entity. Since destruction possesses the nature of appearing and passing away, there is no difference between destruction and the entity; therefore, the universe is not divided into two categories by way of being existent and non-existent"—then what is this "arising"? If it is inherence in its own causes or inherence in *sattā* (existence),...
Or, if it does not exist in the absence [of that nature],
then if it is the acquisition of its own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*),
even though there is equality in that much alone, the establishment of two groups is possible due to internal differences.

Therefore, just as substances, qualities, and actions are mutually distinct from one another by virtue of their own specific natures even though they share the commonality of existence (*sattva*), so too, although there is no difference among things in terms of being objects of knowledge (*prameyatva*), being denotable (*abhidheyatva*), and having a cause (*kāraṇavattva*), it is established that there is a distinction between those [entities] and non-existence (*asat*) due to the difference consisting in the presence of existence (*sattā*) and its absence.

Regarding the fact that destruction is necessarily occurring, we say this: one who asserts that destruction does not depend on any other cause because it is necessarily occurring cannot claim that it is causeless;
for while excluding other causes, one has not excluded the cause itself.
Because a specific negation has as its result the affirmation of the remainder;
furthermore, "inevitability" is either unestablished or inconclusive.
Being questioned regarding this state of affairs, let him explain: is the series of shards inevitably produced from a homogeneous series of jars, or not?

If it were not so, then the destruction of the jar would not be an inevitable occurrence; for indeed, with the physical eye, we do not perceive the destruction of the jar except through the arising of a dissimilar moment. Thus, the inevitability of destruction remains unestablished.

Alternatively, if that inevitability does exist, then the dependence upon causes such as a mallet with respect to that very same inevitable series of dissimilar moments constitutes an inconclusive [reason].
The state of being necessarily destined to perish is not pervaded by independence; therefore, it is not capable of negating the dependence upon other causes.
This very point is indicated by the *Vārttika* passage: "And that fault which arises from destruction without a cause is unavoidable.
Thus, the objection has been stated regarding the case where difference (*anyatva*) is the probandum. (415/11)

Although momentariness was previously mentioned and refuted, nevertheless, your statement regarding momentariness was intended for something else; in that context, "otherness" (anyatva) alone was primary.
Now, however, momentariness itself is to be established as the primary subject; it is by this much that there is a difference between the two sections.

"The qualification contradicts the tenet" means that if there were some entities that were not subject to immediate destruction, then the qualification "immediately destructible" could be postulated; however, in that case, there would be a contradiction with the tenet.
Regarding the term *matvarthīya*:
[the word] *kṣaṇika* is formed by adding the suffix *ṭhan* in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*), according to the rule *ata ini-ṭhanau*.
"Being distinguished by immediate destruction" means being characterized as such.
"At the time of the end of all" [is the meaning].

A single unit of time (*kālakalā*) that lacks prior and posterior parts, established by the science of astronomy (*jyotirvidyā*), is merely a designation for "the final limit of all time" (*sarvāntya-kāla*) and is not real; yet, momentariness (*kṣaṇikatā*) is intended to be real.
Having refuted the statement of the thesis (*pakṣavacana*), he refutes the reason (*hetu*) with the words "those who also... (*ye 'pi*).
Here, it should be understood that by the inclusion of "etcetera" (*ādi*), properties such as existence (*sattva*) and being produced (*kṛtakatva*) are included.

In this regard, whatever exists is all momentary, just like a jar; and sound and so forth, which are the subjects of dispute, exist. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), because momentariness is invariably concomitant with mere existence. But how is the invariable concomitance of momentariness with mere existence established?
It is said: the so-called "existence" of entities is nothing other than their capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*).
For it is impossible that an entity exists and yet does not perform a causal function (*arthakriyā*).
To explain: would such an entity serve as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the cognition of an omniscient one, or not?
If it does not, then either the omniscient one does not exist, or he is not omniscient, precisely because of his lack of knowledge regarding that object.
If it is the objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*), how is it that it does not perform a causal function?
Furthermore, there exists no such thing as a "universal of existence" (*sattāsāmānya*),
nor is there an inherence (*samavāya*) therein by virtue of which it could be called "existent."

Alternatively, if that [capacity for causal efficiency] were absent, then existence would not belong to universals (sāmānya), particulars (viśeṣa), and inherence (samavāya), because it is not admitted that these possess the status of being substrata [of such capacity].

Furthermore, being apprehended by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇagrāhyatā) is simply being an object of a means of valid cognition, which is nothing other than being an objective condition (ālambanapratyaya) with respect to that cognition; and since this is nothing other than the performance of a purposeful action (arthakriyākāritva), it is established that existence is precisely the performance of a purposeful action.
And that [existence] is pervaded by succession and non-succession, because there is no third mode.
For indeed, in those various causal activities of entities, succession and non-succession appear as mutually exclusive.

Thus, if another mode consisting of both succession and non-succession were admitted as being a mixture of these very same successions and non-successions already experienced and determined, then even for the successions and non-successions currently being perceived—

There would be the undesirable consequence of mutual confusion; for if these two—succession and non-succession—were intermingled, then succession as it is perceived would appear to be of the nature of non-succession, and non-succession would appear to be of the nature of succession.
Yet, they do not appear in such a manner.
By this, perception itself—by delimiting succession and simultaneity as mutually exclusive—rejects their commingling everywhere.
If there were identity between these two anywhere, then even here they would be perceived as commingled, being nothing other than those very same [succession and simultaneity].
Therefore, no commingling of these two is observed here.
In this way, it precludes confusion both across different locations and at different times.

Furthermore, regarding the negation of identity (*tādātmya*), because non-perception is qualified by "perceptibility" (*dṛśyatva*), there is no lack of distinction in the negation of things such as *piśācas*, which are themselves imperceptible due to their identity with a perceived pillar, nor of things such as monkeys, which are perceptible. Thus, the negation applies without exception.
As it has been said: "And the qualification is inexpressible.

Succession and simultaneity do not exist in any other manner apart from such [succession and simultaneity]. For there is no identity of the entity itself based merely on the non-difference of its verbal designation;
otherwise, by virtue of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "cow," it would follow that even things like speech (*vāk*) possess horns.
It might be argued:

let there be neither succession nor simultaneity; let there be some other mode designated as "neither-succession-nor-simultaneity," distinct from both succession and simultaneity, by resorting to which stable entities will be employed in causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). However, it is not the case that their causal efficiency, like this other mode, is merely a phantom (*piśāca*).

If that is so, what is lost to us? For those things which are being perceived, experienced, and determined—possessing forms embraced by two modes, namely exclusion from one another in the form of either succession or simultaneity—cannot possibly arise from any other mode, nor can there be any other mode at all. For instance, where there is a restriction of the determination of one thing through the negation of a certain mode, there is no possibility of a third mode.

Just as when a specific mode such as "blue" is negated, there is a determination of the mode "non-blue," and when either of these two modes is negated, there is a rule for the determination of the other— this being the case everywhere regarding cause and effect with respect to that which does not fall within the scope of the negated mode— this is the perception of the contradictory (*viruddhopalabdhi*). For the rule for the determination of one of two [alternatives] by the negation of the other is indeed contradictory to the possibility of the other mode being negated.

Thus, because no other alternative is possible, the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) of entities is pervaded by succession and simultaneity; and since these two [succession and simultaneity] are excluded from a permanent entity, they also exclude its causal efficiency—just as the exclusion of "tree-ness" excludes "śiṃśapā-ness" when it is observed that a mountain ridge consisting of a single rock lacks the former. Thus, the logical connection (*pratibandha*) is established.
For instance, a non-momentary entity cannot perform a causal function (*arthakriyā*) sequentially.
Indeed, entities are observed to be employed in causal functions by means of their own specific form (*svarūpa*).

Whatever entity follows the presence and absence of a particular effect through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), that entity possesses the capacity to produce that effect; and since its form follows the positive and negative concomitance of the effect, it is the form itself [that is the cause].

And since that [entity] exists in the first moment just as it does in the second and subsequent moments, it would produce the entire collection of effects generated in the second and subsequent moments in that very first moment; for it is impossible for that which is capable to delay [its action]. Thus, it does not follow that a non-momentary entity could possess successive operations.
One might argue: "Even though it is capable, it acts successively due to its association with successive auxiliary causes."
That has been stated:
because it cannot withstand critical analysis.
Do these auxiliary causes (sahakārin) provide some benefit to it, or not?
Or [the auxiliary cause] may produce either something distinct from or non-distinct from the entity.

In that case, if it produces a benefit distinct [from the entity], then since the entity does not arise while the benefit is absent, but does arise when the benefit is present, it follows that the benefit alone is the producer of the effect, and not the entity itself;
nor is the entity merely a co-operative factor for the benefit.
It should not be said that [the cause] produces the effect merely through its assistance;
for if the assistance were to produce another assistance, there would be an infinite regress,
whereas if it does not produce one, the status of being a cooperative cause would be absent.

Furthermore, if [the causal complex] produces an impartible assistance, then the entity itself would produce [the effect], and since that entity existed even previously, the auxiliary causes would be useless. Alternatively, if they provide no assistance, the auxiliaries would not be required by the entity, and thus the entity would produce the effect at the very moment it arises.
If it is thought that even those which provide no assistance are auxiliary causes because an entity produces its effect only in their company—
and that they are not disregarded by the entity because the effect does not arise without them—
then [we reply]: if an entity produces the effect by its own nature (*svarūpa*), why does it not produce it in the absence of these [auxiliaries], since its own nature exists even prior to them?
If [the entity] were to produce [the effect] by way of being a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*), then the cooperative causes alone would be the producers, and not the entity itself.

Nor is it correct to argue that the presence or absence of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) depends on both [the entity and the causes], because of the deviation from this rule in the case of a single factor;

for since the effect does not arise even when the entity is present, there is a deviation [from the necessity of the entity]. Furthermore, since the effect arises only when the final auxiliary conditions—the cooperating causes—have come together, there is a deviation regarding the final occurrence of those very cooperative causes.

Because its status as a cause has been definitively established, this [view] is refuted by it: namely, what some say—that an entity, having arisen from its own causes, acts only after a delay, and thus does not act immediately upon arising...
For is that nature of delayed action present in it even at the time of the conjunction with auxiliary factors, or is it not?
If it exists [at that time], then it still would not act;
if it does not exist, how could the entity not be destroyed when its own nature has perished?
Or, if its delayed action is not its inherent nature, why would it not perform its effect immediately upon arising?
Therefore, a non-momentary entity does not perform its causal function either successively or simultaneously;
consequently, whatever effect was produced by that non-momentary entity in the first moment, it would have to produce all of that very same thing in the second and subsequent moments as well.
Because the very nature of accomplishing that task exists even in the second and subsequent moments;

and since it is impossible to accomplish what has already been accomplished, whatever it accomplishes in the second and subsequent moments must be something other than what was accomplished in the first moment— thus, it is merely a repetition of successive steps, and the fault already mentioned applies there as well.

Alternatively, for one who has simultaneously completed all that was to be done, there is no capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) because there is nothing further to be performed in subsequent moments; thus, by virtue of its non-existence, it would follow that it is momentary.

Therefore, since neither succession nor simultaneity—which pervade existence—is observed in a non-momentary entity, existence, being excluded from the non-momentary through the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), is pervaded by momentariness; thus, the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is established.

It is precisely the blue that is not apprehended as having been experienced once its non-momentary nature has been superimposed; rather, it is the very perception of such a blue nature that constitutes the non-perception of succession and simultaneity in that non-momentary entity. This is just as the non-perception of a jar—whose visibility has been superimposed—is simply the perception of the nature of the ground, and the ground arises in that way. There is no such thing as "absence" possessing a physical form that could become an object of cognition.
Furthermore, it must be discussed further:
it might be argued that a momentary entity either possesses the nature of producing causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) or does not.
If it is not non-existent,
and if it possesses the nature of producing that [effect], what use has it for auxiliary causes?
The seed would produce the sprout at the very moment it arises.

Now, one might object: "Once the momentary seed has arisen, being capable, it must indeed produce the sprout. From what does the capability arise? The capability arises from the preceding momentary seed.

If that were so, then since all the moments existing within that continuum are equally seeds without distinction, they would all possess the capacity to produce a sprout; consequently, a seed that has only just been produced immediately after its flower would itself produce the sprout.
This is not so.

The final moment of the seed, having acquired its birth through a succession of subsequent moments characterized by excellence produced by the conjunction of preceding moments of earth, seed, wind, and so forth, is capable of generating the sprout. It does so independently, being accompanied by the efficient co-existent factors such as earth; for even though it is independent of them, it cannot produce the effect without them, since it depends on that single causal complex (*sāmagrī*), and in their absence, that complex is absent.
Nor can there be co-operativity (sahakāritā) on the part of the earth and other factors, because the sprout is produced by those very factors themselves;
for their existence prior to the effect is necessarily indistinguishable [from one another],
and causality consists in nothing more than that.
Nor can it be that those [causes], even when independent, each initiate a different effect, because only that [specific effect] is perceived from them, as their capacity is restricted to that alone.

Nor is there non-action by the others on the grounds that their function has already been performed, for it is impossible [to say] "it is done" regarding a joint action. Furthermore, entities that have attained their presence through their own causes are not sentient; they cannot, after reflecting—"This could be done by one of us; our purpose is accomplished, so what is the use of all of us being present?"—then desist from acting.

Moreover, it is not merely the difference in individual causes that is the cause for the difference in effects; rather, it is the difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), because when that [complex] exists, a difference in effects is observed.
Since there is no difference in the complex that produces non-differentiation, there is no consequence of a difference in the effect.
Furthermore, the mutual conjunction of earth and the other elements arises from the conditions of their approach (*upasarpaṇapratyaya*).
Nor is the reason (hetu) non-common (asādhāraṇa) because there is no contradiction with causal efficiency (arthakriyā) for that which is momentary.

Nor is the statement of the reason a non-essential part of the proof, since the probandum (sādhya) is established simply by proving the pervasion (vyāpti) when the subject of the thesis (sādhyadharmin)—such as sound—is being perceived.
Indeed, a pervasion that encompasses all instances cannot have only the perceptible as its domain.

For it might be suspected by an opponent that [the reason] "existence" has not been excluded from non-momentary things by you, since those things are not perceived; thus, "existence" would be an inconclusive reason for proving momentariness.
Therefore, the pervasion (vyāpti) must be demonstrated as follows: "Whatever is perceptible or imperceptible, all that is momentary.

[Objection: Even so, since momentariness of sound and other such subjects under dispute is established simply through the force of demonstrating the pervasion, the statement of the logical reason remains as useless as before in being a non-constituent part of the proof.
Not so;

for even though things such as a rabbit’s horn do not exist, whatever is similar to existent things—whether visible or invisible—is all momentary. Thus, there is a pervasion (*vyāpti*) that includes all cases, and it is not the case that rabbit’s horns and the like are themselves momentary. This remains true even regarding the subject of dispute.

Even if pervasion is established in the case of sound and so forth, momentariness is not thereby proven; therefore, existence must necessarily be shown as the means for proving their momentariness. Thus, the statement of the reason is not lacking a constituent part of the proof. To this, it is replied:

Existence (*sattva*) is not a valid logical reason for proving momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), because it is either inconclusive (*asādhāraṇa*) or its negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful.

For instance, existence is pervaded by succession and simultaneity; thus, through the non-perception of these two, existence is excluded from the non-momentary. Likewise, existence is pervaded by dependence and independence; thus, through the non-perception of these two, existence is also excluded from the momentary.

Therefore, like the property of possessing odor, it is an uncommon [reason] and not a valid member of a proof. For you must admit that the seeds of earth, air, water, and fire, having reached their final moment, are capable and determined by their prior existence to be the causes of earth, water, fire, and sprouts which have a fixed subsequent production; these very things [are what you claim].
Do they produce [the effect] independently of one another, or dependently?
Has it not already been stated that the earth and other elements, having reached their final moment, produce the subsequent aggregate independently?
Why then entertain this alternative of them being "dependent"?
And [you say they are] "independent.
In that case, is even the seed-moment that produces the capable seed-moment itself entirely independent?
If it is argued that "Oṃ," [we reply:
in that case, all moments of the seed would be independent in producing their own effects, and thus there would be no need for auxiliary causes (sahakārin).
But was it not said that these [moments] are not conscious agents; rather, their presence is restricted by their own specific conditions, and they cannot be hindered by anything else?
Is this farmer, then, not a discerning person? He is indeed discerning, for he exerts effort to bring the seed down from the granary and sows it in the ploughed earth;
