because the capacity of the seed-moment to produce a sprout arises through a succession of excellence produced by its coexistence with earth and other factors, whereas from that which remains in the granary, no sprout would be produced even in a thousand years, he therefore sows it there.
If [you say this], then why is this capable seed-moment not produced solely from its own continuum? If that is so, why would it not depend upon another continuum for its own effect?
Is it not the case that it indeed depends [on others], but for its own production, and not for its own effect?
In that case, its independence is accepted [only] with respect to that [subsequent moment], but not with respect to its own production.
But surely, even regarding its production, its own preceding moment existing within its own continuum remains independent;
thus, each preceding moment, falling within its own continuum, remains independent and exerts itself toward its generation. This is like a seed placed in a granary.
In this way, the farmer would indeed be successful; his labor in agriculture, though fraught with much suffering, would have been rendered fruitful.
Therefore, even against one's will, one must admit that it is only when the [causal] moments reach their final state and are mutually dependent that they produce an effect.

Furthermore, would the seed, upon reaching its final moment, produce the sprout, the earth, the wind, the water, and the fire without depending on them? Does it produce those others by the very same nature through which it produces the sprout, or by a different nature?
It cannot be so, because by that very [cause], earth and the other elements would necessarily possess the nature of the sprout;
for indeed, according to you, it is not possible for an effect to be differentiated when its cause is undifferentiated,
as this would entail the fallacy of the effect's differentiation being accidental.
As you yourselves have stated: "The distinction, or rather the cause of distinction, is precisely this: the attribution of contradictory properties and the difference in causes.
Nor is there a difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), because that too is non-different;
otherwise, there would be no rule governing their coexistence.

A certain specific difference in intrinsic nature (svabhāvabheda) alone, acquired from its own cause, is such that from it various effects arise; therefore, the diversity of effects is not accidental, nor does it entail an over-extension (atiprasaṅga), because such a [specific nature] is not present everywhere. Furthermore, there is no identity between cause and effect, by which the diversity and non-diversity of the cause would necessarily follow upon the diversity and non-diversity of the effect.

If it is argued that just as a single effect arises from many [causes], so too multiple effects will be produced from a single cause; then your laborious effort to establish a single object—such as a whole (*avayavin*), a universal (*sāmānya*), or a conjunction (*saṃyoga*)—as existing in multiple locations is in vain. For even though the locations are manifold, the object residing within them, such as a universal, cannot possibly be manifold.
Because it is non-different from them;

the seed, by way of a different form, is the producer of the sprout and the others, such as the earth, for instance, because the seed is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the sprout through the transformation of its essential part, whereas in relation to the earth and so forth—which are to be produced—it is a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*). Furthermore, it was previously [stated that]...

If it is argued that earth and the other elements are the respective material causes (*upādāna*) of earth and the others, and that their production occurs through the modification of those [causes], then we ask: are these cooperative causes (*sahakārin*) and the material cause one and the same reality, or are they many? If they are one, how can they be a producer by means of a different form? If they are many, is there a difference between those two [the cooperative causes] and the seed, or no difference? If there is a difference, how can the seed be the producer, since the sprout and so forth arise from those two alone?

Or, if there were no difference [between them], how could there not be a difference in the seed, given its identity with that which is different? Or rather, because of their identity, those two would possess only a single form.

Therefore, when earth and so forth—which are distinct from the sprout—are to be produced, the material cause (upādāna) for that [sprout] must first be required by the seed, existing at the same time as the earth and so forth.

In this way, even a seed must necessarily depend upon auxiliary causes such as soil and so forth, which exist at the same time as itself; otherwise, the production of distinct effects could not be established—this must be admitted even by one who does not wish it.
Furthermore, you yourselves have demonstrated that what provides no assistance cannot be an object of dependence.
Furthermore, for that which is momentary, no capacity to assist is possible other than through production, because it is indivisible.
Nor can there be a relationship of producer and produced between two things existing at the same time, just as in the case of the left and right horns of an ox.

Therefore, since it would follow that the effect arises from its own continuum alone, and since a distinction among effects would be untenable, and because there is an absence of dependence on what provides no assistance, [momentary things cannot produce effects].

Since causal efficiency is impossible for that which is momentary—whether it be dependent or independent—the quality of being a unique [specific] existence (*asādhāraṇasattva*) is not a factor for proving momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*).

Now, lest existence be non-unique, one might admit a dependence on [auxiliaries] even for those that provide no assistance, in order to produce the effect; for even they [the auxiliaries] exhibit positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) with the effect.

However, by this same reasoning, even a non-momentary entity will not depend upon successive auxiliary causes—even though those causes provide no assistance—nor will it require the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) of its effect to follow a sequence.
It will produce its effects sequentially by virtue of successive auxiliaries;
and even for that which is capable, the delay in producing the effect is logically explained by the non-proximity of the required conditions.
Nor should it be argued that, merely by virtue of the convergence of auxiliary causes, the accomplishment of an effect produced from them is rendered independent of their intrinsic nature;
for we observe that production occurs only when they are accompanied by those [auxiliaries],
and because production does not occur even when their nature is present [without such accompaniment].

If it is argued that because the effect arises only when there is the co-presence [of the cause], the cause is merely the co-presence itself and not the form as well, then what now becomes of the seed-form? Is it not equivalent to a donkey or similar thing?
If you say "yes" [to this]:
Now, why is it that a sprout does not arise even in the absence of the seed-form, as in the case of a donkey and so forth?
If you say it is because the conjunction of those [factors] is the cause of it,
then when that conjunction is the cause, how is it that the form residing therein is not also a cause?
Nor is its inclusion [in the definition] due to its being unavoidable,
because mere conjunction occurs here and there even in the absence of the form of the seed;
rather, it is the specific form itself that constitutes the seeds and so forth within that conjunction.

Therefore, just as pervasion— which is defined based on both [the pervaded and the pervader]— is defined with respect to the pervader through the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) as "the pervader exists only where the pervaded exists, never its absence," whereas with respect to the pervaded it is defined through the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*) as "the pervaded exists only there and not elsewhere"; likewise, although the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is also defined based on both,
it is defined with respect to the cause through the exclusion of non-connection as "existence prior to the production of the effect."
Thus, it is not that the cause is non-existent;
rather, with respect to the effect,
it is determined in accordance with experience that its existence occurs only when the cause exists— through the exclusion of non-connection— and not when anything else exists.
For it is precisely thus that there is agreement among both worldly people and investigators.

Furthermore, existence is not merely the state of being a cause; rather, it is the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of blue and so forth, as determined in experience. For that [nature], being delimited by its own absence (*svābhāvavyavacchinna*), is employed in various causal functions (*arthakriyā*) in that very form, and not merely because of the fact of performing a causal function.
Let it not be that your own nature is such as to perform multiple causal functions simultaneously without a distinction of form;
therefore, if an omniscient being exists, then that entity, by its very nature, will serve as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the knowledge of that [omniscience].

On the other hand, even if he does not exist, having been produced in that form, although initially ineffective, he will later, due to some cause, obtain auxiliary conditions (*sahakāri-pratyaya*) and be employed in various causal functions.

Thus it is established: even for that which is momentary, since purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) is possible through either succession or simultaneity as appropriate, the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) is unestablished; therefore, "existence" (*sattva*) is an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*) with a doubtful negative concomitance (*saṃdigdhavyatireka*) when the Buddhists seek to prove the momentariness of entities.
For us, however, it is established otherwise, and thus it constitutes a variety of the "unestablished" (*asiddha*).
Thus it is said:
"And the association with contradictory properties characterized by being a producer and not being a producer cannot serve as a reason for [establishing] plurality;
for so-called 'productivity' is not the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the entity, but rather its property (*dharma*)."
Furthermore, the property (*dharma*) is in reality distinct from the property-bearer (*dharmī*).
Nor can the distinction of one thing suffice for the distinction of another, as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
If it is asked: "Since there is no difference in their being other than one another, how can it be said that this belongs specifically to that?"
In this matter, the answer must be stated by means of the very nature of things (*vastusvabhāva*).
Just as it has been said that although there is no difference in their being "other" [than the cause], smoke is the effect of fire alone and not of a seed;
and likewise, even "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is not a reason for momentariness, because it is established otherwise (*anyathāsiddhi*).

Because destruction occurs with a cause, and because it is established that there is no identity between arising and destruction—since [if they were identical] it would follow that the entity is absolutely non-existent, as has already been stated—it was said by the author of the *Vārttika*: "Those [reasons] are either unestablished (*asiddha*), otherwise-established (*anyathāsiddha*), or contradictory (*viruddha*); therefore, they are not valid reasons. (416/15)
The observation of a specific final moment is unestablished (*asiddha*) because it is not established as a property of the preceding moments.

Both existence (*sattva*) and being produced (*kṛtakatva*) are otherwise established (*anyathāsiddha*). Furthermore, every reason (*hetu*) is contradictory (*viruddha*) when momentariness is the property to be proven (*sādhya*).

For instance, existence (*sattva*) or being produced (*kṛtakatva*), because it is not pervasive across the three worlds due to its exclusion from them, is not a valid reason either spatially or temporally; this is because the knowledge of its invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is impossible, and thus it lacks the status of a logical mark (*liṅga*).
This is since it is impossible to grasp the invariable concomitance—whether by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—in a single moment.
Therefore, existence, being produced, or something else that is pervasive across space and time must be made the reason.

And whether that [subject] has a positive form or a negative form (consisting in the exclusion of others), it is non-different and non-momentary across various times; thus it is said to be "contradictory" (*viruddha*) because it contradicts the probandum, which is momentariness.

Regarding the point "because of the perception of a specific property" (*viśeṣadarśanāt*) at the end, its contradictory nature will be stated immediately hereafter. Having for the sake of argument granted that it possesses specific properties, he states its established nature and its inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*), saying "or having granted this... (*upetya vaitat*).
In order to demonstrate that the reason (*hetu*) is both unestablished (*asiddha*) and contradictory (*viruddha*), he says:
"At the end, [the word] 'particular' (*viśeṣa*).
He states that the reason, characterized by perception and non-perception, is otherwise established (*anyathāsiddha*).
As for this reason,
namely "because existence and non-existence possess that [property]" (417.7),
the meaning is: because the cognition of "here" possesses the state of being due to the presence or absence of conjunction.
We do not understand this claim that there is the production of a lamp in another location.

If it is maintained that for a momentary lamp, its capacity to produce an effect in another location arises solely from its continuity (*saṃtāna*), then all moments of the lamp would produce a lamp in another location, and not just some of them within the belly of the primary [lamp].
Furthermore, by virtue of the causal condition of moving away (*apasarpaṇa-pratyaya*), they produce an effect elsewhere than within the interior of the lamp-vessel.
Now, does the causal condition of moving away confer some benefit upon the lamp or not?
It certainly does not confer one; for since a moment (*kṣaṇa*) is indivisible, it is impossible for it to be either benefited or unbenefited.

Furthermore, in the absence of a substratum, there can be no state of being a cooperative cause (*sahakāribhāva*), because if that which provides no assistance were to be a cooperative cause, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); such indeed is your own statement.

Nor is the production of a specific moment of the lamp itself the "assistance" provided by the cooperative causes, since that [specificity] is established from the preceding material cause (*upādāna*) alone, without depending on cooperative causes.
Indeed, it is not possible for those very factors that assist that cause to also be its cooperative causes (*sahakārin*).

Likewise, since nothing at all is contributed by the preceding lamp-moments— even though they arise solely through the capacity of each preceding lamp— none of them would produce the primary effect either in a single location or in another location.

If, on the other hand, even those things that provide no assistance are required for the performance of an effect because their presence or absence conforms to the presence or absence of the effect—as is the case with a momentary lamp—then this is equally true for the position of non-momentariness; such is the summary.
This has been elaborated by us in the *Brahmatattvasamīkṣā* and the *Nyāyakaṇikā*, so we shall desist here.
[The phrase] "not indeed in the case of a clod of earth or the like falling through the air" [is explained as follows].

For substances possessing equal weight, such as a clod of earth and a hawk, the causes [of their rapid descent] are weight, effort, and projection. For instance, when a hawk is released downward from a man standing atop a palace toward a pigeon moving on the ground, the hawk’s effort— generated by the desire to seize the pigeon— its weight, and its projection are the causes of its swift descent.
However, for that which has been projected, both gravity (*gurutva*) and effort (*prayatna*) are causes of falling; for one who is not exerting effort, gravity alone is the cause of falling.
Thus, there is no fault even in the view of the followers of Ulūka (the Vaiśeṣikas). To this, he says:
"And the *saṃskāra* is one."

If it were stated that cognitions occurring at non-simultaneous times have a single object, it would follow as an undesirable consequence (*prasajyeran*) that cognitions of jars, cloths, and so forth, as well as cognitions of lamps and so forth, which possess a temporal sequence, would also have a single object;
therefore, he says:
"those who hold a contrary view."
The reason "because they are denoted by the same word" is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

For there are indeed cognitions denoted by the same word, such as "die" (*akṣa*, *akṣa*), yet they do not have the same object, because their objects—namely, the acts of gambling and so forth—are distinct. Therefore, he says:
"Given that there is co-referentiality with its own causal conditions"—
even so, since there is an inconclusiveness (anaikāntika) due to the very conditions of the lamp,
he says:

Regarding the term "non-deviating" (*avyutthāyī*): one whose nature is to deviate—that is, to wander—is called "deviating" or "wandering. Its non-wandering nature, moreover, is to be understood through the refutation of the proof for momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*).

Since [the state of being] established through the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of that very non-arising cognition is already accomplished, the use of the same word to denote it is merely an elaboration (*prapañca*). 13–14.
NyS 3.2.15: It is not so, because of the appearance of different qualities resulting from the transformation of the milk.
The commentary states: "The manifestation of another quality.
To begin with, the substance exists, and the quality also exists, but it is merely unmanifested.

There was one emergent quality; therein, that which had emerged becomes latent upon the cessation of the preceding quality, and another quality arises—this is the meaning of "that comes to be. // 15 //
The observation that the production of a different substance results from a rearrangement [of parts] is an inference for the cessation of the previous substance.
But here, however, there is a negation [of that view].
For it is precisely the constituents of the milk which, upon the destruction of the milk, produce a distinct substance characterized by qualities born of maturation (*pākaja*).

If, on the other hand, every effect were already existent even prior to the operation of its cause, then the operation of the cause would be useless, because the effect—even as a manifestation—would already exist.
Or, just as that very [action] is not made to exist when it is non-existent, so too are other effects;
and this has been explained by us in the *Nyāyakaṇikā*. // 16 //
NyS 3.2.17: [The argument is] inconclusive because, in some cases, a cause of destruction is not perceived, while in other cases it is perceived.
And having granted that [the objection] is groundless, [it is replied:
because of the possession of the properties of destruction and origination, there is doubt due to the commonality of these properties;
for the destruction and origination of curd and milk are seen to be without cause, whereas the origination and destruction of a jar are seen to have causes.
Thus, here there is a doubt as to whether the destruction and production in a crystal have causes or are causeless.

If it is determined by means of valid cognition that these two indeed have causes, then, because no cause for destruction is perceived, it is determined that the crystal does not undergo destruction, unlike a jar.
This very point has been stated by the author of the Bhāṣya.
Furthermore, it is not as [you claim], namely that [destruction occurs] without a cause of destruction;
nor is it "without a substratum" (*niradhiṣṭhāna*).

For a corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*) must depend upon a subject (*dharmin*) and possess properties similar to those of that subject. Since the production and destruction of a crystal are themselves subjects, they serve as the corroborative instances for the destruction and production of milk and curd by virtue of possessing properties similar to them.
It must be so; however, the production and destruction of the crystal are not themselves apprehended as the subjects (dharmin).
Therefore, they do not serve as examples by virtue of sharing those same properties.

If, however, it were said "because of inherence in a substance," then there would be an inconclusive argument (*anaikānta*) due to color and other qualities that inhere in the atoms of water and so forth; therefore, he says:
"pervading" (*vyāpaka*).
Even so, there would still be an inconclusive argument because of the generality (*sāmānya*) of "selfhood" (*ātmatva*); therefore, he says:
Regarding the phrase "provided that it is a quality":
even so, there is an inconclusiveness (anaikānta) due to the dimension of the self; therefore, he says, "by virtue of being perceptible."
The phrase "of those such as ourselves" is to be supplied [to complete the sense].
The mention of "pervasion" is for the purpose [of excluding] prior connection with qualifiers such as "being a quality" (guṇatva).

If it were stated simply as "because of being perceptible to those such as ourselves," there would be an inconclusive [reason] due to [the case of] universals (sāmānya) and inherence (samavāya); therefore, he says: "provided that it possesses a universal" (jātimattve sati).
In the phrase "because of being dependent" (*āśritatvāt*), it should also be supplied that [the subject] possesses a genus (*jātimat*) and is perceptible (*pratyakṣatve*).
When it is stated that "cognition is impermanent because it is perceptible," there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to the mind (*manas*); therefore, he says:
"one who is not a yogi" (*ayogī*).
Nevertheless, because there is a deviation [from the rule] in the case of the self (ātman), it was stated "provided that it exists as an instrument" (karaṇabhāve sati).
The cognition of avoidance and so forth becomes the instrument.
And sound is the instrument (karaṇa) in the cognition [of it].

Here too, the phrase "provided that it possesses a genus" (jātimattve sati) must be supplied; therefore, there is no inconclusiveness (anaikāntika) due to [the presence of] smell-ness (gandhatva) and so forth. // 17 //
NyS 3.2.18: It [the soul] is not [identical with] either the sense organ or the object, because cognition persists even when those two have perished.
He introduces another point of reflection with the words, "But this is what is being considered.
Now, was it not already established in the *Ātmaparīkṣā* that cognition (*buddhi*) is a quality of the self? Why, then, is it being examined again?
Therefore, the author of the Bhāṣya says:
"Even though it is well-known. The meaning is that although this matter has already been examined, it is nevertheless examined again for the sake of understanding its specific intermediate details.
The author of the Vārttika objects:
"Not a quality. He provides the rebuttal: [it is not so].
"Given that it is non-eternal"—
having reflected thus, the proponent (siddhāntin) adopts the position that [the cognition] arises from sensory contact.
He objects: "I saw"—this is not so. He replies: "Even in the case of memory... (18)
And because objects of knowledge are not perceived simultaneously, [the self] is not the mind.
He proposes: "Let it be so then.
He refutes this: "Simultaneously.
The meaning is that that which has been inferred to be an instrument cannot become an agent by setting aside its very nature as an instrument.

He challenges the commentary which states, "that which is realized through the non-perception of objects of knowledge simultaneously," by pointing out that it employs a qualifying term; he then responds,
"not of all."
He objects again with the words "even so.
The meaning is that the denial of a specific instrument being a quality of knowledge implies that some other instrument must possess the quality of knowledge, yet the self is not an instrument.
"He composes himself because of the occurrence of misfortune";
he explains this very point by saying,
"because of instability."
The meaning is that the knower himself is sometimes the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and sometimes the object of knowledge (*prameya*). That is to say, one person determines another person;
just as this person is, so too is that other person—thus, the determination of one person occurs by means of another person who is already established.
He asks:
"If it is not due to the instrument, then what?
The answer is: "Because of the mastery of the knower."
The meaning is: "Because of the agent's independence.
For when there is a conjunction of the agent, the instrument, and so forth, consciousness is observed in the agent alone, not in the instrument or other factors.
Just as, in the conjunction of clay, staff, wheel, water, string, and potter, agency belongs only to the agent—the potter—and not to the clay and the rest.

The commentary states that "the controller" (*vaśī*) is the "instrument of control" (*vaśyakaraṇa*); however, that is untenable because even a knower is seen to be subject to control in some instances—for example, as in "Yajñadatta causes Devadatta to weave a mat. Therefore, he says:
"And this [is not the case] with the knower."

If, however, someone should desire the mind to possess the quality of cognition, [the author] explains that regarding such a person, the Bhāṣya states "and if it were to have the quality of cognition," which he interprets as "if it were indeed to have the quality of cognition."

He explains the Bhāṣya passage "of the means [consisting of] the nose and so forth" with the words "and just as for the knower. And likewise, that which is the means of cognition for the thinker— that is the mind, the instrument.
Now, to the question "Why then is that [knowledge] also not conscious?", he says:
"Of both.
The remainder of the sense is that the internal organ is all-pervading, whereas knowledge is devoid of another internal organ. // 19 //
Even if it were a quality of the self, the same [objection] would apply.
Now, not seeing the mind (*manas*) as an internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), he raises an objection:
[Nyāyasūtra 3.2.21] "If it were a quality of the self (*ātmaguṇa*),
there would be no production [of cognition] due to the absence of contact between the mind and the sense organs."
"He avoids the undesirable consequence" (*pariharati na prasaṅgaḥ*).

Regarding the commentary (*bhāṣya*) which states "one whose nature is modification" (*vikaraṇadharma*): he is one whose nature is a specific instrument (*viśiṣṭaṃ karaṇaṃ dharmo yasya sa vikaraṇadharmā*), possessing an instrument distinct from the instruments of those such as ourselves.
The meaning is that by this, one becomes a seer of things that are obstructed, distant, subtle, and so forth. // 21 //
NyS 3.2.22: Because no originating cause has been stated.
He explains by completing the commentary beginning with "If, however," etc., as follows: "If,
however" [means] "not at the time of arising."
No proof is stated here;
rather, the meaning is that there exists a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*). He states another interpretation:
"Or in the case of non-simultaneous arising.
He states another interpretation:
"Or in the case of non-simultaneous arising."
He states another explanation:
"videha" (bodiless). For if the mind were to reside in the body, then all cognition would belong to the self, which has the body as its locus.

But when the mind itself does not exist, since there would still be contact between the sense organs and their objects, as well as the existence of the self outside the body, it would follow that cognitions could arise even in a disembodied state;
this is what is meant by "and in the case of the rejection of the internal organ."

Although all cognitions do not arise simultaneously, nevertheless, there is the undesirable consequence that recollections must necessarily arise simultaneously; this is the distinction between this [view] and the previous one.
He states another explanation:
"And when the sense organ and the self are both simultaneously connected with the object."
The sense is that when there is no contact between the sense organ and the mind, there is no determining factor for postulating causality among those [other factors] which are variable. // 22 //
And because no cause for destruction is perceived, if [sound] were to persist, it would follow that it is eternal.
Without limbs—(Sūtra 23).
Regarding this, he states that in the sūtra of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), the word "and" (*ca*) refers back to the preceding sūtras of the prima facie positions.
[The phrase] "that being a quality of the self" (*tad-ātmaguṇatve*) follows from this;
hence, the rest is self-evident (*nigada*).
Such is the explanation. // 23 //
NyS 3.2.24: Because cognition is apprehended as impermanent, it is destroyed by a subsequent cognition, just like sound.
The final cognition is that immediately after which the person attains liberation;
it perishes due to the absence of a cause for its persistence.
These are the causes of persistence. (424)
6) "Dharma and adharma [arise] from those two; because of their absence [of those], [they do not exist].
Now, as to why there is an absence of those two, he says:
"From time."
The meaning is: "having reached the moment for the experience of the final pleasure or pain.
Alternatively, he says that the destruction of the final cognition occurs precisely from the formative impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by itself.
Or [it arises] from the formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
The point is that because no cause for the persistence of a formative force is observed, its destruction occurs.
He asks:
How is it [determined] by time? The answer is: "as many as his births," which means as many as his final body. // 24 //
NyS 3.2.25: Because memory arises from the contact of the mind with that portion of the self where cognition is inherent, there is no simultaneous production [of cognitions].
"If it is because of the cause," he says;
here, first, there is one rebuttal.
This means that one is the primary rebuttal, whereas the other rebuttal is secondary, being according to the opinion of a partial proponent (ekadeśin).

Furthermore, he states "and because they are determinative" (*paricchedatvāt*) to show that memories do not arise simultaneously, because they are determinative, like the cognitions of smell, taste, form, touch, and sound.
He states "others, however" (*apare tu*) to present the rebuttal of a certain partisan (*ekadeśin*). // 25 //
NyS 3.2.26: No, because the mind functions within the body.
This [position] he refutes, saying it is not correct:
for the mind is not dependent on anything, nor is it inherent in anything; rather, [if one claims it is merely] a conjunction, that would lead to over-extension—this is the meaning.
Nor is it the case that "function" (*vṛtti*) means the capacity for its own effect;
for the mind performs its own effect only within the body and not elsewhere, and thus the claim that "the mind is said to be dependent on the body" is also untenable.
This is because the contact between the sense organ and its object—which is the effect of the mind—occurs outside the body. This is the meaning.
He resolves this objection, saying:
"To this we reply.

The meaning is that when the mind is conjoined with whatever body has been acquired through karma, it possesses causal activity characterized by specific knowledge (*vaiśeṣikajñāna*) and so forth; it does not possess such activity when not conjoined with it. Thus, there is no other [cause] for the mind's dependence upon a body.
NyS 3.2.27: It is not a valid reason because it is itself that which is to be proven.
The objection [is as follows]:
"But there is a goal to be accomplished" (Sūtra 27).
There is no refutation [of the soul's existence] because the maintenance of the body is possible for one who remembers.
The rebuttal:
"smara-dhaḥ" (sūtra 28).
That is not so, because the mind possesses the quality of rapid movement.
Again, an objection is raised:
"Not that—He" (Sūtra 29).
NyS 3.2.30: No, because there is no fixed rule regarding the time of recollection.
The rebuttal:
"One does not remember" (Sūtra 30).

A *bhāṣya* is a composition of reflection (*nintā-prabandha*), that is, a composition of recollection (*smṛti-prabandha*). It refers to the contemplation or recollection of some specific meaning (*artha*) that serves as an indicative mark (*liṅga*), a sign (*cihna*), or— in other words— an uncommon characteristic.
A perfected object that has been propitiated becomes a cause for memory for one who possesses its signs.
For this reason as well, he states that the mind is a cause for memory only in dependence upon conjunction with a body, and not otherwise:
"independent of conjunction with a body..."
Thus [ends the section]. 30.
Nor is there a specific conjunction [of the self with the mind] due to the self's impulsion, chance, or its being a knower.

NyS 3.2.32: [The cause of doubt] is the same as in the case of the piercing of the foot by one whose mind is distracted, due to a particular kind of contact. (Sūtra 31) *ātma-ṣaḥ* (Sūtra 31). NyS 3.2.32: It is the same as [the cause of doubt] for one whose mind is distracted, due to a particular kind of contact resulting in the piercing of the foot.
NyS 3.2.33: Because cognitions of the mental application (praṇidhāna), the inferential mark (liṅga), and so forth do not occur simultaneously, there is no simultaneous recollection.
It vitiates.
Vyāsa— nam (Sūtra 32).

The objection "like intuitive knowledge" (*prātibhavat*) means that since the causes of memory— such as prior resolve and so forth— are not present at the moment memory arises, there would follow the undesirable consequence of memories arising simultaneously due to the conjunction of the self and the mind depending on latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), just as in the case of intuitive knowledge. He states the resolution:
Regarding the phrase "because it is the cause of memory for one who exists":
even though the instrument and its sequence are not perceived, they are inferred from the sequence in which the effects arise.
Thus, even intuitive cognition (*prātibha*), which arises from the contact between the self and the mind depending upon a specific human action, is neither without a cause nor devoid of a sequence.
The author of the Bhāṣya asks in order to introduce the principal argument:
"Now, [what about] intuitive knowledge? Having provided a confused answer here, he raises an objection.
If it is argued that this is incorrect because there is no logical reason (*hetu*), he states the essence of the reply:
"Not [of] the instrument (*karaṇa*)."

Even if, in some cases, two cuts occur simultaneously when an axe comes into contact with two pieces of wood at once, nevertheless, a difference in the instruments must be inferred due to the difference between the parts of the axe.

Alternatively, let other instruments perform their effects simultaneously; however, there is no deviation in the rule that the instrument of cognition produces cognitions only in succession, as it has been said: "cognition occurs in a sequence."
Therefore, a single instrument is never capable of producing multiple effects simultaneously.
However, even a single agent can perform many actions at once through a diversity of instruments; thus he says:
"Because for a cognizer whose nature is not subject to transformation, there is no simultaneity of cognitions despite the multiplicity of bodies."
He whose dharma is manifold creation (*vividha-karaṇa*) is described as such; the author of the *Vārttika* explains this with the words, "And this is not a fixed rule.

Indeed, when supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) has appeared, the yogi, having fashioned bodies together with sense-faculties in various worlds and having taken hold of the minds of liberated souls, hastening toward liberation, [perceives] those [objects] acquired through karma simultaneously.

Because of the distinction between pleasure and pain, one experiences them neither with aversion nor with attachment; thus, even for this single [self], cognitions arise simultaneously due to the diversity of the instruments.
And this is the second refutation: that there is no difference in the spatial parts of the self conditioned by cognitions that would cause cognitions to arise non-simultaneously.
[The term] "avasthita" means...
In that very location within his own body where various cognitions regarding diverse objects have arisen, as well as their latent impressions (*saṃskāra*),
the mind— which is situated inside the body— is conjoined with that region.
This is what the author of the *Vārttika* states:
And if [it is argued that cognition occurs] due to contact with that portion of the self (ātman) which is inherent in the cognition,
then this is not a valid rebuttal because it fails to account for all cases.
However, the teacher-like [opponents] state that this leads to the undesirable consequence of the simultaneity of memories.
It is untenable that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) which are situated [in the self] occupy the same location.

Why? Because since the parts (*pradeśa*) of the self are not distinct substances, if all conditioned phenomena were to occupy the same location as the self, the consequence of the simultaneous occurrence of cognitions would be unavoidable. For there cannot exist parts of the self that are other than it, as is the case with a jar; rather, the self itself is one and only one. Thus, the meaning is that all [phenomena] residing in the self occupy the same location.
This has been stated by the author of the Bhāṣya:

"Since the spatial points of the self are not distinct substances, and since there is no difference in their inherence in a single object, the refutation of the simultaneity of recollections is untenable.
As for the phrase "but in the case of the series of sounds," the word *tu* (but) serves to dispel the doubt expressed in the Bhāṣya.
The author of the Vārttika explains this very commentary [with the words] "by means of the proximity of the latent impression" (saṃskārapratyāsattyā).
He asks:
"What is the proximity? To this we reply: "We do not state an answer."

Even though the self is partless, it has been established that the latent impression (saṃskāra) likewise does not reside [in it]; therefore, the meaning is that, as in the case of sound, the presence or absence of auxiliary causes is indeed possible. // 33 //
NyS 3.2.34: Because the undertaking and cessation of activity are caused by desire and aversion in one who possesses knowledge.
Now, it is investigated whether cognition (*buddhi*) itself is co-located with desire and so forth, or not.
In this regard, a doubt arises due to the conflicting views of the Sāṃkhya school and the Nihilists (*vaināśika*). He states that conflict as follows:
Knowledge is a property of the *puruṣa*, yet it belongs to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

The consciousness of the *puruṣa* is one alone, immutable and eternal; however, by virtue of the delusion consisting in the reflection of the principle of the intellect (*buddhitattva*)—which has transformed into the forms of various objects—it appears as if divided, possessing the characteristics of arising and passing away, and is designated as "cognition" (*vijñāna*) and "mental modification" (*vṛtti*).
However, the view that desire, aversion, and so forth— being by their very nature subject to arising and passing away— belong to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is refuted [by the Sūtra]:
"Of the knower" (Sūtra 34).
It turns toward [the internal] and goes inward; that which is both this and the self is the *pratyagātman* (the inner self), and [the argument concerns] that.
This is what is meant:

because desire and other qualities belonging to another are not perceived by someone else through perception occurring in the same substratum as cognition, or else, if they were so perceived, it would follow that Caitra could perceive the qualities residing in Maitra.

Furthermore, because the modifications of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and other qualities are eternally imperceptible, desire and the rest must reside only in the self (ātman) and not in the internal organ. // 34 //
NyS 3.2.35: Because desire and aversion have that as their mark, they are not denied in earth and other [elements].

In this interval, the proponent of the doctrine that consciousness is an emergent property of matter (*bhūtacaitanika*), having found an opportunity, objects as follows: "Because of that mark" (Sūtra 35).
(428/4) If for whomsoever there is initiation and cessation [of activity], for him there is desire and aversion; and for whomsoever these two exist, for him there is consciousness.

Alas! By this sequence, the doctrine of the sentience of the elements (*bhūta-caitanya*), which is our own accepted view, follows—namely, that consciousness resides only in the elements when they have transformed into the shape of a body, because initiation and cessation are observed therein. This is the meaning. // 35 //
Because the commencement and cessation [of action] are observed in the case of axes and other such tools.
The author of the Vārttika states the intended meaning of the phrase "in the case of axes and so forth" (*paraśvādiṣu*).
Regarding the phrase "in the case of axes and so forth" (428.9),

the proponent of the doctrine that the elements possess consciousness (*bhūtacaitanika*) provides an alternative interpretation of the reason— "because of having those as its marks" (*talliṅgatvāt*)— for the sake of establishing his own position.
"In that case, this [is the argument]:

because one observes a difference in the arrangement of parts within bodies, a difference in the activity of the atoms that initiate the body is inferred even in clods of earth and the like; from that [difference in activity], desire and aversion [are inferred], and from those two, consciousness."
The mobile and moving body is fragile and unstable, such as the bodies of worms and the like; the stationary and stable body belongs to gods, humans, and others,
for that indeed endures for a much longer time.
He refutes this as follows:
"Of the clay particles, etc., [of jars and so forth].

Since the commencement [of production] is observed through the rearrangement of the clay that initiates the jar and other objects, whereas it is not observed in the case of sand, there is inconclusiveness regarding the commencement and cessation of production. // 36 //
But restriction and non-restriction are the qualifiers of that [object].
Having thus refuted the proof that consciousness belongs to the elements, he states the proof for consciousness belonging to something other than them:
"But restriction and non-restriction are the differentiators of those" (Sūtra 39).
The restriction and non-restriction of those two, desire and aversion, are their distinguishing features.
This indeed is the distinction between desire and aversion: that having excluded their dependence on the elements (*bhūta*), their dependence on something other than those is established.
Regarding this, he first states the non-restriction.
The engagement and withdrawal of a knower— namely, vibration and non-vibration— are caused by desire and aversion;
they do not reside in their own substratum— that is, they do not reside in the substratum of the desire and aversion themselves—
but rather in the instrument to be employed, such as an axe or the like.

In that case, activity and cessation would occur only with respect to those elements actually engaged [in action], and not with respect to all [factors] including the body and so forth which serve as the instigators; this is the logical consequence of non-universality. Non-universality means the absence of universal application.
Thus it is said:
this is what is meant— the body is not the substratum of desire, knowledge, and aversion,
because it is the substratum of the movement produced by desire and the rest, like an axe or similar tools.
Thus, having explained the differentiator regarding this lack of restriction, he explains the restriction:

"But for that Cārvāka, according to whose view the commencement and cessation [of action] caused by desire and aversion—due to the sentience of the elements—occur in their own substratum, namely the body and so forth;
for that Cārvāka..."
Just as the activity of material elements, characterized by falling and so forth, is caused by a different quality such as gravity,
the obstruction of that very same quality— gravity and the like— by means of conjunction with a supporting substance results in its cessation, namely non-falling and so forth; this [cessation],
occurring in all material elements, is invariably pervaded [by the cause].
But [activity and cessation] do not occur only in those elements that are appropriated by a body;
rather, in this way, activity and cessation caused by knowledge, desire, and aversion would occur in their own substratum even in mere elements.
This is what is meant: whatever properties belong to earth and so forth are observed to exist as long as earth and so forth exist, just as...
If heaviness and so forth, as well as cognition, desire, and so forth, were properties of earth and the other elements, they would necessarily exist as long as earth and the others exist;
yet they are not observed in jars and such things. Therefore, cognition and the rest are not properties of earth and the others.

In this context, the author of the Bhāṣya employed the word *niyama* (restriction) with the intention of suggesting the consequence of universal presence (*sārvatrikatva*), whereas he used the word *aniyama* (non-restriction) with the intention of suggesting the absence of universal presence.

The author of the Vārttika, however, intending to emphasize the restriction that [the suffix] must be applied only [to the specific case], employed the word "niyama" (restriction) in reference to a limited scope;
whereas for a universal application, because there is an absence of such a restrictive determination as stated, he used the word "aniyama" (non-restriction).
Thus, there is no contradiction, as it relies on a difference in intended meaning.

As for one who would violate this rule through the power of intoxication— just as it is said that yeast and other substances, having undergone specific transformations and attained the state of wine, intoxicate, so too earth and other elements transformed into the form of a body possess consciousness, and not otherwise; therefore,
there is no such consequence [of consciousness] in jars and the like.
To this, he replies: "And in a single body.
Just as the power of intoxication exists in each individual part of wine and does not reside solely in the collection as a whole, so too consciousness must exist in each individual part of the body.

Nor can one, out of sheer audacity, maintain that consciousness resides only in the aggregate of the body and not in its parts, for consciousness is still perceived even when three or four parts have been severed.
Therefore, if each of the parts were individually conscious, there would be many conscious beings in a single body.
If it is argued, "Let it be so; what harm is done to us?", we say: no.

If they were independent and possessed conflicting intentions, not even a single effect would ever arise. Furthermore, a restriction to a single intention among many is never observed; at best, such a unity of intention might occur by chance (*kākatālīya-nyāya*), but a fixed rule for this has never been seen before. Since this [possibility] is well known, this objection is set aside, and the critique was stated that the inference regarding the determination of conditions (*pratyaya-vyavasthā*) would not be possible.
We observe the mutual connection of cognitions within a single body, but not in another body; this is the established rule.
This [rule] would hold if there were only one conscious being in a single body and that same being did not exist in another body; otherwise, it would not be so—this is the meaning.
In some places, the reading is "there may be inference from the establishment of the suffixes," which is indeed easy to understand.
Regarding what was stated as "restriction and non-restriction," the author of the Bhāṣya indicates that very inference:
"And a specific activity is observed to be caused by the qualities of another."
Activity characterized by a specific kind of motion is the cause for the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful;

this is the formal argument: this activity within the bodies of mobile and immobile beings is caused by a quality residing in a substrate distinct from its own substrate, because it is a specific kind of activity, just like the specific kind of activity found in axes and the like.

Not only is the specific activity of the body caused by another quality [i.e., the soul], but even the specific activity of the elements that originate it is likewise dependent upon another quality; thus he says:
"The evidence is the arrangement of its constituent parts."
Thus, it is the same [in both cases], because cognition persists even when the sense organ and the object have perished.

For just as cognition is not a quality of the sense organ and the object because it persists even when the sense organ and the object have perished, so too, because cognition persists through the stages of childhood, youth, middle age, and old age— even when the body has perished— [cognition is not a quality of the body].
The meaning is that it is the knowledge of the qualities of the body.

Furthermore, regarding the statement "because the undertaking and desisting of an intelligent being are caused by desire and aversion," the terms "undertaking" and "desisting" do not, for us, intend merely the occurrence of activity and cessation; rather, they refer to a specific kind of movement aimed at the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful.

The author of the Bhāṣya states that because you have countered [the opponent's position] by means of the generality of activity (*pravṛtti-sāmānya*) without understanding this specific instance of activity (*pravṛtti-viśeṣa*), your non-comprehension (*apratipatti*) constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
He explains this with the words "mere action" (*kriyāmātra*).
The author of the Vārttika then comments upon that.
The remainder [of the sentence] is: "And it is incorrect because of a different statement.
This might be the case:

since the reasons such as "because of the aforementioned causality" and so forth, which belong to the sūtras to be stated later, are equally applicable to the refutation of consciousness in the elements (bhūta), the sense-faculties (indriya), and the mind (manas), why is consciousness refuted only in the mind and not elsewhere?
Therefore, he says "of the elements, the senses, and the mind" (bhūtendriyamanasām) [to clarify] "the elements, the senses, and the mind. (37)
NyS 3.2.38: [Pleasure and pain do not arise] from the mind, because of the reasons already stated, because of dependence on another, and because of the arrival of what was not performed.
As it has been said: "He" (Sūtra 38).
He explains [the phrase] "because of the aforementioned reason" as follows:

From the definition of the self—beginning with the statement that "desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain, and cognition are the marks (liṅga) of the self"—up to the conclusion of the examination of its characteristics, all that has been stated is here summarized.

And in this context, by the word "reason" (hetu), the Sūtra concerning desire and so forth is well-summarized; by means of the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), the examination whose object is the state of being a reason is indicated.
The *vārttika* states, "because of the stated nature of the reasons.

The construction is as follows: because the reasons such as "the apprehension of a single object through both sight and touch" possess the nature of reasons as previously described; therefore [the self exists].
By this, the meaning of the word "etcetera" (*prabhṛti*) occurring in the *bhāṣya* has been explained.
Since these aforementioned reasons have been refuted by opponents, he says:
"Because they are not refuted.
The meaning is that they have been refuted merely by words, but not in reality.

In the activities of sustaining, impelling, and arranging, the body and the sense organs are dependent as appropriate, because they are material, like a jar or similar objects; and the mind is also dependent, because it is an instrument, like an axe or similar tools. They proceed under the influence of someone's effort; if, however, they were conscious, they would be independent. Thus, there is a contradiction with the inference that establishes their dependence.
This is the meaning.

However, for one who accepts the authority of the Vedas, yet—having accepted that a person is the unconscious recipient of results—prefers the view that consciousness belongs to the body and so forth, [the author] states the reason for their lack of consciousness:
"And because of the arrival of what was not done."
For the fruit of instruction resides in the agent,
since instruction is characterized by the statement of a means required by the agent.
As the venerable Jaimini has said in this regard:

"The fruit of the treatise belongs to the performer, because that is its characteristic. This has been established by us in the section beginning with "The injunction is the enjoiner," and because from the statement "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," it is understood that the fruit is intended for the agent.

Precisely because of the traditional rule regarding the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) in this very context, it must be accepted by all who follow the path of the orthodox (*āstika*) that whoever is the agent of an action is also the enjoyer of its fruit.
Furthermore, if sentience were attributed to the body and other such factors, then those alone would be the agents of action due to the independence of the conscious principle.
Furthermore, since it is impossible for these [elements] once reduced to ashes to possess a fruit in the next world, one must admit that the insentient self is the possessor of that fruit; and thus,

actions performed by the body and so forth would be experienced by the person (puruṣa), which entails the faults of "attaining what was not done" (*akṛtābhyāgama*) and "the loss of what was done" (*kṛtanāśa*), both of which are rejected by the scriptures.
If, however, the body and so forth are insentient, while the person (*puruṣa*) distinct from the body and such is sentient, then the person is the agent by virtue of his autonomy;

and since the body and so forth are the instruments employed by him, the experience of the fruits of one's own performed actions belongs to those instruments. Thus, there is no contradiction with the scriptures, nor any conflict with the activity of a discerning being.
Such is the intended meaning. // 38 //
By means of elimination and because the previously stated reasons are established.

Now, this is the summary of the established [position], meaning the conclusion. The commentary states: "The explanation of the categories of logical proof is not refuted," and "upon the dissolution, that is, the destruction, of the body."
"Without a connection" (*apratisaṃhitam*) means:

I have seen that what was begun on the previous day is completed on the following day; having formed a connection [between them] by thinking, "What was begun by me must be completed by me," they would not complete it in the absence of such a connection. Or, even if it were completed, Maitra might complete what was begun by Caitra.

For, from that which is undertaken by oneself, there would follow a mass of actions undertaken by others that is indistinguishable and non-excluded; since even one's own [action] possesses the nature of "otherness," it would be lacking finality. To illustrate: in the Vaiśyastoma sacrifice, only a Vaiśya has the entitlement, not a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya; likewise, in the Rājasūya, only a king has the entitlement, not a Brāhmaṇa or a Vaiśya;
and similarly, in a sacrifice for which Soma is the means, only a Brāhmaṇa is authorized, not a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, while a Śūdra is altogether unauthorized.

The sense is this: that final determination (*pariniṣṭhā*) would not exist in a mere continuum of cognitions, because all things possessing the characteristic of existence are distinct from one another by virtue of their difference from the three worlds, and because the universal of "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha-sāmānya*) has already been refuted.
He states the reason for [the cognition] being non-referential (*apratisaṃhita*).
"Because of the absence of recollection. // 39 //
Memory, however, belongs to the self because of its nature as a knower.

The very power of knowledge, which pervades the three periods of time, is the nature of the knower; and that, being distinct from space and the other elements, is the very essence of the self, pervading the three periods of time.

NyS 3.2.41: "Because the causes of memory—arising from [the following]—are not simultaneous: resolve, connection, repetition, signs, characteristics, similarity, possession, the supported and the support, relation, immediate succession, separation, a single effect, contradiction, excellence, attainment, intervention, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, fear, purposefulness, action, passion, merit, and demerit"—[with these words], he asks about the causes of memory by way of the "lion's glance" (siṃhāvalokita) method in order to introduce the subsequent sūtra.
He introduces the sūtra preceded by a statement of its intended meaning (*tātparya*).
Regarding "of the causes of mindfulness" (smṛtikāraṇānām): [this refers to] "to those who have made a vow" (praṇibhyaḥ), according to Sūtra 41.

Retention (*dhāraṇā*) is the holding of the mind through the desire to remember the subject matter (*bhāṣya*). The meaning is the withdrawal of the mind from various objects to which it has become attached.
Alternatively, it is the contemplation of the signs (*liṅga*) of what one wishes to remember, or the direct retention [of that object], or the effort directed toward those signs.
This is the meaning.
As for the phrase "for indeed, the composition":
just as in this very work, topics such as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, being contained within a single text, serve as causes for the mutual recollection of one another.
Or by way of sequence,
as when one recalls the object of knowledge (*prameya*) after having recalled the category of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
or otherwise.
Just as one remembers the objects of knowledge (prameya) by recollecting the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) and the points of defeat (nigrahasthāna),
he states another explanation of the "bond" (nibandha):
"retention" (dhāraṇā).

The branch of *dhāraṇā* was taught by Jaigīṣavya and others. It consists of the mental placement (*upavikṣepa*) or superimposition (*samāropa*) of deities—who possess specific forms, postures, weapons, and ornaments—upon objects already known, such as the network of channels (*nāḍīcakra*), the heart-lotus (*hṛtpuṇḍarīka*), the pit of the throat, the tip of the nose, the forehead, the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), and so forth. The meaning is that once the deities have been thus superimposed there, they are remembered through the perception of those respective parts.
Here, the word "practice" (*abhyāsa*) refers to the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by repetition, which is a quality of the self (*ātmaguṇa*).
By this, both respect (*ādara*) and the causal basis (*pratyaya*) are also included;
for these two, too, serve as causes for memory only by means of depositing a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), just like repeated practice (*abhyāsa*).

Furthermore, it is not intended that the causes of memory exclude one another; rather, through this latent impression, there is indeed a coexistence (*samāveśa*) of all the causes of memory, such as the vow (*praṇidhāna*) and so forth.
However, through the commentaries (*nibandha*) and other sources, one should infer the presence or absence of absorption (*samāveśa*) as appropriate.
Furthermore, the mark (*liṅga*) perceived hereafter—

An example of that which is connected by conjunction (*saṃyogin*) is smoke [as an indicator] of fire. An example of that which is connected by inherence (*samavāyin*) is the case where, although a cow is obstructed by a wall or the like, its horn—which is directly perceived—is present together with the cow; thus, the horn is said to be "inherently connected" (*samavāyi*). However, it is not the case that the horn is inherently connected to the cow, because the cow itself is inherently connected only to its own parts, such as the horn.

The meaning of "inhering in the same object" (*ekārthasamavāyin*) is as follows: the inherence (*samavāya*) in a single object is "inherence in the same object"; that which possesses this is "that which inheres in the same object.
An example of this is: "the hand [inheres] in the foot."

Indeed, in this case, there is inherence (*samavāya*) of a single whole (*avayavin*) both in the foot and in the hand; thus, those two—the hand and the foot—possess inherence in a single object. Therein, by means of one [part] that possesses inherence in a single object which is perceptible (*pratyakṣa*), the other [part], though imperceptible (*apratyakṣa*), is remembered. However, when the meaning is "inherence in a single object," then the example is "color [is related] to touch."
The distinction is that a *liṅga* is characterized by an essential and inseparable connection (*svābhāvikāvinābhāva*), whereas a *cihna* is conventional (*sāṅketika*).
A *grāmaṇī* is a leader.

Although the term "connection" (*sambandha*) applies everywhere, including in the case of vows (*praṇidhāna*) and so forth, nevertheless, by excluding vows and the like, the word "connection" is used here according to the maxim of the "ox and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*) to refer to a different kind of connection.
Nor should it be argued that the inclusion of the other terms is redundant because the word "relation" (*sambandha*) already encompasses everything;
for the author of the Bhāṣya has stated elsewhere that the author of the Sūtras does not concern himself with brevity of expression,
and that clarity of the student's understanding is achieved precisely through such specific designation.
"Because of immediate succession":
for at the hour of Brahmā, immediately upon waking, one should rise; after that, urinate; after that, perform purification; after that, wash the face comfortably and clean the teeth, and so forth.
"Because of separation" indicates grief.
From that, one also remembers the object of grief because of a common purpose; for example,
as there is a single sacrificial session (*satra*) to be performed by at least seventeen persons desiring supernatural power (*ṛddhi*).
In that case, having seen one sacrificer, one remembers another sacrificer due to their similarity;
for example, a religious student (*brahmacārī*) remembers his teacher, who produced in him excellence in the knowledge and discipline of the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*).
But in the case of attainment, it is as when a seeker [remembers what he has obtained].
Because he frequently remembers that sweet food which has been obtained or is yet to be obtained by him;
desire (*icchā*) is affection (*sneha*).
That [affection], however, is aversion toward brothers and the like, or toward a wife and so forth who are disagreeable.
And by means of those two as well, one remembers that object;
the meaning is "by means of action" or "by means of its effect.
Furthermore, through the dharma produced by the practice of dharma, one remembers a previous birth.
Thus, the recollection of the means for pleasure and so forth by one who has just been born is to be understood as resulting from dharma and adharma.
Now, one might ask: since madness and other such factors are also established in the world as causes of memory, why were they not mentioned? To this he says:
"And this [list] is merely an illustration of the causes of memory. (41)
NyS 3.2.42: Because action is perceived as non-abiding.
Having thus established the "lion’s glance" (siṃhāvalokita), he begins an investigation into the subject at hand, namely cognition (*buddhi*).

Regarding the phrase "and in the case of impermanent cognition" (430.9), even if it were stated that [cognition] is dependent on a substance (*dravya*), there would still be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to [the qualities of] form (*rūpa*) and so forth residing in the eye and other sense organs; therefore, he says:
"Because it rests upon a pervasive substance.
Nevertheless, there is an inconclusiveness (anaikānta) due to [qualities] such as selfhood (ātmatva); therefore, he says "provided that it possesses a genus" (jātimattve sati).
Even so, there is an inconclusiveness due to the dimension of omnipresence (vibhutva-parimāṇa); therefore, he says:
Regarding the phrase "provided that it is perceptible to us and others":
cognitions whose objects are the continua of karma and so forth perish very rapidly.
If, in this context, one were to say "because of its illuminating nature," then there would be an inconclusive reason (anaikāntika) due to the self (ātman); therefore, he says:

"Even though it is a cause," [one might object], "there is still an inconclusiveness (anaikānta) with respect to the mind, the ear, and so forth; therefore, he says 'pratyartha' (with respect to each object).

One cognition has a single object and does not have another object as its domain; likewise, other cognitions are also restricted solely to their own respective objects. The mind, the ear, and so forth are not like this, because they possess multiple objects."

But is it not the case that being restricted to a single object (*pratyarthaniyatatva*) is non-pervasive [i.e., not universally true], since when there is simultaneous contact with multiple objects, a single cognition arises even regarding various objects? To this, he says: Since a new object (*artha*) arises at every moment through its own action, and because the sequence of the effect follows the sequence of its causes, the cognition—which is the effect—arises not simultaneously. Because the object is the cause of the perceptual cognition, each individual object, arising in succession, is the cause; thus, it is established that all cognitions, which possess a sequential nature, are restricted to a single object each.
And this restriction (*niyama*) is with respect to another action of the same class, not with respect to the substance;

therefore, even though the cognition of the action has substances and so forth as its objects, there is no contradiction regarding the restriction to each respective object. Furthermore, because the qualification "restricted to each respective object" was previously suspected of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the self (*ātman*), the qualification "instrumentality" (*karaṇatva*) is employed.
He states another formal argument:
"Or else" (*atha vā*).
To prevent the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) due to [the presence of] pleasure-ness (*sukhatva*) and so forth, he says: "provided that it is a quality" (*guṇatve sati*). (431.1)
The term "non-external" (*abāhya*) is stated in order to exclude deviation with respect to [objects] such as visible form (*rūpa*).
Even though the word "persisting" (*avasthita*) is used, the term "perishing" (*dhvaṃsinī*) is employed because perception ceases [even during that time].

Although it might be possible to argue that the single cognition of touch and so forth persists for that duration and will perish due to the destruction of the contact with the object caused by intervention and the like, [the author uses these terms to preclude such an interpretation].

Even the destruction of a non-inherent cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) is observed to be a cause for the destruction of its effect, as in the case of the destruction of duality resulting from the destruction of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*); nevertheless, since momentariness is established by other reasons alone, this [example] should be regarded as merely an incidental corroboration (*abhyuccaya*). For, by the very demonstration of the momentariness of cognitions whose objects are things that perish in a moment, the demonstration of the momentariness of cognitions whose objects are enduring things is also indicated.
"Cognitions have stable objects yet are momentary,
because they are cognitions, like the cognition of an action and so forth.
Having thus superimposed the nature of a self onto cognition— thinking that "cognition alone is the rememberer and the grasper"— the opponent raises this objection.
If it is argued that [the mind] abides by means of mindfulness, he refutes this by saying:
"Not for that very reason."
For it is not the intellect (*buddhi*) that is the rememberer, such that in its absence memory would not arise; rather, it is the self (*ātman*), and that is eternal.
The meaning is that the presence of the intellect, however, is what contradicts memory.

Now, if cognition (*buddhi*) does not exist, how then can memory arise? For an effect cannot exist without a cause. Nor is the self alone the cause; otherwise, since the self is eternal, the arising of memory would also have to be eternal. Therefore, the arising of memory is also a mark (*liṅga*) for the existence of cognition. To this, he says: "And because that [memory] occurs from something else."
This might be the case: if the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by cognition were the cause of memory, then memory would persist as long as that impression exists.
Therefore, he says: "from that [arises] the resolution (*praṇidhāna*), etc."
It is not by the mere fact that a formative force (*saṃskāra*) exists that memory occurs, but rather from its awakening;
and the awakening is occasional, because it is occasional due to factors such as a prior resolution (*praṇidhāna*). This is the meaning. // 42 //
The non-apprehension of the unmanifest [object] is due to its lack of stability, like the non-apprehension of form during a flash of lightning.
The proponent of the stability of the Buddha says: "If [the cognition] were not stable... (43)
NyS 3.2.44: By the employment of a reason, there is the admission of that which is to be negated.
"It vitiates [the argument];

not because of contradiction" means that having asserted the permanence of cognition in general, to then state that cognitions of jars and the like produced by a flash of lightning are impermanent is contradictory.

He states that the apprehension of the unmanifest is established otherwise [than by the existence of the whole] with the words "of the apprehension of the unmanifest," because there is a difference in the cause for the apprehension of the substratum (dharmin).

And that which is the cause for the apprehension of the substratum (*dharmin*) as indistinct is that which apprehends the substratum as possessing only the universal (*sāmānyamātra*); by virtue of that, there is an indistinct apprehension. However, that which [apprehends] it as possessing both the universal and the particular, by virtue of that, there is a distinct apprehension—this is the meaning. For, without relying upon the substratum, such apprehensions are impossible within their own respective objects; this is the meaning of "because of distinctness. [The opponent] says: "without relying upon the substratum," being ignorant [of the fact].
He raises an objection:
"If it be said that there is a contradiction with worldly experience.
He refutes this by relying on the apprehension of the subject (*dharmin*).
"It is not otherwise.
He states another fault:
"And because it is inconclusive."
The explanation of the Bhāṣya is achieved precisely through the explanation of the Vārttika.
The apprehension of that [object] is not like the apprehension of a lamp-flame made manifest by its continuity.
NyS 3.2.46: With regard to a substance, there is doubt because of the perception of its own qualities as well as the qualities of others.
For previously, the sentience of the elements, the sense organs, and the mind was directly refuted, while that of the body was refuted only by way of introduction;

however, at present, the sentience of the body itself is being rejected directly. Thus, because of this difference in intent (*tātparya*), there is no tautology. In reality, however, the Commentator will explain the avoidance of tautology in another manner at the end of the section.
Its being a quality of that [substratum] is established by its perception therein; the words "by an uncontradicted [perception]" are to be supplied as the remainder. // 44-45 //
Because color and the other [sensory qualities] persist as long as the body exists.
It is not because of the non-cessation of its cause—for consciousness, the body is the cause, and that is not yet ceased;
however, it should be understood that the cause of the formative impression (saṃskāra) has indeed ceased. // 47 //
Not so, because of the production of another quality arising from baking.
And that is not so, because of the production of another quality born of heating (*pākaja*).
The meaning is that there is no absolute absence of color (*rūpa*) either in the atom or in the pot. // 48 //
NyS 3.2.49: There is no refutation of things produced by cooking, because their opposites are established.

Having thus stated the difference in nature (*vaidharmya*) regarding whether something is absolute or non-absolute, he states another difference in nature—namely, having an opponent versus not having an opponent—with the words "And for this reason as well":

"Because [the property] of being produced by cooking (*pākaja*) is established as having an opponent, the demonstration of its deviation [from the probandum] does not constitute a refutation of the fact that consciousness (*caitanya*) persists as long as the body exists. (49)
Because it pervades the body.
Because it would lead to the undesirable consequence that there is no established continuity of cognition.

Just as Devadatta’s cognition is not taken up by Yajñadatta, but rather by Devadatta alone—this being the established rule—the meaning here is that within a single body, the cognition of one part does not take up the cognition of another part, or the cognition of the whole. // 50 //
NyS 3.2.51: [The argument is] not [valid], because [the self] is not perceived in the hair, nails, and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "the sūtra of the example": the meaning is that this sūtra is for the purpose of providing an illustration, namely: "The hands, feet, and so forth are not sentient, because they are parts of the body, just like hair, nails, and so forth. // 51 //
NyS 3.2.52: Because the body extends only as far as the skin, there is no [application of the definition] to the hair, nails, and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "because it extends to the skin":
the reason—that hair, nails, and so forth are parts of the body—is unestablished (*asiddha*). The definition of the body is that which serves as the substratum for the sense organs;
therefore, wherever the body is inherent, it must necessarily be accompanied by that which serves as the substratum for the sense organs.
The meaning is that the collection of parts ending with the skin is such [a body], whereas hair, nails, and so forth are not like that, and thus they are not limbs of the body. // 52 //
Because of its dissimilarity to the qualities of the body.
NyS 3.2.54: No, because color and the other [sensory qualities] possess mutual dissimilarity.
NyS 3.2.55: There is no refutation of color and so forth, because they are not supersensuous.
However, the mutual heterogeneity of color and the other qualities is not observed—meaning it is not associated with being a quality of the body.
For it is never seen that those things which possess the heterogeneity of color, such as visibility to the eye or tangibility by the tongue, are not qualities of the body.
Furthermore, the qualities of the body are not excluded [from this category], because such heterogeneity is observed in them.
Therefore, because there is an absence of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) with being a quality of the body, this is merely a point of dissimilarity (vaidharmya).

The dissimilarity from qualities of the body—whether perceptible by external organs or imperceptible—is its being perceived by the mind (mānasa-pratyakṣatva); however, this [perception] is not a probans for consciousness being a quality of the body through positive and negative concomitance.
Rather, the meaning is that it is a probans for its being a quality other than that [of the body].
Because the negation of a specific instance implies the admission of the remainder;
as for the plural form "ye hetavaḥ" (those reasons), it is used with the intention of referring to a single part of the reasons.

When it is argued that consciousness is not a quality of the body because it does not persist as long as the substance [the body] exists, this is shown to be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) by reference to *saṃskāra* (potency); therefore, it is stated that there is an absence of any other cause.
Even so, this remains inconclusive due to qualities produced by heating (*pākaja*); therefore, it is further stated: "provided that no contrary quality is observed."
"Because it pervades the body"—
this is not a proof;
for a reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga) is not a proof, as it lacks a logical reason (hetu).
As they say: "There is a reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga), but not a proof by reductio (prasaṅgasādhana).
[The reason] is "because it is not perceptible by external sense organs.
Nor is there an inconclusiveness (anaikāntika) due to weight and so forth.
The meaning is that these [objects] are indeed imperceptible; they are not perceptible by means of the external sense organs. // 55 //
NyS 3.2.56: Because cognitions do not occur simultaneously, the mind is one.
In the examination of the true nature of the mind, [the matter] has been explained by the Bhāṣya and the Vārttika through a literal recitation [of the texts]. // 56 //
Not so, because multiple actions are perceived simultaneously.
Establishment is the state of being situated. // 57 //
