The perception of that [succession] occurs due to rapid movement, like the sight of a whirling firebrand.
And because of the reasons already stated, [the self] is atomic.
Its arising occurs due to the connection with the fruits of previously performed actions.
When one reflects upon the mind, what connection does the investigation into the cause of the body's origination have? To this, he says: "Indeed, of the mind... and so forth.

(438/10) Since the mind itself is also examined through an investigation into its locus (*adhikaraṇa*), there is no lack of connection with the investigation into the cause of the body's origination. "Examination" (*parīkṣā*) means thorough inspection; and that [inspection] occurs both with respect to the essential nature (*svarūpa*) and with respect to relations (*sambandhin*).
Furthermore, the body is related to the mind, because the mind has the body as its locus.
Therefore, the meaning is that the examination of the body is actually the examination of the mind alone.
Regarding the phrase "at the very time of its arising": *samam* means "as if equal" (*samam iva*).
The meaning is "immediately after arising.
Who says that he does not give?
The meaning is that if [the conditions] are complete, then immediately after arising, he will certainly give.
"Maturing latent karma" (karmāśaya) means that it causes its own fruit to be experienced;
or, it refers to other living beings who share in the experience of that same karma.

For example, karma that is to produce the state of being a *kiṃnara* does not yield its fruit if there is an obstruction by the karma of either the male or the female regarding the enjoyment [of sexual union] by a man and a woman. Those other living beings who are objects of affection, such as brothers and so forth, are called "partakers" (*bhāgin*) of that karma because they partake in the fruits of karma, such as food, horses, villages, and the like; however, due to the obstruction caused by the karma of those living beings—which is denoted by terms such as "misfortune" (*abhāgya*)—[the original karma does not bear fruit].
Or rather, the meaning is that there is no cause characterized by merit (*dharma*) or demerit (*adharma*) acting as a cooperative condition for that action; for,
since there is deviation in the acquisition of villages and the like despite visible actions such as service, an unseen cause (*adṛṣṭa*) must be postulated.
As they have said: "...and that very thing is the cause there, as well as sound... [The commentary explains:
"Service and so forth are seen to be the cause;
and by saying 'as well as sound,' the subject indicates the unseen (adṛṣṭa) object of that [sound]."

Furthermore, those [results] such as villages, being produced from that unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), depend upon the merit (*dharma*) generated by acts such as saluting deities for the sake of removing obstacles in the interim;
therefore, for the completion of its own fruit, the initial merit requires another merit as a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*).
And because of the diversity of cooperative causes, there is no contradiction in the removal of obstacles also serving as a cooperative cause.
The meaning is that, due to the absence of auxiliary causes for that action, the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) is obstructed and does not produce its fruit;
or rather, because that action—which is the auxiliary cause—is obstructed by another more powerful action, the fruit is not initiated.

Having thus explained the absence of auxiliary causes and the obstruction regarding one's own actions, he now demonstrates the absence of auxiliary causes and the obstruction regarding the actions of other sentient beings who share a common experience.
And regarding the actions of other sentient beings:
if it were stated simply that [they] "possess form and so forth," there would be an inconclusive argument (*anaikāntika*) due to atoms (*paramāṇu*); therefore, he says:
"provided they are perceptible by external sense organs."

Since the point is already established by the mere phrase "while being perceptible by the sense organs," the expression "while being perceptible by external instruments" is stated with the intention of merely distinguishing the category of things perceptible by the sense organs from another category, namely those perceptible by external instruments.
(Nyāyasūtra 3.2.61): Its assumption [of a cause] is like the assumption of a physical form from the elements.
No, because it is equivalent to the point to be proven.

The objection that the reason—"because of the incapacity for purposeful action"—is inconclusive (anaikāntika) by means of the example of sand and the like, which is itself equivalent to the probandum, is also refuted;
for since even sand and the like can somehow serve as causes for human purposes, it has been stated that their creation is preceded by the qualities of the Puruṣa. // 62 //
NyS 3.2.63: [The self is not produced by the parents], because they are merely the cause of its birth.

Or, even if the production of sand and such things were not preceded by the qualities of a person (*puruṣaguṇa*), nevertheless, when we reflect upon the production and so forth of the body and observe its difference from sand and the like, we conclude that it must have a distinct causal agent; thus, it is established that [the world] has the qualities of a person as its cause. To this, he says:
"And this comparison is unequal."

(440/16) Now, one might object that the mother and father are not the direct causes for the production of the body; to this he says: "By the words 'mother and father,' [he means] the blood and the semen.
In the phrase "to be experienced," the *kṛtya* suffix is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), according to the rule for words such as *bhavya* and *geya*. // 63 //
Likewise, [the same applies] to food.
He says that there is also inequality for this reason:
"Likewise, regarding food" (Sūtra 64).
He completes [the argument] with the opening phrase of the preceding sūtra:
"Because it is the cause of origination" (utpattinimittatvāt), which is the subject under discussion.
The *kalala*, *arbuda*, *peśī*, *māṃsapeśī*, and so forth, are specific stages of transformation (*pariṇāmabheda*) of the blood and semen that initiate the body. // 64 //
And because there is no restriction regarding the attainment [of the result].
In the case of attainment—(Sūtra 65).
The union of the couple is the "attainment" (prāpti); there is no fixed rule regarding that [union] for the production of a body.
Therefore, because the observed [cause] is inconsistent, there exists that unobserved [cause] from which the creation of the body arises; this is the meaning. // 65 //
Action is the cause for the production of conjunction, just as it is the cause for the production of the body.
The opponent, standing by the side, raises a doubt:
"By all selves.

[The author] replies: "But surely, that body which is acquired through a particular person's unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) is the locus of experience for that person alone; there is no lack of restriction. To this, he says:
Nor is it restricted to a single person;
for merit and demerit arise from the contact between the self and the mind,
and since this contact of the mind with all selves is common to everyone, merit and demerit would belong to all.
The meaning is not, however, that they belong exclusively to some [specific person] alone.
The answer to this is "the body.
With the same intention already stated, one raises an objection: "If it is asked, 'Whence comes their being situated therein—that is, their being situated in a single person?'"
The opponent replies, "Because of its own conjunction.
He asks again, "What restriction is there regarding conjunction?
[The response is: "Just as it is conjoined with the mind by means of one self, so too is it conjoined by means of other selves."
The meaning is that just as [the soul] is conjoined with one mind, so too is it with other minds; thus, there is no distinction in the contact between the self and the mind.
The answer is: "No, because of the mind's restriction as a cause," [referring to] the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*).
For the restraint of the mind is dependent upon [past] impressions, and the restraint of unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) is dependent upon the restraint of the mind;
and because this mutual dependence is beginningless, like that of the seed and the sprout, it does not entail any logical flaw—this is the meaning. // 66 //
By this, the restrictive rule (niyama) has been refuted.

Thus, the specific arrangement regarding the production of the body has been shown as being dependent upon the qualities of the self (*ātman*). However, there are those who maintain that the production of the body is not dependent on karma, but rather on primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and so forth;

for the *prakṛtis* themselves, independent of causes such as merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), being by nature prone to activity through the states of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, initiate their respective transformations.

However, they depend upon merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) merely for the removal of obstructions; just as a farmer, wishing to flood an unflooded field from a full one, floods the other fields by breaking only the embankments between them, so too do the primary natures (*prakṛti*) flood the evolutes (*vikāra*).
As it has been said: "The efficient cause is not the motivator of the primary natures; rather, it serves to break the obstruction, like a farmer."
In response to them, he says:
"By this, the lack of restriction is refuted" (Sūtra 67).

By this—namely, by the statement regarding the lack of restriction in the production of bodies for elements that depend upon karma—the lack of restriction [alleged] for those independent of it is refuted by way of contrast.

Niyama is pervasion (*vyāpti*), meaning that all selves possess a common physical form; aniyama, however, is non-pervasion, meaning that for some self there is one body and for another a different one. For if the production of bodies were dependent upon *prakṛti*, then because *prakṛti* is a single entity and common to all selves, there would be no cause for the non-commonality of bodies.

The mention of "beings" (bhūta), however, is intended as an illustration of the primary cause; it is not merely to show that having a common physical form is a defect when the creation of the body is not caused by karma, but rather to demonstrate that even liberation would not be possible [under such a view]. Thus, he establishes liberation according to his own position with the words, "And it is established."
He shows, however, that in the Sāṃkhya position there can be no liberation, with the words: "if [the self] were independent of karma. (67)
If it is argued that this is caused by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), then that same consequence would follow again at the time of final liberation (*apavarga*).

He raises an objection: "If it is argued that this is caused by the unseen (adṛṣṭa). Here, "the unseen" refers to either the non-perception of the objects of experience, such as sound and so forth, or the non-perception of the distinction between primordial matter (prakṛti) and the spirit (puruṣa).
The meaning is that [the manifestation] is brought about by that.

"It refutes [the objection] in this regard" means: just as there was no seeing previously, so too there is no seeing after the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamādhi*); thus, even one who has not [yet] entered [the path] would transmigrate again. Having raised this doubt, he refutes it.
"And [the body exists] because its purpose has been fulfilled.
Now, an objection is raised: "We do not say that the purpose of the Puruṣa consists in the enjoyment of sound and other objects, such that there would be a fulfillment of purpose;
rather, it is the perception of the distinction between the Puruṣa [and Prakṛti]. And since that [perception] does not yet exist, [Prakṛti] undertakes the body"—thus he explains.
Regarding the phrase "and by the cause that is human effort" (*puruṣārthena ca hetunā*): the particle *ca* is used for emphasis, meaning "by human effort alone. He provides the rebuttal:
Regarding the phrase "and because of its non-performance":
the word "and" (ca) has the sense of "but" (tu);
it serves to exclude the [previous] position.

The meaning is: "What was intended for the sake of which one undertakes bodies—that has not been accomplished, while something else has been done; what connection is there between this and that? He raises an objection: "It is a specific desire to see (*didṛkṣā-viśeṣa*). For seeing is excluded by the negative particle (*nañ*); therefore, he speaks of the desire to see which is rooted in that [seeing]. And since that [desire] does not exist in liberation (*apavarga*), the meaning is that one who is not liberated transmigrates.
"It does not [arise] prior" refutes this. What is meant is as follows:

for the desire to see (didṛkṣā) resides in the intellect (buddhi); it does not exist when the intellect is absent. Furthermore, the intellect is a transformation of primordial nature (prakṛti-pariṇāma). Thus, there would be the consequence of mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*): the desire to see exists when the intellect exists, and the intellect exists when the desire to see exists.
Nor is beginninglessness a valid defense, because both [the self and the mind] would be absent at the beginning of creation;
for us, however, the distinction is that at the time of dissolution, the self and the mind remain, conditioned by merit and demerit (dharma-adharma).
Taking up the theory that the effect pre-exists in the cause (*satkāryavāda*), he raises an objection:
"Because [the cause] possesses all powers. He then refutes it.
"Not because it would entail the consequence of the non-existence of liberation" (444/3).
He analyzes the [concise] connection: "Just as there is a desire to see, so too there is the perception of diversity.

Activity toward primordial matter (*prakṛti*) does not occur for that purpose; and thus, since there is no cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) nor its destruction due to the absence of liberation, there would be no liberation. This is the [consequence].
This is the meaning.
He clarifies this very point:

since the perception of diversity exists, the employment of the Pradhāna for that purpose is illogical; therefore, due to the absence of saṃsāra, its destruction—which is liberation—would not occur. This is the intended sense.
He demonstrates that very absence of liberation when its opposite—saṃsāra—is present:
"And when there is the perception of manifoldness.
The meaning is that as long as the cause is not severed, the effect cannot be severed.
He further demonstrates the conceptual construction (vikalpa) by stating "ignorance" and "non-seeing";
the meaning is that this is because the absence of discriminative knowledge (vivekajñāna) is common to both.
The remainder has its meaning unobscured.
However, others—the Ārhatas—describe *adṛṣṭa* as a quality of atoms;
impelled by its own qualities, it enters the body of earth-atoms and of the mind.

And that [unseen force], arising from its own unseen merit or demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), effects the experience of pleasure and pain for the person (*pudgala*); it is not, however, a property (*dharma*) of the person.
For them, as for the Sāṃkhyas, there would again follow the consequence of [the persistence of] that [unseen force] even upon liberation (*apavarga*).
He establishes this with the words: "of the quality of the atom" (paramāṇuguṇasya). // 68 //
And because mental action is the cause [of rebirth], there is no severance of conjunction.
Furthermore, he states that in this view there would be no departure [from the body], because the mind has karma as its cause. // 69 //
However, he states that "departure" (prāyaṇa) is indeed possible according to our own system:

when the latent impressions (*karmāśaya*) of the karma that initiated the present body have been exhausted, it is logical that the mind withdraws due to other latent impressions of karma that will initiate a future body;
thus, departure has both causes.
The meaning is that it is the cause of approaching and withdrawing. // 69 //
And there would be the consequence of eternality, because death would be impossible.

Now, one might object: "Let there be no severance of the conjunction; why should that not be acceptable? To this he says: "And it would follow that the body is eternal, because death would be impossible.
The meaning is: because the conjunction [with the self] would never be severed.
[Objection: But surely it has been stated that "that which exists and is without cause is eternal"; how then could the body, which possesses a cause, be eternal?
To this he says: by the phrase "the consequence of eternality," we mean the impossibility of death.
The meaning is that destruction would be impossible. In the case of something being accidental— that is, without a cause— there would be no difference between various states of existence (prāyaṇa).

Furthermore, a difference in the time of death is observed: some die while still in the womb, some as soon as born, and some as young children, and so forth; for that which lacks a cause must either exist eternally or not exist at all—meaning it would be like the sky or like a flower in the sky. // 70 //
This would be like the case of the impermanence of the blackness of an atom.
He objects on the grounds that the reason "because of being causeless" is inconclusive, citing the example: "like the blackness of atoms. // 71 //
Not so, because it would entail the consequence of experiencing the results of actions not performed.
He refutes it, saying "and this is not so" (446/2);
that is to say, it is not established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is unproduced, and on the contrary, is contradicted by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and scripture (*āgama*).
The meaning is that its acceptance follows from the admission of that [thesis].

The intention is that even the blackness of an atom is admitted to be produced by baking (pākaja), because it is an earthy color, just like red and other colors, according to the inference: "The blackness of an atom is not without a cause, because it is an earthy color, like red and other colors."
Or, according to the scripture, the meaning of the Sūtra is as follows:
because there would be the undesirable consequence of experiencing the fruit of an action that was never performed.
For just as the quality of an atom itself is eternal and initiates the body and so forth, so too this [Self], being eternal, is not produced by anything.

The sense is that the fruit of that which has not been performed would be enjoyed by persons; consequently, this collection of prescribed activities and prohibited abstentions among the believers would be useless, and the composition of the scriptures would also be purposeless.
This has been explained in great detail in the Bhāṣya.
Its meaning has been explained by the literal commentary. // 72 //
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Nyāyavārtikatātparyaṭīkā* composed by the venerable Vācaspatimiśra.
In this third chapter, there are 75 sūtras in the first daily lesson (ānhika) and 73 sūtras in the second; thus, from the beginning, there are 148 sūtras in total.
In the first daily lesson of the third book (a0), there are 9 sections (prakaraṇas).
In the third daily lesson (ānhika), there are nine sections;
together, there are sixteen sections;
The first daily lesson of the fourth chapter.
The activity is as previously described.
Now, following the sequence of enumeration and definition, it is appropriate to examine *pravṛtti* immediately after the examination of the mind (*manas*).
To dispel the doubt as to why that [pravṛtti] is not examined [here], he states the aphorism:
"Immediately after the mind."
The process of manifestation is as previously described (Sūtra 1).
The meaning is that its remainder has been examined in the same manner as it was characterized;
[the author] asks "But what [remains]?"—
the objects of knowledge (prameya), beginning with the self (ātman) and ending with the mind (manas), have already been examined.
The meaning is that neither the nature nor the effect of the process of manifestation has been examined. The answer is:
"As long as there is a substratum for dharma and adharma."
"Residing in a single substance" means that it exists in the self alone.
"Abiding" means that it is not subject to extremely rapid destruction like cognition and other such mental states.
"Due to inherence in the self" [is the reason].
The qualification "being an effect" (kāryatve sati) is to be understood [as part of the definition];

NyS 4.1.10: The proof of rebirth is established through the eternity of the self.

Arising and cessation, as well as rebirth (*pretyabhāva*), do not exist for a permanent self; therefore, in this [view], rebirth is not logical. For the nihilists (*vaināśika*), however, rebirth is logical by virtue of the arising and cessation of sentient beings.
The form *pretya* (having died) should be understood as having the suffix *-lyap*, as in the expression "he sleeps with his mouth open."

Thus, the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position is that since "becoming" (*bhavana*) and "departure" (*prāyaṇa*) share a common agent—as expressed in the phrase "having become thus, [there is] departure"—the identity of their agent is logically established. However, because the permanence of the self (*ātman*) was established in the preceding sūtra, if there were the production and destruction of a sentient being (*sattva*), there would be the faults of the loss of what has been done (*kṛtahāni*) and the acquisition of what has not been done (*akṛtābhyāgama*). Consequently, one would not engage in activity for the sake of higher prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), and it would follow that the instructions of the seers (*ṛṣi*) would be rendered useless. Therefore, birth and departure are simply the emergence and dissolution of the connection between the eternal self and its own body, sense organs, and cognition; in this way, the state of passing away (*pretyabhāva*) is logically accounted for.
Thus is the established conclusion. // 10 //
From the manifest [arise] the manifest, because perception is the means of valid cognition.

In the context of the investigation into post-mortem existence (*pretyabhāva*), he considers this further point:
if it is asked how this so-called "rebirth as a hungry ghost" (*preta*) occurs,

"from the manifest.
He will refute opposing views later on.
The term "the substratum of the body, the sense organs, the objects, and the instruments" is neuter because it is treated as a singular collective compound (*ekavadbhāva*).
[The author] teaches that inference—which arises from a relationship grasped through perception—is also taught under the category of perception, because it is rooted in perception.

Now, one might object: let the body and the elements such as earth be manifest (*vyakta*) due to their largeness (*mahattva*), their being composed of multiple substances (*anekadravyavattva*), and their specific qualities (*rūpaviśeṣa*); however, how can their fundamental causes, the atoms (*paramāṇu*), be manifest? The arising of an entity from non-existence does not occur, because [an effect] does not manifest without having destroyed [its cause].

Regarding this, some first say: "How can there be the arising of an entity from non-existence? For there is no manifestation without having first destroyed [the prior state]; that is the meaning. Indeed, everything arises precisely from emptiness."
Thus, indeed, it is heard: "In the beginning, this was non-existent alone.
For this very reason, even today the birth of the non-existent is observed, and not that of the existent; for what reason? Because non-existence is its cause.
And this [statement] "without having destroyed [the previous], there is no manifestation" is an illustration;

Therefore, it is established that the universe has a non-existent material cause (asad-upādāna). // 14 //

Now, it might be argued that by the phrase "because [the effect] appears after having destroyed [the cause]," the immediate succession between the destruction of the seed and the production of the sprout has been indicated; and since the production of the sprout follows immediately upon the destruction of the seed, it follows that the production of the sprout is the effect of the destruction of the seed.

the meaning is that while an immediate succession not caused by anything else establishes a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇa-bhāva*), this [case] is caused by an immediate succession of arrangement (*vyūha-ānantarya*); therefore, it cannot lead one to understand that non-existence (*abhāva*) possesses causality.
If the sprout is the effect of a different arrangement [of parts], then why does it not arise while the previous arrangement has not yet perished? To this he says:

If the destruction of the seed is the cause for the arising of the sprout, then when the seed has been destroyed and its constituent parts are mutually separated, why does the sprout not arise even in the absence of a new arrangement (*vyūha*) of those parts? Therefore, since the sprout does not arise from what has been destroyed, the meaning of the Sūtra is that the destruction of the seed is not the cause [of the sprout] in the absence of that arrangement. // 17 //
There is no refutation [of our position] because of the sequential instruction.

Nevertheless, to the question of what the decisive reason is for this [specific sequence], he says:
If non-existence were the cause for the production of a sprout— the remainder being that it would be "indescribable"—

Furthermore, even that which is claimed—that non-existence (abhāva) serves as the material cause because of the arising of what was previously non-existent—is also necessitated by the distinctness and the distinct potencies of effects;

Thus, this view has been refuted by the rejection of the theories of the manifestation of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*) and the manifestation of the indeterminable (*anirvacanīyakhyāti*). Then another says: "The Lord is the cause, because human action is seen to be fruitless" (Sūtra 19).
Let it not be that this manifold expansion of names and forms has emptiness as its material cause; rather, it will have Brahman as its material cause.

And in this way, there is no contradiction of its permanence; for even in transformation, the essence remains unimpaired, and permanence is defined by that very characteristic. As it is said: "That in which the essence is not destroyed is also permanent"—this is one view.

Furthermore, Brahman itself, due to the conditioning of indefinable, beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*), undergoes illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) as the diversity of the phenomenal world of names and forms (*nāmarūpa-prapañca*), just as a single entity such as pleasure appears in various forms of reflection through the diversity of media such as jewels, swords, and so forth.
By this, these two views have been indicated:
that Īśvara is Brahman because of his connection with lordship (*īśanā*).
The power of volition and the power of action constitute "lordship" (īśanā).

For it is heard in scripture: "It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate,'" and so forth.

neither non-existence, nor primordial matter (pradhāna), nor atoms are conscious.

For that [transformation] must occur either in its entirety or in part; in the case of transformation in its entirety, there would be impermanence due to the destruction of its essential nature (*tattva*).

If transformation occurs in part, then because it possesses parts, that very [Brahman] would be non-eternal. If, on the other hand, transformation belongs to that which is pervaded by its essence, and that essence is Brahman,

Furthermore, it is impossible for a single, partless self-cognizing perception to be the object of a contrary cognition.

Furthermore, in the case of Brahman—which is partless and directly perceived through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*)—there can be neither a non-apprehension of its true nature nor an apprehension of it as a universal.
Therefore, the claim that the Lord (*īśvara*) undergoes illusory transformation (*vivarta*) into the diversity of the world is untenable;
however, the Lord may indeed be the efficient cause (*nimitta*) of the world.
If it is asserted that [the Self] alone is the cause of the world without dependence [on anything else], then this objection presents itself:
"Because in the absence of human action, results are not produced.
The author of the Vārttika states the negative concomitance (vyatireka) of this point.
"If God were the cause," [it would follow that] "the effect would be of a single form. To this he says, "of God":
in relation to karma, God would be powerless.
And thus, the meaning is that the reason to be stated later—that "its causes are not employed by God"—is inconclusive (anaikāntika). // 20 //
It is not a valid reason because it is brought about by that [very same thing].

Thus, having refuted both the view that God is the material cause (*upādāna*) and the view that Brahman is the illusory transformation (*vivarta*), as well as the view that God is the independent efficient cause (*nimitta*), he adopts his own intended position:
"Because it is produced by Him, [the world] is not the reason [for His existence]" (Sūtra 21).

For the world, which has atoms as its material cause (*upādāna*), God is the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) in dependence upon the karma of persons; and that karma of persons which He depends upon is itself also caused by God.
Furthermore, we shall demonstrate from what has been taught that it is not the case that something which is depended upon lacks causality.

Therefore, since human effort is brought about by God, the reason for refuting the position that "God, assisted by that [effort], is the efficient cause of the world"— namely, that "in the absence of human action, results would not be produced"— is not a non-reason (*ahetu*).
The meaning is that this is indeed a valid reason for refuting the view that [the world] has God as its efficient cause independently [of human effort].
The commentary states that [the Lord] is another self characterized by qualities (*guṇaviśiṣṭa*).
The author of the Vārttika will establish the qualities of the Lord, such as knowledge and so forth.

He states the distinction [of the liberated soul] from those souls subject to saṃsāra:
"Adharma... [and so on].

Now, one might object: since there is an absence of the performance of ritual action for this [liberated soul], how can there be *dharma*? Likewise, how can there be the sovereignty consisting of powers such as *aṇimā*, which is of the nature of an effect, without action? Thus, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the acquisition of what was not earned (*akṛtābhyāgama*).
To this he says:
"And its quality (dharma) conforms to his volition."
To the question, "Why should he bring this about? he says:
"And thus, there is no loss of the attainment of what one has done oneself.

Let it not be that his sovereignty—the fruit of dharma produced by performance characterized by volition—is merely the result of external ritual practice; rather, let it be the result of the creation of the world. Thus, there is no contingency of attaining what was not done.
This is the meaning. It might be argued:
"The activity of discerning persons does not occur without a purpose, and for Īśvara, who has attained everything that is to be attained, there is nothing further to be attained."
Therefore, since it would be useless for him to create this world,
he says:
"and like one who has attained his goal."
The meaning is that this Blessed One might not have a self-interest [in acting], yet he would proceed to create the world for the sake of favoring others.
Regarding this very point, he states an example:
"Just as this [father] does for his children."
The meaning is that this [Lord] is the father of his own offspring, just as a father [is of his children].
He applies this to the point of the illustration by saying, "so too, the Lord is like a father.

Now, one might object: since other selves are observed to be associated with non-eternal knowledge, the Lord—being distinct from them—cannot possibly belong to the same class as those selves; to this he replies: "And not because of being of the nature of a self."

Even though other selves are conjoined with impermanent knowledge while this [self] is conjoined with eternal knowledge and so forth, it nonetheless belongs to the very same class as other selves because of its conjunction with qualities such as cognition (*buddhi*).
Otherwise, there would follow the absurd consequence that water-atoms and the like would not be "water" and so on, due to their conjunction with eternal color-form (*rūpa*) and other qualities;
for we observe that the color-form and other qualities residing in hailstones and the like are impermanent.

And if this [Self] were not designated by qualities such as cognition (buddhi) and so forth, it would be unestablished due to a lack of means of valid cognition (pramāṇa); thus he says, "by cognition and so forth.
This might be argued: if Īśvara proceeds to create the world out of compassion, then alas! he should create only those who are happy, and not those who are miserable.
Nor should it be said that the diversity of creation is due to the cooperation of merit (dharma) and demerit (adharma) residing in the individual souls (kṣetrajña).

Since a non-compassionate [being] cannot preside over Dharma—which, if not presided over, fails to perform its own function—the compassionate Lord must therefore preside over it. Consequently, because the world is seen to possess diversity through distinctions such as the happy and the miserable, the Lord does not act merely out of compassion; thus, he says:
"of one who proceeds without the loss of the attainment of what was done by oneself."
This is the intended meaning:
although he is compassionate and possesses a greatness that surpasses other beings, he is not able to alter the inherent capacity of things;
therefore, even that which is produced through unrighteousness (adharma)—
Nor is it logical for [the Lord] to be eternal even by virtue of His sovereign power;
nor is it possible for Him to perish without bestowing His fruit upon that which is opposed to its own fruit.
Therefore, since He does not transgress the fixed law (niyati) of the individual souls (kṣetrajña), the Lord cannot fail to preside over unrighteousness (adharma).

Therefore, although He is compassionate, this [Lord], conforming to the intrinsic nature of things and acting as a co-operative cause for merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), ordains the diversity of the world. This is what was stated [in the verse]: "of one who proceeds without the loss of the attainment of the fruits of his own actions. The meaning is: "of one who proceeds without the loss of the attainment of the fruits of whatever action has been performed by persons. [This refers to] the section on the system of the Lord (*īśvara-prakriyā*) in the *Vārttika*.

"And this reason does not turn away from that.
(459/14) The meaning is: this very reason characterized by insentience (*acetanatva*) does not turn away from milk.
Thinking that action (*parispanda*) is movement which conforms to material form (*mūrti*), and that it is not possible for an immaterial, omnipresent Lord (*īśvara*), he raises an objection.
If it is argued that [the Lord] is not the cause because of the absence of action (*kriyā*),

the rebuttal is based on the intention that "action" refers to knowledge, desire to act, and effort, which— though devoid of physical motion— are denoted by verbal roots (*ākhyāta-pada*) and thus constitute action;
this is because the alternative possibilities (*vikalpa*) are untenable.
And when multiple substances are combined simultaneously, [the effect arises] "from conjunctions excluded from non-common effects.

This means that while the non-common effect of each individual conjunction of two threads is a two-threaded piece (*dvitantuka*), it is from conjunctions excluded from those that the common effect characterized as a cloth (*paṭa*) is produced.

It is not only in the case of substances where an action has already arisen and ceased that there is the production of another substance; rather, even in the case of substances where no action has yet arisen, when a prior substance ceases due to conjunctions remaining in place, there is the production of another substance.
Thus he says:
"But when there is the disjunction of one part... and so forth.

By the word "tu" (but), it is shown that there is a specific distinction from the previous case regarding the action that has arisen and ceased. He asks: "Is it only for those devoid of action that an undertaking occurs? and answers: "No; rather, some [actions]... When the motion produced by the action of one [of two bodies] has ceased due to the impelling conjunction (*nodana-saṃyoga*), at the very same moment that the motion ceases in the other substance, another substance arises; because of its inherent nature (*svābhāvya*), it proceeds, and thus there is no fault.

This conscious being, although its very nature is to favor others, ordains the diversity of the world in accordance with the inherent nature of things and by following the latencies of karma (*karmāśaya*).
The meaning is that it does not necessarily obstruct the engagement of men in evil deeds.
Even today, the diverse natures of conscious beings are observed among people who are good, bad, or middling.
Now, if sovereignty were eternal, then the futility of dharma would follow, as that [sovereignty] would not arise from dharma.

Consequently, the statement that "the sovereignty of Īśvara should be understood as the fruit of his own performed karma" would be untenable; such is the sense [of the objection]. He refutes this, saying: "We say it is eternal."
For his powers of knowledge and action are eternal; thus, his sovereignty is eternal.
However, [powers] such as *aṇimā* and so forth are non-eternal, and it was with this intention that the author of the Bhāṣya stated they are the fruit of merit (*dharma*).

The purpose of the Lord’s merit—which presides over the accumulated stores of merit and demerit residing within each individual soul and conforms to the volitions of the soul’s own persistence—is [the manifestation of these powers].
The author of the *Bhāṣya* has stated this while provisionally accepting the existence of God's attributes (*dharma*).

However, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the actual existence of attributes in God; for the production of all effects is established by His eternal powers of knowledge and action alone. Bearing this intention in mind, he says:
"And there is no attribute in God."
If it is argued that there is therefore another self because of its possession of intelligence, [we reply:
by "another self" is meant another embodied being.
And that connection with a body is, for some—such as those in the cycle of existence (saṃsārin)—present; for others—such as the liberated ones like Śuka, Prahlāda, and so forth—it is past.
Therefore, the meaning of the objection is that this Lord, being intelligent, must necessarily be embodied;
that is to say, he must be a distinct self from another self, a distinct body from another body.
Why? Because of the difference in qualities.
If his intellect and other faculties were eternal, there would be no purpose in his assuming a body for the sake of their production; this is the intended meaning.
Now, one might object: "It is precisely this that [proves] atoms proceed when presided over by an intelligent cause.
The meaning is that, through the force of the property of the subject (pakṣadharmatā) aided by reasoning (tarka), his status as an eternal intelligent being is established.

By the passage beginning with "because of the impossibility of restricting [the cause] to each respective object," reasoning (*tarka*) is shown to be an auxiliary to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Thus far, the bodilessness of the Lord has been demonstrated through the distinction of his qualities; now, he states that this [bodilessness] does not tolerate even the conceptual possibility of a connection with a body, by saying:
"Furthermore, because of His being endowed with intelligence."

(465/4) "Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) has as its objects the past, future, and present" means that it possesses direct manifestation (*sākṣātkāravatī*); it does not, however, depend on the sense faculties (*akṣa*), because it is eternal.
And this is an elliptical indication;
it should also be understood that [the phrase] "nor inferential" implies "neither sensory nor based on analogy."
"Unafflicted" (*akliṣṭa*) means that it is not defiled by the affliction (*kleśa*), which is ignorance (*avidyā*).
"Because of being connected with a material substance" (*mūrttimaddravyasambandhitvāt*)... [means: because it is related to a substance possessing form.
The meaning is "because of being conjoined.
And thus, there is no deviation [of the reason] by means of color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth.
And thus, there is no deviation by means of color-form and so forth.

This much is intended by the Teacher: indeed, there are three kinds of entities in the world that are well-known to have conscious agents as their makers, such as palaces, watchtowers, gatehouses, and archways;
and those that are well-known to be the opposite of these.
For example, atoms, space, and so forth;
and those whose conscious creator is doubtful, such as bodies, mountains, and the earth.

In this regard, because there is doubt due to the presence of opposing views among disputants and the absence of any proving or subverting evidence regarding their having a conscious creator, there is uncertainty concerning their being created by a conscious agent.
Moreover, mere non-perception through direct perception cannot constitute a sublation here,
because even for things that exist but are remote by nature— such as atoms and the like— there is no perception by direct means.
And so it is with the mountains, trees, and so forth, which are the subjects under dispute.

[The argument is: Those things which possess origination must be preceded by a creator who possesses knowledge of their material causes (*upādāna*), either because they possess origination or because their material causes are insentient; for whatever possesses origination and has insentient material causes is necessarily preceded by one who possesses knowledge of those material causes, just as a palace or similar structures are.
And so too are the subjects of dispute, such as atoms, trees, mountains, and the like; therefore, it is so.
Furthermore, the fact that these [subjects] possess origination is not unestablished.
Alternatively, its [the earth's] possession of that [consciousness] is established by its having parts and being possessed of action when it is large, just like cloth and other such things.

Nor does this amount to proving what is already established for the Vaināśikas (Buddhists) regarding action as consciousness, or for the Mīmāṃsakas regarding the *kṣetrajña* (individual soul) as consciousness, because even if consciousness were established, those [elements like earth] would still lack knowledge of their own material cause (*upādāna*).

Or, if he possesses that knowledge, then he alone is our Lord; let it be so, for this is a case of proving what is already established—who indeed would desire the attainment of their goal without undergoing hardship?
Nor is the example devoid of the property to be proven, because even things such as cloth have as their makers weavers and others who possess knowledge of their respective materials.

For this very reason, there is no contradiction in the reason; for such a contradiction would exist only if cloth and other such things were produced by an agent possessing knowledge of their material cause.
Nor is this [position] accepted by others either.
It might be argued that the specific property implied by the meaning— such as possessing a body and so forth— is contradictory because it contradicts the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Just as in the case [of the argument] "the mountain possesses fire because it possesses the transformation of grass and so forth," the contradictory reason (*viruddha-hetu*) is sublated by perception—since the cold touch, which is opposed to the manifest hot touch belonging to the fire required for the transformation of grass and so forth (which is itself implied by the presence of fire)—is perceived;

likewise, the knowledge whose objects are the material causes such as earth and so forth has the body, the contact between self and mind, and other such factors as its causes, and it does not occur in their absence. Thus, that [knowledge] is implied by this [reason].
And that [cause] is here sublated by valid cognition;

upon its cessation, his knowledge would necessarily cease, just as a burning fire ceases when its heat and manifestation cease, like frost. No, for it is impossible for the non-pervaded to cease when the pervader has not ceased.
If the cause is not pervasive of the effect, then alas, the discourse regarding the pervaded and the pervader is destroyed!

This would be the case if even the knowledge of the material cause (upādāna-jñāna) of the earth and so forth were an effect [of that creator]; however, since that is accepted as eternal, it does not necessarily cease even when the body and other such factors cease.
For the non-pervaded does not necessarily cease upon the cessation of the non-pervasive.
Otherwise, just as "Maitra possesses horses" would not be the case, "he possesses cows" would likewise not be possible.
Nor is it correct to argue that because impermanent things such as cognitions are frequently perceived, an eternal cognition is impossible;

for it is not the case that because the water-born snowballs and the like are directly perceived to be impermanent in their color and other qualities, the atoms that compose them or the color and other qualities residing in them must likewise be impermanent.
However, permanence is equal in both cases by virtue of having no cause.
Nor is it logical to claim that cognition is pervaded by the body and so forth simply because cognition is perceived in conjunction with them here and there;
for pervasion consists in possessing an essential connection, and that occurs only in the absence of adventitious conditions (*upādhi*).
Furthermore, when cognition coexists with the body and so forth, its limiting condition (*upādhi*) is its being an effect (*kāryatva*).
Cognition, as an effect, does not transcend its own cause—the body and so forth—whereas eternal [cognition], even while transcending them, does not contradict the perception of their concomitance.
Therefore, just as "sound is non-eternal because it possesses the property of having an origin," [so too is the case here].
When the argument "like a pot" is employed, someone might object on the grounds of the diversity of properties between the probandum and the example:
"If sound is impermanent because it possesses the property of being produced—which is a similarity to a pot—then alas, it must also possess form and other qualities like that pot;
if it does not possess form and other qualities through its similarity to a pot, then let it likewise not be impermanent. Thus he objects.

The proponent of the *utkarṣasama* sophistical refutation is indeed defeated; likewise, the proponent of the *utkarṣasama* sophistical refutation must be defeated because he opposes [the argument] by means of a mere similarity (*sādharmya*) that is non-conclusive (*aprayojaka*).
Furthermore, since this [similarity] is easily found in all inferences, it would result in the annihilation of all inference.
This might be so.

The state of having an origin is observed in jars and the like to be pervaded solely by the fact of being preceded by a maker who possesses knowledge of the material cause and so forth; therefore, that much alone could be inferred for the earth and other elements. But how could there be a maker possessing eternal and omniscient knowledge? For that [quality] is certainly not observed in the subject of the illustrative example.
Now, how can the eyes and other sense organs be inferred from the perception of form and so forth on the grounds that it is an action?
For actions such as cutting are not accomplished by means of the sense organs;
rather, they have axes and the like as their instruments.

Now, even though the fact of having the sense organ as its instrument (*indriyasādhanatva*) is not observed in the corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭāntadharmī*), it is established by the force of the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatābalāt*).
For the nature of action (*kriyātva*) residing in the perception of color and so forth leads to the inference of that very instrument which is capable of accomplishing that perception;

and since axes and the like are not capable [of this], the force of the property of being a predicate of the subject brings to mind the eyes and other organs, which are distinct from axes and the like, even though they have never been perceived before. Is this not so?
This is equally applicable to the other case as well.

For it is impossible that there could be a simultaneity in the production of effects—characterized by being non-envious, restricted to specific directions and locations, sensory or non-sensory, mobile or immobile, and so forth—if such omniscient knowledge were non-existent, or even if it were eternal;

indeed, such cognition of the Supreme Lord cannot be an effect produced by a body and the like, because prior to the production of a body, [the Lord] would be insentient, which would lead to the undesirable consequence of having to postulate another Lord to produce the other effects of that preceding time.
Thus, rather than postulating an endless series of such prior and prior states through an infinite worldly construction, it is better to postulate the eternity of the Buddha.
By this, the postulation of the eternity of the body and the sense faculties is also refuted.
By this, too, that which some say—
"Even if it were established that everything possessing an arrangement and so forth has an intelligent cause,
how could there be a single cause for that arrangement and the rest?
Thus [it is said].
That too has been refuted:

their desire to reject the existence of an omniscient being would be fulfilled only if those with physical eyes were capable of seeing atoms, the individual souls (kṣetrajña), or the latencies of karma (karmāśaya) inherent within them.
But this is not the case.

Therefore, rather than postulating many beings distinct from ourselves who perceive supersensible objects, it is better to postulate only one such being, for the sake of parsimony in hypothesis (*kalpanālāghava*).

Nor should it be argued that the production of effects such as bodies and worlds is accomplished solely through the conjunction of the *kṣetrajña* (the individual soul) and atoms—given that the unseen merit (*adṛṣ�ṭa*) matures at certain times—and thus there is no need for an intelligent creator.

Because the property of having an origin (*utpattimattva*) is established as having an essential connection (*svābhāvikapratibandha*) with being produced by an omniscient agent who possesses knowledge of the material causes and so forth—there being no such limiting condition (*upādhi*)—there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

For there is no deviation [in the inference] because we observe that the sense organs and the mind, which are the means for producing cognition, are not known [to exist independently]; and because even insentient milk, which is the cause for the growth of a calf, acts independently of a conscious controller;
and because trees and the like in a forest are seen to arise without effort [on the part of a creator]. Thus, [the reason] does not deviate from the probandum.
This is not correct;
for all of those [entities] are included within the subject (*pakṣa*) precisely because they have become the locus of dispute.
Nor is there a lack of the property of the subject (*apakṣadharmatā*) due to contradiction with non-perception, as in the case of the existence of a rabbit's horn.
Because the subject (*dharmin*) is by nature unfit for perception, it is impossible for the Blessed One to contradict it;

otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the abolition of all inference. As for a horn, however—such as one existing on a rabbit's head or on a calf—it is fit for perception, and since it is negated by non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), it is unfit to be established [as a subject].
This might be so.
It is not mere origination that is tied to a cause possessing intelligence, but rather its specific characteristic;
for upon seeing that [characteristic], even one who has not observed the agent develops the cognition that it was produced, and that cognition arises from the sight of it.

When a thing is observed to have its presence or absence conforming to the presence or absence of an intelligent being—such as a jar—it is not merely because it is produced that [the inference holds], for even the body and the world do not show their presence or absence to conform to that [intelligent being].

Therefore, the general property of "being produced," which depends upon the pervasion of having an intelligent cause as conditioned by this specific qualification (*viśeṣa-upādhi*), is not intrinsically connected to that [cause]; thus, it cannot lead to the inference of it.
Otherwise, by depending on the pervasion of fire conditioned by smoke, one would face the absurd consequence of inferring fire from paleness found even in lilies or pigeons.
To this it is replied:

Let your honors examine this more closely: is the specific characteristic [of being produced] the conformity to the positive and negative concomitance of an intelligent agent, or rather the observation thereof?
If it is the former, that is certainly accepted by those who maintain that bodies, the world, and so forth, have an intelligent cause.

For no one else, unless they accept it, can rightly declare that a cause possesses a presence or absence that does not conform to its effect. Furthermore, if there is no observation [of the causal process], then the cognition that "this was made" cannot arise for one who has not observed the action.

For only that cloth which has been seen by this person to follow the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) with an intelligent cause is its effect, and not a cloth existing in the marketplace.

If it is argued that because one thing of a certain class is observed to follow the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of another, then even another thing of that same class which is not observed to follow such concomitance must likewise be so;

then, alas! since produced things such as jars follow the positive and negative concomitance of an intelligent agent, other things of that same class—such as the body and the world—cannot be excluded by your logic from being likewise [produced by an intelligent agent].
If you say, "Only those things belonging to the class of jars are preceded by an intelligent agent," [we reply: ...
But surely, palaces and the like would not have that [Intelligent Being] as their cause,

because they do not belong to the same class as a pot. Or rather, whatever class of thing is seen to follow the positive and negative concomitance of an Intelligent Being, that very same class— even when its positive and negative concomitance is not observed— must have an Intelligent Being as its cause.
In that case, what kind of class of effects such as palaces and the like has not been observed to have an intelligent cause, such that the body, the world, and so forth— which possess origination—
would not be likewise? Indeed, there is no distinction whatsoever in their belonging to that same class.

As for the argument that, because it is a modification of clay, an anthill—like a jar or similar object—is not the product of a potter, this is due to the contradiction with the non-perception of a potter;
however, if it is preceded by an invisible sentient being, that is indeed accepted.
It might be argued as follows:
Mere origination is not pervaded by having a creator who possesses knowledge of the material cause;

rather, that which has a material cause and so forth knowable by people such as ourselves does not possess such [origination] as that of the body, the world, and so forth. Therefore, [the world, etc., must have a creator beyond our reach].
"It is not preceded by that [knowledge] because of the absence of pervasion"—

this is incorrect. For once the pervasion between "having an origin" and "having an agent who knows its material cause and so forth" has been established first through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), then, regarding the object of the knowledge of the effect, the postulation of the capacity to know its material cause and so forth [is justified].

Because of its establishment through pervasion (*vyāpti*): it has been stated that once the general nature of cognition is established by the force of pervasion, its eternity is established by the force of its being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).

Therefore, since no limiting condition (*upādhi*) is perceived while being sought, the state of having an origin (*utpattimattva*) is intrinsically connected (*svabhāvapratibaddha*) with having an intelligent cause (*buddhimaddhetukatva*).
Nor can it be suspected that "the state of having an origin," which is tied to its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), will continue to exist even after transcending its own correlate;
for if that were the case, it would entail the loss of its intrinsic nature.
It might be argued as follows:

It is argued that there exist counter-arguments (pratipakṣasādhana) in the form of inferences such as: "The earth and so forth are not preceded by an omniscient being, because they are objects of knowledge, because they exist, and so on, like a pot. Thus, due to this state of being counter-balanced (satpratipakṣatā), the inference under discussion is said to be fallacious. Now, does this [inference] negate being preceded by an omniscient being, or does it negate being preceded by a mere knower, the term "all" (sarva) being used for the sake of illustration?

If the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) were [accepted], then it would be established that [the Veda] is preceded by one who perceives only a portion [of reality]; and thus there would be a contradiction with one's own tenets (apasiddhānta),
nor is it even possible.

For it is impossible for limited perceivers such as ourselves to create the earth and other such things; however, if what is to be negated were merely being preceded by a knower, there would be a fallacy of deviation (vyabhicāra) with respect to jars and the like.
Furthermore, [it is argued that] God cannot be the supervisor of atoms and so forth because He is bodiless.

The inference that "divine knowledge, like the knowledge of a liberated soul, is not omniscient and is impermanent because it is a form of knowledge, like the knowledge of persons such as ourselves," requires the establishment of God and His possession of intellect in order to establish the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*); thus, while depending on the very means of proof that would establish those [attributes], this inference ought not even to find its own self, let alone contradict them.

For neither scripture (*āgama*) nor inference (*anumāna*) establishes a creator of the world who is devoid of eternal and omniscient intelligence; rather, they establish Him as possessing such qualities. Thus it is established that your inference, being contrary to those two, cannot possibly arise.

Furthermore, like His intelligence, His will and effort are also to be understood as eternal and included within the proof of His being a creator, because the nature of agency consists in the inherence (*samavāya*) of knowledge, desire to act (*cikīrṣā*), and effort.
And because these [three] are mutually inseparable, when one is established, the other two are established as well.
Thus, it has been stated that the establishment of such a Lord occurs precisely from the fact of having an origin, aided by the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).

Alternatively, let there be the establishment merely of his being an agent possessing knowledge of the material cause and so forth; however, the establishment of the specific qualities [of that agent] follows from the establishment of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) through the inference by elimination (*pariśeṣānumāna*).

For instance, a creator who is cognizant of the body, the world, and so forth, cannot be one whose intellect is non-eternal or limited in scope; because if he were such, it would follow that he is ignorant of his own material cause and other necessary factors.
Indeed, no such person is observed to be cognizant of those causes and so forth, as is the case with people like ourselves.
And because He is directly cognizant of their appropriation and so forth, He is "thus" (tathā).

Indeed, no one other than such a Lord is capable of knowing the distinctions among atoms or the latencies of karma (karmāśaya) inherent in each individual soul (kṣetrajña), as has been explained in detail below. Therefore, He is "thus. Indeed, it is not the case that anyone else is able to know the distinctions among atoms or the karmic deposits residing in each field-knower (kṣetrajña) except for a Lord of that nature; this was elaborated upon previously.
Even though merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) are inherent in another person, God is able to govern them because of their relationship;

for connection is not limited solely to conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*), since the inherence in that which is conjoined with what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya*) is also a form of connection.

Indeed, atoms and the like are conjoined with God, and the individual souls (*kṣetrajña*) are conjoined with them; thus, merit and demerit are related to Him through inherence in that which is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*). Alternatively, there is inherence in the soul itself due to the soul’s conjunction with God, since the existence of an eternal conjunction has already been established.

Even without the assistance of their own inherent properties (*svadharma*), the Lord will cause merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), or even atoms, to turn toward their respective effects, just as one skilled in the science of poisons causes a fragment of poison to turn toward the commencement of its action;

by this, the argument regarding the necessity of a conscious material cause (*cetana-upādāna*) is also explained. However, the author of the *Vārttika* stated "consciousness" (*cetanatva*) as the reason merely as an illustrative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*).
Other reasons, such as "having an origin" (utpattimattva) and so forth, are also to be inferred; and the sacred tradition (āmnāya) confirms this principle through such passages as:

"Under the governance of this Imperishable (akṣara), O Gārgī, heaven and earth stand held apart," "The one God, generating heaven and earth," and "It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate,'" and so on.
And there is this traditional teaching (smṛti):
"This ignorant creature is not master of its own pleasure and pain;
impelled by God, it goes either to heaven or indeed to hell. Furthermore, because [God] is not the cause [of action], the eternality of God's knowledge [is established].

The Śruti demonstrates this: "Without hands or feet, He is swift and a grasper; He sees without eyes and hears without ears; He knows the universe, yet there is no knower of Him; they call Him the foremost, the ancient Person," and so forth.
By this very passage, His bodilessness is demonstrated.
As for the remainder, however, it has been elaborated upon by the author of the Vārttika himself; therefore, we shall desist. // 21 //
NyS 4.1.22: The production of entities occurs without a cause, as seen in the case of the sharpness of thorns and the like.

Thinking that thorns and the like, despite possessing specific configurations, are without a cause because no such cause is perceived, one who likewise considers bodies and so forth— which also possess distinct configurations— to be without a cause,
advances the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) with the phrase "animittataḥ" (due to being without a cause).
Regarding thorns, bodies, and the like, for which no cause is perceived, [the opponent] attempts to include them within the subject class (*pakṣa*) so as not to expose a deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
Alternatively, if such a deviation were exposed, it would result in the destruction of all inference, since such a deviation could be found everywhere.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that because they possess a distinction of configuration (*saṃsthāna-bheda*), even thorns, bodies, and the like must possess a cause, using as examples cloth and so forth, whose causes are established for both parties. // 22 //
Because it is the cause of that which is causeless, it does not follow from being causeless.
Having set forth the view of a certain proponent of the Siddhānta, he refutes it with the words:
NyS 4.1.24: There is no refutation [of our position], because there is a difference in meaning between the "causal" (nimitta) and the "non-causal" (animitta).
The author of the Vārttika himself, having proposed the alternative that thorns and such things are without a cause, refutes it by stating:
"that the birth of thorns and such things is causeless.
This refers to the logic of the relationship between the one who teaches and the one who is taught.
The person who is to be informed is the object (*karman*),
and the person who informs is the agent (*kartṛ*);
both the agent and the object are *kārakas*.

The logical principle regarding the relationship between the object to be communicated and the communicator is that the agent is the cause of the action; yet this very principle is accepted by this [opponent] who asserts that the birth of the body and so forth is without a cause.
Otherwise, he would be a mere mute.
Thus it has been said: "To assert that everything is without a cause while simultaneously communicating [this very point] is a contradiction."
He says, "And because of the employment of a sentence," meaning that it is not only because of the acceptance of the logic of the proponent and the opponent, but for this reason as well:
if you employ a sentence for the purpose of communication, yet claim that everything is without a cause, there is a contradiction. Thus is the meaning.
Nevertheless, it is "unestablished for one of the two properties" (*anyataradharmāsiddha*).
It is unestablished with respect to one of the two properties— that is, the property to be proven called "causelessness"— because causelessness itself is unestablished.
[Objection: Surely, by mere words, what is unestablished for the opponent does not become established, as this would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga). To this, he says:
"Because of the existence of a specific configuration.
This means that since the fact that thorns and so forth have a cause is established by valid cognition through the example of cloth and the like, it is not unestablished merely by words.

But why has the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) not been refuted by the author of the Sūtras himself? To this, Bhāṣyakāra says: "Indeed, this doctrine [of the opponent] is that [the world] is not caused by karma. (24)
NyS 4.1.25: Everything is impermanent, because it possesses the nature of arising and perishing.
Others, however, think that everything is impermanent because it possesses the nature of arising and perishing.
He asks in order to demonstrate the singularity of the reason (*hetu*).
"What is impermanent? [The answer is: "That which exists at some time.
He explains the meaning of the reason [for its impermanence] as "arising."
That which has the nature of arising, when unarisen, does not exist; that which has arisen exists, and that which has the nature of destruction, when destroyed, does not exist;

that which has not yet been destroyed exists. Therefore, because of its non-existence at the prior and subsequent times and its existence in the interim, it is established that impermanence—characterized by occasional existence—is proven, since it possesses the nature of arising and destruction.
This is the meaning. [The author] asks about the nature of the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*):
"What more [is there to say]?"— the answer is "and that which is derived from the elements.
Here, first of all, the author of the Vārttika himself [states]:
He states the answer:
"Because the sūtra stating 'everything is impermanent' has the purpose of providing an illustrative example.
The word *artha* here signifies a cause (*nimitta*), because that sūtra—which is devoted to presenting a thesis and a reason—has the illustrative example as its underlying cause.
The meaning is that a reason does not convey the intended object of the thesis without an example;
he analyzes this very point with the words, "everything is impermanent."
He states another refutation: "And this [argument], namely, 'because it possesses the nature of arising and perishing'... (25).
Not so, because impermanence itself is impermanent.
Having set forth the view of a certain proponent of a partial conclusion, he refutes it:
"Not so, because impermanence itself is permanent. (27–28)
That impermanence [of fire] is like the destruction of fire following the destruction of what is to be burned.
NyS 4.1.28: There is no rejection of the eternal, because its existence is established according to how it is perceived.
He states the ultimate conclusion as taught in the Sūtra:
"Indeed, this... Now, it is said: we do not prove that everything is impermanent; rather, whatever dharma possesses the property called impermanence, all that is impermanent.

Furthermore, even if space and the other [elements] were eternal, there would be no damage to our position; thus, he refutes that [objection] by pointing out that it proves what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

And because non-eternality is absent, there is no fault in the claim that "everything is impermanent. He says this because if a subject (*dharmin*) exists, it would be impermanent through its connection with that [impermanence], yet that very subject might at some time not exist. Therefore, he states:
The property called impermanence does not exist in the absence of a substratum (dharmin).

This might be argued: since jars and the like are understood to possess the nature of arising and perishing, they may be impermanent due to their connection with impermanence; by that very same example, because they possess existence (sattva), space and the like will also be impermanent—thus he teaches.

Then he refutes [the objection] with the words "But again...": because even upon the establishment of the subsequent term, there is the establishment of the eternality of that term's referent. // 28 //
NyS 4.1.29: Everything is eternal, because the five elements are eternal.
This is another extreme view: everything is eternal. Why? Because the five elements are eternal.
Indeed, this effect—such as cows, jars, and so forth—is perceived as being composed of the five elements; for people designate them as "the jar is clay" or "the body is clay.
And the elements are eternal, because their destruction is not admitted by the Naiyāyikas.
Therefore, the prima facie position is that entities such as cows, jars, and so forth, are eternal. // 29 //
NyS 4.1.30: [Sound is non-eternal] because the causes of its production and destruction are perceived.
Derivatives of the elements are indeed distinct from the elements themselves; for cows, jars, and the like are not the most subtle atoms.
As it was stated in the second chapter, if they were as imperceptible as atoms, it would follow that nothing at all could be perceived.
Therefore, because they are possessed of the contradictory properties of being perceived and not being perceived, derivatives of the elements are distinct from the elements.

And thus, because the causes of their arising and destruction are perceived, they are not eternal, even though the elements themselves are eternal; this is the established conclusion, stated as: "Not so, because the causes of their arising and destruction are perceived. (30)
There is no refutation [of the definition], because it is included within that definition.
Thinking that there is identity [of the body] with the elements due to their similarity in nature, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādin) says once again:
"Because they are included within the characteristics of those [elements], there is no denial of the permanence of cows, jars, and so forth, on account of the permanence of the elements. (31)
NyS 4.1.32: [The non-existence of the soul is not established] because its origination and its causes are perceived.

Intending to show that the equilibrium of the elements (*bhūtasāmya*)—which is possible even though cows, jars, and so forth are effects of the elements—does not lead to the understanding that they are identical in essence with those elements, he says:
"Not [so], because their production and their causes are perceived" (32).

Furthermore, if the production and destruction of entities were not real, how could there be the engagement of discerning people who, desiring them, seek the causes of production for what is desired and the causes of destruction for what is undesired? Thus he says:
Regarding the phrase "the cause of arising and destruction":
furthermore, he states that the reason (*hetu*) is non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*), for there is no pervasion in the case of sound, action, cognition, and so forth;
and it has been stated that what is non-pervasive is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
For the thesis is that "everything is eternal.
In this regard, it is "inconclusive" (*anaikānta*) because of both existence and non-existence;
that is to say, it is "inconclusive" because it does not have a single, definitive conclusion (*anta*) characterized by either existence or non-existence.
The author of the Vārttika will state this very point from the perspective of the meaning: "Because the thesis (pakṣa) is situated at both extremes.
The construction is: "Because the thesis is situated at both extremes, which consist of the existence and non-existence of the reason.

He expresses this same point through an objection and its refutation—beginning with the words "svapnaviṣaya" and so forth—to show that there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) if one were to assume falsity in the absence of a subverting factor (bādhaka).
Having stated the meaning as expressed in the Bhāṣya, the author of the Vārttika himself says: "And of everything," etc.
The phrase "to the extent that by which it is established" means that it is brought about by the act of establishing.
The remainder has a meaning that is not obscure.
Not so, because the establishment [of distinctions] would be untenable.
Thus, having refuted the doctrine of the Sāṃkhyas, he introduces the doctrine of the Svāyambhuvas in order to refute it:
"Others describe everything as eternal in another way;
indeed, this transformation of the substratum (dharmi) is threefold, consisting of the forms of property (dharma), characteristic (lakṣaṇa), and state (avasthā)."
For example, gold is the *dharmin* (the substratum), while its transformations (*pariṇāma*) are such things as the *vardhamānaka* (a type of golden ornament) and the *rucaka* (a necklace).
The transformation of the characteristics (*lakṣaṇapariṇāma*) of the *dharma*, however, consists of the future state and so forth.
Indeed, when this goldsmith breaks a *vardhamānaka* and fashions a *rucaka*, at that time the *vardhamānaka*...

Having abandoned the characteristic of the present, [the gold] attains the characteristic of the past; meanwhile, the *rucaka* (necklace), having abandoned the characteristic of the future, attains the state of the present. Once it has attained the state of the present, however, the *rucaka*, undergoing the states of being new and old, becomes subject to transformation of state (*avasthā-pariṇāma*). And these states of being new and old, which depend upon the characteristic of the present, are transformations of characteristic (*lakṣaṇa-pariṇāma*). Thus, this threefold transformation belongs to the substratum (*dharmin*); and the attributes (*dharma*), characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and states (*avasthā*) are both different from and non-different from the substratum.
And thus, because they are non-different from their substrates (*dharmī*), these properties (*dharma*) are eternal;
yet because they are different [from one another], they are subject to arising and destruction—thus both [states] are logically established.

Now, an objection is raised: if the substrates possess the nature of undergoing appearance and disappearance, then since they would be non-existent prior to their arising and non-existent after their destruction, how can the eternity of all things be established? To this, he says: "And that which arises..."
It exists even prior to its arising;
the phrase "in the form of the substratum" is to be supplied.
It also exists when it has ceased.
Here too, the phrase "in the form of a substratum" is to be understood as the ellipsis. He refutes [this view]:
"No, because a systematic determination is untenable" (Sūtra 33).

The meaning is that the determination of arising and passing away—in terms of their essential nature (*svarūpa*), time (*kāla*), specific distinction (*viśeṣa*), and relation (*sambandhin*)—is untenable [if they are not distinct from the substrate].
This is what is being said: first of all, difference (*bheda*) and non-difference (*abheda*), being properties established through mutual exclusion, cannot coexist in a single locus.

Therefore, one who desires a distinction between the characteristics (*dharma*), the temporal phases (*lakṣaṇa*), and the states (*avasthā*) on the one hand and the substrate (*dharmī*) on the other, for the sake of establishing arising and passing away, must admit their impermanence (*anityatva*).
Regarding the establishment of permanence by accepting the existence of the effect even while it is still being produced— as the Sāṃkhya does— the author of the Vārttika says:
"And he who asserts that what has ceased to exist still exists even after its cessation."
This is easy to understand. // 33 //
Everything is distinct, because the characteristics of entities are distinct.
This is yet another extreme view of the Buddhists: that everything is discrete because the characteristics of entities are discrete.

Neither the Sautrāntikas nor the Vaibhāṣikas maintain that there is any such thing as a substance distinct from form and the other [sensory objects], nor that there is any whole distinct from its parts. // 34 //
NyS 4.1.35: It is not so, because a single entity is produced by multiple characteristics.
