He refutes those [objections] with the following:
"Because a single entity is not produced by multiple characteristics" (Sūtra 35).
Because a single composite entity, such as a jar, is produced as something connected with manifold characteristics. // 35 //
Moreover, there is no refutation [of our position] precisely because of the established definition [of the categories].
"Moreover" (athāpi) means "furthermore" (api ca).
And [the phrase] "when the collection of atoms is not perceived" (aṇusamūhe cāgṛhyamāṇe) means:
The meaning is that it is beyond the senses due to its extreme subtlety.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "this was also stated subsequently":
moreover, after the Buddha had set forth the reason "because of the distinctness of the characteristics of existence," he later said this.
To the question "What was that said?",
he replies:
"Because there is no single entity, [there is only] a collection."
Thus [he says]. He refutes what was stated above: because a single [unit] is untenable, the collection does not exist at all.
He explains what was stated [previously]:
"There is no single entity (bhāva) because the term 'entity' is applied to a collection. He then explains the refutation of this [position].
"Because a single [entity] is untenable. He elaborates on this with the words, "For a collection of one...

By stating that there is no such thing as a single entity—that is, by asserting the negation of the unity of any given entity—and by saying that the word "entity" (bhāva) is applied to a collection, he himself admits that very point.
"Now, is it not the case that a collection (*samūha*) is admitted, but not a single entity (*eko bhāva*)? To this he says:
"For a collection is a unification of the one. Thus, by this, there is a contradiction between the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*).
It has been stated;
now, he says "because the term for an entity (bhāva-śabda) is applied to a collection" in order to show the contradiction of the proposition by the reason.
The Vārttika states:
"Its application is as follows.
(475/9) The word "jar" has multiple objects; thus, it refers to multiple objects in an ultimate sense, whereas the oneness of the jar is merely conceptual.

Nor is it excluded by the term "single word" (*ekapada*); thus, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to a single word, because even that has multiple ultimate objects as its referents—this is the meaning.
It might be argued:

since from words such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*) one understands many things, such as color-form (*rūpa*) and so on, as well as the base (*budhna*) and so on, how can there be a single object? To this, he says:
Regarding the relation of container and contained (*ādhārādheyabhāva*):

even if there were a plurality of meanings for words such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*) and so forth, nevertheless, the oneness of each of those respective objects cannot be denied; thus, the position desired by the opponent is not established.
However, granting [the opponent's point] for the sake of argument, it is said that even a plurality of meanings is not possible here.
"And because there would be an infinite regress of division within the aggregate" (476/19).

If only the aggregate exists and not any single entity whatsoever, then when that aggregate characterized as a jar is being divided, no distinction such as "small," "smaller," or "smallest" could be perceived; for since it is an aggregate consisting of the jar, potsherds, gravel, powder, and atoms, it would possess infinite constituent parts. This...
There would be no distinction such as "the Great Vehicle is large" and "the Small Vehicle is smaller.

Therefore, by one who seeks to establish this gradation, the cessation of a collection [of atoms] must be asserted in some instance; and since that is not possible without a single non-composite entity, it follows that a single [indivisible atom] must be accepted—this is the meaning.
One who does not understand the point stated raises a doubt: "Now, if you think...

(477/5). It should be understood that the expressions "the collection of form and so forth" and "the four non-substantial entities" are intended to show the distinction between different intermediate views.
The reply is by means of demonstrating what has already been stated:

"In this very view... This is a renewed suspicion regarding that which was previously refuted—namely, "then you would be postulating an infinite aggregate"—in order to bring about a contradiction with scripture (*āgama*).
Since the occurrence of one is impossible, there can be no occurrence of many;
therefore, that which was called "many" must be abandoned.
The remainder has been explained by the commentary on the Bhāṣya. // 36 //
NyS 4.1.37: Everything is non-existence, because the mutual non-existence of entities is established.
Now he raises the proponent of emptiness:
"This is another extreme:
the thesis that 'everything is non-existent'."
The reason for this is that "the mutual non-existence (itaretarābhāva) among entities is established.
All of this— consisting of the means of valid cognition, the objects of valid cognition, and the resulting cognition— is non-existent and void,
because the mutual non-existence among entities is established.

The author of the Vārttika explains: "Because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with words denoting existence, due to both the negation of the state of being non-existent and [the presence of] the cognition of existence.

Indeed, these [categories] such as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are experienced as being the objects of the cognition "non-existent" and of the negative particle (*nañ*), precisely because they do not possess the nature of one another.

Therefore, the words expressing them stand in coreferentiality with that [cognition]; consequently, the means of valid cognition and the rest are non-existent, like a cloth that has neither been produced nor destroyed.
Furthermore, are these entities permanent or impermanent? If they were permanent, they would be non-existent, as they would be devoid of all causal efficacy;
for it has already been stated that a permanent thing can never be employed toward any effect, since neither gradual nor simultaneous action is possible for it.
If, however, they are impermanent, then if their very nature is destruction, they would not exist even in the first moment, just as they do not exist in the second and subsequent moments.
Either these things have destruction as their inherent nature when they exist, or if they do not have that as their inherent nature, they would not perish even in another moment.

Indeed, it is not possible for something produced from its own causes as blue to ever be made yellow, even by a thousand causes; thus, the fact that impermanent things have destruction as their inherent nature must be accepted even against one's will.

Therefore, we consider it logical that the ultimate reality of entities is indeed emptiness; however, through conceptual construction, they appear as if they truly exist, though they lack objective reality. Thus, "all entities" means all words denoting entities.

And the formal argument is: all words denoting entities have non-existent things as their objects, because they stand in grammatical coordination with both non-existent referents and negations, like the word "cloth" when it has not yet arisen or when it has perished.
Regarding this, the author of the Vārttika states the following refutation of the objection raised in the Bhāṣya, which was not in accordance with the Sūtra.

This refers to the contradiction between the two terms of the proposition (*pratijñāpada*) and between the proposition and the reason (*pratijñāhetu*). "Having identical case endings" means having case endings that express an identical referent, but it does not mean merely having identical case endings, because words with different case endings can also exhibit grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
As in the case of "Caitra reads," and as in the case of "I do not regard you as a blade of grass"—
it is impossible for there to be a cognition [of that object] without its corresponding causal condition.

For that which is absolutely non-existent (*atyantāsann*), being devoid of any description (*anirūpākhyam*), whether as "everything" or as a "positive entity" (*bhāvaḥ*), is not within the range of verbal expression.

Indeed, it was established in the second sūtra itself that neither the non-existent (*asat*) nor the indeterminable (*anirvacanīyam*) is within the range of manifestation; rather, it is only the existent (*sat*) that manifests through the nature of another existent.
And so, how could even the absolutely non-existent ever be within the range of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*)?
"The rest is in the Bhāṣya" means that the contradiction between the proposition and the reason has been explained in detail in the Bhāṣya. // 37 //
Not so, because things are established by way of their own intrinsic nature.
Having departed from the Sūtra, the author of the Bhāṣya says the following in order to state a refutation based on the Sūtra itself;
for the refutation is connected with the Sūtra:
"Not because of the establishment of the intrinsic nature of entities" (Sūtra 38).
The claim that "everything is non-existent" is not tenable.

Why? Because things possess an established intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); the intrinsic nature of entities such as substances (*dravya*) and so forth consists of properties such as existence (*sat*) and so on.
Alternatively, intrinsic nature is the essential form (*svarūpa*) of entities by which these entities are distinguished from one another according to their respective natures.

Alternatively, because the cognition "it is non-existent" is qualified by the terms "as a cow" or "as a horse," the cognition "it is not a cow" establishes the existence of the cow itself by excluding the cow while connecting [the object] with horses and so forth; the same applies to horses and other things. Thus, since the nature of entities is established by their own essence, there is no such thing as "non-existence. Having cited the sūtra, "Not because of establishment by way of intrinsic nature" (*na svabhāvasiddheḥ*), the author of the Vārttika explains it according to its literal form and then demonstrates its intended meaning through a series of questions.
Regarding the phrase "of the preceding sūtra" (pūrvasūtrasya):

by means of the passage beginning with "And what is intrinsic nature? (kaśca svabhāvaḥ) and ending with "the entity is established" (siddho bhāvaḥ), the author of the Vārttika shows the threefold commentary on the sūtra provided by the author of the Bhāṣya.
The meaning is that a "common property" (sāmānyo dharmaḥ) is a shared quality, such as permanence and so forth.
By means of a preliminary question, he establishes the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the cognition of non-existence with the entity itself.
[The question is: "How then?

The word "non-existent" (*asat*), indeed, denotes that very existence which is qualified by the absence [of another]; it applies to a cloth characterized by the quality of whiteness. Thus, the application of both the cognition and the designation of "non-existent" with a term denoting an entity is logically established.
The meaning is that there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the two terms.

Furthermore, some entities (*bhāva*) are eternal and some are non-eternal. Among these, the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) of the eternal has already been established in the refutation of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅgabhaṅga*).
As for the non-eternal, an entity does not have destruction as its intrinsic nature; rather, having arisen from its own causes with an existent nature, it perishes due to other causes.
As for what was said—that blue cannot be made yellow—we reply: it is indeed possible to make a blue cloth yellow, just as an unbaked black pot becomes red through contact with fire.
If you argue that the quality of blueness cannot be turned into yellowness, then surely it is also impossible to turn existence into non-existence.
Just as the states of being black and red occur successively with respect to a jar, so too do the existence and non-existence of the jar occur with respect to its shards; thus there is no fault.
There is no establishment of intrinsic nature because of its relativity.
The proponent of emptiness challenges what was stated [previously], namely, "because of establishment by way of intrinsic nature" (svabhāvasiddhi), with the following:
"There is no establishment by way of intrinsic nature because of relativity" (Sūtra 39).
For indeed, all things possess distinct intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*), and their distinctness is dependent upon something else.

To illustrate: blue is distinct in relation to yellow and so forth, but not by its own intrinsic nature. In this same way, shortness, length, priority, posteriority, fatherhood, sonship, and so on, are to be understood as mutually dependent. And that which is dependent on another is not intrinsic (*svābhāvika*), just as the redness of a crystal is [not intrinsic] when it depends on a hibiscus flower; such is the meaning of the objection. (39)
It is improper because it is self-contradictory.
[The opponent] objects: "This is incorrect because it is contradicted [by scripture]" (Sūtra 40).
He explains that with the words "yadi" (if).

Now, one might object: "If the absence of both occurs through this sequence, let it be; our desired conclusion is already established. To this, he replies: "In the case of dependence and in the case of non-dependence."

For the distinction of magnitude consists of length and shortness, and that is innate to entities; it is merely their relative superiority or non-superiority that depends upon mutual apprehension. Thus, the shortness of a sugarcane stalk compared to a bamboo pole is its non-superiority, consisting in being measured by a number of cubits associated with a lower count; the length of the bamboo pole is its superiority, consisting in being measured by a number of cubits associated with a higher count. And this [distinction] is defined in dependence upon the definition of its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).
But it is not the case that its production is dependent upon a counter-correlate;
this is not a property of the thing itself that depends on prior or posterior [entities].
Furthermore, difference (*bheda*) is distinctness, and as a qualifier of the thing, it does not depend on another entity for its production, but rather for its own determination.

In the same way, paternity is also established as being merely the generative power itself, whose definition is dependent upon the definition of that which is generated, but whose own production is not dependent upon it.
This has been explained by us at length in the *Brahmatattvaparīkṣā*.

Furthermore, qualities such as priority and posteriority, although their production is dependent on another due to having comparative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) as their cause, cannot be denied, as they sustain the course of worldly affairs.
And it is not the case that, merely by this much, the entity which is their substratum is not independent; thus everything is cleared up.
It might be argued: "Length and so forth will be merely dependent [upon something else], so what is the use of their having an intrinsic nature (vastusvabhāva)?
To this, he says:
"And since there is no establishment by way of intrinsic nature" (481/1):
dependence is the capacity for dependence, the connection with the purpose of dependence.
The author of the *Vārttika* himself states the refutations, saying that "in every respect, this is contradictory."
This has been explained by the word itself. // 40 //
The absolute determination of number is not established, because of the impossibility and possibility of a cause.
The commentary is intended to introduce the subsequent sūtra.
Now, these are the "one-sided numerical doctrines" (*saṃkhyaikāntavāda*); that is, those doctrines in which there is a numerical one-sidedness.
The meaning is that immediately after the doctrine of emptiness, they are now to be examined.
Therein, he first establishes the non-duality of Brahman:
"Everything is one; why? Because of the lack of distinction in its existence. This is his underlying intention.
To begin with, this manifold proliferation of name-and-form (nāmarūpa-prapañca) cannot manifest while being distinct from the Light (prakāśa),
because that which is insentient (jaḍa) lacks the capacity for self-manifestation.
Nor is it logical to say that it manifests by departing from the Light.
Indeed, no connection with manifestation is possible for this [object] in the interim.
If it is argued that the relation is that of object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*), we say no; for that which is incapable of acting upon anything cannot possibly possess the status of a subject.
Nor is it correct to say that cognition produces a fruit with respect to an object,
because that is impossible in the case of past and future objects;
yet, it is not the case that those two do not function as objects.

Therefore, since it is impossible for the manifold of names and forms (*nāmarūpa-prapañca*), which is distinct from cognition, to be manifested, we rightly perceive that this [manifold] is a transformation (*vivarta*) of cognition itself.
Nor is it tenable to claim that jars and other objects, which possess the nature of light, are themselves subject to arising and passing away and are mutually exclusive;
for there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to apprehend their mutual exclusion.

For when something is excluded from something else, that exclusion is apprehended through the apprehension of both; however, cognitions—which are distinct in character, abide solely in their own nature, and are unaware of one another's affairs—are not even capable of apprehending another cognition, let alone excluding it from itself.
Furthermore, the apprehension of an exclusion, which has as its cause the apprehension of the object to be negated and the locus of negation, cannot possibly arise simultaneously with its own cause.
Because there is no causal relationship between such two [entities], which are like the left and right horns [of a cow].
Furthermore, it is not logical that a single momentary consciousness should first apprehend the locus of the negation and the object to be negated, and only afterwards apprehend the negation;
for that which is momentary and lacks succession cannot possess an operation characterized by succession.
Nor is it logical to claim that one cognition apprehends the locus of the negation and its object of negation, while another cognition performs the negation;
for if that were so, it would follow that Caitra could have a cognition of negation regarding an object even when it has been apprehended by Maitra.
Furthermore, it is not correct to say that the very apprehension of the nature of the cognition itself constitutes the apprehension of its negation.

For this would indeed be the case if there were identity between the intrinsic nature [of an entity] and its exclusion from others. In that regard, either the entity would have exclusion as its intrinsic nature, or exclusion would have the entity as its intrinsic nature. In the former alternative, because exclusion is insubstantial (*tucchatva*), entities that are non-different from it in their intrinsic nature would themselves be insubstantial.

Consequently, through another turn of phrase, there would be the undesirable consequence of a doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*). However, in the latter alternative, since exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is simply an entity (*bhāva*) in the form of a positive injunction (*vidhi*), and they are excluded by way of being such positive injunctions, entities are not mutually excluded from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*). This is what was stated [by the author]: "because there is no difference in their existence" (*sadaviśeṣāt*).

(482/1) However, we do not deny that the diversity of entities is based on beginningless, indefinable ignorance (*anirvacanīyāvidyā*). Nor is there any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to apprehend a distinction between the knower and the act of knowing, precisely because of the aforementioned distinction.
Therefore, there is no mutual distinction among objects of knowledge, nor is there a distinction between them and the act of knowing.
Nor is there any difference between the knower and his knowledge, nor any mutual difference among various cognitions;

therefore, it is established that non-duality (advaita) is the truth: Brahman is indeed the Light itself, self-luminous, immutable and eternal, a mass of bliss, wherein the manifold and diverse world of names and forms is manifested by beginningless ignorance.
For this very reason, there are scriptural passages such as:
"Brahman is indeed one without a second; there is not the slightest diversity here.
He goes from death to death who perceives here any kind of diversity. And so forth.
Having thus presented the absolute unity [of all things], he states the absolute duality: "Everything is twofold; why? Because of the distinction between the eternal and the non-eternal.
For there exists no other category apart from the eternal and the non-eternal upon which entities could be established as having a triad or more.
He states another view: "Everything is threefold."
He demonstrates that very point:
"the knower, the object of knowledge, and the act of knowing.
Even the act of cognition (*jñapti*) is [included], because it too is being known.
The sense is that it does not exceed what is to be known (*jñeya*).
He states another opinion:
"And all [of them] are fourfold."
[The author] shows [this]:
the knower (*pramātṛ*), the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the object of knowledge (*prameya*), and the result of knowledge (*pramiti*).

If the so-called result of knowledge is not accepted as a reality distinct from the means of knowledge and the others, then—due to the absence of the primary action that is the result of knowledge—how could there be the knower and the rest?
And how could there be syntactical unity or a diversity of grammatical factors (*kāraka*) without the act of illumination?
We do not deny that the object of cognition (*prameya*) may be designated as such subsequent to the state of being the fruit of valid cognition (*pramā*);
yet, by this much alone, it does not cease to be a distinct reality.
Thus,
others also [should be understood] according to their respective possibilities;

such as "primordial nature and the person" (prakṛti-puruṣau), or "the five aggregates" (pañca-skandhāḥ), or "the bound soul, the fetter, its severance, and the Lord" (paśu-pāśa-taducchedeśvarāḥ), and so forth.
In this regard, he demonstrates through a sūtra an investigation that culminates in the refutation of the absolutism of number.
The absolute [monistic] doctrine of number is not established, because of both the impossibility and the possibility of a cause. (Sūtra 41)
If the meaning of the proposition is that "everything is one, and [that one] is twofold, threefold, and fourfold without distinction," then a proof distinct from that must be stated;
for the thing to be proven cannot itself be the proof.
And thus, because the means of proof is distinct from that [object], there is no absolute establishment of its being an object of cognition;
nor is there any self-cognition whatsoever, since even things such as knowledge and lamps are cognizable by something else.
And how an object can be a cognitive domain even when it is distinct from cognition will be explained on the occasion of refuting the Vijñānavāda.
Nor is the difference between the object and cognition impossible to apprehend;

for instance, in the experience "I perceive blue," the blue—characterized by a non-white form and not being the locus of the "I"-notion—is the object of one's own direct experience. The same applies to the mutual distinction between blue and other such objects.
Otherwise, when instructed, "Bring the jar," one might close one's eyes and go to sleep; or when instructed, "You may sleep," one might fetch water—
this being due to the absence of anyone capable of discerning [the meaning] for someone from anything in any way.
Nor is it correct to say that this conventional usage of difference is based on an indefinable, beginningless ignorance (*anirvacanīyānādyavidyā*),
because the theory of the manifestation of the indefinable (*anirvacanīyakhyāti*) has already been refuted.
Therefore, this cognition of difference, which is established by the common experience of all people, cannot be dismissed merely by examining its causal basis.

Rather, from the clearly perceived effect characterized by the cognition of difference, one must postulate a cause of such a nature that, by means of it, the cognition of the manifold world (prapañca) arises without obstruction.
And that [cause] is indeed perception itself.

For instance, while determining a blue object, one determines its difference from yellow and so forth, through the sense-object contact characterized as "qualification of the conjoined" (saṃyuktaviśeṣaṇatā).

For one who experiences blue as "blue" and yellow and so forth as "yellow" and so forth— whether experiencing them or remembering them— is able to comprehend them as the locus of negation and the object to be negated; even if their mutual difference has not been grasped through the mere form [of the object],
it is not the case that they do not manifest with distinction, for if they did not manifest as distinct,
there would be no relation of limit and limited between these two, blue and yellow, whose own natures have been grasped.
And thus, it is incorrect to say that their difference can be grasped through direct perception by having grasped those two [entities] first;
for "difference is not established by another means of knowledge because of mutual dependence;
there is no cognition of the form 'this is not that' or 'this is not here' without [prior] difference."
By this, the difference between the cognizer and cognition is also explained.

Cognizers are inferred to be distinct because of the established distribution of various experiences of pleasure and pain, and because the distinction between the deaf, the blind, the one-eyed, the learned, the fool, the transmigrating being, and the liberated one is logically possible;
for it is impossible for contradictory attributes to coexist in a single entity simultaneously.
Even if this [non-duality] could somehow be rendered possible through mere conceptualization, it leads to the "cow-dung-and-milk" analogy—that is, it results in a total confusion of categories.

Thus, because they contradict direct perception, scriptural passages such as "one only, without a second" have their literal meaning untenable; consequently, bypassing their primary sense, they must rely upon a secondary figurative application, just like the statements "the sacrificer is the sacrificial grass-bundle" or "the sun is indeed the sacrificial post."
As the venerable Jaimini has stated: "But it is a figurative statement" and "Its establishment [is through inference]," therefore non-duality does not exist.
Not so, because it exists as a constituent part of its cause.

And it has been stated that, because the means of proof is distinct from the object to be proven, even those [theories] that maintain an absolute difference in number have their meaning refuted. // 41 //
Nyāya Sūtra 4.1.42.
On this point, the proponent of the prima facie view says:
"No, because the cause is not a constituent part [of the effect]" (Sūtra 42).
He explains this [verse]: because the cause possesses a portion of the probandum (*sādhya*).

Whether there be one or two or more [reasons], some single part is the means of proof (*sādhana*); thus, there is neither a different number [of reasons] nor an absence of the status of being a means of proof—this is the meaning. // 42 //
Because it is partless, [the reason] is not a valid logical reason.
He refutes [this]: "Because it lacks parts, it is not a valid reason" (Sūtra 43).

Regarding the phrase "because of being a part": if there were some part of the probandum (*sādhya*), then the absolute unity [of number] would not exist; thus, in this thesis-meaning that "everything is one," nothing whatsoever is excluded or set aside (*apavṛjyate*) such that it could serve as its proof. Now, why is it that the probandum itself is not the reason (*hetu*)? [The answer follows: because...
He says:
"And [the view] regarding the self. The word "and" (*ca*) indicates a reason.
Furthermore, he states that these extremist numerical views are false doctrines because they contradict means of valid cognition such as direct perception.
"These indeed are the proponents of absolute enumeration (saṃkhyaikāntavādins).
The word "indeed" (khalu) is used for emphasis.
The meaning is: by means of the rejection of that difference in objects—such as a post or a person—which is produced by specific qualities like [the presence of] knots, hollows, hands, and so forth.

If they function by admitting a distinction in their specific causal efficacy (*viśeṣakāritārthabheda*), even so, they abandon their absoluteness; the meaning is that the number "one" and so forth are not absolute.
Alternatively, if it is argued that [the number] is produced by a universal (*sāmānyakārita*), the meaning is that only the mere number is accepted, but not its absoluteness through that [universal].
"This is indeed our own position," he says, "for even so, nothing is contradicted.
As for those who say that existence-in-general (*sattāsāmānya*) alone is reality while particular differences (*bheda*) are merely conceptual (*kālpnika*), he addresses them by saying:
"And not without difference."
As they say:
"A universal cannot exist without particulars, any more than a rabbit's horn."
It might be argued: "In the investigation of rebirth (pretyabhāva), what occasion is there for these extremist views (ekāntavāda) to be examined?
To this, he says:
Regarding the word "they":
in monistic views such as Advaita and others, rebirth (*pretyabhāva*) would not be real, but rather merely conceptual;
and it is not only rebirth, but all sixteen categories (*padārtha*) as well.

Therefore, for the sake of the thorough discernment of that knowledge which consists in the true cognition of these [categories], there is the discernment of knowledge through the discernment of the objects of knowledge;
it is for this purpose that these have been examined.
Thus, by this sequence of arguments, death and rebirth (*pretyabhāva*) has been examined. // 43 //
There is doubt because the fruit may be produced either immediately or at a later time.
Now, following the order of the enumeration, the fruit is examined.
In this regard, there arises a doubt as to whether the fruit of the Agnihotra and other such rites occurs immediately or at a later time.
This is what is meant:
Immediately following the action, suffering as well as worldly status and so forth are perceived; for people of the world praise him, saying, "This man is righteous, he is most excellent.
Therefore, should his fruit consist of only this much, or is there also a future result such as heaven and so on?

What is the conclusion? If the fruit of the action were [only] heaven and so forth, then since the action would not be the cause in its own essential form—because it has long since ceased when that [result] arises—[it could not produce it].

Furthermore, in the hypothesis that there is an *apūrva* (unseen potency), one would have to postulate numerous *apūrvas* belonging to both the primary and subsidiary elements; nor do these produce the fruit immediately upon their arising, so one must further postulate other auxiliary factors for them. Thus, due to the excessive burden of postulating unseen entities (*adṛṣṭa-kalpanā-gaurava*) and because it does not contradict the observation of results occurring immediately thereafter, its fruit—such as heaven and the like—is not something pertaining to another world.

Rather, it is precisely that which is seen immediately [after death]. Even in that case, since the result would be suffering, there would be a contradiction with the teaching; therefore, the result is merely the acquisition of worldly status, praise, and so forth. And because these are causes of pleasure, they are somehow designated by terms such as "heaven" (*svarga*). For the use of the word "heaven" for a cause of pleasure is indeed observed in common usage, as in: "Sandalwood is heaven," or "Fine garments are heaven"—this being the logical conclusion.
This being the case, we reply:

first of all, it has been established through the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) that the word *svarga* denotes pleasure, as in: "That happiness which is unmixed with pain, not followed by distress, and brought about by mere desire—that is the referent of the word *svarga*. Thus, its denotative function regarding pleasure is determined.

Moreover, since the application of that term to sandalwood and the like is accounted for by its being a denoter of that [pleasure], it is not reasonable to assume multiple meanings—as they say: "it is improper for a word to have multiple meanings. Therefore, this word *svarga* is primary in denoting the aforementioned distinct pleasure.
And likewise, in the case of the expression "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*), since the primary meaning is possible, it is not proper to assume a figurative sense.

Nor is it right to abandon the primary meaning out of fear of postulating multiple unseen results (*adṛṣṭa*), because when something is established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is improper to subject it to questioning regarding its necessity.
As they say:

"One must be diligent in perceiving what has not been heard for the sake of establishing what is heard; one should not, however, pay heed to laxity regarding what has already been heard. Likewise: "Even very many unseen things are to be postulated if they possess a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
Furthermore, the immediate visible results such as the rows of people [in the assembly] are not the fruit of performing the *homa* and other rites, but rather the fruit of perceiving them.

Because there is an absence of worldly censure and the like even for those who are free from hypocrisy and who practice in secret, it is well said in the Bhāṣya: "Not immediately, because [the fruit] is to be enjoyed at a later time.
Thus, by such activity, a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) characterized as merit (*dharma*) or demerit (*adharma*) is produced.

This "refinement" (saṃskāra) of the person is not to be understood as being produced by bathing and the like; rather, it is called a "refinement" merely by virtue of being an attribute of the person. In ultimate reality, however, although this property resides in the person, it serves as its intermediate operation (avāntaravyāpāra) when an action is to produce its fruit.
The *vārttika* states that this results in immediate suffering and so forth.
This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with an *atadguṇasaṃvijñāna* (non-qualificative) sense, such as "suffering and so forth.
By this, the "row of worldly people" and other such things are expressed. (484/1) 44.
It is not immediate, because it is to be experienced at a later time.
NyS 4.1.46: There is no production at a later time because the cause has perished.
Prior to its production, it would exist like the fruit of a tree [on the tree before it has fallen].
It is incorrect to say that heaven is heard of as the fruit,
because in the expression "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*), heaven is heard as a qualification of the person and is therefore not something to be accomplished; therefore,
he says:
And it should be understood that the action taught is not purposeless;

for this instruction from a reliable authority (āpta) indeed declares that the action to be instructed is a desired means [to an end]. In that regard, since there is a requirement for the action to be desired, the qualification of the person is also required, and thus its status as something to be accomplished (sādhya) is established.

For in this way, [the goal] such as membership in the ranks of the world would be accomplished by the performance of the *agnihotra* and other rites, provided that the performance of the *agnihotra* and so forth were taught for one who desires that—just as it is taught for one who desires heaven.
And this is not the case; thus he says, "nor desiring heat and so forth," meaning "desiring worldly status and the like."
The remainder has a meaning that is not obscure. // 45 // 46 // 47 //
It is neither non-existent, nor existent, nor both existent and non-existent, because of the mutual incompatibility between existence and non-existence.
Now this is considered: is this fruit, prior to its arising, existent, non-existent, both existent and non-existent, or neither?
Here, intending to state the non-existence of the fruit by refuting all these positions, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) argues:
"This fruit, prior to its production..."
It is neither non-existent, nor existent, nor both existent and non-existent.
To the question, "Why is it not both existent and non-existent? he says:
"Because of the contradiction between existence and non-existence."
Because they possess mutually contradictory properties (*dharmatva*), "dharma" means intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);
the meaning is that [they are so] due to contradiction. Now, why is it not the case that it is neither? To this [it is said]:
He said:
"Nor is it the opposite of both.
The proponent replied:
Prior to its arising, that which possesses the nature of arising is certainly non-existent. // 48 //
NyS 4.1.49: It is certain that what possesses the property of arising is non-existent prior to its arising;
why? Because we observe both arising and passing away.

Now, it may be objected: "The Sāṃkhyas declare that what is non-existent does not arise and what is existent is not destroyed; how then is this [your position] possible? To this he says: "Because of the observation of arising and passing away" (Sūtra 49).

The meaning is that just as there is neither origination nor destruction for the power of consciousness (*citiśakti*), which is eternal by nature, so too these two would not exist for a result that is eternal.
"For it is not the case on the side of existence" means:
on the side of the theory that the effect pre-exists (*satkāryavāda*).
"Nothing whatsoever is produced":
from this proposition, no knowledge of reality arises;
furthermore, some doubts and the like do not cease.
The concealment of ignorance is the concealment of doubt and error.
For the Great Principle (mahat) is perceived as the characteristic of its cause, the Pradhāna; indeed, the Pradhāna is perceived through the Great Principle.
In the same way, for that [Great Principle], there is the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), which means its nourishment or grossness.
"It occurs later" means after the state of being merely a cause. // 49 //
But that which is established merely by cognition is non-existent.
As for what was said regarding "the restriction of appropriation":

if there were a restriction of appropriation on the part of the person— such that one desiring a cloth appropriates only threads and not vīraṇa grass, while one desiring a mat appropriates vīraṇa grass— then [the argument holds].
Therefore, because the capacity of those respective causes for their respective effects is fully known, and that capacity is established through inference, this is stated:
"But that [cause] is non-existent, being established only by the intellect" (Sūtra 50).

The meaning is that, because the effect does not exist [prior to its production], it is produced by this very cause and not by another; thus, it is established by inference through the intellect (*buddhisiddha*).
Now, regarding the position that the effect is non-existent (*asatkāryapakṣa*), as for the threads...

If you argue that there would be no such restriction as that the cloth has *tūla* fibers as its material cause (*upādāna*) and not *vīraṇa* grass or the like, that is incorrect; for even though non-existence is common to all things, it is established by the particularity of their own nature (*svabhāva-viśeṣa*) that only a certain thing produced from its own causes is capable of generating a specific effect, and nothing else. Furthermore, according to the theory of the pre-existent effect (*satkāryapakṣa*), the universe has *pradhāna* as its material cause, and because of its identity with that [cause], it is of the same nature as its cause.

If every member of the class of effects were of the nature of everything, then there would be no restriction such as "this is here," "this is not there," "this is now," "this is not then," or "this is this very thing and not that," because there would be no cause for the distinction of one thing from another.
Therefore, he says that one who asserts the non-existence of a horn in a donkey contradicts his own established tenet by implying that a horn exists even in a donkey.
And one who says that "because it does not exist, the horn of a donkey is not produced"—
this is a mere "sweetness on the tongue" (guḍajihvikā), for while existence and non-existence are equal [in being predicates], that which has a cause is what is produced.

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), however, the restriction of production is postulated based on the restriction of the causal capacity [of that which is non-existent]; but if everything were existent in its entirety, there would be no cause for such restriction, as has already been stated. He teaches: "Now, what is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the non-existence of the effect (*asatkārya*)?"

For inference cannot serve as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding this matter, because its locus (*āśraya*) is unestablished; nor can it be perception, because even by that [perception], what is non-existent cannot be determined independently—this is the intended meaning. Understanding this intention, he states the reply: "There is no inference, whether in the case of non-existence or in the case of existence."

Just as for us there is no inference regarding the non-existence of an effect due to the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*), so too, even when the effect exists, there is no inference because of that very same unestablished locus. Where, then, is there inference? To this [it is replied]:
He says: the construction is that there is inference because there is no disagreement regarding the subject (*dharmin*).
The meaning is that, this being so, its locus (*āśraya*) is established.
He asks again: "Where?"
If there is no disagreement regarding the locus (*dharmin*), then where is the dispute? The answer is: "that which is common to both," because the locus is the basis for the discussion.
He analyzes the arguments specifically of those who maintain the theory that the effect pre-exists in the cause (*satkāryavāda*), with reference to them: "The cloth is merely the threads.
This means that [the cloth] is non-different from the threads.
"By way of its being an effect" means that the effect is both different and non-different from the cause.

The position that the effect is non-existent (*asatkāryapakṣa*), however, was not presented because it is [already] well-known and because there are no intermediate logical complications (*pratibandha*) involved.
"It has been established" refers to the second chapter.
"Prior to the time of perception" means prior to the operation of the causes.

The examples of the "fourth" (*turya*) and so forth are intended merely to express the absence of any specific configuration (*saṃsthāna-viśeṣa*), and do not intend to refer to prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*).
Regarding the phrase "abiding in a particular capacity," the remainder of the sense is "prior to the operation of the cause.

Here, we too state that there is the proving of what is already established (*siddha-sādhana*), because [the effect] exists prior to its own operation which is the cause for the production of the cloth.
"Threads are indeed delimited by specific potencies.
Thus he sets forth the proof for the pre-existence of the effect according to the opponents:
"The threads are for the purpose of manifesting what already exists, because they are invariably taken up by one who desires that [effect], just like a spade and other such tools. (489/1)
For just as a digging tool reveals water that already exists by removing the earth,
[the opponent] refutes this by stating:
"If manifestation is of something already existing, then it follows that the effect must also be like the manifestation."
The meaning is that just as there is the arising of a manifestation that is itself non-existent, so too there is the arising of an effect that is non-existent;
the example "like a shovel and so forth" is deficient in the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*).
Thus he says, "even that which... One must explain from what this non-attainment (*aprāpti*) arises;
for attainment (*prāpti*) is indeed conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and that is a quality (*guṇa*).

Furthermore, a quality (guṇa) would perish either through the destruction of its substance (dravya) or through another opposing quality. In this case, neither the obstructing substance nor the water being obstructed has been destroyed, such that their conjunction (saṃyoga) might perish; therefore, the production of another opposing quality must be asserted, and that very quality which opposes the conjunction is disjunction (vibhāga).
The meaning is that it is so stated.

Having refuted the position that "non-attainment" (*aprāpti*) is the absence of attainment (*prāpti*), he anticipates and refutes the position of exclusion (*paryudāsa*) with the words, "Now, [if it is argued] regarding attainment...
He then raises a further objection: "Or, [if it is argued] that it is arising in a different location..."
Furthermore, we do not accept conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or disjunction (*vibhāga*) as qualities (*guṇa*).

Rather, the meaning is that disjunction occurs precisely when a substance arises in a different location, and conjunction occurs precisely when [substances] arise without an interval. He refutes this by saying "in a different location."

Because of the employment of a qualification, separation is not the arising in a different location. Why? [Because] the qualification "arisen" [is applied to what is] "arisen" [only] in the sense of being distinct by virtue of being in a different location. For a qualification imparts its own coloring to the qualified object, but not the coloring of another. Indeed, the meaning is that a blue qualifier does not produce the cognition of red in a lotus for one who is not deluded.
Furthermore, since we—who deny the momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga) of entities—deny arising in a different location, "separation" is not arising in a different location.
[The opponent] suspects that this is because separation is momentary.
For, having arisen from the contact of the sense organ, it must produce a cognition of its own object through separation.

The meaning is that it does not exist for such a long duration because, being momentary, it perishes as soon as it arises. He refutes [the opponent's view] with the words, "not in the manifestation of the universal" (*na sāmānyābhivyaktau*).
He analyzes this point as follows:

First of all, it is said that the produced (*utpanna*) distinction (*vibhāga*) manifests the universal (*sāmānya*). Production (*utpatti*) consists in inherence in its own cause or inherence in existence (*sattā*); that which is qualified by this is "produced."
Thus it is said:

according to those for whom the cognition of particulars is preceded by the grasping of the universal, it is stated that the universal does not manifest itself at that time, but produces its own cognition at a subsequent moment.
What is meant by this is that we do not, like the Buddhists, accept momentariness characterized by existence only during preceding and succeeding moments.

We shall explain [the nature of] disjunction and the others; however, it is characterized by extremely rapid destruction, and that [characteristic] can be described as being distinct from things like jars, which endure for two or three moments or for a long time. // 50 //
"Because of the difference in their substrata, like the production of fruit from a tree; therefore, this is not a valid reason."
One who considers the self—which is distinct from the body and so forth—to be eternal, a transmigrator, and non-existent, says:
"Because it occurs apart from its substratum, like the production of fruit on a tree; therefore, [the opponent's reason] is not a valid reason" (Sūtra 51).
The watering of the roots and the production of the fruit have the single tree as their locus;
however, for ritual acts such as the fire-oblation (*homa*), the body is the locus.
But the body is not the locus of the future [result] such as heaven, because that [result] exists even when the body has perished.

Therefore, because heaven and the like are distinct from their substratum—just as the production of fruit from a tree—this example shows that the oblation (homa) is not the cause for heaven as its result. This is the meaning. // 51 //
NyS 4.1.52: There is no refutation [of the self] because pleasure has the self as its substratum.
Intending to establish that there exists a self—a creator distinct from the body and other such things, capable of enjoying the fruits of heaven—he says:
"There is no refutation [of the self] because pleasure resides in the self" (Nyāyasūtra 4.1.53).
This is not so, because the fruits are specified as being sons, cattle, women, attendants, gold, food, and so forth.

[The opponent] objects: "Let it be that heaven and so forth have the self as their locus; nevertheless, the reason [for the cessation of activity] is not pervasive, because there is a turning away from fruits such as sons.
[The author] replies: "No, because of the mention of fruits such as sons, cattle, women, retinues, gold, food, and so forth" (Sūtra 53).
Because the fruit is produced through connection with them, there is a metaphorical designation of the fruit as being in those [factors].
He avoids [that objection]:
because the fruit is produced through connection with them, there is a metaphorical designation of the fruit as being in them (Sūtra 54).
Even heaven is not desired as heaven per se, but rather as an object of enjoyment;
such being the case, what need is there to mention sons and the like?
They too are desired solely as objects of enjoyment, for it is not their own nature that is the object of enjoyment, but rather the pleasure produced by them that is the object of enjoyment.

Therefore, because happiness arises from the connection with sons and others, and because that [happiness] originates from them, the meaning is that the term "fruit" (phala) is applied to those sons and others just as it is to the [actual] fruit.
By this very explanation of the meaning of the Sūtra, the Bhāṣya and the Vārtika are also explained. // 54 //
The arising of birth is indeed suffering, because it is associated with various forms of affliction.
Following the [discussion of] the fruit, there is the examination of suffering;
in this regard, let this be the examination: "Suffering has the characteristic of affliction as it is being experienced.
But as for this pleasure which is felt as agreeable by each individual, how can that be suffering? Because it contradicts experience."

If the body, the sense organs, and the intellect are suffering because they are causes of suffering, why do they not become pleasure simply because they are causes of pleasure? This excessive timidity is contrary to the entire course of worldly life, as they say: "One does not refrain from sowing rice just because there are wild deer."
"For indeed, monks, pots are not placed on the fire because there is no meat.

Therefore, just as one seeking meat who, having removed the thorns, eats the meat, incurs the harm arising from those thorns; so too, a discerning person, having removed suffering, will enjoy the pleasure achieved through the means of the senses and so forth. And since the causes for avoiding various sufferings are observed and their efficacy is seen through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the proponent (pūrvapakṣin), intending this, speaks as if in doubt, using the "sugar-on-the-tongue" (*guḍajivhikā*) method.
He asks:
"What is this? This is the response of the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin).
The author of the Sūtras says "others. With that very intention, the proponent asks, "How so?
The answer is: "Indeed, it is not witnessed by the whole world."
But for what purpose is this instruction on the cultivation of suffering?
To this the Commentator says: it is for the sake of the abandonment of suffering.
Of what kind [of person] is there the abandonment of suffering? To this he says:

The "experience" (*anubhava*) is the undergoing of the continuous succession of birth and death; it is the attainment [of that]. One who is weary because of the cultivation of the teaching on suffering caused by that [attainment], and who possesses the conviction that it is enough [to be done], is for that very reason one who desires to abandon suffering—thus the connection should be made.
The opponent asks according to his own intention.
By what reasoning? The answer is:
"All classes of sentient beings are like phantoms."

Arising is the attainment of sense objects that serve as the causes of pleasure and pain; its configurations are the worlds, from the realm of truth (satyaloka) down to the Avīci hell. This is what is meant: The term "arising" refers to the manifestation of the various realms of existence, which function as the causes for experiencing pleasure and pain. These realms are the structural arrangements of those objects, extending from the highest heaven, Satyaloka, down to the lowest abyss, Avīci. By this it is intended to be said: [that all these worlds arise from the mind].
If it were possible to attain happiness by means of abandoning suffering, then what wise person would ever renounce such happiness, which is to be experienced as agreeable?
Yet, no such happiness exists anywhere, because it is impossible to grasp anything that is entirely devoid of suffering, since all things are invariably accompanied by suffering.
Indeed, it is not possible to take up the honey alone from food mixed with poison after having removed the poison.
Therefore, this is not a rejection of pleasure; rather, it is the cultivation of the perception of suffering within pleasure itself that is being taught. // 55 //
In this regard, the sage provides the reason:
"The arising of birth is indeed suffering, because it is subject to various afflictions" (Sūtra 55).
Birth is origination; it must be contemplated as nothing but suffering because it is associated with manifold afflictions. // 55 //
Nor is there [a lack of proof] even for pleasure, because it is produced in the interval.
But why, then, is it not suffering by its very nature? To this he says: "Because of the production of intervals of pleasure" (Sūtra 56).
Indeed, this enumeration of suffering is not a denial of happiness; it is merely a description of suffering and an analysis of suffering. // 56 //
There is no refutation [of the existence of a self] because, for one who experiences sensation, the fault of seeking [objects] does not cease as long as affliction has not ceased.
Furthermore, he says that the cultivation of the perception of suffering is not a rejection of pleasure on the grounds that it is suffering;
for one who experiences "this is a means to my pleasure" desires that means to pleasure,
and since that [means] is a cause of affliction in the many ways already described, there is the instruction to cultivate the perception of suffering.
When a desire that is desirable for one who desires it is fulfilled— that is, when it is accomplished—
then immediately thereafter another desire or longing quickly afflicts this person; even upon attaining heaven and the like, he desires sovereignty over his own realm and so forth.
Thus, regarding the attainment of that [state], the meaning is that his desire for the Prājāpatya and other [worlds] is afflicted by the suffering of praying for the means to achieve them.
The construction is: "He obtains the earth in such a way that it extends all around to the ocean's rim. // 57 //
And because there is a misconception of pleasure regarding what is actually a variety of suffering.

"Now, even if he experiences pleasures in the interim, nevertheless, perceiving the intermingling with suffering, he will desist of his own accord even without instruction; so what is the use of teaching him the contemplation of suffering? To this, he says:
And because of the conceit of pleasure regarding what is actually a variety of suffering. (Sūtra 58)

For those who have reached the culmination of the scriptures and possess discernment, because of their connection with various afflictions, there is indeed the firm conviction that pleasure in its entirety is nothing but suffering;
for they are like the eyeball. Just as the eyeball is pained even by contact with a tuft of *iṣīkā* grass, while other parts of the body are not, so it is due to the softness of their minds.

The discerning are pained [by worldly things], whereas the undiscerning—regarding even the falling of a fresh lotus petal, moist with the lac-dye from the feet of a woman whose eyes are like those of a doe agitated by a lover’s quarrel, as a source of pleasure upon their heads in secret—their bodies bristling with horripilation like a coat of mail, their eyes overflowing with tears of intense bliss, find contentment;
it is toward them that this instruction is meaningful. This is the sense.
"Be born and die"—thus it runs on.
It is born again, it dies again; having been born, it dies; having died, it is born. This means a continuous accumulation of the activity of running on. [The opponent] objects:
"Why is it not said that birth itself is suffering?"—the meaning of this question is:
if the instruction on the cultivation of suffering applies to birth as well, then what is the purpose of the restrictive particle *eva*? He provides the answer:
Regarding the term *janmavinigrahārthīya*: *vinigraha* means cessation; since that itself is the purpose (*artha*) toward which it proceeds, it is called *janmavinigrahārthīya*.
And as for the statement "possessing the suffix denoting possession" (matvarthīya),
this is what is meant: [the suffix is used] to express the sense of possession.

One must contemplate that birth is nothing but suffering; one should not form even the slightest notion of happiness therein, for it leads to a succession of manifold misfortunes and results in obstacles to liberation. // 58 //
NyS 4.1.59: There is no liberation because of the continuous succession of debts, afflictions, and worldly activity.
Immediately after the enumeration of suffering, liberation was enumerated and— *the remainder is that it was defined*— now that [liberation] is being rejected.
There is an absence of liberation due to the continuous succession of debts, afflictions, and worldly activity. (Sūtra 59)
The author of the Bhāṣya explains that:
"Because of the connection with debt," for it is indeed so.
"...Having discharged the three debts, one should fix the mind on liberation;
desiring liberation without having discharged them, one goes downward through delusion...

The meaning is that because one's life comes to an end precisely by the discharge of the three debts, there is no opportunity to fix the mind on liberation, and thus there is an absence of final release (*apavarga*).
Because of the persistence of the afflictions (*kleśa*), there is no liberation;
the meaning is that cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) cannot be severed as long as its cause has not been cut off.
This same explanation applies to the phrase "because of the persistence of [rebirth] activity" (*pravṛtty-anubandhāt*). // 59 //
NyS 4.1.60: Because the term "primary" (pradhāna) is untenable, there is a restatement by means of the term "quality" (guṇa), as this is appropriate for the purposes of censure or praise.
Having thus presented the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa), he begins the established conclusion (siddhānta): "To this it is replied:
as for what was said regarding the 'inseparable connection with debt' (ṛṇānubandha)..."

In order to establish that the word *jāyamāna* (being born) is a secondary term (*guṇaśabda*) because its status as a primary term (*pradhānaśabda*) is untenable, [the author] first states that the word *ṛṇa* (debt) is a secondary term, so as to provide an illustrative example.
He explains this by saying, "because of the impossibility of it being a primary term.
He then elaborates upon that.
Regarding the phrase "by debts":
this is not a primary designation;
rather, it is a censure, meaning that like one who is indebted, he is not independent and lacks the qualification for those various actions.
But in the absence of that [external cause], the term "independent" is used as a praise;
thus, the word "being born" is a figurative expression and not primary.
But why is he not [considered] primary? To this he says:
because one who has just been born from the mother lacks the qualification. Why is there no qualification? To this he says:
Because eligibility belongs to one who both desires [the result] and is capable.
Why "one who desires"? To this he says:
because in the injunctions for ritual action, such as "One desiring heaven should offer the Agnihotra," there is the scriptural mention of a connection with desire (*kāmasaṃyoga*).
Furthermore, even though a child desires the attainment of pleasure and the avoidance of pain, he does not, through discernment, desire heaven, sons, cattle, food, and so forth.
And since there is activity only for one who is capable,
the Veda— in the form of an authoritative instruction— cannot enjoin an object that is impossible for one who lacks the capacity.
Furthermore, a child is not capable [of such action] due to his lack of knowledge and other such factors.
For this very reason, animals, gods, sages, the lame, Śūdras, and those who do not belong to a lineage of seers (ṛṣi) have no entitlement [to Vedic rites], because they lack the requisite capacity.
He states that this kind of practice is not only Vedic, but also worldly.
And this does not differ from the worldly [view]. He explains that: "First, the worldly [person] is one who speaks what has been understood and is blameless."

The meaning is this: that which is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is irreproachable, free from redundancy, and independent—such a thing should be taught; it is that which does not fail to exist.
He states that the observation of indicative marks (*liṅgadarśana*) corroborates this meaning as established by logic (*nyāya*):
"And the mantra and brāhmaṇa texts, bearing the marks of the householder's life, declare ritual action."

The mark of the householder's state is the wife; that ritual action in which she [participates] is described as such. For example: "The clarified butter is to be inspected by the wife," and "The wives sing the *udgītha*."
"Let the two, wearing linen garments, establish the sacred fires," and so forth.
By this, it has been stated that the stage prior to the householder's life is not bound by debts; now he says that even the subsequent stage is not bound by debts.
And when there is entitlement for one who possesses the desire [to act], then, provided that the desire does not change, the statement regarding "living until old age" (jarāmarya) is justified.
Therefore, by that aforementioned repayment of debt, since there is no opportunity for liberation at the end of one's life, that [debt] is repaid;
thus, the explanation of the "unchanging entity" (avipariṇāma-padārtha) does not cease.
Furthermore, the explanation of the term "of the fourth" (turīyasya) is "of the fourth" (caturthasya).
Generally, when seventy-five years have passed, the thirst for wealth diminishes; however,
regarding the state of extreme union [with death], the mention of "by old age" is redundant,
because it is already established by the phrase "or by death"— this is the remaining sense.
If it is argued that this is merely an indication of incapacity due to either old age or death,
and therefore for whom [the injunction] would be futile,
he says:
"It is not tenable that one who is incapable is liberated.
This might be the case:

although there are other injunctions for the householder such as sacrifices and the like, nevertheless, the statement "being born, [one is] with three debts" will enjoin sacrifices and so forth even for the child; anticipating this doubt, he refutes it with careful deliberation.
Furthermore, it might be argued that what is enjoined is restated for the sake of desire (*kāma*), and thus the purpose is established.

However, in the phrase "one who is being born" (*jāyamāno vai*), there is no injunctive suffix; therefore, by its own natural sense, it is understood as a restatement of something already established. But if the establishment of that matter is not possible through another sentence or any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in any way whatsoever, [then it must be taken as an injunction].

One might imagine its status as an injunction based on the principle that "therefore, from the absence of [other] words, it is an injunction" because it conveys something not previously known; however, since there exist hundreds of sentences containing case-endings that enjoin that very same meaning, who indeed would imagine its injunctive nature by mere whim?

Therefore, we consider it logical that the restatement of what has been enjoined is indeed proper, and that the word "being born" (*jāyamāna*) is rightly understood as having a secondary (metaphorical) sense.
This might be argued:
the word "being born," without its meaning being figurative, naturally denotes the separation from the mother's womb.
One should rather assume that it functions in a secondary sense (jaghanyavṛtti) out of deference to the restatement;
it is better, therefore, to assume an injunction in accordance with the primary meaning.
This being so, the direct Vedic statement (śruti) remains respected.
Moreover, even an infant possesses the capacity for the production of a result, because he is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) with respect to that result.
Therefore, although one who has just been born lacks the capacity to perform the practices that are the means to a result, he nevertheless possesses the capacity for the production of the result;
and since the purpose lies in the result itself, not in its means, [the capacity exists].
He says: "For the means of accomplishing the result are the object of effort, not the result itself.

This is the underlying intention: An injunction (vidhi) indeed enjoins a person as an agent with respect to its own operation; and since effort is its operation, it is possible [for it to exist], yet it cannot be turned away from its object, and thus it requires its own object.
Furthermore, its direct fruit cannot be its object;
rather, it may be so only by virtue of being intended as a goal.
Yet, this effort does not reach fulfillment merely by that much, so long as one has not attained that which is to be directly accomplished.

The means to that [result] must be directly accomplished; thus, it fulfills the human effort directed toward the aim of the result for as long as the means remains its object. However, a child who does not know that means lacks the capacity for it.
And how could one who is incapable and thus a non-agent engage himself with effort?
And since it would not otherwise qualify [as an agent], it is established that the word "jāyamāna" (being born) must necessarily be understood in its secondary sense [of "one who has been born"].

Furthermore, because it is enjoined as "being born," the meaning is that it is prescribed prior to the statement regarding the debts (*ṛṇavākya*), and also subsequent to the statement regarding the debts.

Regarding what was stated there—that renunciation (*pravrajyā*) is indeed prescribed—he, being questioned, says: "If it is argued that this is because there is no explicit injunction [for it]," he dispels that doubt by saying:
"No, for even in the case of a prohibition, there is no lack of an injunction."
He analyzes the doubt with the words "by means of perception" (*pratyakṣataḥ*).

For the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Authority, having set out to teach what is beneficial for living beings out of compassion, teaches that one should resort to the householder's state alone; from this we understand that there are no other stages of life (*āśrama*) that are beneficial for living beings—this is the meaning.
Therefore they say: "The teachers [hold] that there is only one stage of life (aikāśramya), because the householder's state (gārhasthya) is directly enjoined.
He analyzes this refutation, stating: "It is not a prohibition.

For the Smṛtis, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas are found to uncontestably enjoin the four stages of life; if these were prohibited by direct Vedic revelation (śruti), then, due to that contradiction, it would be like the case of the total veiling of the Audumbarī post.
In that case, there would be no authoritative means [of knowledge],
nor is the negation of that [fourfold stage system] directly understood from the Veda.
Therefore, the meaning is that the fourfold āśrama system ordained by Smṛti and other sources, being unprohibited by the Śruti, cannot be abandoned.
And he states that there is no inference of its prohibition based on the absence of an injunction, saying:
"And because of the context.

This means that because the instruction regarding the householder's life is the subject at hand, it is that alone which is enjoined, not another stage of life; however, this is not because other stages of life do not exist.

For grammar, while explaining words, does not imply the absence of means [of knowledge] such as perception and the rest. Furthermore, let it be granted that there is no direct injunction in the Veda; nevertheless, we do perceive explicit statements concerning the four stages of life (*cāturāśramya*) which describe liberation along with its means, and these are perceived as direct perceptions. Because they refer to something not previously known, these are indeed injunctions regarding liberation together with its means.
And he says that they will belong to the four stages of life (*cāturāśramya*), stating:
"The *Ṛgveda* and the *Brāhmaṇa* declare liberation (*apavarga*)," and "Death is beyond ritual actions."
It indicates that the renunciation of action is the means for attaining liberation (*apavarga*). By the term "immortality" (*amṛtatva*), liberation is shown.
It clarifies, through another scriptural passage, this indicated renunciation of action as the means for attaining liberation.
"Not by action, nor by progeny"—
by "the further shore beyond the firmament" (*nāka*),
he indicates ignorance (*avidyā*).
The meaning is "beyond ignorance.
By the phrase "placed in the cave," he shows that it is not within the scope of worldly means of valid cognition (*laukikapramāṇa*).
[He further describes it as] "beyond darkness."
Ignorance is darkness; beyond that is [the state] "having the color of the sun," which means it is eternally luminous.

Thus, by this, the state of devotion to the Lord (*īśvarapraṇidhāna*) as a means to liberation has been stated. Having cited the *ṛc* verses, he cites the *brāhmaṇa* passage with the words "Now, the *brāhmaṇa* passages.
By the words "sacrifice" (*yajña*) and so forth, the householder stage of life (*gṛhasthāśrama*) is shown. [The word] "austerity" (*tapas*)...
"Evam" refers to the stage of the forest-dweller (vānaprasthāśrama);
"brahmacārī" refers to the stage of the student (brahmacaryāśrama).
He now states the fruit characterized by worldly prosperity (abhyudaya) for these [stages].
"All these indeed" refers to the fourth stage of life;
"established in Brahman" refers to that very stage.
"Of such a nature" (tathākratuḥ):
*kratu* means intention (*saṃkalpa*).
He who previously existed as one possessing desire, he now becomes one who is free from desire.
Not desiring desire, avoiding it— in order to establish that avoidance— he did not desire; its explanation is "free from desire" (niṣkāma) and "one whose desire is the Self" (ātmakāma).
One whose desire consists of the self endowed with isolation (kaivalya) becomes one whose desires are fulfilled through its attainment;
the meaning is that for him there is no further vital breath, and thus he becomes eternal.
He concludes the subject under discussion with the words "therein, as has been said."
Furthermore, he cites another scriptural passage that speaks of the four stages of life (*cāturāśramya*),
beginning with "those who [follow] the four...
From this as well, this teaching regarding "until old age and death" is intended for those who seek results.
Thus he says:
"And for one who seeks the fruit. // 60 //
Because of the superimposition [of qualities] upon the self, there is no negation [of its existence].
Having asked, "How does one recite [the Veda]? [the answer is:
There is no prohibition against [reciting] within oneself because of the act of mental superimposition (samāropaṇa). (Sūtra 61)
Because of the internalizing (*samāropaṇa*) of the fires of the self, there is no prohibition against liberation from the bonds of debt; thus,
by this artifice, the direct injunction for renunciation (*pravrajyā*) has also been shown for one who has emerged from worldly desires but whose intellect is perverted.

"For one who has formed the conviction that 'these pursuits are sufficient [to be abandoned] as they are causes of misfortune,' and for whom, precisely because of this, the desire for fruits has ceased, the enkindling of the fires within oneself is prescribed.
Thus, the meaning is that when the injunction for renunciation is laid down for one who has risen above these pursuits, then those *brāhmaṇas* which speak of that [state] become appropriate. // 61 //
And because the final accumulation of the sacrificial vessels is impossible, there is an absence of fruit.

Indeed, when the sacrificer has died, the sacrificial vessels are placed upon the sacrificer’s body according to their respective order of age, and then the final sacrifice (*antyeṣṭi*) is performed. In that case, if the ritual were conceived as being without distinction throughout life until old age (*jarāmarya*), it would follow that all rituals must end with the piling of the vessels; the meaning is that it would follow that rituals must continue until death. [Objection: But surely it is precisely this—that rituals end with the piling of the vessels—that is intended? To this, [the author replies]:
He said:
"In that case, there is the emergence from seeking.
Therefore, it is not the case that the fruit is the instigator of the agent without distinction.
The phrase "absence of fruit" (phalābhāva) means that, without distinction, there is an absence of the agent's purposefulness regarding the fruit;
by this, the contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning renunciation through desire is demonstrated.

Thus, the Vedic revelation (śruti) regarding the four stages of life (cāturāśramya) has been stated. Now, he says "and because of the prescription of the four stages of life" to show that the traditional law (smṛti) and other sources are also instructors of the four stages of life.
He raises an objection: "If it be argued that this [the Smṛti] is not authoritative."
The scripture of the Supreme Lord—who is the creator of the world, supremely compassionate, and omniscient—must be accepted as authoritative because it was spoken by a reliable person (*āpta*).
The meaning is: since the reliability of Manu, Vyāsa, and others is not certain, how can there be certainty regarding the authority of the works composed by them?
The answer is: "by means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇena*).
This might be so:

let the authority of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas be granted because they are authorized by the Veda; but from what source is the certainty of the authority of the Dharmaśāstras composed by Manu and others? To this, he says:
"And if there were non-authority... [etc.]
The meaning is that because they are accepted by all people, those [traditions] also possess authority.
However, the Smṛtis of Buddha and others are accepted by Mlecchas and others who revile the Veda, but not by the Āryas; therefore, the meaning is that they cannot be considered authoritative.
Furthermore, there is no possibility of a lack of authority on account of the identity between the seer and the proclaimer.

Those very same individuals who were the seers of the Veda and the performers of its meaning are the ones who proclaimed the Itihāsas and other texts—namely, Vālmīki, Vyāsa, Vaiśampāyana, Manu, and so forth.

Furthermore, Vedic rituals depend upon the procedural requirements (itikartavyatā) found in the Smṛtis, while Smārta rites depend upon Vedic elements such as mantras; thus, all of this would be untenable if the Dharmaśāstras lacked authoritative status.

And although it is possible that Manu and others, being endowed with knowledge of dharma, dispassion, and sovereignty, taught [the law] even from their own experience, nevertheless, it is more reasonable that the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and so forth are rooted in the Veda;
for it is said:
"The entire Veda is the root of dharma, as are the Smṛti and the conduct of those who know it."
Whatever dharma has been proclaimed by Manu for anyone at all, [that should be observed].

By such elaborate statements of their own as, "All that has been declared in the Veda, for it consists of all-knowledge," they have firmly established the Veda alone as their very self. Now, one might ask: why is this matter, which falls within the scope of history (itihāsa) and so forth, not stated by the Veda, which is perceived through direct perception? From its non-mention [therein], we understand that this was surely not intended by the author of the Vedas. Thus, although this [objection] has already been refuted, it is refuted once more for the sake of firmness and because of the fixed distinction of subject matters, as expressed by the phrase "viṣayavyavasthānācca" (and because of the restriction of the scope). 62.
NyS 4.1.63: For one who is fast asleep and does not perceive dreams, there is liberation due to the absence of afflictions.
Regarding what was also stated—that liberation does not occur because of the non-interruption of the connection with the afflictions (*kleśa*)—he refutes that:
"For one who is in deep sleep, there is liberation due to the absence of afflictions when no dreams are seen" (Sūtra 63).
He explains this as follows: "Indeed, for one who is in deep sleep... and so forth.

The state of deep sleep is cited because it is established by common worldly experience (*loka-siddha*).
