Although the selves are likewise liberated from afflictions (*kleśa*) during the state of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), that state was not cited because it is not established by common worldly experience.
However, this much is the distinction regarding the state of liberation: that in this [state], even the latent impressions of the afflictions (*kleśa-vāsanā*) do not exist.
Even when the afflictions are severed during the state of deep sleep and the state of cosmic dissolution, their latent impressions (vāsanā) still persist. // 63 //
For one whose afflictions have been eliminated, there is no further engagement for the sake of rebirth.

Regarding the point that [the cycle continues] "due to the persistence of activity," he says in response: "For one whose afflictions have been eliminated, there is no activity for the sake of rebirth" (Sūtra 64).
"Of the embodied being.

He explains this: even when passion, hatred, and delusion have been exhausted, there is no further activity for the sake of re-linking [to a new birth]. We have already established how the grains of karma, when enveloped by the husks of the defects (*doṣa*), are capable of producing the sprout of birth.
The meaning is "not merely [those].
He raises an objection regarding the futility of action:
if there were futility, it would follow that the scripture—which teaches that actions are the means to achieve results—would lack authority (*aprāmāṇya*).
Such is the intended meaning.
He refutes [the objection] with the words "not by the ripening of karma.
The ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) is the experience of that [karma], which is enjoyment (*bhoga*). // 64 //
It is not so, because the continuum of afflictions is intrinsic.
The proponent of the prima facie view says: No, because the continuum of afflictions is innate. (Sūtra 65)
An exponent of a particular school within the Siddhānta says:
"Just as there is non-eternality due to non-existence prior to production, so too there is non-eternality even when [non-existence] is inherent."
The state of being prior [to that] (Sūtra 66).
The construction is as follows: it is like the impermanence of that state which exists in milk and so forth prior to the production of curds and so forth. // 66 //
It is like the case of the non-eternality of the blackness of an atom.
But another partial proponent (ekadeśin), illustrating by means of existence itself, says:
"Or like the blackness and impermanence of atoms" (Sūtra 67).
The scriptural tradition stating, "That which is this dark form belongs to food," declares that the blackness of the atoms of earth is beginningless;
the intention is that by the word "food" (anna), clay (mṛd) is denoted.
Here, he first refutes the partial proponent (ekadeśin) with the words, "Indeed, of that which exists... and so forth.
He refutes the second proponent who holds a partial view:
it is not tenable that the blackness of atoms is beginningless, because no cause for it has been heard of.
The blackness of atoms must be an effect, since it is a quality of earth.
On the contrary, there is a reason for impermanence, namely, "like blood and so forth.

However, because it differs from the nature of human effort, water, blood, and the like, its designation as "beginningless" is based merely on the fact that it is not preceded by [deliberate] effort; thus, there is no contradiction with scripture. // 67 //
And [it is] not [the case that the self is the agent], because passion and so forth have conceptual construction as their cause.
Having thus refuted the two partial views, he states the supreme concentration:
"But this concentration [is not so], because passion and the like do not have conceptualization as their cause" (Sūtra 68).
He explains the letter *ca* as having the sense of a collective inclusion (*samuccaya*) of what has not been mentioned:
"because of being caused by karma, and because of being mutually caused";
the remainder [of the sentence] is that there is a collection of what was not stated.
Therein, he analyzes the phrase "because it has conceptualization as its cause" by saying "from false conceptualizations.
Although conceptualization (*saṃkalpa*) is the longing for an object previously experienced, nevertheless, its prior portion— the experience itself— is what must be understood here.
Because aspiration is a form of attachment, the meaning is that false experience is volition (*saṃkalpa*). [Objection:
But how can there be a diversity of effects from a single false cognition? To this, he says:
Regarding the phrase "from those things that cause attachment, provocation, and delusion":
because these words are listed in the *bhavya-geya* group, the suffix is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).
Delusive conceptualization is the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of false cognition.
He analyzes the fact that passion and the other afflictions have karma as their cause.
By the word "karma," birth is indicated by way of its category.
He states that passion and the other afflictions have a mutual causality by saying "itaretara.
This might be so.

Although the afflictions (*kleśa*) are impermanent, nevertheless, because there is no cause for the cessation of their producer—namely, false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*)—there is an absence of liberation due to the persistence of those very afflictions; therefore, he says:
"all [this] is from the absence of conceptual constructions (*asaṃkalpa*)."

Furthermore, it has been stated that the continuum of afflictions (*kleśasaṃtati*) is beginningless. Why? Because all these internal entities (*ādhyātmika-bhāva*)—the body, the sense faculties, and so forth—are called "internal" because they function with reference to a self (*ātman*).

Now, if there were the cessation even of things that are beginningless, then alas, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the cessation of even those things characterized by non-arising; therefore, he says:
"And this being so, nothing whatsoever is characterized by non-arising.
The meaning is that only those things such as passion (*rāga*) which are characterized by arising are admitted to possess the property of passing away.

Now, it may be argued: "Granted that passion and the like, which are caused by false knowledge, would cease upon the cessation of false knowledge; but as for those [passions] which are caused by karma, how can they cease? Furthermore, there is no cessation of passion and the like upon the cessation of karma, because one who possesses passion and the like lacks the cessation of karma."
Therefore, there would be no liberation; to this he says:

And karma, which brings about rebirth in a particular class of beings, does not become a cause for the arising of passion and the like because the mental constructions consisting of false knowledge have been destroyed by the knowledge of reality.
False knowledge alone is the cause of all passions and the rest.

The intention is that it has been stated that karma is the cause [of rebirth] because karmas, through the restriction of their respective classes (*nikāya*), set in motion passion and the other afflictions.

Now, one might object: "Just as passion and the rest cease when false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) ceases even though karma still exists, so too, even though karma exists, the fruit should not arise once false knowledge has ceased.
To this, he says: "But the experience of pleasure and pain is the fruit."
The Vārttika states:
"For if there were a connection with 'as long as life lasts' (*yāvajjīva*), then the phrase 'or by old age' (*jarayā ha vā*) would be meaningless;
because the sense is already conveyed by [the phrase] 'or by death' (*mṛtyunā vā*). Without stating this, the author of the Vārttika has set forth the second argument mentioned in the Bhāṣya.
By the phrase "because [he] himself is incapable," it is meant that [the Brahmin is the recipient] because he is the means for the sacrifice;
that is to say, because he is the performer of the sacrifice.
He clarifies this very point:
because the sacrificer becomes a constituent part of the sacrifice, as the venerable Jaimini has stated: "And the person [is a constituent], because he exists for the sake of the ritual action."

Karma, which depends on volition (*saṃkalpa*) and so forth, has passion (*rāga*) and the like as its cause. (498/20) Whatever karma is the cause of a particular type of birth manifests only that latent tendency of false knowledge (*mithyājñāna-vāsanā*) appropriate to that birth; by means of this, it becomes the cause of passion and the rest. [The opponent] objects:
Regarding the phrase "of pleasure and so forth":

just as action accompanied by false knowledge is the cause of passion and the like, so too is it the cause of its fruit when accompanied by that [false knowledge]. Thus, the meaning is that for one who possesses the knowledge of reality in their final body, even though action exists, it would not be a cause for the fruit; this is how he provides the rebuttal.

"Not because of independence" means that in order to exhaust the manifold impressions (*karmāśaya*), even though he is undeluded, unattached, and free from aversion, he experiences the fruit of action as if he were deluded, attached, and averse; thus,
action produces its own fruit independently of passion and the like, and by that means, there is this experience of the fruit.
It is not the cause of bondage; rather, for those who are deluded and so forth, it is the experience of the fruits of the causes of bondage that constitutes bondage.
And that [experience] is produced by actions accompanied by passion and the like, not by those independent of passion and the like—thus it is clarified.
Thus ends the first *āhnika* of the fourth chapter in the *Nyāyavārtikatātparyaṭīkā* composed by the venerable Vācaspati Miśra. **The Second Āhnika of the Fourth Chapter** NyS_4.2.1:
Through the knowledge of reality regarding those things caused by defects, there is the cessation of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*).
Thus, doubt, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and the objects of valid cognition (*prameya*) have been examined.
As for the purpose (*prayojana*) and the others, wherever there was doubt, they were examined by this method of successive application (*atideśa*).
Thus, all sixteen categories beginning with the means of valid cognition have been examined.
It has been stated that the knowledge of the reality (*tattvajñāna*) of these [categories] is the cause for attaining the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).

In that regard, it has also been stated that the knowledge of the reality of the objects of cognition (*prameya*) is the direct cause of the supreme good, whereas the knowledge of the reality of the others is so by way of being an auxiliary to that [knowledge].
This is now to be examined here: is the knowledge of the reality of each of the objects of cognition, beginning with the self (*ātman*), the cause for attaining the supreme good, or rather...
The author of the Bhāṣya introduces this investigation with the words: "Of which one part among these?"— that is to say,
does it apply to each and every one of as many objects as there are things to be known?
The meaning is: as many selves as there are according to the distinction of each individual living being, and as many sense organs as there are.
A bystander asks the proponent: "What is the distinction here?
The proponent replies: "Not even one in each [body]."

The prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it is incorrect to say that the attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) results from the knowledge of the reality of the means of valid cognition and so forth, because [the term "knowledge"] cannot logically apply either to the whole or to a part thereof. He states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*):
"False knowledge is indeed delusion (*moha*). The word *vai* expresses the rejection of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), while the word *khalu* has the sense of "because.
The prima facie position is untenable because false knowledge is delusion.

Knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna) is not conducive to the supreme good (niḥśreyasa) merely by the cessation of ignorance; rather, it is so through the destruction of the root cause of saṃsāra by means of its very nature as a perceived fact.
Furthermore, it is not ignorance of reality that is the cause of saṃsāra, but rather false knowledge (mithyājñāna).
Therefore, knowledge of reality is the cause of liberation (apavarga) because it stands in opposition to and destroys that [false knowledge].
"Let this be so; nevertheless, what does it have to do with the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa)? To this he says:
"And that false knowledge, in whatever object it operates...
For it is the self and other things connected to one's own [self] that, when determined erroneously, become the cause of saṃsāra; therefore, it has precisely those as its object.
False knowledge is what must be removed, not the knowledge whose object is the inner self and so forth; therefore, whether false knowledge regarding that [inner self] ceases or does not cease—
using the example of one's own self and so on—
it has no utility whatsoever toward the cessation of saṃsāra.
But for one who applies [knowledge] therein, the knowledge of reality is difficult to attain;
thus he asks: "What, then, is that false knowledge?"
Indeed, there are various conflicting views among disputants.

Some say that the direct realization of non-dual Brahman— which is a mass of pure consciousness and bliss, purified by the shaking off of the manifold proliferation of name-and-form— is the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
Others, however, [define it] as the discriminative knowledge of the difference between the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*;
others [call it] the knowledge of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya-jñāna*);
and the elders [describe it] as the vision of a permanent self distinct from the impermanent body, senses, and so forth.
Thus, there is a question regarding this misconception; the answer is:
the grasping at a self in what is not-self—the delusion that "I am"—is the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*).
First of all, the knowledge of the Self as a single mass of non-dual bliss is not the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*),
because difference, being established by direct perception, cannot be denied in the absence of a subverting proof (*bādhaka*).
Furthermore, luminosity and bliss cannot be the very nature (*svabhāva*) of the Self if they are distinct from the attributes (*dharma*) of the Self.

The Śruti text, "Brahman is truth, consciousness, and bliss," intends bliss and consciousness as powers; thus, their grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is somehow possible through their being possessed of those qualities, even though they are distinct.
If, however, there were non-difference between bliss and consciousness, the simultaneous use of the two terms would be untenable due to their being synonyms.
Furthermore, in the expression "the sun is supreme light," there is no non-difference between "supreme" and "light," because even that which is not light can possess supremacy.

Since light can occur even in things that are not inherently luminous, such as fireflies, this [argument] is trivial. Furthermore, the discernment of the difference between the *sattva* and the *puruṣa* is untenable, because it is impossible for such discernment to arise from *sattva* alone, which is itself a product of primordial nature (*prakṛti*). Since the existence of the Pradhāna is rooted in the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), its refutation follows directly from the refutation of that doctrine.

Since the non-existence of the self in persons and phenomena has been refuted by the demonstration that the doctrine of momentary destruction is itself untenable, it is well said that the grasping at a self where there is no self—the delusion "I am"—is the conceit of "I. For this very reason, every being, even a worm, harbors such a wish for a self, thinking: "May I not cease to be; may I continue to exist."
Such an attachment as this occurs for one who determines the body and so forth to be the self, but not for one who knows the true nature of the self.
Indeed, seeing the body and so forth as distinct from himself—like a snake from its slough—he does not feel affection for it; due to the absence of affection, he does not suffer, nor does he grieve.
Having shown that for one who lacks knowledge of reality there is cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), he states that for one who possesses knowledge of reality there is the cessation of cyclic existence:
"But he for whom [there is] suffering...

Thus, since in the manner described it is the case that delusion and knowledge of reality are the causes of cyclic existence and liberation respectively, the preceding summary begins: "Therefore, by those seeking liberation, the sufferings of rebirth and its fruits must be known," and so forth.
The terms "practicing," "repeatedly exercising," and "cultivating" are synonymous expressions intended to demonstrate the firmness of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Having clarified the meaning, he recites the Sūtra regarding this point:
"From the knowledge of reality concerning the causes of defects, there is the cessation of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*)."
The summary of the meaning of the treatise is restated; the meaning is that the summary of the purport of the treatise is restated by the second sūtra.

As for the commentary (*bhāṣya*) beginning with "But what indeed, sir?", it is inappropriate because liberation is not caused by knowledge of the mere object, but rather by knowledge of the true nature of the objects of cognition (*prameya*);
therefore, the author of the Vārttika says:
Regarding the phrase "of other objects" (*viṣayāntarāṇām*):
the meaning is that "as many objects as there are" does not refer merely to objects (*viṣaya*) in general, but rather refers to objects of cognition (*prameya*).
The rest of the commentary (*vārttika*) is easy to understand. // 1 //
NyS 4.2.2: Form and the other sense objects, which are the causes of defects, are produced by conceptual construction.

It has been stated that the notion of self regarding the body and other non-self entities must be eliminated. In this regard, when the question arises as to where first the notion of self should be eliminated, he says:

"But indeed, by means of the sequence of higher discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*). Higher discernment is the knowledge of reality born of meditative absorption (*samādhi*); and since that is easier to accomplish with respect to its object, it is appropriate for the beginner to apply effort toward that very thing first.
The Sūtra:
The causes of defects are the objects, such as forms and so forth, which are produced by conceptual construction. (Sūtra 2)
The meaning is that they are made objects by that [mind] through false knowledge and volition;
"desires" (kāmāḥ) refers to things worthy of being desired. // 2 //
But the misconception of a "whole" (avayavin) is caused by that [collection].
Others, indeed, while seeking to eliminate the notion of a whole (*avayavin*), deny the whole itself; addressing those who deny it, he says: "Beyond this, [the Sūtra states]:
'But the conceit of a whole is caused by that' (Sūtra 3)."

The *nimitta* (sign) consists of features such as the whiteness [of the teeth] and so forth; the objects qualified by these are the *saṃjñās* (notions). A lover, experiencing the individual parts of his beloved—such as her teeth, lips, nose, and so on—becomes attached to her.

The *vyañjanas* (minor marks) are the parts of the whole; because they are perceived together with it, their *anuvyañjana* (counter-mark) is the resemblance to them, through which that [resemblance] is superimposed upon it.
And such indeed is the conduct of women:

"If she possesses limbs languid from the weight of breasts that have the grace of the temples of the elephant who is the sole vehicle for the sport of the Bodiless One (Kāma), and a luster as pure as molten gold;"
If my beloved were not embraced, and if the *Siddhasaṃjīvinī* herb had not been discovered, how could we endure otherwise the pain of the arrows of the God of the Uneven Bow?
This person, plunging into this river of Love— which is delightful with the sandbanks of her hips and the whirlpools of her navel-region,
graced by the lotus of her face and the surging waves of her eyebrows— has cast off the exhaustion caused by the fire of long separation.
But those who possess discernment, contemplating the perception of the impure, say:
"Women are leather bags sewn together with sinews and veins, filled with marrow, bones, spleens, livers, and even excrement."
The sages also said:
"Because of its place of origin, its seed, its support, its outflow, and its end,
and because it must be purified by external means, the wise indeed know the body to be impure."
He states the purpose of cultivating the perception of the foul: "for one who cultivates that."

Now, one might ask: "In that case, do the parts (*avayava*) and the secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*) have no object [for the perception of impurity], and is there only the supreme object of the perception of the foul (*aśubhasaṃjñā*)?
To this, he says:
"And even when the two kinds of objects exist."

Although this object characterized by a desirable woman is indeed twofold, nevertheless, for the sake of abandoning passion and the like, its status as an object of notions such as "limbs" and so forth is set aside, and its status as an object of the notion of "impurity" is adopted; the meaning is that this is done to produce detachment.
Regarding this very point, he provides an illustration:
As in the expression "mixed with poison":
it is not that honey and poison do not exist in an ultimate sense; rather, the designation "poison" is applied there for the sake of cultivating detachment—this is the meaning. // 3 //
NyS 4.2.4: Doubt arises because knowledge and ignorance are each of two kinds.

Thus, having stated the instruction on *prasaṃkhyāna* according to his own view, he introduces the refutation of the *prasaṃkhyāna* favored by others. Now, the Vijñānavādin, intending to refute the [external] object, establishes the refutation of the composite whole (*avayavin*).
Indeed, the notions of "parts" (*avayava*) and "subtle characteristics" (*anuvyañjana*) pertain to specific objects.
In that regard, since the mere object does not exist, how could there be the notions of parts and secondary characteristics?
To refute these, first the possessor of parts (the whole) is refuted, and afterwards the atom; thus, the intention is that consciousness alone, devoid of an object, is established.
In this context, since an investigation is preceded by doubt, he first states the doubt:
"Doubt arises from the twofold nature of knowledge and ignorance" (Sūtra 4).
Apprehension is knowledge, and non-apprehension is ignorance.
That which exists is apprehended, such as water in a pond;
that which does not exist is apprehended, such as water in a mirage in the desert.
That which exists is not perceived, such as a treasure buried deep in the earth;
that which does not exist is not perceived, such as a jar or similar object when the ground is visible, because it would be capable of being perceived under those same conditions.
Thus, due to this twofold nature of knowledge and ignorance, there is doubt regarding the existence of a whole (*avayavin*).
The meaning is: even if the whole (*avayavin*) is perceived, there is still doubt;
and even if it is not perceived, there is likewise doubt. NyS 4.2.5: That [doubt] does not arise, because the previous reason is well-established.
In this regard, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin), intending to refute even the reason for the denial of the whole (avayavin) that will be stated later, says:
"That [is] not doubtful, because the previous reason is well-established" (Sūtra 5).
[This refers to] the possessor of parts (*avayavin*).
However, the author of the *Vārttika* himself refutes the doubt [that it might be the cause], stating:
"The twofold nature of knowledge and ignorance is not the cause of doubt" (502.21). 4–5.
Furthermore, doubt does not arise even because the occurrence [of the reason] is impossible.
The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādin) says: "Because the occurrence [of the self] is untenable. (Sūtra 6)
NyS 4.2.7: Because the parts do not subsist either wholly or partially [in the whole], the whole does not exist.

Following common worldly understanding— that "the tree stands in its branches and so forth," or "the branches and so forth are the tree"— the author of the Vārttika conceptualizes [the relationship] as "parts" and "the whole. Consequently,
it follows that a part would be a single substance.
Why? Because they subsist in a single substance.
To the question, "Let that be so; what is the fault? he says:
"And there is no substance consisting of a single entity that can serve as a substrate without perishing."
The ellipsis is "because it would entail that what is produced is eternal. Regarding the phrase "by means of a part of the whole" (*avayavyekadeśena*):
the meaning is that the constituent part (*avayava*) exists in the whole (*avayavin*) by means of those parts of the whole which are themselves [parts].
For this whole does not have other parts as its constituent portions within its own parts; and because it does not reside in those [parts], the whole would be non-existent.
If it were begun by a single part, there would be the consequence of its production being continuous.
For it is said that the operation of the parts is for the sake of conjunction, and the causes of that [conjunction] are required;

since there is no requirement for conjunction regarding the production of a single substance, the composite (avayavin) would be produced as long as there is a part, and thus a part not occupied by a composite would never be seen—this is the meaning. (7–8)
And because it does not exist separately from its parts.

If it existed apart from its parts, the whole would be perceived [independently]; yet no other substratum for it is perceived. Furthermore, you yourself as a proponent have admitted that a visible part is not the locus of this [whole]. With this intention, he says:
"And it would have to be eternal. (9)
Nor are the parts the whole.

But as for one who thinks that the whole (avayavin) is merely a property (dharma) of the parts, yet is neither absolutely different nor non-different from the parts—since if it were different, the relationship of property and possessor of property would be untenable, like that between a cow and a horse; and if there were non-difference, that relationship would likewise be untenable because it would be identical to the nature of the possessor of the property itself—he says this in response: "The whole is in some way different and in some way non-different from the parts, and it is merely a property of the parts. To him, [the author] replies:
And the whole is not [identical to] its parts. (Sūtra 10)
It has already been stated that difference and non-difference cannot both coexist in a single locus as mutual negations.

Nor can there be a relationship between property and property-possessor (*dharmadharmibhāva*) when there is absolute non-difference. Therefore, just as a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is accepted to exist only between certain things despite their absolute difference, so too must a relationship between property and property-possessor be accepted to exist only between certain things.
And such is the refutation; this is the meaning.
And since the whole (avayavin) exists in a part by means of one of its parts, it follows that the whole would be merely a collection of parts. This is the meaning:
for that which exists in a part is called the "whole."
If the parts of the whole reside in the constituent parts by way of their own parts, then the whole would exist only in those parts;
and since those parts are manifold, it follows that the whole is merely a collection of parts.

Regarding the claim that "the whole (avayavin) exists in one part or one location," the whole does not reside in any single part at all, because its constituent parts reside in their respective locations. Furthermore, since the whole is apprehended only through those [parts], it ought to be perceived precisely where its own part resides.
And thus, since a single part of the cloth exists in one thread, the cloth would be perceived in that single thread; such is the meaning. // 10 //
NyS 4.2.11: Since there is no differentiation within a single entity, the application of words denoting differentiation is untenable; therefore, the question is invalid.
The proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntavādin) says:
"Even in the absence of other members [of the syllogism], it is not a non-reason because it does not apply [to the subject]. (NyS 4.2.12)
Furthermore, regarding the thesis that "the whole does not reside in its own parts by way of partial presence," the reason "because of the absence of other parts" is not a valid reason (*ahetu*).

Why? Even if there are other parts belonging to the whole, it is still the case that those other parts reside in the other parts of the whole; what, then, has this to do with the mode of residence of the whole itself?
Moreover, one who maintains the thesis that "one [entity] resides in many" should not be questioned as to whether it resides "in its entirety" or "by way of partial presence. Why?
Because it would involve a contradiction for a single whole to exist either entirely or partially through a plurality of things that are inherent in a single object;
relying on this, he says: "If the whole does not exist neither partially nor entirely, then how does it exist?"
If it is objected that this is doubtful because no other form has been specified,
he states a parable with a touch of irony:
"Just as threads that are not variegated produce a variegated cloth."
It is said that the Naiyāyikas accept that a variegated cloth is produced from non-variegated threads;
however, this is incorrect.
For a single variegated color residing in the cloth is not possible, as that would contradict their own statement.
For "various" (*nānā*) is said to be "manifold" (*citram*); how then could it be one? Therefore, what is expressed by "the manifold is not one" is expressed by "the manifold is one.
As they say: "...if you claim that the manifold is one, this is a most wonderful and great thing!"
Nor is it correct to say that it is blue, yellow, and so forth— many such non-pervasive [qualities]— that constitute the locus of the term "variegated" (*citra*),

because colors and the like are pervasive (*vyāpyavṛtti*). These very subjects under dispute, blue, yellow, and so forth, must be pervasive within their substratum, because they belong to the class of color (*rūpajātīyatva*).
"Like the form residing in a white cloth"—this mockery is justified, as it is like saying that threads which are not variegated produce a variegated cloth. He refutes this:
because [the cloth] is the substrate for a form that is not perceived [in the threads].
By one who says, "Let the form of the whole (avayavin) be specified," [it must be asked]:

since that which has parts is a "whole" (avayavī), and a part (avayava) is its cause, while the possessor of those parts—the whole—is the effect; from where does this acceptance of the relation of cause and effect arise?
Furthermore, there exists no such thing as a "reductio ad absurdum" (prasaṅgasādhana) that constitutes a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).

However, this would be mere reasoning (*tarka*); and the meaning is that this [reasoning] cannot establish an object as valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) without the procedural requirements (*itikartavyatā*) of valid knowledge.

Furthermore, as for the example of a variegated cloth-form which you cited with the intent of derision: whatever your underlying intention regarding it may be, this example appears to us based on your statement alone.
Moreover, since an example must be a point of non-dispute between the proponent and the opponent, your attempt to prove it is futile.

Nevertheless, even while accepting this "wondrous doctrine" (citravāda), we say to you: "We shall establish that the variegated form belongs to the cloth," for the purpose of refuting the mockery that pervades your own intention.
The point is that the very experience—"the variegated form of the cloth"—is here the uncontradicted means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
The Buddhist reveals his own position, saying: "If [you say] there would be the consequence of multiplicity."
He refutes [this], because the word "variegated" (citra) has both a single and a multiple object as its referent.
If "variegated" were said to apply only to the multiple, then there would be a contradiction; however, the term "variegated" is indeed employed even with respect to a single thing.

Therefore, the meaning is that there is no contradiction for this [consciousness] in its unity. The teacher says: "No, because it is not observed in a single [instance]," meaning that such an experience apprehending a variegated [object] is not observed in a single [moment].

The point is this: where indeed are words that function independently of the speaker's intention not easily found? He refutes [the objection] with the words, "not so, because it would involve abandoning what has been accepted" (507/1).

To begin with, the word *citra* cannot be understood as a synonym for multiple things (*aneka*), nor can it enter into grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the term *aneka* in the expression "multiple variegated things" (*anekaṃ citram*).

Since the simultaneous employment of synonymous terms is logically untenable, yet we observe the usage "many variegated [colors]," it must be accepted that just as white things are many, so too are variegated things many. Thus, the meaning is that just as for one who does not accept a single white [color], the acceptance of the multiplicity of white [colors] is lost, so too for one who does not accept a single variegated [color], the acceptance of the multiplicity of variegated [colors] is lost.
He states another objection:
"Now, [if you say] it is manifold and not variegated. He refutes this:
"Even so," he objects;
"or perhaps they are not variegated."
He thus refutes [the objection] by saying, "And so, nothing at all [is lost].

For we indeed accept that a variegated color (*citra-rūpa*) is produced in the whole (*avayavin*) by means of white, green, red, and other colors inherent in its parts, which serve as its non-inherent causes (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*). He explains this with the example of the interior of a folded cloth.
Thus;
"another fold" means another side;
he avoids it.
"This has been stated by you yourself.
Thinking that even a single quality initiates [the effect], he raises an objection: "In that case, there would be a variegated cognition."
"It is concentrated, not attached.

Now, one might object: "Should not the color of the whole (avayavin), which is produced from variegated and non-variegated [parts], also be pointed out just like yellow and so forth? Since it cannot be pointed out, it does not exist.
To this, he says: "To this extent."
The meaning is that even though it is inexpressible, it is being experienced and cannot be denied;
for example, the great difference in sweetness between sugarcane juice and other substances.
To begin with, it is not logical for the whole to be perceived through the form and other qualities of its parts.

Visual perceptibility is not observed in one substance by way of the form of another substance; indeed, air is not visually perceptible by way of the form of earth and so forth—this is the meaning. He concludes the subject under discussion with the words "Therefore."
The meaning is that they are non-conceptualized and non-examined. (508/5) // 12 //
The perception of that [collection] is like the perception of a mass of hair by one suffering from ophthalmia.

NyS_4.2.14: Due to the sharpness or dullness of the sense organ within the limits of its own object, the apprehension of the object occurs accordingly; there is no operation [of the sense] upon what is not its object.

"Because the whole (avayavin) is not established, there is no apprehension of anything at all"—thus the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin), having been confronted with this objection, says the following.

The sūtra, bhāṣya, and vārtika beginning with "Because its apprehension is like the perception of a mass of hair by one suffering from ophthalmia" have their meanings clear to both the prima facie and the final positions. 13–14.
And in this way, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress of parts and sub-parts until the dissolution of the world.
Furthermore, he states that this alternative regarding the mode of subsistence is untenable because it contradicts the nature of the substratum:
"And thus there would be the consequence of [an infinite regress of] parts and wholes until the dissolution of the world" (Sūtra 15).
In this regard, three positions are possible:

[the position that] this consequence— the non-existence of the whole (avayavin) resulting from the impossibility of its existence in its parts— is refuted either at the time of cosmic dissolution (pralaya), or at the level of the atom (paramāṇu), or it is not refuted anywhere at all.
In this regard, this sūtra is based on the first and second alternatives:

just as the conceptualization of existence (*vṛtti-vikalpa*) regarding a gross object such as a jar would, due to the absence of that [object], cease at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*)—since it would reside in its parts and their parts, and those too would be absent—at that time, dissolution cannot be an object of perception devoid of all description. Therefore, due to the absence of an object of perception, the conceptualization, being without a basis, does not even find its own self.
And this [phrase] "up to the dissolution" is an illustration;
it should also be understood as "down to the atom.
Since even atoms, being beyond the senses, lack the status of being objects of perception, the state of conceptual construction having no basis remains exactly as it was.
This has been stated: "Or [the world] would cease from the partless atom. Now, as for the phrase "even so": NyS 4.2.16: "There is no dissolution, because of the existence of atoms."
Moreover, this is the meaning:
furthermore, this was stated—"until the dissolution"—having accepted the possibility of dissolution;
however, in reality:
There is no dissolution, because atoms exist eternally. (Sūtra 16)
He states the proof for its partlessness:
"But the atom is indeed partless. (16)
Or else, [the atom] is beyond the point of division.
Now, one might ask: why does this division of parts and wholes not continue infinitely? To this, he says:
"Or [the process stops] beyond the atom" (Sūtra 17).
*Truṭi* and *trasareṇu* are not different in meaning.
The particle of dust known as *trasareṇu* is that which resides in a sunbeam passing through a lattice.
If, beyond the *truṭi*, a division of parts does not persist for two or three steps, then, due to the non-termination of the division of parts, [the atom is established].

Because substances are innumerable, the state of being an atom (*truṭi*) would cease to exist; even an atom would then have the same magnitude as Mount Sumeru. The meaning is that, since they possess infinite parts, there is indeed no distinction between them.
Or rather, until the dissolution (*pralaya*) or until the cessation [of conceptualization].

In the view that [the world] consists of atoms at the time of dissolution, there is no cessation of conceptualization, yet the object of perception does not exist; thus, conceptualization is without a basis.

The meaning is that, since everything possesses infinite parts and is as if permeated by conceptualization, there is an absence of objects of perception, and therefore conceptualization is without a basis.
This is an illustration by way of number:
"And so many atoms, when aggregated, attain the state of a *truṭi*.
However, if [the atom] possesses parts (*sāvayavatva*), the meaning of the word "atom" (*paramāṇu*) must be stated.

What is meant by "atom" (*paramāṇu*)? It is an atom (*aṇu*) characterized by being "ultimate" (*parama*), in the sense that there is nothing smaller than it. Therefore, if there were something else even smaller than that, it would not be an atom characterized by ultimacy; this is the meaning. Alternatively, if the parts of the atom possessed different dimensions, they would necessarily have dimensions smaller than [the atom] itself.
Therefore, it is not the atom (*paramāṇu*) itself that is being negated; rather, the parts of the atom are themselves called "atoms," and because they lack further parts, they are not effects.
You, however, having superimposed the notion that an effect produced by atoms is itself an "atom," negate it through the threefold analysis of its existence. // 17 //
That [creation] is untenable because of its interpenetration with space.
Now, the proponent of non-apprehension (anupalambhika), addressing one who thinks that everything is non-existent, says:

"Because it is interpenetrated by space, it is impossible for that atom to be partless; but if it were to have parts, its non-existence would follow from the dilemma regarding its mode of existence. Thus, emptiness alone is the reality of all things."
Even though conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is without foundation, being produced merely through the imagination of worldly convention, it leads one to understand ultimate emptiness;
for even false cognitions are seen to be causes for the realization of reality,
just as the continuous stream of perceptions of an elephant from afar regarding a tree is the cause for the comprehension of the true nature of that tree.

The sense is that many such [objections] are to be imagined, such as: "Just as a line-drawn cow or a gavaya [is not the real thing], so too is the cognition of 'gavaya-ness' [not the real thing]. The author of this Vārttika refutes this by stating:
"If it is asserted that the atom is impermanent because of its interpenetration with space (ākāśa), one must ask what the meaning of 'interpenetration' (vyatiśreḍa) is."
Thus:
"Or else, [the reason] would be the non-omnipresence of space. (NyS 4.2.19)
NyS 4.2.20: Since internal and external [space] are stated to be the causes of other substances that are effects, it follows that they do not exist in that which is not an effect.
(511/4) The statement "internal and external" is a statement regarding another cause of the effect;
(512/3) the meaning is that "another cause" refers to a specific cause, and it is a statement concerning that.

Having [provisionally] accepted the parts of the atom, [the author] states that space is not the cause of its division; thus, by the phrase "due to the interpenetration of space," he refers to the division—that is, the separation—caused by space.
The meaning is that space is not the cause of the disjunction between two substances being divided; rather, it is action [that is the cause].
That which is unobstructed on all sides and lacks constituent parts in its center is called a "void" (*supira*).
This refers to a whole (*avayavin*) that is continuous and unobstructed on all sides, by way of its own constituent parts.
This is what is meant:
that which has parts situated around it without any interval, and which lacks anything in its center—that is a cavity (*suṣira*).
It is connected with every material thing (*mūrtimat*).

It appears that the author of the Vārttika’s acceptance of the conjunction of the partless (aja-saṃyoga), when asserting that all reality consists in being connected with everything that possesses form, is merely a bold assertion (prauḍhivāda). // 19–20 //
And because conjunction and sound are all-pervasive, [ether] is omnipresent.
NyS_4.2.22: Non-obstruction, non-resistance, and omnipresence are the properties of space.
It might be argued:

"If space were all-pervading, then because it would obstruct corporeal substances, there would be an obstruction of their movement and the production of a different configuration, as occurs with a boat in a flood of water; yet this is not the case.
Therefore, space is not all-pervading. To this, he says:
Non-obstruction, non-resistance, and omnipresence are the properties of space. (Sūtra 22)
The meaning is that precisely because there is no mental projection (*avyūha*) and no obstruction (*aviṣṭambha*), his sovereign power (*vibhutva*) is unimpeded (*apratyūha*). // 22 //
And because the configuration of corporeal things is possible, there exists the reality of constituent parts.
Furthermore, the proponent of emptiness objects:
"Because the occurrence of shape is possible only for things possessing form, there must be the existence of parts" (Sūtra 23).
The commentary (*vārttika*) sets aside the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

Although the aphorism (*sūtra*) mentions "possessing form" (*mūrtimat*) merely in the sense of being related [to something], the author of the commentary explains it as a statement of the reason (*hetu*):
"Atoms possess parts because they possess form, like a jar and so forth."
(513/19) He states another argument: "Because it possesses shape" (saṃsthānavattvāt). // 23 //
And because conjunction is possible.
He recites another sutra together with its commentary:
"And because conjunction is possible" (Sūtra 24).
Thus:
NyS 4.2.25: There is no refutation [of the objection], because it would lead to an infinite regress and because an infinite regress is untenable.
He points out the redundancy; [the opponent] replies, "Is this not so? (514/4). He refutes it.
"It is not that its purpose has been fulfilled":

"Form" (*mūrti*) refers to the sixfold dimension (*parimāṇa*) of a non-pervasive substance (*dravya*). The states of extreme shortness (*paramāṇutva*) and extreme minuteness (*paramahasvatva*) reside only in an extremely subtle substance; however, by including the pervasive [substance], there are eight kinds of dimensions, including extreme largeness (*paramamahattva*) and extreme length (*paramadīrghatva*).
Furthermore, because it possesses supreme magnitude and supreme length, and is all-pervading and omnipresent, it is not a material form (*mūrti*).
This is because of the statement of the Great Sage (*pāramarṣa*): "Material form is the dimension of a substance that is not all-pervading.

As for what is called "configuration" (*saṃsthāna*), it is a conjunction known as "accumulation" (*pracaya*) residing in things such as jars; it is the cause for the manifestation of universals such as "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*).
Conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is merely conjunction; it is not, however, "attainment after non-attainment.
Therefore, there is no tautology.
This [point] refutes that doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
As for the argument "because it possesses form," the proponent of emptiness (śūnyatāvādin), with the conviction that [all things] end in dissolution, says: "Now then... and so forth.
The proponent says: "The end is partless.
The meaning is that the state of having dissolution as its limit has already been established below.

Now, one might object: "Surely, since disjunction has been refuted below [in the case of destruction], let it be that disjunction does not end with dissolution; rather, it will have a further end. What is the point of insisting that its limit is the atom? To this, he raises the doubt: "Suppose, then, that disjunction has an end. He then refutes it:
"That is not tenable" means that there can be no quality when the possessor of the quality does not exist.
And only this many kalpas are possible.

Regarding these, he says that in the first kalpa there would be the faults of uncertainty and contradiction; in the second, the consequence that the division would lack a substratum; and in the third, the consequence that the atom would be immeasurable.
Thus, "this collection of kalpas would be only this much."
By asserting that division terminates at the atom (*paramāṇu*), you accept an atom that is partless yet possesses form.
However, if [division] were infinite, it would follow that a discrete object (*truṭi*) is immeasurable, which is a contradiction.
Furthermore, if [division] terminated at the dissolution of the world (*pralaya*), it would follow that division lacks a substratum, which is a contradiction.

The meaning of the term "having parts" (sāvayava) is not merely that which is composed of homogeneous parts, but rather that which is supported by them; for instance, a substance such as a cloth, though composed of threads and the like, is also supported by those very threads and so forth. [Objection: Even if this is so, from what does its "having parts" follow? To this, he says:
The "part" (*avayava*) is its substratum—that is, the substratum of that effect-substance (*kāryadravya*) which is composed of constituents of the same genus.

Therefore, being composed of parts (*sāvayavatva*) is a specific property of an effect. Consequently, by asserting that "atoms (*paramāṇu*) are composed of parts," one is effectively saying that the atom is a specific effect;
and for an atom to be a specific effect is a contradiction.
(515/2) But if [atoms] were infinite, it would follow that they are immeasurable due to their fragmentation.

Indeed, that which is imagined as partless, owing to its extreme subtlety, is called an "atom" (*paramāṇu*); by this, what is meant by "atom" is that it is partless and unproduced. What is meant by "having parts" (*sāvayava*) is that it has parts and is produced.
The meaning is that there is a contradiction between the two parts of the proposition (*pratijñā*).
Now, lest there be non-apprehensibility (*aprameyatva*) of the atom, you might maintain that the atom is preceded by a single [other] atom;
the rest has its meaning self-evident.
If it is argued that [the term] is spoken with reference to two substances:
for, regarding the conjunctions of a central atom with its neighboring atoms on the sides, the conjunction of that central atom with the atom in front does not reside in the atom behind the center;
likewise, the conjunction of the central atom does not at all reside in the atom in front of the center.
Thus it should be understood in other cases as well;
since all six [elements] occupy distinct locations, their co-location is unestablished.
Now, if it is said with reference to a central atom that is related to [other] atoms—that the six types of conjunctions exist as dependent upon it—the author replies:
"Nothing is contradicted.
This might be so.

He restates the objection raised by others—that because atoms are conjoined and occupy the same location, they would all be conjoined and occupy the same location, resulting in the absurd consequence that a composite object would be no larger than a single atom—with the words:
"As for this [which has been said]... (yatpunaretat).
He refutes that [position] with "That is not so":
where something is inherent in another, that is its substrate, just as substance is for color and other qualities.
Atoms do not inhere anywhere; rather, it is their conjunctions that do so.
Therefore, while it may be granted that the conjunctions—which possess spatial location—occupy the same location, this cannot be said of the atoms themselves, because they lack spatial location.
Thus he explains.
Now, as for the phrase "the effect and the cause":
just as in the case of "the jujube fruit in this bowl," where the jujube fruit occupies the very location of the bowl, so too do its parts occupy the locations of their own parts.
And it is not only *samavāya* (inherence) that serves as the basis for the relation between a locus and its occupant; rather, *saṃyoga* (conjunction) does so as well.
For in this case, the cognition of the supported and the support—such as "the jujube fruit is in the bowl" or "whiteness is in the cloth"—is not distinguished [as being distinct entities].
Therefore, because many substances are observed to occupy the same location, the example is not unestablished; such is the meaning. He refutes that [objection] as follows:
This has been refuted by not accepting [that premise].
We deny that substances occupy the same location through inherence (*samavāya*), but not through conjunction (*saṃyoga*);
for it is through inherence that occupying the same location is the adversary of grossness (*sthaulya*).
Just as odor, taste, color, and touch—though occupying the same location—do not initiate grossness, for what reason? Because these formless [qualities] co-inhere in the same location.

But as for material things possessing touch, which occupy different locations through their co-inherence yet are mutually conjoined—if they were to initiate grossness, what would be contradicted? Therefore, if those joined by conjunction were to initiate grossness, what would be contradicted? Thus, by means of conjunction...

It is not the state of occupying the same location that is denied, but rather [coexistence] through inherence (*samavāya*) that is denied; for it has been established that such [inherence] is incompatible with grossness.
This was stated while provisionally accepting the view that conjunctions occupy the same location.
In ultimate reality, however, the locus of the conjunction between a bowl and a jujube fruit is the bowl and the jujube fruit themselves.

He states that conjunctions also occupy distinct locations, establishing that the conjunction between the pot and the jujube fruit resides in the parts of the pot and the parts of the jujube fruit; thus he says:
"Nor are the conjunctions [unitary]," and so forth. He concludes:

Regarding the statement "because the six [atoms] occupy the same location," as for what was further stated: "it is not logical for that which possesses a distinction of direction and location to be a single entity."
It is said that for a single atom as conceived by you, there are six spatial directions;

yet, since there can be no internal division within a single [atom], there would have to be six atoms [occupying those directions]. He refutes this, asking: "Who says that there is a distinction of spatial directions [within it]?"
The meaning is that space (*dik*), being unitary in its essential nature (*svarūpa*) and all-pervading, possesses no internal differentiation.

If space is indeed one, then how can there be these various distinctions in cognition and designation regarding an atom—such as "this atom is to the east of that" or "this is to the west"? To this, he says:
"And the distinctions of direction and place are the conjunctions of directions. Even though space is one, [an atom] is conjoined with a location proximate to the place where the sun rises.

That atom which is conjoined with a location distant from this [central] one is the eastern [atom]; likewise, that which is conjoined with a location proximate to the place where the sun sets is the western [atom]. With respect to those two atoms—the eastern and the western—that conjunction with a location distant from the places of sunrise and sunset is the "middle" (madhyavatī).

In this way, those two atoms situated on the sides of the central atom, which are connected to a horizontal direction and stand in a straight line with it, are the southern and northern atoms; likewise, proximity to the sun when it is at midday and distance from it constitute smallness, while being delimited by the former number and being delimited by the latter number constitute abundance.

Therefore, even for a single atom, the conjunctions with other atoms are merely partial [occupancies] that do not pervade the whole. Likewise, for space as well, the conjunctions with even a single [atom] are merely its parts. Thus, this simultaneous conjunction of an atom with six [other atoms] is caused solely by its corporeality (*mūrtatva*), not by its having parts (*sāvayavatva*);
therefore, it cannot prove that the atom has parts.

Therefore, that which is stated by opponents as a *prasaṅgasādhana*—namely, "whatever is devoid of parts is not conjoined with six [other atoms], just like consciousness; and so is the atom"—is refuted. This is because the pervasion of conjunction with six [atoms] by having parts (*sāvayavatva*) is unestablished, since such conjunction is instead necessitated by corporeality (*mūrtatva*).
Even the occurrence of shadow and light on an atom is possible because a single conjunction does not pervade [the whole].
Now, it was asked how an infinite regress (anavasthā) is not established; to this, the Commentator says:
"Because in the case of an infinite regress, there would be an infinity of constituent parts of the substance for every locus."

The author of the Vārttika refutes the reasons, such as "because of possessing activity" and so forth, by considering them in every possible way; as for those [reasons] beginning with "because of possessing activity," they are [rejected] on the grounds that they are unestablished (*asiddha*).
The meaning is that for one who does not accept a whole (avayavin) such as a jar, it is impossible for a jar or the like to exist.
Furthermore, because the possessive suffix *matup* is observed to denote something other than its base, it is contradictory;
the meaning is that for one who does not accept action as something distinct from the atom, the use of the possessive suffix *matup* is contradictory. // 25 //

But the non-perception of the true nature of entities resulting from their analysis by the intellect is like the non-perception of the existence of a cloth when the threads are pulled away; thus, there is no perception of that [inherent nature].

The Vijñānavādin says: regarding this which you call "cognitions," if a cloth were distinct from its threads, it would be perceived as separate from them, just as a cow is perceived as distinct from a horse; yet it is not so perceived. Therefore, this notion that "this is a cloth" is a false cognition.
The notion of a "thread" is also a false cognition, because it is not perceived as distinct from its constituent parts; likewise, the notion of a "part" is also false.
Thus, by this sequence, when even atoms are analyzed by the intellect, no external object exists, since its true nature is not perceived.

Whether [an object] be gross or subtle, all cognitions whatsoever are false, for they apprehend their own internal forms as if they were external objects. Now, while it may be granted that cloth and other such things possess parts, atoms—being partless—cannot be analyzed away by the intellect; therefore, through the analysis of entities by the intellect, their true nature is perceived. To this [it is replied]:
He said:
"Even atoms, when divided part by part, continue until their dissolution."
Let atoms be partless; however, when they are mentally analyzed through their six conjunctions, their true nature is perceived. // 26 //
NyS 4.2.27: It is not a valid reason because it is contradictory.
He refutes this as follows:
"Because it is contradictory, it is not a valid reason.
That whose true nature is not perceived when it is being analyzed must be distinguished from something else.
Because that [destruction] would be impossible in the absence of a limit (*avadhi*);
and thus, by means of that limit, it must abide somewhere.
For it has been stated that if there were no such abiding, the consequence would follow that the break (*truṭi*) is immeasurable.

Therefore, it must reside either in the atoms or in their conjunctions. And thus, that from which a thing is analytically separated is itself the ultimate limit of its reality, which is apprehended in its true nature. Consequently, it is established that there is no contradiction, because when all things are analyzed by the intellect, they are found to be untenable.
He states another refutation:
"the non-arising of all entities.

(250/5) Since the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is also an entity, if that [means of valid cognition] were not established because it is included within those [entities], then the result would be the non-arising of all entities; such is the meaning. // 27 //
Because it has that as its substratum, there is no separate apprehension of it.
Because it has that as its basis, it is not perceived separately. (Sūtra 28)
One who asserts "because they are not perceived as distinct" should be questioned:
does this mean there is an absence of conventional usage based on difference, or an absence of actual difference,
or that [the cloth] is not perceived in another location apart from the threads?
Thus [it is argued].
First, the initial [position] is not tenable, for while the threads are cognized by a cognition of distinct appearances, the cloth is cognized by a cognition of non-distinct appearance.
Nor is the second [position] tenable.

Because threads occupy the region of the warp-threads, and a cloth occupies the region of the threads; therefore, the fact that [the cloth] is not perceived elsewhere than in the threads—that is, its non-separate apprehension—is logically possible even if there is a difference [between them], by virtue of its being dependent upon them. Thus, it cannot lead to the conclusion of non-difference. As for the Bhāṣya: "But through mental analysis, there is a separate apprehension of entities, even in the case of atoms which transcend the senses."
Where indeed both the part and the whole are perceptible by the senses, there is a distinct apprehension for those who lack discernment;

that is to say, it is extremely clear that there is a distinct apprehension of the wholes—which are visible through direct perception and dependent upon those parts—from the atoms which are beyond the senses and known only through inference. // 28 //
And because the understanding of the meaning [of a treatise] arises from the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
Now, he states the separate apprehension of the whole (*avayavin*), even when its sensory constituent parts are being analyzed according to their true nature:
"And because the object is understood through a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇataś cārthapratipatteḥ*).

That which exists—the substance that is a whole, such as a cloth—and the manner in which it exists, namely, by way of inhering in its own parts and by way of being a substratum for qualities; [all this is established through valid cognition].
That which does not exist— such as a rabbit’s horn—
and that which exists through the relationship of cause and effect— all that is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) through perception.
The commentary is easy to understand. // 29 //
NyS 4.2.30: [The non-existence of the self is established] by means of the impossibility and possibility of the instruments of valid cognition.
NyS 4.2.31: This conceit regarding the means of valid cognition and the objects of valid cognition is like the conceit regarding objects in a dream.

Regarding what was stated— that because of the establishment or non-establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no non-establishment of all things— the Proponent of Consciousness (*vijñānavādin*) objects:
"This conceit regarding the means of valid cognition and the objects of cognition is like the conceit regarding the objects in a dream" (Sūtra 31).

Indeed, the relationship between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the object of cognition (*prameya*) is not real; rather, it depends upon conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) based on beginningless predispositions (*vāsanā*). For just as objects do not exist in a dream yet appear through mere conceptual construction, so too is the emptiness of external objects established by this conventional, non-ultimately real relationship between the means and object of cognition, which is observed among conditions (*pratyaya*) as ultimately real.
The meaning is that it has already been explained previously that even false cognitions can serve as causes for the realization of reality.
The author of the Vārttika explains this:
"Just as there are no objects in a dream... (31).
Or rather, it is like an illusion, a city of Gandharvas, or a mirage.
[Objection: "Granted that dream-cognitions have such a nature; but what follows for those waking cognitions which are directed toward pillars or jars? For they are utterly different [from dreams].
To this, he says:
"Illusion, Gandharva-city," and so forth.
The meaning is that even waking cognitions are seen to be of this same nature by the thousands, and these cognitions of pillars, jars, and so forth are not distinct from them. // 32 //
NyS 4.2.33: There is no proof because of the absence of a reason.
He refutes this as follows:
"Because of the absence of a reason, there is no proof" (Sūtra 33).
And the conceit regarding the objects of a dream is like memory and mental construction.
The author of the Commentary (Bhāṣyakāra) explains this:
"Like the conceit of objects at the end of a dream.
Although the word *anta* denotes a part, it is used here for the state (*avasthā*) merely in the sense of being dependent upon it.
This means "in the state of dreaming.

What is being said is this: for one who maintains that dream-cognition is not in accordance with reality (*ayāthārthya*), since that [lack of correspondence] would otherwise be untenable, a waking cognition must be stated as its sublater (*bādhaka*).
And since a cognition that is itself incorrect is not capable of sublatting it, the correctness (*samīcīnatva*) of the waking cognition must be admitted.
And thus, the statement "like the perception of objects at the end of waking" is untenable.
If it is argued that this is merely an explanatory gloss (*vārttika*),

the meaning is that the very nature of being a cognition (*pratyayatva*), when accompanied by the example of dreaming, is the reason for the falsity of the conceit regarding the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*).
And because there is an absence of capacity in the opposite case,
the qualification "by one who has previously awakened" was stated with a specific intention;
however, since it is now stated with the intention of [showing] non-perception, there is no tautology.
Here, the Vijñānavādin states the proof for his own position:
"Objects do not exist apart from consciousness, because they are objects of apprehension,
just like sensation."
This is the intended meaning here:

For an external object to be the apprehended (grāhya) of consciousness, it must be either by its mere existence, or by being a cause, or by depending on the same causal complex (sāmagrī), or by being the locus for the fruit deposited by the cognition.

It cannot be by its mere existence; for one thing cannot be the object of another merely by existing, because since mere existence pertains to all other objects as well, all things would become objects of all [cognitions], resulting in the absurdity of everyone being omniscient.
Nor is mere existence a determinant of being an object, since even that which is non-existent can be an object;
for this very reason, the status of being an object does not consist in being a cause.
Furthermore, since the eye and other [faculties] are also causes of consciousness, it would follow that objects are [the causes] of visual consciousness;
moreover, consciousness would not manifest as having a present appearance,
because due to momentariness, the object-moment that produces it perishes at the very time the produced consciousness arises.
If, however, objectivity (*viṣayatva*) were based on dependence upon a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatva*), then the appearance of the present would be justified.

But that [justification] is not tenable, because it would be over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*) due to its pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*) even in the case of grasping the past and future which are non-existent; for it would follow that even a moment of the sense organ (*indriya*) and so forth, being dependent on a single causal complex, would become an objective support (*ālambana*).

If it is argued that "the objective support is that which serves as the locus for the fruit deposited by consciousness," then what is produced in the object by consciousness? It is "manifestness" (*prākaṭya*). Nor is this a property of the object like whiteness and so forth, which is common to all persons.
For even a property of an object (*arthadharma*) produced by knowledge is seen to be unique (*asādhāraṇa*) with respect to the possessor of that knowledge;
just as, for example, duality— which is a property of an object produced by enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*)— is unique only with respect to the person who possesses that enumerative cognition.
That is not so, because it is not all-encompassing.

Indeed, there exist thousands of cognitions regarding past and future objects produced by means of verbal testimony and inference; yet these are not capable of producing a result with respect to the object, because at that time the object is non-existent.
Indeed, it is impossible that there exists a subject (*dharmī*) which is non-existent and unarisen in nature, yet possesses a property (*dharma*) that is not destroyed and is present in nature.

If you argue that cognition arises from its own causes endowed with the power to manifest both itself and its object, and that it is of such a nature that only a certain thing is its object and not everything—
well then, sir, since a power must reside in something capable of being acted upon (*śakya*), it must be stated what it is that this [cognition] is capable of acting upon.
If it is argued that [the object] is the purpose, we say no.

First of all, this [cognition] is not something to be produced by the object, because it is the object itself that produces the cognition. Furthermore, it has already been stated that the result does not reside in the object.

Furthermore, when the object of power (śakya) does not exist, the possibility of power (śakti) cannot arise; therefore, the claim that consciousness without an aspect (anākāra) perceives an external object is a mere fantasy.
Let it be rather that [consciousness] possesses an aspect and has an external object as its domain;
for indeed, cognition possessing the aspect of blue and so forth has blue and so forth as its object.
Since blue is its intrinsic nature,
this must be addressed here:
does it constitute an object because of a state of similarity in every respect, or rather because of a state of similarity in some respect?

First of all, there can be no complete similarity between an object, which is insentient by nature, and cognition, which is luminous by nature; for if there were complete similarity, cognition too would become insentient, resulting in the loss of its status as cognition.
Furthermore, if there were similarity only in part, then since that [partial similarity] exists in every case, every cognition would perceive every object.

Moreover, a cognition arising from the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*)—the cognition of blue—is not so similar to the object blue as it is similar to the cognition of blue; thus, by virtue of both the immediately preceding condition and its similarity [to that condition], [it perceives the preceding cognition rather than the external object].
This [definition] would be the object, but that is not the case;
therefore, neither similarity nor co-arising constitutes the definition of an object.

Suppose it is argued: "Let there be both similarity and co-arising with the mental attention (*manaskāra*), the sense-faculties (*indriya*), and so forth; nevertheless, that which one determines (*adhyavasyati*) is its object. And since one determines the thing (*artha*), the thing alone is its object, not the mental attention and so forth."
Now, what is this "ascertainment" (adhyavasāya)?
It is certainly not apprehension, for two forms are not apprehended; there is the experience "this is blue," but not "in the blue.
If it is argued that ascertainment is the superimposition of one's own form onto the external object—
Does that [superimposition] occur when the external object is being perceived, or when it is not being perceived?
For it has been stated that two blue things do not manifest;
nor can one superimpose something upon a locus of superimposition without first apprehending that locus.

For one does not superimpose silver, which is white and lustrous, upon that which stands before one without having experienced it. Moreover, if the external object were not being apprehended, there would be no restriction regarding purposeful activity;
for since other things would be indistinguishable from it insofar as they are also unapprehended, it would follow that activity could occur toward them as well.
Furthermore, in the system of cognition with forms (*sākārajñānavāda*), there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of external objects, because they are not perceived.
[Objection: But surely the occasional nature of the forms such as blue is itself the proof.
For instance, if something occurs only occasionally even when [the internal cause] is present, it must depend on something else.

If it is argued that just as cognitions—which manifest as a continuous movement even when steps exist—depend on other [simultaneous] continua, so too, even though the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) exists as a continuum, all six evolving cognitions (*pravṛttivijñāna*) arise only occasionally because the conditions for the maturation of their latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are occasional;
[we reply: surely, the latent impression is the capacity of the storehouse-consciousnesses falling within a single continuum to produce their respective evolving cognitions, and of that [capacity]...

Maturation (*paripāka*) is the orientation toward the production of an effect; and its condition (*pratyaya*) is the preceding moment existing within its own continuum (*svasantāna*), because the dependence on another continuum is not admitted. And in that case, all [moments] falling within the continuum of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) would become causes of maturation.

Or rather, not even one [moment] [is capable], because there is no distinction [between them]. If it is argued that "there is a difference in capacity due to the difference between moments, and because that [capacity] is occasional, the effect is occasional," then surely a single moment would possess the capacity to produce a cognition of blue and the capacity to produce the awakening of that capacity, whereas another moment would not possess those.
Or, if [the cause] were a sentient being, how could there be a difference in capacity due to a difference in moments?
Since all [factors] residing in the continuum of the *ālayavijñāna* are capable, when a capable cause is present, the non-production of the effect is untenable.

However, if [the cause] depends solely on its own continuum, then the occasional nature of the thing to be negated is contradicted by its permanence; this contradiction is perceived through [the observation of] that [permanence].
Thus, the occasional nature of [cognition], when excluded, is established as depending upon another cause; this constitutes the proof of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*).

Nor can the active cognitions (*pravṛttivijñāna*) have other mental continua as their cause, because since those other continua are eternally present—and since, being non-spatial by nature, distance is impossible between them, and since no distinct external entity is admitted—there is no possibility of temporal remoteness either, given that the appearance of previously non-existent beings is not admitted.
This inference [of yours] is the acceptance of external objects by the Sautrāntikas;
that is incorrect.

Even if blue and other cognitions arise solely from the cause of their own continuum, since their occasional occurrence is established, the reason is inconclusive because its negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful.

Now, it was argued that "the difference between moments is not the cause of the difference in effects; rather, it is the difference of the imagined continuum—which lacks all causal capacity—that is the cause of the difference in effects, and not the difference of the ultimately real moment which is the cause of the difference in effects. What [is the meaning of this]?

Another [opponent] ought to say this: "Venerable sir, is it not the case that if the difference between moments is the cause for the difference in capacities, then distinct moments would not possess a single capacity? And thus, when a cognition of blue has been produced by one particular moment, that cognition of blue would not arise from subsequent moments?"

If those that are distinct do not possess a single capacity, then how, for the proponent of external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*), can there be a single stream of cognition with the form of a blue lotus arising from distinct streams of blue lotuses?
If it is argued that the cognition of blue is indeed different from another stream of blue lotuses; [we reply:]...
We too say that the cognition of blue at one moment is indeed different from that at another moment.
Therefore, a certain such distinction of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) arises which produces a certain particular effect and not another effect.
Consequently, even for a cognition possessing an aspect (*sākāra*), the object is not its objective domain (*gocara*).
And that which is not within the range [of perception] cannot be inferred;

nor is inference, like direct perception, a means of accessing external objects. Therefore, the author of the *Vārttika* has rightly stated: "Objects are not distinct from the mind, because they are objects of cognition, just like sensation.
For while objects such as blue and so forth are established for both parties in the debate, there is a disagreement regarding whether they are different from or non-different from the mind.

In this regard, the difference of these [objects] from consciousness, which has been accepted by others, is being refuted; and whatever is refuted is so on the grounds of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*). Thus, the reason "because of being an object of apprehension" (*grāhyatvāt*) is an apprehension of what is pervaded by the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*). The difference from consciousness is the thing to be negated; its contradictory is non-difference from it.
Being an object of apprehension is pervaded by that [non-difference]; the very apprehension of that [being an object of apprehension] is the non-apprehension of that which is to be negated.
In this regard, the following must first be stated:
if there were a pervasion of the state of being an object (*grāhyatva*) by non-difference, that would exclude difference; however, its pervasion is not by non-difference.
For instance, that which is perceived as blue, gross, and discrete—its discreteness and grossness are not the nature of cognition.
For magnitude consists in pervading various directions and locations;
and it is not possible for a cognition—which is partless and does not consist of multiple directions and locations—to pervade various directions and locations.
As it has been said:
