Therefore, the appearance of grossness exists neither in the object nor in the cognition, because that [grossness] has been refuted in the case of a single [atom]; since it is impossible even in the case of many [atoms],
the division of the object likewise cannot be of the nature of cognition.
If that were its true nature, then cognition would, in the ultimate sense, be disconnected from the object;
therefore, this [self] must also be accepted as non-existent because it is not cognition.
Furthermore, since there can be no identity between the existent and the non-existent, one must—even if unwillingly—admit that the non-self (anātman) also appears in consciousness.
And thus, even though it exists, it will be manifested.

Now, one might ask: how can consciousness, which does nothing to an object that lacks self-nature (*anātman*), be a manifester of that object? Or, if consciousness does nothing at all, how can it be a manifester of grossness (*sthaulya*)?
If it is argued that [the cognition arises] from its own nature (*svabhāva*), here too this [objection] is not barred by a staff.
For whatever is the nature of something does not depend on anything else, just as a logical mark (*liṅga*) does not depend on anything else in its connection with its own probandum (*sādhya*).
And since the cognition of an object arises from its own nature, it does not depend on anything else for its belonging to that [object].

If it is asked, "How can there be knowledge of an object when there is no connection?", then how indeed can there be a connection between two related things? If one were to postulate another connection, there would be an infinite regress.
Therefore, just as a connection itself exists between two related things without requiring another connection, [so too does cognition exist].
In the same way, it is identical for cognition as well: it [relates] to an object without depending on another relation.
Nor does this lead to an over-extension;
for a certain cognition, having arisen from its own causes, has only a specific object and no other.
Intrinsic natures do not deserve to be subjected to such interrogation as: "Let it be thus," "Let it not be thus," or "Why does it not exist?

If it is asked, "How can visual consciousness have form as its object if it performs no function?", is this said with the intention of referring to visual consciousness as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or with the intention of referring to it as a result (*phala*)?
If it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then it is not ineffective in that regard, because it is the cause for producing the acts of avoidance, acquisition, or indifference.

If, on the other hand, it is the result (*phala*), that is incorrect; for how could a result ever be effective? Indeed, the arrival at a city produced by Caitra’s journey does nothing toward the production of the conjunction or inherence of Caitra with the city.
Thus, since it has the object as its domain by virtue of its own nature, no further thing need be produced by cognition.

It has been stated that the fact that cognition has the object as its domain consists in its being tied to the object; for when the cognition of a cognizer is examined by a subsequent reflective cognition (*anuvyavasāya*), it cannot be examined without the examination of the object.
How [could there be a relation] to the action if it were not inherent in the action?

If it is argued that this is due to dependence on that [the universal], what is this "dependence"? If it is defined as having its own definition dependent upon the definition of that [universal], then this is the same here as well, provided one does not harbor a dogmatic attachment elsewhere.

Therefore, since the object of apprehension (*grāhya*) is not pervaded by difference, the property of being an object of apprehension—being pervaded by the opposite [of difference]—is not able to exclude difference.
While this refutation remains substantial, the author of the Vārttika states another refutation: "Feeling consists of pleasure and pain, while consciousness is cognition.
Having granted [the opponent's position], he says: "Or rather, consciousness is non-different from feeling."
Just as a fingertip cannot be touched by that very same fingertip, so too knowledge cannot be grasped by that very same knowledge.

Now, it is argued that grasping (*grahīti*) is not something graspable, for it possesses no state of being an object (*karmabhāva*). Something becomes an object by virtue of possessing the fruit of an action; however, in this case, there is no further fruit.
Rather, grasping is said to be "graspable" because its nature is self-manifesting and its illumination is independent of anything else.
If this [consciousness] itself were not manifest, objects would not be manifest either, for their manifestation is dependent upon its manifestation.

For instance, whatever has its manifestation dependent on the manifestation of something else becomes manifest only when that [other thing] is manifest, just as [an object] whose manifestation depends on the manifestation of a staff [is not seen when the staff is not seen].

The object possesses illumination dependent upon the illumination of cognition, and this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). Nor does it follow that consciousness cannot be self-cognizing simply because no self-cognition other than cognition has been observed; for a reason is not a prover merely through being seen or not seen, but rather by its inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) with its own probandum. And that connection is established through the operation of a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) against the contrary case. Thus, in this matter, there is no need for an illustrative example.
He said:
"Action and the act of doing are not one and the same. This is the intended meaning here.

Furthermore, what is this so-called "manifestness" (*prakāśatva*) of objects that consists in their dependence on the manifestation of consciousness? For no other manifestation is produced in the object by the manifestation of consciousness.

Moreover, the manifestation of the probandum (*liṅgin*) depends on the manifestation of the probans (*liṅga*); yet it is not the case that [the probandum] manifests while the probans is manifesting, but rather when the manifestation of the probans has ceased.

If it should be argued that there is no manifestation of the object distinct from cognition, and that the manifestation of cognition is itself both the manifestation of the object and its own self-manifestation (*svasaṃvedana*).
If that is so, what follows? For it is not the case that the self is dependent upon itself;
nor is it established that cognition alone is the illumination of both oneself and another.
Indeed, the illumination of cognition is mental, whereas the illumination of an object is sensory.

Furthermore, the manifestation of an object does not depend upon the illumination of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇajñāna*), but rather depends upon the existence (*sattā*) of that means of valid cognition; however, it is well known that nothing depends upon a result (*phala*).

Thus, it is established that this consciousness under dispute is distinct from its own self-manifestation, because it is being manifested, just as the manifestation of one sentient being [depends on] the manifestation of another sentient being.
Therefore, with this underlying intention, it was stated that action (*karman*) and activity (*kriyā*) are not one and the same.
By this, the argument that there is no difference between the blue object and its cognition because they are necessarily perceived together (*sahopalambhaniyama*) should be understood as refuted.
For there is not even the perception of both the object and the cognition simultaneously; how, then, could there be such a necessity?

Now, if it is argued that "simultaneous apprehension" (*sahopalambha*) as stated [in the scripture] is the logical reason (*hetu*), then it is contradictory (*viruddha*), because the meaning of "simultaneity" (*saha-artha*) is impossible if there is no difference [between the two].
This matter has already been elaborated upon in the *Nyāyakāṇikā*; however, for fear of prolixity, it is not further detailed here, and thus we shall desist.
He too must explain the observed diversity of cognitions by means of a causal sequence (*anuvaya*).

It is not possible for the diversity of cognitions—such as blue, yellow, and so forth—to be based merely on the continuity (*saṃtāna*) [of a single stream]. Nor can it be based on the influence or proximity of another stream, since cognitions are devoid of spatial location.
The meaning is that, in its own nature, spatial separation is impossible; nor is there temporal separation, because there is no manifestation of previously non-existent beings.
[The opponent] objects: "This is a mere stream of consciousness, like a dream."
The meaning is that even in the absence of external objects, there exists an internal cause for the differentiation of consciousness.
He refutes this with the words "so 'pi" (that too),
meaning that even dream-cognition is indirectly based upon external objects.
Having accepted that dream-cognition is not caused by external objects, he says:
"Now, even in the case of the dream-position (*svapnapakṣe*). Here, *varga* means "position" (*pakṣa*).
Furthermore, it should not be said that one consciousness is the object of thought and another is the thinker;
the point is that this is because we do not admit the existence of a distinct objective support (*ālambana*).
However, this was stated even while provisionally accepting that dream-cognitions lack external causes.
But he says that the state of having external signs alone is the ultimate reality:
"And these which are dream-cognitions," and so on,
including "to me as well."
The word "api" (even) is used in the sense of possibility; the meaning is that, in my position, it is possible that all cognitions are false.
The rest is easy to understand.
False sleep;
and it must be said that the clarity of consciousness in the absence of an object is inexpressible.

Clarity is the apprehension of the universal, the particular, and their possessor; lack of clarity is the apprehension of the universal alone. And this [distinction] is difficult to establish when the object is non-existent, because it is impossible for a mental image of that [object] to arise—this is the meaning.
If it is argued that consciousness is seen even when an object does not exist, [we reply:
while cognitions such as those of dreams, illusions, gandharva-cities, and mirages persist, let them be caused by defects in the objects, the sense faculties, or the mind;
however, as for these cognitions of a river filled with pus which persist for all people, they cannot have external objects as their cause because of the presence of such defects.

Because [cognition] has defects as its cause, and because there is no persistence of many [objects], and because if it were produced by the contact of unimpaired sense-faculties with their objects, it would contradict the form of the "desire for water" (a mirage); therefore, it is correct that cognitions possessing various forms arise and perish independently of external objects, having acquired their birth from the diversity of beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*). This is the meaning of the objection.
The statement "there are no rivers there" was made out of a firm adherence to one's own view;
it was not intended [as a final conclusion] because of the contradiction and other such faults.

Because of the differences in taste, potency, and post-digestive effect (*vipāka*) between human blood and water, and because the taste, potency, and post-digestive effect of water are observed [in the former], once it is ascertained that a river is full of water,

the ascertainment that it is full of pus for *pretas* is false; when this falsity is ascertained, one must postulate the persistence of a defect (*doṣa*) due to the persistence of that [false perception], and that defect is precisely the karma that brings about the *preta*-body.
As it has been said: "The hungry ghosts (preta) are born from the ripening of identical karma.
Furthermore, it is conceived that the latent impression (vāsanā) of karma is in one place, while its fruit is in another.
(524/6) "Benefit" refers to sons, cattle, food, and so forth.

If that [benefit] were consciousness, then since the karmic impression (*vāsanā*) resides in whichever continuum of cognition (*jñānasantāna*), the resultant consciousness appearing in the form of a son and so on would reside in that very same place; thus, co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established.

However, if the result—sons, cattle, food, and so on—were of the nature of an external object (*artharūpa*), there would be a lack of co-referentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), and the consequence would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). This is the intended meaning.
He refutes that [objection] by stating, "Because it is not accepted.
The meaning is this: sons and the like are not the result (*phala*) in their own nature, but rather the joy caused by them;
for it is that very joy which is desired by the conscious agent, and because the result is characterized by that [desire].
Having established the point by means of a *muktaka* (independent) argument, he states the formal syllogisms (*prayoga*), beginning with "from my own mind.
If "mind-only" were taken as the subject (*pakṣa*), then there would be no illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*); therefore, it is said "from my own mind."

Because of the qualification "provided it is not the locus of my own ego-sense," there is no deviation [of the reason] by way of one's own mind. Furthermore, since the reasons are intended for the purpose of refuting superimposition, the subject is not "incapable" (asamartha).
NyS 4.2.35: The destruction of false perception arises from the knowledge of reality, just as the delusion regarding the objects of a dream is destroyed upon waking.
Furthermore, having first established that perceptions of "I" lack an external object, one must then prove that cognitions of reality likewise lack an external object.

The absence of an external object for those [cognitions] depends upon a subverting cognition (*bādhaka*), and the subverting cognition here negates the conceit of superimposed silver and the like, but it does not negate the common feature of the object (*arthasāmānya*) situated before one—namely, its white and luminous nature.

Therefore, even by following the subverting cognition, it is not the case that false cognition lacks an external object; thus he says that the example "like a dream" is deficient in the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*).

This being the case, if false cognition (mithyājñāna) has the primary [internal organ] as its locus, then the destruction of false perception occurs through the sublation of it by the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna), just like the disappearance of the conceit regarding objects in a dream; however, there is no negation of the universal (sāmānya) either—this is the remainder [of the argument].
The rest is in the Bhāṣya.
The commentary is easy to understand. // 35 //
And it is the same for cognition, because the existence of its cause is perceived.

But as for that Mādhyamika who, having employed a false cognition to deny external objects by means of an example, then uses that very same example to establish the non-existence of consciousness and the fact that things cannot withstand analysis—
against him he says:
"And because the existence of the cause of cognition is likewise perceived" (Sūtra 36).
For if the object were negated, this [argument] might indeed hold;
however, when that [object] is established, the existence of cognition is likewise established without impediment.

And there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for one who speaks thus, while at the same time attempting to establish the inability of entities to withstand analysis by means of a non-existent *pramāṇa*.
O Devānāmpriya, one of praiseworthy wisdom, this mere conceptualization is not sufficient as a means for the knowledge of reality;
nor is the false cognition of an elephant the basis for the knowledge of the reality of trees and so forth, but rather the mind that is properly directed.
It is a specific contact between the sense faculty and its object.
This [contact] did not exist at the time of false cognition;
nor does the habitual practice of delusion conduce to correct knowledge, for it only strengthens delusion itself. Thus, everything is clear.
Thus, this Mādhyamika cannot deny the false cognition that is being experienced;
and it has been stated that one who accepts such a false cognition must explain its cause. (36)
And because of the distinction between the real and the primary, the twofold nature of false cognition is established.
And because of the distinction between the real and the primary, the twofold nature of false cognition is established. (Sūtra 37)
The meaning is that by means of a false cognition (*mithyābuddhi*), its own cause is indicated; therefore, there is a twofold nature of the cause of false knowledge.

In a case where the cognition "this is a person" arises with respect to a post (*sthāṇu*), the reality (*tattva*) is the post, which is the primary [object]; "person" refers to that which was previously a person.
Having thus established cognitions regarding form (*rūpa*), the author of the Bhāṣya proceeds to establish cognitions regarding odor (*gandha*) and so forth as well.
And [the object] such as odor is the cognizable (*prameya*). He concludes:
"Therefore, this is incorrect. // 37 //
From the practice of a specific kind of meditative concentration.
It has been stated that the cessation of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) results from the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) regarding those things caused by the defects (*doṣa*).
Now, how does this knowledge of reality arise? It does not [arise] first from scripture (*āgama*).
Alternatively, knowledge of reality arising from birth alone is not capable of bringing about the cessation of the ego-sense;

for even in those who have gained such knowledge regarding the causes of defects, the defects of the ego-sense persist as before. Furthermore, direct realization is untenable due to the absence of a means [to achieve it].
The answer to this is the following sutra:
"From the practice of the reality of meditative concentration" (Sūtra 38).
The commentator explains the term *samādhi*:
"But that [is the state] of the mind which has been withdrawn from the senses.
By this, he eliminates distraction.
This is the conjunction with the Self of the mind—which has been withdrawn from the senses and is being held by a sustaining effort in some region of the heart-lotus, which is the Self’s own abode.
Indeed, this [conjunction] exists even in the state of deep sleep; therefore, it is said that [the mind] is "characterized by the desire to know reality."

And that practice consists in the repeated production of effort directed toward that object; from that [practice], characterized by devotion, continuity, and long duration, the cognition of reality arises. // 38 //
Not so, because of the predominance of a specific object.
He introduces this sūtra of objection with the words, "As for what was said, 'for when that exists'":
"And because there is activity due to hunger and so forth" (NyS 4.2.40).

The meaning of the sūtra is that for those whose minds are carried away by the objects of the senses, concentration (dhāraṇā) does not occur; likewise, due to the absence of its practice, there is no direct realization of the Puruṣa (sattva). // 39 // 40 //
Its arising occurs due to the connection with the fruits of actions performed in the past.
He introduces the Samādhāna-sūtra:
"Let this be the sign for emerging from meditative concentration," thus [ends] the sūtra.
Its arising occurs due to the connection with the fruits of actions performed in the past. (Sūtra 41)
The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: the concentration previously performed has its fruit as a formative force (*saṃskāra*); its continuity is its stability; [the mind remains] because of that.
The author of the Commentary explains this.
Regarding the term "previously performed":
it is called *praviveka* because one is distinguished (*pravivicyate*) by means of it; it is an excellent formation (*saṃskāra*), and that is a property of the self (*ātma-dharma*).
Why, then, is this imperceptible *saṃskāra* postulated?
To this he says: "For [if it were] fruitless..."

For even many specific efforts, being transitory and unable to coexist with one another, are not capable of bringing about the direct realization of reality; therefore, the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by them are postulated, for it is through their stability that they can function collectively—this is the meaning.
NyS 4.2.42: Instruction on the practice of yoga in forests, caves, sandy banks, and so forth.
The "culmination of accumulation" (*pracayakāṣṭhā*) is the limit of accumulation (*pracayāvadhi*), beyond which no further accumulation exists.

The meaning is: in that cultivation of meditative concentration (*samādhibhāvanā*) which is preeminent due to its possession of those auxiliary factors, there is the effort toward meditative concentration; thus it is called "cultivation of meditative concentration. // 42 //
The same undesirable consequence would apply even in the case of liberation.
The proponent of the prima facie view says:
"If it is because of the predominance of a particular object. Indeed, such is the power of this external object that—
The opponent's misconception is that the Self will produce cognition independently of the sense organs and other such factors. // 43 //
NyS 4.2.44: No, because what has already been established necessarily occurs.
The sūtra of the established conclusion:
"No, because that which is certain to arise is not yet accomplished" (Sūtra 44);
this has been explained.
The meaning is that rice grains do not indeed become shriveled husks even when fully threshed, without the accumulation of contact with a pot, water, and fire. // 44 //
And its absence occurs upon liberation.
For that purpose, there is the refinement of the self through restraints (yama) and observances (niyama), and through yoga by means of the methods prescribed for internal discipline.
Is it only a specific state of meditative concentration that is the means for attaining knowledge of reality?
Not so; rather:
For that purpose, the purification of the self is achieved through restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*), as well as through yoga by means of the methods prescribed for the inner discipline.
This is the common means for accomplishing dharma for those in all stages of life (*āśrama*):
non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness.
Thus says Yama:
"Restraint" (niyama) refers to that specific means of dharma which belongs exclusively to a particular stage of life (āśramin).

By the term "yoga," he indicates the *Yogaśāstra* of Patañjali by means of its subject matter. "Yogācāra" refers to what is prescribed as the duty of an ascetic (*yati*), such as solitude, specific dietary rules, not staying in one place, and so forth.
The meaning is that these [remedies] are also means for removal through the sequential arising of the knowledge of reality. // 46 //
The practice of grasping knowledge and engaging in discussion with those who possess that same knowledge.
Now, if these are the means to liberation through the sequence of generating the knowledge of reality, then what is the use of *ānvīkṣikī*? To this he says:
"The practice of grasping knowledge and conversing with those who possess that knowledge" (Sūtra 47).
He explains that: "for the sake of that" refers to what has been under discussion.
*Ātmavidyā* is *anvīkṣikī*.
"Practice" (*abhyāsa*) means constant performance; the meaning is exertion therein.
He states the purpose: for the sake of the maturation of wisdom (*prajñā*). Maturation, moreover, is the cutting off of doubt.
[Is it] something distinct from the body and so forth?
There is a doubt as to whether there is a self or not.
Its "cutting away" for the world is the knowledge of reality regarding the self; its "inclusion" therein is what is determined by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
and its "authorization" is by means of reasoning (*tarka*). // 47 //
One should approach that [teacher] with those who are free from malice and who desire the excellence and welfare of their disciples, teachers, fellow students, and superiors.
A fellow religious practitioner (*sabrahmacārī*) is one who studies together.

One who is different from a teacher, a pupil, or a fellow student, yet is instructed by the scripture and seeks the excellence of the disciplined—namely, the excellence characterized by liberation—is "faithful" (*śrāddha*).
Because faith is observed toward their final liberation (*apavarga*), it is inferred that there was a practice of the means thereto in a previous existence.
Therefore, even for them, it should be made to appear through the power of impressions from previous lives;
"one should approach" means one should go before [the deity] and come to know [it] together with the Guru and others.
This is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), the understood meaning (*gatārtha*). // 48 //
Or, even if it is devoid of a counter-argument, [the rejoinder may apply] when there is a desire for a specific purpose.
Thus, by means of this, it has been stated that the determination of reality occurs through engaging in debate with teachers and others.
However, if one should think that adopting a position and a counter-position is offensive to the teacher and others, and therefore even debate is not appropriate; [then the following is said].
In this regard, the following sūtra applies:
"Or, even if lacking an antidote, [there is no fault] if there is a purpose and a desire for that purpose" (Sūtra 49).
"He should approach him who explains [it]"—this phrase continues [from the previous context].

Desiring to acquire wisdom from another, such as a teacher, one who declares their wish to understand reality by manifesting a desire to know the truth asserts the distinction of the self from the body and so forth; thus, without establishing a fixed position for their own side, they [seek] their own view through the refutation of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) via the investigation conducted by the teacher and others.

One should purify one's own philosophical system by means of establishing the definitive tenets (*siddhāntavyavasthāpana*). Furthermore, it is connected [to the following]: one should purify the views of the various proponents (*prāvāduka*), which are mutually contradictory, by abandoning what is illogical and adopting what is logical. // 49 //
Wrangling and cavil are for the purpose of protecting the determination of truth, just as the covering of thorny branches is for the purpose of protecting the growth of seeds.
Now, one might object: "If such a state of affairs belongs to *vāda* alone, then *jalpa* and *vitaṇḍā* would be abandoned in the determination of truth. To this he says:
"And some, due to attachment to their own position, overstep the rules of logic;
in that case [the following applies]."
The sūtra states: "Wrangling and cavil are for the purpose of protecting the determination of truth, like the covering of thorny branches to protect the growth of seeds" (Sūtra 50).
He explains this as: "for those who have not yet produced the knowledge of reality. (50)
NyS_4.2.51: Discussion by means of those two [objections] after having raised a dispute.

It is not only for those striving for that [liberation] that there are frivolous arguments (*jalpa*) and destructive criticisms (*vitaṇḍā*), but also for one who is despised by others due to their lack of knowledge, world-weariness, and so forth.
Regarding this, the sūtra states: "Debate by means of these two [frivolous argument and destructive criticism] is *vigṛhya-kathana* (sūtra 51).

This refers to one who, out of the arrogance of false knowledge manifested through his own philosophical system, or out of a perverse cleverness, or due to a lack of true knowledge and dispassion, or out of a desire for gain, honor, and fame—
When those who hold false reasons— lords and supporters of the people— engage in the refutation of the Vedas, Brahmins, the afterlife, and so forth, the proponent,
seeing no valid refutation against them due to a lack of presence of mind,
resorts to *jalpa* and *vitaṇḍā*. Having entered into debate through *jalpa* and *vitaṇḍā*, he establishes the truth for the sake of protecting the sciences.
Lest there be a corruption of the Dharma among the subjects who follow the conduct of their lords due to a confusion of their intellects—
this too is the purpose of *jalpa* and *vitaṇḍā*;
it is not for the sake of visible gains such as profit or fame.

For a Sage, who is supremely compassionate and engaged in the welfare of others, does not teach a method for the removal of another's impurity that has a visible purpose [for oneself]. This is from the *Śaṅkāvārttika*.
[The phrase] "because the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is all-pervading" [is used as a reason].
The intention regarding this will be stated below.
He refutes it;
the meaning is that [the Sāṃkhya view] has already been answered by those who criticize the Sāṃkhya.
Suspecting [the opponent's position], she reveals her own intention:
"By the movement and observation of one's own limbs.
As long as effort does not arise in a portion of the self delimited by the hand, so long no action occurs there; and effort cannot occur there without the contact of the self and the mind.
Furthermore, there is no perception without the conjunction of the mind with a sense faculty;
nor is it possible for the mind, being atomic, to be in simultaneous contact with multiple sense faculties and the hand at once.
Therefore, the meaning of the objection is that the mind must be all-pervading (*vyāpaka*).
He refutes [the objection] because of the simultaneity of the conjunction of the body, self, and mind, due to the simultaneous arising of effort and perception.
In that regard, movement occurs in one's own limb due to the connection of the self with the body.

Dependent upon the desire to move the hand, an effort arises in the form "I shall move the hand" through the conjunction of the self and the mind; there, from the conjunction of the self and the mind possessing that effort, action arises in the hand.
Although the conjunction of the self with all its limbs is not distinguished [as being different], nevertheless, a specific effort produced by a specific desire performs action only in the hand;
elsewhere, there is no impelling of the eye from the conjunction of the self with that which possesses effort.
And although these two efforts do not arise simultaneously, nevertheless, due to their extreme subtlety, the difference in time is not perceived.
Now, one might ask: how can a conjunction or an effort residing in one part of the self produce an effect in another location where there is no conjunction or effort? To this, he says:
"And the self has no parts."
The *Pariśiṣṭavārttika* has been explained by means of a commentary on the *Bhāṣya*. // 51 //
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā* composed by the venerable Vācaspati Miśra.
In the first *āhnika* of the fourth *adhyāya*, there are 67 *sūtras* and 24 *prakaraṇas*.
In the second *āhnika*, there are 51 *sūtras* and 6 *prakaraṇas*.
Including all from the beginning, there are 460 *sūtras* and 60 *prakaraṇas*.
Now begins the fifth chapter.

NyS 5.1.1: *sādharmya-vaidharmya-utkarṣa-apakarṣa-varṇya-avarṇya-vikalpa-sādhya-prāpti-aprāpti-prasaṅga-pratidṛṣṭānta-anutpatti-saṃśaya-prakaraṇa-ahetu-arthāpatti-aviśeṣa-upapatti-upalabdhi-anupalabdhi-nitya-anitya-kāryasamāḥ*.
Now, since the categories beginning with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have been enumerated and defined, what remains for which the purpose of this fifth chapter exists?
Since it is begun [here], he says:
"The multiplicity of *jāti*s arises from the various ways of counter-arguing by means of similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*)," according to the *Bhāṣya*.
The author of the *Vārttika* states its meaning as follows:
"Of the *jāti*s that have been stated in brief," and so forth.

(529/1) Although it would have been appropriate to define the specific varieties of *jāti* and *nigrahasthāna* immediately after the general definitions of *jāti* and *nigrahasthāna* in the first chapter, nevertheless, because these are numerous, there might be a delay in the examination of the objects of cognition (*prameya-parīkṣā*); yet this [examination] is required by the students.
However, without an examination of doubt and the other categories, an examination of the objects of knowledge (prameya) is not possible.
Therefore, the Sage, out of consideration for his disciples, first carried out that examination;
immediately thereafter, he proceeds with the remaining definitions of the specific types of futile rejoinders (jāti) and points of defeat (nigrahasthāna).

The examination of *jalpa* (disputation) and *vitaṇḍā* (cavil) follows immediately [after this], and since they are its constituent parts, there is an intermediate connection consisting of the *jāti*s (futile rejoinders) and *nigrahasthāna*s (points of defeat); thus everything is consistent.
He states the general definition which is useful for the specific [definitions]:
"In that regard, what is called *jāti*... and so forth.
The phrase "employed by the cognition of negation" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
This introduces the commencement of the chapter (āhnika).
"Because there is a prohibition against the application of the genus (jāti).

The meaning is that avoidance, being a form of general cognition and so forth, does not depend upon specific cognition. He provides the resolution: "No, because the purpose for undertaking [the discussion] has already been stated."
This very point is made to remind [the opponent] that the application [of the argument] is easy for oneself as well;
that is, when the judges ask, "Which *jāti* is this?", it is easy for oneself to apply [the response].

Alternatively, when the truth has been attacked by one who hates the science of existence (*sadvidyā*), and the means for its immediate refutation does not occur to mind, it is better to face uncertainty than to suffer certain defeat before the witnesses—thinking, "How might I at least achieve the defeat of my opponent?"
By means of cognition, one employs the notion of birth, as if scattering dust;
for by that, reality is established in the world.
Otherwise, the world would proceed upon a wrong path.
Furthermore, ordinary people do not possess the intelligence to refute the fallacious arguments (kuhetu) raised by those hostile to knowledge merely by using nails, slaps, and the like to repel them.
Therefore, with the intention that such methods as nails and slaps should not be taught by the author of the treatise, he says:
Or [it is] "for the sake of refuting what is good and the means [to it].
Because its object is not reality, the means is in fact not good from the perspective of ultimate truth; yet it is called "good" because a refutation does not immediately appear.
The word "and" (ca) in the phrase "desiring gain, honor, and fame" is used in the sense of a cumulative conjunction (anvācaya).
The purpose in protecting the truth is well-known; the meaning is that when that [purpose] exists, this [protection] is also pursued as a secondary consequence.
He introduces another view in order to refute it: "By means of an improper proof," etc. (503).

2) Even though he knew that the proof concerning the true nature of reality was invalid, at the time of debate, it did not occur to him to demonstrate its invalidity due to a lack of presence of mind (*apratibhā*).
While merely remembering, "This is invalid," he employs a *jāti* (futile rejoinder). This is what is meant by [the statement] "due to ignorance of the fault in the proof.
Alternatively, even though he knows [the truth], he employs a *jāti* under the pretext of a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) in order to point out the fault of that proof.

The meaning is that [the opponent] refutes the proof by means of a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum), thinking: "If my [critique] is merely a fallacious refutation, then your [argument] is likewise a fallacious proof; for if your proof were valid, then mine would also have to be valid.
He now refutes this position of the opponent.
Regarding the phrase "etattu" (but this):

for if one were to state a *jāti* (futile rejoinder), there would be two points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), namely, overlooking a point that should be challenged (*paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa*) and challenging one who is not to be challenged (*niranuyojyānuyoga*). Therefore, it is said, "having understood [it].
If, however, he does not understand it, why then would he employ a *jāti*?
The point is this: for one who forgets even what was previously practiced merely upon seeing it, what need is there to mention one who has not brought to mind a previous birth?

By this, the application of the five *jātis*—namely, *sādharmyasama*, *vaidharmyasama*, *vikalpasama*, *sādhyasama*, and *saṃśayasama*—is refuted when an inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) probans is employed, since the alternative of being either conscious or unconscious is impossible.
"Prior and posterior states" refers to a logical response to a logical proof.
[The opponent says: "An improper reply to an improper proof is [itself] improper.
[The author replies: "But is it not said that these are 'balancing the similarity' (*sādharmya-sama*) and so forth?

And in reality, there is no equality between 'balancing the similarity' and the like on one hand and the original proof (*sthāpanā*) on the other; for if that were the case, it would follow that they are mere futile rejoinders (*jāti*). To this, he says:"
"The application [of the reason] is for the sake of equalization" means that the equality is based on conceit and is not real;
the ellipsis is "in which application the similarity itself is equal."
Thus it has been said: "The application for the purpose of equalization, which possesses an equivalent meaning, should be understood as 'sādharmyasama' (equal by similarity).

Having stated the equality in its essential nature (*svarūpa*) through this analysis—namely, that "the dissimilarity itself is equal"—he states the equality by way of the absence of a specific reason for distinction, saying "or the absence of a specific reason.
To those who say that all *jātis* (fallacious rejoinders) are to be employed against all *āśepas* (objections), he replies:
The application of all *jāti*s [fallacies] involves all possible *apadeśa*s.
(531/2) *Apadeśa* refers to the statement of a reason (*hetu*).

Furthermore, in cases such as "equal by similarity" (*sādharmyasama*), the word "equal" (*sama*) is used because it signifies that the proponent of the proof (*sādhana-vādin*) and the proponent of the *jāti* are on equal footing.

Regarding those who think that the proponent (*vādī*) and the opponent (*prativādī*) are equal because they are alike in their use of similarity (*sādharmya*), [the author] says: "The equality of the proponent and the opponent is not the meaning of the *sumārtha* (correct point); the opponent is one who employs futile rejoinders (*jāti*).

Because when a conclusion is drawn through similarity and dissimilarity, the opposite of that property is established, there are the two [futile rejoinders] based on similarity and dissimilarity (*sādharmya-vaidharmya-sama*). (Nyāyasūtra 5.1.2)
By completing the sūtra with "the two negations" (*pratiṣedhau*), he establishes the masculine gender.

Otherwise, since *jāti* (fallacy) is the subject under discussion, it would have been expressed as "similarity and dissimilarity through grammatical coreferentiality" (*sādharmya-vaidharmya-sama*). The meaning is that when the application of the reversal of those properties has been made, it is for the purpose of establishing the reversal of the probandum (*sādhya*).
In the Bhāṣya, an illustration is provided: "The self possesses activity because it is conjoined with qualities that are the causes of activity for a substance.

Indeed, there exists in the self a quality that is the cause of activity, namely effort (*prayatna*) or the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*); likewise, in a clod of earth, there is a quality that is the cause of activity, namely conjunction with a substance possessing touch and velocity.
When [the argument] has been thus presented, the opponent objects on the basis of similarity alone, saying: "The self is inactive because it is all-pervading, like space.

In this case, the proof (*sādhana*) is fallacious and the rejoinder is not a *jāti* (futile rejoinder), because there is an essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*) between all-pervasiveness and inactivity.
Therefore, the author of the *Vārttika*, disregarding this [objection], [proceeds as follows].
He states another example:
"For instance, 'Sound is impermanent because it has the property of being produced. This, however, is a correct proof, whereas the [opposing] response is a fallacy."

When a similarity is stated, there is the "equal by similarity" (sādharmyasama); when a dissimilarity is stated, there is the "equal by dissimilarity" (vaidharmyasama). Likewise, when a similarity is stated, there is the "equal by dissimilarity," and when a dissimilarity is stated, there is the "equal by similarity. // 2 //
Its establishment is like the establishment of "cowness" through the [perception of] a cow.
But how is this "balancing the birth" (jāti)?
Furthermore, why does the "balancing the point of the argument" (prakaraṇasama) not constitute a correct rejoinder? To this he says:
"And the rejoinders to these two, namely those based on similarity (sādharmya) and dissimilarity (vaidharmya), [are as follows]."
Its establishment is like the establishment of a cow from the nature of "cowness" (Sūtra 3).

This would be so if the probans were a means of cognition solely by virtue of positive and negative concomitance; in that case, due to the absence of the apprehension of a specific relation, there would be the fallacy of "balancing the context" (*prakaraṇasama*). But this is not the case, because that which possesses an essential connection is the means of cognition. And "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) is essentially connected with "impermanence."
However, there is no natural connection between incorporeality and eternality, because it is subject to deviation in the case of cognition, action, and so forth.
Therefore, since its specific character is not apprehended, it is not a "neutralized" (prakaraṇasama) reason;
just as a cow is established as such from "cowness" due to a natural invariable concomitance.

The Bhāṣya statement, "not because of a connection with the dewlap and so forth," contains the term *sāsnādi* as a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the qualities themselves are not included in the reference (*atadguṇasaṃvijñāna*).
By this, deviating features such as the horns and so forth are understood.
The Vārttika states: "Because of the non-connection of one [feature], and because of the non-exclusion of another."
(532/11) Because a single entity [such as a cow] does not possess concomitance with [the universal "cowness"], there is a lack of concomitance due to deviation in the case of horses and so forth.

This means that because a single instance of a dissimilar property, such as having a solid hoof, does not fail to exclude [non-cows] among cows alone—since it is also excluded from buffaloes and the like. // 3 //

NyS 5.1.4: Because of the variation in properties between the subject and the example, and because both may themselves be subjects to be proved, there are the sophistries of parity through addition (utkarṣasama), subtraction (apakarṣasama), praise (varṇyasama), censure (avarṇyasama), and alternative (vikalpasama).

The sophistries of parity based on addition (*utkarṣasama*), subtraction (*apakarṣasama*), praise (*varṇyasama*), blame (*avarṇyasama*), and alternative (*vikalpasama*) arise from the variation of properties in the subject and the example, as well as from both being equally unproven. (Sūtra 4)
Because it is equally unproven in both cases, it is "equal to the point to be proven" (sādhyasama).
By the statement, "of the five *jātis*, [the definition is] from the variation of properties in the probandum and the example," exactly five definitions are indicated.
And these are distinguished from one another by their respective designations as *jātis*.

When it is stated, "Sound is impermanent because it is produced, like a jar," if the opponent objects by means of a reductio (*prasaṅga*) as follows: "If sound is impermanent because of its similarity to a jar due to being produced, then for that very same similarity to a jar, sound must also possess color and other such qualities;
if it does not possess color and other such qualities, then let it not be impermanent either."
Furthermore, there is no specific reason why, because of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), it must be impermanent rather than possessing form and so forth (*rūpādimat*).

Thus, when one adduces an exaggeration (*utkarṣa*) based on the diversity of the properties of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), that is "balancing the exaggeration" (*utkarṣasama*).

Likewise, when that same diversity of properties between the probandum and the example is distinguished by means of diminution (*apakarṣa*), that is the definition of "balancing the diminution" (*apakarṣasama*).

*Varṇyasama* (balancing the description) and *avarṇyasama* (balancing the non-description) arise when, due to the diversity of properties (*dharma*) in the probandum (*sādhya*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), one generates the contingency that they lack the nature of being the probandum or the probans respectively.

However, *sādhyasama* (balancing the probandum) consists in the contingency of [the reason] possessing the members of the syllogism (*hetv-ādy-avayava*) based on the connection with "describability" (*varṇyatva*), which is caused by the alternative possibilities regarding the properties of the probandum and the example.
For this very reason, the author of the Sūtras provides the reason for *sādhyasama* as "because both are equally to be proved" (*ubhayasādhyatvāt*).

The author of the Bhāṣya also, by stating that [the proponent] must possess the capacity of the members of the proof such as the reason (*hetu*) and so forth, considers the resulting [objection] to be "equal to the point to be proven" (*sādhyasama*).
Regarding this, the author of the Vārttika says:
"In the case of the statement 'A jar is impermanent,' what is the reason?"

(533/9) Nor should it be argued that if the term for the definition (*lakṣaṇapada*), being qualified by a difference in designation (*samākhyābheda*), has distinct meanings, then the designatory terms themselves should serve as the definitions and the term for the definition is redundant; for it is only when conjoined with the term for the definition that they convey the distinction between the objects to be defined (*lakṣya*). // 4 //
NyS 5.1.5: There is no refutation on the basis of dissimilarity, because the establishment of the conclusion follows from some degree of similarity.
The rejection of these six types of arguments:
"Because a conclusion is established through even a slight similarity, there is no refutation on the basis of dissimilarity" (Sūtra 5).

That property (*dharma*) of a subject (*dharmin*) for which a natural connection with the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is established—that is, which exists—is the means of proof (*sādhana*) for that property to be proven; it is subsumed under that property to be proven, and likewise by the word "therefore" (*tathā ca*). This means by the term of the application (*upanaya*).

Regarding the claim that the alternative between eternal and non-eternal is like the alternative between being produced by disjunction and not being produced by disjunction, he says: "The property of having origination as its nature is both positive and negative concomitant; the property of being produced by disjunction is not so."

The meaning is this: by offering an answer that is "equal to the dilemma" (*vikalpasama*), it was stated that just as the dilemma is established— namely, that while a pot possesses origination, it is not produced from disjunction— in the same way, even though sound possesses origination, it may be eternal like [the sound] produced from disjunction, whereas the pot is non-eternal.

In that regard, first of all, the property of having the nature of origination (*utpattidharmakatva*) is observed in things such as a jar when impermanence is present, but it is not observed in things such as space when impermanence is absent; therefore, it is determined to be intrinsically connected with impermanence. However, no such natural connection has been apprehended between the property of having the nature of origination and being produced by disjunction (*vibhāgaja*) or not being produced by disjunction (*avibhāgaja*), such that whatever possesses origination would necessarily be produced by disjunction.
Nothing could be non-produced by division.
Therefore, one who states a futile rejoinder (*jātyuttara*) based on the parity of doubt (*vikalpasama*) must, with great persistence, assert that sound is eternal because it is produced by division;

in this regard, the following applies: just as the property of having an origin (*utpattidharmakatva*) serves as a reason for impermanence through positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*).
Thus, being produced by disjunction (*vibhāgaja*) is not an *anvaya-vyatirekin* (positive-negative) reason with respect to the permanence of sound;
for that [reason] is uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*). This is the meaning. He states its uncommonness:
For nothing other than sound that is produced from disjunction has been observed to be either eternal or impermanent.
[Objection: But is it not observed that a disjunction produced by disjunction is indeed impermanent? To this he says:
"It possesses the previously mentioned qualification."

Sound is preceded by the disjunction of the cause alone, whereas disjunction is preceded by the disjunction of the cause and the non-cause; thus it is established that being preceded by the disjunction of the cause alone is the unique (asādhāraṇa) characteristic—this is the meaning. Furthermore, because the example is valid through the extension of the property to be proven (sādhyātideśa).
Having stated the refutation of the six types of jāti, he states another refutation for those [jātis] such as varṇya, avarṇya, and sādhya-sama:
"And because the example is established through the extension of the property to be proven" (Sūtra 6).
He explains that by saying "the example is the probandum," he here presents a refutation of those who propound fourteen types of futile rejoinders (*jāti*).
As for what was stated here regarding the redundancy of the *jātis*:

The meaning is that, according to [the opponent], the difference or non-difference of the characterized (lakṣya) depends on the difference or non-difference of the characteristic (lakṣaṇa); since this characteristic is one, there are not six genera. Therefore, the point is that [fallacies] such as *utkarṣasama* are included within *vikalpasama* itself. [The author] refutes this:
There is no tautology;

for the five definitions, together with the specific words that serve as their respective subjects (*lakṣya*), constitute six definitions because they are both to be established—this is so not only because of the difference in the subjects, but also because of the observation of a difference in formulation.
[The author] raises an objection:

If it is argued that there is a distinction between universals (jāti) due to a distinction between the objects characterized (lakṣya), and that this leads to an infinite regress, [the author] refutes this, saying: "No, because of the lack of definite determination."
There is no definitive enumeration of these individual instances (lakṣya) because they are infinite.

The meaning is that there are twenty-four classes (jāti) by way of including their defining characteristics (lakṣaṇa). He provides an illustration of the distinction [of instances] even though there is no difference in their defining characteristics.
For it is said that [the fallacy] is "equal to the point at issue" (*prakaraṇasama*) alone;
the rest is easy to understand. // 7 //

NyS 5.1.8: Because there is no distinction whether the reason (hetu) reaches the probandum (sādhya) or does not reach it, and because that which does not reach it cannot establish [the probandum], these are the two sophistries of "reaching" and "not reaching" (prāptyaprāptisama).
"Acquisition and non-acquisition are equal" is the term to be defined (*lakṣya*);
the remainder is the definition (*lakṣaṇa*).
That which is non-existent is established, but not that which is existent.
Since it has already been attained— because attainment is impossible for that which is non-existent—
it is therefore not something to be proven.

Moreover, by whatever means something is attained, in that same way the Gaṅgā has reached the ocean; it is united with the ocean and non-different from the ocean. One should also observe that in the same way, if there were no difference [between them], there would be no relationship of probandum and probans, because that relationship is based upon distinction.
But the "balancing by non-attainment" (*aprāptisama*) is indeed quite clear.

Now, one might ask: since the proof and the negation are one and the same when both attainment (*prāpti*) and non-attainment (*aprāpti*) are combined, how can balancing by attainment and balancing by non-attainment be distinct?
To this he says: "The teaching of the distinction between these two is due to the speaker's intention. (535/9)

The meaning is that even though the negation of the means [of cognition] is a single entity, there is an intention to express it as distinct based on the difference in the alternatives, namely "having reached" or "not having reached.
However, when there is an intention to express non-distinction, there is only one answer.
For example, by intending the plurality of trees, the plural form "trees" (vṛkṣāḥ) is used; yet, by intending the unity of that number of trees, the singular form "one forest" (ekaṃ vanam) is used.
Thinking that the general definition of a *jāti* (futile rejoinder) is "an opposition based on similarity or dissimilarity by means of an example," [the opponent] objects;
[the author] refutes this, saying, "[That is not so], because the definition of a *jāti* is absent," [and adds],
"[Your objection arises] from a failure to fully understand the meaning of the Sūtra."

In the Sūtra, it is not intended that the similarity must be with the example; rather, the similarity is with any existing property that is not the probandum, or the similarity is by means of a reason that has not [yet] been reached. Thus, there is no lack of consistency with the general definition. // 8 //

NyS 5.1.9: There is no refutation [of the argument], because we observe the production of jars and other objects, and because [the body] is subject to affliction through malevolent magic (*abhicāra*).

Regarding the refutation: the sūtra states, "Because we observe the production of jars and other objects," and he explains this as follows: for the staff and other tools that have come into contact with the lump of clay, there is no lack of distinction [among them], as there is between the Ganges and the ocean.
"By means of the clay particles abandoning their previous configuration.
The action to be accomplished (*sādhya-karma*) is that [configuration], and since those clay particles are already established, there is no deviation [from the rule].
However, the jar is the result, not the thing to be accomplished.
This is the intended meaning.

As for the question "What is the meaning of non-attainment?", the intended meaning is that if something were to be an instrument (*sādhaka*) without having attained [its object], there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
The answer is that its status as a means of accomplishment exists without mutual contact;
otherwise, however, this [status] would already be established by the mere mention [of the term].
The rule is that demerit (pratyavāya) accrues only to the one for whose sake an act of sorcery is performed by means of the Śyena sacrifice and the like, and not to anyone else;
here too, causality with respect to the action is observed,
just as in the case of ground known as "mud."
The rest is easy to understand. // 9 //

NyS 5.1.9: The two [futile rejoinders], *prasaṅgasama* and *pratidṛṣṭāntasama*, consist respectively in opposing an argument by failing to state the reason for the example and by means of a counter-example.

The two [fallacies] known as *prasangasama* and *pratidṛṣṭāntasama* consist respectively in an objection based on the failure to state the reason for the example and an objection by means of a counter-example. (Sūtra 9)

The cause of the example is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); because that [cause] is not pointed out, there is the "balancing by consequence" (*prasaṅgasama*). For the "balancing by the probandum" (*sādhyasama*) indeed entails, in the case of the example, the members such as the reason (*hetu*) just as it does for the probandum.

The meaning is that it entails the necessity of the example being established through the employment of the five-membered syllogism regarding impermanence. However, the "balancing by consequence" (*prasaṅgasama*) entails that the impermanence residing in the example must be established by the mere means of valid cognition; thus, there is no tautology.
The *bhāṣya* [states] that even for the proof, the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) which proves the impermanence residing in the example must be stated.
The *vārttika* asks: "In the case of 'the pot itself is indeed impermanent,' what is the reason?"
The meaning is: "What is the proof for this? The commentary provides a counter-example (*pratidṛṣṭānta*):
"Since space is seen to be inactive while possessing the qualities of being intangible and so forth, why [is it not the case] by virtue of this counter-example?"
The connection with qualities that cause action does not establish the very absence of action in the self; this is the remainder [of the sense].

If, however, this were an argument based on non-uniformity—namely, that even that which is endowed with qualities causing action is seen to be inactive, as in the case of space—then that would be a valid response.
But since this is not so, it is a *jāti* (a futile rejoinder).
He raises an objection:
"Of the conjunction of air and space. He refutes it:
This is not so, because of the occurrence of properties similar to those [of the sky];
that is, because it is possible for a substratum possessing properties similar to those [of the sky] to possess action.
To the question, "If it is of such a nature, why does it not act in space? he says: "But as for that..."

But as for one who thinks that the cause is manifested solely by the unity of the production of the effect, and not also by the manifestation of the similarity between the perceived cause and effect—for him, the author states the refutations beginning with "yadi ca" (if, however).
NyS_5.1.10: Its cessation is like the cessation of the application of the material cause of a lamp.
If the subsequent [example] is for the purpose of making something known, then the example is not unknown;
the remainder [of the definition] is "because there is a consensus of intellect among worldly investigators" (NyS 5.1.11).
Furthermore, when the counter-example serves as the reason, the example is not without a reason.
And how could that be a cause? That is to say, how could it be a cause?
Because it is accepted as such.

The meaning is that because my own example is accepted, yours is not an example. Even if one were to argue, "Just as my [example] is not an example, so too is yours," even then there is a contradiction; for if the non-example-status of my [example] is to be proven by means of a counter-example, it is by that very counter-example that the non-example-status of my [example] must be established.
If that [lamp] is not an example, then the lamp's lack of being an example is the very point to be proven; thus, it is contradictory—this is the meaning. // 9 // 10 // 11 //
NyS 5.1.12: The "balancing by non-origination" (anutpattisama) occurs because there is no cause prior to origination.
The author of the Bhāṣya explains by means of an example: "It has been stated that 'sound is impermanent because it follows immediately upon effort, like a jar.
From the non-hearing of that [sound], due to the absence of its cause, there would be an absence of impermanence, which is its effect; consequently, permanence would result."
Because there is no other category [of existence] apart from permanence and impermanence. // 12 //
Since that which has arisen exists in such a manner, and since its cause is logically established, there is no negation of the cause.
The refutation of that [objection] is as follows:
Since a cause is established for an entity that has arisen from a state of being, there is no negation of the cause. (Sūtra 13)
For one must oppose [the position] by means of the property of sound being eternal through its non-arising;
yet it is not possible for that which has not arisen to be both "sound" and "eternal," nor can it be characterized by the property of non-arising.
The meaning is that since sound is both produced and subject to production, and is non-eternal, it is not possible to object on the grounds of its non-production.
By the phrase "because of the occurrence of a cause," the meaning is the refutation of [the claim] that it follows immediately upon effort.
Regarding what was stated—that because of the absence of a cause for the effect of impermanence, permanence would follow—the author of the Vārttika says:
Furthermore, this reason is indicative (*jñāpaka*), not productive (*kāraka*).

For when a productive cause ceases, it causes its own effect to cease; however, an indicative cause does not do so even in its absence, because treasures and the like buried deep in the earth for a long time are not thereby eliminated.
Consequently, the qualification "prior to arising" is meaningless.
For arising is the connection with existence for that which previously did not exist; if this [connection] is admitted to exist even prior [to arising], then the qualification "prior" is redundant.
The meaning is that, in the absence of arising, it would always possess the property of non-arising.

Others, however, considering that this is merely the *jāti* (futile rejoinder) called "balancing the implication" (*arthāpattisama*) because it was stated that there is an absence of cause prior to production, offer this rebuttal: "When it is said that sound is non-eternal because it follows immediately upon effort, by the very fact of that statement, its eternity would follow from not following immediately upon effort; thus, since the counter-position is established through implication, this is the *jāti* called 'balancing the implication'. Such is their misconception.
When this has been established, those very same people say regarding this [matter] that there is no such restriction;
he now refutes that view of others with the words "But this... and so forth.
He raises an objection:
"If it is argued that this is not a *jāti* because it lacks the defining characteristics of a *jāti*,
the meaning is that a *jāti* is a counter-argument based on similarity (*sādharmya*) or dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), and there is no similarity or dissimilarity whatsoever for the *anutpattisama*."
He refutes [the objection] by stating:
"Not by means of unarisen [properties], because they lack a cause, due to their similarity [to non-causes].
Just as unarisen threads are not the cause of a cloth, so too, prior to the production of the sound, the property of being immediately following effort (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) is unarisen.
The meaning is that there is a general definition [of the *sādharmyasama*] as an opposition based on similarity, namely: "It is not the cause of impermanence.

By this much, the distinction between the *arthāpattisama* and the *anutpattisama* is shown; for in the case of the *anutpattisama*, there is a negation of the effect through similarity with non-arisen non-causes, whereas in the *arthāpattisama*, there is a negation by superimposing a meaning contrary to the actual sense of the sentence. // 13 //

NyS 5.1.14: When the general property and the example are equally perceptible by the senses, [the fallacy] "balancing the doubt" (saṃśayasama) occurs because of the commonality of being both eternal and non-eternal.
The example for the reason (*hetu*) "being produced immediately after an effort" is a jar.

For just as the perception of specific features exists as the cause of certainty (*niścaya*), so too the mere perception of common characteristics (*sādharmya*) exists as the cause of doubt (*saṃśaya*); thus, there must also be doubt. This is the meaning.
He clarifies the purpose of the sūtra’s meaning through both objection and resolution.
The "balancing by doubt" (saṃśayasama) and the "balancing by similarity" (sādharmyasama) are thus [distinguished]. // 14 //

NyS_5.1.15: If there is doubt due to similarity, there is no doubt due to dissimilarity; or, if there were doubt in both cases, it would lead to the consequence of perpetual doubt. Furthermore, because the universal is not admitted to be eternal, there is no refutation [of the universal]. This is the aphorism for its rejection: "If there is doubt due to similarity, there is no doubt due to dissimilarity; or, if there were doubt in both cases, it would lead to the consequence of perpetual doubt. Furthermore, because the universal is not admitted to be eternal, there is no refutation [of the universal]. (Sūtra 15)

The meaning of the sūtra is that the mere perception of commonality is not the cause of doubt, but rather it is [the perception of commonality] accompanied by the non-perception of specific features; however, when there is the perception of specific features, being devoid of that [non-perception], it is not a cause.
"Or in both ways" means by means of both the perception of similarity and the perception of specific features.
"And because the permanence of the universal is not admitted"—the meaning is that the commonality (*sādharmya*) is not admitted to be a cause of doubt because it is permanent. // 15 //
NS 5.1.16: The "equal to the point at issue" (prakaraṇasama) [fallacy] occurs because the process of proof is established through similarity to both sides.
This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) because of the similarity to both;
it should also be understood as being due to the dissimilarity to both.
The author of the Bhāṣya explains this by saying: "by both—namely, by the eternal and by the non-eternal."
And the second [reason] initiates a counter-argument based on similarity with the eternal, stating: "Sound is eternal, because it is audible, like the nature of sound (*śabdatva*).
Now, what happens to the first reason when the second proof is set forth? To this he says:

"This being the case, the reason 'because it follows immediately upon effort' (*prayatnānantarīyakatvāt*), though stated by way of similarity with the non-eternal, does not transcend the context (*prakaraṇa*)."
"Do not overstep the context; what is the fault? To this he says: "Because one does not overstep the context, one does not overstep the determination (*nirṇaya*).
The meaning is that there is no failure to achieve the determination.
Having thus shown the rebuttal against one who argues for impermanence, he speaks to one who argues for permanence:
"And this is the same when it is stated by way of similarity with the permanent."

Thus, two types of *prakaraṇasama* (the "neutralized" reason) have been stated by way of similarity (*sādharmya*); likewise, he addresses the two types of *prakaraṇasama* by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) to both proponents who put forward proofs for permanence and impermanence, stating: "This is the same," and "Because of the dissimilarity from both."

"Because it possesses the dissimilarity to eternal space due to its being produced, and because it possesses the dissimilarity to impermanent jars due to its being intangible"—thus there are four types of *prakaraṇasama*.
According to the *Pūrvapakṣavārttika*, this [is included] among the *saṃśayasama* and *sādharmyasama* fallacies. (540)
"The establishment of its distinction [from the other fallacies] is due to its not sharing the common characteristics of both sides.

For in the case of the *prakaraṇasama* (the "equal to the point at issue"), one proceeds with the thought: "By means of the certainty of my own position, I shall refute the proponent's proof of his position.

However, in the cases of *sādharmyasama* (the "equal by similarity") and *saṃśayasama* (the "equal by doubt"), the refutation consists merely in bringing about an equivalence with the proponent's proof.
However, the distinction is that [the opponent's position] is not established through the ascertainment of a counter-argument (*pratipakṣa*).

Here, moreover, it is not by means of a proof (*sādhana*) that mere equality is brought about, but rather by means of refutations (*dūṣaṇa*); it is on this basis alone that a formal argument (*prayoga*) possessing equal force should be understood as "equal" (*sama*). // 16 //

NyS 5.1.17: Because the establishment of the counter-position occurs through the very process of inquiry, the negation [of that position] is untenable, since the counter-position is thereby established.
The refutation of this [objection] is as follows: Since the matter is established by means of the counter-argument, the negation is untenable because the counter-argument is valid. (Sūtra 17)

At that time, when two proofs are such that no distinction between them is perceived, what is this arrogance of the opponent, thinking: "I must refute the proponent's proof by means of my own proof for my own position"?

If he desires the establishment of his own position through his own proof while both are of equal strength, then even if he does not wish it, the proponent must likewise be made to accept the establishment of his position through his own proof.

Otherwise, having relied upon the establishment of the probandum through his own proof, [the opponent's objection] would clearly be like the maxim of the royal court: "This is the established rule of the king's family."

This being the case, when the Sūtra and Bhāṣya are to be applied [to this context]: since the establishment of the subject matter (*prakaraṇa*)—that is, the probandum (*sādhya*)—is achieved through the counter-argument (*pratipakṣa*), which is itself a means of proving the counter-position (*pratipakṣasādhana*), it follows that the refutation of the opponent's argument is untenable; for the refutation of the other's argument occurs by way of establishing one's own probandum through one's own means of proof (*svasādhana*). Thus, because the establishment is equal, the negation of the opponent's argument is logically impossible.

Why is the negation untenable? To this it is said: "because the counter-position is established. By stating that the establishment of the process—that is, the establishment of one's own probandum—results from a proof similar to the opponent's proof, the respondent has effectively stated that the establishment of the process results from the counter-position (*pratipakṣa*). [Objection: If this is so, then the fallacious reason called *prakaraṇasama* (the "equal-to-the-issue") should not be pointed out by the respondent, as it would result in a futile rejoinder (*jāti*). To this he says:

Furthermore, the establishment of a formal argument (*prakriyāsiddhi*) arises from the failure to ascertain the true nature of reality. When an opponent employs a proof with the intent of refuting the proponent's thesis by means of determining their own thesis, that becomes the futile rejoinder (*jāti*) known as *prakaraṇasama*. One who employs a counter-argument with the thought, "By way of providing an equal counter-position (*satpratipakṣa*), I shall render the proponent's proof inconclusive," is not a speaker of a futile rejoinder, because he is a speaker of a valid response.

Since the fallacy of the reason known as *satpratipakṣatā* (the presence of a counter-argument) has been established as being like *anaikāntika* (inconclusiveness) and other such defects, the example of *prakaraṇasama* (the neutralized reason) is shown by the phrase "due to the non-determination of the truth. This [fallacy] is the *viruddhāvyabhicārī* (the non-deviant contradictory) according to the *Vārttika*.
Regarding the phrase "the answer has already been stated":
when two parties, each possessing equal strength, accept the establishment of their respective probanda from one and the same [reason], the deviation (vyabhicāra) is established for both as a result.
Furthermore, a "non-deviant contradiction" (viruddhāvyabhicārī) is not possible.

For non-deviation is indeed inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), and that [concomitance] consists either in the fulfillment of five conditions or four conditions; the meaning is that this does not exist in the case of a "non-deviant contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) reason. // 17 //
Nyāyasūtra 5.1.18: Because the reason is not established in any of the three times, it is "equal to the non-reason" (ahetusama).
The Sūtra, Bhāṣya, and Vārtika have been explained by means of the commentary on the examination of the general nature of the means of valid cognition. // 18 //
Since the probandum is established by means of the reason, there is no non-establishment [of the reason] in the three times.
And because a negation is untenable, there is no negation of that which is to be negated.
Nyāyasūtra 5.1.21: Arthāpattisama (the equalizing by implication) occurs when the opponent's position is established through an implication.
He applies the sūtra by means of an illustration:
"Sound is impermanent.

The meaning is that while you assert that sound is impermanent due to its similarity to the impermanent, you are, by virtue of its similarity to the permanent, actually asserting the permanence of sound—though without using words.
There is a distinction [between this and] *sādharmyasama* and the others because there is no description of the proponent's intention. // 21 //

NyS 5.1.22: The objection that the loss of the thesis follows from presumption (arthāpatti) because it was not stated is untenable; for since it was not stated, [the charge] lacks certainty, and because presumption itself is inconclusive.
The sūtra refuting this is as follows:

"The occurrence of the loss of one's position [is not established] because it was not stated; and because the implication (*arthāpatti*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), since it was not stated" (Sūtra 22).
He explains that [by the phrase] "without establishing the capacity":

indeed, that very thing which cannot be accounted for by the meaning of the statement without a further assumption is obtained from the statement itself; as when it is said, "Devadatta is fat and does not eat during the day," the implication is that he eats at night;

or as when it is said, "One should bring about heaven through sacrifice," the implication is that one does so "by performing the intermediate apūrva"—for such is the capacity of the sentence-meaning in establishing its own consistency.
However, when the probandum is being established through a non-deviant similarity (*sādharmya*), it does not follow by implication that it must also be established through a deviant similarity;
for the latter lacks the capacity to bring about the meaning of the sentence,
since the meaning of the sentence is established even without it.

If, however, that which has not been observed to possess causal efficacy were understood even when unstated, then while you are asserting the eternality of sound, its impermanence—though unstated—would have to be accepted;
and thus there would be the exclusion of the very eternality you intend to establish.
This is what he says:
Since the establishment of the unmentioned side of impermanence would, by implication, entail the abandonment of the side of permanence—
given that opposition can also be established through the reverse—
it is said to be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), as this [reason] is equal for both sides.
He states that [the reason] is inconclusive due to deviation, saying:
"And this is not merely because of the opposite.
For indeed, the opposite of non-eating is not necessarily conceived as eating everywhere simply from the negation of eating.
For the term "heaviness" (dhanatva) is intended to indicate a specific excellence of gravity conducive to the stone's falling, but it does not prevent the falling of other things.
The Vārttika is easily understood. // 22 //

NyS 5.1.23: "The 'balancing by non-distinction' (*aviśeṣasama*) occurs because, if there is no distinction due to the occurrence of a single property, it would follow that everything is non-distinct, since the occurrence of existence is common to all."

If, because of the similarity to a jar—namely, the property of being produced immediately after an effort—there were no distinction between sound and a jar regarding what is called impermanence due to their common property of existence (*sattva*), it would follow that all things would be indistinguishable from everything else.

However, this is not the case; for although there is a similarity between sound and a jar in terms of being produced immediately after an effort, their impermanence is not thereby rendered non-distinct.
Thus, this negation is "balancing the non-distinction" (aviśeṣasama).
The explanation of "non-distinction" is that both [the example and the subject] possess impermanence.
"The *deśya-vārttika* is not distinct from the *sādharmyasama* [fallacy]," and "the *parihāra-vārttika* is not [distinct] from the *ekasamasta*. // 23 //
There is no negation [of the probans] because in some cases the property is untenable, while in others it is tenable.
The aphorism refuting this is as follows:
"In some cases there is an absence of negation because those properties are impossible, and in other cases because they are possible" (Sūtra 24).

In some cases, when there is a commonality such as being produced immediately after effort, it is possible for that property— the property of the pot, namely impermanence— to belong to sound and so forth along with the pot; however, in other cases, when there is a commonality such as mere existence, it is impossible for the property of mere existence to belong to sound along with mere existence, and thus there is no negation [of the probandum].
This is the construction [of the sentence].
What is meant is this: it is similarity endowed with inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) that is the indicator, and not mere similarity.
