furthermore, since the agent and the object are the most highly favored among the various *kārakas* with respect to the productive activity (*bhāvanā*), there is a rule for expressing their number, and thus the expression of the *kāraka* itself is not established [as the primary meaning].

Furthermore, this definition is over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*), because even nouns such as *pācakaḥ* (the cook) and *pākyaḥ* (the thing to be cooked) denote a collection of action and its factors (*kriyā-kāraka*).
Dissatisfied with that definition, he subsumes verbal forms (*ākhyāta-pada*) by means of two other definitions.
A verb (*ākhyāta*) denotes an action qualified by a number of its factors (*kāraka*), as well as its temporal connection.

In expressions such as *pacati* (he cooks) or *pacyate* (it is cooked), an action qualified by the number and by a time—such as the present and so forth—of either the agent or the object is perceived. Furthermore, regarding time, it is stated in some places that it merely exists.

However, that is not what is intended by the definition [of an *ākhyāta*] in cases such as *pacati* (he cooks) or *yajeta* (he should sacrifice), because the connection with those [factors] is not perceived there.

By this definition, verbal forms (*ākhyāta*) such as *tiṣṭhati* (he stands) and *svapiti* (he sleeps) are not included, since neither the grammatical participant (*kāraka*) nor its number is perceived; therefore, he states a second definition in order to include them:
"And it denotes merely the meaning of the root (*dhātvartha*), qualified by the expression of time (*kāla*). Thus, it is called "denotation" (*abhidhāna*).
Regarding the phrase "in usage":
particles (*nipāta*) are those whose forms are not distinct from the meaning of either a noun or a verb.

For example, conjunctions and so forth are expressed as distinct from the meanings of nouns or verbs that are to be conjoined—such as by means of nominal words for conjunction, alternation, and so on—because the genitive case is employed therein.

Whether they [the particles] denote a combination (*samuccaya*) or an alternative (*vikalpa*), words such as *ca* do not express their own meaning—whether it be the meaning of a noun (*nāman*) or the meaning of a verb (*ākhyāta*)—as distinct from that. Those particles are so described because their forms (*rūpa*) are manifested or explained (*pratipādyante*) as being differentiated from the meaning of a noun or the meaning of a verb; "form" refers to that which is manifested as distinct. Furthermore, prefixes (*upasarga*) are those which, when employed nearby—that is, when used immediately before [a verb]—illuminate (*avadyotaka*) an action; and "illumination" is intended here as a figurative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).

Prefixes (*upasarga*) are understood to have both additional meanings and contrary meanings, as in examples such as *abhyāgacchati* (he approaches) and *pratiṣṭhate* (he stands firm). The author of the Vārttika establishes that this constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) by stating:
"having admitted... (*abhyupagateti*).
And just as a deviation from the subject (*arthāntara*) is a point of defeat for the proponent and the respondent, it should be understood as such for the opponent as well. // 7 //
NS 5.2.8: It is meaningless, like the specification of a sequence of phonemes.
The suffix *-vat* is used in the sense of "like," as in the expression "like the description of a sequence of phonemes.

In this context, when a Dravidian attempts to demonstrate the permanence of sound (*śabdanityatva*) to an Ārya who does not understand his language using his own tongue, that [utterance] constitutes the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) known as "the meaningless" (*nirarthaka*), because he, knowing the Ārya's language, resorts to it merely to conceal his own incapacity.

Alternatively, if he employs a proof in his own language because he is unacquainted with that [opponent's] language, he is defeated in the former case by way of "misapprehension" (*vipratipatti*) and in the latter by way of "non-apprehension" (*apratipatti*).
For even if the proof possesses actual capacity, it is like being mute; since the noble words that convey the meaning are not understood, the attempt to convey them is futile.

In this very context, the sequence of phonemes (*varṇakrama*) has been shown by the author merely as an illustration; it is not, however, an actual example of a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), for if it were, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even the "cheek-drumming" [of a fool] would qualify as such. For instance, the speech of a Dravidian person, which is prompted by a desire to express a specific meaning, is not like the mere enumeration of phonemes or the "cheek-drumming," because they share the common characteristic of being non-expressive. Thus, the "enumeration of phonemes" serves as the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
For this very reason, the author of the Bhāṣya says:
"of such a kind"; the meaning is that it is not, however, exclusively this [kind].
"Vārttika, example, and Bhāṣya"—
this means that such is the manner of the examples.
"Because of the non-employment of a proof" [is the reason].

The meaning is that the proof (*sādhana*) consists of a five-membered statement intended to communicate to another; since that [scripture] is not accepted as such, even though it communicates [its own tenets] according to its own system, it does not communicate them to the Noble Ones (*āryas*).
NyS 5.2.9: That which, though stated three times by the proponent, is not understood by either the assembly or the opponent, is called "the unintelligible" (avijñātārtha).
A statement which is not understood by the assembly and the opponent, even though it has been uttered three times by the proponent using a common terminology—
since the comprehension of the meaning for the assembly and the opponent generally occurs after that many repetitions, and that is usually three—
it is therefore said to have been "uttered three times."
But surely, it is impossible for a proponent who uses a common convention to state something three times and yet have its meaning remain unintelligible;
or, even if such a thing were possible, the assembly and the opponent would simply be dull-witted, and there is no fault on the part of the expounder when the dull-witted do not understand.
For it is not the case that because a deaf person does not hear a song, there is some fault on the part of the singer. To this, he says:

That which has an ambiguous word-meaning is, for example, "The white one runs," when there is no determining factor such as context; that which employs an unintelligible usage is, for example, "jarbharī-turpharītū";
and that which has an uncomprehended meaning is due to causes such as being pronounced too rapidly, and so forth.

He states that this constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) with the words "asāmarthya" (lack of capacity). The *Vārttika* has its meaning established by the explanation of the *Bhāṣya*. // 9 //
NyS 5.2.10: That which lacks a coherent meaning due to the absence of a logical sequence between what precedes and what follows is *apārthaka* (meaningless).

Where there is no connection—due to the lack of logical sequence between multiple words that are unconnected, or between multiple sentences that are uttered without rapidity, such that their meanings cannot be understood as related—that is considered "meaninglessness" (*apārthakatva*). This is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) because it is purposeless. Why?

Because the employment of words or sentences is intended for the communication of the meaning of a collection or the meaning of a sentence; since that [communication] is absent, it is meaningless. This is the sense.
He provides an example of the lack of connection between the preceding and following parts of a sentence:
"For instance, 'ten pomegranates, six cakes'.
He then provides an example of the lack of connection between the preceding and following parts of words.
"A sacrificial pit and a deer skin":
*rauruka* means relating to the *ruru* deer.
It must be caused to drink;
the elder is not one who lies down.
The author of the Vārttika raises an objection.
Regarding the phrase "of the meaningless (*nirarthaka*) and the nonsensical (*apārthaka*"):

for the utterance of speech has as its purpose the communication of another; since in that regard neither the meaningless nor the nonsensical can cause another to understand, there is no difference between the two.
Nor is it appropriate to accept them as distinct merely on the grounds that in one case there is a mere sequence of phonemes, while in the other there are words.

The meaning of the objection is that since in one case there is the employment of a sentence (*vākya*) and in another the employment of a word (*pada*), it would follow that even among the "meaningless" (*apārthaka*) types of fallacies, a distinction must be made based on internal subdivisions. He refutes this, saying:
"It is divided."
He asks:
"How? The answer:

In that context, "meaningless" (anarthaka) refers to a mere phoneme devoid of a denotable object; however, here "pointless" (apārthaka) refers to words—whereby "words" (padāni) are so called because the denotable object is reached (padyate) or understood through them—and even sentences (vākyāni), which possess denotable objects, yet are disconnected [from one another]. There is a great difference between the "meaningless" and the "pointless," both of which lack a denotable object and a purpose.
But there is no such distinction between these two types of purposeless sentences and words as would lead us to respect their internal subdivisions.

However, if one intends merely to express the absence of the purpose of convincing another, then there would be no distinction among any points of defeat (nigrahasthāna), because in all cases there would be an absence of convincing another; or, if such convincing were present, the occurrence of a point of defeat would be untenable. // 10 //
NS 5.2.11: A statement in which the members [of the syllogism] are inverted is "untimely" (*aprāptakāla*). (Sūtra 11)

He explains that the sequence of the members of the argument, such as the proposition (*pratijñā*) and so forth, follows their respective definitions according to the requirements of the subject matter; that is, the sequence does not deviate from their definitions. This has already been stated by us in the first chapter:

others understand through speech that expresses what is required, and not otherwise. In that regard, at the outset, the statement of the probandum (*sādhya*) is required by others, but not the statement of the proof (*sādhana*).
In that regard, if one were to employ only the first means of proof (sādhana) at the outset, how could one state what is required?
And how can one who states what is not required be called an "expositor" (pratipādaka)?

Thus, all the statements of the reason (hetu) and so forth must possess a sequence; they cannot convey meaning without a sequence, because the comprehension of the meaning occurs precisely by following the sequence of the facts, even when the words are in a reversed order.
Thus, the meaning of the thesis and the other members is such that it cannot be understood without their specific order.

Since there is no expectancy for you regarding a reversal of the members, and since the connection between word-meanings is preceded by that [expectancy], the lack of connection constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*); this is the meaning.
Regarding the *Vārttika*, some say: "Even so, [the conclusion] is established."
As they say here as well: "There is no restrictive rule regarding the order [of words], because there is no difference between the two cases in terms of the accomplishment of the intended meaning.

If it were argued: "This is our convention (*samaya*), just like the word 'artha' [which has a fixed meaning], that the meaning must be understood through this specific sequence and not by any other; therefore, it is understood only in that way and not by another sequence," to this he replies: "And because no such convention is accepted."

The cognition [of meaning] occurs with respect to words alone based on convention, not with respect to sentences; for the understanding of meaning arises from a sentence even when that sentence is newly composed by a poet, independent of any prior convention.

It might be argued that even in sentences a fixed order of sequence is observed—for instance, one says *pācayāṃ babhūva* ("he caused to cook") and not *babhūva pācayām* ("he became having caused to cook"). To this he replies: "And because of usage. The meaning is that while worldly usage is restricted in that regard, here (in the case of mantras), usage is seen even when there is a transposition of the constituent parts.
He refutes this as follows:
"As for the claim that 'it is not so, because it is established even in this way,' the answer to that is: this is like the word *prayoga*."
He explains this very point:
just as the word *gāvī*, when employed in the sense of the word *go* itself, conveys the object characterized by a hump and so forth;
although the communication of meaning by words is not inherent (*svābhāvika*), it nevertheless proceeds today based on the convention established by the Supreme Lord.

To that extent, they remain correct; for this very reason, there is a difference in words corresponding to a difference in meaning for those [words] which possess the convention established by the Supreme Lord (pārameśvara-saṅketa).
However, even if they are employed regarding an object, words that lack that convention are incorrect and constitute linguistic corruption (apabhraṃśa).

Furthermore, with reference to that [correctness], the injunctions such as "one should speak using correct words" and the explanatory passages (arthavāda) expressing censure regarding dharma—such as "a mantra is deficient if [wrong] in accent or phoneme"—as well as the established authority of the Vedas, have been set forth.
In the second chapter [it was stated]:

"Nor is this the meaning—that all those things which are correct (*sādhu*) are causes of Dharma; rather, when the performance of Dharma and speech corresponding thereto have arisen, it is restricted that they must be performed by means of correct words alone."
This being the case, since words such as *go* and *gāvī* are seen to be used by Āryas without distinction, one must consider whether all of these are equally correct (*sādhavaḥ*),
or whether only one is correct and the comprehension of the others arises from it as their source.

In that regard, when the correctness of a single word is postulated, and the comprehension of the meaning from the other words is thereby established on the basis of their being derived from it, it is not logical to postulate correctness for every one of them.
As the venerable Jaimini has said: "It is illogical for there to be multiple words [for the same thing].
In that regard, when the inquiry arises as to which among these is incorrect—namely, which one of these [words]—the truth in that matter is determined through specialized application (*abhiyoga*).
That which is remembered without contradiction as correct by those most proficient in the science, such as Indra, Pāṇini, and others, is determined to be correct; anything else is incorrect.

Therefore, although worldly people understand the meaning of "cow" and so forth from words such as *gāvī* and the like, and thus their linguistic practice concerns only perceptible objects, [the correctness of the standard forms remains established].

Nevertheless, for those who investigate, the process of inquiry is as follows: when the oldest person ought to have used the word "cow" (go), he inadvertently used the word "gāvī"; thereupon, the next oldest person inferred the word "cow" and thereby cognized the universal cowness (gotva).
As they say:
When a child, while learning, utters "Amba!
Amba!", though it is indistinct, those who know it reach a certain conclusion regarding what is distinct.

Thus, when a correct word (*sādhu*) ought to be employed, if a corrupt form (*apabhraṃśa*) is used instead, some meaning is expressed by that [corrupt form] only through the mediation of the correct word. Consequently, bystanders, having inferred the original word (*mūlaśabda*) from this [corruption], understand the meaning; they do not realize that "this person understood this meaning directly from the word *gāvī* itself. Thus, they come to regard that very [corrupt form] as the denoter of "cowness" (*gotva*), and [apply it] to others...
He became an elder (*vṛddha*).

From that time forward, this delusion regarding the denotative capacity of words that have lost their connection to the original form (*mūlaśabda*) persists only with respect to the corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*); for one who is more senior and knows both [the original and the corrupt], the comprehension of word-meaning follows the original form, whereas for people of the present day, it arises from the corrupt form alone. For this very reason, even the lack of formal grammatical derivation (*anavākhyāna*) serves a purpose.

If this distinction between correct words (*sādhu*) and corrupt words (*apabhraṃśa*) did not exist, then because knowledge [of the distinction] would be absent, it would follow that the performance of dharma would become impossible. This is because both the injunction (*niyamavidhi*)—"one should speak with correct words"—and the prohibition (*niṣedha*)—"one must not speak like a barbarian (*mleccha*), nor should one use corrupt speech"—would be difficult to comprehend due to uncertainty regarding their scope. For a word is correct (*sādhu*) in that specific meaning for which it was established by the Blessed Lord, and incorrect (*asādhu*) elsewhere; just as the very same word *aśva* is correct when referring to a poor man, but incorrect when referring to a horse.

Just as any medicinal herb touched by the tip of a mongoose’s fang destroys snake venom, so too a word that has been established by convention by the Lord (Īśvara) is a correct word (*sādhū*) and is conducive to *dharma*, while no other is.

In cases where there is a dispute between Āryans and Mlecchas regarding the meaning of words such as "barley" (*yava*) or "boar" (*varāha*), the meaning accepted by the Āryans must be adopted based on the supplementary Vedic statements (*vākyaśeṣa*), and not the meaning accepted by the Mlecchas; for in those instances, the latter would contradict the supplementary Vedic statements.

However, regarding those words whose usage has not been observed among the Āryas but are employed by Mlecchas alone for specific meanings— such as *pika*, *nema*, *tāmara*, and so forth— which yet are used in the Veda,
their meaning must be determined solely from the usage of the Mlecchas; for they are experts in that regard and because their usage does not contradict the usage of the Āryas.

This being the established case, the more extreme ravings of those devoid of the study of Nyāya and Mīmāṃsā are to be disregarded; therefore, it was well said: "like a word devoid of its formal application," and "the grammatical analysis of words is not useless.
He now demonstrates, preceded by a question, the reason for the fixed order of the members of a syllogism, such as the proposition and so forth.
Regarding how this was previously [stated] as "firstly," he restates the second point of objection and provides the rebuttal:
"As for that which was said, 'because of not accepting the convention'..."
Thus, one who explains the sequence of meanings as they actually occur according to their own strength of derivation is not to be censured—that is, he is not to be reproached.
For in a technical treatise (*śāstra*), sentences are employed for the purpose of summarizing meaning;
indeed, the summary of meaning in a treatise is not performed in an arbitrary manner, as if it were a mere collection of all that exists or a description of everything that has occurred.

It is logical that the same should be done in formal debate as well; for in debates and the like, just as there are the proponent's and opponent's positions, the speaker is also subjected to examination, and what has been examined is established by scripture. // 11 //
NyS 5.2.12: That which is deficient by even one of its members is called "deficient" (nyūna).

It has been established that the five members beginning with the proposition (*pratijñā*), when combined, constitute the means of proof (*sādhana*). If there is deficiency, there is no means of proof; and in the absence of that [means], there is no establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*).
The meaning is that an effect produced by a complete causal complex (*sāmagrī*) does not arise from a mere portion of that complex.

The opinion of others is presented with the words "But some," meaning that some assert that there is no ground for defeat called "deficiency of the proposition" (*pratijñānyūna*). He refutes this, stating, "But this is not tenable."
Is it that [the deficiency of the thesis] is not a separate point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), or rather that it is not a point of defeat at all?
He states this very point by asking: "Is he defeated or not?
He states the fault in the first alternative with the word "yadi" (if).
In the second alternative, he states the fault with the words "atha na nigrahaḥ" (if it is not a point of defeat).
The meaning is that it has been stated that the thesis (*pratijñā*) is a constituent part of the proof (*sādhana*).
And as for what you say— that it is merely the adoption of the *Diṅnāga* system—
this is refuted;
this too [is refuted].
The meaning is that there is a great difference between a proven fact (*siddha*) and a thesis to be proven (*sādhya*), or between a tenet (*siddhānta*) and a proposition (*pratijñā*). // 12 //
NS 5.2.13: That which contains more than the reason and the example is "redundant" (adhika).
This is the commentary [of Patañjali]: "This is the acceptance of a restriction.
Regarding this, the inquiry is: "How is this goal accomplished? For, since the goal is established by a single means alone, the statement of another means would be purposeless;
because a means that expresses no distinction once the action has been completed falls outside the logic of being a "means" (*sādhana*).

However, where there is an inquiry from either the opponent or the assembly as to how many means of proof (*sādhana*) are possible for this probandum (*sādhya*), in that case all those means of proof, however many they may be, must indeed be stated; for if only one or another were mentioned, it would result in defeat (*nigraha*).
Thus, he sets forth the opinion of those who say that [stating] more than that is not a ground for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
"And that [certainty] does not arise from firmness"—
thus he refutes [the opponent's view] by stating "not for the sake of firmness.
If certainty were what constitutes firmness, then it would arise from a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) alone, because that which does not produce certainty is not a *pramāṇa*.
Now, if you say that its clarity is what constitutes certainty, that has already been answered.

Furthermore, there is no grasping of the universal, the particular, and their possessor; for even with thousands of inferences, those [cognitions] have as their object only the substance possessing the universal.
You raise an objection: "But you say that both are indicators."

The meaning of the objection is this: "Our definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not 'the capacity to cognize an object not yet apprehended,' by which [definition] a second means of cognition would be invalid once the object has been apprehended by one;

rather, a means of valid cognition is simply that which cognizes, and this quality is no different for a second [cognition] as well. He refutes this, saying: "It is true that both [cognitions] inform [us]."

It is the person who errs here, who makes known an object already known without it being sought after; the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), however, does not err, for it necessarily proceeds by its own capacity.
If it proceeds and presents the object of knowledge once the desire to know has arisen, there is no fault on its part.

For a sickle is not "non-cutting" when grain has not been harvested; therefore, it is established that the censure falls upon the person, due to his disregard for the cause [of inquiry] and because it would lead to an infinite regress. // 13 //
NyS 5.2.14: Furthermore, the repetition of words and their meanings is called "redundancy" (purukta), except in the case of a restatement (anuvāda).
NyS 5.2.15: Repetition (punarukta) is the restatement by means of the word *syāt* of that which has already been established through the force of the meaning.

Therefore, by these two sūtras, what was actually a single point of defeat (nigrahasthāna) has been stated as threefold in some way, with the intention of expressing internal subdivisions for the sake of elaboration.
That same [point of defeat], namely repetition (punarukta), occurs in some cases through the recurrence of the word, in some through a different synonym, and in some through the meaning.
[The opponent] objects: "No, because it does not constitute a defeat."
He maintains that this is true;
for while the skill of the speaker is considered in the case of frivolous talk and cavil,
one would be unskilled in the employment of redundant speech.

Because the means of proof (sādhana) has been stated without regard [for the capacity of the thesis], the object to be proven (sādhya) remains unestablished; since that [object] is not fully understood, the proponent is defeated. Furthermore, what is intended [by this fault] is either futility (vaiyarthyam), pointlessness (anarthakyam), or having a contradictory purpose (viruddhaprayojanatvam).
For instance, when there is a redundant statement, one whose mind is distracted by pursuing its purpose fails to grasp it immediately from the initial utterance.

Thinking that even a well-known matter is as if unknown, one would be unable to ascertain it; consequently, one who has set out to provide an exposition would fail to provide it. Thus, because the purpose would be both contradictory and futile, this constitutes a logically established ground for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). // 15 //
NyS 5.2.16: Non-reproduction is the failure to repeat what has been understood by the assembly after it has been stated three times.
He explains [the phrase] "of the meaning of the sentence already understood.
He states the justification for this being a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*): "If one does not restate [the opponent's position], upon what basis could one state a refutation?"
Some maintain that this *vārttika* is not a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*),
because the opponent's state of either confusion or lack of confusion is established by means of the subsequent examination of the merits and defects of the response.
He analyzes this with the following [verse]: "Because it possesses qualities and defects.
Therefore, what purpose is there in uttering the utterance? This is the remainder [of the argument].
For there is indeed someone—this is the reading found in some places.
In this context, the two particles "tatra" and "asti" are to be understood as introducing the sentence.

Because men possess diverse dispositions, someone may be capable of providing an answer but not of repeating it; yet, one who states a correct response does not deserve defeat merely on account of that failure to repeat.

Now, if non-reproduction (*ananubhāṣaṇa*) were not a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), then one who begins to reproduce [the opponent's argument] but fails to reproduce it all would not be defeated; therefore, he says: "But for one who, having begun, does not carry it through, yet might state a correct reply (*saduttara*), there would indeed be a defeat consisting merely in humiliation (*khalīkāra*), but not a subversion of his status as a speaker of truth. He thus resolves this objection of the Venerable One (*bhadanta*) with the words: "Not because of a failure to understand the subject matter of the reply."
For a refutation must concern the object to be refuted; indeed, it is impossible to state a refutation when the object to be refuted has not been mentioned.

Certainly, the defects of the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), the example (*udāharaṇa*), the application (*upanaya*), and the conclusion (*nigamana*) cannot be established as defects without first stating their own nature. Thus, one who does not utter [the original argument] is not entitled to state its defect.
This being so, it is contradictory to say: "He does not utter [the argument], yet he states a rejoinder (*uttara*)."

It might be argued that the opponent need not refute everything, because by refuting even a single member [of the syllogism], the proof is already invalidated, making the statement of further faults redundant.
Indeed, one who has been killed cannot be killed again even if protected from death; likewise, that which has already been refuted cannot be refuted once more.

Therefore, even though there may be a multiplicity of points to be refuted (*dūṣya*), one must refute at least one; and likewise, since not everything is to be refuted during the restatement (*anubhāṣaṇa*) of all [the opponent's arguments], that which is to be refuted must be restated again. Thus, in the restatement of everything, there would be two grounds for the opponent's defeat (*nigrahasthāna*): the restatement twice and the restatement of what is not to be refuted.
Consequently, it follows that the opposite is the case—that *anubhāṣaṇa* itself is a ground for defeat. Therefore...
He says: "And because there is no formal proposition (*apratijñāna*).
He analyzes this point: "This is not being proposed [as a rule]:

that everything must first be uttered as a single continuous text, and only afterwards should the subsequent [objection] be stated by way of restating what is to be refuted, such that both the restatement of the object of refutation and the double restatement would be faults; rather, it may be done in whatever manner [is appropriate]."
The following must be stated in reply:

since it is not logical for one who is responding to provide an answer when the basis for that answer is absent, only the basis itself should be restated; for without that, the answer cannot be formulated.
Therefore, it is correct that non-reproduction consists solely in the failure to restate that [basis], and not in the failure to restate everything; such is the meaning.

But surely, by the prescription that *apratibhā* (lack of ingenuity) is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), it is also understood that *ananubhāṣaṇa* (failure to repeat) is one as well, since the latter is a specific instance of the former. Indeed, one is not defeated merely by the fact that one does not repeat; rather, while failing to repeat, one does not comprehend the object of refutation, and not comprehending it, one does not formulate a response therein; thus, one is defeated by *apratibhā*.

Thus, this very non-reproduction (*ananubhāṣaṇa*) is a specific instance of lack of ingenuity (*apratibhā*); therefore, the status of being a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) established for lack of ingenuity is also established for this specific instance.

Just as the possession of a dewlap and so forth is established for a cow, it is also established for a brindled cow (*śābaleya*), yet they do not undertake a separate effort to establish the possession of a dewlap and so forth in that case anew.
To this we reply:
First of all, non-reproduction (*ananubhāṣaṇa*) is not a specific variety of the general category of "inability to respond" (*apratibhā*), because of the diversity of human capacities.
Someone, even while knowing both the refutation and the point to be refuted, may be unable to reproduce it due to a deficiency in their power of speech.
Therefore, since non-reproduction can occur even when there is no lack of ingenuity (*apratibhā*), non-reproduction is not a specific sub-type of lack of ingenuity.

Someone might repeat the object of refutation but be incapable of formulating a response; such a person is defeated by *apratibhā* (lack of ingenuity), not by *ananubhāṣaṇa* (failure to repeat), because the latter is subsumed within the former’s capacity.

On the other hand, someone else may not even know the object to be refuted; he is defeated by *ajñāna* (ignorance). In the case of ignorance, failure to repeat is not necessarily present, for one who possesses a good memory might be able to recite the mere form of the syllables uttered by the proponent even without understanding their meaning, which makes repetition possible.
However, *apratibhā* must necessarily occur, for it is impossible that one should not know the object to be refuted yet claim to know its refutation.

Nevertheless, there is a distinction in terms of their essential nature (*svarūpa*); for the ignorance regarding the object of refutation that constitutes "non-reproduction" (*ananubhāṣaṇa*) is not the same as the ignorance regarding the object of refutation that constitutes "inability to respond" (*apratibhā*). Therefore, although the ignorance of non-reproduction and the ignorance of inability to respond are equal in having the non-statement of a reply as their result, they are presented separately with the intention of expressing their internal distinctions. [This applies to] "that which has been stated three times."
Even after stating this three times, one who does not understand due to extreme dullness has no entitlement to engage in formal debate; such is the intended meaning. // 16 //
And ignorance is that which is not cognized.
He explains that [point] with the words "by the assembly of one who has understood the meaning.
Here, the author of the Vārttika applies the general definition of a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*): "A point of defeat arises from non-comprehension" (sūtra 1.2.19). // 17 //
Non-rejoinder (aprati-bhā) is the failure to provide a reply.
He explains that [with the words] "the opponent's position," etc.,
showing contempt for the Vārttika by means of reciting its verses and so forth.

For when one is engaged in a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) consisting of shifting to another subject (*arthāntara*), by introducing [the new subject] under the pretext of establishing that [original point] through a series of related arguments, one does not demonstrate ignorance regarding the original topic; however, in this case, there is indeed such ignorance because of the introduction of the matter with such a distinction.

Furthermore, this should be understood as "inability to respond" (*apratibhā*) when a correct proof is being presented; but when a fallacious proof (*sādhanābhāsa*) is being presented, it constitutes "neglecting what requires inquiry" (*paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa*). // 18 //
NyS 5.2.19: *Vikṣepa* (evasion) is the interruption of the discussion by resorting to the necessity of [dealing with] the effect.

Having accepted the presentation of both a proof and a refutation, while remaining in that very state and being clearly perceived [by the assembly], one perceives either the firmness of the opponent or the harshness of the members of the assembly, and then abruptly shifting the task, cuts off the discussion that was previously accepted; in that case, it is the point of defeat called "distracting" (*vikṣepa*).
By this [term] "inability to respond" (*apratibhā*), one should understand that even silence is included,
because being occupied with other business is merely an indicative mark for the interruption of an accepted debate.

Furthermore, this is not a separate point [of defeat], because there is no interruption of the debate through the introduction of tangential arguments under the pretext of thinking, "I shall establish exactly what was relevant to the matter at hand."

In this case, however, it is due to the interruption of the discussion. Furthermore, this [interruption] is not included among the fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*). For distraction does not conform to the property of any particular logical mark (*liṅga*), nor is it employed for the sake of establishing the probandum under discussion, such that it would constitute a fallacious reason.

Moreover, distraction (*vyāsaṅga*) is not a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*), because one withdraws only after having accepted the debate and failing to state a reason immediately thereafter. Furthermore, if this person were to state a correct reason and then withdraw because he was unable to support it, would he not be defeated by this much alone? Or would he be defeated by a fallacious reason? Rather, he is defeated solely due to his distraction.
However, the distinction between the meaningless (*anarthaka*) and the nonsensical (*apārthaka*) is quite clear.
For in this case, the speaker does not lack a common convention [with the listener], which would render it meaningless;
nor are the words or sentences here disconnected in their sequence, which would render it nonsensical.
Nor is there contempt, by which there would be a lack of presence of mind (*apratibhā*).
Therefore, it is established that distraction (*vikṣepa*) is a separate point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). // 19 //
NyS 5.2.20: Matānujñā (concession of the opponent's position) is the attribution of a fault to the opponent's position by accepting a fault in one's own position.
He explains that one who, having accepted a fault pointed out by another regarding his own position, [responds].
How is it known that he accepts it? To this, he says:

Regarding the phrase "without having extracted": the sense is that if one does not accept [the opponent's position], one would have to extract it. As for the *Vārttika*, its meaning is: "but rather by means of another's property which has not been surrendered and not taken."
(559/13) Others maintain that this is not a point of defeat because it is an application of a consequence (*prasaṅga*).
For example: "If you are a thief because you are a human being, then you too must be a thief."

And this is not accepted by you; therefore, because of its inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*), "this is not a valid reason"—this reversal of the reductio (*prasaṅga-viparyaya*) follows. Consequently, since he has not admitted the thief-nature of the self by this [statement], it is "admission of one's own position" (*matānujñā*);
the meaning is that this is not a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). He refutes this, saying: "But this is not so."
Why? For this very reason.
Why? Because he is defeated precisely because he raises an objection (*prasaṅga*) when a further response ought to be made.
For if a proponent were to say to the opponent, "Truly, I am indeed a thief," could he then possibly establish the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*)?

Therefore, when the correct reply ought to be that "being a man" is not the cause for being a thief, but rather "connection with another's property taken without permission," if instead one offers a semblance of a reply, this indicates that he certainly does not know the proper reply; because of his ignorance of the proper reply, he is defeated. And that ignorance of the reply, when pointed out by the opponent as being "Matānujñā" (Admission of One's Own Position), is called Matānujñā. // 20 //
NyS_5.2.21: Neglecting to press for a point of defeat when the opponent has reached a point of defeat is "overlooking the censurable" (paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa).

"He is one who should be questioned" (paryanuyojya) means that he possesses the justification for defeat, that is, its establishment through valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). However, this [fault] should not be pointed out by the proponent (*vādin*), for a sane person does not point out a flaw in his own proof.

Nor can it be by the opponent, for no one who is not insane would condemn himself. Rather, knowing what ought to be questioned, why would he overlook it? Therefore, that point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) must be pointed out either by the moderator of the assembly or by the assembly itself when questioned by both the proponent and the opponent. In this regard, in a debate (*vāda*) that concludes with the determination of truth, the assembly alone emerges victorious because both parties are defeated. This is also the case in informal discussion (*jalpa*) and destructive criticism (*vitaṇḍā*), which proceed with the aim of examining human capability rather than seeking the truth.
The opponent is defeated;
for even though the proponent was employing fallacious arguments, he has nonetheless paralyzed the opponent by presenting a correct proof. Regarding the opponent...

The distinction is that "inability to respond" (*apratibhā*) consists in the failure to offer a reply, whereas "overlooking the point to be questioned" (*paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa*) consists in the failure to respond when a fallacious proof (*sādhanābhāsa*) has been presented.
Some maintain in their *Vārttika* that it is not so, because of the mention of "another's speech";
for where the opponent remains silent, one demonstrates by that very silence the opponent's unfitness to provide a reply.

This indicates that he is a proponent of fallacious proofs (*sādhanābhāsa*), for even when he points out a fault where no valid fault exists, he provides a defective reply and thereby merely indicates a fault in that proof itself. Indeed, the elders teach: "When a proof is defective, one should provide a [pointed] rebuttal."

Therefore, whether there is no statement or a different statement, "neglecting what ought to be addressed" is not a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), because in either case there is no neglect; this is the meaning.
He refutes that with "and that is not so":
for one who knows a correct fault in the proof should state that very fault.
Thus, this person, whether speaking at an opportune moment or not, certainly does not understand the fault correctly;

for the intention of a person whose status as an authoritative source (*pramāṇa*) is established is indicated by gestures and the like, but not that of one whose status as an authoritative source is unestablished.
As they say:

"Even knowing that it has been well said— 'Whatever is spoken by a sophist beyond the scope of Śruti and Smṛti should be determined as faulty, exactly as it is heard, if it is indeed faulty'— why does this person say something else? (21)
NyS 5.2.22: To charge someone with a point of defeat when it is not a point of defeat is "objection against one who is not to be objected against" (niranuyojyānuyoga).

And this is not identical to *apratibhā* (lack of ingenuity), for that is a failure to respond further, whereas this is a failure to respond precisely by way of providing a superior answer to what is unsurpassed; thus there is a great distinction.
By this alone, all types [of fallacies] are subsumed under the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
Furthermore, there is no distinction between these and the pseudo-reasons (*hetvābhāsa*);
for those belong to the proponent’s points of defeat, whereas this belongs to the opponent’s.
Thus there is a great distinction.
For this very reason, you also have the verse:
"A statement lacking a member of proof, and the failure to point out a fault in those two [the thesis and the reason]."

"But another point of defeat (nigrahasthāna) is not tenable, thus it is not accepted"—by this, the author of the Bhāṣya shows that this "objection against one who should not be censured" (niranuyojyānuyoga) is a specific variety of "inability to respond" (apratibhā), which consists in a simple negation (prasajyapratiṣedha). The meaning is: due to a false determination (mithyādhyavasāya), that is, through a superimposition (samāropa), regarding the definition of a point of defeat.
The commentary is easy to understand. // 22 //
NyS 5.2.23: Having accepted a tenet, the consequence of engaging in a debate characterized by a lack of consistency is "contradiction of a tenet" (apasiddhānta).

The explanation of the term *abhyupetya* is "having promised (*pratijñāya*) the existence of some matter in such a way. Regarding the phrase "due to the reversal of the promised matter" (*pratijñātārthaviparyayāt*), it means "due to the reversal of the accepted matter," which is to say, due to the reversal of the tenet (*siddhānta*).
This is the explanation of [the Sūtra] "Because of non-restriction" (aniyamāt).
In that regard, he states the Sāṃkhya position:
"Just as it is not existent," and so forth.

To state this in another way: "it is not that [the existent] ceases from here" is an alternative explanation of the same point, and "the non-existent does not arise" is an alternative exposition of the same principle. Having accepted this established doctrine (siddhānta) of the Sāṃkhyas, he introduces a discussion regarding its opposite in order to establish his own position; thus, he demonstrates the establishment of his own thesis.

The proposition (*pratijñā*) is that it is logical for there to be a single primordial nature (*prakṛti*) of the class of objects that are manifest and perceived; "of the modifications" (*vikārāṇām*) is a restatement of that which is manifest;
"because of the observation of continuity" (*anvayadarśanāt*) is the reason (*hetu*).

"Of those things endowed with clay" is the example based on similarity (*sādharmyodāharaṇa*); likewise, "this manifest diversity is perceived as being endowed with pleasure, pain, and delusion" is the application (*upanaya*).

He states the conclusion (*nigamana*): "Therefore, because of the observation of this endowment, when the question arises as to by what [the manifest world] is endowed, the answer is: 'by pleasure and the rest'.
Thus, "all modification has a single primordial nature" is this very discourse.
Having thus spoken while accepting the [Sāṃkhya] tenet, the Sāṃkhya is questioned by the Naiyāyika;
he is asked for the sake of refutation:
"Now, how is it to be defined that 'prakṛti is the cause of transformation'?"

Thus questioned by the Naiyāyika, the Sāṃkhya gives this answer: "That which, while persisting—such as clay—undergoes the cessation of one attribute and the emergence of another attribute, such as a jar or a water-pot, wherein that other attribute, such as a bowl or a vase, arises as something previously non-existent—that [substratum] is the primordial material cause (prakṛti), such as clay;
and that which is the attribute which ceases or emerges is the modification (vikāra)."
In this example, he applies the fallacy of contradicting one's own tenet (apasiddhānta).

This proponent, by reversing or deviating from the meaning of his proposition or his established tenet, leads the discussion into error; for he has indeed asserted that "from non-existence nothing appears," that "what exists is not produced," and that "what exists does not perish."
Nevertheless, why is the established doctrine (siddhānta) sublated by this [perception], and why is it not rather the perception that is sublated by the established doctrine? To this he says:
"Of the existent and the non-existent.

For this [perception] is established by worldly means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), whereas the established doctrine is established merely by formal admission and lacks the status of a means of valid cognition.
Therefore, by this [position], the established doctrine is sublated by something more powerful.
This means that it would follow that even for things possessing the properties of clay and so forth, these would not exist;

that is to say, for those possessing real properties, both arising and destruction—observed as the commencement and cessation of activity—would not occur, not only for intelligent agents but for [all] things as well.

When the Sāṃkhya, thus positioned, is questioned by the Naiyāyika—if he accepts that there is the acquisition of self-nature (*ātmalābha*) for the non-existent and the loss of self-nature for the existent—then he falls into the fallacy of contradicting his own tenets (*apasiddhānta*).

If, however, he does not accept this, his thesis (*pakṣa*) is not established. For he has made the transformation (*vikāra*) the subject of his thesis on the basis of its having a single primordial material cause (*ekaprakṛti*); yet, since transformations cannot be defined [if they do not arise from the non-existent], in their absence neither the meaning of the proposition nor the meaning of the reason is established, because the locus of the reason is unestablished (*āśrayāsiddhatva*).

"Surely, since this contradicts the meaning of the thesis— namely, that there is the cessation of the existent and the arising of the non-existent— it would constitute either a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) or a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) known as 'contradiction of the thesis' (*pratijñāvirodha*). Anticipating this objection, the author of the Vārttika says:
Regarding the phrase "apart from the meaning of the proposition":

here, the reason—"modifications have a single primordial nature because they possess a single primordial nature"—is not manifested as being pervaded by something contrary to the probandum such that it would become contradictory (*viruddha*).

Nor is the fact that modifications have a single primordial nature verbally opposed by the reason of "homogeneity" (*samanvaya*), such that there would be a contradiction with the proposition (*pratijñāvirodha*).

Regarding the contradiction between the proposition and the reason based on mere abundance, the author of the Vārttika stated that there is a contradiction because it contradicts the permanence of the universal "cowness" (gotva) as established in his own system.

Moreover, in that case [the former], the teaching of the inconclusive (anaikāntika) is sublated by a stronger established tenet (siddhānta), whereas here, the established tenet itself is sublated. Since the latter is weaker, there is no redundancy of examples. Therefore, where there is a contradiction with the meaning of the proposition (pratijñā), that is either the contradictory fallacy of the reason (viruddha-hetvābhāsa) or a contradiction of the proposition (pratijñāvirodha).

In this case, however, since there is a contradiction with another admission apart from the meaning of the original proposition, it is established that in *jalpa* and *vitaṇḍā*, a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) occurs due to the incapacity of the person who asserts mutually contradictory meanings before and after. // 23 //
And the fallacies of the reason (hetvābhāsa) are as previously described.
He explains [the term] "and fallacious reasons" (*hetvābhāsāś ca*).
If some point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) remains unmentioned, that should be included by means of the word "and" (*ca*).
He states the doubt to be refuted by the phrase "as previously stated" (*yathoktāḥ*), which is a part of the sūtra.

Furthermore, one might raise the following objection: "Do fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) become points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) simply by virtue of possessing another characteristic? For instance, just as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—namely perception and the rest—are characterized as 'objects of cognition' (*prameya*) because they are the instruments for apprehending [an object], yet those very same things are 'means of valid cognition' (*pramāṇa*) by virtue of being the instruments that bring about valid cognition, and are 'objects of cognition' (*prameya*) by virtue of being pervaded by valid cognition;

thus, by means of a different characteristic, the means of valid cognition themselves would incur the status of being objects of cognition. It is in response to the possibility of such a doubt that [the author] says:
The Blessed One, the author of the Sūtra,
said "as has been stated," thereby concluding the entire meaning of the treatise.
These [categories], beginning with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), have been enumerated, defined, and examined.
The word "iti" marks the completion of the treatise.
The author of the *Vārttika* summarizes [the work] with the words: "of the *jātis* along with their elaborations."
"Regarding the definition of the points of defeat (nigrahasthāna):
this indicates in brief that even the types of futile rejoinders (jāti) are included among the points of defeat for the opponent,
and it serves as the conclusion of the treatise."
The meaning is that by this [verse], these [categories] beginning with the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) have been enumerated.
Whatever merit has been gained from rescuing the exceedingly aged cows of Uddyotakara, who were submerged in the mud of difficult and flawed compositions—
[that merit is dedicated] to the bull-bannered Lord Śiva, the bridge across the ocean of saṃsāra and the cause for the pacification of all suffering. // 1 //
May the Lord be pleased by this entire fruit offered by him.
May this creeper of a commentary— fragrant with the birth of the knowledge of reality, possessing a multitude of hidden meanings, bearing the fruit of the nectar of liberation,
with lovely sprouts of elegant sayings, rooted in direct perception, authoritative scripture, and great logic, and pleasing to the mind— be a source of joy for the wise, like a lotus-pond for bees.
O cruel ones, this salutation with joined palms has been made; this body is offered by me here for you to strike as you desire.
I entreat you: do not defile the rivers of fame of others with showers of dust in the form of false words. // 3 //
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the *Nyāyavārtikatātparyaṭīkā* composed by the venerable Vācaspati Miśra.
And this treatise is completed.
May there be auspiciousness.

In the first *āhnika* of the fifth *adhyāya*, there are 43 *sūtras* and 17 *prakaraṇas*; in the second *āhnika*, there are 24 *sūtras* and 7 *prakaraṇas*. Combined, these total 67 *sūtras* and 24 *prakaraṇas*.
According to the *Nyāyasūcīnibandha*, the figures specified for this *Nyāya-śāstra* are: 5 *adhyāyas*, 10 *āhnikas*, 84 *prakaraṇas*, 528 *sūtras*, 1,960 *padas*, and 8,385 *akṣaras*.
